title: ‘Harry Potter And The Cursed Child’ Posts Big Gain As Summer Slips Away – Broadway Box Office
summary: Broadway held steady as the summer season came to a close with the Labor Day holiday, with the 25 productions grossing a total $26,258,361 for the week ending September 6. The total reps a small 2% increase over the previous week and about a 4% jump over last year at this time. Total attendance was […]
content:
Broadway held steady as the summer season came to a close with the Labor Day holiday, with the 25 productions grossing a total $26,258,361 for the week ending September 6.

The total reps a small 2% increase over the previous week and about a 4% jump over last year at this time. Total attendance was 220,836, down a negligible 1% from the previous week and up 3% year-to-year.

All of the productions reported at least some gains over the previous week, likely boosted by tourism over the long holiday weekend. The biggest gain – $240,630 – was made by Harry Potter and The Cursed Child, taking in $1,819,963 as Tom Felton settled into his second week back from vacation.

The week’s sell-outs were Hamilton, Just In Time and Oh, Mary!, with Hadestown, MJ, The Lion King and The Rocky Horror Show all coming in at 99% of capacity. Coming close to that mark with at least 90% of seats occupied were & Juliet, Buena Vista Social Club, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Operation Mincemeat, Paranormal Activity, Schmigadoon!, The Book of Mormon and Titanique.

Watch on Deadline

At the lower end of the attendance spectrum, with fewer than 70% of seats filled, were Six, Stranger Things: The First Shadow and Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York).

Top five earners for the week were Hamilton ($2,187,028); MJ ($1,849,850); Harry Potter and the Cursed Child ($1,819,963); The Lion King ($1,714,434); and The Lost Boys ($1,281,191). Hamilton had the top average ticket at $204.66, with the overall Broadway average at $118.90.

In the 15th week of the 2026-27 season, Broadway has grossed season-to-date $489,296,981, down about 5% from last year at this time, with total attendance of 4,011,339 down just 1% year-to-year.

All figures courtesy of The Broadway League. For more box office information visit the League’s website.

title: Netflix Orders New Series Take On ‘Lonesome Dove’ From ‘East of Eden’ Showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart
summary: “Lonesome Dove,” which was originally adapted into an Emmy- and Golden Globe-winning CBS miniseries starring Robert Duvall in 1989, is getting a new take at Netflix. The streamer announced Tuesday that it had ordered “Lonesome Dove” to series, from co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart. Kazan and Stuart are also the co-showrunners on Netflix’s upcoming […]
content:
“Lonesome Dove,” which was originally adapted into an Emmy- and Golden Globe-winning CBS miniseries starring Robert Duvall in 1989, is getting a new take at Netflix. The streamer announced Tuesday that it had ordered “Lonesome Dove” to series, from co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart.

Kazan and Stuart are also the co-showrunners on Netflix’s upcoming limited series “East of Eden.” Kazan and Stuart were hired by Teton Ridge Entertainment, which holds the rights to “Lonesome Dove,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning western novel from author Larry McMurtry first released in 1985. The CBS miniseries was a smash, attracting 26 million viewers and spawned multiple sequels (“Return to Lonesome Dove,” “Streets of Laredo,” “Dead Man’s Walk,” “Comanche Moon”) as well as the 1994 syndicated “Lonesome Dove: The Series.”

Here’s the logline: “Gus McCrae and Woodrow Call renew their spirit of adventure as they face an uncertain future, embarking on one final, perilous cattle drive from the Rio Grande to the untamed wilderness of Montana in pursuit of a dream that they have perhaps already outlived. These two former Texas Rangers lead an unforgettable cast of characters across the American west in this sweeping odyssey defined by unrequited longing, unbreakable friendship, brutal frontier justice, and an unwavering pursuit of a meaningful life.”

Popular on Variety

Teton Ridge acquired the rights to “Lonesome Dove” last year; at the time, it announced that development would begin with the first book in the series, “Lonesome Dove,” followed by the rest of the tetralogy, including “Streets of Laredo,” “Dead Man’s Walk” and “Comanche Moon.” The novels focus on members of the Texas Ranger Division, spanning from when Texas was a republic until the start of the 20th century when it was part of the U.S.

Kazan and Stuart will serve as co-showrunners/writers/executive producers, while EPs also include Thomas Tull, Jillian Share and Jen Gorton of Teton Ridge Entertainment; Jon Jashni; Diana Ossana; and Curtis McMurtry of the McMurtry Estate. Diana Ossana, McMurty’s longtime creative partner, is also an exec producer.

“’Lonesome Dove’ is one of the great American stories, and there was no question we wanted to follow Zoe and Jeb wherever they went next,” said Netflix head of scripted series, U.S. and Canada, Jinny Howe. “After ‘East of Eden,’ we know exactly what they’re capable of — the depth of character, the sweep of place, the emotional precision. This material deserves that level of care. In their hands, it’s going to be something extraordinary. We’re excited to partner with Teton Ridge to bring this legendary story to life.”

In a joint statement, Kazan and Stuart said that “we come to this material with love and respect, and can’t wait to hit the trail with Gus and Call and the rest of these beloved characters.” And Teton Ridge Entertainment president Jillian Share added: “‘Lonesome Dove’ is the kind of story that only comes along once in a generation. Its characters, scope and deeply human portrait of the American West have made it an enduring classic, and we see an extraordinary opportunity to bring Larry McMurtry’s world to a new generation of audiences.”

Said Ossana: “‘Lonesome Dove’ has been part of my creative life for decades, an important part of Larry’s and my partnership journey. Its characters, landscape, and profound understanding of friendship, love, loss, and human longing have stayed with me, and it is deeply meaningful to help bring this newly imagined, extraordinary world of ‘Lonesome Dove’ to a contemporary generation while preserving the emotional truths that make all of Larry’s work timeless.”

title: Telluride Takeaways: From Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti’s ‘Debut’ to Nathan Fielder’s Audacious Dare to the Doc Branch
summary: On my last morning in Telluride, halfway through breakfast at Butcher & Baker, Kenneth Branagh stopped at the table on his way to a Q&A for “Into the Breach,” the National Theatre documentary he produced. He had a story. A night earlier, he’d ridden the gondola up in pitch darkness with Willem Dafoe, Tom Hiddleston […]
content:
On my last morning in Telluride, halfway through breakfast at Butcher & Baker, Kenneth Branagh stopped at the table on his way to a Q&A for “Into the Breach,” the National Theatre documentary he produced. He had a story. A night earlier, he’d ridden the gondola up in pitch darkness with Willem Dafoe, Tom Hiddleston and Andrew Scott — four of the best actors alive, each with a film at the festival, sealed in one cable car with nothing to look at and nothing to do but talk. All anyone could hear was Dafoe. Branagh, laughing, called it “the wisdom of Willem.” A voice in the dark, no face attached.

I half-believed it until a few hours later, waiting out my flight at Montrose, when I ran into Hiddleston on his way back to the U.K. He told the same story, unprompted.

Popular on Variety

That’s the festival. The Telluriders have gone home, Venice wraps in a few days and we came down the mountain knowing more about this Oscar race than we did going up. Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic “The Odyssey” is still the one to beat. It won’t be a cakewalk. Here’s what else I carried down.

“The Debut” handed Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti their moment.

Jesse Eisenberg’s third feature behind the camera premiered Saturday night. By the next day, it was the hottest ticket in town. “The Debut” drops Moore’s Mona, a meek suburban homemaker who lands a bit part in a community theater musical, into the front of the best actress race. It’s the funniest, warmest thing she’s done in years. Giamatti, whom Eisenberg calls his “favorite actor,” plays the tyrant director shaping her. During one rehearsal scene between them — a master-class, no other word for it — the Telluride crowd applauded in the middle of the movie. You rarely see that happen once at a festival. It happened again before the credits.

Moore already has an Oscar for “Still Alice,” and she’s the one to beat. Giamatti is the sentimental story coming up underneath: twice nominated for “Cinderella Man” and “The Holdovers,” never a winner and here he is doing the loosest work of his late career in a supporting turn built to be embraced. Eisenberg wrote seven songs for the fictional show. The one they’ll push is “This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out),” which Moore performs, and it’s headed for a best original song campaign.

Nathan Fielder attempts the impossible.

The festival’s best-kept secret came Sunday night, when ticket holders filed into the Werner Herzog Theatre with their phones locked away for “You Can See Everything,” the Elizabeth Holmes documentary Fielder co-directed with Lance Oppenheim, whose narrative feature “Primetime” premiered in Venice a day earlier. Holmes invites Fielder and his skeptical crew to film her in the 34 days before she reports to prison. The shoot spirals into a three-year descent. Portions are recreated with an A-list actor who is eligible for Oscar attention, though not SAG.

Now comes the hard part, which is the documentary branch, which has never embraced this kind of nonfiction filmmaking. Voters who prize the observational and the sincere tend to bristle at a movie where the filmmaker is this present and this implicated. The circus around Fielder guarantees the kind of coverage most nonfiction contenders would trade a lung for. Whether the branch rewards it is the whole question. Nobody has made a movie quite like this. Almost nobody has won an Oscar for one.

Jordan Firstman in “Club Kid” A24

“Club Kid” has a real play for the old guard.

Jordan Firstman’s directorial debut had its North American premiere Friday, and its trajectory keeps getting more serious than anyone bet on. Firstman writes, directs and stars as Peter, a washed-up New York party promoter whose life on the dance floor stops cold when the 10-year-old son he never knew about (British newcomer Reggie Absolom) turns up at his door.

Strip away the club scene and the online-comedian brand, and you have a classically built story about a man-child being handed a kid. I expected that this would struggle to appeal to the older industry demographic. I was wrong. In fact, it seems to register incredibly well with older Academy voters, at least the ones I chatted with on the mountain.

Veteran actor Colleen Camp, who first came to the festival in 1977, made the case for the film’s tonal control better than any campaign deck could. “I always say, always hire somebody funny to do something dramatic, because you’ll get so many interesting things,” she said at the post-screening Q&A. “And what [Firstman] did in this movie is even in the most dramatic moments, they’re brilliantly ironic and they’re funny.”

Firstman described how his script reversed course on him over two years of writing. “I started the script from kind of a cynical place of looking around at the scene and just not feeling good about it — looking at the excessive drug use and the sex, and being a part of it and feeling bad about myself and feeling bad about my community,” he said. “What happened was that making this film in the community — we shot at real parties, in the queer spaces in New York — my empathy really opened up in the production of the film.” That shift is on the screen, and it’s what voters will feel without necessarily being able to name it.

By the end of the panel, it came down to one word, spoken loudly by Firstman: “love.”

L.A. BOLA NEGRA. Guitarricadelafuente as Sebastián in La Bola Negra. Cr. Carla Oset/Netflix © 2026. ‘La Bola Negra’ Carla Oset/Netflix

“La Bola Negra” commands the room.

Respect is the currency at that altitude, and Los Javis have it. Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi arrived off a Cannes run that ended with the directing prize, and the Telluride word-of-mouth only got louder. Chris Pine, Sofia Coppola, Rian Johnson and their Netflix stablemate Danny Boyle (“Ink”) all turned up for the screening.

Shot on 35 mm and inspired by the unfinished Federico García Lorca work of the same name, “La Bola Negra” moves across 1932, 1937 and 2017, tracing three generations of gay men through nearly a century of Spanish history.

A subtitled Netflix title the festival can’t stop buzzing about is exactly where you want to be heading into the international feature race, and the streamer is hunting well beyond that category. And even though stars Guitarricadelafuente and Penélope Cruz weren’t on the mountain, the film played so well that it shows it can exist in the awards echo chamber without them (which says a lot).

“Wild Horse Nine” Searchlight Pictures

“Wild Horse Nine” made the two-stop drop look easy.

Of the titles that ran the Venice-to-Telluride relay this year, Martin McDonagh’s landed with the most confidence. Searchlight Pictures’ “Wild Horse Nine” bowed in Venice competition on Sept. 3 to a 13-minute standing ovation, the Lido’s first real roar of the fall. Two days later, it turned up as Telluride’s surprise patron screening, timed to John Malkovich’s Silver Medallion tribute.

Malkovich was the biggest takeaway. Twice nominated and never a winner, he called the script the kind you see “every 25 years.” The double premiere vaulted him near the front of best actor, trailing only Matt Damon in “The Odyssey” and another Telluride player, Andrew Scott in “Elsinore.” Sam Rockwell, who won supporting actor for his last McDonagh outing, is back in that conversation, with the open question of whether Steve Buscemi joins him.

Kate O’Flynn, Paul Jesson and Marion Bailey in “Tender Loving Care” Thin Man Films Ltd and Bleecker Street

“Tender Loving Care” is Mike Leigh in a minor key, and it wrecks you anyway.

If this is the last Mike Leigh film, and the final shot plays like a man who knows it might be, it’s a hell of a way to leave. “Tender Loving Care” follows two social workers and was built the usual Leigh way: no script, no plot, just months of assembling people until they exist.

Marion Bailey, who plays Birdie, figured out the assignment before the assignment existed. “I could see as he was going through, he was crossing off people and I thought, what’s the sort of person he’s looking for? And then it dawned on me — he’s looking for someone who has a sense of humor,” she said. “The ones he was crossing off my list were people who don’t have a sense of humor.” Then she added the part only a Leigh veteran gets to add: “You get a call from Mike to say, ‘Do you want to come on board? I don’t know what the part will be. I’m not sure how it’ll work out, but would you like to do it?’ Yes, please. You don’t even stop to think about it.”

The film’s dedication to Dick Pope hangs over it, and longtime producer Georgina Lowe explained how the succession happened. Lucy, who came up under Pope as a camera trainee on “Meantime” and operated on “Hard Truths,” took over the cinematography after a British Society of Cinematographers function where Pope received a posthumous lifetime achievement award. “I don’t think Mike heard this, but Pat turned to Lucy and said, ‘You should shoot the next one,’” Lowe said. “Simultaneously, Mike had thought that. It just made total sense.”

Paul Jesson gave the film its thesis in a single line, asking what a movie about caring for people means right now. “It’s also a good antidote to a world which, by and large, is being run by bullies and thugs,” he said. “The state of the world at the moment is pretty terrifying, really. A lot of people try to close their eyes, cover their ears and get on with their own private lives. And it’s hard to know what to do apart from that, other than look after the people they’re close to.” That’s the movie, and the campaign.

Andrew Scott stars as Ian Charleson in ELSINORE, a Focus Features release.

Credit: Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC Anthony Dickenson

Everybody wrote a love letter to acting this year.

Step back from the horse race and the weekend had a through-line: acting itself, in films made largely by and for the people who do it. Two of the marquee titles orbit the same building. “Elsinore” is Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in the last year of his life, holding on long enough to play Hamlet at London’s National Theatre. “Into the Breach,” the documentary Branagh produced, tells the story of that same theater, with Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Gary Oldman and Ian McKellen around a table sorting out what the stage cost them and what it gave back. One film stages a great actor’s final bow. The other rounds up living legends to explain why it mattered.

“The Debut” is the same subject from the bottom of the ladder: Moore as a suburban nobody who discovers, in a community theater musical, that performing might be the truest thing she’s ever done and nearly comes apart proving it. A drama, a doc and a comedy, all circling what it costs to disappear into someone else.

The actors branch is the largest bloc in the Academy, and nothing moves a room of performers like a film that treats performance as life or death. Telluride just handed them three.

The gondola is the place to get honest polls.

Nothing tells you how ticket holders are responding to a movie like a gondola ride to or from the Chuck Jones Theatre. On a ride up Sunday morning, you get to listen to the festival unfiltered, which, of course, came with the secret screening speculation that swung from a Frank Ocean project to the eventual Fielder documentary. But then you get to hear about people’s reactions to the Bill Gates talk at Elks Park that half the car caught the tail end of, and the running argument over which “Martin McDonagh is the real Martin McDonagh.” (Whatever that means?)

One producer I chatted with had the most useful read of the weekend on “La Bola Negra,” which he claimed everyone kept calling too long. “I felt that it was long, but I was never bored,” he said. “I was pretty engaged. It felt pretty robust the whole time.” That distinction can matter most. It’s not about whether voters check their watches, but whether they mind. Turns out they don’t.

However, he was less forgiving elsewhere about “Fjord,” Cristian Mungiu’s Romanian Palme d’Or winner. “I didn’t think there was any character work between the two of them [Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve]. I didn’t get their relationship at all,” he said. “They got these incredible actors and it didn’t just match. I wanted to hear more about their beliefs. I wanted to get more into it, be challenged more. It left me a little cold.”

Interestingly, I spoke to someone else immediately after getting off the gondola who said “Fjord” is the best thing they’ve seen this year.

The pendulum can swing rapidly between voters and titles.

Other notes from the mountain

Stephen Beresford, who wrote “Elsinore,” lost his passport and couldn’t make it to Telluride. That didn’t stop his leading man from having a moment.

Andrew Scott had company for that reaction. After the screening, Oprah Winfrey, a Telluride regular this year behind Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s “Everest: The Other Side,” found Scott outside and cried in his arms. If you want to know how a movie is landing on the mountain, watch for who’s weeping in the lobby or outside.

(That’s also “A Long Winter” writer and director Andrew Haigh weeping alongside them)

Winfrey also threw a party, and by the chatter, all anyone could talk about was who got the invite, who didn’t and how you could possibly get one. Spoiler alert: I wasn’t one of them.

title: Hurricane Marie’s Waves Undermine Multimillion Dollar Malibu Beachfront Home, Causing Sinkhole; Several Other Properties Red Tagged
summary: While many Angelenos were busy dealing with unseasonable rain from the remnants of Hurricane Marie, beach communities have been hit hard by high tides and massive waves associated with the storm. Among the most-impacted enclaves are Malibu, where a sinkhole opened up under one multimillion dollar beachfront home; Pacific Palisades, where the waterfront has been […]
content:
While many Angelenos were busy dealing with unseasonable rain from the remnants of Hurricane Marie, beach communities have been hit hard by high tides and massive waves associated with the storm.

Among the most-impacted enclaves are Malibu, where a sinkhole opened up under one multimillion dollar beachfront home; Pacific Palisades, where the waterfront has been further eroded away from the remaining pilings of homes razed by last year’s fire; Long Beach, where very rare wave action inside the breakwater and high tides have combined to trigger evacuations; and Dana Point, where a number of seaside estates were red tagged.

The Malibu sinkhole opened up along the sand in the 31600 block of Sea Level Drive East. That’s in the secluded Point Lechuza community near Broad Beach. Photos from the scene show the house still standing on pilings driven into the sand, but the driveway gone and portions of the street falling into the waves below.

Watch on Deadline

A sinkhole caused by pounding surf opened in the driveway of a Malibu home and caused a gas main rupture Tuesday morning.

Read more: https://t.co/7KI5yWLdWF pic.twitter.com/u8dkrdyXo7 — Spectrum News 1 SoCal (@SpecNews1SoCal) September 8, 2026

Los Angeles County Fire Department crews responded to a call at the scene at about 5:45 a.m. Tuesday and found not just the wreckage, but a gas main rupture.

The Southern California Gas Company was summoned to shut off the gas, according to a fire department spokesman.

“There is a sinkhole there, but the home is not occupied,” he said.



The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department and the county fire department closed the private road.

Malibu’s Building Safety Division and SoCal Gas were working to assess the situation, and the city reportedly red-tagged five homes, prohibiting entry.

“The city’s Building Safety Division and Southern California Gas Company will continue to assess the situation to determine safety concerns for the surrounding area, and will provide updates as they become available,” city officials said in a statement.

Malibu officials said they are “actively monitoring and responding to coastal erosion issues in areas including Pacific Coast Highway in the Palisades Fire burn area and at Westward Beach due to strong waves and high tides, in close collaboration with partner agencies.”

Malibu residents are expressing fears about the continued impact of forecasted strong storm systems on the iconic coastline and nearby shops and roads. pic.twitter.com/8UPD0UUD3P — CBS LA (@CBSLosAngeles) September 8, 2026

A high surf advisory and coastal flood advisory are in effect until 11 p.m. Tuesday for portions of the Los Angeles County coast, while a coastal flood advisory were extended to 11 p.m. Wednesday for Orange County.

Over the weekend, Hurricane Marie aimed waves with 10-foot faces directly at the shores of Malibu and Orange County, both of which face south. The storm remained well offshore but sent considerable moisture toward the area. That, coupled with evening high tides well over 7 feet, caused flooding at parking lots in Seal Beach and Zuma Beach, and sea water “flowing into homes and streets” in Long Beach, according to the NWS.

Waves crashing above rooftops in Long Beach from historic swell smashing the Alamitos Peninsula. Residents have evacuated along the boardwalk. #CA #LongBeach #Flood #Waves pic.twitter.com/q4qj2deTOJ — Jonathan Petramala (@jpetramala) September 8, 2026

The Long Beach Fire Department reported Monday night that approximately 20 homes were evacuated along Seaside Walk, from 63rd to 67th Place, due to the seawall being compromised and damage to the boardwalk.

There were also reports of damaged and cracked concrete in between several of the homes.

“These evacuation orders are being issued out of an abundance of caution while the Building Department evaluates the structural integrity and condition of these homes,” LBFD said in a statement.

In South Orange County’s tony Dana Point, about a dozen high-priced homes were red-tagged as uninhabitable after damage from the high waves undermined at least one beachfront building’s slab foundation.

#BreakingNews: High surf and coastal erosion have damaged multiple homes in Dana Point, prompting residents of the Capistrano Bay Community to call for an emergency declaration. https://t.co/aSzasq10gr pic.twitter.com/Ogxk58zTFh — KTLA (@KTLA) September 8, 2026

This weekend’s damage may only be a prelude to what’s in store for beachside communities this winter, with the National Climate Prediction Center last month forecasting “a greater than 90% chance of a very strong [El Niño] event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27.”

That would mean not just mudslides in the hills of coastal communities, but potentially even bigger surf pounding their already-eroded beaches.

“The city is preparing for potential strong storms, strong waves, heavy rain, mudslides and coastal erosion that are possible along the entire Southern California coast due to the forecast strong El Niño conditions,” Malibu officials said today.

City News Service contributed to this report.

title: John Mulaney Looking To ‘Get Smart’ At Warner Bros – The Dish
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Talk about a dead ringer when it comes to casting: We’re getting word that 4x Emmy winner John Mulaney is eyeing to star as wisenheimer Agent Maxwell Smart in Warner Bros’ upcoming reimagining of Get Smart. The project is early in the works with Now You See Me: Now You Don’t scribe Seth Grahame-Smith penning […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Talk about a dead ringer when it comes to casting: We’re getting word that 4x Emmy winner John Mulaney is eyeing to star as wisenheimer Agent Maxwell Smart in Warner Bros’ upcoming reimagining of Get Smart.

The project is early in the works with Now You See Me: Now You Don’t scribe Seth Grahame-Smith penning the screenplay. Chuck Roven and Andrew Lazar are producing.

The spy comedy series Get Smart was created by Mel Brooks and Buck Henry and ran for 138 episodes from 1965-70. The first four seasons of the James Bond spoof aired on NBC, while the final season was shown on CBS. Don Adams starred as bumbling know-it-all agent Maxwell Smart (Agent 86) opposite Barbara Feldon (Agent 99) and Edward Platt, who played the Chief. They work for a secret U.S. government counterintelligence agency called Control, which was in a constant battle with evil org, Kaos. While Smart always has the upper hand over Kaos, he often was incompetent. Get Smart won seven Emmys including two for Outstanding Comedy Series.

RELATED: Buck Henry Dies: ‘The Graduate’ Writer, ‘Get Smart’ Co-Creator & Early ‘SNL’ Favorite Was 89

Watch on Deadline

The opening sequence was a classic, showing Adams’ Smart walking through a ridiculous number of locked barricades before arriving at a phone booth, in which he picked up the phone and dialed a number, before dropping into Control headquarters. The series was followed by a 1980 feature film, The Nude Bomb, which was made without Brooks and Henry, as well as the 1989 made-for-TV sequel to the series, Get Smart, Again! which starred Adams and Feldon. For a beat there was a 1995 revival series starring Adams, Feldon, Andy Dick, Heather Morgan and Elaine Hendrix that aired on Fox for seven episodes in early 1995. Then there was a 2008 feature film adaptation from Warner Bros., produced by Roven and Lazar and starring Steve Carell as Smart, Anne Hathaway as Agent 99, Alan Arkin as the Chief and Dwayne Johnson as Agent 23. The pic was programmed as a summer tentpole and opened to $38.6M stateside and made $130.3M domestic, and $230.6M worldwide.

Mulaney also is a Critics Choice- and WGA Award-winning writer, comedian and actor. This summer, he became the first comedian ever to headline Wrigley Field and ended up selling out the iconic ballpark.

Mulaney just announced Mulaney Takes Manhattan, a special nine-show New York City run from January 7-15 that takes him to nine iconic venues over nine nights, from Comedy Cellar and Blue Note to Carnegie Hall and Radio City Music Hall, culminating in a finale at Madison Square Garden. The shows are part of Mulaney’s latest stand-up tour, John Mulaney: Mister Whatever.

He has hosted Saturday Night Live six times and next will appear in Amazon MGM Studios’ upcoming David O. Russell feature Madden, starring Nicolas Cage as the famed football coach and NFL commentator.

RELATED: ‘Madden’ Teaser Trailer: Boom! Nicolas Cage Transforms In David O. Russell’s Biopic

Mulaney won Emmys for Outstanding Writing for a Variety Special in 2025 (SNL: 50th Anniversary), Writing for a Variety Special in 2023 (John Mulaney: Baby J), Writing for a Variety Special in 2018 (John Mulaney: Kid Gorgeous at Radio City Hall) and Outstanding Original Music and Lyrics in 2011 (SNL).

Grahame-Smith is repped by WME and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. He has a story credit on the Warner Bros’ hit Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, which amassed more than $452M WW. He also wrote Now You See Me: Now You Don’t, which grossed close to $247M at the global box office, and The Lego Batman Movie, which minted over $312M WW.

Mulaney is repped by WME and Shreck Rose Dapello.

title: Netflix Orders ‘Lonesome Dove’ Series From Zoe Kazan & Jeb Stuart Based On Larry McMurtry’s Novel
summary: Larry McMurtry’s classic Lonesome Dove novel is returning to television as a Netflix series. The streamer has greenlighted the Western drama from Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart, co-showrunners of Netflix’s upcoming East of Eden limited series, and Teton Ridge Entertainment. Independent studio Teton Ridge Entertainment, which focuses on American West stories, announced in February that it […]
content:
Larry McMurtry’s classic Lonesome Dove novel is returning to television as a Netflix series. The streamer has greenlighted the Western drama from Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart, co-showrunners of Netflix’s upcoming East of Eden limited series, and Teton Ridge Entertainment.

Independent studio Teton Ridge Entertainment, which focuses on American West stories, announced in February that it had acquired the rights to the Lonesome Dove literary franchise for film and television. It brought in Kazan and Stuart to write the adaptation and took the package out in late April. By early May, in a very competitive situation, Lonesome Dove had laded at Netflix with a straight-to-series order.

As to why it took four months for the streamer to confirm the show, word is that there were some gaps in the complex web of necessary rights that had to be secured before Netflix could proceed with the greenlight, a process that has now been completed.

Watch on Deadline

Lonesome Dove, which is envisioned as an ongoing series, follows Gus McCrae and Woodrow Call who renew their spirit of adventure as they face an uncertain future, embarking on one final, perilous cattle drive from the Rio Grande to the untamed wilderness of Montana in pursuit of a dream that they have perhaps already outlived. These two former Texas Rangers lead an unforgettable cast of characters across the American west in this sweeping odyssey defined by unrequited longing, unbreakable friendship, brutal frontier justice, and an unwavering pursuit of a meaningful life.

Kazan and Stuart are taking on McMurtry’s Pulitzer Prize-winning novel after tackling John Steinbeck’s East Of Eden for the upcoming Netflix limited series starring Florence Pugh, which premieres Oct. 1. The duo served as co-showrunners on East of Eden, which was written by Kazan.

“After our singular experience on East of Eden, we are thrilled to be teaming with Netflix again, along with Teton Ridge Entertainment, to bring Larry McMurtry’s western classic to life,” Kazan and Stuart said in a statement. “We come to this material with love and respect, and can’t wait to hit the trail with Gus and Call and the rest of these beloved characters. Yee-haw.”

Kazan and Stuart executive produce Lonesome Dove alongside Thomas Tull, Jillian Share and Jen Gorton of Teton Ridge Entertainment; Jon Jashni; late McMurtry’s longtime creative partner Diana Ossana; Curtis McMurtry of the McMurtry Estate.

“Lonesome Dove is one of the great American stories, and there was no question we wanted to follow Zoe and Jeb wherever they went next,” said Jinny Howe, Netflix Head of Scripted Series, UCAN. “After East of Eden, we know exactly what they’re capable of — the depth of character, the sweep of place, the emotional precision. This material deserves that level of care. In their hands, it’s going to be something extraordinary. We’re excited to partner with Teton Ridge to bring this legendary story to life.”

Published in 1986 by Simon & Schuster, McMurtry’s novel — the first in the Lonesome Dove book series — spent 24 consecutive weeks in hardcover and 28 consecutive weeks in paperback on NYT’s Bestseller list, selling over 4 million copies.

It was turned into a hit 1989 miniseries by CBS. Starring Robert Duvall and Tommy Lee Jones, the four-part Lonesome Dove pulled in an some 26M viewers and won a Peabody, seven Emmys and two Golden Globes. The subsequent books in the Lonesome Dove series were also adapted into miniseries.

“Lonesome Dove is the kind of story that only comes along once in a generation. Its characters, scope and deeply human portrait of the American West have made it an enduring classic, and we see an extraordinary opportunity to bring Larry McMurtry’s world to a new generation of audiences,” said Jillian Share, President, Teton Ridge Entertainment. “We’re thrilled to partner with Netflix and for Zoe and Jeb to reimagine this landmark story while preserving the heart and spirit that have made Lonesome Dove so beloved.”

Stuart is repped by UTA, Kaplan Perrone, and Hansen Jacobson. Ossana is repped by UTA.

title: ‘A Common Story’ Review: A Stunningly Played Study of a Couple Whose Inability to Articulate Their Emotions Drives Them Apart
summary: Far too often, relationship dramas devolve into screaming matches with a predictable crescendo that exhausts both actors and audiences: They’re using words, but since few writers have the caustic wit of Edward Albee, what they say is more tiresome than trenchant. Perhaps because debuting director Anna Foglietta is first an actor, she understands that silences […]
content:
Far too often, relationship dramas devolve into screaming matches with a predictable crescendo that exhausts both actors and audiences: They’re using words, but since few writers have the caustic wit of Edward Albee, what they say is more tiresome than trenchant. Perhaps because debuting director Anna Foglietta is first an actor, she understands that silences are more powerful than screeches, even more so when a couple want to express themselves but just can’t find the words. “A Common Story” is a revelation, not just in an Italian film landscape that too often falls back on verbal assaults, but more broadly, thanks to Foglietta’s sensitivity to the spaces between speech, and the superlative performances from Alba Rohrwacher and Guido Caprino, who have never been better.

This sensitivity to voids is revealed in the opening montage, consisting of empty rooms in university buildings, their vacant stillness a troubling indication of absence. It’s the perfect visualization of the empty-nest syndrome experienced by parents Erika (Rohrwacher) and Mauro (Caprino), bringing their only child Irene (Ksenia Borzak) to college. She’s probably the first member of the family to seek higher education, and mom and dad are super proud. Once back home, they fall into their usual patterns: Mauro works in construction with his father Marcello (Elio De Capitani), and Erika is a supermarket cashier.

Popular on Variety

Her days always had a structure that reflected her sense of purpose: she’d get up early each morning to bake a bundt cake for breakfast, check in on her mother Altea (Caterina Casini) after work to bring groceries, clean the house, cook the meals. She was useful, and being useful signified she had a role to fill that brought meaning to her life. Now she’s nearly 45, her daughter is out of the house, and she finds herself suddenly adrift without the self-analytical tools to understand what she’s feeling.

Being needed is her reason for waking up in the morning, but Irene is away and self-sufficient Altea is busy with her friends. Perhaps if she could talk about her feelings with Mauro, they’d be able to negotiate the changes together, but notwithstanding a deep love, they’re not people who’ve ever talked about their personal psychology. Unequipped to find the words that could identify her state of mind, Erika begins to fall apart.

The building blocks of “A Common Story” can be found in countless feminist texts describing the lack of self-worth felt by women whose circumscribed lives seem meaningless when their perceived usefulness is over. But what about the women unable to articulate those emotions, who don’t have access to such texts and for whom the words “mental health provider” might as well be gibberish? Erika is incapable of understanding her depression because she can’t name it, and without the vocabulary she’s unable to share her despair with Mauro, who watches his wife’s disintegration with bewilderment.

As a man, he’s meant to hold everything together; after all, he’s in construction, he fixes things. But he can’t fix this. Making matters worse, his father’s constant barbs have emasculated him, and when he learns that Marcello sold the business without letting him know, it feels like his role as the anchor of the family has been smashed. Following a humiliation at a family luncheon, Erika and Mauro have an argument; Foglietta first discreetly shoots them at a distance, through the windows of their parked car, then as Erika starts to shout, the angle shifts to the other side, until the camera is very close and the meltdown is as raw as it’s going to get.

It’s a wrenching moment, and a rare one in a film with barely any cuts within a scene (DP Andrea Benjamin Manenti’s careful framing meaningfully creates barriers within the fixed field of vision). It’s also the only time their voices are raised, yet they still can’t find words to convey their vulnerability. Filling the quivering void is their intense need for each other, and an inability to understand how to make themselves whole again.

Home alone, no longer driven to bake a cake or organize the house, Erika calls a telemarketer after seeing an infomercial for a face cream. The slick saleswoman asks questions about her skin type, which she can’t answer because she’s never thought about herself that way before, and after excitedly imagining what this product will do, she hangs up disillusioned: no longer able to fulfill the roles of daughter and mother, she also can’t become the kind of woman shaped by a consumer-driven society.

The scene highlights Rohrwacher’s delicate vulnerability and her masterful way of capturing Erika’s inner life, at once hollowed out yet in turmoil. It’s the character’s perplexity that’s so heartrending, perfectly matched by Caprino’s subtlety in conveying Mauro’s incomprehension at what’s happening to his marriage. With eyes, body language and the charged spaces between words, the two performers show us a couple on the verge of collapse, whose love for one another holds out the promise of salvation.

title: ‘Company’ Stars Nick Nolte, Adelaide Clemens on the Film’s Power of Stillness
summary: The vital act of storytelling drives Casey Affleck’s “Company.” Knowing those stories and the people in them also passes on lessons learned involving grief, regret and forgiveness. The film premieres in competition at Venice. “Company” stars Nick Nolte, Adelaide Clemens, Ben Mendelsohn, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee Cowan and Atticus Affleck. The film jumps […]
content:
The vital act of storytelling drives Casey Affleck’s “Company.” Knowing those stories and the people in them also passes on lessons learned involving grief, regret and forgiveness. The film premieres in competition at Venice.



“Company” stars Nick Nolte, Adelaide Clemens, Ben Mendelsohn, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee Cowan and Atticus Affleck. The film jumps between 1975, 1953 and 1903, connected by stories in each era. Much of the film involves just two actors in a shot, or one actor in a beautifully composed shot.

“When Casey sets up the camera, you know by the angles that he’s shooting from that it’s going to be much more intimate,” says Nolte.



Nolte’s Tom is an old man living alone. It’s winter, and he sees a young woman passed out on the snow outside his isolated cabin. He brings Alice (Cowan) in, warms her up and she tells him a story about a couple living in a cabin quite like his in 1903.



“It was the script, and it was so delicate,” Nolte says of what drew him to the project. “It had these silences and gaps, and the storytelling was obvious. I just found that intriguing. It wasn’t like any script that normally comes in. You know, it was one of those special ones.”



Nolte didn’t want to play Tom as necessarily a hermit, though, as we do discover his story as the film unspools. “I looked at him as somebody that wanted to not be with humanity in general. He was a reclusive, and he lived in isolation, and he’d probably be a trapper.”



Affleck’s direction is quite intentional, with each scene meticulously framed and lit, allowing stillness to permeate. Nolte’s expressive eyes and face do a lot of the work in each scene as Alice talks. “It was really about listening, just really listening to the story,” he says.



In the 1903 segment, Clemens and McNairy play a couple on an isolated farm, who, like Tom, find and rescue a young person from the snow. Caleb (Atticus Affleck) intrigues Rebecca (Clemens), as he brags about his world travels and personal philosophy with a familiar mix of confidence and insecurity — she’s wary, and his presence creates delicious tension.



“As I’ve gotten older, and I’ve worked more in the industry, I’ve started to learn the power of a two shot, and I’ve also started to learn that you need really skilled professionals to execute that in a powerful way,” she says. “You need an incredible cinematographer who we have on this film, Marcell Rév — everything was so beautiful.”



Clemens says that working with Casey is “what you dream of” because he is an Oscar-winning actor himself.



“Directors will often do a two shot, but then they’ll cover it as well. But if you have two actors who are in an environment where they’re supported, then you can have a really powerful scene, and you can see our whole bodies,” Clemens says of the framing, noting that she and her colleagues had to use their whole bodies. “We tell this whole story from the shins up. It wouldn’t be executed in the way it was if we didn’t have Casey trusting us.”



Clemens brought a “Buddha-like” demeanor and maternal depth and empathy to Rebecca, whereas Atticus Affleck had to leave everyone wondering about his truth. Clemens says that while he was well-prepared for the film, and “rehearsed intensely,” his performance was natural and “didn’t feel like a performance … He was amazing.”



Have some people in Hollywood figured out how to continue to spotlight Hollywood’s greats? “I’m 86, and real limited in the kind of roles I can play now, but I find that without the work, there just isn’t any reason to keep on going,” says Nolte, who has more projects on deck. “You know your creativity is tied into it, and as long as I’m physically capable, I encourage them to consider me. I haven’t thought about retiring.”

title: Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s ‘All of a Sudden,’ Abinash Bikram Shah’s ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Lead Asia Pacific Screen Awards Nominations
summary: Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s “All of a Sudden” and Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” led nominations for the 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards with three nods apiece, as the Asia Pacific Screen Academy unveiled a 36-film slate from 32 countries and regions ahead of the Oct. 30 ceremony in Australia. “All of a Sudden” (France, […]
content:
Hamaguchi Ryusuke‘s “All of a Sudden” and Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” led nominations for the 19th Asia Pacific Screen Awards with three nods apiece, as the Asia Pacific Screen Academy unveiled a 36-film slate from 32 countries and regions ahead of the Oct. 30 ceremony in Australia.

“All of a Sudden” (France, Japan, Germany, Belgium) and “Elephants in the Fog” (Nepal, Germany, Brazil, France, Norway) are both nominated for best film, best director and best performance. Hamaguchi and Shah face off in the director race against Sompot Chidgasornpongse for “9 Temples to Heaven,” Aung Phyoe for “Fruit Gathering” and Jennifer Peedom for “Tenzing.”

Three more films round out the best film category with two nominations apiece: Shahrbanoo Sadat’s “No Good Men” (Germany, France, Norway, Denmark, Afghanistan), also up for best performance; Levan Koguashvili’s “Guria” (Georgia, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Bulgaria, Türkiye, U.K., Norway, Saudi Arabia), also nominated for best cinematography; and Chidgasornpongse’s “9 Temples to Heaven” (Thailand, Singapore, France, Norway, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Qatar).

Popular on Variety

APSA also recognizes best screenplay, best cinematography, best youth film, best animated film and best documentary film, with best performance remaining an ungendered category.

According to the Academy, 69% of directors with nominated films are presenting their first or second feature, a trend most pronounced in the youth and animation races: all five best youth film nominees are helmed by first-time directors, and every best animated film contender comes from a first- or second-time filmmaker.

The lineup also highlighted several cross-border pairings, including Virginie Efira and Okamoto Tao, jointly nominated for best performance for “All of a Sudden,” and Ervin Han and Raúl García, the Singaporean and Spanish directing duo behind best animated film contender “The Violinist.”

Tracey Vieira, chair of the Asia Pacific Screen Academy, said: “When you look across this year’s nominations, what really stands out is the level of collaboration behind these films. We are seeing filmmakers and creative teams from countries across the Asia Pacific working together, and in many cases partnering with countries well beyond the region, to bring these stories to the screen.”

Three projects backed by the MPA APSA Academy Film Fund earned nominations this year: “9 Temples to Heaven,” funded in 2021; Sara Ishaq’s “The Station” (Yemen, Jordan, France, Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Qatar), funded in 2019; and Anthony Chen’s “We Are All Strangers” (Singapore), funded in 2023. Submissions for this year’s fund remain open through Sept. 25.

Mandy Walker ASC ACS, the APSA international jury president, said: “Watching and celebrating movies from other cultures only enriches our own experiences and views of the world. I have the honor to be heading the International Jury this year to recognize the achievements of these talented filmmakers.”

The Asia Pacific Screen Forum will run Oct. 28–30 on the Gold Coast ahead of the awards ceremony, with sessions on financing, distribution and cross-border collaboration alongside a masterclass with Walker. Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate said: “The Gold Coast is proud to be a creative crossroads for the Asia Pacific, and APSA is a big part of that story.”
