title: ‘NCIS: New York’s LL Cool J & Byron Balasco Preview Latest Spinoff; Tease Potential Crossovers
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The new CBS series NCIS: New York is gearing up for its explosive premiere on October 6, with the release of new photos and an interview with star LL Cool J and showrunner Byron Balasco, both of whom are also executive producers. The images below are from Episode 102 titled “Family Business,” and Episode 103 titled “Carousel.” […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The new CBS series NCIS: New York is gearing up for its explosive premiere on October 6, with the release of new photos and an interview with star LL Cool J and showrunner Byron Balasco, both of whom are also executive producers. The images below are from Episode 102 titled “Family Business,” and Episode 103 titled “Carousel.”

The project heralds the return of R. Scott Gemmill (The Pitt) to the NCIS Universe. Gemmill, who executive produced and served as showrunner on NCIS: Los Angeles, developed NCIS: New York with Balasco.

In the pilot, after years of special assignments and covert ops, Special Agent Sam Hanna (LL Cool J) returns to his hometown of New York City for a brand-new mission. When Sam’s friend and Navy reservist Jack Halloway is found dead, he requests permission from Assistant Special Agent-In-Charge Robyn Wells (Jennifer Beals) to investigate his friend’s death.

Robyn pairs Sam with roguish agent Nick Schaeffer (Scott Caan), who introduces him to the rest of the team: clean-cut Wyatt Sellers (Shane Harper), bright-eyed Addy Ross (Jacqueline Byers), and hacker-turned-computer guy Sean Sullivan (Devin Druid). As the team investigates Jack’s death, they work together to gather key information that can help find the culprits.

“CAROUSEL” (L-R): LL Cool J as NCIS Special Agent Sam Hanna and Scott Caan as NCIS Special Agent Nick Schaeffer in ‘NCIS: New York’ Episode 3 ‘Carousel’ Emily V. Aragones/CBS

DEADLINE: We learned about Sam being in Dubai in the NCIS crossover at the end of last season. Can you flesh out more about what he’s been up to and how he ends up in New York?

BYRON BALASCO: Yeah, Sam has been a lone wolf, sort of a samurai, traveling the world on very high-stakes solo missions in all parts of the globe in dangerous hotspots. So when we find him in Dubai, he’s finishing up one of these missions when he, in the middle of it, gets a call from somebody who’s very important to him. He can’t get the call because he’s in the middle of the mission, and he realizes missing that call might have put this person in jeopardy. So that brings him back to New York. It’s a very emotional reason. It’s a very close personal case to him. So he feels like he needs to go to New York and handle this one himself.

LL COOL J: New York is totally different; it’s a lot grittier, it’s more character-driven. New York is the main character and the star. Sam hasn’t been in New York in many, many years. So he has to get re-acclimated to that. Plus, he’s a man looking for redemption in many ways because of different things that he’s been through over the course of his career in law enforcement. It’s pretty special and a great contribution to the NCIS Universe in general.

DEADLINE: LL, you’re a native New Yorker. Does it feel extra special to start this new chapter back home?

LL COOL J: Yeah, it’s real cool. It’s different, too, because I’m a New Yorker, but we’re going to parts of New York I’ve never seen. We’re visiting all the various parts of New York: the underbelly, the main parts. It’s a lot of fun in that regard.

“Family Business” (L-R): LL Cool J as NCIS Special Agent Sam Hanna and Scott Caan as NCIS Special Agent Nick Schaeffer Cara Howe/CBS

DEADLINE: Bryon, what can you share about the pairing of LL and Scott Caan? What makes them the perfect crime-fighting duo?

BALASCO: As actors, they have incredible chemistry together. They’re both extremely magnetic. They both have very strong personalities and personas that really bounce well off of each other. There’s a little bit of an opposites-attract kind of thing with them that plays really well. They’re really specifically great for New York because they both have a very complicated, emotional, and loving relationship with the place that raised them. Having them both in New York together, dealing with the past, the present, and the future together in different ways makes a very compelling watch.

DEADLINE: LL, you and Scott Caan are like the movie Twins starring Arnold Schwarzenegger and Danny DeVito. Will you guys joke around about the obvious differences between you two?

LL COOL J: That’s on the table, of course. Everything’s on the table. We play with all the obvious things, yeah, no question.

BALASCO: They make a great team. Nick was born and raised in New York. He’s a man who has a lot of loyalty and feels very indebted to the city, and wants to pay it back. In terms of him and Sam, they’re kind of different guys. Nick is more extroverted, more kind of outwardly in your face, whereas Sam’s a little introverted. It’s a constant battle between Nick getting Sam to open up while Sam resists. Through that process, they become really, really close. You’ll see the bond forming between them.

DEADLINE: The casting of Jennifer Beals was received by the fandom with great excitement. What can you guys share about who she will play?

LL COOL J: She brings gravitas as the boss, Special Agent in Charge Robin Wells. She’s telling these characters what to do and leading the ship. It’s really powerful how she helps bring these characters to life.

BALASCO: What’s interesting about Robin is that she’s not your do it my way or the highway kind of boss. She really understands what each team member needs and how to lead them. You can’t treat everybody the same because not everybody is the same. What’s so special about her leadership is that she’s deeply sensitive to the cases, but always professional, and guides us down the right path. Part of her story is that she is seen by the powers that be as somebody that we could have big plans for. But she’s very conflicted about that because she loves her job.

“Carousel” (L-R) LL Cool J as NCIS Special Agent Sam Hanna Emily V. Aragones/CBS

DEADLINE: The NCIS Universe is vast. Any chance we could see any crossovers or appearances by NCIS favorites in Season 1?

LL COOL J: There might be. I’ll put it to you like this: I welcome crossovers. I think crossovers are great, and they’re fun.

BALASCO: We’ll have to see what happens. I mean, we’re all in the universe, so you can kind of expect anything like that to happen.

DEADLINE: How about some familiar faces from NCIS: Los Angeles? Say, Chris O’Donnell and Eric Christian-Olson?

LL COOL J: All welcome. Super welcome.

BALASCO: All things are possible. We’re still in the beginning of our journey here.

title: New Goldenrod Platform Helps Productions Secure Texas Film Boost
summary: As sweetened production incentives roll out in Texas, an Austin-based company wants to help filmmakers capture the maximum possible rebate from the Lone Star State and beyond. Its new platform called Goldenrod is now live for productions based in Texas, with pilot projects in Kentucky and Louisiana. The launch announcement is timed to the Toronto […]
content:
As sweetened production incentives roll out in Texas, an Austin-based company wants to help filmmakers capture the maximum possible rebate from the Lone Star State and beyond.

Its new platform called Goldenrod is now live for productions based in Texas, with pilot projects in Kentucky and Louisiana. The launch announcement is timed to the Toronto Film Festival at a moment of great attention to state incentive packages and a potential national benefit that’s currently being drafted by lawmakers in Washington.

Goldenrod offers productions (film, television, commercial and video game) purpose-built technology alongside in-person incentives consulting. Filmmakers are welcome to bring early-stage projects to strategize before shooting starts. Goldenrod monitors compliance during production and manages final submissions through approval and payment.

Watch on Deadline

The expanded Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program that passed last fall established a $1.5 billion fund, or $300 million every two years for a decade. The base incentive rate for qualifying film and television projects is 5% to 25% depending on in-state spend (a minimum of $250,000), with uplifts possible. It’s a cash rebate system, which pays out faster than a tax incentive.

“Incentives compliance is genuinely hard to get right,” says producer and Goldenrod co-founder Russell Wayne Groves (Family Movie, Stages), founder of The Ranch Productions in Austin. “The administrative load pulls you off set, off the creative work, and if you miss something, you’re either leaving significant dollars on the table or facing disqualification entirely.” He compares Goldenrod to a TurboTax for production incentives. “You focus on the work, we make sure you’re maximizing every dollar you’re entitled to, and your financiers always know exactly where things stand.”

The other founders are Ted Griffis and Brandon Thomas of Austin-based post production studio TBD Post (Iron Lung, Netflix’s The Long Game, Apple TV documentary Fathom), and Tara Khanna, former Incentives Team Lead and Senior Production Incentives Specialist at the Texas Film Commission.

The company takes a deposit upfront and a percentage of incentives captured.

Texas’ production profile has been rising, including a shoutout by David Ellison last month. The Paramount CEO named it as one of a few states he’d consider to relocate the Hollywood studio absent settlement talks on an antitrust lawsuit. California Attorney General Rob Bonta is leading a dozen states to block Paramount’s planned merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.

A federal tax incentive like those available in many other countries was recently resurfaced by President Trump and is creating major industry buzz. It could be paired with state benefits to offer a substantial package encouraging projects to film in the U.S. Production drives jobs and spending in local economies across both red and blue states.

Groves tells Deadline he was the first to onboard Goldenrod with his SXSW-premiering film Stages and about 10 productions have beta tested the service. The ideal scenario is “someone that has a budget and a schedule, and we help make sure the budget is optimized for the benefit of that project. In the state of Texas, if you don’t use it, you lose it. So we want to make sure that you’re getting the most out of whatever your budget is.”

Texas has 35% residency requirement for cast and crew to qualify for the rebate. “So, if you if you were at 30% and you were on week four of five, you … need to hire an extra five people to fit in that box. That is what we’re trying to flag.”

At least 60% of production must be completed in state.

“We’re going to move extremely quickly after TIFF,” Groves says. Beyond Texas, Kentucky and Louisiana, Goldenrod has a list of about 16 more states to tap, hoping to eventually expand across the U.S.

“I love Texas. I’m from Texas … But I think this has to be state agnostic. Each state is different. Something we want to do on the front end is to say, before you apply, let’s do a review. If this is not the appropriate spot for you to do this, in this state, let’s look at another state.”

At TIFF, The Goldenrod team will be meeting with filmmakers and film commissions and host a party with XYZ Films on Sunday where it will be handing out ‘golden tickets’ for prospective clients to log into the platform and crunch some numbers.

title: Doc Talk Podcast: ‘Remake’ Director Ross McElwee On Love, Loss And Grieving For His Son
summary: Adrian McElwee, son of the filmmaker Ross McElwee, was such an interesting child, full of precocious wisdom. For instance, when his father asked young Adrian during a seaside trip, “Why do you think you like fishing so much?” the boy spontaneously replied, “I don’t know. I just love the deep surprise of the ocean.” The […]
content:
Adrian McElwee, son of the filmmaker Ross McElwee, was such an interesting child, full of precocious wisdom. For instance, when his father asked young Adrian during a seaside trip, “Why do you think you like fishing so much?” the boy spontaneously replied, “I don’t know. I just love the deep surprise of the ocean.”

The elder McElwee would include his son in many of his films and later, when Adrian entered adulthood, they worked together on documentaries. But Adrian’s fate was not to be a happy one. The boy who displayed such joy and promise as a child experienced periodic depression as an adult and slipped into drug addiction.

In McElwee’s documentary Remake, which just aired on the PBS series POV, he explores his relationship with Adrian and his son’s struggles after he came of age, which culminated with Adrian’s untimely death at the age of 27. The film has won awards around the world including the Impact Golden Globes Prize for Documentary at the Venice Film Festival, the ReFrame Award for Creative Use of Archive at IDFA in Amsterdam, and the True Vision Award at True/False in Columbia, MO.

Watch on Deadline

McElwee joins the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss the film and what he learned about himself during the making of Remake. No film could be more heartbreaking, yet there are touches of humor throughout. The director tells us about striking that delicate balance and whether he sees this as his final film.

Music Box Films acquired Remake and the company also released a restored version of McElwee’s 1985 documentary Sherman’s March, the film that launched his career and inaugured a new style of documentary filmmaking where the director – through on camera commentary and voice-over – guides the viewer through the subject matter. The influence of that style can be seen in many successive films including You Can See Everything, which just premiered at Telluride, and The Oldest Person in the World, directed by Sam Green. On the pod, McElwee talks about the making of Sherman’s March, which becomes a significant storyline in Remake.

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

Watch the trailer above, and check out the poster below. Based on the 2012 visual novel by Kinoko Nasu and developed by Type-Moon (the Fate […]
content:
A witch-meets-boy tale is brewing early next year. Crunchyroll has acquired anime feature Witch on the Holy Night and set it for a January 29 release in North American theaters. Watch the trailer above, and check out the poster below.

Based on the 2012 visual novel by Kinoko Nasu and developed by Type-Moon (the Fate franchise), the pic follows Aoko Aozaki, an ordinary high school girl who actually is a magician lives in the modern world, though she is still only an apprentice. As she spends her days living alongside her housemate, Alice Kuonji, striving to become a full-fledged Magician, Aoko meets a boy. It’s the beginning of one young girl’s story — the tale of a witch.

Distributed by Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures Entertainment, Witch on the Holy Night will be available in both Japanese with English subtitles as well as dubbed in English. The pic is animated by ufotable, the toon production house behind last year’s theatrical smash Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba Infinity Castle I, which grossed an astounding $793.6 million worldwide.

title: Dan Schneider Loses ‘Quiet on Set’ Defamation Suit on Appeal
summary: The producers of the documentary series “Quiet on Set” have prevailed in a lawsuit brought by former Nickelodeon showrunner Dan Schneider, who claimed that the show implied that he was a child sex abuser. Schneider sued for defamation in 2024, alleging that the series had falsely portrayed him as being responsible for or having facilitated […]
content:
The producers of the documentary series “Quiet on Set” have prevailed in a lawsuit brought by former Nickelodeon showrunner Dan Schneider, who claimed that the show implied that he was a child sex abuser.

Schneider sued for defamation in 2024, alleging that the series had falsely portrayed him as being responsible for or having facilitated sex abuse committed by others. He won the first round in court, as a judge found enough merit in the claims to deny the defendants’ motion to throw out the case.

But the defendants — Warner Bros. Discovery, Sony and producers Mary Robertson and Emma Schwartz — filed an appeal, and on Thursday a three-judge panel ruled unanimously in their favor. The judges found that while the show does depict Schneider as a bad boss, it does not cross the line to a defamatory implication of child sex abuse.

Popular on Variety

“The documentary clearly distinguishes between the lamentable conduct that its participants attribute to Schneider — gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior, and inappropriate sexual innuendo — and the child sexual abuse explicitly attributed to three named individuals, two of whom are discussed at length,” wrote Judge Melanie Ochoa, for the panel. “‘Quiet on Set’ also affirmatively states that Schneider’s employer investigated his conduct and, while it confirmed some inappropriate behavior, it found no evidence of child sexual abuse. Schneider’s attempt to find an alternative meaning than what is expressly stated in the documentary is unavailing.”

Schneider was responsible for creating a series of hit shows on Nickelodeon, including “The Amanda Show,” “Drake & Josh,” “Zoey 101,” “iCarly,” and “Victorious.” Amid allegations of abusive conduct, Nickelodeon cut ties with him in 2018.

The series, “Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV,” ran on Investigation Discovery in March 2024. Schneider posted a video apology shortly afterward, saying he was “embarrassed” by his past behaviors.

In the lawsuit, Schneider’s attorneys argued that while the show did not come out and directly accuse Schneider of sex abuse, it did juxtapose accusations of “inappropriate behavior” with pictures of Schneider with his arm around child actresses.

The show also delved into the cases of Brian Peck, a dialogue coach who was arrested for child sex abuse, and Jason Michael Handy, a production assistant who was also accused of sending an explicit photo to a child actress.

Schneider argued that he had nothing to do with those cases, and that the series created a false impression by linking him to them.

But the panel ruled that it could not go along with that argument, given that “the only such abuse discussed is explicitly attributed to named perpetrators and the documentary expressly states that an investigation into Schneider found no evidence of abuse.”

The defendants prevailed under California’s anti-SLAPP statute, which allows an early mechanism to strike lawsuits intended to stifle speech on matters of public interest.

Gerry Silver, Schneider’s attorney, said in a statement he was disappointed in the result.

“We are disappointed by the Court’s decision to reverse the Superior Court’s well-reasoned anti-SLAPP ruling, and we are evaluating our options for further review and appeal,” Silver said. “However, we are pleased that the Court acknowledged that the makers of ‘Quiet on Set’ presented absolutely no evidence that Dan was sexually abusive towards any of his cast members and agreed that any such allegation is provably false.”

title: Dan Schneider’s ‘Quiet On Set’ Defamation Suit Shut Down By Appeal Judges In Big Win For WBD
summary: Just under two years after Dan Schneider was given a green light on his Quiet on Set defamation lawsuit against Warner Bros Discovery and others, a trio of appeal judges just handed the former Nickelodeon producer a big defeat. Slamming Schneider for relying on “a theory of defamation by implication,” the Golden State’s Second District […]
content:
Just under two years after Dan Schneider was given a green light on his Quiet on Set defamation lawsuit against Warner Bros Discovery and others, a trio of appeal judges just handed the former Nickelodeon producer a big defeat.

Slamming Schneider for relying on “a theory of defamation by implication,” the Golden State’s Second District Court of Appeal panel stated Thursday it will “refrain from splitting hairs to find an allegation of child sexual abuse where the only such abuse discussed is explicitly attributed to named perpetrators and the documentary expressly states that an investigation into Schneider found no evidence of abuse.”

What the panel did not refrain from was reversing the November 2024 ruling by LA Superior Court Judge Ashfaq G. Chowdhury denying the anti-SLAPP efforts by Warner Bros Discovery and Maxine Productions to have the iCarly creator’s suit dismissed. They concluded in the 37-page order “that Schneider has not shown a likelihood of success on the merits of his defamation claim.”

Watch on Deadline

Schneider filed the defamation suit against Warner Bros Discovery, Maxine Productions, Sony Pictures and Quiet on Set producers Mary Robertson and Emma Schwartz of defamation soon after the disturbing Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV after the series premiered in March 2024.

At the time. Schneider insisted Quiet on Set was a “hit job” that resulted in the annihilation of his “legacy and reputation.” A big hit viewerwise for ID, Quiet on Set examined two child sexual abusers who work on his shows — dialogue coach Brian Peck and former production assistant Jason Handy. In his 2024 filonmg, Schneider asserted he had “no knowledge of their abuse, was not complicit in their abuse.”

WBD did not responded today to Deadline’s request for comment on the ruling and their reversal of fortune.

The appeal was argued by Gibson Dunn attorneys before Judge Rashida Adams, Anne Egerton and Mark Hanasono n August 17. The Theodore J. Boutrous, Ilissa Samplin, Zachary Freund, and Connor Sullivan-led team of Gibson Dunn was brought on board after the defendants saw their move to get the case tossed out rejected in late 2024.

To that, the trio determined the 2024 Investigation Discovery limited series “clearly distinguishes between the lamentable conduct that its participants attribute to Schneider— gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior, and inappropriate sexual innuendo—and the child sexual abuse explicitly attributed to three named individuals, two of whom are discussed at length.

They add: “Quiet on Set also affirmatively states that Schneider’s employer investigated his conduct and, while it confirmed some inappropriate behavior, it found no evidence of child sexual abuse. Schneider’s attempt to find an alternative meaning than what is expressly stated in the documentary is unavailing.”

title: Netflix Debuts ‘Friday Night Lights’-Inspired NFL Pregame Opener Directed By Peter Berg & Narrated By Kyle Chandler: “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts, Can’t Lose”
summary: Ahead of Thursday’s game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia, Netflix released a Friday Night Lights-inspired pregame opener. Directed by Peter Berg and narrated by FNL Emmy winner Kyle Chandler, the clip titled “For the Love of Football” taps into the nostalgia of fans of the film and TV […]
content:
Ahead of Thursday’s game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia, Netflix released a Friday Night Lights-inspired pregame opener.

Directed by Peter Berg and narrated by FNL Emmy winner Kyle Chandler, the clip titled “For the Love of Football” taps into the nostalgia of fans of the film and TV series.

The series and film followed the fictional Dillon Panthers as Coach Taylor (Chandler in the series) inspired them to achieve greatness.

“And so it begins, right here, right now, today. You are going to win,” Chandler narrates as music similar to the Friday Night Lights theme song plays in the background. “You’ll use your eyes to win. Your eyes will show you the truth. You’ll recognize it whether you like it or not, without wishing you were seeing something else.”

Watch on Deadline

Chandler’s narration continues: “The truth on the field is never something else. You will not look away. You will feel the truth together in your hearts. Your eyes will see clearly. Your hearts will feel fully.”

RELATED: As NFL Season Kicks Off, Here Are Five Things In The Media Mix For 2026

As the narration goes on, images of various NFL teams play alongside young football players and cheerleaders from the Watts Rams youth football program.

“You will play with your eyes clear and your heart full. If you can do that, and then do it again and again, I assure you, you cannot lose,” Chandler continues. “Clear eyes. Full hearts. Can’t lose.”

The spot is the first of four openers Berg directed for Netflix, which also will stream games on Thanksgiving Eve, Christmas Day and Week 18 of the 2026 NFL season.

Watch the Friday Night Lights-inspired opener in the video above.

title: Jimmy Kimmel “Play-Acting” Over James Talarico Interview & FCC Threats, White House Claims
summary: In the latest twist in the Jimmy Kimmel-James Talarico interview drama, the White House is now accusing the ABC late-night host and his network of spinning a fake tale of federal strong-arming. Put another way, Team Trump insists there was never pressure put on Kimmel and ABC from the Trump administration to scuttle an interview […]
content:
In the latest twist in the Jimmy Kimmel–James Talarico interview drama, the White House is now accusing the ABC late-night host and his network of spinning a fake tale of federal strong-arming.

Put another way, Team Trump insists there was never pressure put on Kimmel and ABC from the Trump administration to scuttle an interview with the poll-topping Texas Democrat and Senate hopeful.



“Jimmy Kimmel is play-acting — as he often does — to create a false narrative about this administration’s policies,” Assistant White House Press Secretary Davis Ingle said Thursday.

“Chairman Carr has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate.,” Ingle added of Carr, the FCC chairman, just before the second night of Donald Trump‘s GOP midterm convention aka pageant reconvenes. “Any media outlet blindly amplifying Kimmel’s egocentric delusion should insist on proof. Of which they will find none.”

Watch on Deadline

ABC parent company Disney had no comment on the response from the White House when contacted by Deadline. The lack of response is unsurprising given that the company is the midst of an escalating legal and regulatory First Amendment clash with the FCC over station license renewals and charges of political thumbs on the scale.

Wednesday’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! monologue had some distinct déjà vu of what Stephen Colbert went through on CBS last year with Talarico, who is looking to flip the Lone Star state for the Dems for the first time in decades. The L.A.-based Kimmel revealed that an on-air sit-down with Talarico would not air on ABC tonight.

After naming off various political candidates including Trump, who Kimmel has talked to over the years, the Live! host put federal regulatory enforcement under the spotlight. “[The] FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions,” Kimmel said. “Guest bookings, it would seem, they don’t like.”

“And so, out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he stated. “It will be posted on YouTube instead.”

James Talarico Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Interestingly, Talarico, who is in Los Angeles today and Friday for a series of deep-pocket Hollywood fundraisers, was not officially listed as a guest on Kimmel before the host made his announcement. In a separate interview with MS NOW’s Symone Sanders Townsend today on The Weeknight, Talarico called the Kimmel situation the “most dangerous form of cancel culture.” With the knowledge that much of the consumption of late-night shows actually happens online anyway, the candidate went on to say: “I’m still hopeful that we can have this interview on the air. So we’ll see what happens tonight.”

Between Trump in Texas and Talarico in California, we certainly will.

At the same time, with the wounds still fresh from Disney’s sudden sidelining of Kimmel for almost a week a year ago over affiliate fallout from a remark he made about the tragic assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, there is a tendency for some to get lost in the weeds of this. There is also a tendency for some to start shouting about equal-time rules without a read of the fine print.

The equal time rule requires broadcasters that feature political candidates offer comparable airtime to rivals — if it is requested. Daytime and late-night talks shows have long operated under the assumption that they fell under an exemption for news and news interview programming. But in January, Carr issued guidance suggesting that such talk shows may not be free from the rule.

The equal time rule also is often misunderstood. It applies to political candidates in a certain cycle. So, for instance, Ted Cruz’s appearance on The View this week makes no difference because he’s not up for reelection this midterm.

Carr has argued that nothing is preventing late-night or daytime talk shows from featuring a political candidate as a guest. They just have to be prepared to offer time to rivals as well.

As ABC pushes back on Carr’s investigation of The View, the network’s argument is one of selective enforcement as the FCC chairman has not singled out other broadcasters, like conservative talk radio. The network has also pointed to a 2002 letter from the FCC confirming the show’s exemption from the equal time rule. The network also has characterized the equal time rule as unworkable, given that its stations may be on the hook not just for major party candidates but also third-party rivals.

Again, let’s see what happens tonight.

Worth noting that when the now axed Colbert’s interview with Talarico was shifted over to YouTube, it got a huge number of views and the candidate raised more than $2.5 million in just over 24 hours. That might be history worth repeating itself for the Texas Democrat, false narrative or not.

title: Jack Huston, Chazz Palminteri & Kathleen Chalfant Join Hulu’s ‘Chicks’ Pilot
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Jack Huston (Spider-Man Noir, Boardwalk Empire), Chazz Palminteri (A Bronx Tale, Bullets Over Broadway) and Kathleen Chalfant (The Copenhagen Test, The Affair) have joined Ellen Pompeo and Jodie Whittaker in the Hulu pilot Chicks. From writer and executive producer Katie Robbins, Chicks is a family dramedy set in the rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods of old Boston. It follows Chickie (Pompeo) and Doreen […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Jack Huston (Spider-Man Noir, Boardwalk Empire), Chazz Palminteri (A Bronx Tale, Bullets Over Broadway) and Kathleen Chalfant (The Copenhagen Test, The Affair) have joined Ellen Pompeo and Jodie Whittaker in the Hulu pilot Chicks.

From writer and executive producer Katie Robbins, Chicks is a family dramedy set in the rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods of old Boston. It follows Chickie (Pompeo) and Doreen (Whittaker), two estranged half-sisters who are both struggling to get by when their wise-guy dad unexpectedly kicks the bucket. Their only inheritance is a legacy of two-bit crime that inspires them to run increasingly audacious frauds. As their con grows, so does their odd-couple bond, as they each start to fill the father-shaped hole in the other’s heart.

In a series regular role, Huston plays The Clooney, a devilishly handsome businessman who’s charmed by Chickie’s store and maybe her too…

Watch on Deadline

Palminteri will guest star as Salvatore Mastrangelo, Sr., Chickie and Doreen’s dad. A man who moves down the street with a swing in his step and a swagger in his soul, Sally, Sr., is a neighborhood institution and fixer, a ladies’ man with four ex-wives (not that anyone’s counting), and an even bigger portfolio of small-time cons.

Chalfant plays Aunt Sister Donna of Compassionate Trinity, Chickie and Doreen’s paternal aunt, who is mean as spit and tougher than any wise guy on the block.

Chicks is based on an original idea from Robbins that she developed for Pompeo, inspired by conversations the two had on the set of their first project together, the Hulu limited series Good American Family. Pompeo and Robbins exec-produce alongside the latter’s Calamity Jane partner, Laura Holstein.

Huston is repped by 111 Media, Altitude Management, CAA, and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Palminteri is repped by Innovative Artists & Liebman Entertainment. Chalfant is repped by DGRW & AMT Artists.

title: CBS Files Motion to Dismiss Former ‘Matlock’ Writer’s Lawsuit Alleging Racist, Sexist Comments: ‘We Stand Firmly Behind Our Producers’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: CBS Studios has filed a motion in Los Angeles Superior Court under the anti-SLAPP statute to strike a lawsuit filed earlier this summer by former “Matlock” writer John Lowe. The CBS Studios filing included multiple declarations disputing his allegations against three of the show’s executive producers. Lowe’s suit against CBS Studios, showrunner Jennie Snyder Urman […]
content:
CBS Studios has filed a motion in Los Angeles Superior Court under the anti-SLAPP statute to strike a lawsuit filed earlier this summer by former “Matlock” writer John Lowe. The CBS Studios filing included multiple declarations disputing his allegations against three of the show’s executive producers.

Lowe’s suit against CBS Studios, showrunner Jennie Snyder Urman and executive producers Nicki Renna and Jeffrey Lieber alleged that “racially stereotyped comments about his body and genitalia” were made toward him and other Black cast and crew members, creating a “hostile work environment.”

In its filing, the studio threw its full support behind Urman, Renna and Lieber, while countering many of Lowe’s allegations. Lowe’s attorney Ron Zambrano told Variety that they had not yet been served the motion yet, so he couldn’t comment on the specifics, while writing, “But I am confident we will successfully oppose the motion as the complaint was drafted with that possibility in mind.”

Popular on Variety

“We take allegations of discrimination and harassment very seriously,” a CBS Studios spokesperson said. “Today, with the filing of our motion to strike, we took our first step toward challenging the baseless complaint filed by former ‘Matlock’ writer John Lowe. As stated in the motion and following a thorough investigation, we are confident that Lowe’s accusations are demonstrably inaccurate and maliciously fabricated, and will not allow them to go unchallenged.

“False allegations are deeply damaging, both to those wrongly accused, and to anyone with a serious and legitimate claim of discrimination,” the spokesperson added. “We stand firmly behind our producers and look forward to the truth coming to light.”

In his lawsuit, Lowe — who worked on “Matlock” from October 2023 to July 2024 (as CBS Studios noted, not in 2025, as Lowe’s complaint stated) — claimed he was terminated from his position as a form of retaliation, as it came two weeks after reporting an alleged incident in which Urman referred to Juneteenth as “Coonteenth.”

In declarations, Urman, Renna, Lieber and other witnesses disputed this, and said that Urman “never used that word (and) did not say it to Ms. Renna, to Lowe, or to anyone else.”

Lowe had also in his complaint detailed an alleged incident claiming that Urman brought in her dog to the writers’ room, “citing that her children ‘didn’t like the aesthetic’ — referring to the dog’s black color.” He claimed he was coerced into taking the dog for nearly a year, while other staff were present, a move he felt “was racially motivated and designed to single him out for humiliation based on his race, not for any creative or production reason.”

In declaration, Urman, Renna and Lieber said it wasn’t Urman’s dog, nor did she place it on Lowe’s lap or comment on the dog’s appearance, nor was she present when Lowe asked to adopt the dog.

As for Lowe’s claims that Renna said Black cast member Eme Ikwuakor “can barely read” and allegedly called Lowe late at night and said she “was in bed wearing only her underwear,” the producers said in their declarations that Lowe made it up.

And regarding Lowe’s allegations of sexually charged comments, the producers declared that “Lowe’s sexuality or his sex life was never questioned, nor was his body ever commented on.”

Meanwhile, in her declaration, Urman said that in January 2026 — 18 months after his departure from “Matlock” — Lowe sent an email to Urman demanding $10,000. Urman said she reported the email to the company’s HR representative, and that Lowe’s first complaint to the company’s HR representative came after that demand for $10,000 and after Urman had contacted HR about it.

Back in June, CBS Studios said it had investigated the allegations and didn’t find any merit to them: “We are committed to maintaining a safe and respectful environment for everyone and take all workplace complaints seriously,” a company spokesperson said at the time. “In this instance, a thorough investigation was completed, and we were unable to find support for his allegations. We look forward to vigorously defending this lawsuit.”

At the same time, Lowe’s attorney, Ron Zambrano, sent this statement: “There is no excuse for this blatant racism and harassment. CBS should be ashamed for allowing it, and the ‘Matlock’ showrunner and producers should be held accountable. Mr. Lowe was subjected to degrading and unlawful conduct. He deserved to be treated with dignity and respect, as everyone should expect in the workplace, not subjected to these outrageous and illegal racial slurs and sexual harassment without any connection to his work on the show.”

In the filing, CBS Studios said Lowe’s complaint was “filled with fabrications and outright lies that it resembles a grotesque work of fiction more than a court pleading. Lowe was never subjected to race or sex harassment as he claims, and as this case progresses, Defendants are confident that Plaintiff’s malicious and unsupported attacks will be publicly exposed for what they are: retaliation by a desperate man who was not renewed as a writer because his performance deficiencies detrimentally impacted CBS’ ability to convey the messages it desired.”

title: TIFF Opens With Siân Heder’s Crowd-Pleasing ‘Being Heumann’ — and Apple Has Its Next Oscar Contender
summary: “Being Heumann” opens on a New York sidewalk that doesn’t allow Judy Heumann to climb it. There’s no curb cut or ramp. Just a woman and her wheelchair. Director Siân Heder holds on it — and then Judy gives the middle finger. And it immediately hooks the viewer in for the ride. At least that […]
content:
“Being Heumann” opens on a New York sidewalk that doesn’t allow Judy Heumann to climb it. There’s no curb cut or ramp. Just a woman and her wheelchair. Director Siân Heder holds on it — and then Judy gives the middle finger. And it immediately hooks the viewer in for the ride.

At least that was the case for the audience inside Roy Thomson Hall, who sat with rapt attention as Heder’s film opened the 51st Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday night. The film is Heder’s first since “CODA,” the Sundance sensation which went on to win the best picture Oscar, a first for Apple Original Films and any streaming company. It chronicles the true story of how Heumann and her motley crew of activists fought for equal rights by waging a 28-day sit-in protest that helped pave the way for the Americans with Disabilities Act.

”I don’t want to make a biopic about you. I want to make ‘Dog Day Afternoon’ with disabled people,” Heder said she told Heumann when she pitched herself to direct the project.

Popular on Variety

After the screening — which ran with open captions, ASL interpreters and live captioning for the onstage portions — Heder sat for a Q&A with her actors to discuss how they made the film and her critical decision to cast actors with disabilities. Heder’s choice created a massive opportunity for actors like Madeley who has been a wheelchair user since birth.

Madeley already idolized Heumann, known as the “Mother of the Disability Movement” — “She was funny. She was fierce. She was cheeky. She was naughty. She was sexy,” Madeley pointed out.

“That is a gift for any actor to be able to play with all of those different things,” Madeleu continued. “But that was a challenge as well, and I knew the pressure that so many disabled people are waiting to see a character like this on the big screen, myself included.”

The British actress — a BAFTA nominee for “Don’t Take My Baby,” and familiar to others from “Doctor Who” — has been very good in things you may have missed. Here she is the whole ballgame, and she plays Heumann without a single note of the saintly patience that biopics tend to hand their disabled subjects. Madeley’s Judy is funny, tactical, horny and even a little bit of an asshole sometimes. She is passionate about the right things and furious in a way that keeps finding new gears.

The movie also shows what Heder can do with real money behind her. “CODA” was a small film about a small town, shot at the scale its budget allowed and beloved for its intimacy. “Being Heumann” is a period piece with a sprawling cast — the activists’ 28-day occupation of the San Francisco Federal Building, the longest occupation of a federal building in U.S. history, was staged with hundreds of people. From there, they bring their fight to Washington, D.C. and, finally, to secretary Joseph Califano’s front door. Apple funded the film, and Heder makes the leap look easy. Give a good director resources and you find out what she was doing without them.

The ensemble around Madeley — Michael Patrick Thornton, Russell Harvard, Daniel Durant and a deep bench of disabled performers who describe themselves in the film as “radical crips” — is cast with an authenticity most productions still treat as a “nice-to-have.”

“As disabled kids, you grow up being told like there’s this ceiling that’s made of vibranium that’s always hanging over you, and no matter what you do, you’re not going to be able to break out of this box, and confined to trying to do whatever society thinks that you can do,” said Charlie Rush-Reese, a blind performer who makes his acting debut in the film. “Being part of this project really not only inspired me to continue to chase my dreams and know that event a black kids in Minnesota can grow up to be in a movie like this, but … that [it] would inspire other disabled people to go out and chase their dreams.”

Oscar nominee Mark Ruffalo, a decade after he brought “Spotlight” to Toronto, plays the bureaucrat stalling on Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act with the weary decency of a man who thinks the math is on his side. While he doesn’t have the role or screen time needed to propel his way into the supporting actor race, if the film gets big enough, you can never count him out.

Dylan O’Brien, Rob Delaney and Ray Fisher round out the cast.

“My first thought when I signed up for the project was, ‘This would be such a fucking punk rock summer to be a part of,’” said O’Brien, who plays a local reporter who embeds himself with the activists and publicizes their efforts. But, making the movie was more meaningful than he anticipated. “Evan did not necessarily realize how galvanized he would be along with them, and that reflects my experience.”

The film allows Heder to do something American movies rarely do. Without spoiling where the film goes, “Being Heumann” treats its disabled characters as full romantic and sexual beings: for example, there’s an intimate scene between a disabled performer and a nondisabled one that is played for tenderness and desire, not a learning lesson.

Moreover, the film reinforces that that disability rights movement was never just about ramps and regulations for one community. It is, and has always been, about seeing this minority group as people who have the right to be wanted and not as a set of limitations someone else can see from across a room.

The ultimate result is, plainly, a crowd-pleaser — the good kind — engineered by someone who knows the difference between manipulating its audience and bringing genuine care and heart to a story. It’s funny while also being inspiring, and specific without being alienating. That matters this weekend for one concrete reason and that’s the People’s Choice Award. Toronto’s audience vote carries more Oscar-season weight than any jury prize, and the pipeline is well-worn — “Nomadland,” “Green Book,” “12 Years a Slave.” If “Being Heumann” takes it, the conversation changes overnight from “Will it play?” to “How far can it go?”

In the Oscars landscape, we can see a few possibilities.

Madeley belongs in the best actress discussion, and a win in Toronto would strengthen her position there. Screenplay is alive as well — Heder and Rebekah Taussig wrote from Heumann’s memoir, “Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist and Heder already owns an adapted screenplay Oscar for “CODA.”

The film is a natural for the Academy’s casting category, given the scale and integrity of the ensemble Heder assembled. Add in production design with a 1977 New York, San Francisco and Washington, all rebuilt with period specificity.

And best picture is not out of reach for a movie made by an Oscar-winning director, backed by the studio that won the category the last time she showed up at the big show.

The campaign won’t have to manufacture that poignancy. The real Heumann died in 2023, having spent a lifetime making the country hold a door it kept trying to close. That message could be a strong factor.

”Being Heumann” debuts in theaters on Nov. 6 before streaming on Apple TV.

title: ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s First Film Since ‘CODA’ Is a Bold and Stirring Dramatization of the Protest That Launched the Disabled-Rights Revolution
summary: "Being Huemann" isn’t as transporting a movie as "CODA" was, yet it’s a stirring drama cut from the same cloth of cathartic empathy.
content:
There’s a quality that liberal social-protest dramas tend to have in common. They’re usually about revolutionary moments we’ve come through and are on the other side of, so they can encourage the audience to feel — with a touch of sanctimony — that yesterday’s revolution was never anything but today’s common sense. That’s been true of many movies, even some fine ones, about the Civil Rights movement or the gay rights movement. It’s true, as well, of a movie about the fight for union rights like “Norma Rae.”

But when you watch “Being Heumann,” a drama about the astonishing 1977 protest that launched the disability-rights revolution (it opened the Toronto International Film Festival tonight), the film doesn’t give you that sanctimonious “Oh, of course” feeling. That’s because the director, Siân Heder, who made a splash five years ago with “CODA” (this is the first film she’s made since), takes pains to preserve, as emotion and drama, the radicalism of what the movie is about.

Popular on Variety

“Being Heumann” features a cast of disabled actors playing disabled people, and the actors have a raw, piercing, in-your-face quality that burns away any hint of sentimental complacency. But Heder uses the authenticity of her casting in a super-sly, double-edged way. She’s following up on what she did in “CODA,” where she placed deaf actors like Troy Kotsur at the center of her story in a way that mainstream movies almost never had. The humanity of her characters transcended their disabilities — yet in a way that’s too simple, since the movie insisted on how central the disabilities were to their identities. In addition to telling a great story, “CODA” busted through our pieties about how we characterize people.

“Being Heumann” isn’t as transporting a movie as “CODA” was, yet it’s a stirring drama cut from the same cloth of cathartic empathy. And it’s also structurally bold. The movie chronicles a sit-in, sparked by the disabled-rights leader Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley), that lasted for 28 days, as Huemann and her fellow protesters entered the Federal Building in San Francisco to confront the officials there, and wound up staying in the building — not because they’d planned it that way, but because that’s how the situation evolved. They were rolling with the punches, the politics, the media, and their own desperate impacted lives of messed-up righteousness. They wouldn’t take no for an answer, and “no” was the only answer they were getting. What they were fighting for was nothing less than the right to be treated — and seen — as full human beings.

Heder echoes the spontaneity of that journey, and mirrors it in how the film invites us to relate to its inspiringly prickly ensemble. The performances have a casual purity, and are often quite forceful, yet when the protesters first come together and we’re getting to know them, there’s a part of us that surveys them and says: Look, it’s a person with MS. It’s a blind person. It’s a deaf person. It’s a woman in a wheelchair. It’s a man wearing a brace on his head attached to a plastic orb he uses to tap out letters to say words. At first, the film all but inevitably encourages us to define each character by his or her disability — and the moment we’ve done that, we’ve actually tumbled, without realizing it, down a small rabbit hole of prejudice.

The movie opens in 1972, when Judy, in New York City, leads an early protest, all to try to get the government to pass Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, an anti-discriminatory measure that will guarantee the rights of disabled people to take part in all programs that receive federal funding. (That, of course, is most of American life.) Heder, who has a sixth sense for how to place the camera in a way that’s subjective and electrifying, introduces Judy, who’s been disabled since she was a child and is in a wheelchair, as she’s making her way through the puddles of midtown Manhattan (with Iggy Pop’s “The Passenger” on the soundtrack), experiencing herself as an encumbrance. When she reaches the building her protest is organized to stand in front of, the whole event (the protesters chanting “Sign 504!”) falls on deaf ears. So she says “Let me down,” meaning down into the street, and she then wheels herself out there and stops a Mack truck right in the middle of Madison Ave. That’s Judy Heumann. As played by Ruth Madeley, who looks like Bonnie Hunt but acts like an officious Joan of Arc, she’s hellbent on gaining the human rights that no one apart from disabled people seems to realize they don’t have.

Cut to five years later. It’s 1977, and Section 504 has been passed into law by the U.S. Congress; it passed by a few votes from people who, the movie suggests, barely knew what they were doing. Nevertheless: a victory, right? Not quite. Section 504 will not become law until Joseph Califano, the U.S. Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare under President Jimmy Carter, signs it into law. And he’s hedging; he doesn’t want to do it. Why not?

This is where the film becomes morally captivating. Carter was the most dogged liberal president of the last 60 years, and Califano — played with weary mid-century bureaucratic testiness by Mark Ruffalo — was a veteran ally of the Civil Rights movement who, in spirit, is very much a card-carrying liberal. Yet he’s a stubbornly conventional one. For him, it’s all about the money — and if Section 504 passes, it will mean that everything from schools to buses to sidewalks will have to be made over to accommodate the needs of disabled people. He says that will cost $2.4 billion (in 1977, an astronomical sum). He says: We can’t afford it. But what he means is (and this is the non-liberal side of liberalism): We can’t afford it just for those people.

Judy Heumann, living in San Francisco, is helping to organize a nationwide series of protests by disabled people against the oppression they’ve been living under. Section 504 is now law; they just want the HEW Secretary to sign it. Yet what they’re really fighting is the oppression of being treated as cripples — a hard-wired social prejudice that dictates, quite often, that they can’t go to school or get a job. (Judy talks about how they wouldn’t let her into school until she was 10 because she was considered a “fire hazard.” Which is often the excuse.) And the only way they’ll be able to do any of those things is if the federal government coughs up the money because it understands what disabled people need to live a full life: ramps that go alongside stairways, cut curbs that provide spaces for wheelchairs, and the demand that educators, and employers, do not look at disabled people and see a problem but, rather, a person with all the potential that implies.

This is a true upsurge in consciousness, reinforced by how we come to embrace the humanity of everyone onscreen. Judy has gathered up protesters with many different disabilities, and at one point we see how their priorities clash. The sit-in at the San Francisco Federal Building, which was the longest in U.S. history, takes its spirit from the Civil Rights movement, and from Gandhi too, when Judy goes on a hunger strike. One of the protesters, Brad Lomax (Antwan Tolliver), is a Black Panther, and his Panther comrades help out, bringing food to sustain the journey. Yet what’s dramatic and at times scaldingly funny about “Being Huemann” is how the characters’ fury brings them to life, whether it’s Kitty (Madeline Delp) turning her librarian personality inside out or Hale (Andrew Pilkington) tapping out the eloquence of his outrage. Judy Heumann truly sparked a revolution, though it would be 13 years before the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 was signed into law. And as “Being Heumann” captures with subversive gusto, the real disability revolution — the one in which we look at someone with a disability and just see another person in front of us — is still a work in progress.

title: ‘Burgundy’ Review: An Attractive, Light-Bodied Wine Doc With a Good Nose but No Legs
summary: “Everything that follows is true. Exactly as we dreamed it,” reads the opening title of “Burgundy,” from award-winning documentary duo Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, with an almost legible wink. It’s a sweet start to a sweet movie, but in retrospect it sounds a little defensive, as though the pair are aware that, especially compared […]
content:
“Everything that follows is true. Exactly as we dreamed it,” reads the opening title of “Burgundy,” from award-winning documentary duo Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, with an almost legible wink. It’s a sweet start to a sweet movie, but in retrospect it sounds a little defensive, as though the pair are aware that, especially compared to their last two lovely films — 2020’s “The Truffle Hunters” and 2024’s “Gaucho Gaucho” — “Burgundy” feels less like an incisive portrait of a particular arcane lifestyle than a rambling reverie about it. Amiably riffing on the viticultural tradition of the eponymous winemaking region of eastern-central France, “Burgundy” has more fragrance than substance and even then, too quickly loses its bouquet.

If dream it is, however, it’s a pleasant one — no night terrors in these terroirs — especially given that the directors, who are also responsible for the scrumptious cinematography, find so much material for their trademark, eye-catchingly pictorialist visuals. As perky ’60s pop songs play, perfectly composed chateaux-tableaux that are so crowded with billiard tables, oil paintings and antique tchotchkesthey feel like slightly sardonic wealth critique, we are first introduced to Bertrand Devillard, patriarch of a winemaking estate that dates back 160 years. Bertrand is a hands-on boss, and even when relaxing by the pool or doing a little skeet shooting, a worried one. His grandson Melchior is more interested in the world of high finance than in taking over the family business that would naturally be his inheritance.

Popular on Variety

That there would be plenty of people from outside the clan willing to step into that breach is proven by Enzo, a handsome young man with the throwback good looks of a midcentury matinee idol (he self-consciously models himself after his hero, Jean Gabin) whose ambition is one day to run his own vineyard. For the time being he comes to work on Bertrand’s estate, learning the ropes from the bottom up — cleaning the massive vats, stomping the season’s harvest, sampling wines he could never otherwise afford in an effort to educate his palate. Amusingly sketch-like intros then round out the rest of the cast, which includes Enzo’s eventual girlfriend, Céleste, a trainee sommelier; Patrick, the maitre’d of a nearby 3-Michelin-Star restaurant; and Guillaume, a recently separated wine critic whose adventures in dating, therapy and physio (for RSI due to lifting 100 glasses a day) make him the droll comic relief in a film whose tone is rarely serious enough to need relieving.

As in their other feature docs, Dweck and Kershaw’s craftsmanship is superb — they’re at least as meticulous and detail-oriented as their proudly finicky subjects. And the deliberately stilted restaging of interactions that likely originally happened in a much less picturesque manner is an inextricable part of their approach. So too are editor Pauline Gaillard’s sharp cuts, which are often timed exactly to coincide with the moment that someone lost in faraway thought finishes swirling their mouthful of Pinot Noir and hocks it unceremoniously into a nearby receptacle.

Less successfully, this time out the directors further break strict documentary protocol by including some whimsical 8mm footage, usually of Enzo and Céleste’s burgeoning relationship, which is again nicely shot but feels reversed in, as though it was only included as filler when the actual storylines were found to be getting bit sparse. An entire sequence in which the pair go to the movies to watch “Bonnie and Clyde” and then enact their own heist as pastiche versions of Faye Dunaway and Warren Beatty, is just a bit too cute and a digression too far from the film’s ostensible topic.

“The Truffle Hunters” followed several leathery Piedmontese old-timers and their absurdly touching relationships with their truffle-snuffling dogs. “Burgundy,” by contrast, has no natural source of such effortless, warm-hearted charm and without it, the portraiture sometimes veers closer to caricature. Perhaps for the first time, the limitations of Dweck and Kershaw’s deliberate, constructed style make themselves felt: when messy real life intrudes, the film rather flounders. Enzo abruptly goes off-script, so to speak, and quits the Devillard estate to try his hand at mussel farming and pouf! The narrative of a dedicated striver following his long-cherished dream evaporates at the revelation that maybe his lifelong fascination with viticulture was not so lifelong after all.

The filmmakers hastily shift course and retool the final third of “Burgundy” as a kind of star cross’d lovers romance, when Céleste also quits her apprenticeship and moves to Paris, and the young, sundered couple can be portrayed as pining for one another. Not only is this pivot a little hard to invest in, given we’ve been burned before, more grievously, it takes the main focus of the action away from the very region and wine culture the film is purportedly celebrating.

It is possible that true wine experts will respond to those parts of “Burgundy” that unabashedly ennoble the various different disciplines within the wine arts. Film lovers, on the other hand might be left unsatisfied by an approach that strains the limits of documentary realism to no particular end, save to further mythologize an already singularly rarefied sphere. And even if “Burgundy” is for oenophiles rather than cinephiles, presumably they too will be a little let down by a vintage that is fruity and full of promise at the first sip, but that loses its complexity — if not its easy drinkability — long before the last.

title: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Sparks $3.5M+ In Previews On Thursday – Box Office Update
summary: Warner Bros and Alcon’s Practical Magic 2 is off to a solid start in previews with an estimated $3.5M to $4M after showtimes that began at 2PM. Those figures are higher than the previews of Sandra Bullock’s romantic adventure pic Lost City ($2.5M, $31M 3-day opening) and the George Clooney and Julia Roberts romantic comedy, […]
content:
Warner Bros and Alcon’s Practical Magic 2 is off to a solid start in previews with an estimated $3.5M to $4M after showtimes that began at 2PM.

Those figures are higher than the previews of Sandra Bullock’s romantic adventure pic Lost City ($2.5M, $31M 3-day opening) and the George Clooney and Julia Roberts romantic comedy, Ticket to Paradise ($1.1M previews, $16.5M opening). The preview cash is also a notch above Warner Bros/MRC’s Wuthering Heights $3M Thursday which turned into a $32.8M 3-day opening. Even if this $70M net production files an opening between $30M-$35M domestic, it’s not cursed. Practical Magic 2 will have the power of PLFs this weekend, notably Dolby Cinema. Alcon financed 50% of the Bullock and Nicole Kidman reteam.

Critics are harsh on the sequel at 36%, but they also tried to cast a bad spell on the original 1998 movie at 29% Rotten. That pic opened to No. 1 at $13.1M back on Oct. 16-18, 1998 and finaled at $46.7M domestic, and $94.4M worldwide with a B- CinemaScore (sometimes moviegoers in their CinemaScores can be harder on features based on novels). The international outlook for part 2 in 77 territories sans China is between $18M-$23M.

Watch on Deadline

‘Hope’ Neon

NEON’s Na Hong-jin directed and written sci-fi alien invasion movie, Hope, opened yesterday to $1.1M at 1,506 theaters. That included $305K in previews. The pic is expected to do the mid-single digits in its 5-day debut. The pic was a smash in its home country of South Korea grossing over $36M and ranking No. 1 two weekends in a row. Michael Fassbender and Alicia Vikander play aliens in the pic.

Also opening this weekend is Disney’s documentary Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger and Angel Studio’s Runner.

Tonight’s previews are estimates from sources. We’ll have the actual reported figure from Warner Bros in the AM.

title: Jimmy Kimmel’s James Talarico Interview Posted To YouTube As Host Calls Out Trump And FCC: “They Want To Make Our Editorial Decisions For Us”
summary: Jimmy Kimmel’s interview with James Talarico was posted to YouTube on Thursday evening rather than the late-night host’s ABC broadcast amid concerns over an FCC enforcement action. “Why are they so scared of you?” Kimmel asked Talarico at the outset of the 20 minute interview, noting that Stephen Colbert also posted a sit down with […]
content:
Jimmy Kimmel‘s interview with James Talarico was posted to YouTube on Thursday evening rather than the late-night host’s ABC broadcast amid concerns over an FCC enforcement action.

“Why are they so scared of you?” Kimmel asked Talarico at the outset of the 20 minute interview, noting that Stephen Colbert also posted a sit down with the Texas U.S. Senate candidate in February over concerns it would invoke the the rule.

“They are worried that we’re going to win this race in Texas,” Talarico said. “But we are the underdogs until the last vote is counted.”

For decades, daytime and late night TV talk shows have operated on the assumption that they were exempt from the FCC’s equal time rule, which requires broadcasters who feature candidates to provide comparable time to their rivals, if it is requested.

Watch on Deadline

But in January, the FCC under chairman Brendan Carr, appointed by Donald Trump, issued guidance to broadcasters that TV talk shows may not be exempt, a move that critics saw as a regulatory effort to crackdown on daytime and late-night hosts the president does not like. Weeks later, the FCC started an investigation of The View after it featured Talarico as a guest. The equal time rule includes an exemption for news coverage and news interviews.

ABC has pushed back against the FCC’s actions, releasing a 2002 letter from the FCC affirming that The View was exempt. The network also has argued that the FCC is selectively enforcing the rule, as its January guidance did not address talk radio, where conservative hosts routinely feature political candidates, including Talarico’s Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

Kimmel opened his interview by noting that, until recently, the FCC has long recognized that late-night talk shows have been exempt, pointing to Donald Trump’s guest spots.

“When he was running, he was on the show two times, but now I guess he doesn’t like me anymore, or the First Amendment, and so the FCC has threatened me or threaten my show, our network, even our local ABC stations, because they want to make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept,” Kimmel said. “And so tonight we’re bypassing the public airwaves and hosting this YouTube interview on YouTube, even though our government would clearly prefer that we not do it at all.” The FCC does not regulate streaming platforms.

In a statement earlier on Thursday, a White House spokesman claimed that Kimmel was creating “a false narrative about this administration’s policies.

“Chairman Carr has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate,” a spokesperson said.

Carr has not commented, but previously said that the TV talk shows are free to feature political candidates, but they may be on the hook to offer time to their competitors. He also suggested that the Colbert interview was a publicity stunt designed to drive up fundraising for Talarico.

In his monologue on the Jimmy Kimmel Live TV broadcast, Kimmel challenged the White House’s statement. He told the audience that he would be interviewing Talarico but viewers would not see it. He called the threat of FCC action “yet another attack on free speech, something that is all too familiar for the show for us.” Kimmel also said that he would “love” to interview Paxton, but the rule would not just apply to Talarico’s GOP rival. “Our affiliates in Texas would have to give equal time to as many candidates as there are on the ballot. There’s about 10 candidates on the ballot,” Kimmel said. ABC’s legal team has argued that offering all candidates such time is untenable.

The interview was otherwise a pretty standard sitdown for Talarico, giving him the opportunity to repeat some of his campaign themes, including how his life has been shaped by religion and Jesus Christ.

It was also clear that Kimmel was a fan of Talarico, and he even ran a portion of one of his campaign ads.

He said, “I’ve been following you for a long time. I’ve been watching your videos. I think what you’re doing is great. I really do. … You hit on something that used to be on all of the bumper stickers. ‘What would Jesus do?’ I think Jesus has been co-opted by this MAGA enterprise in this way. It makes no sense when you really think about it. Would Jesus be throwing people into vans and separating them from their children? Would Jesus be taking kids off food stamps? … This is not the Jesus that I learned about growing up. And you bring it right back to the Bible, to the real teachings of Jesus, and it is it is very authentic.”

If the past is any guide, the Kimmel interview may ultimately draw more attention that Talarico would have gotten via a standard broadcast. His interview with Colbert has drawn 9.5 million views on YouTube, far more than the show’s average.

title: Stephen King Calls Mike Flanagan’s ‘Carrie’ Miniseries “Brilliant”
summary: Stephen King has weighed in on Mike Flanagan’s adaptation of Carrie, and he has a positive review. The supernatural horror miniseries premieres on October 7 on Prime Video with Summer H. Howell in the title role. Ahead of its release, the author of the 1974 novel the series is based on shared his take on […]
content:
Stephen King has weighed in on Mike Flanagan‘s adaptation of Carrie, and he has a positive review.

The supernatural horror miniseries premieres on October 7 on Prime Video with Summer H. Howell in the title role. Ahead of its release, the author of the 1974 novel the series is based on shared his take on the remake.

“Mike Flanagan’s version of CARRIE is brilliant,” King wrote on Threads. “What it has to say about social media is shocking and true.”

Carrie follows misfit high‑schooler Carrie White (Howell) after having spent her life hidden away inside the walls of her home with her fiercely protective mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan). Following her father’s unexpected death, Carrie enters the public high school ecosystem and is forced to navigate a viral bullying scandal that tears through her community.

Watch on Deadline

Carrie also faces the relentless pressure and casual cruelty of the social‑media age, and the awakening of mysterious telekinetic powers that rise alongside her adolescence.

King’s son, Joe Hill, also took to social media to share the series trailer and give a positive review.

“I was watching this trailer for Carrie on Instagram and thinking how good it looks and suddenly found myself fighting back tears,” Hill posted on Threads. “Never had that happen before, watching a preview. Maybe I’m getting a bit soggy in my fifties, I don’t know. Looks so good tho—Mike Flanagan sure can make em.”

Carrie was first adapted into a film in 1976, with Brian De Palma directing a screenplay written by Lawrence D. Cohen and Sissy Spacek as Carrie. A direct sequel, directed by Katt Shea, The Rage: Carrie 2 was released in 1999, with Emily Bergl playing Rachel Lang, Carrie’s younger half-sister.

In 2002, a television film directed by David Carson and based on a screenplay by Bryan Fuller debuted on NBC, with Angela Bettis as Carrie.

Before the new miniseries on Prime Video, Kimberly Peirce directed a 2013 remake starring Chloë Grace Moretz.

Prime Video’s Carrie also stars Siena Agudong (Sue Snell), Alison Thornton (Chris Hargensen), Joel Oulette (Tommy Ross), Josie Totah (Tina), Arthur Conti (Billy), Thalia Dudek (Emaline), Amber Midthunder (Miss Desjardin), and Matthew Lillard (Principal Grayle).

title: ‘The Housewife’ Review: Naomi Watts Is Chilling In Disturbing Post-Holocaust Drama With A Surprising Twist – Toronto Film Festival
summary: In 2015, Alyssa Hill’s startling Holocaust-themed script made the Black List of best unproduced screenplays. Now, a decade later, it has finally been made, and somehow the timing is just right for this challenging and pertinent portrait of a woman who lived a lie, hiding in plain sight until an intrepid young New York Times […]
content:
In 2015, Alyssa Hill’s startling Holocaust-themed script made the Black List of best unproduced screenplays. Now, a decade later, it has finally been made, and somehow the timing is just right for this challenging and pertinent portrait of a woman who lived a lie, hiding in plain sight until an intrepid young New York Times journalist uncovered her shocking secret right in the heart of Queens circa 1964, almost 20 years after the horrific events she has kept hidden, even from her husband, in a completely different life in post-war America.

I say the timing is eerily right since antisemitism and wholesale immigration cleansing has made a comeback, unthinkable after the horrors of the Nazis and concentration camps, and even as recently as this week in Germany where a far-right extremist party scored an election victory, the latest sign of a resurgence for the worst aspects of German history.

Enter one of the key opening-night world premieres at the Toronto Film Festival with the debut of the deceptively titled The Housewife. Naomi Watts plays Austrian-born Hermine Ryan, seemingly as a typical Queens, NY, 1950s housewife. She’s happily married to construction worker Russell Ryan (Luke Evans), bakes cakes for her neighbors and is a member of the women’s garden club — generally almost a June Cleaver persona in her community.

Watch on Deadline

NYT reporter Joseph Lelyveld (Tye Sheridan) has been tipped by famed Nazi hunter Simon Wiesenthal about a suspected former concentration camp guard living in the suburbs, perhaps under an assumed name. He tracks the suspected man down but first encounters his wife, Hermine, who invites him in, even acting motherly and cooperative to the point where Lelyveld feels the tip is a dead end. The planned front-page story has to be delayed despite the insistence of his anxious editor, Abe (Ron Leo).

Lelyveld worked closely with immigration officer Anthony DeVito (a very fine Michael Imperioli), who makes a startling discovery: It is not the husband, but rather the formerly known Hermine Braunsteiner who was in fact a vicious guard responsible for leading hundreds of Jews to their deaths. Female guards are rarely heard of, much less depicted in movies, making The Housewife a unique entry into the canon of films made on this subject.

The revelation comes relatively early, so it is not a spoiler alert. The story, inspired by real events, proceeds with Lelyveld confronting Hermine who denies all of it, claiming she was never a guard and unaware of the horrors at the camp. It becomes a bit of a cat-and-mouse game, Hermine’s secret life at risk, until the reporter can actually go to print, but does he have the facts needed? Suddenly her past is public record, the effort to deport her begins, and director Ben Shirinian’s impressive debut feature film becomes a psychological drama laced with moral ambiguity.

What The Housewife shows most effectively is human nature, how one person can embody the worst, most monstrous aspects of humanity, and then lock it away (literally in the case of her Nazi medal she quietly prizes but keeps hidden) to become a model American citizen. In an enormously tricky and risky performance, Watts is stunning as she plays both aspects, deep in denial of who she was and unapologetic for the mask she has been wearing, even with her husband who never knew. It is also nice to see Sheridan dive into a different kind of role than we have seen him do in the past, a conflicted but honest reporter confronted with a complex story he could not have imagined. Also, though in for just a couple of scenes, Lena Olin is superb and riveting as Rachel Berger, a reluctant eyewitness to Hermine’s atrocities but a key person who tells the frightening truth at Hermine’s deportation hearing which becomes as nail-biting as any courtroom drama you may have seen.

What works well here, and sets this exceptional film apart from what we have seen many times in dealing with this subject, is that there are no flashbacks to the actual scene of the crimes as it were, not a single shot of Hermine in a camp. The truly frightening thing is seeing her as she lives quietly all these years later, an upstanding citizen with a past finally uncovered that could have remained undiscovered if not for the efforts of Wiesenthal, one dedicated journalist, and the power of a free press.

Producers are Robbie Brenner, Kevin McKeon, Lee Broda, Jonathan Lim and Matt Paul. Appropriate for its TIFF debut, Canadian Shirinian’s film was shot in Montreal doubling effectively for New York.

Title: The Housewife

Festival: Toronto (Opening Night)

Director: Ben Shirinian

Screenwriter: Alyssa Hill

Cast: Naomi Watts, Luke Evans, Tye Sheridan, Lena Olin, Michael Imperioli, Ron Leo

Sales agent: CAA

Running time: 1 hr 42 mins

title: Donald Trump’s GOP Midterm Convention Fails To Get A Bounce In Cable News Viewership
summary: The first night of Donald Trump’s midterm convention failed to generate a ratings bounce for Fox News, with the audiences comparable or even slightly below regular primetime programming. Fox News’s coverage of the convention dominated the primetime hours on Wednesday, drawing an average 2.3 million viewers. But that is less than its September, 2025 primetime […]
content:
The first night of Donald Trump‘s midterm convention failed to generate a ratings bounce for Fox News, with the audiences comparable or even slightly below regular primetime programming.

Fox News’s coverage of the convention dominated the primetime hours on Wednesday, drawing an average 2.3 million viewers. But that is less than its September, 2025 primetime viewership, when it averaged 2.54 million viewers.

During Donald Trump’s speech from 9 p.m. ET to 11 p.m. ET, Fox News averaged 2.5 million viewers. A year ago, during the month of September, Hannity drew an average of 2.89 million in the 9 p.m. ET hour and Gutfeld! garnered an average of 2.94 million at 10 p.m. ET.

CNN‘s primetime coverage averaged 441,000 viewers, compared to a 543,000 average in September, 2025. MS NOW posted 1.1 million viewers in primetime, an uptick from an average of 810,000 during the month a year ago. In contrast to Fox News and CNN, MS NOW carried little of Trump’s speech and stayed on analysis from Jen Psaki and Lawrence O’Donnell and their guests.

Watch on Deadline

The figures are from Nielsen via Fox News.

title: Venice Final Cut Winner Machérie Ekwa Bahango on ‘Madi Makambu’ and Why She Wants Congo to Be Seen: ‘We’re a Great Nation That Needs to Write Its Own History’
summary: Machérie Ekwa Bahango wants Congo to be noticed by the industry.  “Through my films, I would like Congo to be seen as part of the world. Not for the labels people stick on it, but for what it really is,” she tells Variety.  “The subjects in my films are difficult, but they are issues that people […]
content:
Machérie Ekwa Bahango wants Congo to be noticed by the industry.

“Through my films, I would like Congo to be seen as part of the world. Not for the labels people stick on it, but for what it really is,” she tells Variety.

“The subjects in my films are difficult, but they are issues that people face in the Congo. We’re a great nation that needs to write, and rewrite, our own history.”

In her upcoming film “Madi Makambu,” awarded Final Cut’s La Biennale di Venezia Prize at the Venice Film Festival, she focuses on two lovers, Madi and Djino. Their lives take a turn when Madi gives birth to a child that Djino is not the father of, after experiencing a denied pregnancy. Though she doesn’t want to care for the baby, she must confront her past.

Popular on Variety

Jurors Tareq Al-Ibrahim, Mariette Rissenbeek and Tamara Tatishvili said the project invites audiences to follow a “genuine and electrifying young female protagonist, trying to navigate the violence and social injustice that is her unchosen reality.”

“I’m inspired by my everyday life, and everything that’s happening around me. The topics of my films come to me naturally, as if they’re asking me to tell their story,” Ekwa Bahango says.

She has been talking about women since her short “Sema.”

“The process of creating that film and working with women who had survived rape and violence in the eastern part of my country made me realize that my cinema could be a voice for resilient and strong women.”
