“When I look back at my first feature [‘Maki’la,’ which premiered at Berlinale], which was about children living on the streets, my understanding [of their situation] was still very limited at the time. Everything became clear through the female characters I developed.”

Ekwa Bahango is a self-taught filmmaker.

“The kind of cinema I want to make requires freedom and vulnerability. I think a film school would have certainly taken that away from me.”

She adds: “The challenge at the local level is primarily financial. It also stems from the fact that people aren’t yet aware of cinema’s strength and power. Many think that making films is just for fun and they don’t take us seriously. As a result, they don’t invest in us.”

Abroad, the world is still catching up with Congolese cinema, too.

“Particularly in the West, the challenge is to gain acceptance for this cinema, which doesn’t yet have a defined identity – and to accept it for what it is in its current form. There’s a tendency to expect one general model of African cinema, but Africa comprises more than 54 countries. Each of them has its own cinema. Little by little, we will get there.”

“Madi Makambu” is produced by CL1 D’oeil Studio and co-produced by Boucan Films.

“I live in a very intense society. We say: ‘Every day, we wake up to a new challenge’. My films aim to capture this unpredictability,” she says.

“The most beautiful thing we have in all of this, I think, is love. It’s what allows us to believe, be resilient and keep going. We need love in the Congo – and in the world. It’s the only thing that will soothe our sorrows.”

title: France, South Korea Take Center Stage as Global Film and TV Leaders Confront Industry Upheaval at Lumiere Summit: ‘Culture Itself Is Becoming a Driver of Growth’
summary: From Hollywood heavyweights and festival chiefs to exhibitors, broadcasters, streamers, heads of state and industry figures from more than 60 countries converged at a historic site in the south of France, where pine trees, sculpture gardens and sun-drenched terraces offered a postcard-worthy backdrop to timely conversations about an industry in upheaval. The Lumiere Summit gathering […]
content:
From Hollywood heavyweights and festival chiefs to exhibitors, broadcasters, streamers, heads of state and industry figures from more than 60 countries converged at a historic site in the south of France, where pine trees, sculpture gardens and sun-drenched terraces offered a postcard-worthy backdrop to timely conversations about an industry in upheaval.

The Lumiere Summit gathering on Sept. 7 in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — a famous site in France’s medieval history — took its name from the Lumière brothers, the French inventors who pioneered cinema in the 1890s. The first of its kind assembly was hosted by two world leaders with an interest in asserting their influence in entertainment on the world stage: French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

For Macron, the stakes go far beyond the film and television business. The event was meant to rally forces as creative industries reckon with the rise of social media platforms, the transformative promise of AI and tumultuous global political landscape. It’s no accident that France and South Korea were motivated to flex some muscle in a business traditionally dominated by the U.S. Both countries have tangled with President Donald Trump over tariffs and security concerns in recent months.

Popular on Variety

Some concrete declarations regarding trade were unveiled at the held on the stunning grounds of the Fondation Maeght art foundation and museum complex. The discussions were held in a setting packed with priceless works by some of the 20th century’s biggest names (Braque, Calder, Chagall, Kandinsky and Miró, to name a few), which added weight to conversations about difficult issues, from the impact of social media scrolling on youth to concerns that the business model of YouTube et al is fundamentally undercutting art.

Macron didn’t hold back in suggesting that social media platforms that rely on revenue-sharing agreements with users are a danger to the centuries-old model in which artistic works are commissioned with financing support upfront from patrons or platforms. He also pointed to the rising tide of political censorship that threatens creative freedom and artists who push boundaries.

“We have to be ready to resist because this model is what has been created over decades by a lot of artists, by the states and the different governments. It’s extremely important and I really believe it’s part of our DNA,” Macron told Variety at the summit.

The summit had the feel of a diplomatic event — complete with sword-bearing members of the Republican Guard lining up along a narrow red carpet to announce Macron’s arrival and a large delegation that accompanied South Korea’s Lee Jae Myung.

Macron also nodded to the rising tide of political pressure being applied to arts and cultural institutions in Europe, the U.S. and beyond.

“If there is a debate or if it is threatened by some populist parties or some extremes, we have to resist because I think it’s part of what we are. Culture and art is part of what France is. It’s part of our soft power outside and it’s a very important economy as well,” Macron said.

That belief — that culture is simultaneously an economic force, a source of soft power and something that requires active protection — became the thesis for the gathering, the first of this scale in a century. Macron and Lee Jae Myung emphasized the urgency of the need to act as AI tools and

A number of initiatives were unveiled at the event, notably:

** A pact between France and South Korea to build up film, TV, animation and gaming creative sectors, backed by $1.1 billion in investment. 2026 marks 150 years since France and Korea began diplomatic relations.

** The IRIS initiative (International Resilience Initiative for Independent Screens) that brings together several dozen filmmakers and industry leaders into a coalition deigned to help support specialty and art house theaters worldwide.

** An effort to create a world congress of state film commissions and related entities that will meet twice a year in an effort to shore up the future of independently financed films.

** A proposal to accelerate preservation efforts on behalf of vintage films in danger of being lost to film degradation.

** In a response to the AI boom, 120 of the Lumiere Summit’s 200 participants endorsed a declaration that pledged to prioritize human creation, copyright and cultural diversity in the artistic process.

If there was one common thread that cut across the conversations held about the future of filmmaking, exhibition and changing audience tastes, it was the impact of the unprecedented volume of content that now washes over consumers. Macron and Lee Jae Myung spoke passionately about the need to pay more attention to “the quality of images” that we are exposed to.

For Canal+ Group chairman Maxime Saada, that question has become increasingly pressing “in the face of AI” and the enormous success of TikTok and other social platforms. “People have never had access to so much content, they have never watched so many things and spent so much time watching,” said Saada, who recently made a five-year deal with French film guilds to invest $1.1 billion in French and European cinema starting in 2028. “But there is some kind of worry about what they’re watching, and the quality of what they’re watching.”

Donna Langley, chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment, said the impact of AI makes the question of “image literacy” particularly urgent. Rather than rejecting the technology outright, she argued that the industry should establish clearer ways for audiences to understand how what they are watching has been made. “AI isn’t all bad. We don’t want to take innovative tools away from storytellers and filmmakers, but I do think that it’s incumbent upon all of us to focus on this idea of disclosure,” she said. “So we all know what we’re looking at.”

Thierry Frémaux, Cannes Film Festival chief, stressed that instruction in media literacy is crucial. “Education for children, for the new generation, for what they have to know about history of cinéma and the history of images, because so much of what they know comes from the internet,” Frémaux said.

For CNC president Gaëtan Bruel, president of France’s CNC, the provocative topics and concerns raised about the long-term effects of online media gave them a good starting point for meaty discussions. Macron appointed Bruel to run France’s national film body in spring 2025. Almost immediately, he asked him to begin organizing a summit devoted to the future of cinema and the moving image. Bruel said the idea grew out of Macron’s concern about “the darker side of our image-saturated civilization” and the increasingly urgent question of how societies relate to screens.

Another possible source of concern may have been U.S. President Donald Trump threatening to impose a 100% tariff on all foreign-made films.

“We could see that many of the industry’s old dividing lines had become obsolete, yet the industry had not fully drawn the consequences,” Bruel said. “We wanted to create a genuinely global framework, not simply for discussion, but for thought and action.”

Bruel proposed the Fondation Maeght — France’s first foundation dedicated to modern art — as an intentionally unconventional setting. “The place did not call for convention-center panels; it called for conversations, in the sculpture garden, on the terraces and among the artworks.”

Organizers arranged nearly two dozen panel sessions throughout the day, letting participants choose among six smaller conversations at several points during the day, while leaving room for informal chats in the gardens.

During the outdoor lunch, Macron sat alongside Brigitte Macron amid a mix of political and entertainment heavyweights including Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, Disney’s Dana Walden, NBCUniversal’s Donna Langley, Sony Pictures’ Tom Rothman, George Clooney (fresh off his Venice Golden Lion honor), Paramount Skydance’s Andy Gordon, Mediawan co-founder Pierre-Antoine Capton, Cannes Film Festival President Iris Knobloch and CJ Group’s Miky Lee in gardens of the Fondation Maeght.

Guests ate beneath the trees at long tables set among the foundation’s stone walls and sculptures, making the gathering feel at moments more like an unusually high-powered Riviera garden party than an international policy summit.

But beneath the conviviality, the conversations reflected a degree of anxiety about where the industry is heading. For many of those attending, perhaps the clearest takeaway was how similar the problems confronting very different corners of the industry have become.

Netflix’s Sarandos, who didn’t take part in a panel but participated in a private meeting with Macron and other studio heads, left the summit with a feeling that more such collaborative efforts are needed to steer electronic media into its next century. Despite different business profiles, the industry’s largest conglomerates have much in common. “Everyone has the same problems. Everyone has the same challenges, and the more we can get together, the more creative we can be about the solutions,” Sarandos told Variety.

“We live in a time of multilateralism in almost every aspect of our lives, including in the arts,” he said. As regulators weigh updates to the EU’s audiovisual regulations, which could impact how Netflix does business on the continent, Sarandos stressed the need for a level playing field between broadcasters, streaming services and video-sharing platforms such as YouTube.

YouTube is highly viewed but not subjected to any French production investment obligations because it is not a producer of original content per se. Netflix does face French regulatory curbs on how it operates in the country. Asked about the YouTube effect in France and elsewhere, Sarandos told Variety, “We should all compete on this level. We compete with everyone on the TV screen. So if they’re on the TV screen, they’re a competitor.”

Donna Langley, chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment, similarly pointed to the significance of bringing together industries and cultures that increasingly face the same technological and economic disruption.

“Yes, we’re in the Hollywood film industry, but we are a global industry,” Langley said. “To be able to come together with different cultures and different countries to tackle some of the biggest challenges that we know we’re going to be facing even more as the future unfolds — whether it’s with AI, new technology, or just the disruption in general — I think it’s very important.”

The need for YouTube to start directly investing in content was raised at several points throughout the day, notably by Macron in his opening speech. TF1 boss Rodolphe Belmer opined during his panel that “YouTube has established itself on the TV screen and is already capturing a significant share of the TV advertising market without carrying comparable local investment obligations” as broadcasters and streamers. YouTube’s revenue-sharing model was directly called out by the two heads of state as a threat to the artistic community.

Canal Plus Group CEO Anna Marsh said the distance some guests had traveled underscored that urgency. “You can really feel an outreach from all sorts of executives, whether we’re producers, distributors, exhibitors, channels, pay, free, digital,” Marsh said. “There’s a common goal to tell better stories, to engage audiences, and to make sure also that the young generation remain as passionate as we are about content that matters and content that will stand the test of time.”

For SXSW festival artistic director Peter Debruge, one of the more unusual aspects of the summit was seeing that spirit extend even to organizations that typically are ruthlessly competitive.

“This is such a competitive industry, and I think that this whole event brings together people who are usually rivals, who are fighting for the same eyeballs, the same box office dollars,” he said. Debruge sat on a panel with other heads of festivals who set up a WhatsApp group to continue the conversation beyond the event. He said that even though they remain rivals, they all share the same goal which is to showcase “risky movies or audacious auteur work.”

Anonymous Content CEO Darren Walker echoed Saada’s concerns. “We’re overwhelmed with images,” Walker said. “That doesn’t mean that we are smarter, better informed, or that we’ve experienced more joy and enjoyment because of that.” For Walker, there’s an important distinction between volume and value. “It’s not just about the volume. More importantly, it’s about the quality and the consistency of excellence,” Saada said.

Langley said AI had made the concept of image literacy particularly important to teach in schools. Rather than rejecting the technology outright, she argued that the industry should establish clearer ways for audiences to understand how what they are watching has been made. “AI isn’t all bad. We don’t want to take innovative tools away from storytellers and filmmakers, but I do think that it’s incumbent upon all of us to focus on this idea of disclosure,” she said. “So we all know what we’re looking at.”

Lynette Howell Taylor, producer and president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, said she was encouraged to hear that human-created storytelling remains the focus of every conversation about technology. “No matter who you’re talking to, they come back to the power of storytelling. They continue to say it’s about human storytelling.”

Macron’s full-throated defense of protecting cultural distinctions also reverberated through discussions about local production, artists’ rights and freedom of expression.

Metropolitan FilmExport co-founder and president Victor Hadida said “placing culture at the center of all our concerns is a huge step” because culture lies “at the heart of our societies — and indeed, of our very conception of democracy.” He pointed out the summit’s focus on independent production, movie theaters, distribution, cultural heritage and education, while pointing to the economic case for supporting culture as well. “Culture itself is becoming a driver of growth,” Hadida said.

Anonymous Content’s Walker likewise said one of the messages he was taking away was “the importance of elevating and exalting and rewarding artists and standing with them,” particularly amid what he described as growing authoritarianism around the world and threats to artists.

Moroccan filmmaker and producer Nabil Ayouch struck an even more urgent note, citing his concern about the state of democracies and the erosion of freedom of expression. “That’s why we absolutely must be very vigilant about the need to strengthen the circulation of creative works. When we consider younger generations, media literacy, and just how important it is for young people to have very open minds about art given the state of the world, and in light of the major challenges that lie ahead,” he said, before adding, “We must encourage films to travel by all possible means, including through cinemas.”

Stéphane Sitbon-Gomez, France Télévisions head of channels and programming, meanwhile, saw the summit as evidence that France’s recent efforts to bring together global alliances around cultural and creative industry policies is gaining traction with other countries.

“The Americans are involved. That’s a real success for the French government,” Sitbon-Gomez said. “I remember a few years ago when we weren’t even on the radar.” The executive pointed to France’s audiovisual tax credit and France 2030 investment plan as part of a strategy that had helped make the country a stronger production hub. “I think we have a French industry on the rise, one that’s capable of exporting its products, and this is recognized by international players,” he said.

Sitbon-Gomez’s point about American involvement carries more historical weight than it might first appear. The last time France tried to convene the world’s film industry with comparable ambition was almost exactly a century earlier, in the autumn of 1926, when the Congrès international du cinématographe met in Paris. The event is remembered in industry lore for Hollywood’s chilly response to France’s initiative. At the time, which was also a moment of upheaval for filmdom as talking pictures replaced silent films as the norm for high-end films, American players kept their distance rather than cede ground to the French on leading the film business. That the biggest names in American film and streaming instead made the trip to the south of France for this summit says something about how much the balance of power, and America’s stake in a multilateral conversation about the industry’s future, has shifted.

The question of how locally rooted films and programs can travel internationally produced some of the summit’s most concrete conversations.

Sang-Hyun Yoon, CEO of Korea’s CJ ENM, said he met with executives from Canal Plus and France Télévisions about bringing more French content to Korean audiences and more Korean programming to France. “It is difficult to build meaningful global collaboration through the power of content alone,” Sang-Hyun Yoon said. “We also need stronger collaboration among local platforms. If local platforms can work together in this way, I believe that these partnerships between platforms will become another very important element in taking content across borders and accelerating its globalization.”

The debate around theatrical and streaming distribution also surfaced throughout the day.

Exhibitors in France are for the most part opposed to collaborating with streaming services due to the country’s strict windowing rules, but Laure de Boissard, Pathé Cinémas’ managing director, said French cinemas could find opportunities to work with platforms on selected films, pointing to titles designed for the large screen. She cited Netflix’s upcoming “Narnia,” which was shot for IMAX, as an example of a film that could potentially have a short special theatrical release in France without delaying its streaming debut. But she said Netflix appears “to be closed off by principle to discussion.” “I find that a bit of a shame,” she added.

De Boissard was also cautious about the IRIS initiative aimed at art house cinemas. As Pathé is a vertically-integrated French group, she wondered if it would still qualify as independent circuit. “What does ‘independent’ actually mean?” she asked. “Especially since no one around the world has the same definition. There are very different systems. There’s already a lot of inequality. We shouldn’t let this exacerbate it.”

For Cinema United head Michael O’Leary, meanwhile, theatrical exhibition is entering what he described as an “opportunity phase.” “For the first time in a number of years, the industry is on its front foot,” said O’Leary. “I visit a lot of small, one-screen theaters in rural areas, and the technology is the theater owner standing in the lobby when people come in and talking to them about how their summers are going, how their mother’s doing,” he said.

Andy Gordon, chief strategy officer and chief operating officer for Paramount Skydance, said what distinguished the summit was Macron’s insistence on what should happen next. “I thought it accomplished what President Macron was after. I thought it opened a lot of conversation,” Gordon said. “And as always, he ends every discussion with a follow-up plan, which is unique and special.”

Frémaux, meanwhile, said the gathering shouldn’t be viewed as an end in itself. “The best outcome for this day is not to forget this day,” Frémaux said. “And in one month, two months, one year, to remain faithful to what we all said, and think about it, in order to be ready for the future and for this summit to have a legacy.”

Yet, the test now is whether the momentum can outlast Macron’s presidency. He is set to leave office in May, and the far-right Rassemblement National — a party with little enthusiasm for culture — is leading in polls ahead of the 2027 election. But for now, organizers have at least secured a marker of continuity — a second Lumière Summit is slated to take place in Greece next year, a first sign that the initiative is intended to survive beyond a single event, and beyond Macron himself.

Naman Ramachandran contributed to this report.

title: Oscars: Singapore Selects Anthony Chen’s ‘We Are All Strangers’ for International Feature Race
summary: “We Are All Strangers,” written and directed by Anthony Chen, has been selected as Singapore’s official entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) said. The pick was made by a Selection Committee drawn from eligible members of the Singapore Film Commission Advisory Committee (SFCAC). Set […]
content:
“We Are All Strangers,” written and directed by Anthony Chen, has been selected as Singapore‘s official entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) said.

The pick was made by a Selection Committee drawn from eligible members of the Singapore Film Commission Advisory Committee (SFCAC).

Set in contemporary Singapore, the film centers on family relationships and unexpected life changes. It stars Chen’s frequent collaborators Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler, with Andi Lim and Regene Lim rounding out the cast. Earlier this year, it became the first Singaporean film selected for the main competition at the Berlin Film Festival in the festival’s 76-year history, competing against 21 other international films for the Golden Bear.

“We Are All Strangers” completes Chen’s Growing Up trilogy, which began with “Ilo Ilo” in 2013 and continued with “Wet Season” in 2019. The two earlier films have collectively won more than 50 international accolades, including 12 Golden Horse nominations and five Golden Horse Awards, along with “Ilo Ilo”‘s Caméra d’Or win at Cannes. Both films previously served as Singapore’s Oscars entries, at the 86th and 93rd Academy Awards respectively.

Popular on Variety

Produced by Chen’s Giraffe Pictures and supported by IMDA, “We Are All Strangers” opened in Singapore cinemas in August and is rolling out progressively across international markets. Paradise City Sales is handling world sales. Film Movement holds North American distribution rights, and the film is currently screening at the Toronto Film Festival, marking its debut on the continent.

Yvonne Tang, assistant chief executive at IMDA’s Media Industry Group, said, “After careful deliberation by the selection committee, we are proud to present ‘We Are All Strangers’ as Singapore’s official entry to the 99th Academy Awards. Anthony has a remarkable ability to tell stories that are deeply rooted in Singapore while resonating with audiences around the world. We’re excited to celebrate this latest milestone with Anthony, whose talent, dedication, and belief have driven the trilogy over the past 10 years. We also hope Singaporeans watch and support this film.”

Chen said it meant a great deal to have the film picked to close out a project he has poured a decade into, and that watching every installment of the trilogy go on to represent Singapore has been a defining achievement for everyone who helped make them. “These stories belong to Singapore, and presenting this final chapter of the trilogy on the global stage is a privilege for me as a filmmaker,” he said.

title: Charli xcx Announces U.K. and Europe ‘Music, Fashion, Film’ Tour Dates, With Audrey Hobert Opening
summary: Charli xcx is bringing the “Music, Fashion, Film” tour overseas. The avant-garde pop star has announced six U.K. and Europe dates in February 2027, including in Dublin, Ireland; Glasgow, Scotland; Manchester, England; London, England; Amsterdam, The Netherlands; and Paris, France. “Sue Me” and “Bowling Alley” singer Audrey Hobert will open for all dates. Charli is […]
content:
Charli xcx is bringing the “Music, Fashion, Film” tour overseas.

The avant-garde pop star has announced six U.K. and Europe dates in February 2027, including in Dublin, Ireland; Glasgow, Scotland; Manchester, England; London, England; Amsterdam, The Netherlands; and Paris, France. “Sue Me” and “Bowling Alley” singer Audrey Hobert will open for all dates.

Charli is about to kick off the tour for her latest album — which saw her ditch her signature autotune and dance beats for something a bit more rock ‘n’ roll — in the U.S. and Canada. She plays Philadelphia on Friday night and then arrives in Brooklyn for two shows, hitting Toronto, Boston, Washington D.C., Atlanta, San Diego, Los Angeles (for two shows), Glendale and Las Vegas.

The sign-up for presale access is live now through Sept. 15 on Charli’s website, with artist pre-sale tickets going live on Sept. 16 at 11 a.m. BST/12 p.m. CET. General on-sale begins Sept. 18 at 9 a.m. BST/10 a.m. CET.

Popular on Variety

“Music, Fashion, Film” was critically acclaimed, with Variety‘s Jem Aswad calling the album a “sonic palette cleanser to launch the post-‘Brat’ era in earnest — familiar but sufficiently distanced from the past, leaving her free to go basically anywhere she wants in her next chapter.”

See all of Charli’s U.K. and Europe tour dates, as well as their venues, below.

Feb. 13 — Dublin, Ireland at 3Arena

Feb. 15 — Glasgow, U.K. at OVO Hyrdo

Feb. 17 — Manchester, U.K. at Co-Op Live

Feb. 19 — London, U.K. at the O2

Feb. 22 — Amsterdam, The Netherlands at Ziggo Dome

Feb. 24 — Paris, France at Accor Arena

title: San Sebastian Competition Title ‘Border’ Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Paris-based international sales company Reel Suspects has boarded worldwide sales on Chinese filmmaker Ah Biao’s feature debut “Border” (“Bian Jing”), which will world premiere in the official selection of the San Sebastián Film Festival, where it competes for the Golden Shell. The cast includes Zheyan Li, Feng Qi, Sanming Han, Gang Zheng and Tao Guo, […]
content:
Paris-based international sales company Reel Suspects has boarded worldwide sales on Chinese filmmaker Ah Biao’s feature debut “Border” (“Bian Jing”), which will world premiere in the official selection of the San Sebastián Film Festival, where it competes for the Golden Shell.

The cast includes Zheyan Li, Feng Qi, Sanming Han, Gang Zheng and Tao Guo, in a Hong Kong-U.S.-South Korea-Japan co-production.

The story centers on an impoverished young miner living a muted existence in a remote town where emotional reticence is the norm among men. A mysterious young woman disrupts his routine, awakening a curiosity he thought long dormant. Drawn to follow her into unfamiliar territory, he abandons the familiar comforts of his old life, not realizing she is hiding something about who she really is.

Popular on Variety

“We’re thrilled to bring ‘Border’ to audiences at San Sebastián and to see the film presented in official competition,” said Matteo Lovadina, Reel Suspects CEO. “Ah Biao is a remarkable new voice with a distinctive cinematic vision, and we believe this is the beginning of a very exciting journey for him. He is undoubtedly a filmmaker to watch, and we’re delighted to be introducing his work to international audiences at such an important moment in his career. ‘Border’ presents a distinctive cinematic aesthetic rooted in Eastern experience. Through image, sound, performance and space, it draws on the language of cinema itself to explore the existential struggles of human experience. Its strikingly fresh audiovisual expression reveals another dimension of contemporary Chinese-language cinema.”

Ah Biao, who was born in Shanxi, China, and is now based in Bangkok, works as a director, screenwriter and cinematographer. “Border” is his first feature, placing him in San Sebastián’s main competition lineup alongside veteran directors Mike Leigh, Pablo Larraín, Nicole Garcia and Yeşim Ustaoğlu.

Borderless Films produced “Border,” with Jenny Man Wu as producer alongside fellow producers Lili Tong, Tyler Hill and Xue Ma. “For us, bringing a fully independently produced first feature to San Sebastián’s official competition is especially meaningful,” said producer Jenny Man Wu. “The film was carried forward by a deeply committed team who believed in Ah Biao’s vision and found ways to sustain it at every stage of its production.”

The film also figures among 24 titles in the running for this year’s Sebastiane Award, an honor Basque LGBTIQA+ association Gehitu gives to the film judged the strongest portrayal of queer lives and experiences.

Lovadina launched Reel Suspects in 2005 as a Paris-based boutique sales outfit specializing in independent film and up-and-coming directors, building an international reputation for elevated-genre fare alongside a roster of acclaimed first features and established names. The company’s current slate also includes Israel Cárdenas and Laura Amelia Guzmán’s “Interior Apartement Dia” and Zoe Berriatúa’s “Buffet Libre.”

title: French TV Disruptor Jeremy Zag Talks Building ‘Miraculous’ Universe, Plans For A Live-Action Series & Latest On Katy Perry Animated Movie ‘Melody’
summary: Fans of Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir can expect a live-action version of the animated series, its co-creator Jeremy Zag has said. Meanwhile, his studio, Zag Entertainment, is also making headway on Melody, an animated feature film with Katy Perry. Zag co-created French animated show Miraculous through Zag. He was feted as Deadline’s […]
content:
Fans of Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug & Cat Noir can expect a live-action version of the animated series, its co-creator Jeremy Zag has said. Meanwhile, his studio, Zag Entertainment, is also making headway on Melody, an animated feature film with Katy Perry.

Zag co-created French animated show Miraculous through Zag. He was feted as Deadline’s 2026 French TV Disruptor this week at Unifrance’s Rendez-Vous market, recognizing his work creating animated series and movies that have travelled the world.

He received the accolade in the historic surroundings of the Montivilliers Abbey in Normandy, France. Ahead of being presented with the award, the animation boss sat down with Deadline to talk about his work, and tease some of what’s next.

Zag explained how with Miraculous and other work he always sets out to create a whole universe, spanning TV and film as well as games and merch. “I really believe in the power of a brand, and I believe that from a little drawing, you can create a giant franchise,” he said.

Zag decamped to L.A. to build Miraculous into a global franchise. He took creative inspiration from U.S. superhero culture, but also learned some American business smarts to create a universe of characters. The Zag team has a raft of new superheroes ready to join Ladybug, and Zag also teased a live-action Miraculous series.

“We’re going to keep the DNA of what people love about Miraculous,” Zag said about the project. “We are moving forward now. The team is here, the producers are here, the writers are here.”

Chloé LECLERCQ

Giving Deadline the latest on Melody with Katy Perry, Zag told us things are moving forward.

“Katy is very involved in the movie; she’s playing a main character, she’s working on the songs, and she’s also working on the story,” he said. “We are incredibly happy because we are also working with Gary Trousdale, the director of Beauty and the Beast.”

He added: “It’s about believing in yourself. It’s a little girl who wants to sing, but she doesn’t believe in herself.”

Zag talks about creating an animation legacy. “My dream is to leave behind me some franchises that will help the new generation to believe in themselves… and obviously to create crossovers between them all,” he said. “The final dream is to create a Zag World.”

Check out the video for more on all the above and to see why Zag earned the Disruptor tag.

title: BBC Stokes Anger By Curbing Cab Rides For Night Shift Workers… As Senior Managers Spend $17,000 On Taxis In Three Months
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The BBC has sparked unrest among staff with plans to slash taxi usage for night shift workers. Bosses at the UK broadcaster want to change the qualifying time for expensable cab fares, meaning employees would have to leave work 30 minutes later or start 30 minutes earlier for the BBC to foot the bill […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The BBC has sparked unrest among staff with plans to slash taxi usage for night shift workers.

Bosses at the UK broadcaster want to change the qualifying time for expensable cab fares, meaning employees would have to leave work 30 minutes later or start 30 minutes earlier for the BBC to foot the bill for a car journey.

Bectu and the National Union of Journalists are fighting the taxi changes, which the BBC has put forward as part of its 2027 pay offer. The BBC’s improved offer of a basic 1.5% pay rise was rejected by the unions, with further talks set to take place over the coming weeks as the spectre of industrial action looms.

BBC employees are unhappy about the below-inflation pay rise, and the cab curbs have only exacerbated unease. BBC journalists, who contribute to 24-hour news coverage, are particularly exercised about the proposals, with one insider describing them as “unreasonable.”

Watch on Deadline

Another accused the corporation of “pissing about around the edges” as it seeks to save £500 million ($674 million) over the coming years. Critics have also raised concerns about the safety of women who need to travel to and from work at night time.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster is “looking at all our operating costs” as it seeks to make savings. They added: “The safety of our staff remains paramount, and the changes have been designed to bring the BBC more in line with others in the industry and reflect the greater availability of public transport, particularly in London.”

The cab curbs come as the BBC recently published senior management expense claims for the first quarter of its 2025/26 financial year. The BBC’s highest-paid staff claimed more than £13,000 ($17,600) on taxi journeys in the three months from April to June 2025. This was up 6% on the same period in 2024, according to an analysis by Deadline.

The expense claims were made before the BBC introduced new cost control measures in April 2026, cracking down on travel costs and other outgoings, including attending conferences, awards, and events. A spokesperson said the BBC has “strict guidelines” for taxi usage, which apply to all staff.

BBC director general Matt Brittin told staff this week that he was unimpressed by some of the expense claims, which pre-dated his arrival. “When I look at it, there are some things there that don’t make any sense to me, and I wouldn’t want to happen under my watch,” he said. “We have to spend our money very carefully, and I think we’re all very conscious of that.”

Brittin added that pay talks had been a “pretty difficult process for everyone” and he acknowledged that strike action was a possibility. Any industrial action would be subject to a ballot of union members.

title: Pierce Brosnan Says Tom Hardy ‘MobLand’ Feud Was “Storm In A Teacup”
summary: Pierce Brosnan has said that it is all happy families on the set of Paramount+’s MobLand. At the Season 2 premiere in London, Brosnan was asked about the behind-the-scenes drama involving Tom Hardy, who reportedly clashed with showrunner Jez Butterworth and had timekeeping issues on set. “Oh my God, it was a storm in a […]
content:
Pierce Brosnan has said that it is all happy families on the set of Paramount+’s MobLand.

At the Season 2 premiere in London, Brosnan was asked about the behind-the-scenes drama involving Tom Hardy, who reportedly clashed with showrunner Jez Butterworth and had timekeeping issues on set.

“Oh my God, it was a storm in a teacup, really,” the James Bond star told Press Association. “I love the dude. I love Tom Hardy. I’m a massive fan of the man’s work. Truly.

“We are rock solid as a company, as a family. Everyone shows up for work, and everybody’s just there on the spot. It moves very fast so it’s not like we go out and socialise and go to the pub or anything like that.”

Hardy added that it was a “privilege” to work with Brosnan and Helen Mirren. “In many aspects, of course, I look up to them. Coming up, these are actors that came before me,” he told PA.

Watch on Deadline

“So to be able to work with them is a privilege, but also to be able to enjoy them, watching them spread their wings with their range now as well, and play against their type in some aspects, and really enjoy that is a beautiful thing to watch as a human being.”

Mirren also joined the chorus. “The relationships are amazing. Obviously, Pierce and I have an extraordinary chemistry on-screen and off-screen. We’re very, very fond of each other. We respect each other enormously,” she said.

The actors are set to be reunited in Season 3, which was confirmed by Paramount earlier this month after a meeting in London between Hardy, Butterworth and series executive producer David C. Glasser, where they hashed things out

In Season 2 of MobLand, produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios, the Harrigans struggle to show a unified front as rising rivals threaten their fractured criminal empire – and Harry Da Souza (Hardy), their street-smart and formidable ‘fixer,’ must walk a dangerous tightrope when tensions within the family intensify. As violence spills into every corner of their lives, loyalties snap, safety proves temporary, and the battle for power leaves no room for mercy.

Alongside Hardy, Brosnan and Mirren, Season 2 also stars Paddy Considine, Joanne Froggatt, Lara Pulver, Anson Boon, Mandeep Dhillon, Jasmine Jobson, Teddie Allen, Emmett J. Scanlan, Johnny Flynn, Ophelia Lovibond, Janet McTeer, and Toby Jones.

MobLand is executive produced by Glasser, Ritchie, Butterworth, Hardy, Ivan Atkinson, Dean Baker, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari and Keith Cox.

Following Season 2’s September 18 premiere on Paramount+, new episodes from MobLand‘s ten-episode second season will be available to stream weekly on Fridays, culminating in the season finale on November 20

title: Cricket Legend Virender Sehwag To Host ‘Rise And Fall’ Season 2 For Prime Video
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Indian cricket legend Virender Sehwag is swapping the bat and pads for a suit and microphone. The sporting superstar, known as the Sultan of Multan, has been unveiled as host for Season 2 of Rise and Fall, Prime Video India’s reality series to replace Ashnee Grover. This marks the first time he’ll front a […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Indian cricket legend Virender Sehwag is swapping the bat and pads for a suit and microphone.

The sporting superstar, known as the Sultan of Multan, has been unveiled as host for Season 2 of Rise and Fall, Prime Video India’s reality series to replace Ashnee Grover. This marks the first time he’ll front a streaming TV show.

Sehwag’s role was revealed in a trailer that you can watch above. The 1-minute 44-second trailer sees him playing versions of Albert Einstein, a doctor, a teacher and a karate yellow belt in a series of vignettes before a skyscraper building flashes on screen and the retired batsman switches to a sharp suit. “In Rise and Fall, the game of up and down is going to be very twisted,” he says to camera.

Sehwag has long been eyed as an on-screen presence thanks to his sharp wit and straight-talking style. He retired from cricket in 2015 after a glittering career in which he became one of India’s most destructive opening batsmen and the country’s vice-captain for large portions of his international career.

Watch on Deadline

Numerous Indian cricketers have taken the TV pathway as their careers wound down with former Test team captain Rohit Sharma recently announcing a show, Family Full House, for Sony Entertainment Television and the likes of Ajay Jadeja and Shikhar Dhawan also fronting shows. Sourav Ganguly is the current presenter of Bigg Boss Bangla, the Bengali-language version of Big Brother, which kicked off its most recent season on August 30.

Rise and Fall Season 2 was announced in March after the first run became a huge hit for Amazon’s MX Player, which has since been subsumed into Prime Video. The show is a remake of the Studio Lambert format for UK network Channel 4, though that version was cancelled after one season due to low ratings. The Indian show, from Banijay Asia, has been the breakout for the format.

Set across the contrasting worlds of a penthouse and the basement in the same highrise building, the game brings together 15 celebrities, who are divided into two groups, the Rulers and the Workers. While the Rulers enjoy the privileges of the penthouse, the Workers navigate the realities of the basement. Should the Rulers. Over the course of challenges, members of the Workers are able to replace Rulers in the penthouse, changing their fortunes and the tide of the game.

“The love and excitement audiences showed for Rise and Fall in its first season gave us the perfect reason to take this unique power game forward,” said Amogh Dusad, Director and Head of AVOD Content, Prime Video India. “Season 2 brings a fresh set of personalities into a format where power is always in motion, and every decision carries a consequence.

“With Virender Sehwag stepping in as host, we’re bringing a whole new energy to the show; his wit, spontaneity, and fearless personality make him an exciting fit for the game. We’re excited for audiences to experience the drama, strategy and entertainment in Rise and Fall Season 2, and watch it on Prime Video for free.”

Sehwag compared the gameplay to a professional match. “Cricket has taught me one thing – no match is won before the final ball, and Rise and Fall Season 2 takes that unpredictability to another level,” he said. “As a host, what excites me about this game is that there are no easy wins and no fixed positions. The biggest challenge isn’t just getting to the top but knowing how to stay there. You have to know when to attack, when to defend, and, most importantly, when to read the game before it reads you.”

Deepak Dhar, Founder and Group CEO of Banijay Asia, said the “overwhelming response that Rise and Fall received in its debut season reaffirmed the strength of its unique premise, where power, strategy and human behaviour come together to create an unpredictable game.”

No launch date or contestant casting as been revealed yet, but the show will stream free on Prime Video and the MX Player Android app, which is still available under a a new identity – MX Player by Prime Video.

content:
The 2026 Toronto Film Festival kicked off Thursday, September 10, and features a slew of world premieres including the official opening-night film Being Heumann, Oscar winner Siân Heder‘s follow-up to her Best Picture winner CODA. The event’s 51st edition features 10 days of premieres, gala presentations and more as the third leg of the fall festival tour (along with Venice and Telluride) that helps set the agenda for awards season.

Among the fest’s world premieres are the latest from such filmmakers as Green Book double Oscar winner Peter Farrelly (I Play Rocky), Shakespeare in Love Oscar nominee John Madden (Onwards & Sideways), Chris Rock (Misty Green) and Anton Corbijn (A Talent for Murder).

TIFF also will feature the world debuts of Prima Facie, from British director Susanna White starring three-time Oscar nominee Cynthia Erivo, and The Assassin(s) from Korean filmmaker Hur Jin-ho, whose A Normal Family played Toronto in 2023.

RELATED: TIFF Centrepiece To Showcase 54 Features With Kamila Andini’s ‘Four Seasons In Java’ & Avi Nesher’s ‘Our Loves’ Among World Premieres

Among others screenings are Friends star Courteney Cox directing debut Evil Genius, Tim Blake Nelson’s prison thriller The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd, One Battle After Another breakout Chase Infiniti’s The Julia Set and director Rebel Wilson’s The Deb follow-up Girl Group.

Scroll below to read about Deadline’s reviews out of TIFF 2026, and click on the link to read the full versions. Keep checking back as we add more.
