title: Toronto Premiere of ‘Le Faux Soir’ Crowns Great Year for Walloon Cinema, Built on Belgian Region’s Creative Freedom, Can Do Attitude
summary: It is no wonder Belgian cinema has risen internationally in recent years. Cinema is, after all, a language, and Belgian filmmakers come from a country built on the need to understand language as a bridge—between its regions, its people, and its idioms. The country has three official languages—Dutch, French and German—and is divided both regionally […]
content:
It is no wonder Belgian cinema has risen internationally in recent years. Cinema is, after all, a language, and Belgian filmmakers come from a country built on the need to understand language as a bridge—between its regions, its people, and its idioms. The country has three official languages—Dutch, French and German—and is divided both regionally and culturally into three highly autonomous regions: Flanders, in the north; Wallonia, in the south; and the Brussels-Capital Region, right in the middle.

The Walloon region has experienced a great year in cinema, set to be crowned by the world premiere of Michaël R. Roskam’s “Le Faux Soir” at the Toronto International Film Festival—with the film then heading to San Sebastián in a prominent slot as the festival’s closing gala. The latest by the renowned “Bullhead” director chronicles the real-life story of how the Belgian resistance pulled off an almost unfathomable feat: at the height of the Nazi occupation of the country in 1943, a resistance group organized a fake edition of Le Soir, the country’s largest newspaper, appropriated by the Germans as a propaganda machine.

Popular on Variety

The film marks a homecoming for Roskam after working on Hollywood projects over the last few years. The director says the film led him to reflect how Belgians are often “too modest about their own history.”

“There is something deeply Belgian in its combination of courage, restraint, pacifism and humor: an ability to resist without losing a certain sense of irony or self-awareness,” continued the director. “That spirit is central to the people behind ‘Le Faux Soir,’ but it also feels very present in Belgian history—and, in some ways, in Belgium today. It has given me a renewed sense of pride in where I come from.”

It is extra special to have such a high-profile Toronto this year, given that 2026 marks the 40th anniversary of Wallonie-Bruxelles Images (WBImages), the agency for the international promotion of film and audiovisual works from the Fédération Wallonie-Bruxelles. Speaking with Variety from a busy Venice, where the agency presented Ann Sirot and Raphaël Balboni’s “Diane in the Loop,” WBImages director Hervé Le Phuez says his team can feel “genuinely proud of the work accomplished” by the agency in the last four decades.

“What makes us particularly happy is to see how well and how widely our films travel internationally, and how many of our producers and other film professionals are now working across borders,” he adds, noting recent co-productions such as “A Man of His Time” and “Forever Your Maternal Animal.” “The number of international co-productions involving Wallonia-Brussels producers every year is probably one of the best indicators of this strong international presence.”

Le Phuez clarifies that both WBImages and the Film and Audiovisual Center of the Wallonia-Brussels Federation are responsible for supporting audiovisual production at the Communities in Belgium level. “Rather than looking at filmmakers from one particular region, we are interested in creators who contribute to what we could call a ‘Belgian attitude’ in terms of characters, storytelling, cinematographic language, and the way they look at the world.”

“Although these films are Belgian, they often carry the voices of talents coming from very different regions, countries, cultures and linguistic backgrounds,” he notes. “This openness and our ability to welcome filmmakers from different backgrounds is one of the strengths of Belgian cinema [and] one of the reasons why [it] remains so diverse, dynamic and internationally relevant.”

This is a truth evident in the Walloon presence in Toronto, spearheaded by “Le Faux Soir” and Lukas Dhont’s Cannes-winning queer war drama “Coward.” Both films were made in collaboration between Flanders and Wallonia, with “Le Faux Soir” being a majority Walloon production and “Coward” a majority Flemish one.

Ronni Shalev, whose short film “2:Love” is also world premiering in Toronto, adds to this line of thought from an immigrant perspective. “As an immigrant to Belgium, I was pretty blown away by the financial support that is offered to beginner auteurs who have a strong artistic vision,” he says.

“I was amazed by the freedom given to auteurs,” he adds. “I was encouraged to propose a compelling artistic proposal and to bring it to life, with a strong emphasis on materiality and originality. In animation, this often translates to longer and more expensive productions, but I felt that I was being encouraged.”

Shalev believes this creative freedom and encouragement ties “into a larger Walloon ethic of a do-it-yourself and can-do-istic approach to art.” “People tend to decide on a project here, however grandiose, and figure out how to make it happen as they go along. I think that this approach lends a hand to having very unique and idiosyncratic voices in cinema—both on a narrative and a visual level.”

Sameh Alaa and Robin Vouters’s short film “The Day I Smoked a Cigarette With My Father” is also world premiering at TIFF, and producer Delphine Duez of Belgium’s White Boat Pictures mirrors Shalev’s thoughts. “There is a very particular energy in Walloon and Belgian cinema today,” she says. “Young filmmakers are not necessarily trying to reproduce what has already been done. They are taking risks, blending genres, working with materiality, the body and the intimate, and inventing their own cinematic languages.”

Looking at the crop of films coming out of Wallonia and Belgium more widely, Roskam says it is “encouraging” to see the “range of voices currently at work.” “New generations are emerging, while established filmmakers continue to make ambitious work. The number and diversity of films being developed across the country is impressive.”

“Many completely independent films are made and create a strong feeling of possibility,” Shalev adds. “This is crucially made possible by the ‘statut d’artiste,’ a social status given to artists that ensures they are paid a salary by social security during the weeks in the year when they don’t have a work contract. A welfare state utopia, in effect. These benefits and opportunities are currently under threat of being dismantled and erased by Belgium’s current right-wing government. But so long as they exist, they make the local cinema scene rich with ideas and experimentation.”

Duez adds that, while Belgium is recognized for the quality of its crews, “what strikes us most is the human dimension of the industry.” “People are willing to give their time, their talent and their experience to a project—and, importantly, to the next generation.”

“Even very experienced and senior professionals are often ready to put themselves at the service of a young filmmaker when they feel that the project has that essential spark,” she adds. “There is less of a rigid industrial hierarchy. People meet each other more easily, personalities emerge, and collaboration can remain very direct.”

Le Phuez concurs, emphasizing Belgium’s “virtuous circle” of production and financing. “We have three different levels of public competence and, consequently, three different support schemes for cinema, which can be combined and allow filmmakers to put together significant financing for their films.” Still, the agency director believes the “greatest strength” of their creators is an “ability to preserve their originality despite the growing uniformization of the global world.”

“They manage to remain true to their own voices while reaching audiences internationally,” he says. “And we think that is something really valuable.”

title: Catherine Deneuve on Playing a ‘Punk Fairy Godmother’ in Léa Domenach’s Venice-Bound ‘A Man’s Skin,’ a Feminist Medieval Musical (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Catherine Deneuve needed little convincing to play a “punk fairy godmother” in Léa Domenach’s “Peau d’Homme” (“A Man’s Skin“) the Venice-premiering medieval musical that reunites the famed French actor and up-and-coming director three years after “Bernadette.” “A punk fairy godmother — first of all, that idea alone would have been enough,” Deneuve told Variety in […]
content:
Catherine Deneuve needed little convincing to play a “punk fairy godmother” in Léa Domenach’s “Peau d’Homme” (“A Man’s Skin“) the Venice-premiering medieval musical that reunites the famed French actor and up-and-coming director three years after “Bernadette.”

“A punk fairy godmother — first of all, that idea alone would have been enough,” Deneuve told Variety in a phone interview alongside Domenach a few days before the Lido premiere. “I thought the script, the characters, the situations — it was like a musical, and I really liked that. It’s very original and it’s fun.”

Set in the 15th century, “A Man’s Skin” follows Blanche, a young woman who is given a magical “man’s skin” that allows her to become Léonard and discover freedoms, power and sexuality largely denied to her as a woman.

Popular on Variety

“A Man’s Skin” is adapted from Hubert and Zanzim’s graphic novel of the same name. Producers Antoine Rein and Fabrice Goldstein at Karé Productions acquired the rights and brought the project to Domenach, who co-wrote the adaptation with Clemence Dargent. Alain Attal’s Trésor Films, one of France’s top producers, then joined Rein and Goldstein. Playtime is handling international sales, while Diaphana Distribution will release the film in France. The film is closing Venice’s Giornate degli Autori out of competition.

Domenach said she was drawn to the project but wanted to make it more playful. “The comic book is great, but I thought it had a somewhat tame side to it,” Domenach said. “I told the producers: ‘I’m adapting the comic book because I like the underlying message, but I’ll turn it into a comedy to bring it to life.’”

“I really wanted to create a sort of bubble of joy to address some pretty serious issues — religious fanaticism, homophobia, sexism — which are, after all, fundamental issues, and even the drought; the kingdom is suffering from a drought,” she continued. “We see what’s happening today. Everything has to resonate a bit with our times, but in a lighthearted way so that it reaches as many people as possible, too.”

Some of the characters in the film are directly inspired by real-life politicians. Tancrède, played by Eddy de Pretto, is a religious zealot whom Domenach openly describes as a Trump-like figure.

“That’s just part of the comedy. The parallels have to be explicit to make people laugh; otherwise, we miss our mark a bit. I think Tancrède is Trump — but he represents all those political figures who are initially seen as buffoons and who, over time, come to be taken seriously.”

“There are plenty of them,” she said. “There’s Trump, but not just him. There’s the Argentine president, there’s Jordan Bardella. There was a time when there was Berlusconi. Berlusconi was someone no one took seriously, and yet he governed Italy. It’s Trump today, but there have been others in the past, and there will be others tomorrow.”

When Bardella’s name came up, Deneuve interjected: “He’s grotesque!” Bardella is the 30-year-old deputy of Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party which is currently leading polls in the 2027 presidential election. And when Domenach said there would likely be more such figures in the future, Deneuve shot back: “I hope not!”

That political undercurrent dovetails with the film’s feminism that Domenach sees as a direct continuation of “Bernadette,” in which Deneuve played the wife of former French President Jacques Chirac, a fierce and opinionated first lady. The movie (whose English title is “The President’s Wife”) had a healthy run at the French box office, scoring nearly 900K admissions, sold to major territories around the world and earned a Cesar nomination for best first film.

“There’s a kind of continuity. It’s funny — even when you think about the two characters, Bernadette and Blanche. What I find interesting is that these two women were never really destined to step out of their comfort zones, take control, or forge ahead. They were raised to lead somewhat ‘perfect’ lives, and then, all of a sudden, they break the mold, much to our delight, in a way,“ she said.

“They share a bit of that in common. And, indeed, both films are very feminist and proudly so,” she continued.

Domenach said one of the most significant departures from the graphic novel was shifting the center of gravity toward the female characters. “In the comic book, the main character is a man, it’s Léonard. But with the adaptation, we really wanted the women to truly take up all the space they need.”

She said she deliberately brought together women from different generations and with different relationships to feminism.

Deneuve herself resisted the idea of being easily categorized. “I really like women, but I’m not a die-hard feminist,” she admitted.

For Domenach, that difference is precisely what makes the film’s perspective more compelling.

“That doesn’t stop us from having a debate, working together, and finding common ground on fundamental issues,” she said, “such as sexism, or what a man can do versus what a woman can do.”

The filmmaker said the movie’s themes feel especially relevant in a moment when progress on gender and LGBTQ rights appears uneven.

“On the issue of gender, things are moving forward, but at the same time, more and more people are voting for the far right. Nationalism is on the rise. Things are becoming more radical on both sides,” she said.

“There are also many young gay people getting beaten up on the street,” she continued. “It feels like things are moving forward in some ways, but in other ways, it feels like we’re taking a big step backward. I feel like we’re making gains in some areas and losing ground in others.”

While it tackles serious topics, “A Man’s Skin” is also unapologetically lighthearted. Music and dancing run throughout the film, something Deneuve said immediately appealed to her. She’s played in several iconic musicals throughout her career, notably Jacques Demy’s films , from “The Young Girls of Rochefort” to “The Umbrellas of Cherbourg” and “Pean d’âne,” but also in Francois Ozon’s “8 Women” and several films directed by Christophe Honoré, notably “Beloved.”

“It’s wonderful when you get the chance to sing in a movie. I mean, when a movie is a musical, there’s something else added to the script beyond the songs. It’s a whole other world when it’s a musical. It really is a whole other world. I really enjoyed it.”

Deneuve said has a long personal relationship with singing that goes well beyond her screen work. “I’ve always sung — in my daily life, with my family, in the car, with my sisters and my father,” she said. “There were always songs and poems — ones I still remember from when I was a child. It’s incredible, actually.”

She recalled one particularly memorable taxi ride, while laughing. “One day, I took a taxi, and when we arrived at our destination, the driver said to me, ‘Only Italian construction workers sing in cars these days.’”

The film also carries echoes of “Peau d’Âne,” as hinted by its French title, and Domenach said that was intentional.

“Since the comic book’s title itself was already a tribute — ‘Peau d’Homme,’ ‘Peau d’Âne’ — I wanted there to be little nods to it,” Domenach said. “It was the first movie I ever saw in a theater.”

Deneuve said she still had fond memories of Demy’s film. “For those who loved ‘Peau d’Âne,’ it’s remained something a little bit magical,” Deneuve said. “I understand very well the idea of revisiting an element from the film in relation to the music, in relation to a song.”

In spite of its high concept and topnotch cast – which also includes Karin Viard, Stefan Crepon and Laurent Stocker — Domenach said “A Man’s Skin” proved difficult to finance.

Her longtime producers Antoine Rein and Fabrice Goldstein, who were behind “Bernadette,” were eventually joined by Alain Attal, whose credits include some of France’s biggest hits, from Gilles Lellouche’s “Beating Hearts” to Guillaume Canet’s “Little White Lies.”

Domenach said the film was initially supposed to be released in France by Warner which had handled “Bernadette” but the distributor has since scaled back on distributing French movies locally.

“So finding a new distributor, and also taking on such an ambitious project involving singing, dancing, and a period film — all while tackling such serious subjects — was a huge gamble,” she continued. “It was very complicated.”

Domenach said the hurdle to finance “A Man’s Skin” reflected how tough the market has become to finance “mid-range films.”

“It’s one of the few countries where you can still make original projects like this, but unfortunately, more and more often on a shoestring budget,” Domenach said of France. “Today, either we manage to make these very big, very expensive films, or it has to be an arthouse film budgeted under €3 million. But I’m part of the mid-range film scene, and that’s very complicated.”

Deneuve jumped in, saying “Mid-range films are the ones that have suffered the most.” The actor revealed that she had recently experienced that difficulty herself.

“I completely agree with her because, personally, I know I had a project that was supposed to happen around the end of the year, but it didn’t come together financially,” she said. “There are a lot of projects that aren’t getting off the ground anymore, and these are the so-called middle-of-the-road films.”

When asked whether attaching her name to a movie was still a decisive factor in getting it made, she pushed back on the idea. “Life in the film industry isn’t like that anymore. You know, I’m very aware of that. For me, it’s no surprise.”

Now, the film arrives in Venice, where Deneuve said she feels particularly at home. She was famously married to Marcello Mastroianni with whom she had a daughter, Chiara Mastroianni, who is also an actor.

“I have mostly good memories,” she said of Italy. “Plus, I’m lucky — I speak Italian fluently. So it’s true that you feel like you’re in a foreign land because Italy is really very different, but even so, I don’t feel out of place since I understand everything and everyone.”

The Venice Film Festival itself has a particular place in Deneuve’s career. She won the Volpi Cup there for “Place Vendôme” in 1998 and returned in 2022 to receive the festival’s Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.

Deneuve arrives on the Lido this year after another characteristically busy stretch. Earlier this year she was back in Cannes competition with Marie Kreutzer’s “Gentle Monster,” opposite Léa Seydoux, after also appearing in Asghar Farhadi’s ensemble drama “Parallel Tales.” She also has Stéphane Demoustier’s “Forty Love” coming up, while “A Man’s Skin” is due to open in France in January 2027.

title: ‘Rojo’ Director Benjamín Naishtat on Awaited Toronto, San Sebastián Title ‘Glaxo,’ the Impunity of Power and Connecting via Genre
summary: “At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Nobel Prize winning author Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks at the beginning of “Conversation at The Cathedral.” In “Glaxo,” one of the most awaited of Latin American films this year, director Benjamín Naishtat charts what he describes as the whole of Argentina’s loss of innocence, which […]
content:
“At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Nobel Prize winning author Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks at the beginning of “Conversation at The Cathedral.”

In “Glaxo,” one of the most awaited of Latin American films this year, director Benjamín Naishtat charts what he describes as the whole of Argentina’s loss of innocence, which again has its origins in 1950s dictatorship and is equally pervasive.

After the lighter turn of co-directing “Puán,” a “deliciously droll” makeover movie, said Variety, in “Glaxo,” which world premieres in Toronto’s Special Presentations, Naishtat returns to the disturbing collective psychology portrait of “Rojo,” charting the impunity of power — a cop, and the Glaxo corporation — and a tale of betrayals in its central coming of age section.

Popular on Variety

Set along three timelines — Florida, outside Buenos Aires, on June 6, 1956, and then Chivilcoy, a town in the sticks also outside the Argentine capital one year later and then in 1984.

Esteban Bigliardi as Flaco in ‘Glaxo’ Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures

In the first, with Argentina under military dictatorship, based on historical facts depicted by Argentine writer Roberto Walsh in a trailblazing example of a non-fiction novel — police commissioner Folcada arrests 12 men listening to a boxing match, and then is leaned on by his boss to make an example of them.

One year later, now a civilian and a wealthy ranch owner, Folcada has moved to Chivilcoy with his stunning wife, Negra Morcada (Lali Espósito, notable), dazzling four teen friends — Miguelito, Verdemann, “Bicho” and Lucio.

“This is the story of a betrayal,” says narrator Miguelito. In fact it’s the story of multiple endemic betrayals driven by the exercise of unaccountable power and the misjudgment of adolescence, under the weight of which four teens’ seemingly “Stand by Me” friendship unravels.

If “Rojo” was a “witheringly provocative examination of temporary moral eclipse becoming permanent moral apocalypse,” as Variety noted, “Glaxo” delivers a broader historical take on the same Argentinean dark ages.

It delivers a pedigree producer package as a production of Brazil’s RT Features (“Paper Tiger,” “I’m Still Here”), produced by Argentina’s Rei Pictures (“Zama,” “The Settlers”). The film is inspired by novel “Glaxo,” from the film’s co-writer, Hernán Ronsino, which was partly inspired in turn by Walsh’s “Operation Masacre.” This deep concern for heritage – historical, literary, cinematographic – is one of the film’s sources of emotion.

Variety talked to Naishtat before the Toronto world premiere of “Glaxo,” after which the film segues for its European bow in main competition at San Sebastián.

Two first questions. At the beginning of the “Conversation in The Cathedral,” Mario Vargas Llosa famously asks: “At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” It seems that to a certain extent Hernán Ronsino and you in “Glaxo” are asking the same question about Argentina. Also Miguelito, the narrator, says “This is the story of a betrayal. It seems to me that this is the story of many betrayals….

Benjamin Naishtat: I think that’s a very good analysis of the film, and basically this reading is obviously connected to Hernán Ronsino’s novel. When I read the novel for the first time, two things struck me. First, its very austere style, almost like an American police crime novel, but also closely related to Argentine writer Rodolfo Walsh, the author of “Operation Massacre,” a book that has a strong connection to “Glaxo.” The film “Glaxo· also has a string connection to “Operation Massacre,” an underground film from 1973 by Jorge Cedrón, a filmmaker who isn’t very well known but who is very important in the mysterious history of Argentine cinema. I wanted to mention that because it’s important. But going back to your point, yes, I think it really is an open question for the audience.

To what extent does “Glaxo” suggest any answers?

Naishtat: I don’t think the film tries to give us an answer but it simply presents us with the question. As an audience member, I’m more interested in leaving with more questions than with simple answers. That’s what we tried to do with this project: generate questions in a historical echo going backwards, but posing possible hypotheses about when Argentina got screwed and also about Argentina’s present. I think we tried to analyze the current state of Argentina from a different angle and from a different perspective.

One possible hypothesis comes in the prologue, set on June 9, 1956, turning on Police Commissioner Folcada, which suggests the terrible impunity of power. The other might be the terribly limited prospects of people like Miguelito living in Chivilcoy, a town outside Buenos Aires, where the two latter parts of the film is set.

Naishtat: The impunity of power is a good point. It relates to your earlier question and is a good starting point in relation to what impunity means in Argentina. In fact, the historical episodes depicted in the prologue — historical episodes that occurred in 1956 — remain unpunished to this day. Those responsible for that massacre never had to pay a price for what they did.

Regarding Miguelito and his life opportunities, I do share your view, but it’s also related to the film being not only a thriller but melodrama and also a coming-of-age story. I personally love the coming-of-age genre. What’s fascinating is that it connects you to an age we’ve all lived through — adolescence — in which love, and even more so, falling in love, has a devastating power over you. Without knowing who we are, we already have the capacity to fall in love in a way that we will never again experience. And that’s dangerous. So I tried to play with those themes a little bit by telling a story about adolescent love.

You’ve mentioned genres. The film plays with their different registers and has multiple echoes from other films.

Naishtat: This is my second collaboration after “Rojo.” with cinematographer Pedro Sotero. “Rojo” was a language exercise in relation to thrillers and television from the ‘70s. “Glaxo” has three different languages in the same film. So we have a prologue, which relates to clandestine Latin American films from the ‘70s, filmed as if it was shot on Super 16mm, with texture, like using only a single lens, and with very precarious shooting and lighting conditions.

Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures

Then we have the main 1950s section, which tries to play with Italian and American melodrama, like films such as “A Place in the Sun” or “Giant” by George Stevens, which were strong points of reference for the images in that section. Then we have the film-noir section set in the 1980s, shot in CinemaScope with anamorphic lenses to generate maximum atmosphere, which honestly, was a lot of fun. We’re both huge cinephiles. Pedro and I love genre cinema, and I think we’re convinced that the future of cinema, if there is one, is a popular future, let’s say within the popular genres — being able to talk to the audience and bring complexity to popular genres. In other words, recovering the complexity that popular genres used to have in other eras.

The credits say that “Glaxo” is a production of Brazil’s RT Features produced by Argentina’s Rei Pictures. That speaks volumes of the comparative current state of the two countries’ film industries.

Naishtat: Yes. This is very important. As the film’s credits say, the producer of the film is Rodrigo Teixeira and his Brazilian production company RT Features and Rei Pictures is a minority co-producer on the Argentine side. The film was shot entirely in Brazil, which is very strange, because it’s set entirely in Argentina and so it was a very difficult decision for me. Rodrigo and I wanted to shoot it in Argentina, but the current state of Argentina made that impossible. The cuts and the freezing of public funding for the film industry have been brutal for Argentine cinema. There are fewer productions now and less of a presence in the major markets and the major festivals. And perhaps what will become even more evident in the coming years will be the total lack of promoting new talent and new voices. There used to be a very interesting generation making their first features not only in Buenos Aires, but in Córdoba, in other cities, in Patagonia — genuinely interesting voices. This government, which is waging an open war on culture in general, is, in my opinion, a fascist government, an enemy of culture, one that has no cultural politics whatsoever. It doesn’t even have conservative politics, it has no politics at all; the politics is that there are no cultural politics and this is derailing the life plans of many people.

I personally can keep working because, as you know, this is my fifth film and I’ve been able to secure financing in Brazil with Rodrigo Teixeira, or in France, or in other places. But if I had to start my career today, I’d have to work somewhere else. I wouldn’t be able to work in cinema, and this is what’s happening in Argentina, which is very sad. I think it’s important to call this out, because as you know, we’re a country with a great filmmaking tradition and it is now in very serious danger.

title: Thailand Bets on Film Tourism to Turn Movie Locations Into Travel Destinations
summary: The Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) has launched “Amazing Locations: From Scene to Scenic,” a campaign built to convert the country’s rising profile as a filming destination into lasting tourism, as productions ranging from “The White Lotus” to “The Challenge” Season 42 continue to draw international attention to Thai locations. TAT deputy governor Nithee Seeprae […]
content:
The Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) has launched “Amazing Locations: From Scene to Scenic,” a campaign built to convert the country’s rising profile as a filming destination into lasting tourism, as productions ranging from “The White Lotus” to “The Challenge” Season 42 continue to draw international attention to Thai locations.

TAT deputy governor Nithee Seeprae says the campaign grew out of watching how quickly the “set-jetting” trend has taken hold among travelers who plan trips around what they have seen on screen.

TAT frames the push as part of a broader strategy to make Thailand a top-of-mind choice for global productions, pointing to the strength of its local crews, production infrastructure, studio facilities and incentive programs as the pillars of that pitch. The campaign’s specific job, as Seeprae describes it, is to bridge filmmaking and travel: encouraging filmmakers to turn Thailand’s varied landscapes into cinematic backdrops while steering travelers toward the real places they recognize from the screen.

Popular on Variety

“We have seen firsthand how tangibly it benefits destinations and local communities when a film or series puts a place on screen,” Seeprae says. “It genuinely inspires people to travel, and we have seen that pull firsthand, audiences putting Thailand at the top of their must-visit list simply because they fell in love with it on screen first.”

The numbers back up the strategy. Seeprae says the country’s cash rebate program has drawn in upward of 100 foreign productions to date, funneling more than THB20 billion ($608 million) toward Thai crews and local economies. The rebate program itself is administered by Thailand’s Dept. of Tourism rather than TAT, though the agency promotes it as part of the country’s broader pitch to filmmakers. He points to Koh Samui as a case study: after the island appeared in the third season of “The White Lotus,” online interest in the destination jumped 88% and hotel reservations there grew 44%, figures he says have been echoed by titles including “The Hangover Part II” and “Jurassic World: Rebirth.” Recent Thailand shoots also include the Bollywood blockbuster “Dhurandhar,” Sam Raimi’s “Send Help,” the survival sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and “John Rambo.”

Seeprae says this year’s push doubles down on undiscovered locations rather than simply revisiting places already familiar to international audiences. He points to Isan provinces such as Nong Khai, Bueng Kan and Ubon Ratchathani, along with Nakhon Si Thammarat in the south, as places with striking scenery and a distinct sense of place that international productions have yet to explore. He cites director Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s body of work as proof that cinema can give an entire region “a place in the world’s imagination.” As part of the campaign, TAT is running trips that bring filmmakers, producers, influencers and cultural figures into these locations along both a B2B track focused on production logistics and a B2C track aimed at travelers.

The push comes as Thailand’s production sector matures well beyond service work. Nicholas Simon, founder and producer at Indochina Prods., has watched the local crew base grow from working transportation on shoots to running productions worth well over $100 million. “Crew who were working 15 years ago as transport coordinators are now line producing $100 million projects,” Simon says, pointing to Thai nominees at the Creative Emmys for “The White Lotus” and “Alien: Earth,” and a Thai costume designer from “The Creator” who is now a voting member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

“Jurassic World: Rebirth” behind the scenes Everett Collection

Simon credits “The White Lotus” and “Alien: Earth” with changing how Hollywood sees the country itself, rather than as a stand-in for somewhere else. Those productions, he says, also introduced the industry to Thailand’s art department talent, and “the film incentive has driven a new wave of productions scripted Thailand for Thailand.” Simon adds that under-filmed regions such as Songkla, Ranong and the natural rock formations of the north and northeast still hold plenty of unexplored ground, noting that “The Creator” alone shot across 17 of Thailand’s 76 provinces.

That maturity has pushed Indochina into original content through its new venture, TSixtySix. Producer Cod Satrusayang, head of studio at TSixtySix, says, “We think given the right support and the right stories, Thailand can become the next Asian wave following in the footsteps of South Korea,“ adding that clients who once came to Thailand purely for service work are increasingly asking about local stories too. Satrusayang says the biggest remaining gap is screenwriting talent able to work within structure, and that streamers willing to back genres beyond horror and romance are reshaping what gets developed. TSixtySix has a heist film releasing early next year and a coming-of-age drama shooting in late January, with Satrusayang predicting demand for Thai content will keep rising.

The country’s reputation as a source of acclaimed auteurs reinforces its appeal as a location, according to Raymond Phathanavirangoon, producer and founder of the SEAFIC Script Lab. Wong Kar Wai shot much of “In the Mood for Love” in Thailand because, Phathanavirangoon says, “there are locations in Thailand that seem untouched by time since the 1950s-1960s.” He notes that European filmmakers have told him Bangkok’s futuristic skyline could support a science-fiction film in the vein of “Alphaville,” and points to the local production “A Useful Ghost” as an example of a film built around unusual local settings. Phathanavirangoon says specificity, not international polish, is what makes Thai stories travel, citing “9 Temples to Heaven” and the Burmese Busan winner “Ma — Cry of Silence” as films that succeeded by staying rooted in local culture rather than chasing a global audience.

Phathanavirangoon says independent filmmakers are often the ones expanding what audiences associate with Thailand beyond its best-known landmarks. He points to Udon Thani, near the Phu Phra Bat Historical Park, and a growing contemporary arts scene anchored by museums such as Dib and MAIIAM, as the kind of settings independent directors are now drawing on. Director Chantana Tiprachart’s upcoming “Esarn Seven,” shot north of Udon Thani, is one example he cites of a film built around a region rarely seen on screen.

Producer Cattleya Paosrijarern, whose work centers on independent and auteur cinema, says international shoots and homegrown storytelling can coexist without one undermining the other. “Even with line production, we always push to be creative partners, not just vendors,” Paosrijarern says.

She says international funding is welcome but “the money must serve the artist’s vision,” and argues that hyper-local Thai stories only resonate abroad “when it’s backed by quality,” pointing to knowledge, vision and sustained policy support as the real drivers of that continuity. Her upcoming slate includes “Tremble Like a Flower,” the debut feature from visual artist Pathompon Tesprateep, and “Esarn Seven.”

Thailand’s location appeal extends into unscripted television. “The Challenge” Season 42 shot across Bangkok, Pattaya and the Chonburi region, and executive producer Justin Booth says the decision came down to more than scenery. “Thailand has some of the most professional and polished art department personnel anywhere in the world, and you’re able to access that level of talent at a better price,” Booth says. He adds that the range of environments within a compact area gave producers flexibility to design challenges they could not have built elsewhere, comparing the local infrastructure favorably with other countries that have hosted the franchise.

Season 42 also splits its 24 competitors into three teams competing for a share of $500,000, reviving the “Cutthroat” format the show first used in 2009. Booth says the cast made the timing right for the format’s return, and that viewers should watch how team dynamics evolve after a run of seasons built around pairs and individual competition. Asked whether he’s conscious that viewers might want to visit places the show has featured, Booth says that outcome isn’t the production’s primary goal but is one it keeps in mind. “The whole point of turning ‘The Challenge’ into an international competition show was to showcase these locations while also reaching a new or different audience,” he says.

Host T.J. Lavin says Thailand delivered some of the most memorable moments he has filmed for the show, from a season-opening challenge staged in downtown Bangkok to the daily rhythms of life in the country. “It was one of the most incredible and fun places that I’ve ever been,” Lavin says. “Not to mention, foot massages on the daily were amazing.” He says the humidity added real physical difficulty to the competition, thickening the air enough that “even some of the easiest tasks become difficult.”

Thailand’s locations are also central to “Inherit,” the horror feature set to premiere as a gala presentation at the Toronto Film Festival. Director Banjong Pisanthanakun says finding the right physical spaces shapes his films as much as the scripts do. For “Inherit,” he says the main family house “actually combined three real locations plus a sound stage to create a single location that matched the exact mood we wanted.” Pisanthanakun says Thailand’s horror tradition, which he calls part of the culture’s “modern cultural heritage,” continues to travel internationally alongside newer genres such as the family drama “How to Make Millions Before Grandma Dies” and the thriller “Bad Genius.”

Star Davika Hoorne, who plays a centuries-old demon matriarch in the film, says she hopes international audiences take away more than scares. “For audiences around the world, ‘Inherit’ is more than just a horror film, it’s also a glimpse into Thai culture,” Hoorne says. “I hope people feel both the thrill and the heart, and walk away pleasantly surprised.”

Several of these voices are set to share a stage in Toronto. TIFF is hosting a summit panel titled “From Scenic to Scene: How Thailand Shapes Global Cinema,” billed as an exploration of how landscape, local culture and incentives turn the country into what organizers describe as “a global story engine.” Pisanthanakun and Satrusayang are the featured guests, with Phathanavirangoon moderating and Seeprae delivering opening remarks.

For TAT, the ambition extends well past any single title. Seeprae says success five years from now would mean Thailand being recognized as “a prototype destination for filmmaking,” with productions returning to explore regions beyond the familiar and the resulting tourism sustained rather than a brief moment of interest.

title: Venice Film Festival Takeaways: Malkovich Storms the Oscar Race, Political Movies Dominate Buzz and More
summary: Is Venice still vibrating from all the rounds of applause? It’s become customary for audiences at the festival’s premieres to clap and cheer for a seeming eternity after the credits roll. (Often to the visible discomfort of the actors and filmmakers, who look like they don’t know what to do with themselves when the hurrahs […]
content:
Is Venice still vibrating from all the rounds of applause?

It’s become customary for audiences at the festival’s premieres to clap and cheer for a seeming eternity after the credits roll. (Often to the visible discomfort of the actors and filmmakers, who look like they don’t know what to do with themselves when the hurrahs rage into double digits.) Call it a Champagne (or Aperol spritz — we’re in Italy, after all) problem for stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and director Martin McDonagh, whose dark comedy “Wild Horse Nine” was embraced with a rousing 13-minute standing ovation inside the Lido’s famed Palazzo del Cinema. But that didn’t turn out to be the festival’s biggest reception — later in the week, Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem received 15.5 minutes of applause for their marriage-in-crisis drama “Bunker, and on Thursday, Gaza documentary “NAZA” was greeted with a massive 24.5 minutes, the longest of any recorded ovation at a major film festival.

And for all the complaints that Hollywood has basically abandoned film festivals, there was no shortage of celebrities to elicit big reactions from crowds. Robert Pattinson (“Primetime”), Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem (“Bunker”) and Oasis’ Liam and Noel Gallagher (“Don’t Look Back in Anger”) were among the boldface names hoping to turn festival kudos into awards chatter or box office plaudits.

Popular on Variety

As Venice wraps up and festivalgoers take their last bites of pasta and sips of spritzes, here are takeaways from the floating city.

George Clooney Steals the Show

Only Clooney could become the talk of the fest without even having a movie to promote. The A-lister traveled to Venice not for a new project but to receive the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. (If that has a familiar ring, Clooney played a movie star who accepts a career honor in Italy in last year’s “Jay Kelly.”) Indeed, Clooney was everywhere this year, making appearances at a press conference, the opening-night ceremony and a master class. He had a lot to say about the power of art in times of turmoil, the importance of free speech and the fraying state of democracy. And he found time to teach festivalgoers a new term: “There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people. I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now, but we’ll get through it.” We believe you, George!

Malkovich Storms Into the Oscar Race

Get ready to see a lot of Malkovich. The beloved character actor is drumming up awards buzz for “Wild Horse Nine,” in which he plays an eccentric CIA agent reflecting on his life. McDonagh has a pretty good track record of getting his actors from the Lido to the Academy Awards. Rockwell and Frances McDormand won Oscars for 2017’s “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri,” while Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson were nominated for 2022’s “The Banshees of Inisherin,” both of which bowed in Venice. Recognition feels long overdue for Malkovich, whose last nomination was more than three decades ago, for 1993’s “In the Line of Fire.” Matt Damon and Tom Cruise, you might have some competition…

Politics, Politics, Politics

Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera wasn’t exaggerating when he called this year’s lineup “the most political ever.” The 83rd edition was packed with films about hot-button issues like right-wing media barons (“Ink”), right-wing trolls (“Musk”), conflict in the Middle East (“NAZA”) and ICE (“They’re Here”). Offscreen, it’s become de rigueur to probe actors and directors at film festivals about the state of the world — a conversation that escalated at Berlin after jury president Wim Wenders said filmmakers should “stay out of politics.” Maggie Gyllenhaal, who is presiding over the Venice jury, disagrees. At the jury press conference, she called movies “fundamentally, unavoidably political” and challenged people to “hear stories about the most corrupt, most perverse people.” Her reasoning? “It opens up the opportunity to find empathy.”

A Record-Breaking Embrace

Audiences, for their part, seem just fine with politics at the forefront. “NAZA,” a devastating exposé about the systems behind the Israeli military’s remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, elicited the longest standing ovation in film festival history. (Or, at least since journalists began reporting on the trend.) The documentary was met with 24.5 minutes of applause, surpassing the ovation for last year’s Gaza-set drama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” and that of Guillermo Del Toro’s “Pan’s Labyrinth” at Cannes in 2006, both of which clocked in at 22 minutes. Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are two of the four filmmakers behind 2025’s Oscar-winning doc “No Other Land.” Given the warm reception for and timeliness of “NAZA,” will the duo find themselves back in the awards conversation?

Where Are the Women?

Gyllenhaal may be jury president, but she’s just as confused as everyone else about the dearth of women-directed films in the main competition lineup. (She didn’t select the movies, after all.) Only two titles up for the Golden Lion — “Woman Unknown,” a drama by May el-Toukhy, and “NAZA,” with Szor co-helming — were directed by women. “I guess it’s finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal deadpanned at her press conference. In all seriousness, though, she puts the blame on the powers that be. “There’s a systemic problem,” she said. “It’s harder for women to get films financed.”

A Star Is Born

Lance Oppenheim, the 30-year-old director known for non-fiction work like “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire,” emerged as a major talent to watch. A24’s “Primetime,” his debut feature film, was one of the buzziest of the festival, scoring an enthusiastic seven minutes of applause as audiences embraced Pattinson’s immersive performance as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen. And that was just the fanfare on the Lido. The next day in Colorado, Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder unveiled their top-secret documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, titled “You Can See Everything,” which became the talk of Telluride Film Festival. It’s safe to say Oppenheim will be getting plenty of use out of his tuxedo over the next few months.

Feeling Hot, Hot, Hot

This year’s hottest accessory? Electronic and handheld fans. Temperatures on the Lido were sweltering, which left A-listers on the verge of overheating on the red carpet. At their respective premieres, Jack O’Connell (“Ink”) had to take off his thick Dunhill coat before blotting the moisture on his face and shirt; Parker Posey (“Wild Horse Nine”) continuously waved herself with a decorative fan while mouthing about the brutal heat during the movie’s long standing ovation; and Pattinson (“Primetime”), wearing a suave all-white suit, dabbed the sweat off his forehead with napkins before posing for a cast photo. Stars, they’re just like us!

title: CBS Wants Ex-‘Matlock’ Writer’s Racial & Sexual Harassment Suit Dismissed; Says Claims Are “Fabrications & Outright Lies”
summary: On the eve of the 2026-2027 TV season, CBS is seeking to dismiss a scathing lawsuit brought by an ex-writer for the show, claiming that the scribe’s allegations of racial and sexual harassment are “fabrications and outright lies.” Back in June, John Lowe claimed in an unspecified damages seeking filing that showrunner Jennie Urman Snyder […]
content:
On the eve of the 2026-2027 TV season, CBS is seeking to dismiss a scathing lawsuit brought by an ex-writer for the show, claiming that the scribe’s allegations of racial and sexual harassment are “fabrications and outright lies.”

Back in June, John Lowe claimed in an unspecified damages seeking filing that showrunner Jennie Urman Snyder and producers allowed “sexually explicit and discriminatory conduct” to fester. Among other things, the suit in L.A. Superior Court alleged that Snyder referred to the Juneteenth holiday with a racial slur, and that another producer made a sexually suggestive late-night call to him.

Now, CBS’s legal team — representing CBS Studios and other defendants Snyder, Nicki Renna and Jeffrey Lieber — have responded to Lowe and his lawyers with a stern rejection of the claims. They assert that the “allegations that he was unlawfully terminated as a writer on Matlock and that he is entitled to recover lost wages implicate California’s anti-SLAPP statute and support the instant motion to strike because Defendants’ decision to not reengage Lowe as a writer was a creative decision in furtherance of their exercise of free speech on a matter of public interest.”

Watch on Deadline

Getting specific, for instance, CBS’ legal team wrote that Lowe was hired on the Kathy Bates-starrer in October, 2023 and departed in July, 2024, and not in July, 2025. They pointed to Snyder never using the claimed racial slur and that others did not witness it.

CBS’ legal team wrote, “Lowe was never subjected to race or sex harassment as he claims, and as this case progresses, Defendants are confident that Plaintiff’s malicious and unsupported attacks will be publicly exposed for what they are: retaliation by a desperate man who was not renewed as a writer because his performance deficiencies detrimentally impacted CBS’ ability to convey the messages it desired.”

A CBS Studios spokesperson said, “As stated in the motion and following a thorough investigation, we are confident that Lowe’s accusations are demonstrably inaccurate and maliciously fabricated, and will not allow them to go unchallenged.

“False allegations are deeply damaging, both to those wrongly accused, and to anyone with a serious and legitimate claim of discrimination. We stand firmly behind our producers and look forward to the truth coming to light.”

title: On 25th Anniversary Of 9/11, NY1 Anchor Pat Kiernan On “Putting Yourself Back In That Moment”
summary: Memories of September 11 are still overwhelming for many New Yorkers, but NY1 anchor Pat Kiernan finds value in looking back on that indelible day 25 years later. “It’s worthwhile for me just to refresh my memory on what played out at what moment, and also kind of to put yourself back into that moment,” […]
content:
Memories of September 11 are still overwhelming for many New Yorkers, but NY1 anchor Pat Kiernan finds value in looking back on that indelible day 25 years later.

“It’s worthwhile for me just to refresh my memory on what played out at what moment, and also kind of to put yourself back into that moment,” he told Deadline in an interview at New York‘s Paley Center for Media. The center hosted a panel with Kiernan and six other current and former journalists recalling the day’s coverage on the anniversary.

Unedited YouTube footage of Kiernan’s morning broadcast was posted earlier this week to X by Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reporter Daniel McFadin and has racked up 10.4 million views. “You get 15 minutes of news from the Before Times,” McFadin wrote in his post. “Then the world changes.”

As that blue-sky morning took a radical turn, reporters scrambled for actionable intel in a dial-up internet age. “We got very lucky that we had two quality eyewitnesses call in in the first couple of minutes,” Kiernan recalled. “That allowed us to stay on the air, speak to them, get their descriptions at the same time as we were mobilizing the team.”

Watch on Deadline

Word of an incident at one of the World Trade Center towers reached the newsroom during a commercial break. “The next commercial break on NY1 was three weeks later,” he remembered.

While Kiernan and others initially referred to the situation as a fire, with wide shots of the towers showing puffs of smoke coming out of the north tower, it soon became clear that a plane had hit the building. (One caller noted a plane’s tire had fallen to the sidewalk below.)

“My mind immediately goes to how different it would be today between social media, FaceTime, pictures from from anywhere with a layer of AI and not being sure if the pictures are legitimate,” Kiernan said.

Pat Kiernan (Paley Center) Paley Center

His boyish looks notwithstanding, Kiernan is now one of the deans of New York television, approaching his 30th anniversary on NY1. The network launched in 1992 as a news outlet only available to subscribers of Time Warner Cable, now Charter Spectrum. Then, as now, the cable system reached only the five boroughs of New York City, giving NY1 a loyal, concentrated audience of more than 1 million daily viewers in the capital of media and finance.

“As the story went on, it developed very quickly and there was a there was a national news lane and there was a NY1 lane,” Kiernan said. “We were fully focused on what was happening in the city.” Part of that responsibility was to attend to the thousands of New Yorkers whose loved ones were missing, with their hand-made fliers becoming one of the indelible images of the tragedy.

“The thing that we could do that was helpful to the community was to be in lower Manhattan, to be down with the families in Greenwich Village that stood at that wall with a picture of my my missing loved one,” the anchor said. “We did that for hours, literally almost handing the microphone to them and saying, ‘I know your situation is desperate. Here’s here’s your chance to speak to the city.’ Which was compelling for our viewers and therapeutic for the people who were in that desperate moment.”

Other participants in the Paley panel, which was moderated by former CNN anchor Paula Zahn, recalled the significant limitations of technology 25 years ago. “Half the staff had a Blackberry, the other half had a Nextel,” said Nina Pineda of WABC-TV. “We couldn’t even take pictures.” She recalled detouring en route to the burning towers to relay a bystander’s camcorder video to the station newsroom, with the resulting delay becoming moot when her station’s antenna was lost in the Trade Center’s collapse.

Jonathan Capehart, an MS Now host and PBS political analyst who was working for Mike Bloomberg’s mayoral campaign on 9/11, joined other panelists in recalling how difficult it was to confirm information. “We were hearing the rumors,” he said. “But you couldn’t corroborate.” John Miller, then a leading national reporter on ABC News, included a mention on air of a car bomb being found at the State Department, a detail that later proved inaccurate.

Kiernan was in the Deadline interview about how a 9/11-scale event would be covered in today’s media landscape, which is marked by smaller media institutions along with Substackers, influencers and an atomization of voices.

“There are two offsetting trends,” he said. “The favorable trend is that it is possible to get information and move video from anywhere in the city and anywhere on the planet. So that allows us to be in more places, more quickly, to verify stories, to get information to our reporters, to get information from our reporters. That’s offset by all of the impact of declining audiences and changing audience habits.”

Traditional media’s infrastructure, he added, “is not as robust as it was.” At NY1, “We’ve been lucky that we have retained a lot of that audience, and we’ve still got a sizable team. But you look around the city, we had two 24-hour all-news radio stations at the time that this happened. We had an active newsroom at Channel 9 that doesn’t exist anymore. … The Times had a metro section and more reporters who were on the ground familiar with these stories. So, that’s the team that knows how to step up in a moment like this. And collectively in the city, there are fewer people who are in a position to do that.”

Barbie Zelizer, a professor at U. Penn’s Annenberg School for Communication, emphasized on the panel the potency of the coverage on the day of 9/11. Still photographs, she emphasized, such as those taken by fellow panelist Matthew McDermott, were “instrumental” because they were “able to present something real.” They “bore witness” to the tragedy but also “invited people in” to understand it in a way that video or text never could.

Zelizer also said things are not quite as different as they seem 25 years later.

“There are different platforms, there are different technologies, there’s a different speed at which we get information,” she said. “But we’ve always had misinformation and disinformation alongside real information.”

title: Saban Acquires & Dates Sharks Vs Whales Thriller ‘Alphas’ With Martin Henderson, Teagan Croft & Charlotte Vega
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Saban Films has acquired U.S. rights to Alphas, the survival thriller that puts great whites and killer whales on a collision course. The film, which stars Martin Henderson (Virgin River), Teagan Croft (Titans) and Charlotte Vega (Wrong Turn), is being lined up for a theatrical release in early 2027. In Alphas, “after a string of great white […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Saban Films has acquired U.S. rights to Alphas, the survival thriller that puts great whites and killer whales on a collision course.

The film, which stars Martin Henderson (Virgin River), Teagan Croft (Titans) and Charlotte Vega (Wrong Turn), is being lined up for a theatrical release in early 2027.

In Alphas, “after a string of great white attacks threatens a quiet surfing beach town, killer whales are enlisted to drive the sharks out. But when the alpha great white proves too powerful to stop, a former local surfing legend (Henderson) and a retired orca trainer (Vega) make one last, terrifying move: unleash the most dangerous killer whale ever known.”

Pic is directed by Liam O’Donnell from a script by Frank Hannah and a story by Hannah and Christopher Tuffin. The film is produced by Christopher Tuffin for Strong Island, Renee Tab for Sentient Entertainment, Joel Chikapa Phiri and Tshepiso Chikapa Phiri for Known Associates, XYZ Films, and executive-produced by Timo Argillander and Andrea Scarso on behalf of IPR.VC.

Watch on Deadline

The deal was brokered by Nate Bolotin for XYZ and Jonathan Saba for Saban.

“Monster movies have always given us something bigger than life to be scared of,” said Shanan Becker and Jonathan Saban, Co-Presidents of Saban Films. “Godzilla started it. Jaws made it real, because the scariest monster isn’t the one we dream up, it’s the shark already swimming beneath us. Alphas finally gives that shark something to be scared of, too.”

“We built Alphas to take the shark movie audiences know and flip the food chain,” added producer Christopher Tuffin. “When the only thing that can save the beach may be more dangerous than sharks, every choice becomes terrifying.”

title: ‘R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2’ Launches At TIFF Market, Details Revealed With Cassandra Peterson AKA ‘Elvira Mistress Of The Dark’ Joining Cast

Stine’s Pumpkinhead. Written and directed by Jem Garrard, who also helmed the original R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead, the sequel continues author Stine’s Pumpkinhead story. The synopsis reads: “When […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Blue Fox Entertainment will launch international sales at the TIFF market to R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2, the upcoming Tubi Original sequel to the young-adult horror film R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead.

Written and directed by Jem Garrard, who also helmed the original R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead, the sequel continues author Stine’s Pumpkinhead story. The synopsis reads: “When a new Pumpkinhead curse awakens in Redhaven, Sam and Becka must stop it before it claims the entire town.”

Bean Reid, Adeline Lo and Matty Finochio return to star in the sequel, with additional casting due to be announced at a later date. Joining the returning cast is Cassandra Peterson, best known as character ‘Elvira, Mistress of the Dark’, who takes on the role of Cassandra, “a wise and ancient witch whose arrival could prove pivotal to the events unfolding in Redhaven”.

The film is slated to premiere on Tubi this fall as part of the streamer’s Terror on Tubi horror hub. Pic is produced by Front Street Pictures, the film is executive produced by James Mattagne, Joan Waricha, Harvey Kahn, Yvonne Bernard, Dan Bernard, Jem Garrard, Allen Lewis, and Rama Diallo.

Watch on Deadline

R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead premiered on Tubi in 2025. Inspired by an episode of R.L. Stine’s The Haunting Hour, the film “follows teenager Sam after his brother Finn mysteriously vanishes and everyone in town—including Sam’s mother—seems to have forgotten he ever existed. With Halloween approaching, Sam, his friend Becka and eccentric local Rusty must uncover the truth and break a harvest curse before it is too late.”

The original film stars Bean Reid, Adeline Lo, Kevin McNulty, Bob Frazer, Matty Finochio and Seth Isaac Johnson.

“R.L. Stine’s stories have been a gateway into horror for generations of young audiences, and Pumpkinhead brings that same spirit of adventure, scares and fun to a new generation,” said Lisa Gutberlet, President of Blue Fox Entertainment, about the Goosebumps writer. “We’re thrilled to continue our relationship with Tubi and bring R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead 2 to our international buyers at TIFF. Jem Garrard has created another exciting chapter in the mythology, and we’re looking forward to sharing it with audiences around the world.”

The acquisition expands Blue Fox Entertainment’s international sales relationship with Tubi, following multiple collaborations, including Buzzkill starring Siena Agudong and Brec Bassinger, and Aliyah’s Interlude.

R.L. Stine’s Pumpkinhead series is not related to Stan Winston’s 1988 cult monster movie Pumpkinhead, which also spawned a film franchise.

title: Ben Silverman, Emmanuelle Chriqui, Keshet & More On Advisory Board Of New Platform Connecting Jewish Creators With Investors — TIFF Market
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Former NBC Co-Chairman Ben Silverman, Micah Green (CEO of 30 West), Tanya Cohen (Co-CEO of Made by Us), actress Emmanuelle Chriqui (Entourage), producer Anthony Bregman (Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind) and Keshet International are among the advisory board members of new platform Shooq, which aims to connect Jewish creators with investors keen to […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Former NBC Co-Chairman Ben Silverman, Micah Green (CEO of 30 West), Tanya Cohen (Co-CEO of Made by Us), actress Emmanuelle Chriqui (Entourage), producer Anthony Bregman (Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind) and Keshet International are among the advisory board members of new platform Shooq, which aims to connect Jewish creators with investors keen to accelerate Jewish storytelling.

The group, overseen by veteran producers Ari Pinchot and Jonathan Rubenstein, is aiming to help finance film, TV, podcasts and digital media that “strengthen Jewish identity, combat antisemitism and bring top level Jewish stories to global audiences”.

Named after the Hebrew word for marketplace and launching this week during the Toronto Film Festival and market, the group aims to connect creators with investors, media funds, studios, foundations, philanthropists, and mission-driven funding partners.

Watch on Deadline

According to its founders, the platform already features narrative features, TV series, podcasts and social media video content. Funders are being sought to finance development, production and marketing with each project curated by the Shooq platform to match it with an appropriate financier.

Unlike crowdfunding platforms, Shooq isn’t designed to raise or manage funds directly, but more as a matchmaking platform with funders creating profiles outlining their investment interests, requirements, preferred genres, funding ranges, and areas of focus. When a project aligns with those criteria, Shooq facilitates a direct introduction between the creators and the potential funder. Any investment or grant discussions take place directly between the parties. Funders can also showcase their own projects for additional funding. According to the founders, the site already features funders from the investment and philanthropic arenas.

Shooq is also offering funders access to industry consultants and “optional reporting tools and impact metrics for mission-driven funders seeking to measure their project’s cultural and social outcomes”. Participation is free and funders can participate anonymously, depending on their preference.

Founders Pinchot and Rubenstein produced the Roast of Anti-Semitism comedy show in LA and run the Jewish Writers Institute with the Maimonides Fund.

“Great stories shape culture,” said Pinchot. “Many investors and philanthropists have been eager to support meaningful [Jewish] media but lacked both a trusted way to curate projects and an efficient mechanism and/or the means to fully finance them. Shooq is the solution.”

Jonathan Rubenstein added: “We can’t afford to keep competing with one another for the same limited resources. We need to come together under one roof, pool our resources, and give our best [Jewish] storytellers the support they need to get impactful projects made to reach audiences around the world. That is what Shooq is designed to do.”

title: Robert Pattinson Is Having His Best Year Ever With ‘Primetime,’ ‘The Drama,’ ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Dune 3.’ Will the Oscars Recognize Him?
summary: Four Robert Pattinsons are better than one, and that makes his upcoming Oscar run a bit more complicated. In “Primetime,” Pattinson sits alone in a dim Florida room, reading a stranger’s chat logs aloud: “I will undress you as you undress me.” He’s playing Chris Hansen, host of the hidden-camera series “To Catch a Predator,” […]
content:
Four Robert Pattinsons are better than one, and that makes his upcoming Oscar run a bit more complicated.

In “Primetime,” Pattinson sits alone in a dim Florida room, reading a stranger’s chat logs aloud: “I will undress you as you undress me.” He’s playing Chris Hansen, host of the hidden-camera series “To Catch a Predator,” the man who turned police stings into television events that battled for ratings against the likes of ABC’s “Lost.” It’s the most uncomfortable thing Pattinson has ever done on screen (yet). It could also be what finally gets him an Oscar nomination.

At 40, he’s yet to be recognized despite acclaimed turns in “Good Time,” “The Lighthouse” and “The Rover.” This year, Pattinson has stacked the deck.

Popular on Variety

The evidence is all over the 2026 film year: indies, franchises and, in the middle of it all, shooting the next “Batman” movie with Matt Reeves.

Courtesy of A24, Venice Film Festival

In Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” which played in competition at Venice (earning a seven-minute standing ovation) and opens Sept. 25 through A24, Pattinson has what looks like his clearest awards vehicle. Kristoffer Borgli’s dark comedy “The Drama” gave him another showcase opposite Zendaya back in the spring. Then came Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” which became one of the year’s billion-dollar phenomena. And still to come, on Dec. 18, Denis Villeneuve’s final installment, “Dune: Part Three,” will give him a showier, villainous supporting turn as the shape-shifting Scytale.

Four movies, two possible categories and two very different campaigns to juggle. Nobody’s asking anymore whether Pattinson belongs in the race. The question is how the studios — and Pattinson — choose to play it.

“Primetime” seems to be the obvious one.

Oppenheim, a documentarian who also helmed the Telluride surprise documentary “You Can See Everything” alongside Nathan Fielder, is making his narrative feature debut. His Hansen is a showman, the connective tissue of an anti-hero origin story à la “Joker” with Joaquin Phoenix and “American Psycho” with Christian Bale. The film isn’t out to canonize him. Instead, it watches everything that made him larger than the premise of the show: the ratings, the crew, the wannabe actors playing decoys and the audience who gobbled it up at home.

Pattinson doesn’t ask anyone to root for Hansen, rather he asks them to sit with a man they’ve known from television and watch him squirm.

We’ve seen a character get embraced like this before. Phoenix won lead actor for “Joker,” an ugly, uncomfortable character in a movie that split the room and still ran the table. “Primetime” operates in a similar space: loud enough to start a fight, familiar enough as an American story to give voters a way in.

And Pattinson isn’t the only highlight.

Skyler Gisondo, best known for roles in shows like HBO’s “The Righteous Gemstones” and most recently as Jimmy Olsen in James Gunn’s “Superman,” is terrific as Dan Plumb, the hopeful actor hired to play the bait. In many ways, he’s best in show. Also great alongside Gisondo is Emmy winner Merritt Wever (“Nurse Jackie”), who gives the producer an edge as the operation’s compromises pile up.

And then there’s the real Hansen, who has been angling his way into the rollout with countless interviews and comments about the film. If nothing else, the movie now comes with a sideshow, and sideshows keep a title in the conversation. Look what Elon Musk did for “The Odyssey.”

Unfortunately, Pattinson is a prime target for a vote-splitting scenario.

He’s very good in Borgli’s comedy “The Drama” as a museum curator whose wedding quietly comes apart. In another year, it might have been the campaign. But it came out in April, and “Primetime” is the more recent entrant in the lead race.

There’s also the fact that the lead actor race is incredibly competitive, with his “Odyssey” co-star Matt Damon in the thick of it, along with Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”), John Malkovich (“Wild Horse Nine”) and, still to come, Tom Cruise (“Digger”) and perhaps even his “Dune: Part Three” co-star Timothée Chalamet.

The supporting race could be the leaner pathway.

©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection

In “The Odyssey,” Pattinson plays Antinous, ringleader of the suitors circling Penelope, and one piece of Nolan’s huge ensemble behind Damon’s Odysseus in what’s turning into one of the year’s biggest films. Best picture contenders of that size can float a supporting player, especially one the industry already respects. The question for Universal is whether the part is big enough, and sticky enough, to be worth the political capital. Could he split votes with his co-star John Leguizamo, or come along for the ride?

“Dune: Part Three” is the other option, and potentially the showier one. Scytale is a bigger swing, Villeneuve is in his corner and Warner Bros. has a prime December date and real money in the franchise. The first two “Dune” films drew 15 Oscar nominations between them, so the Academy plainly takes the series seriously beyond the craft categories. But none of those nominations have been for acting.

Either one could carry a real supporting push. But one wonders, could Pattinson actually land more than one nom?

Jamie Foxx pulled it off in 2004, winning lead actor for “Ray” and landing a supporting nod for “Collateral.” Cate Blanchett did it in 2007, with a lead nomination for “Elizabeth: The Golden Age” and a supporting nomination for “I’m Not There.” The most recent was Scarlett Johansson in 2019, with “Marriage Story” and “Jojo Rabbit.” In addition, when you have a year of multiple titles, the Academy looks for the “representation”-type of film like they did with Jessica Chastain (nominated for “The Help” in a seven-film year) and Philip Seymour Hoffman (nominated for “Charlie Wilson’s War” in supporting actor, with two lead acclaimed works in “Before the Devil Knows You’re Dead” and “The Savages”).

And let’s not forget, actors can now be double-nominated in the same category following an Academy rule update earlier this year.

That’s no guarantee for any of this. “Primetime” might play too harshly for a chunk of the Academy, while “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three” could be technical players with other actors to be recognized.

Nonetheless, Pattinson stopped having us ask the question if he was a great actor a while ago. What’s left is for the Academy, and its four Pattinsons before them, to talk themselves into checking the right box.

title: ‘Hombre al Agua’ Review: Gael García Bernal Directs and Stars in a Sputtering, Screwball-y Dramedy About One Man’s Identity Crisis
summary: Sifting through Gael García Bernal’s recent roles — from the namesake conquistador of Lav Diaz’s “Magellan,” the grieving wife-guy in Piero Messina’s droopy sci-fi “Another End,” and the fast-aging family man of M. Night Shyamalan’s “Old” — won’t give you much insight on “Hombre al Agua,” which translates as “man overboard.” Except that unlike those international […]
content:
Sifting through Gael García Bernal’s recent roles — from the namesake conquistador of Lav Diaz’s “Magellan,” the grieving wife-guy in Piero Messina’s droopy sci-fi “Another End,” and the fast-aging family man of M. Night Shyamalan’s “Old” — won’t give you much insight on “Hombre al Agua,” which translates as “man overboard.” Except that unlike those international productions, García Bernal’s third directorial feature caters to the home side as a quasi-popular Mexican dramedy whose gags and in-jokes will play — if for anyone — more effectively to a Spanish-speaking crowd.

That’s not to make excuses, but to put in context, what is also a sputtering, screwball-y film about masculine roles in a waning patriarchal society. Get the script’s nuances or not, this awkwardly low-energy undertaking doesn’t make much of a case for García Bernal as a director, but as a star text in the mode of “Déficit,” his 2007 directorial debut, it’s got a fair bit to chew on by its own prismatic design. A TIFF slot will follow its premiere in Venice’s Spotlight section, and García Bernal’s profile is sure to fuel a healthy festival run.

Popular on Variety

Bits of narration from an offscreen speaker give the film a fairytale feel, a vibe matched by the rustic splendor of its chateau setting, where Camilo (García Bernal) lives with his athlete wife Jauna (Esmerelda Pimentel) and baby daughter. Camilo’s fortune, we learn from the opening address, came by a stroke of luck when he saved Juana’s businessman father Abel (Jorge Salinas) from drowning. Eternally grateful, Abel swiftly moved the Cuban lifeguard to Yucatán and placed him in a cushy corporate post at one of his companies. Jauna’s affections were secured shortly after — though apparently a jadedness has set into the marriage when the present timeline kicks off, and a rushed sex session devolves into a minor spat over who must tend to the crying babe. And does Juana even want to be touched by her husband? Facing the other direction, she asks him to make love to her with a different accent; to pretend that he’s another guy — maybe a Colombian dude. “From Cartagena or Bogota?” Camilo mutters.

“Hombre al Agua” then spins out into a game of shifting identities as a flurry of eccentric characters settle into the couple’s household. There’s Fabiana (Débora Nascimento), a statuesque Brazilian actress shadowing Jauna to prepare for a role as a pole-vaulter. Silvina (Natalia Oreiro), the Argentinian mistress and baby-momma of Abel, suspiciously begs Camilo to keep an eye on her while he recovers from a car accident. His daughter’s no-nonsense nanny, Malvina (Anna Diaz), side-eyes her bougie employers, while Silvina’s scruffy ex-husband, Ricardes (Manuel Garcia Rulfo), creeps around the gardens, occasionally drawing Camilo into a heart-to-heart. Meanwhile, at the factory Camilo manages for Abel, he’s a fumbling boss-man tasked with firing veteran workers and curbing their efforts to organize.

The scenarios are vaguely zany, as when Fabiana Method-acts her way into Camilo’s bed, but the winding chattiness of the comedy is flatter than it is dry — like a bubbly beverage left too long uncapped. Pivots into a black-and-white Brazilian telenovela, which Camilo tunes into nightly while on baby duty, feed into the film’s nesting-doll narrative on paper, but in practice make for annoyingly gratuitous flourishes. In any case, the procession of masks, roles and stories (or versions of a story) that filter throughout make sense for what is ultimately an actor’s movie about the instability of a life lived as a series of parts. The web of characters make for a vaguely amusing assembly of nationalities, types and stereotypes, but insofar as they reflect back Camilo’s selves, that aspect is far too bleary and imprecise to build out a convincing personal crisis.

As the unravelling of a relationship, however, “Hombre al Agua” has a bit more going for it when Jauna decides to direct a movie about her own life, casting Fabiana (whom she may or may not be sleeping with) as herself and Robbie (Ricky Martin, making a brief stunt appearance) as a version of Camilo. Buried resentments come out through the script, and when Robbie unexpectedly drops the part, Camilo steps in to play himself, allowing for one of the film’s more arresting scenes, in which Jauna tenderly directs a sort of couple’s therapy between Camilo and Fabiana-as-Jauna.

It’s the peak for a movie that otherwise proceeds lifelessly though a few more unearned and perfunctory twists. Blowhard Abel, who is running for local office and wants Camilo as his right-hand man, turns out to be a Faustian figure whose influence must be denounced. Avenues for Camilo’s enlightenment while still remaining distinct and vivid personalities, the women impose change on García Bernal’s hapless hero, who might be the least interesting among them.

title: Italian Director Tommaso Usberti’s Toxic Masculinity Drama ‘Before the War’ Scores Top Venice Critics’ Week Prize
summary: Paris-based Italian director Tommaso Usberti’s romance “Before the War,” a reflection on racism and toxic masculinity set in the Northern Italian plains, is the big winner of the Venice Critics’ Week where it scooped the grand prize and the award for best producer.  “Before the War” — which is the only Italian entry in the […]
content:
Paris-based Italian director Tommaso Usberti’s romance “Before the War,” a reflection on racism and toxic masculinity set in the Northern Italian plains, is the big winner of the Venice Critics’ Week where it scooped the grand prize and the award for best producer.

“Before the War” — which is the only Italian entry in the section dedicated to first works from around the world — is the tale of a young man named Guido, raised within a Northern Italian racist milieu, who becomes attracted to a Kosovar immigrant named Sonia.

“He has earned respect from his peers through violence in the racist and macho environment he grew up in,” says the synopsis. But when Guido meets Sonia, something shifts. He finds himself torn between the world that made him and the one that she is opening up for him.

Popular on Variety
