🥸 New identity: Spain’s Mediapro will relaunch as Imagina on January 1, 2027, following a major company review and “several months of reorganization.”

🏆 Awards: John Turturro is set to receive the Golden Eye Award at the Zurich Film Festival, which kicks off later this month.

📋 Lineup: The Zurich Summit has revealed its second batch of speakers including Oscar winner Edward Berger and Constantin Film CEO Oliver Berben.

⛰️ “Oh, the hills are alive”: Prime Video got the YA gang together, with a campus-style retreat in the Bavarian alps including stars from Off Campus, Boys of Tommen, Love Me Love Me 2, Maxton Hall and Our Fault: London.

❌ Stop right there!: Donald Trump‘s administration took exception to UK government plans to compel online video giants like YouTube to promote “public service media” content from outlets like the BBC.

✒️ Signed: Arcade, the management company of The Sidemen, has signed a host of creators, including comedian Max Fosh, as it relaunches as an entertainment business.

🎥 Trailer: For Pablo Larraín’s Netflix miniseries My Sad Dead.

Photo of the Week

Getty

Burstyn With Pride – There was barely a dry eye in the room as the sparkling Oscar winner and nonagenarian Ellen Burstyn collected the Golden Lion For Lifetime Achievement Award in Venice on Monday.

International Insider was written by Jesse Whittock and edited by Jake Kanter. Zac Ntim contributed. Send any tips, comments or ideas for international coverage to jwhittock@deadline.com and mgoldbart@deadline.com

title: Minka Kelly Reacts To ‘Ransom Canyon’s Cancellation After “Two Beautiful Seasons”
summary: Minka Kelly is focusing at the positives as she bids farewell to Ransom Canyon, which was canceled by Netflix after two seasons. Kelly, who starred opposite Josh Duhamel in the Texas romantic drama, posted a video of her and Duhamel’s characters Quinn and Staten’s romantic journey, which saw plenty of ups and downs during the […]
content:
Minka Kelly is focusing at the positives as she bids farewell to Ransom Canyon, which was canceled by Netflix after two seasons.

Kelly, who starred opposite Josh Duhamel in the Texas romantic drama, posted a video of her and Duhamel’s characters Quinn and Staten’s romantic journey, which saw plenty of ups and downs during the two seasons.

She accompanied the compilation of some signature Quinn-Staten scenes, largely from Season 1, with a message to the show’s fans.

She sounded philosophical about the cancellation, writing, “All good things must come to an end. And so it is,” before sharing her gratitude.

Watch on Deadline

“Thank you all for giving us two beautiful seasons,” she said, adding, “Thank you forever my Ransom Canyon family.”

Ransom Canyon follows childhood friends-turned-star-crossed lovers Staten Kirkland (Duhamel) and Quinn O’Grady (Kelly) who never seem to be able to get their timing right.

The duo were tested again in the second season with Quinn getting briefly engaged to someone else but by the end, unlike the Season 1 finale which saw Staten and Quinn split up, they were in a good place — and very much together. In fact, as opposed as Season 1, the Season 2 closer of Random Canyon did not have any jaw-dropping cliffhangers, which would bring some consolation to fans who had invested in the series and its characters for two seasons.

April Blair served as showrunner, creator and executive producer. Executive producers included stars Duhamel and Kelly as well as Dan Angel, Bradley Gardner and Joe Fazzio.

title: Paramount Argues States’ Antitrust Suit Will ‘Collapse Under Scrutiny’
summary: Paramount’s lawyers filed a legal response to the states’ antitrust lawsuit against the Warner Bros. Discovery merger on Friday, sketching out arguments and defenses it may use at a trial next March. Among other defenses, Paramount’s lawyers said they may claim that the coalition of 12 states lacks the authority to regulate the merger, “which […]
content:
Paramount’s lawyers filed a legal response to the states’ antitrust lawsuit against the Warner Bros. Discovery merger on Friday, sketching out arguments and defenses it may use at a trial next March.

Among other defenses, Paramount’s lawyers said they may claim that the coalition of 12 states lacks the authority to regulate the merger, “which is vested in the U.S. Department of Justice.” However, states do have the authority to bring claims alleging harms caused by conduct violative of federal antitrust law.

Paramount also noted that Cinema United, the trade group for theater chains, has called for a settlement.

Popular on Variety

“Day by day, the weak case against this Merger gets even weaker,” the company argued, adding that it also plans to challenge the states’ market definitions. “Plaintiffs’ case amounts to a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny.”

California led the state coalition in suing to block the merger in July, arguing that the deal will create unlawful concentration in the basic cable market and in the wide-release and blockbuster theatrical markets. The DOJ had earlier approved the merger, issuing a memo laying out its reasoning for why the deal should be allowed to go forward.

States typically work with the DOJ in antitrust cases, but under the Trump administration California and several others have often charted their own course.

Paramount has repeatedly argued that the deal will be pro-competitive, and will result in more movies and TV shows.

In its answer to the complaint, the company denied the states’ allegations — a requisite formality to establish a legal controversy. The company also added a few pages of argument, alleging that the states’ case ignores the broader context of an industry in rapid transition to streaming.

“The way audiences consume content is changing rapidly. Streaming services now have greater viewership than movie theaters and cable television,” Paramount argues. “Plaintiffs’ case depends on ignoring this reality. It involves a series of gerrymandered markets based on cherry-picked data from the past. The alleged markets are not the product of sound economic analysis or current market realities. They have been invented for one purpose and one purpose only: to trigger a presumption — any presumption, no matter how weak — in the hopes the Court will look no further.”

The Writers Guild of America has filed its own lawsuit arguing that the merger will reduce the marketplace for writers’ work. That case is set to be heard alongside the states’ challenge at trial on March 2, 2027.

Paramount has agreed not to close the deal until a ruling is issued after the trial — though it is asking the court to require the plaintiffs to post a $1.88 billion bond as the price of continuing the litigation. A judge is set to hear arguments on that request on Sept. 24.

Meanwhile, a court will hold a two-day settlement conference in the antitrust case with the parties in late October. That’s a standard part of civil procedure and does not indicate whether a deal is in the offing.

title: Jimmy Kimmel’s Pulled TV Interview With James Talarico Hits 5 Million Views in 24 Hours on YouTube
summary: Jimmy Kimmel’s pulled TV interview with James Talarico, the Texan Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, has crossed 5 million views in the 24 hours since it was posted to YouTube. It was revealed during Wednesday night’s episode of “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” that the interview would not air on his ABC show because of threats […]
content:
Jimmy Kimmel‘s pulled TV interview with James Talarico, the Texan Democrat running for the U.S. Senate, has crossed 5 million views in the 24 hours since it was posted to YouTube.

It was revealed during Wednesday night’s episode of “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” that the interview would not air on his ABC show because of threats from Donald Trump’s FCC against the network’s affiliate stations. “Out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” Kimmel said on air. “It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV.”

This, of course, is not Kimmel’s first conflict with the FCC. Chairman Brendan Carr’s threatened ABC after the host’s comments about the assassination of Charlie Kirk in 2025, and the network later suspended him for nearly a week.

Popular on Variety

Talarico is no stranger to FCC feuds either. In February, the agency told “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” that it couldn’t broadcast an interview with him. The segment was posted to the show’s YouTube Channel instead, where it reached more than 9 million views.

The pulled TV interview between Kimmel and Talarico started with the late night host asking the Texas senate candidate why Trump and the FCC are so scared of him. Talarico responded: “Well, they’re worried that we’re going to win this race in Texas. But we are the underdogs until the last vote is counted. We’re not just going up against the most corrupt politician in Texas. We’re going up against this entire corrupt system.”

Watch the full 20-minute interview in the video below.

title: ‘The Julia Set’ Review: Chase Infiniti Confirms Her Movie-Star Mettle in Niki Byrne’s Riveting Math-Geek Bad Romance
summary: In "The Julia Set," she portrays a numbers genius in the most convincing way possible — by wearing her virtuosity lightly and casually, as if it were second nature (which, for someone like Julia, it is). But she also makes Julia a highly focused and mature young woman who is still, by virtue of age and inexperience, just naïve enough to be poised between assertion and following the lead of a dude she should have steered clear of.
content:
There are two major pieces of news to come out of “The Julia Set,” the nothing-short-of-terrific new movie that premiered tonight at the Toronto Film Festival. It’s the first movie to feature Chase Infiniti since her breakout role as the Leonardo DiCaprio character’s daughter in “One Battle After Another,” and the first piece of news is that it confirms her movie-star mettle and astonishing quality of lyrical wised-up innocence as an actor.

She plays Julia Fischer, a math prodigy who’s a freshman in college, and who makes the mistake — though she chooses it with big dark wide open eyes — of falling into a romantic relationship with her ridiculously good-looking dream-preppie teaching assistant, played by Christopher Briney (from “The Summer I Turned Pretty” and the musical version of “Mean Girls”).

In “The Julia Set,” Infiniti portrays a numbers genius in the most convincing way possible — by wearing her virtuosity lightly and casually, as if it were second nature (which, for someone like Julia, it is). But she also makes Julia a disciplined and mature young woman who is still, by virtue of age and inexperience, just naïve enough to be poised between asserting herself and following the lead of a dude she should have steered clear of. “The Julia Set” isn’t some moralistic cautionary melodrama. It’s a true drama about how Julia, like all of us at some point, falls into a thorny experience she’s not ready for, and how it shapes her.

Popular on Variety

The other piece of news, though, is that Niki Byrne, who wrote and directed the movie (her first feature), is a star in her own right — a born filmmaker who knows how to lure the audience in ways both heightened and supple. She’s every bit as sharp a dialogue writer as she is a director. “The Julia Set” could be called a coming-of-age movie, and it certainly has a lot to say about the insidious qualities of a bad romance, but part of its excitement is that it’s not every day that we get to see the convincing tale of a math genius. Julia’s off-the-charts intelligence, which Infiniti embodies with exquisite conviction, changes the stakes of the movie; we’re rooting for her emotional salvation, but we’re also rooting for her to dazzle the universe with her talent. The film could have been called “Good Willa Hunting.”

Infiniti makes Julia a brilliant but grounded person who has very little ego invested in her talent. When her freshman TA, Pascal, takes a special interest in her, and starts to flirt with her, we feel the tension even more than we would have 10 years ago, because the very notion that a TA would try to date one of his students is more of an official no-no than it used to be. Yet Julia is aware of all that. And even as the film is too, it shows us we why she and Pascal are drawn to each other. They’re both beautiful, and they’re beautiful math geeks, which means that they’re actually the rare people who can understand each other. Niki Byrne stages their heady shop-talk exchanges with a flippant density that keeps us hanging on every word.

It doesn’t take us long to pick up on the dynamic that’s going to toxify this relationship. Pascal is turned on by Julia’s intelligence. But he’s also subtly, insanely competitive with it. He invites her to join his advanced study group, presided over by the demanding Dr. Zatlan, played by the German actress Nina Hoss with a stern hauteur as mesmerizing as it is misanthropic. She’s training the members of the study group to enter the Putnam Competition, a fabled math test, consisting of just 12 questions (it’s been around for 100 years), that is widely considered to be the most difficult math test ever devised. The school is competing in it as a team, but so is each individual. For Julia, it could mean a ticket to MIT, a school she actually got into (along with Harvard and the University of Chicago and several others), but here she is attending her modest local college instead, because it’s the place that offered her the best scholarship, and she wanted to stay near her family: her loving mother (Carmen Ejogo) and beloved older brother, Evan (Alex Dillard), who has Down syndrome.

The first sign that something is up with Pascal — apart from the fact that no movie character since the age of John Hughes can look like this without being serious trouble — is when he performs disappointingly on a sample test, only to stalk out of the class, slap himself in the face, punch the bulletin board, and yell “Fuck!” It only gets worse from there. Some viewers, schooled in the new absolutist morality, may say: With red flags being waved in her face, why doesn’t Julia just ditch this loser? But what the movie is saying is: It doesn’t always work that way. Byrne stages a superb sequence in which Pascal takes Julia to meets his parents. His father is a legendary mathematician, Aleksander Mandelbrot, played by Jason Isaacs in the most sly performance he has ever given. We can see that Aleksander is a narcissist who gets off on competing with his son, but what a magnetic dick! The scene in which he plays chess with Pascal is brilliantly done — we see their whole life story in that game. And Pascal’s mother, played with mournful spirit by Gillian Anderson, humanizes the whole situation.

Chase Infiniti leads us through “The Julia Set” by making her performance a true character study. Her Julia is cool and cunning and together; she’s also in over her smarter-than-everyone-else’s head. She wants to be a prodigy, a worldly success, a devoted daughter, and to be in love — all good things. But in this movie they’re often in extreme conflict. And Infiniti makes Julia radiant in that very confusion. There is, of course, a climactic math competition. There is Adderall abuse and a car accident, and there is some next-level gaslighting. There are reckonings. Yet it all flows, because Niki Byrne unfurls this story with such panache and precision yet such effortless conviction. It’s clear that Byrne, along with Chase Infiniti, is going to be a major player. Just watch the movie and do the math.

title: Lil Durk Acquitted in Murder-for-Hire Trial
summary: A Los Angeles federal jury on Friday found Grammy-winning rapper Lil Durk not guilty of murder-for-hire, conspiracy and stalking resulting in death charges in the 2022 killing of rapper Quando Rondo’s cousin, according to the Los Angeles Times. Prosecutors alleged that rapper (real name: Durk Banks) directed hit men to target rapper Quando Rondo, born […]
content:
A Los Angeles federal jury on Friday found Grammy-winning rapper Lil Durk not guilty of murder-for-hire, conspiracy and stalking resulting in death charges in the 2022 killing of rapper Quando Rondo’s cousin, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Prosecutors alleged that rapper (real name: Durk Banks) directed hit men to target rapper Quando Rondo, born Tyquian Bowman, for revenge after the death of his friend Dayvon Bennett, a.k.a. the rapper King Von. However, prosecutors claimed, the gunmen fatally shot Bowman’s cousin Saviay’a Robinson at the crowded Los Angeles shopping mall the Beverly Center. Prosecutors said three gunmen fired 18 rounds at the vehicle in which Bowman and Robinson were riding.

Popular on Variety

Deandre Wilson and David Lindsey, who prosecutors claimed was one of the gunmen, were also on trial and were convicted on the charges of conspiracy to commit stalking, stalking using a dangerous weapon and stalking resulting in death, but were acquitted on the murder-for-hire charges. Wilson’s attorney had claimed that he was just a “passenger” during the murder.

One prosecutor, Assistant U.S. Attorney Ian Yanniello, said, “No one is saying he was the one on the ground with a gun in his hand in Los Angeles, but you know this story doesn’t happen without him, and it doesn’t make sense without his leadership,” adding that Durk “used his money, his power, and his influence to try to kill his biggest opp.”

The prosecution relied largely on testimony from three cooperating witnesses: Kacey Hester — also known as OTF Jam — and Keith Jones, as well as Durk’s former assistant Kavon Grant.

Defense attorney Brian Steel described the three as unreliable “snitches, cooperators, rats” hoping to receive lighter sentences.

“[Grant] has manipulated the people in this case, he has manipulated the FBI, the LAPD, and respectfully, has been manipulating the members of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” said another defense attory, Drew Findling. “Well, folks, it is time for you to say … ‘He will not manipulate us.’”

Durk, 32, is a key figurehead in the Chicago drill music scene, which has spawned numerous rap stars including Chief Keef, Lil Reese and G Herbo. His past five solo albums debuted in the top five on the Billboard 200, and his 2023 single “All My Life” featuring J. Cole hit No. 2 on the Hot 100. Earlier this year, that song won a Grammy for best melodic rap performance.

The incident that allegedly spurred the shooting took place in Atlanta in 2020, after Bennett scuffled with Bowman outside a hookah lounge and was fatally shot by someone in Bowman’s entourage.

The trial was a media circus, with crowds of fans and tourists surround the courthouse and celebrities including Kanye West and the rapper MGK turning up to support Durk.

title: Ocean Way Festival Canceled In Santa Monica Due To Beach Erosion & “Can No Longer Be Safely Held As Planned”
summary: Ocean Way Festival has been canceled because of beach erosion caused by Hurricane Marie. The two-day festival was scheduled for Saturday, September 26, and Sunday, September 27, with headliners The Killers and Olivia Dean, along with artists like Jack White, Sublime, Alvvays, Khruangbin, Durand Jones & The Indications, and Hiatus Kaiyote. “Due to the impacts […]
content:
Ocean Way Festival has been canceled because of beach erosion caused by Hurricane Marie.

The two-day festival was scheduled for Saturday, September 26, and Sunday, September 27, with headliners The Killers and Olivia Dean, along with artists like Jack White, Sublime, Alvvays, Khruangbin, Durand Jones & The Indications, and Hiatus Kaiyote.

“Due to the impacts of Hurricane Marie, the City of Santa Monica has canceled the inaugural Ocean Way Festival,” event organizers said in a statement on Friday, September 11. “Storm surf and runoff has caused significant beach erosion and the festival can no longer be safely held as planned.”

The statement also noted that “plans are already underway to bring the festival to Santa Monica in 2027,” adding, “Refunds are being processed automatically, and no further action is required on your part. Please allow a few business days for the refund to appear in your account. Thank you for your support. See you soon.”

Watch on Deadline

Other artists scheduled to appear included SG Lewis, 54 Ultra, Hot Chip DJs, DJ Harvey, Austin Millz, Vandelux, Heidi Lawden, Blond:ish, Poolside, Carlita, Good Neighbours, Coco & Breezy, Nala, and Erez.

Ocean Way Festival is not the first L.A.-area festival canceled this year. In August, the inaugural LA Jazz Festival was canceled and postponed until 2027, citing “last-minute public safety and municipal costs associated with the final permitting” of the event, according to a statement NBC4 shared.

The jazz festival included “Jazz on the Beach” concerts at Dockweiler Beach and featured musical performances by John Legend, Janelle Monáe, Parliament Funkadelic featuring George Clinton, Charlie Wilson, Raphael Saadiq, Original Koffee, Terrace Martin, Poncho Sanchez, among others.

title: Gary Oldman Says HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ TV Series Will Be “More Satisfying” Than The Movies
summary: Gary Oldman is weighing in on the HBO adaptation of the Harry Potter saga and says one key difference from the films will make it “more satisfying” for fans. In a new interview, the actor who played Sirius Black across multiple movies in the Harry Potter universe revealed why he thinks the TV series will […]
content:
Gary Oldman is weighing in on the HBO adaptation of the Harry Potter saga and says one key difference from the films will make it “more satisfying” for fans.

In a new interview, the actor who played Sirius Black across multiple movies in the Harry Potter universe revealed why he thinks the TV series will have an advantage over the films.

“We had to cut a lot, and still we could only get the films down to, like, three hours,” Oldman told Entertainment Weekly. “I believe [the TV series is] gonna do it pretty much word-for-word, which I think, as a viewer, would be more satisfying.”

Oldman, who first appeared in the films in 2004’s Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, said that “a lot of character detail was sacrificed,” which the series could develop further.

Watch on Deadline

The actor said he was “grateful” to be part of the Harry Potter franchise, calling it a “phenomenon,” and added, “I don’t think you’re ever gonna see again.”

“When you think of that initial cast, someone in the story who doesn’t get a lot of credit anymore is Chris Columbus, who set the world up and cast it,” he said. “We were extraordinarily lucky to have those people come back again, and again, and again, and literally grow into those roles.”

Oldman would reprise his Sirius Black role with a cameo in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. He then appeared in 2007’s Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix. The actor’s last appearance was a cameo in 2011’s Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows — Part 2.

The Harry Potter series will debut in Christmas 2026 on HBO and stream on HBO Max.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone‘s logline reads, “There is nothing special about Harry Potter – or so his Aunt Petunia tells him. But when a mysterious letter of admission to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry arrives, it opens the door to a hidden world of magic, friendship and adventure. Yet behind Hogwarts’ enchanted walls lie dark secrets. Harry must find the courage to prove himself against the darkest wizard of all.”

The series stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid, Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom, Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy, Leo Earley as Seamus Finnigan, Elijah Oshin as Dean Thomas, Tristan Harland as Fred Weasley, Gabriel Harland as George Weasley, Ruari Spooner as Percy Weasley, Alessia Leoni as Parvati Patil, Sienna Moosah as Lavender Brown, Finn Stephens as Vincent Crabbe, William Nash as Gregory Goyle, Warwick Davis as Filius Flitwick and Sirine Saba as Pomona Sprout.

title: ‘The View’s Sunny Hostin Defends AI As “New Art Form” Amid “Gatekeeping In Hollywood Around Black & Brown Creative Content”
summary: Sunny Hostin received pushback from her co-hosts on The View as she defended the use of AI in Hollywood. Hostin, who recently licensed her name and likeness to AI company Fountain 0, argued that generative AI should be considered a “new art form,” noting that it can help the entertainment industry show more Black and […]
content:
Sunny Hostin received pushback from her co-hosts on The View as she defended the use of AI in Hollywood.

Hostin, who recently licensed her name and likeness to AI company Fountain 0, argued that generative AI should be considered a “new art form,” noting that it can help the entertainment industry show more Black and Brown representation.

“I partnered with this company because I’ve written a trilogy, and for six years I’ve tried to get my films or my stories made into series and films, and the gatekeeping in Hollywood around Black and Brown creative content is insane,” the former prosecutor said. “I cannot get New York Times best-selling books onto the screen to tell diverse stories to diverse communities.”

She continued, “With AI, that cuts out the gatekeeping. You get to make your film. You get to have a director … It’s a way to go to a streamer and say, ‘Here’s the product. Will you license it? Will you show it?’ It’s a way, I think, to get Black and Brown stories told.”

Watch on Deadline

Joy Behar noted that with AI, “real people are not working,” and Hostin added, “The real people are not getting jobs in Hollywood. Black and Brown actors are not getting the jobs.”

Alyssa Farah Griffin jumped on Behar’s point and said, “I worry you’re closing the doors to those roles being played by Black and Brown actors and being replaced by AI.”

“That would be great if the studios would not gatekeep and allow the stories to be told,” Hostin replied.

Griffin also said generative AI is “pulling from intellectual property of all the existing actors out there,” and they aren’t getting residuals for it.

One thing that’s for sure is that the AI “train has left the station,” as Hostin said, who added, “This is something that’s here. It’s not going away, and I think that there are going to be enormous benefits.”

Ana Navarro asked Hostin whether she felt any ethical issues with working with an AI company, and Hostin said she “thought about it a lot” before signing away her likeness.

“I think that diverse stories need to be told,” Hostin said before Behar interjected to say, “We’ve said that already. I’m saying that those same people that you’re worried about are now out of work.”

Hostin defended that point, saying, “I’m not the person putting them out of work because the studios just won’t make these projects.”

Behar then said, “Force them to do it rather than have a robot replace Black people in movies.”

Hostin closed out the topic, saying, “I don’t think it’s ever going to take away the arts. I think it’s a different art form.”

Watch the full exchange from The View in the video below.

title: Gary Oldman Predicts HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Series Will Be ‘More Satisfying’ for Fans Than the Movies
summary: Gary Oldman, who played Sirius Black in four “Harry Potter” movies, said he believes HBO’s forthcoming TV series adaptation set in the Wizarding World will be a bigger crowd-pleaser than the Warner Bros. films. That’s because the movies were significantly abridged from J.K. Rowling’s original books, whereas HBO’s “Harry Potter” is including far more of […]
content:
Gary Oldman, who played Sirius Black in four “Harry Potter” movies, said he believes HBO’s forthcoming TV series adaptation set in the Wizarding World will be a bigger crowd-pleaser than the Warner Bros. films.

That’s because the movies were significantly abridged from J.K. Rowling’s original books, whereas HBO’s “Harry Potter” is including far more of the source material, the British actor said in a recent interview with EW.

“We had to cut a lot [for the ‘Harry Potter’ movies], and still we could only get the films down to, like, three hours,” Oldman said, adding that “a lot of character detail was sacrificed” in the process. “I believe [the HBO series is] gonna do it pretty much word-for-word, which I think, as a viewer, would be more satisfying.”

Popular on Variety

Oldman has previously opined that Sirius Black, a character he loves, did not get enough screen time in the movies. “He wasn’t in it enough. He turned up and then he went through the veil,” Oldman told IndieWire in 2024. Oldman’s Black first appeared in 2004’s “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban,” but he had only cameos in “Goblet of Fire” and “Deathly Hallows Part 2″ and a brief appearance in “Order of the Phoenix” before his character is killed off.

That said, Oldman told EW he is “proud” and “grateful” to have been part of the “Harry Potter” films “because it is such a phenomenon, the like of which I don’t think you’re ever gonna see again.”

“When you think of that initial cast, someone in the story who doesn’t get a lot of credit anymore is [director] Chris Columbus, who set the world up and cast it,” he said. “We were extraordinarily lucky to have those people come back again, and again, and again, and literally grow into those roles.”

Oldman will next appear in Season 6 of Apple TV’s “Slow Horses,” which premieres Sept. 16.

Season 1 of HBO’s “Harry Potter” TV show has wrapped and will premiere on HBO and HBO Max on Dec. 25. The second season, which will be based on the second book in Rowling’s beloved fantasy series, is currently in pre-production at Leavesden Studios outside London.

HBO has not announced casting for the role of Sirius Black in the series to this point. The cast of HBO’s “Harry Potter” series includes Dominic McLaughlin in the title role alongside Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley; John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore; Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall; Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape; Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid; Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom; and Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy.

Meanwhile, Oldman once said that his performance as Sirius Black in the movies was “mediocre,” but he later clarified that he didn’t mean to “disparage anyone out there who are fans of ‘Harry Potter’ and the films and the character who I think is much beloved.”

“What I meant by that is, as any artist or any actor or painter, you are always hypercritical of your own work,” he told Variety in 2024. “If you’re not, and you’re satisfied with what you’re doing, that would be death to me. If I watched a performance of myself and thought, ‘My God, I’m fantastic in this,’ that would be a sad day.”

title: Jeremy Thomas, Legendary British Producer and Oscar Winner, Dies at 77
summary: Jeremy Thomas, one of the film industry’s most highly respected independent producers with a body of work spanning more than half a century, has died. He was 77 years old. According to his team, Thomas passed away peacefully at his country home in Oxfordshire late on Friday Sep 11, surrounded by his family and loved […]
content:
Jeremy Thomas, one of the film industry’s most highly respected independent producers with a body of work spanning more than half a century, has died. He was 77 years old.

According to his team, Thomas passed away peacefully at his country home in Oxfordshire late on Friday Sep 11, surrounded by his family and loved ones.

Across his career, Thomas — who founded the Recorded Picture Company and later co-founded Hanway Films — helped bring to life more than 80 features, championing the work of both international cinema and daring auteur filmmakers in the process.

Among numerous accolades and awards, Thomas won a best picture Oscar for Bernardo Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor” in 1988, one of nine Academy Awards for the film. He would make features across 17 years with the Italian director, one of several filmmakers with whom he’d have enduring working relationships.

Popular on Variety

Within his vast library of films, Thomas also produced Jonathan Glazer’s debut feature “Sexy Beast,” David Cronbenberg “Crash,” Christopher Hampton’s “A Dangerous Method” and Nagisa Oshima’s “Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence.” Other directors he collaborated with, many across multiple films, would include Jim Jarmusch, Stephen Frears, Julien Temple, Takashi Miike, Matteo Garrone, Werner Herzog, Terry Gilliam, Richard Linklater, Karel Reisz, Phillip Noyce, David Mackenzie, Jerzy Skolimowski, Ben Wheatley and Wim Wenders.

Working to the last, Thomas produced Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard,” starring Rooney and Kate Mara, which premiered at this year’s Venice Film Festival. Meanwhile, at the current Toronto Film Festival, his latest collaboration with Miike, “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” is due to world premiere on Sep 14.

In 2006 Thomas received a European Film Award for Outstanding European Achievement in World Cinema. In 2021, Thomas came to Cannes as the subject of Mark Cousins’ documentary “The Storms of Jeremy Thomas,” recounting his numerous trips to the festival and work as a producer. He recently appeared in Luca Guadagnino’s documentary “Joie De Vivre,” which also premiered in Venice, about the cinema, art, and life of Bertolucci.

The son of director Ralph Thomas (who directed many “Doctor” films) and nephew of Gerald Thomas (who directed all of the “Carry On” films), Thomas was born in London in 1949. He began working in the industry immediately after leaving school, helping in the cutting rooms for films including “The Harder They Come” and “Family Life,” eventually rising to edit Ken Loach’s 1973 TV short “A Misfortune.”

While he originally wanted to be a director, Thomas shifted to producing, with his first producer credit being the 1976 feature “Mad Dog Morgan,” which he made in Australia at the age of 27 for director Phillipe Mora. He later returned to the U.K. and produced Skolimowski’s 1978 horror “The Shout,” the first for his newly-launched Recorded Pictures Company banner. The film went to Cannes, where it competed for the Palme d’Or and won the Grand Prix de Jury prize.

title: Liam Neeson on the ‘Rage’ Behind ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’ and Turning Producer for First Time to Tell Story of Irish Scandal
summary: Liam Neeson was in his home in upstate New York in late 2017 when he was sent a link to a New York Times article about a shameful episode in Ireland’s history. Almost a decade on and he tells Variety he’s “still coming to terms with my reaction to it.” The piece, written by Dan […]
content:
Liam Neeson was in his home in upstate New York in late 2017 when he was sent a link to a New York Times article about a shameful episode in Ireland’s history.

Almost a decade on and he tells Variety he’s “still coming to terms with my reaction to it.”

The piece, written by Dan Barry, laid bare the shocking revelations from a Catholic home for mothers and babies in County Galway on Ireland’s West Coast, where over the course of several decades until the early 1960s almost 800 infants and children had been buried in unmarked graves, unceremoniously dumped in a sewage tank and forgotten about.

At the center of the article was Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian whose tireless dedication and unwavering sense of moral justice, often in the face of indifference (and, in the case of the Catholic Church, resistance), would help bring the appalling story to light. Corless’ work had already sparked national fury in Ireland, but Barry’s words would bring it to a wider, international audience, including one of the Emerald Isle’s most famous stars.

Popular on Variety

“There certainly was a growing rage, an embarrassment,” says Neeson on his first thoughts after reading the article. “I was brought up a Catholic. I was an altar boy for a bunch of years, and I was kind of staggered by it. And, for the first time in my professional life, I remember thinking: ‘Whatever my celebrity status is in this business, I want this story to be shown to more people.”

So “viscerally struck” was Neeson that he decided to take a leap from his prolific on-screen career (he passed 100 film credits a few yearsa go) and turn producer for the first time, optioning the article for what would become “The Lost Children of Tuam” (the same name as the article), which now screens in Toronto having had its world premiere on home soil at the Galway Film Fleidh. “I just had to respond to it a some way,” he says.

Directing from a script by Rebecca Lenkiewicz (“She Said”) is acclaimed Irish filmmaker Frank Berry, best known for “Michael Inside” and, more recently, “Aisha.”

“When I saw those films, I thought — this is the man to tell this story,” says Neeson, who would also bring on board producers including frequent collaborator Jules Daly and Irish powerhouse Element Pictures.

“Frank wonderfully eavesdrops with his camera and allows the story to breathe. And especially with this, you do not want to highlight the horror. You just let the story breathe, and the horror will reveal itself.”

Frank Berry while filming ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’

Berry may have been brought onto the film a few years after Neeson acquired the rights to the article, but says he was instantly “aware of the immense responsibility” involved. “There’s a lot of people in Ireland and throughout the world who are affected by religious institutions, so that was on our minds every single step of the way. How would survivors feel when they’re watching this scene or when they’re listening to this dialog?,” he says. “But we started at the very beginning at the core of the of the film, which is this amazing character in Catherine Corliss, and we let Catherine lead us.”

Speaking at “The Lost Children of Tuam” world premiere in Galway, where she was the star attraction, Corliss — portrayed by Monica Dolan in the film — told the audience about first hearing that Neeson was interested in speaking to her. “And she said she nearly fell off her chair,” says Berry.

Neeson would eventually go to meet Corliss in her home (“I did not arrive by helicopter,” he notes). “And I had a wonderful afternoon just listening to her, assuring her this would come to the screen and for her to please exercise extraordinary patience,” he says. “I said: ‘Schindler’s List’ took over 10 years.'”

“The Lost Children of Tuam” would take almost 8 1/2 years. But it was wait everyone was prepared to make to get it right.

Much of the film was shot in on location in and around the town of Tuam itself — “it was very important for us to be authentic,” says Berry — where the director met a number of survivors of the home. Some of them would go on to appear as extras (Neeson says that, beyond a period where “it was in my head for about 10 seconds,” there was never any question about him starring on screen).

“As with all my films, it’s really important to have lived experience at every part of the process,” says Berry. “It keeps conversations alive and fresh all the time.”

Monica Dolan plays Catherine Corless in ‘The Lost Children of Tuam’

But it wasn’t just those who had connections to that particular home who were drawn to the project and wanted to get involved.

“There’s so many religious institutions in Ireland that have hurt people, and that pain is is very, very palpable in Irish society,” says Berry. “From Mother and Baby Homes but also the secondary school system, even up into the 80s, and the Magdalene Laundries, which were open until the 90s.”

As he notes: “There are survivors everywhere — and that’s why we made the film, and that’s why what Catherine’s doing, is so important. A lot of that pain is is hidden in Ireland and there’s a lot of wounds in Ireland that need air.”

For Corless, her devotion to the story and her support for the film came with on core goal: to excavate the area around the home, to have the children reburied respectfully and for them to be remembered.

“So this is this film is part of that journey, and that’s the goal she’s looking at. And she’ll rest when that happens,” says Berry.

For Neeson, who asserts that “The Lost Children of Tuam” may be his solitary producer credit, he cites a a line from someone else to underline the importance of Corless’ work.

“As the wonderful late Irish journalist, Con Houlihan, once said regarding mortality and memory, ‘to be forgotten is to die twice.'”

title: Maisie Williams Thriller ‘Ignition’ Bought by Saban for North America (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: “Ignition,” the upcoming high-concept thriller led by Emmy-nominated “Game of Thrones” star Maisie Williams, has been acquired for North America. WestEnd Films — which launched the film in Cannes — has closed a domestic deal with Saban on the film, directed by Emmy-nominated filmmaker James Erskine (“Copa 71,” “Billie,” “Sachin: A Billion Dreams”). The deal comes following […]
content:
“Ignition,” the upcoming high-concept thriller led by Emmy-nominated “Game of Thrones” star Maisie Williams, has been acquired for North America.

WestEnd Films — which launched the film in Cannes — has closed a domestic deal with Saban on the film, directed by Emmy-nominated filmmaker James Erskine (“Copa 71,” “Billie,” “Sachin: A Billion Dreams”). The deal comes following international sales including U.K. (Signature Entertainment), Spain (Twelve Oaks), Portugal (NOS), the Middle East (Falcon Films), CIS & Baltics (Arna Media), Eastern Europe and Israel (Forum Film).

Currently in post-production, “Ignition” sees Williams — currently on screens in “Practical Magic 2” — play a woman whose drive to London is thrown into chaos when an anonymous caller informs her that a bomb has been planted in her car. Trapped and cut off from any outside help, she’s forced to follow the terrorist’s instructions, her every move watched, with no choice but to deliver the ticking bomb to its target — the Royal Albert Hall. As the clock counts down, she must use all her wits to survive and, as the synopsis describes, “uncover why she has been entangled in this elaborate terror plot.”

Popular on Variety

The film co-stars BAFTA nominee Rory Kinnear (“No Time to Die,” “The Diplomat”) and Lovi Poe (“Bad Man,” “Seasons”).

“Ignition” — which was filmed using real locations and on live roads using remotely operated multi-camera systems — was produced by Victoria Gregory (“Maiden,” “Man on Wire”), Erskine, Sean Sorensen (“Black and Blue,” “Worth”), Adriel Thomas, Jason Maza (“Twist,” “10×10”) and Mark Stewart (“Heist,” “Escape Plan”). The deal was negotiated by Maya Amsellem, managing director at WestEnd Films, on behalf of the filmmakers, and Bill Bromiley, vice chairman of Saban Films.

“Maisie’s performance leaves you on edge, brilliantly bringing to life James Erskine’s terrific script,” said Bromiley. “We are proud to be a part of it, and to be working with Maya and the team at WestEnd.”

Added Maya Amsellem: “We’re delighted to have Saban on board for ‘Ignition.’ They immediately understood James’s bold vision and the film’s strong commercial potential. It’s a gripping thriller with a fantastic lead performance from Maisie, and we’re excited for North American audiences to experience it.”

WestEnd, which acquired the film under WeLove, its label dedicated to promoting female-driven stories and championing female talent, will continue international sales at TIFF.

“Ignition” was produced by New Black Films under its New Bright Films label, together with Playhouse Pictures, Sharp House and in association with Royal Viking Entertainment, Epic EV Studios, Vectorscope Films and C’est Lovi Productions.

Executive producers include Williams, Michael Safai, Montgomery Blencowe, Jon Levin (“All The Empty Rooms”), Randy Jones Toll (“Roofman”), Steven J. Toll (“Roofman”), Ian Sharp and Pat Wintersgill.

title: ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Director Gabriel Martins on Black Brazilian Representation in His Films: ‘It’s a Life Project To Me, Not Just Cinema’
summary: In 2022, Gabriel Martins made waves at the Sundance Film Festival with “Mars One,” a sprawling ensemble drama chronicling the life of a Black Brazilian family. At that time, the industry was still wrestling with what a post-pandemic future would look like and, despite “Mars One” having a strong festival run, Martins struggled to secure […]
content:
In 2022, Gabriel Martins made waves at the Sundance Film Festival with “Mars One,” a sprawling ensemble drama chronicling the life of a Black Brazilian family. At that time, the industry was still wrestling with what a post-pandemic future would look like and, despite “Mars One” having a strong festival run, Martins struggled to secure financing for his follow-up.

Four years later, with Netflix on board, the director returns to a major festival with “On Behalf of My Son,” world premiering in the prestigious Platform section of the Toronto Film Festival, then heading to San Sebastián, where it plays in competition.

The drama reunites Martins with Rejane Faria, who seesaws between the visceral and the poised in her embodiment of Vicentina, the mother of a bus driver who apparently killed himself and dozens of passengers in a planned suicide crash. As the woman begins to pull at the complicated threads that made up her son’s psyche on the days leading up to the accident, she decides to contact the victims’ families and apologize on behalf of Wesley. “On Behalf of My Son” is produced by Martins’ Filmes de Plástico for Netflix Brazil, and stars Maíra Azevedo, Renato Novaes, Karine Telles, Giovanna Heliodoro, Thalma de Freitas, and Grace Passô.

Popular on Variety

Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s premiere in Toronto, Martins notes how “Mars One” came out at a time when “Brazilian cinema was trying to recover” not only from the impact of COVID-19 but also from the major budget cuts for culture and political instability under the Bolsonaro government. “This partnership with Netflix came at a very important moment,” he notes.

“‘On Behalf of My Son’ was an older project than ‘Mars,’ a project I’ve tried to make possible for many years, but it was very complex,” he goes on. “We needed several locations, a large ensemble; the theme was dense… I think the film comes at a very opportune time. We were ready, as a production company, to make a film this big and make it the best it could be. Those were four years of maturing and making the most of all the doors ‘Mars One’ opened to us.”

Having Netflix’s support gave Martins a much more robust budget and the possibility to deliver a film that remains intimate and heartfelt while also displaying a higher production value – including a memorable crash scene. “Netflix arrived as a partner at a time when the idea was already consolidated, and we had a very strong script,” he says of what the streamer thought of balancing the two. “What you see onscreen was already very clear to us, and they came into the project wanting to support this idea of working on a story that would challenge the audience but was also universal.”

Higia Ikeda, director of films at Netflix Brazil, echoes that thought: “Netflix is proud to partner with visionary storytellers like Gabriel Martins. It’s amazing to see how such a particular Brazilian story can connect with audiences across different cultures.”

“‘On Behalf of My Son’ is a true testament to how sophisticated and diverse Brazilian cinema has become,” she adds. “Through its reflection on grief, solitude, forgiveness, and how life’s encounters shape us, the film invites us all to appreciate the power of human connection. We’re proud to partner with a unique Brazilian production company like Filmes de Plástico to bring such a sensitive and powerful story to the world.”

Courtesy of Denise dos Santos/Netflix

But the film could have ten times its budget and still not work without a central performance as powerful as Faria’s, who is almost unrecognizable onscreen. The duo first met in 2013, when the actress was working with Maurílio Martins, one of the founding members of Filmes de Plástico, on the short film “Quinze.” “My understanding of cinema came from working with them. I left that film and made some more, learned some more, and eventually reunited with Gabriel in ‘Mars One’ and now ‘On Behalf of My Son.’”

“Vicentina was a major challenge, something completely different from anything I had done before,” she adds. “Gabriel didn’t write the character for me, as I was too young for it when he wrote it, but since the film took a decade to get made, I inched a little closer to her in age, and our relationship also narrowed. He knew I could make it work and get her to the place he wanted. I gave all of myself to the role; I became a completely different person.”

Faria credits the “trust” Martins had in her, as well as his sharp direction, with the success of her performance. “We achieved something great and very new when compared to the work we’ve done before. I had a great desire to see a different side of myself, and this character, who required a lot of makeup and had completely different body language, allowed me to step out of myself.”

With “Mars One,” Martins became the first-ever Black director to be chosen by Brazil to represent the country at the Oscars. With “On Behalf of My Son,” the director once again brings a large Black ensemble to the screen, showcasing the strength of Black creatives in a country that still struggles with representation despite having the second-largest Black population in the world, and the largest outside of Africa. Martins cast the film himself, saying it is one of the things that “makes him the happiest” about the project.

“I love watching these people; it was incredible to be on set with these people, and putting them in the spotlight is aggrandizing,” he continues. “It’s a life project, not just cinema to me. It’s a project that involves wanting to see a better world, and that goes through directing people’s gaze to these stories, to interesting people. It makes me want to shoot more and more. Arriving at such a major festival, a festival that has a lot of influence, with this cast, is a great life experience for me.”

Faria emphasizes that working with such a diverse cast “becomes bigger than the film.” “To have the film play [in Toronto], to see the impact on everyone who’s involved makes me so happy, and amplifies the political aspect of it, too.”

“The political comes alongside my well-being and that of all involved,” she goes on. “ We were very, very happy with how we made the film, and we yearned to have our peers with us. When Gabriel offers the opportunity of having a majorly Black ensemble, he turns a desire we have all had for so long into a real possibility: the desire not to walk alone. To not experience success alone, but to bring others with you. Opening these doors is so important. It is a major step, and it says a lot about not only what we have already achieved but what we are yet to achieve.”

“On Behalf of My Son” will open in select cinemas in Brazil Nov. 5, arriving on Netflix globally Nov. 20.

title: First Clip of ‘Club Kid’ Star Jordan Firstman as U.S. Voice Cast Lead in Cannes Breakout ‘Jim Queen’ (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Jordan Firstman, fresh off directorial debut “Club Kid” – acquired by A24 for release this November – leads the English-language voice cast of “Jim Queen.” Variety reveals the exclusive first clip here: The animated comedy, directed by Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athané, premiered at Cannes to rave reviews. Variety’s Guy Lodge called it a “hilarious rare […]
content:
Jordan Firstman, fresh off directorial debut “Club Kid” – acquired by A24 for release this November – leads the English-language voice cast of “Jim Queen.”

Variety reveals the exclusive first clip here:

The animated comedy, directed by Marco Nguyen and Nicolas Athané, premiered at Cannes to rave reviews. Variety’s Guy Lodge called it a “hilarious rare shot of broad comedy that plays like a queer ‘South Park’ on literal steroids.”

“Club Kid,” which Firstman starred in, wrote and produced, also took Cannes by storm, sparking a bidding war.

Popular on Variety

He’s currently in production on Season 2 of the hit HBO series “I Love LA,” and has also starred in FX’s “English Teacher” and Mubi’s “Rotting in the Sun.” He’s represented by UTA, The Lede Company and Frankfurt Kurnit Klein & Selz.

Firstman is joined by Mateo Lane, currently on his third international stand-up tour, “We Gotta Catch Up!” Most recently, Lane made his Broadway debut as Billy Flynn in “Chicago” at New York’s Ambassador Theatre, the longest-running American musical in Broadway history.

Nicole Byer (“Nailed It!”), John Cameron Mitchell (“Hedwig and the Angry Inch”), Bob the Drag Queen (“We’re Here,” “RuPaul’s Drag Race”) and Wendie Malick (“Shrinking”) round out the cast.

M’saada Nia and Wolfie Trausch lead casting and recording of the English language version of the film, while Moby and Lindsay Hick’s Little Walnut is producing the English-language version alongside Bobbypills.

Global Constellation is privately screening the English-language version, featuring the U.S. voice cast, to North American buyers at TIFF over the weekend, as U.S. distribution rights are currently in negotiation.

Following its buzzy Cannes premiere – which Thierry Frémaux hailed as “one of the most beautiful in the festival’s history in terms of atmosphere, comparable to what ‘The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert’ once was” – the film was released in French theaters by The Jokers Films on June 17, debuting at #3 at the box office – behind only “Toy Story 5” and “Backrooms.”

To date, “Jim Queen” is edging close to 400,000 admissions and $3 million at the French box office, and is rolling out theatrically across more than 25 international territories in the months ahead.

U.S. distribution rights remain available and are currently in negotiation.

Produced by Bobbypills founder David Alric and Arthur Delabays, “Jim Queen” starts when Heterosis, a mysterious virus that turns gay men straight, sweeps through the Parisian gay scene. Jim, the six-packed sovereign of the Gym Queens, goes from Pride royalty to social outcast. With only Lucien, a freshly out twink with more heart than abs, still by his side, Jim must race to find a cure before the disease erases the community that once worshipped him.

Co-written with Simon Balteaux and Brice Chevillard, “Jim Queen” is produced by Bobbypills, one of Europe’s leading adult animation studios. It’s behind James Gunn’s “Creature Commandos,” the first television series and first official chapter of the DC Universe, for DC Studios and Warner Bros. Animation.

Its credits also include “Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix,” produced with Ubisoft Film & Television for Netflix, as well as the adult animated series “Crisis Jung” and “Vermin,” both streaming on Netflix.

“Let’s face it – gay guys are obsessed with the way we look. It can be tough in this world, because you have to be in shape and you have to be young. I’m 43, and guys look at me differently,” Balteaux told Variety back in May.

“I used to be a Gym Queen myself. Now, I’m going to be a Daddy. It’s the next step, so I’m making fun of myself too. Although I’ll still go to the gym tomorrow.”

Nguyen added: “There’s a lot of toxic masculinity in the gay community, too. You think it’s enough to say you’re gay, only to realize you don’t fit the standards because you weigh too much. It was very liberating to write this, and to write these jokes, because we talked about what we’ve experienced.”

Co-produced by Umedia (“The Count of Monte Cristo,” “Night of the Zoopocalypse”), it’s executive produced by Moby and Lindsay Hicks for Little Walnut in the U.S., and Katarzyna Janiak and Jacek Świgost for Timeless Studios, Arthur Cohen for Momentum Entertainment, and Fabien Westerhoff for Global Constellation.

“I guess we made a political film, but it’s also because laughter can be a weapon,” said Balteaux.

“We’re very lucky – we live in a country where ‘Jim Queen’ could be made. But we still think of those in Senegal and trans people, also in the U.S. Maybe it will lighten their reality a little.”

title: Nashville Board Approves Renaming Airport For Dolly Parton
summary: Nashville International Airport is a step closer to being renamed to honor the late country superstar Dolly Parton. The six-person board of the Metro Nashville Airport Authority voted unanimously on Friday to approve the proposed renaming. Details, such as the exact wording of the new name, are still to be hashed out in the coming […]
content:
Nashville International Airport is a step closer to being renamed to honor the late country superstar Dolly Parton.

The six-person board of the Metro Nashville Airport Authority voted unanimously on Friday to approve the proposed renaming. Details, such as the exact wording of the new name, are still to be hashed out in the coming months.

“Today, the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority voted unanimously, 6-0, to begin the process of modifying the airport’s name in honor of Dolly Parton,” the board said in a statement. “While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated.”

The vote, the statement explains, is the first step “in a multifaceted process.”

Watch on Deadline

“In the coming months,” the statement continues, “we anticipate having more definitive plans to share regarding the next steps and implementation. We are grateful for the tremendous support and enthusiasm from our community and Dolly’s fans around the world. We look forward to sharing additional details as plans are finalized.”

Parton died August 25 following a cancer diagnosis that became public only after her death. Her passing prompted a massive outpouring of grief and tributes from across the world.

Following Parton’s death, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced plans to rename the airport in her honor, noting, “At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”

The renaming, though, was first proposed last year, with a petition for the move signed by more than 175,000 people. Among the signees was singer Sheryl Crow.

Changing the name could take some time, and considerable amounts of money. The New York Times estimates that the cost of the renaming would be in the millions of dollars.

title: How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’
summary: Slow Horses star Rosalind Eleazar says she fights hard for roles that “people don’t immediately assume I could play.” The latest example of this is her titular role in Misty Green, the new film from director-writer-producer Chris Rock, in which he also stars. Misty Green is a Hollywood actress who no longer has the town at her feet. […]
content:
Slow Horses star Rosalind Eleazar says she fights hard for roles that “people don’t immediately assume I could play.” The latest example of this is her titular role in Misty Green, the new film from director-writer-producer Chris Rock, in which he also stars.

Misty Green is a Hollywood actress who no longer has the town at her feet. A fast and loose substance abuse lifestyle has knocked her down from acclaim to disdain and forced her to beg for even minor auditions. Yet, Misty is like “a jaguar” — to use Eleazar’s term. She swirls around Los Angles with a swaggering brio that belies her penurious circumstances.

“If someone was to give you a breakdown of Misty Green I wonder if they would immediately go, ‘Rosalind Eleazar for that part?’” she tells me via Zoom from the Dolomites region of the Italian Alps. “I think people may associate me more with, I don’t know, something like being a lawyer,” she says. So Eleazar felt going after the role was “a long shot”, but she connected to Misty the moment she read Rock’s script. More importantly, she wanted the part. “It’s a dream role,” she says.

Watch on Deadline

Bigger names than hers were chasing it too.

Having seen her work on stage and screen since the beginning of her career — which includes appearances on stage with the likes of Matthew Broderick and Ralph Fiennes; holding her own playing a memorable Yelena opposite Toby Jones, Richard Armitage, Aimee Lou Wood and Ciarán Hinds In Uncle Vanya at the Harold Pinter Theatre in the West End, and in The House of Bernarda Alba with Harriet Walter at the National Theatre and many TV films and series — Misty Green is undoubtedly the outstanding performance of her career, and by far one of the year’s best.

The East-London-based actor admits “there were tears. I was crying when I thought I didn’t get it… As an actor, one thing I do share with Misty is that you go on this roller-coaster of emotions after you’ve auditioned and it’s out of your hands now, and the next day, you’re like, Oh, I think today I might get a call, and you just live in this endless hope. Then three days go by… So your emotions are constantly going like that,” she says.

She’s in the Dolomites on a hiking holiday with her producer and actor husband Gabriel Lo Giudice (The Wanderer: Destinations Unknown) ahead of arriving in Toronto for TIFF, where she’s planning to meet up with Gary Oldman and some of the acting team behind the motley crew of Apple TV’s Slow Horses.

Then, on Saturday, September 12th, comes Eleazar’s big night — Misty Green will have its world premiere at Roy Thompson Hall.

Rosalind Eleazar in ‘Misty Green’ A24

Next month, the movie will have galas during the BFI London Film Festival and A24 will give Misty Green a limited release from October 9th. Daniel Kaluuya, Adam Driver, Anna Kendrick also star.

Looking back over the whole auditioning process, Eleazar is incredulous over what she put herself through. Still waiting to hear whether or not she’d landed the role, she was in her London apartment “meditating, and I was trying to connect and talk to Chris in my mind,” she reflects with a rueful grimace then a smile. “At one point I genuinely thought I had connected to him, and then whilst I was on set, I said to Chris, ‘Do you remember? Did you ever at one point feel me talking to you?’ He just looked at me and went ‘No,’” she sheepishly divulges.

”You’re lucky if roles like Misty Green come once in a lifetime,” she says, “and I’m so happy that that somehow has worked out for me.”

After two auditions over Zoom in London, the London Academy of Music & Dramatic Art graduate flew to Los Angeles for chemistry tests with Rock, who plays a director who understands that hidden beneath Misty’s armor of pain is an artist with proper talent.

Once the part was hers, Eleazar sprang into action. She took singing lessons — performing “One Night Only” from Dreamgirls is one of the movie’s many highlights — and Rock tasked her with watching some movies, including Klute with Jane Fonda and Donald Sutherland.

An aspect of Eleazar’s performance that fascinates me is the sultry physicality with which she infuses Misty. “I move very differently to Misty,” she says, explaining how the 5Rhythms method played a significant role in developing her walk for the movie. The 5Rhythms practice is a movement and dance practice created by Gabrielle Roth intended to liberate the mind and body.

Eleazar played around with where she felt Misty’s natural tempo stood.

Rosalind Eleazar. Photo: Will Aldersley

“Obviously, throughout the day and through the course of whatever, her tempo changes,” she says, noting that Misty “has quite a lot of sexual energy to her.” The way Misty moves, Eleazar remarks, marks her as “someone that is also wanting to be noticed and someone that is wanting to be respected.”

Eleazar broke out the Misty walk on the streets of LA. “It has to become like second nature, rather than something that on the day of film you suddenly feel self-conscious with because it’s not in your body,” she says. The street test helped her pare down the walk to what she describes as “a floaty staccato,” which allows Misty to “turn corners incredibly fast.” That means, Misty can catch you off guard, giving her a quite languid quality until she springs like the “jaguar” label Eleazar gave her.

Eleazar, who studied Spanish, Mandarin and psychology at the U.K.’s Nottingham University, says she has “a lot of compassion generally for people that come out into the world punching and surviving, and they have these layers upon layers of protection because of whatever’s happened early on in their life, and they’re not immediately likable or lovable, and it takes time to love Misty. She’s not someone that you necessarily easily warm to.”

Eleazar is generally drawn to larger-than-life characters, she says. In all her parts, from her Jacky Bast in Kenneth Lonergan’s 2017 television adaptation of Howards End onwards, she suggests there’s a commonality. “They’ve all been quite big in some way,” she says. “They’re eccentric and sort of Shakespearean, and I find that I enjoy looking for the humanity in those sort of larger-than-life characters.”

Two days prior to auditioning with Rock in LA, she’d read with Ralph Fiennes in London for Rebecca Lenkiewicz’s play Small Hotel, which premiered at the Theatre Royal in Bath with Fiennes and Francesca Annis in the fall of 2025. There’s a slim chance of it transferring into the West End in 2027, if scheduling doesn’t get in the way.

Rosalind Eleazar in ‘Small Hotel’ Marc Brenner

For some reason Judi Dench becomes a topic in our conversation. When I remark that I still replay in my head the Cleopatra the great dame performed opposite Anthony Hopkins in Shakespeare’s Antony and Cleopatra at the National Theatre in 1987, Eleazar’s eyes light up. “Cleopatra is my dream role!” she cries. She’d love to play Medea and Elektra too.

Surely working with Oldman, Saskia Reeves, Jack Lowden, Kristin Scott Thomas, Ruth Bradley, Christopher Chung, Aimee-Ffionn Edwards, Kadiff Kirwan and others on Slow Horses is like being in a theatrical repertory company, because they all come from theater backgrounds?

Nodding admiringly, she says that the cast often takes tea with Oldman who “sort of watches over all of us and is interested in you and what you’re doing and is always a champion of your work.”

She connected with Kaluuya in part because they both hail from the theater, although Misty Green is the first time they’ve worked together. “We would take lots of long walks together and discuss our shared history for the characters and also sharing our own stories. And he’s just an insane actor… I love dangerous actors — Anna [Kendrick] and Adam [Driver] too — you feel you can jump off together and see where you land,” she says, adding that her scenes with Kaluuya were incendiary. “Every take was so different and that beautiful trust you have with someone…”

In the film, Rock’s character raises questions about racism and sexism in Hollywood but those subjects are not the film’s main concerns, a point that Eleazar concurs with. “Misty Green isn’t about race,” she says. However, she and Rock did have a conversation about it. “I think that there are places for different types of films, and this character was able to just exist, and there’s a universality to her. It didn’t matter that she was my skin color, that’s not the leading narrative of the film,” she says.

And off screen whenever she has “potentially experienced certain things” related to race “I privately deal with it, and I kind of think to myself, well, let my work do the talking. I would love to be known as someone that is a solid actor rather than other things. But it doesn’t mean that I’m unaffected by it. Let’s say I’m not unaffected by sexism and racism in our industry,” she says.

If Misty Green takes off for her the way I feel it will, then Eleazar’s going to be very busy. Could she move to Hollywood for work? She has an American passport. “I can I can work there if I started doing a lot more American projects and if it made sense. I do love living in London though, and still loads of shows are made out of the U.K. and in Europe.”

Smiling, Eleazar looks directly at me and says: “This sounds incredibly cheesy, but when part of your dream is starting to become true, it’s actually also quite frightening, because you’re like, oh my gosh, I have portrayed this character in this movie, and I’m incredibly proud of all of our work. And it’s now at the stage of sharing with other people, and it feels exposing. But at the same time, I’m incredibly excited by it, and I’m feeling grateful. What an opportunity I had. And Chris giving me that opportunity — it was a long shot.”

Misty Green will premiere 9.30pm, September 12th at Roy Thompson Hall at the Toronto Film Festival.

title: Kling AI’s TIFF Market Panel Illuminates Tech Challenges and Human-Led Solutions in AI Filmmaking: ‘The Script Is Still the Blueprint’
summary: Kling AI hit the opening morning of the inaugural TIFF: The Market with a lively, well attended panel, “A New Creative Paradigm: Consistent, Cinematic AI Video Powered by Kling AI,” geared towards a Canadian industry audience of animation and live-action film creators eager for up-to-date insight into their roles and human skills in rapidly evolving […]
content:
Kling AI hit the opening morning of the inaugural TIFF: The Market with a lively, well attended panel, “A New Creative Paradigm: Consistent, Cinematic AI Video Powered by Kling AI,” geared towards a Canadian industry audience of animation and live-action film creators eager for up-to-date insight into their roles and human skills in rapidly evolving production workflows.

The panel, moderated by Tony Pu, Kling AI’s head of creator community and industry partnerships, Europe and North America, continued the discussion started at Kling AI’s Cannes Film Market session, where the company announced it had signed on as exclusive global technological brand partner on Evolutionary Films’ animated feature “Minibots.”

Direct from the frontlines, “Minibots” producer and co-founder of Evolutionary Films Diane Shorthouse and AI filmmaker and founder of Amissa Studios Issa Sissoko (who has worked and consulted for the likes of Antoine Fuqua, Darren Aronofsky, and Doug Liman) discussed the practical realities of AI-assisted filmmaking with a focus on existential aspects of the work. Both panelists and their teams utilize tools from Kling AI’s AI creative productivity platform.

Popular on Variety

The fundamental job of a producer is still to serve the director’s creative vision, Shorthouse said, but the tools are different.

“The script is still the blueprint, so I’m not thinking about prompts, I’m thinking about shots,” she said. “Where does the camera need to go? What does the performance need to be? What does it need to cut to? What are the elements or the assets that we need to get there? Who has the best skills [and] where could be using AI artists to do that?

“We start with production designers to design what’s happening. We’ll generate 20 shots of something, and 19 are going to be wrong. But those 19 are important. It’s human judgment that you need to know what’s wrong.”

When pre-visualizing scripts with producers and directors, Sissoko is helping producers and directors not only identify potential problems but also make smart decisions on what needs to be filmed and where money needs to be spent.

“We collaborate with VFX teams as well,” he said. “They might have something ready in 3D, and they want us to kind of slap the skin on it, give them an overall idea of what the cut might look like.”

In hybrid production, Sissoko says the challenge today is reducing dependence on what the AI model generates, finding ways to blend the AI with the real footage in seamlessly. “Getting the AI to not only keep the actor’s performance intact but add to it is very tricky,” he said. “That’s one of the things that I work on.”

In both animated and live-action film contexts, the panelists agreed that greater control in AI film workflow environments is what they’re looking forward to in the coming months. “I need them to obey me more,” Shorthouse said, prompting an amused reaction from the panel and audience. “So if I say, I want this character here in this costume in this environment but just change the eye line, I just want it to just change that not everything else.”

“Every 90 days there’s a huge improvement – I mean, if you’re going from three-second-generated videos to 15 seconds with more consistency across the board,” said Sissoko, who got into the industry making concept trailers, which he uses as an example. “If you can take a pitch deck, have a conversation with a producer and cut together a trailer that gets the story picked up, you are creating work for a lot of people, you’re helping make someone’s dream come true.”

Shorthouse’s advice to emerging filmmakers in the room is to hands-on learn the craft. “Know what shots you want, how things work from cameras to lighting to performances, and then experiment with AI,” she said. “And put all your knowledge of filmmaking into the prompts.”

Sissoko said he tells people who are starting to use AI in filmmaking that learning to write is the most crucial skill. “Before anything, learn how to write stories. [It] will help you with the prompts, as well.”

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Becomes Universal’s Highest-Grossing Film of All Time
summary: On a box office voyage for less than two months, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has become the highest-grossing film in the history of Universal Pictures. The 114-year-old film company announced the milestone on Saturday, when the Matt Damon-led epic’s weekend haul will bring its domestic earnings to $601.2 million, with an international tally of $1.083 […]
content:
On a box office voyage for less than two months, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has become the highest-grossing film in the history of Universal Pictures.

The 114-year-old film company announced the milestone on Saturday, when the Matt Damon-led epic’s weekend haul will bring its domestic earnings to $601.2 million, with an international tally of $1.083 billion in ticket sales. That’s a grand total of $1.68 billion around the world and a slew of records set along the way.

“What Chris and Emma [Thomas] have created will go down as one of the most ambitious and brilliantly executed films in cinematic history. A generational event that galvanizes moviegoing itself,” said Donna Langley, chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment.

Popular on Variety

Nolan’s meticulously hand-crafted movie, shot across the globe and starring some of the biggest names in Hollywood, recently reclaimed the top box office position in its eighth weekend in theaters. The project represents the biggest opening of Nolan’s career, ahead of “The Dark Knight Rises,” and is now the Oscar winner’s highest-grossing film ever. It was produced by Thomas and Nolan via their Syncopy banner, with executive producer Thomas Hayslip.

More superlatives: “The Odyssey” is the top-grossing R-rated film in history, as well as the biggest earner ever for IMAX. While based on 3,000-year-old IP, the movie is the first non-sequel film to gross over $1 billion overseas since 2009.

It’s not just an undeniable victory for Nolan. Earlier this summer, Variety reported about the legacy marker “The Odyssey” represents for Langley. She brought Nolan into the Uni fold after his decisive departure from Warner Bros. in 2021, paving the way for the best picture winner “Oppenheimer” and, now, the best picture hopeful “Odyssey.”

This weekend’s numbers further cements Universal’s box office dominance in 2026, leading all studios with 26% of the market share and grossing nearly $5 billion to date in 2026. The studio is the first to cross $4 billion at the global box office this year and the first to cross $3 billion at the international box office.

title: Courteney Cox on Her TIFF True-Crime Drama ‘Evil Genius’: ‘The Story Is So Unbelievable’
summary: Courteney Cox feels as if she was meant to be a director. “I notice everything,” she says. “I love actors, I love people, I love human stories.” Cox is best known for acting — including marquee roles in “Friends” and in the “Scream” franchise. But she’s long had a hand in directing, from episodes of […]
content:
Courteney Cox feels as if she was meant to be a director.

“I notice everything,” she says. “I love actors, I love people, I love human stories.”

Cox is best known for acting — including marquee roles in “Friends” and in the “Scream” franchise. But she’s long had a hand in directing, from episodes of her sitcom “Cougar Town” to music videos to the 2014 feature “Just Before I Go,” and she stepped behind the camera once again for “Evil Genius,” which debuts as a gala presentation at the Toronto Intl. Film Festival Sept. 12.

With “Evil Genius,” which dramatizes the people and plots behind the “pizza bomber” tragedy in 2003, Cox says she was inspired by “what I would consider my first film,” the Lifetime movie “TalhotBlond.” That film, which Cox directed, was adapted from a 2009 true-crime documentary of the same name by Barbara Schroeder, which probed a love triangle that ended in death. Tapping into true crime again, Cox was inspired by Schroeder’s 2018 doc series “Evil Genius: The True Story of America’s Most Diabolical Bank Heist,” which tackled the infamous pizza bomber case, in which the compelling and clever Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong seemed to mastermind a plot to send a patsy in to rob a bank outside Erie, Pa., with a bomb strapped around his neck.

Popular on Variety

“The choices these people made were so absurd,” Cox says. “I really wanted to go deeper and find out, Why? Why were these their choices?” But Cox’s vision hewed away from the darkest version of the story: “I wanted to have some sort of understanding for these characters, and I wanted the film to be really bright.”

What results is a snappy modern noir in the vein of a Coen brothers film: Patricia Arquette, as the overseer of utter mayhem, is at her snappy, domineering best, alternately alluring and terrifying. “We weren’t reduced to either loving or hating her,” Cox says. “We were uncovering all parts of her.”

Cox had the good luck of access to “hours and hours of tape” from the Schroeder documentary series, and they informed Arquette’s performance — as did a certain inherent humanity.

“I can see Patricia’s heart,” Cox says. “It beats right out of her chest. Every time Patricia laughs, it’s absolutely real.”

In order for the film to work, the main schemer couldn’t solely be, well, an evil genius. “You don’t want to just hate someone the whole time,” Cox says.

Recent Emmy winner David Harbour, as the man still trapped in Arquette’s thrall even after their romantic relationship has ended, has, Cox notes, “a boyish charm” — a quality the film harnesses to tragic ends, as Harbour’s overgrown boy is susceptible, still, to manipulation.

Constructing the cluttered homes through which Arquette’s and Harbour’s characters romp and plot, Cox was in a sort of heaven. “I suffer from acute awareness,” she says, “because it’s very hard for me to not notice everything around me.
