It’s a blessing and a curse — I call it my superpower, but it also keeps me late.”

The plot to rob the bank is hatched in a home in which very few things have ever been thrown away. “Lifetimes of collections of junk,” Cox says with glee. “It was perfect for me, because I was able to get in there and actually make it look the way my vision of a hoarding house would look.”

In the end, though, the film came down to the human story. Arquette’s character “can be a very over-the-top, me, me, me, selfish lady,” Cox says. The tapes aided in providing a lens into the side of her she didn’t share with her conspirators. “We needed to find the humanity, and her vulnerability.”

Though the film is drawn from a notorious crime story, Cox is hopeful that at least some of the audience will come in fresh: “Anyone I’ve shown this film to,” she says, “says that the story is so unbelievable, it drives you to want to know more.”

title: ‘Sámi Blood’ Director Amanda Kernell Explores Forgiveness in ‘Brace Your Heart’: ‘It Can Be a Matter of Survival’
summary: “Brace Your Heart” director Amanda Kernell is ready to talk about forgiveness.  “What can be forgiven? And what if you live in a place where everything has to be, because it can be a matter of survival?,” she wonders. In Kernell’s new film — unspooling at TIFF and the San Sebastián Film Festival — young […]
content:
“Brace Your Heart” director Amanda Kernell is ready to talk about forgiveness.

“What can be forgiven? And what if you live in a place where everything has to be, because it can be a matter of survival?,” she wonders.

In Kernell’s new film — unspooling at TIFF and the San Sebastián Film Festival — young Ejva (Elli Sara Valkeapää) is forced to tend to her late father’s reindeer herd. Her family depends on her, but she’s struggling. She accepts help from Heaika (Andte Gaup-Juuso) while falling for his cousin. But it comes at a price.

“How do you free yourself from trauma, both as an individual and as a group, when you’re so dependent on each other? You can leave everything behind, but there must be another option. Even though you might still have to stay with the people who put you through something violent,” says the director.

Popular on Variety

The film, sold by TrustNordisk, premiered its trailer with Variety here.

Kernell, who has Sámi roots, previously talked about her community in “Sámi Blood.”

“It’s not just some problem I ‘made up’ for my character — it’s something I see in real life. I really want to know what the solution is,” she stresses.

“In reindeer herding, which most of my family on my father’s side does, you have to work together. It’s a matter of life and death. There’s no phone coverage, the ice is thin and the weather changes all the time.”

She adds, “There are many suicides in this world, but there are also people who are surviving and finding the light on the other side.”

She took the title from a saying meant to prepare young Sámi reindeer herders for a difficult future.

“You need to harden your heart in order to survive. Maybe that’s how you get through difficult things, traumas and death — and a life that’s very close to death. But it’s not the path to love,” notes Kernell.

Ejva doesn’t want to do that either: “She can’t allow her heart to harden.”

Kernell says, “In film school [Kernell graduated from the National Film School of Denmark], they used to say: ‘Why did the Gods choose this specific person to go through all this? Because they needed it.’ It sounds brutal, but she needed it — just to find her way up.”

She adds: “This is very nerdy, but in psychology, they say that words can free you. There might be a point to confrontation. When you talk about what you fear the most, something might change inside of you. Your nightmare can go away. It makes me hopeful.”

Kernell wanted to reflect the realities of the reindeer herding, which required a larger scale than she was used to.

“With my cinematographer, Sophia [Olsson], we had to deal with helicopters, snowmobiles and trains. We wondered: ‘We are only interested in emotions, so why are we filming all these snowmobiles?’ But there are places that scream loneliness, and we tried to find them,” she recalls.

“I’ve always admired my cousins, who have been doing this since we were teenagers. According to some statistics, it’s the deadliest profession in Sweden after being an army pilot. I wanted the film to be achingly close to reality. You see a teenager moving reindeer alone on a mountain. It’s not CGI.”

The film made her think about how we define our value through work.

“There’s this fear: What if I lose my ability to work? Who am I then? Many people feel this way,” she points out.

“I hadn’t thought about this before, but when I made [second feature] ‘Charter,’ I had a severe concussion. I couldn’t read, I couldn’t see. Everything was blurry for months. Being a reindeer herder who can’t work properly must be like being a director who can’t see. Fortunately, I can do it again.”

title: Kamila Andini Says Anger Is ‘Liberating’ as She Brings Furious ‘Four Seasons in Java’ to Toronto
summary: Kamila Andini’s “Four Seasons in Java” is her fifth feature film, but this marks her third time at the Toronto Film Festival after “The Seen and the Unseen” (2017) and “Yuni” (2021) that won the Platform Prize and became Indonesia’s official Oscar entry.  It follows Pertiwi, starring Putri Marino (“Cigarette Girl”), who comes back to […]
content:
Kamila Andini’s “Four Seasons in Java” is her fifth feature film, but this marks her third time at the Toronto Film Festival after “The Seen and the Unseen” (2017) and “Yuni” (2021) that won the Platform Prize and became Indonesia’s official Oscar entry.

It follows Pertiwi, starring Putri Marino (“Cigarette Girl”), who comes back to her hometown after being held in prison for 20 years for killing a young man in self-defense during an attempted rape.

This marks Andini’s second collaboration with Marino after “Cigarette Girl.” Marino had already been cast when Andini was still writing the screenplay before they even filmed the Netflix sensation.

Popular on Variety

The Indonesian auteur is known for her tender portrayal of women’s struggle, but this film may be her most furious work. “I didn’t think I was that furious, but as I was researching for a script, I wanted to curse a lot,” Andini explains. She adds that while the subject is frustrating, she needs to express anger as it can also be liberating.

During the preparation process, Andini recalls an intensive period of character development with Marino. “This may be my film with the most character workshops,” she says. Set in a fictionalized town reminiscent of a Western, the film required Marino to train Pertiwi in a range of skills, from horseback riding and handling electricity to fighting.

For Indonesian filmmakers, film festivals have become an important gateway to the international market, helping introduce the country’s cinema to global audiences. “Indonesia is nobody’s top of mind when it comes to Asian cinema,” Andini says. “We’re not even top of mind in Southeast Asia, as Thailand and the Philippines are recognized more,” she adds.

That’s also why Andini and many other Indonesian filmmakers have been actively participating in international project markets. For them, these platforms are no longer just about securing financing, but also about introducing Indonesian stories and culture to the international industry and building greater familiarity with the country’s cinema.

Another strategy Andini has adopted is creating separate festival and theatrical cuts of her films. When she submitted “Yuni” to TIFF in 2021, feedback from her international partners suggested that the film had too many characters. She reworked the film, cutting several characters from the festival version.

Her first film at TIFF, “The Seen and Unseen,” had few characters; she cut some in “Yuni,” but in “Four Seasons in Java,” she doesn’t hold back. Instead, she wants the international audience to experience the vibrancy and communal spirit of Indonesian society.

“Four Seasons in Java” does not have a festival cut. This time, Andini brings many characters without cutting them.

Despite this, Andini is aware that Asian characters can sometimes appear visually similar to North American audiences, so she worked with costume designer Hagai Pakan (“Cigarette Girl”, “Yuni”) to give each character a distinct visual identity

“Four Seasons in Java” premieres in Toronto before coming back to Indonesia on Oct. 8. The film will also play at the Busan International Film Festival

title: ‘Being Heumann’ Producer Kevin Walsh Readies Star Vehicles For Paul Rudd & Sam Rockwell, Series With Casey Affleck: TIFF
summary: EXCLUSIVE: In the wake of a splashy Thursday night TIFF opening night premiere of the Sian Heder-directed Being Heumann, producer Kevin Walsh has two star vehicles happening quickly. He’s next readying Reasonable People, a drama that Cory Finley will direct with Paul Rudd and Sam Rockwell starring. On the series side is The Hawk, which […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: In the wake of a splashy Thursday night TIFF opening night premiere of the Sian Heder-directed Being Heumann, producer Kevin Walsh has two star vehicles happening quickly. He’s next readying Reasonable People, a drama that Cory Finley will direct with Paul Rudd and Sam Rockwell starring. On the series side is The Hawk, which will mark the first major TV series starring vehicle for Casey Affleck. Walsh produced Manchester By The Sea, the film which won Affleck his Oscar and reunited with Affleck on The Instigators.

The Hawk is a crime thriller for Hulu, written by Dave Collard, with Walsh exec producing along with Collard, Affleck, Davey Holmes, Danny Feldheim, Patrick McNamara and Rob Hochberg. Adapted from the Brian Haig-authored book series that began with The President’s Assassin, Affleck will play Sean Drummond, a brilliant JAG lawyer brought in by the CIA after six people are systematically shot and killed in a private DC mansion. Discovering the executions were just a warning shot, Drummond has 72-hours to unravel the conspiracy and prevent a national crisis.

Hulu has committed to shoot a pilot, and the network has ordered other scripts and will likely green light a first season by January. Series is part of a TV slate Walsh Co has assembled under TV group head Danny Feldheim.

Watch on Deadline

On the film side, Cory Finley’s Reasonable People script will be taken to market seeking backers, with Rudd and Rockwell starring and Walsh lead producer. Pic is a Hatfield-McCoy-style feud set in a contemporary suburban setting. The drama begins after a reckless car crash leaves an architect’s teen daughter brain-damaged. The driver is the son of a wealthy developer, and the tragedy ignites a bitter war of revenge between fathers. It quickly spirals out of control and threatens to destroy both families. Rudd plays the architect and Rockwell plays his drifter brother who shows up after the accident and escalates the stakes between the warring families.

From left: Casey Affleck, Paull Rudd, Sam Rockwell Getty Images

Walsh ran film for Ridley Scott’s Scott Free before hanging his own shingle and establishing Apple as his base. He has hatched projects including the Hikari-directed Foster The Snowman, and the Justin Lin-directed That Man From Rio, to star Sydney Sweeney.

Walsh ran Scott Free when the director legend made such big scale films as Napoleon, House of Gucci and The Last Duel. Being Heumann — which Walsh produced alongside director Heder, David Permut, John Beach and Kevin Cleary – brought logistical challenges all it own. And it was harder than Heder’s previous film, the Best Picture Oscar winner CODA.

Being Heumann chronicles Judy Heumann as she galvanized a group of handicapped activists into a 28-day takeover of the Federal Building in San Francisco. The goal was to put pressure to have signed into law legislation that would force government buildings to give accessibility to the handicapped. The results were historic; it changed the world for a group kept invisible because of the inability to get access able-bodied folks took for granted. One of the challenges of shooting the film was to accommodate a cast led by Ruth Madeley, most of whom have physical disabilities. Heumann’s is a true hero tale but there is virtue in how Heder could have followed CODA with a mainstream film and a big payday. Instead, she struggled to mount a movie that once again shines a light on people who are too easily marginalized or forgotten.

“There were 12 disabled leads and 40 disabled cast members on certain days,” Walsh told Deadline. “We had to produce a movie within the movie. That’s the real story here, how Sian took all the political capital in Hollywood that she had after she won Best Picture and was like, “Where can I assert this?” She was offered Marvel movies, big franchise movies, you name it, she could have had her pick. But she chose to tell the story that she was really close to. And I think the thing about Sian is, she’s such a rare bird. She can write, she can direct, but she’s also an incredible leader. She’s relentless and so exacting about getting it right. And it’s such a great thing where you have the combination of those three things, and a determination to do things with care and painstaking detail.

“She will not stop until something’s absolutely correct,” Walsh said. “She’s charming and funny and people love her and they like getting behind her. What impressed me most was how she wouldn’t stop and trying to make it better and better and better. But I think she’s drawn to movies about people who have been counted out. She gets behind that and it speaks to who she is as a person.”

Apple, which acquired CODA as it was becoming a Sundance Festival sensation, staked Heder from the beginning on Being Heumann, and it could be another awards season sleeper for Apple. Though it is period – the cast had to surrender their more comfortable wheelchairs for the ‘70s versions that were spectacularly uncomfortable – it is impossible to watch the federal building takeover and not feel that it was a righteous version of the January 6 storming of the Capitol in DC, after a MAGA crowd, emboldened by Donald Trump’s baseless claims of election fixing. They broke into the Capitol to try and stop the certification of Joe Biden’s presidency, assaulting officers with bear spray and brute force. The Heumann-led group took what for them was an extreme action – they called themselves ‘radical crips’ – in pursuit of basic human rights. Theirs was a peaceful protest, and eventually they got the populace on their side. The cast all knew that, and sacrificed to bring that struggle to the screen.

“Because this is a 1977 period movie, we had to transfer them from their normal wheelchairs to period wheelchairs we retrofitted,” Walsh said. “We were giving them breaks every couple hours, getting on-demand masseuses, making sure they had the right nutrients and the right food. If you experience a spinal cord injury, there’s this disrupted communication between the brain and the spinal cord that creates spasms. I found myself one day clutching the hand of one of our actors, Antwan Tolliver, as he’s riding out a spasm because nobody else was there with him. We had this team circling these people at all times, making sure they were healthy and Sian created this world of support.

“The most poignant story, there’s this brilliant actor named Michael Patrick Thornton, who was just on Broadway with Keanu Reeves, and who is a disabled actor,” Walsh said. “He had been working for 25 years in the movie business, and we got him into a makeup trailer one day. We had ripped the end off the makeup trailers and put doors in place and then put lifts outside the trailers so the cast could access it. And this seasoned actor starts to cry and we all wondered what was wrong?

‘He goes, “I’ve been working 25 years and I’ve never seen the inside of a makeup trailer, ever.” It was his first time. And so we did all that work to create this environment where everybody felt like they were the same. That is something we are all very proud of, creating that world.”

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Slays ‘Jurassic World’ To Become Universal’s Highest Grossing Movie Ever At Global Box Office With $1.68B
summary: By the end of this weekend, The Odyssey will have crushed the ultimate record, becoming Universal’s highest grossing movie ever at the global box office with $1..684 billion. The pic will sail above Universal’s previous record-breaker, 2015’s Jurassic World which ended its run at $1.677 billion. By Sunday, The Odyssey will count $601.2M million domestic and […]
content:
By the end of this weekend, The Odyssey will have crushed the ultimate record, becoming Universal‘s highest grossing movie ever at the global box office with $1..684 billion.

The pic will sail above Universal’s previous record-breaker, 2015’s Jurassic World which ended its run at $1.677 billion.

By Sunday, The Odyssey will count $601.2M million domestic and $1.083 billion international becoming the 12th highest-grossing film ever and the third-biggest non-franchise title of all time.

The Odyssey experienced an amazing 6.33x multiple at the global box office and returned to the No. 1 position globally in its eighth weekend, dropping only 9% domestically.

Watch on Deadline

As we’ve reported, The Odyssey quite some time ago became Christopher Nolan’s highest grossing movie of his career, both domestic (clicking past Dark Knight‘s $534.9M) and worldwide ($1.085B).

“What Chris and Emma [Thomas] have created will go down as one of the most ambitious and brilliantly executed films in cinematic history. A generational event that galvanizes moviegoing itself,” said Donna Langley, Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment.

Among the records that The Odyssey has broken:

Opening

-Biggest opening for director Christopher Nolan ahead of Dark Knight Rises internationally and globally ($139.6M international, $264.1M worldwide).

-Biggest opening weekend for Imax 70MM domestically ($6.3M)

-Biggest Universal R-rated opening weekend domestically ($123.5M).

Cume:

–Highest-grossing film for director Christopher Nolan domestically, internationally and globally.

–Highest-grossing R-rated film of all time (beating Deadpool & Wolverine‘s $1.33B).

–Highest-grossing film ever for Imax ($486M+ WW).

–First non-sequel and non-remake to gross over $1 billion internationally since 2009.

–Second-highest-grossing film of the year (after Sony’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day which is approaching $935M+ by Sunday).

In addition to this global milestone, The Odyssey is also the highest-grossing Universal Pictures film of all time in 45 international markets, including Australia, France, Italy, India and Korea. The Odyssey remains the second-highest grossing Universal Pictures film domestically behind Jurassic World ($653.4M).

Universal continues to lead all major studios with more than $4.92 billion to-date. The studio was the first to cross $4 billion at the global box office this year and the first to cross $3 billion at the international box office.

title: ‘The Family Stone’ Sequel Set At Searchlight With Claire Danes, Rachel McAdams, Sarah Jessica Parker & Many More Returning
summary: Some exciting news heading into the holiday season: Searchlight has announced a sequel to the beloved 2005 holiday film The Family Stone, with nearly the entire cast returning. This includes Claire Danes, Rachel McAdams, Dermot Mulroney, Craig T. Nelson, Sarah Jessica Parker, Luke Wilson, Tyrone Giordano, Elizabeth Reaser, Paul Schneider, and Brian White. The one big […]
content:
Some exciting news heading into the holiday season: Searchlight has announced a sequel to the beloved 2005 holiday film The Family Stone, with nearly the entire cast returning.

This includes Claire Danes, Rachel McAdams, Dermot Mulroney, Craig T. Nelson, Sarah Jessica Parker, Luke Wilson, Tyrone Giordano, Elizabeth Reaser, Paul Schneider, and Brian White.

The one big exception is of course Diane Keaton, who passed away in October 2025 at the age of 79.

The new film, titled The Families Stone will seemingly pay loving tribute: It picks up 20 years after the death of her character, matriarch Sybil Stone — something that was depicted in the original film — as the Stone family again reunites for Christmas, only to face the season’s biggest surprise: their father (Nelson) has unexpectedly invited the woman he’s fallen in love with to meet the family.

Production is set to take place in New York this fall.

Watch on Deadline

Nelson reprises as patriarch Kelly Stone, with Danes back as Julie Morton, McAdams as Amy Stone, Mulroney as Everett Stone, Parker as Meredith Morton, Wilson as Ben Stone, Giordano as Thad Stone, Reaser as Susannah Stone, Schneider as Brad Stevenson, and Brian White as Patrick Thomas.

Tom Bezucha has returned to direct from his own script, with original producer Michael London back to produce alongside Shannon Gaulding for Groundswell Productions, along with Parker and Alison Benson for Pretty Matches Productions.

SVP of Production Taylor Friedman and Creative Executive Daniel Yu are overseeing the project for Searchlight Pictures, reporting to Heads of Production and Development DanTram Nguyen and Katie Goodson-Thomas.

Celebrating its 20th anniversary last year, The Family Stone watches as Everett Stone (Mulroney) brings his tightly wound girlfriend Meredith (Parker) home to meet his liberal, bohemian New England family over the holidays. A disastrous visit leads to romantic complications, shifting loyalties and the revelation that Keaton’s Sybil is terminally ill.

A heavily rewatched Christmas favorite, the film grossed over $92M worldwide in its December 2005 release with 20th Century Fox. Parker was nominated for a Golden Globe for her performance.

She’s repped by CAA — which also reps filmmaker Bezucha — and Schreck Rose Dapello.

Danes is repped by Signpost Management, WME, and Ziffren Brittenham; McAdams by WME and Magnolia Entertainment; Mulroney by Paradigm; Nelson by UTA and Forward Entertainment; Wilson by WME; Reaser by UTA; Schneider by Innovative Artists and Finley Management; and White by Buchwald and Zero Gravity Management.

title: Brian Duckworth Dies: Country Musician, Member Of Taylor Made Band Was 56
summary: Brian Duckworth, the country musician who performed with his brother and sister as the band Taylor Made, died Monday, September 7, at his home in Clarksburg, W. Va. He was 56. His death was announced by family. A cause of death was not disclosed. Taylor Made, which featured Duckworth, his brother Greg Duckworth and sister […]
content:
Brian Duckworth, the country musician who performed with his brother and sister as the band Taylor Made, died Monday, September 7, at his home in Clarksburg, W. Va. He was 56.

His death was announced by family. A cause of death was not disclosed.

Taylor Made, which featured Duckworth, his brother Greg Duckworth and sister Wendy Williams, released its single “Things You Don’t Grow Out Of” in 2012 and, the following year, was named by Nashville’s MusicRow Magazine as Independent Artist of the Year. The siblings would opens for such major acts as Dierks Bentley and Miranda Lambert.

Watch the official video for “Things You Don’t Grow Out Of” below.

Watch on Deadline

While the band continued to perform, Duckworth would keep his job as a dump truck operator.

“He was the ‘Truck Boss,'” his family wrote in announcing his death, “a job he truly enjoyed because it allowed him to spend his days outdoors. Whether working or relaxing, Brian was happiest surrounded by nature.

“Music was also a special part of his life,” the statement continues. “He loved to sing and proudly performed with his family band, Taylor Made. Brian never passed up an opportunity to share his voice, earning him the affectionate nickname ‘Nashville’…Brian’s love of family, music, and the outdoors will forever remain in the hearts of all who knew and loved him.”

In a Facebook tribute, Duckworth’s niece, Brianna Duckworth Kazner, wrote, “I grew up watching my dad, Aunt Wendy, and Uncle Brian perform at fairs and festivals until I was finally old enough to join them on a few occasions. As I’ve gotten older and started writing my own music, I knew the guy to call whenever I got creatively ‘stuck.’ He truly had such a way with song lyrics that I knew without a doubt Uncle Brian would pull me out of the songwriter’s slump.”

Duckworth is survived by wife Tina Scheuvront Duckworth; six children, four grandchildren, and five sisters and brothers.

title: Jeremy Thomas Dies:  Legendary UK Producer Of ‘The Last Emperor’ & ‘Crash’ Was 77
summary: Jeremy Thomas, one of the UK’s most prominent independent film producers of the last 50 years, died on September 11. He was 77 years old. His family announced his death in a statement on Saturday. “Jeremy Thomas, the celebrated British producer of The Last Emperor and of over 40 other films, has died, at the […]
content:
Jeremy Thomas, one of the UK’s most prominent independent film producers of the last 50 years, died on September 11. He was 77 years old.

His family announced his death in a statement on Saturday.

“Jeremy Thomas, the celebrated British producer of The Last Emperor and of over 40 other films, has died, at the age of 77,” it reads. “Thomas passed away peacefully at his country home in Oxfordshire late on Friday 11th, surrounded by his family and loved ones.”

Thomas racked up more than 80 credits over his career including Nagisa Oshima’s Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence, Bernardo Bertolucci’s Oscar-winning The Last Emperor, Jonathan Glazer’s Sexy Beast and David Cronenberg’s Crash.

News of Thomas’ death broke on the final day of the 83rd Venice Film Festival, featuring Werner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard in the main competition on which Thomas was a producer.

Watch on Deadline

At the festival press conference last week, Herzog credited Thomas for coming up with the idea of casting Kate and Rooney Mara in the lead roles of two sisters who act and speak as one at heart of the drama, enabling him to move on with the 40-year gestated project.

Thomas also appeared as interviewee in Luca Guadagnino’s seven-hour documentary Joie de Vivre. Notes, Thoughts, Words, Reflections, Faces, And Visions Concerning Bernardo Bertolucci And The Cinephilia Of The 20th Century That No Longer Exists, with Hanway Films, the sales company he owned for decades before it was sold to Charles Cohen, taking on sales ahead of its Venice premiere.

Thomas was born on July 26, 1949, into a filmmaking family. His father directed more than 40 features including classics such as The 39 Steps and many of the pictures in the comedic Doctor franchise, while his uncle Gerald Thomas was known for the Carry On films.

After school, he took various jobs in the film industry, eventually moving into editing to take assistant editor credits on films such as The Harder They Come and The Golden Voyage of Sinbad and first assistant editor on Ken Loach’s A Family Life.

He moved into producing in 1974 with the Australia-shot feature Mad Dog Morgan, starring Dennis Hopper.

Shortly after, he founded the London-based independent production house, Recorded Picture Company (RPC), kicking off its activities with Jerzy Skolimowski’s The Shout, which won the Grand Prix de Jury at the Cannes Film Festival in 1978. He would go on to found production and foreign sales company Hanway Films in 1998 with Peter Watson and Stephan Mallmann.

Early highlights of his prolific career included Nagisa Oshima’s Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence (1983), starring David Bowie as a prisoner of war in a Japanese camp; Nicolas Roeg’s Bad Timing (1983) and Eureka (1984) and Insignificance (1985) and Stephen Frears’ The Hit.

A crowning achievement was Bertolucci’s epic independently-financed picture The Last Emperor, which took three years to make and went on to win nine Oscars in 1987 and become a commercial success.

Thomas would continue to work with Bertolucci, producing The Sheltering Sky (1990), Little Buddha (1992), Stealing Beauty (1996) and The Dreamers (2003).

One of his most talked about productions was David Cronenberg’s 1996 adaptation of J.G. Ballard’s novel Crash, which sparked a backlash when it world premiered in Cannes in 1996 and then became mired in a censorship battle.

The Cannes habitué Thomas was also the subject of a documentary, Mark Cousins’s The Storms Of Jeremy Thomas, in which the writer and director accompanied the producer on his annual pilgrimage to the festival.

In an interview with Deadline’s Disruptors magazine ahead of the film’s premiere in Cannes in 2021, Thomas said there were a number of Ballard books he still wanted to adapt, but added, “My time is limited”.

Thomas was a revered and widely beloved figure in the global film business, as passionate and knowledgeable a film producer as you could find, and someone for whom cinema was far more than a career. It was a way of life. This was never truer than during his annual pilgrimage to the Cannes Film Festival, where he launched so many films. He would set off from London in an old motor car — another of his passions — and drive down to the Riviera, often with friends including Luc Roeg, son of Nicolas Roeg.

In Cannes, Thomas would do his business from the same Carlton suite, a stage he occupied for decades, entertaining the great and the good of the film business.

Thomas was also known for throwing great parties in Soho, the area he made his home for so many years out of his famous HanWay street office. He was widely known for being a gentleman, a shrewd businessman, a true film lover and someone who made cinema his life.

“Based in London throughout his career, but a dedicated internationalist in taste and temperament, Thomas worked with directors from all over the world (Japan, Italy, Germany, the USA, Canada, Poland, Australia),” read the statement announcing Thomas’ death.

“He was celebrated by them as a dedicated enabler of auteur work at the highest level. He received an Outstanding European Achievement in World Cinema awar from the European Film Academy in 2006,” it continued.

“The roll call of international directors includes: Bernardo Bertolucci, David Cronenberg, Matteo Garrone, Jerzy Skolimowski, Nagisa Oshima, Richard Linklater, Bob Rafelson, Jim Jarmusch, Takeshi Miike, Terry Gilliam. But he was also instrumental in fostering the early careers of many great British directors, producing highly ambitious work: from Jonathan Glazer, Stephen Frears, Julien Temple, Ben Wheatley and David Mackenzie. He was working to the last – his latest collaboration with Takeshi Miike premieres in Toronto on Monday — the 14th September.”

Miike’s Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is world premiering as a Special Presentation. Further upcoming films include Becoming Capa, which is currently in post-production.

In his later years, Thomas suffered from cancer but continued to work tirelessly. He was married twice, first to Claudia Frohlich (m. 1977; div. 1981)​ and then to Eski Thomas née Vivien Coughman in 1982. He is survived by his wife and three children, Jessica, film and TV agent Jack, and Joshua.

Andreas Wiseman contributed to this report.

title: ‘Oasis’ Review: A Sleek, Strange Parable about Bullying and Bonding at the Most Difficult Age
summary: The difficult teenage years are sometimes characterized as a wasteland, but more resemble a forest for the interdependent trio at the sinking heart of Jannis Lenz’s “Oasis,” the German-born, Austrian-trained filmmaker’s creepy, controlled debut feature. Retreating to the woods surrounding their German hometown, three ostracized high-schoolers create an arcane shared reality that provides them with […]
content:
The difficult teenage years are sometimes characterized as a wasteland, but more resemble a forest for the interdependent trio at the sinking heart of Jannis Lenz‘s “Oasis,” the German-born, Austrian-trained filmmaker’s creepy, controlled debut feature. Retreating to the woods surrounding their German hometown, three ostracized high-schoolers create an arcane shared reality that provides them with comfort, support and the opportunity to explore boundaries in a uniquely non-judgmental way. But Lenz’s steady, sorrowful film radiates ambivalence about whether that’s a good thing or whether, in finding each other, these kids will be lost to the world. That’s the thing about forests; you can lose sight of them for the trees.

Lukas (Florian Geißelmann) is a quiet boy: sensitive, artistic, keeps to himself. Basically, all the descriptors that, after the fact, people use to describe a school shooter, apply to him, right down to a rarely seen, perfectly delinquent lop-sided smile. Yet he is not actively unpopular, despite the significant teenage handicap of having a father, Martin (Godehard Giese) — Lukas’ sole parent since the not-too-long-ago death of his mother — who is a teacher at his school. It is only when Lukas befriends big, wounded Andi (Anton Petzold) the son of a soldier recently posted to the base nearby, that he sees his small store of social capital start to dwindle. It doesn’t bother him too much initially, he can always rely instead on his best friend, Maya (a breakout Mathilda Smidt) who lives, apparently un-parented, in a big, airy house nearby and attends a specialist music school. Maya’s vocal exercises, as her class practise their plosives and sibilants, open the film on an appropriately strange, rhythmic note.

Popular on Variety

Cinematographer Alexander Dirninger (who also co-wrote the elegantly spare screenplay with Lenz) observes the slow-building action with such cool, detached dispassion that it always takes some time to understand the behavior we’re watching. This habit of withholding — that does get a little wearing during a stretched-out middle third — is unsurprising, given that Lenz apprenticed with some of the major figures from the school of severe Austrian formalism (his movie could be glibly summarized as “Michael Haneke goes to High School.”) It’s a few scenes before we realize, for example, that when Lukas methodically cuts the shoulder pads out of his dead mother’s blouses and tapes them around his torso, he is not acting on some dysfunctional grieving instinct. He’s constructing a homemade flak vest, for when he meets up with Andi in the woods to shoot paintball guns at each other. His taped-up tee is not exactly Kevlar. Lukas comes home with a livid, baseball-sized bruise blossoming on his shoulder.

After that first paintball-gun chase, Lukas and Andi sit in a field smoking cigarettes and barely talking, letting the whomp-whomp from the nearby wind turbines fill the companionable silence — the sound design, by Nora Czamler and Benedikt Palier (who also provides the disquieting, echoey score) is particularly superb. But there is a lot going unspoken here. That very day a video has started to circulate on social media, of Andi being cruelly humiliated by his classmates. In the coming days, he reacts to the mounting taunting with occasional defensive outbursts, that inevitably bring him to the attention of the school authorities.

Lukas, likely afraid of being targeted himself, rarely intervenes (“Why don’t you ever do anything?” Andi will later shout at him). But he does introduce Andi to Maya and somehow, the three of them gel, gently coaxing each other into more and more peculiar, unsavory, sex-adjacent-but-never-actually-sexual games of touching and biting and bruising. Less of an outlet for their inarticulate feelings of shame and anger, these rituals become an inlet, leading them deeper into (possibly unhealthy, but who’s to say?) emotional co-dependence, while estranging them further from their peers.

Martin is alarmed by his son’s surly withdrawal from their amicable father-son dinners and impromptu Guitar Hero sessions. But then all of the adults involved — Martin, the principal, the school staff and the concerned parents of Lukas and Andi’s classmates — believe they know their kids’ best interests, while only having the vaguest notion of what really interests their kids. Lenz’s film draws a faint parallel between the group dynamics among the teens and those among their purported guardians, as though the instinct to make yourself more integral to the herd by picking on its most vulnerable member is one that does not lessen with age, it simply metastasizes into a more sophisticated variant.

In an effort to sway his sympathies away from Andi, the school counselor (Britta Hammelstein) tells Lukas “Sometimes the victim role is a personal choice” which is an insane statement for a therapy professional to make. But no matter, like all efforts to separate them, it only brings the threesome closer together, and toward ever more intimate acts of mutual masochism and self-harm. Are these games a valuable pressure-valve that can defuse antisocial behavior or are they an early stage of escalation to actual, non-consensual, outward-directed violence? Are they an exorcism or are they practise? As Lenz’s taut, self-contained narrative releases some of its rigor in a rather underwhelmingly open-ended final act, it does give one to wonder what happens to this little club’s arcane rites and secret ceremonies when the safe, accepting space that fostered them turns out to be less oasis than mirage.

title: ‘Diablo 5’ Set for Spring 2029 Release
summary: “Diablo V” is in development at Xbox’s Blizzard Entertainment. The new game is targeting a Spring 2029 release date, Blizzard announced Saturday during the opening ceremony for fan festival BlizzCon 2026 at the Anaheim Convention Center. “Diablo V” will be set a century after the events of “Diablo IV” (which released in 2023) and, in […]
content:
“Diablo V” is in development at Xbox’s Blizzard Entertainment.

The new game is targeting a Spring 2029 release date, Blizzard announced Saturday during the opening ceremony for fan festival BlizzCon 2026 at the Anaheim Convention Center.

“Diablo V” will be set a century after the events of “Diablo IV” (which released in 2023) and, in a first for the video game franchise, take place in a world where Sanctuary has fallen.

According to the description for “Diablo V,” “For the first time, players will enter a Sanctuary where Diablo has triumphed and its heroes have been defeated. At the heart of Diablo V lies a defining question: what must you become when the world has already fallen?”

Popular on Variety

The first “Diablo” was released in 1996, marking 2026 as the 30th anniversary for the franchise. Since then, Blizzard says the “Diablo” games — which now consists of four mainline entries, the most recent being the release of “Diablo IV” in 2023 — have seen more than 130 million players worldwide to date.

“Diablo V” was not the franchise’s only big news revealed during BlizzCon Saturday. Blizzard president Johanna Faries opened the show by announcing a “Diablo” animated TV series is currently in development at Netflix.

Per Blizzard’s statement on the TV project, “After decades of bringing entire universes to life through our games, we’re partnering with some creative powerhouses to tell even more stories beyond gaming across new screens. A new animated series set in the world of ‘Diablo’ is in development with Netflix. More details will be shared in the future, but this is only the beginning, with even more taking shape across our universes.”

Fellow Blizzard brands had plenty to share during BlizzCon 2026’s opening ceremony as well, including news that a new “StarCraft” open-world shooter game is in active development and eyeing a 2030 release.

Variety will be on the ground at BlizzCon Sept. 12-13 and readers can follow along with our coverage of the event here.

Watch the trailer for “Diablo V” in the video below.

title: NFL TV Favorites Like Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Greg Olsen, Kirk Herbstreit Could Play for New Teams Next Season
summary: The NFL is ready to kick off its first Sunday of a new season, but a good part of the game won’t be taking place on the field. Even as play-by-play stalwarts like Fox’s Greg Olsen, ESPN’s Joe Buck and Troy Aikman and Amazon’s Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit give fans real-time details and analysis […]
content:
The NFL is ready to kick off its first Sunday of a new season, but a good part of the game won’t be taking place on the field.

Even as play-by-play stalwarts like Fox’s Greg Olsen, ESPN’s Joe Buck and Troy Aikman and Amazon’s Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit give fans real-time details and analysis for Fox’s Sunday afternoon pigskin sessions, ESPN’s “Monday Night Football” and Amazon’s “Thursday Night Football” they may be thinking about something else. Each of these chroniclers of the gridiron knows his contract with the media company backing their prominent perches ends after the current season, according to three people familiar with the situation.

TV networks rushed to line up top talent to call games after the NFL struck a pivotal 11-year rights deal in 2021. At the time, the thought from many TV sports chiefs was that they had to spend money to make money. Tony Romo carved out new terrain at CBS Sports in 2017 after revealing a knack for predicting game play — all but forcing CBS to re-sign the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback to a multi-season pact in 2020 valued at around $17 million a year.

Popular on Variety

Since that time, most of CBS’ contemporaries have followed suit. When ESPN signed former Fox Sports mainstays Joe Buck and Troy Aikman to deals in 2022 to call “Monday Night Football,” it was seen as a critical move that would help the Disney-backed sports-media giant soothe what had become a troubled relationship with the NFL. Amazon lured NBC Sports’ Al Michaels and ESPN’s Kirk Herbstreit to serve as the voices for “Thursday Night Football.” And Fox secured the services of none other than Tom Brady, a move that crowded out sportscaster Olsen.

Now Fox Sports, ESPN and Amazon must decide whether they need the services of these popular (and sometimes high-priced) veterans going forward, at a time when the NFL appears keen to gain new cash from its relationships with U.S. media companies.

The focus on the booth is different than in years past, when the bigger sports-TV salaries went to the guys crowded around a round table in studio shows like “The NFL Today” or “Fox NFL Kickoff.” “You would never see a big name call games professionally,” says Gideon Cohen, executive vice president of broadcast and new media at Athletes First, a sports management firm. “Now, you have big names that are considering it because of the profile and the amount of money.”

People familiar with the market estimate top football-booth personnel can earn between $15 million and $20 million per season. Fox Sports, Amazon, ESPN and CBS Sports all declined to make executives available for comment.

With media economics in massive flux, some companies may question how much they can pay top announcing talent — and the end of a contract could give them a chance to examine their cash flow. At Amazon, it’s understood that Al Michaels is on a year-to-year contract, while Herbstreit, who also plays a pivotal role in calling college football games for ESPN and makes regular appearances on the popular “College GameDay,” works a superhuman schedule during football season.

“If they make a change there, they may make a change across the board,” suggests Tim Scanlan, vice president of sports broadcast at Octagon, a sports-management and representation firm that is part of Omnicom Group. Indeed, he says, there’s no guarantee that media companies will continue to pay top dollar as the entire sector grapples with exponential increases in many sports rights fees.

“The price of live events just keeps going up,” says Scanlan. As that happens, he adds, “you start to look for savings in production and talent.”

Some companies may not be able to afford ditching their high-priced football analysts. Inside ESPN, it’s widely acknowledged that the decision to lure Buck and Aikman away from Fox has paid dividends. ESPN and the NFL had a rockier relationship when the network fielded what was considered a weaker group of announcers. During the 2018-2019 season, ESPN even dispatched former NFL defensive tackle Booger McFarland to ride an elevated chair set up on the sidelines at the line of scrimmage.

As a result of signing Buck and Aikman, ESPN “did get better games” on the NFL schedule, says Scanlan. “Ratings went up, and they got a couple of Super Bowls” in their most recent NFL pact. “You could argue that it really paid for itself. And my sense is that they’ll be renewed because they’ve got another Super Bowl to handle.” The first Super Bowl to air on ABC in about two decades is slated for February 14, 2027. ESPN has already entered into negotiations with Buck and Aikman to renew their deals, according to a person familiar with the matter.

A tricky situation at CBS Sports could add more drama. Romo will miss at least the first few games of the new season, owing to his arrest for operating a vehicle while intoxicated near Milwaukee over the summer. CBS has elevated studio analyst and former NFL player J.J. Watt to sit alongside the venerable Jim Nantz at the start of this year’s cycle, and has not offered any timeline for Romo’s return. If Watt becomes CBS permanent choice on its top NFL team, it could open other developments.

And then there’s Greg Olsen’s situation at Fox. After Buck and Aikman left, Olsen was elevated to the network’s top NFL calling team. Once Brady arrived, however, Olsen was moved back to the second Fox group. Olsen has been open about his desire to be part a top duo, though there is speculation that Brady, who has many different business opportunities, can’t stick to a season-long role at Fox for many years. At Fox Sports, it’s understood that Olsen does good work and executives are mindful that he has been a team player amid personnel changes.

The TV networks still have reason to please the NFL. The league has an option to renew its current 11-year deals starting after the 2029 season. Keeping top talent in the booth clearly helps relationships with the league, and none of the media conglomerates can afford to lose NFL access altogether. “Nobody wants the NFL product to be weakened,” says Scanlan.

Some new announcer candidates might take the field in the not-too-distant future. What if Travis Kelce, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end who already has an established media presence with a popular podcast, decides to retire?

Still, the networks’ coffers aren’t infinite. The more sports fees go up, the less cash there is for top salaries, new series and more personnel. Eventually, something has to give. That’s when TV companies stop playing football and start considering financial chess. When it comes to the NFL, says Scanlan, “you want to be careful with any decision you make.”

title: ‘StarCraft 3,’ an Open-World Shooter Game, Coming in 2030; First Look Revealed
summary: A new “StarCraft” game is coming from Blizzard Entertainment in 2030 and a first look at the title has already been revealed. While technically “StarCraft III,” the game will be titled “StarCraft.” Per Blizzard Entertainment, “StarCraft” is an open-world, story-driven sci-fi shooter that takes place “decades after the events of StarCraft II” and is “a […]
content:
A new “StarCraft” game is coming from Blizzard Entertainment in 2030 and a first look at the title has already been revealed.

While technically “StarCraft III,” the game will be titled “StarCraft.” Per Blizzard Entertainment, “StarCraft” is an open-world, story-driven sci-fi shooter that takes place “decades after the events of StarCraft II” and is “a brand-new game in the StarCraft universe.”

The original “StarCraft” launched in 1998. The new installment will mark the first mainline title in video game franchise since “StarCraft II: Legacy of the Void” debuted in 2015. This new “StarCraft” game is set in the Koprulu Sector, 70 years after “StarCraft II: Legacy of the Void.”

Per Blizzard Entertainment, “This is just the beginning. Led by Dan Hay, ‘StarCraft’ is early in development, and we’ll have more to share over the coming years, including gameplay reveals, deep dives into the world, and more.”

Popular on Variety

The “StarCraft” news was announced Saturday during BlizzCon 2026 (the first edition of the Blizzard fan-festival event hosted since 2023) at the Anaheim Convention Center. Also revealed at the BlizzCon opening ceremony was an animated TV series adaptation of Blizzard Entertainment’s popular “Diablo” video game franchise, which is currently in development at Netflix.

Variety will be on the ground at BlizzCon Sept. 12-13 and readers can follow along here for our coverage of the event, a celebration of all things Blizzard Entertainment, from “StarCraft” to “Diablo” to “World of Warcraft” to “Overwatch.”

Watch the first teaser for the new “StarCraft” game in the video below.

title: Searchlight’s Matthew Greenfield On Getting People Into Movie Theaters & Finding New Talent On YouTube — TIFF: The Market
summary: Searchlight Pictures boss Matthew Greenfield broke down how YouTube has become fertile ground for finding new stories and filmmakers. The Searchlight Pictures boss also spoke about the battle with familiarity and the need for original ideas to get people into movie theaters in the streaming age. After Obsession and Backrooms, studios and producers are scouring […]
content:
Searchlight Pictures boss Matthew Greenfield broke down how YouTube has become fertile ground for finding new stories and filmmakers. The Searchlight Pictures boss also spoke about the battle with familiarity and the need for original ideas to get people into movie theaters in the streaming age.

After Obsession and Backrooms, studios and producers are scouring YouTube for the next big property originating on the Google-owned video sharing platform.

“YouTube is an incredible resource, and we’re always looking for new storytellers,” Greenfield said.

“One of the things that’s super exciting about [YouTube] is that it used to be that we would find, collectively in the industry, new talent from short films, from first features, from short stories. But all of those had to go through gatekeepers in one form or another.

Watch on Deadline

“With YouTube, obviously, people can go direct and find and build their own audience. And we can find things that wouldn’t have come through the standard [avenues]. So, for sure, it’s an exciting place to find new talent.”

Greenfield was speaking at TIFF: The Market, the Toronto Film Festival’s shiny new film and TV market, which also has a conference strand to take the temperature of the industry.

The Searchlight exec talked about there being a battle with familiarity that needs to be waged to get people into theaters. “Familiarity is the challenge that we have to battle against,” he said. “How do we tell stories that feel new, that feel fresh, that feel interesting, that feel worthy of a theatrical experience?”

He continued: “Everybody has to decide every time they go to a movie: should I pay X dollars, make a real effort, get out of the house, travel, pay to see a movie in the theater, which is a great experience if you’re seeing something you love. Or, should I stay at home and watch everything that has ever been made in the history of human culture?”

Greenfield was speaking at a live recording of industry podcast The Town.

title: Venice 2026 Winners: Best Actress Goes To Mathilde Arcel For ‘Woman Unknown’; While John Malkovich Wins Best Actor For ‘Wild Horse Nine’
summary: Venice Film Festival has kicked off with first prizes announced in the Orizzonti sidebar, Immersive Competition and Venice Classics. In main competition prizes, hotly tipped John Malkovich won Actor for his performance in Wild Horse Nine, which will further fuel to Oscar hopes for the actor. The actor, who is currently on set, was unable […]
content:
Venice Film Festival has kicked off with first prizes announced in the Orizzonti sidebar, Immersive Competition and Venice Classics.

In main competition prizes, hotly tipped John Malkovich won Actor for his performance in Wild Horse Nine, which will further fuel to Oscar hopes for the actor. The actor, who is currently on set, was unable to make to the ceremony so sent a video message instead.

Mathilde Arcel won best actress for performance as a nanny and housemaid hiding a dangerous secret in post World War Two Denmark in May El-Toukhy’s psychological thriller Woman Unknown, the only film directed by a solo female director in competition.

In the Orizzonti section, Best Film went to Ann Sirot and Raphaël Balboni’s Diana in the Loop about a young woman who decides to avenge the rape of her mother, which took place three years before she was born.



Watch on Deadline

Laleh Marzban receives Orizzonti Best Actress Award for “Moragheb (Falling House) Getty Images

Other notable prizes in the sidebar included Best Actress for Laleh Marzban for her brave hijab-less performance in Iranian drama Falling House as a young woman whose dreams of pursuing a modelling career outside of Iran are thwarted by a tyrannical prison guard father.

She dedicated the prize to all the women of Iran declaring in Farsi that the country was going through one of the most painful and difficult times of its history.



“I want to mention the people of my homeland, Iran, who are living under the greatest pressure ever. I would like to dedicate this award to the women of my country, who have paid the highest price for even the smallest form of freedom. Today more than ever, they continue to carry forward their dreams, their courage, and their hope,” she said.

Italian actor Riccardo Scamarcio won Best Actor for his performance in The House of the Monkey as a the father devoted of a disabled son, who becomes increasingly close to his teenage nephew seeing in him the son he always wished for. The film also won Best Screenplay for director Tommaso Landucci and cowriter Damiano Femfert.

Scarmarcio dedicated his prize to all the fathers in the world as well as UK producer Jeremy Thomas whose death at the age of 77 was announced earlier in the day.

The Lion of the Future – Luigi De Laurentiis Award for a Debut Film went to Cameroonian-French director Auguste Bernard Kouemo Yanghu’s House of the Wind exploring the impact of migration to Europe. The drama revolves around 80-year-old Josette who lives alone in Yaoundé, Cameroon, having encouraged her to leave in search of better lives elsewhere.

Tonight’s ceremony, hosted by Italian actors Greta Scarano and Nicolas Maupas, ends a politically charged 83rd edition with a record-breaking ovation for bombshell Israeli documentary Naza and a warm response to Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem in Bunker among the many highlights.

Other memorable moments included Lifetime Achievement Golden Lion Awards for George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn.

Maggie Gyllenhaal and her jury will mete out eight prizes including the Golden Lion for best film. The winners of the Orizzonti sidebar, Venice Classics and Immersive competition, the Lion of the Future – Luigi De Laurentiis Award for a Debut Film, will also be announced this evening.

title: ‘ER’s Big Payday: How Hit Medical Drama Scored Record $13M An Episode From NBC – Book Excerpt
summary: ER was an instant hit when it premiered on NBC in October 1994. But the project had not been an easy sell: it was created by an author, Michael Crichton, with no television record and conceived in a style drastically different from any other medical drama. Add to that a cast of then-largely unknowns and […]
content:
ER was an instant hit when it premiered on NBC in October 1994. But the project had not been an easy sell: it was created by an author, Michael Crichton, with no television record and conceived in a style drastically different from any other medical drama. Add to that a cast of then-largely unknowns and ER coming from an outside studio, indie Warner Bros. Television, and NBC got itself a bargain when it picked up the two-hour pilot to series.

That all changed four years later. With ER dominating the ratings and pop culture and its cast, led by George Clooney, all bonafide stars, NBC had to dig deep into its pockets to keep the medical drama on the air amid interest from rivals CBS and NBC. The dramatic negotiations and their stunning outcome — a new license fee of a whooping $13 million an episode — are being revisited by decorated entertainment journalist Lynette Rice (How To Save a Life: The Inside Story of Grey’s Anatomy) in her latest book, ER: The Oral History, which is being published on September 15 by St. Martin’s Press.

Here is a peek at the chapter about the behind-the-scenes battle, which includes interviews with Bob Daly, who oversaw negotiations on the studio side as Warner Bros. Chairman and Co-CEO; Leslie Moonves, who, as President and CEO of Warner Bros. Television, had developed and sold ER (and Friends) to NBC before becoming President of Entertainment of CBS in 1995; and ER executive producers Christopher Chulack and Jack Orman; with previous comments by former NBC Entertainment President Warren Littlefield.

Watch on Deadline

The High Price Of Healthcare

ER generated many headlines in its early years, but none were quite as astonishing as those that circulated in 1998 when NBC renegotiated the license fee that it paid to air the medical drama. After almost four years of stalled talks, the network finally agreed to fork over an unprecedented $13 million an episode for the drama, or $286 million per year for twenty-two episodes. According to estimates at the time, NBC was making roughly $500 million in profits from the show; the astronomical renegotiation gobbled up more than half of it.

NBC could have gotten away with paying far less for the series; after season 1, Warner Bros. TV had tried to renegotiate the roughly $3 million per episode the network was paying so it could plan for the future and start giving raises to the popular ensemble. But NBC wasn’t ready to haggle over their standard four-year deal. Even though it was raking in big advertising dollars for its Thursday-night lineup that included the pricey Seinfeld, NBC had already renegotiated a new license fee for the Warner Bros.–produced Friends after its first season because comedies typically hold up better than dramas. ER, no matter how impressive its ratings were, would have to wait.

For a fleeting moment, NBC’s lackadaisical attitude left open the possibility that the network was about to lose one of its biggest assets. And Leslie Moonves, who had left Warner Bros. TV soon after developing ER to head up programming at CBS, was eager to pounce.

Bob Daly: They didn’t really realize what they had. At least, I don’t think [President of NBC West Coast] Don Ohlmeyer did. Unlike when they reimbursed us for Friends, they didn’t want to really reimburse us for what we had to give the talent for ER. So, I said, “Okay, we’re going to take a chance on this one. We won’t ask for more money. The hell with them. We will eat it, and they’ll pay through the nose if it goes more than five years. They’re going to really pay for it this time.” So, I gambled on it.

Warren Littlefield: We’d already made a billion dollars before the renegotiation began.

Leslie Moonves: The studios would always come back and renegotiate with the networks, and the networks would give them more money. It happens all the time. When I heard that Don Ohlmeyer didn’t want to step up at that point, I went to Bob Daly and made him a ridiculous offer to bring the show to CBS. I believe it was $12 million [an episode]. I’m not 100 percent sure, but it was up there. We figured out how much money ER was earning, and with the ratings it was getting, I think the number I offered was break even for the network. And I said, “Okay, if we get ER here to CBS, what’s that going to do for the rest of the schedule?” Also, ER had a special place in my heart. ER was one of my babies back in the day.

Bob Daly: When you have a hit show, the actors’ agents always come in for more money after year two, or it depends on how big a hit it is right away. I never had a problem giving people more money. But if I gave more money, I asked for more time. So, let’s say it was year two or three of the show. We would increase their salary for years four and five, which we had a contract on, and they would give us years six and seven. Obviously, it was to the advantage of the studio and the network to agree to do it because it’s good to get the sixth and seventh year or whatever it might be, so you don’t get held up.

Before negotiations officially opened at the start of 1998, ABC under Michael Eisner and Bob Iger had also been kicking the ER tires. If the overtures from the competition weren’t enough to pressure Ohlmeyer into finally making the deal, it was the call he received from Jerry Seinfeld that did. Over the holidays in 1997, the comedian reached Ohlmeyer in Aspen to say he wanted to end Seinfeld the following spring. At the time, Ohlmeyer told the Hollywood trades that Seinfeld’s call wasn’t necessarily im- petus for the deal, but it “shifted the dynamics somewhat. You’re never going to want to lose ER, but I think not having Seinfeld turned the Bunsen burner up even more.”

Bob Daly: They were feeling a lot of pressure. They couldn’t afford to lose ER. So, we made the deal, but I put two other conditions on it that’s never been put on the television show. I said, one, we have Thursday night at 10:00 and you can’t move the show. It’s going to stay there. Two, was that after we closed this deal, NBC had no rights on the talent. They had no more creative control over the show as far as talent was concerned. George was going to leave after five years, and that’s it. As for the rest of the talent, if somebody left for any reason, NBC couldn’t renegotiate the deal. The talent stayed and there was never a problem, but I wanted insurance that it never was going to be a problem.

Leslie Moonves: You want to know the truth? I rarely watched ER after I left Warner Bros. TV. It was too painful. Isn’t that silly, though? I rarely watched Friends after I left, too.

Bob Daly: To be honest, we originally wanted more than $13 million. My guys felt, and they probably were right, that we could have pushed them for another million or so. But we had a very good relationship with NBC. We had a lot of shows on NBC. So, there was a point where I didn’t want to offend them more than I was doing. I basically said to our people, “We don’t want to be pigs here.” I did that because I wanted them to call me up to thank me, as opposed to calling me up to scream at me. Ohlmeyer was really stretched out at that point. That was a huge increase in li- censing. I was a former network guy. I knew the pressure that they were receiving. Once you get a deal that you don’t even expect to get, why push them more than that? It just didn’t make sense.

Warren Littlefield: We didn’t own ER. We just rented it. After the first four years, we rented it for a lot more.

The cast and crew got to enjoy the sudden largesse, too. The five main cast members — George Clooney, Julianna Margulies, Noah Wyle, Eriq La Salle, and Anthony Edwards — were each gifted $1 million checks while others like Laura Innes, Gloria Reuben, and Alex Kingston got $500,000. Meanwhile, executive producers John Wells, Michael Crichton, and Steven Spielberg pooled $6 million and distributed it to the crew.

Christopher Chulack: Spielberg and Crichton and John had profit participation, and they gave everybody a little stipend. It was very nice. They didn’t have to. It wasn’t a million dollars, but it was substantial.

Jack Orman: It was one of the most amazing things that I’ve ever seen in Hollywood, because most people would not have done that. I remember seeing an editor crying right outside one of the buildings, and I walked up to him and said, “What’s going on?” He was like, “I can buy a house now.”

Bob Daly: Everybody was shocked. It was a huge deal. The only deal that was better than the amount of money we got for ER was when [Warner Bros.] released Jon Peters and Peter Guber to go to Sony. [In 1989, the two studios settled a bitter contract dispute after the WB sued Sony for poaching the Batman producers.] We got like $750 million.

With additional sourcing from Top of the Rock: Inside the Rise and Fall of Must See TV, Warren Littlefield, 2012. Adapted from ER: The Oral History, by Lynette Rice. Copyright 2026 by Lynette Rice. title: Courteney Cox Is Ready To Direct A ‘Scream’ Movie: “I Think I Should”
summary: As Courteney Cox returns to the director’s chair for her sophomore feature Evil Genius, she’s ready to take on a franchise she’s been with for 30 years. While discussing the TIFF true-crime film at the Deadline Studio, the Golden Globe nominee revealed she’d be open to directing an upcoming installment in the Scream franchise, in […]
content:
As Courteney Cox returns to the director’s chair for her sophomore feature Evil Genius, she’s ready to take on a franchise she’s been with for 30 years.

While discussing the TIFF true-crime film at the Deadline Studio, the Golden Globe nominee revealed she’d be open to directing an upcoming installment in the Scream franchise, in which she’s starred as Gale Weathers since the original 1996 movie.

“I think I should, honestly. Nobody knows more about that movie than I do,” said Cox. “I mean, and the creator, and Wes Craven, and the writers, and everybody who’s been in it. But I think it’d be great and fun and a good publicity thing. Get on it.”

Cox most recently reprised her role as reporter Gale Weathers in Scream 7, which reunited her with Neve Campbell’s “final girl” Sidney Prescott. Despite holding the franchise’s lowest Rotten Tomatoes score with a 30% critics rating, the Kevin Williamson-helmed installment was the highest-grossing sequel with nearly $208M globally.

Watch on Deadline

Following the record-breaking franchise haul, Spyglass has tapped sister duo Lilla and Nora Zuckerman to write the upcoming eighth film.

Official petition to have Courteney Cox to direct #Scream8 | The Deadline Studio at #TIFF2026 pic.twitter.com/t0xsbEGQ59 — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 12, 2026

Meanwhile, Cox is promoting her latest directorial outing with Evil Genius, the true-crime story of the infamous “pizza bomber” case, devling into the more deeply human story of deception, desperation, and the line between victim and villain.

Directed by Cox from a script by Courtenay Miles, Evil Genius stars Patricia Arquette, David Harbour, Tom McCarthy and more.

title: Mia Wasikowska Fills Out the Screen As ‘Agata the Writer’ in Kuba Dorabialski’s Venice Drama: ‘It’s Our Responsibility to Understand Each Other’
summary: Mia Wasikowska fills out the screen in Kuba Dorabialski’s “Agata the Writer.” Metaphorically and figuratively, as one especially arresting sequence shows her in close-up looking directly at the audience and recounting the rest of the story.   “I was so curious about it,” she says.   “Luckily, when I’m doing something, I don’t think too much about […]
content:
Mia Wasikowska fills out the screen in Kuba Dorabialski’s “Agata the Writer.” Metaphorically and figuratively, as one especially arresting sequence shows her in close-up looking directly at the audience and recounting the rest of the story.

“I was so curious about it,” she says.

“Luckily, when I’m doing something, I don’t think too much about how it’s going to be perceived. Kuba sent me some references, which I thought were really interesting, and it felt organic. But then, when I was watching the scene, I thought: ‘Ok. That’s enough of my face’!”

Popular on Variety

Known for blockbusters like “Alice in Wonderland” and high-profiles dramas “Stoker” or “Jane Eyre,” Wasikowska has been pursuing arthouse fare in recent years.

“I was really excited about making a film that didn’t follow a typical narrative structure. I feel like we have tunnel vision about how to tell a story and make a film,” notes Wasikowska. She also executive produced the film.

“This brings back the sense of exploration. I’m very proud it was made in a market that’s increasingly myopic about how it’s done.”

A Whitefalk Films and Produktion Productions production – sold by French sales company MMM Film Sales – sees Wasikowska as Agata, a Polish-Australian writer who arrives in Sarajevo to write about the war. She wants to speak to the survivors, but they question her motives. Not to mention, weird artworks start to mysteriously disappear from the house where she’s staying.

Dorabialski wanted to combine cinema and literature in the film.

“How do you make these two very different but also very interconnected forms of expression work? Reading is a solitary practice, and we experience cinema collectively,” he states.

He was been back and forth about the title pretty much until the premiere in Venice.

“And then, suddenly, I felt affection for it. I have a lot of affection also for writers too. The essence of everything I’m interested in is this very particular magic of literature. But where it falls short is silence and stillness. Even a novel that explores silence has to fill that void with language. Cinema has the audience in chains, dictating how long stillness lasts,” he says.

“I think these two forms complement each other beautifully.”

Dorabialski comes from the world of video art, where “formal experimentation is not only kind of acceptable – it’s necessary.”

“Cinema felt really exciting to me precisely because it has rules. There’s a definite beginning and end time; there’s a dark room and a screen. We’re just brains in a void. I was excited by some of that formal restriction.”

Wasikowska and Dorabialski both have Polish roots, but in the film, Agata heads to Sarajevo instead.

“I was interested in the idea of Slavic identity outside Eastern Europe and what it means to be part of this linguistic ethnic group,” he explains.

“Much of my work has examined historical similarities throughout Eastern Europe, politically and linguistically. Bosnia and Poland are about as far apart as two Slavic cultures could be, but the concept of Eastern Europe is formed from outside that territory. It’s always the West and the Anglophone world looking at this region and othering this group. I guess I’m playing the insider-outsider game here.”

He knew that Wasikowska would be the right Agata.

“Partly it’s because she has this Polish-Australian connection, but primarily because of the way she chooses and approaches her roles. I knew she could handle the challenge of playing someone who’s very pensive, restrained, quiet and detached.”

He adds: “Even in the final act of the film, where there’s nothing but Mia’s face, we’re still listening to the story and engaging with its content. Every time I watch it, I notice all the small decisions she made that give depth to her expressions.”

Wasikowska hasn’t really explored her roots before. Edward Zwick’s “Defiance,” about a Jewish underground resistance movement, came the closest.

“I haven’t had the opportunity to do that too much. But just from growing up, it’s very familiar to me,” she says.

“My mum and grandma were immigrants, and I observed their experience of trying to find belonging while being nostalgic about Poland. I’ve also traveled back to Poland many times. I connected with that in the script, and with Kuba. I understood the search for belonging and the feeling of being in between cultures even when somewhere feels familiar.”

That’s Agata’s struggle as well, as she’s desperately trying to figure out how to write about a conflict she hasn’t experienced. And whether it even makes sense.

“To me, what’s meaningful is the intention of trying to understand other people and things we haven’t lived through. That’s what it means to be human. It’s our responsibility to try to understand each other,” says Wasikowska.

And, according to Dorabialski, artists have a responsibility to respond to the world in which they live.

“It’s not like you go to church and all your sins are forgiven just because you’ve made an artwork about Gaza. But shouldn’t we expect art to create change? I’m not convinced that it does, especially in any kind of lasting, meaningful way. But artists have to do it anyway.”

title: Maggie Gyllenhaal’s Venice Jury Didn’t Award ‘Woman Unknown’ the Golden Lion Just Because It Was Directed by a Woman: It ‘Was Like a Laser Beam’
summary: Maggie Gyllenhaal kicked off her term as Venice jury president by calling out the lack of women filmmakers in the running for the prestigious Golden Lion. And on Saturday night, she concluded it by awarding the prize to the only film solely directed by a woman: May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown.” But at a press conference […]
content:
Maggie Gyllenhaal kicked off her term as Venice jury president by calling out the lack of women filmmakers in the running for the prestigious Golden Lion. And on Saturday night, she concluded it by awarding the prize to the only film solely directed by a woman: May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown.”

But at a press conference after the awards ceremony, Gyllenhaal rejected the notion that she and her fellow jury members were making any sort of “political statement,” as one journalist put it, with their selection. “I actually didn’t see ‘Woman Unknown,'” she deadpanned. “I just was like, ‘It’s made by a woman and so, Golden Lion!'”

Speaking sincerely, Gyllenhaal continued: “I will say that, of course, I anticipated that question. There are many movies that women made that I don’t like and some that I actively, strongly don’t like, just like films made by men. I have one vote just as each member of this jury does, and so all of the decisions that we make are always complicated, always involve a lot of conversation.”

Popular on Variety

She sighed and added, “I think I’m tired of talking about this same subject over and over. I will continue to do it, but just for a minute, here in this incredible place, I just want to celebrate a beautifully made movie that I felt was like a laser beam just for the well-made movie that it is.”

Gyllenhaal’s jury also consisted of “The Voice of Hind Rajab” director Kaouther Ben Hania, Hong Kong filmmaking giant Johnnie To, Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat, French director and screenwriter Xavier Giannoli, “The Brutalist” composer Daniel Blumberg and U.S.-based Italian film academic Francesco Casetti.

She also explained the jury’s decision to award “Woman Unknown” star Mathilde Arcel with the Volpi Cup for best actress. “You’re allowed to give two awards to a Golden Lion winner if the second award you want to give is unanimous,” Gyllenhaal said. “So we unanimously allowed to award Mathilde, who I’d like to say publicly, for all the press, is going to blow our socks off.”

The only other movie in competition involving a woman director was “NAZA,” which was co-helmed by Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham. The powerful documentary about the conflict in Gaza took home the special jury prize.

Asked about it during the press conference, Gyllenhaal said she admired the film’s “immense bravery and intelligence.” She added that her fellow juror Ben Hania helped illuminate her to the fact that “the way in which it’s shot and put together is about systems.”

“I know Jonathan Glazer, who made ‘Zone of Interest,’ was one of the producers — it reminded me a little bit of ‘Zone of Interest’ in that way, which is also about systems,” she continued. “And one of the things that I loved about the film was the way that it non-literally expressed that.”

See the full list of Venice award winners here.

title: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’
summary: Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77. Terry Gilliam, who worked with Thomas on “Tideland” and “The Man Who Killed Don Quixote,” told Variety, “Jeremy Thomas loved making movies. He loved every aspect of the business, […]
content:
Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.

Terry Gilliam, who worked with Thomas on “Tideland” and “The Man Who Killed Don Quixote,” told Variety, “Jeremy Thomas loved making movies. He loved every aspect of the business, but most of all he loved directors. The list of those he worked with is almost endless and I was one of the lucky ones. His taste in filmmaking spanned the globe. He was fearless in getting some very unlikely films financed and released, often to worldwide success. The list is remarkable in range and absolutely unforgettable in quality. Most of all, he was a joy to work with. As your producer you always felt protected and encouraged, rare qualities to experience, especially when lack of time and money are swirling around you, raging at your head. Filmmaking is not cheap and the pressures are intense but Jeremy always remained calm and supportive. He was a rare and very unique gem in the world of producers.”

Luca Guadagnino, who recently put Thomas on camera for his Venice-bowing documentary “Joie De Vivre” to talk about Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci (with whom he made five films), offered Variety a statement about the producer.

Popular on Variety

“Jeremy Thomas’ death leaves a gigantic void. The space he was fulfilling was a space of pure cinema. Someone who knew how to collaborate with filmmakers and make them better, and how to be himself — a great filmmaker,” he said. “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci. He was a generous man. He was a kind man. He was a man full of stories to tell, but at the same time, very curious to hear others people’s stories. I regret not having been able, in my life, to be produced by the great Jeremy Thomas, and I say a very moved goodbye to him.”

Thomas was greatly admired and loved by fellow British producers, such as Danny Boyle’s producing partner Andrew Macdonald. Macdonald told Variety that “Jeremy and I bonded over his father [director Ralph Thomas] and my grandfather both producing films for Rank in the 1950s. He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.” Macdonald’s grandfather was Emeric Pressburger, the co-writer, co-director and producer of “The Red Shoes” and “Black Narcissus,” among other classics.

Producer Stephen Woolley, whose credits include Oscar-nominated films like “The Crying Game” and “Carol,” told Variety that Thomas was a “colossus.”

Woolley said, “I first met the maverick and international producer in Tokyo at a buyers’ screening of his movie ‘Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence.’ Jeremy Thomas was the person in 1981 in Japan who didn’t suggest but insisted that I be a film producer!!!! He was a huge inspiration and a massively undervalued genius and necessary rebel in our industry… he sided with the subversives and movie anarchists and we loved him dearly… and I have to thank him for my career following in similar footsteps avoiding nationalistic stereotypes and embracing the world of cinema.
