“I tend to revise my script a lot while shooting, and I write it with that process in mind,” Yoon says. “That’s why I prefer to film in chronological order so I can really connect to the following scene. Of course, it doesn’t always work as I intend to,” she laughs.

Another ingredient of her movie’s authenticity is her casting process. She found the central pair, Sim Su-bin (“Teach You a Lesson,” “Filing for Love”) in the role of Jin, and first timer Kim Eo-jin as Du-jae through auditions. Both are relatively unfamiliar faces, even to Korean audiences, so Yoon built the surrounding ensemble to help them carry the film. “I was worried that if the older actors were too famous, they’d take the focus away from them, so I needed to balance this,” she says.

Once shooting began, she made a point to let her young leads embody the material. “As in my previous film, an emerging actor was playing the protagonist, so if the actor prefers to do a scene in a different way than I envisioned, I try to adapt,” Yoon explains. “I encourage the actors to find the intimacy that feels right for them. I know how they talk and behave, I don’t want them to stick to the script but use their own words.”

Only the second Korean film selected for the section after Yoon Ga-eun’s “The World of Love” last year, “The World Before” will be headed to the San Sebastian Film Festival‘s New Directors competition later this month.

title: ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation
summary: In “Masc,” director Bertil Nilsson pulls off a nifty trick: He observes an observer. Usually a film’s protagonist has the dominant POV, but here, Robin (Joshua Griffin) is trying to find his personality by observing other men in his orbit. He almost never initiates the action and is mostly reticent about his reactions, but he […]
content:
In “Masc,” director Bertil Nilsson pulls off a nifty trick: He observes an observer. Usually a film’s protagonist has the dominant POV, but here, Robin (Joshua Griffin) is trying to find his personality by observing other men in his orbit. He almost never initiates the action and is mostly reticent about his reactions, but he takes note of everything. This makes for a fascinating watching experience for the audience, as they find themselves in Robin’s shoes, trying to figure out how to behave. In the process “Masc” becomes a thoroughly unique experience.

Robin is queer, biracial and neurodivergent, so society forces multiple identities on him. In the span of a year, he changes his appearance five times and tries on different jobs, places and people to hang out with. He works as an apprentice handyman and lab assistant, tries to immerse himself within a therapy group and seeks camaraderie with different guys his age. In the process, he takes on their mannerisms and models his personality on them, tries to figure out why they behave the way they do. It’s an intense journey that’s also internal; the strength of the film, and of Griffin’s performance, lies in how tangible and visceral they make that progress.

Popular on Variety

Nilsson wrote “Masc” based on a story he crafted with Griffin, and it plays as an organic collaboration between filmmaker and actor. Whether or not they improvised the situations that they put Robin in together, those play so naturally that the film sometimes has the feel of an observational documentary, which is exactly as it should be with such a sensitive character study.

But “Masc” is also clearly a work of fiction. Not only does Nilsson place the audience in Robin’s purview, he also creates scenes that tell us how he imagines things, how he wishes situations would transpire. In one immaculately crafted and tenderly portrayed scene, Robin stays overnight with a friend, Benji (Tega Alexander). The audience is privy to his vacillating feelings about his friend, how he hopes the night will go, and what he fears it might become. It is a vivid portrait of his innermost feelings and anxieties.

Griffin is tremendous, carrying the film on his shoulders as he appears in almost every frame. He has amazing physical control, making even the solitary scenes captivating; his presence, both jittery and grounded, conveys the complexity of Robin’s constant observation and recording of other people. When he is alone, there’s clear relief in the easier, more rhythmic way he moves. In closeup, his eyes broadcast all that the character is feeling; always watchful, always taking note of everything and everyone. The performance makes a moving and empathetic endeavor of the character’s search for a blueprint of life and personality.

Griffin’s vulnerability is most pronounced in a long scene where Robin spends time with his father (Lincoln Conway) — finally, he is not observing and just being, even if he’s not entirely comfortable. He still has fears of being unloved, but he’s at his most unguarded. Perhaps this familiar form of masculinity is the one he’s been searching for all along.

What makes “Masc” compelling is the way Nilsson turns observation into a mode of self-construction. Robin studies the men around him as though they might offer a grammar for being, borrowing their gestures, routines and affect in an attempt to locate something stable within himself. Yet the film understands identity not as something waiting to be discovered, but as something continually negotiated through imitation, desire and rejection. “Masc” shows that for those who exist outside prescribed ideas of masculinity, becoming oneself can first require learning how to read everyone else.

title: Shuhua’s Acting Debut and Breaking Free From the ‘American Girl’ Label: Director Feng-i Fiona Roan on Toronto Title ‘Happily Ever After’
summary: “Happily Ever After,” the follow-up feature from Taiwanese director Feng-i Fiona Roan, is bowing in the Toronto Film Festival’s Special Presentations lineup, arriving amid heightened attention following the success of her acclaimed debut, “American Girl.” “American Girl” premiered in the Asian Future section of the Tokyo International Film Festival before earning seven Golden Horse Award […]
content:
“Happily Ever After,” the follow-up feature from Taiwanese director Feng-i Fiona Roan, is bowing in the Toronto Film Festival’s Special Presentations lineup, arriving amid heightened attention following the success of her acclaimed debut, “American Girl.”

“American Girl” premiered in the Asian Future section of the Tokyo International Film Festival before earning seven Golden Horse Award nominations and winning three prizes, including best new director. During the Golden Horse celebrations, Roan received a gentle but prescient warning from Oscar-winning filmmaker Ang Lee.

“Director Ang Lee reminded me that the second film is always the hardest,” Roan tells Variety. “Being able to present my second feature at TIFF as its first stop is very meaningful to me. I also hope it can open up more conversations and opportunities.”

Popular on Variety

Drawn from Roan’s childhood and family history, “American Girl” earned widespread acclaim but also prompted some observers to question whether the filmmaker could move beyond autobiography.

“From the development stage of ‘Happily Ever After,’ I was determined to break away from that label,” Roan says. “I was entering a different phase of my life and was even planning my own wedding at the time. This fictional story went from nothing to a complete screenplay within a year, but it also captured the emotional shifts that my friends and I were experiencing at different stages of our lives.”

“Happily Ever After” closely examines the subtle emotional dynamics between two sisters. The story initially placed greater emphasis on the younger sister, played by Shuhua, before evolving into a dual-protagonist narrative.

“While developing the screenplay, I watched ‘Frozen’ for a second time and suddenly realized how remarkably well it balances the narrative arcs of its two sister protagonists,” Roan says. “I went back and analyzed the screenplay for that reason, then used what I learned to refine the rhythm of my own script.”

Beyond the expectations surrounding Roan’s second feature, the film has attracted attention across the film, television and music industries for casting K-pop star Shuhua in her film debut.

“When we met Shuhua, we only asked her to read two scenes,” Roan says. “Her confidence and personality came through so naturally that we decided on the spot.”

During production, Roan sought to create an authentic sense of family among the cast. Rather than addressing Shuhua by her real name or her character’s name, everyone on set simply called her “little sister.” Before filming began, Shuhua was also invited to name the cat that appears as the family pet.

Shuhua’s own experience as the middle child in a family of three daughters gave her a deeper emotional connection to the role, according to Roan.

“I gave her only one note: Before making any movement or delivering any line, she had to have a motivation,” Roan says. “Only after you have convinced yourself can your performance move the audience.”

Asked how she hopes international audiences will view contemporary Taiwanese cinema, Roan draws on her experience living in the U.S. and her observations from attending international film festivals.

“Filmmakers from the previous generation, such as Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang, naturally still have enormous international visibility,” she says. “Their particular time and circumstances allowed them to pursue their artistic practices to an extremely high degree, and those achievements have secured their place in film history.”

Roan believes her own generation brings a stronger awareness of genre and a greater willingness to experiment with different forms.

“Every festival feels a little like a social experiment,” she says. “We bring different stories to international audiences and observe how they respond and what kinds of thoughts those stories provoke.”

Alongside the classics of Taiwanese cinema, Roan cites French New Wave pioneer Agnès Varda as a formative influence. She also points to Ozu Yasujirō’s cycle of films about fathers marrying off their daughters, Kore-eda Hirokazu’s family dramas and Greta Gerwig’s explorations of women’s inner lives.

“My favorite film this year is ‘The World of Love,’ by South Korean director Yoon Ga-eun,” Roan says.

During the early development of “Happily Ever After,” Roan immersed herself in reading, including Taiwanese author Kevin Chen’s novel “Ghost Town.” Stories exploring family, identity and self-worth fed into her new fictional direction while allowing her to retain the emotional honesty of her earlier work.

As the film meets its first international audience in Toronto, Roan is eager to exchange ideas with filmmakers from around the world. Above all, she hopes “Happily Ever After” will spark a conversation around the question embedded in its title: What does it mean to be happy on your own terms?

title: Cannes Prize-Winning Nepal Oscar Entry ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Sells Wide for Best Friend Forever (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” has been sold to distributors across 10 territories, Best Friend Forever has revealed, as the Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize winner plays at the Toronto Film Festival with Nepal’s Oscars international feature submission also confirmed. New deals put the film with MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin […]
content:
Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” has been sold to distributors across 10 territories, Best Friend Forever has revealed, as the Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize winner plays at the Toronto Film Festival with Nepal‘s Oscars international feature submission also confirmed.

New deals put the film with MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin in Spain, Vedette in Benelux, Trigon in Switzerland, Lev Cinema in Israel, Jayantii in Australia, EFAR Films in India, PT Falcon in Indonesia and the Film Development Council of the Philippines. An inflight deal with Silk Route rounds out the announcement.

These join previously announced deals with Arizona Distribution and Les Valseurs Distribution in France, missingFILMs in Germany and Austria, Imovision in Brazil and The Tea Folks Films for local Nepal distribution. A pan-Latin America deal is expected shortly; North American rights are in advanced negotiations.

Popular on Variety

The film – which follows Pirati, matriarch of a Kinnar community in a forested Nepalese village, as she investigates the disappearance of one of her daughters during a nightly patrol against wild elephants – also leads the Asia Pacific Screen Awards nominations, picking up nods for best film, best director and best performance.

“Elephants in the Fog” is produced by Underground Talkies Nepal, Les Valseurs and Die Gesellschaft DGS. Co-producers include Enquadramento Produções, Bubbles Project, Zischlermann Filmproduktion, Storm Films, Jayantii Creations and ZDF/Das kleine Fernsehspiel & ZDF/ARTE.

Shah previously directed the short “Lori,” which received a Special Mention at the Cannes Short Film Competition in 2022.

Best Friend Forever also heads to TIFF with Midnight Madness titles “Vintage Violence” by Eugene Kotlyarenko and “Half” by Samjad, French adult animation “Blaise” – which took best film honors at both the Annecy Contrechamp competition and Fantasia – and Canada’s Oscars submission “Nina Roza” by Geneviève Dulude-De Celles.

The Brussels-based company launched at Cannes in 2019 as a sister outfit of Paris-based Indie Sales, and is managed by Martin Gondre, Charles Bin and Indie Sales co-founder Nicolas Eschbach.

title: Ali Asgari Doesn’t Believe in a Bright Future After Iran’s January Massacre – Just ‘A Bit of Light’
summary: Iranian director Ali Asgari has no desire to repeat clichés about great expectations for things to come. “In Iran, we don’t have high hopes for the future anymore,” he states.  “We’ve been waiting for good news for so many years, and it never came. But I do believe in these small specks of light. For […]
content:
Iranian director Ali Asgari has no desire to repeat clichés about great expectations for things to come.

“In Iran, we don’t have high hopes for the future anymore,” he states.

“We’ve been waiting for good news for so many years, and it never came. But I do believe in these small specks of light. For now, let’s just stick to them so that we can take the next step.”

Talking to Variety after the premiere of his sixth feature “A Bit of Light,” Asgari – also behind “Disappearance,” “Terrestrial Verses” and “Divine Comedy” – said he wanted to “celebrate simple things.”

Popular on Variety

“Right now, especially in my country, we are forgetting about them. We’re forgetting about our families and helping others. We are surrounded by disaster every day, all the time, always expecting something horrible to happen,” he says.

“When we wake up, we don’t know if we’ll be able to handle it until nighttime. We’re all living in a dangerous world right now. If after watching this film someone goes to their mother and takes her hand, that’s enough.”

Family is certainly on the mind of his protagonist, a kind doctor (played by Misagh Zareh) who becomes disillusioned after his arrest. With his medical practice shut down, he’s ready to end his life. He’s a practical man, though, so he decides to tell his family and make suitable arrangements.

“Some doctors in Iran were the only witnesses to what was really happening after the massacre in January. They faced so much death and saw so many injured. We couldn’t even talk about it,” he notes.

In January, after weeks of protests, the authorities opened fire on demonstrators.

“I saw so many families mourning their children. It had affected so many people’s lives. This man still feels connected to his family, and he knows he has to prepare them for what he wants to do. That’s just the way he is.”

He keeps his pain to himself.

“Usually, when we think about sadness or depression, we think of very expressive acting or directing. I took a simpler approach. I told [Misagh]: ‘I only want to see it in your eyes and on your face’.”

Asgari, who got to show the film in Venice’s main competition, thought a lot about Italian filmmakers.

“I studied in Italy, basically. I’ve been inspired a lot by Italian neorealism and people like [screenwriter] Cesare Zavattini. It was important for me to show the everyday life of a country, and I see many similarities between [Iran] and neorealism’s depiction of Italy after the war.”

“We are experiencing a horrible tragedy: war and massacres. That’s why it’s so important to focus on normal life.”

His characters can’t ignore what’s happening entirely – they cook and talk about Trump – but they still need to keep going.

“While writing the screenplay, we thought a lot about the absurdity of it all. Albert Camus wrote about Sisyphus rolling a rock to the top of a mountain. Then the rock would roll down, and he had to start over. That’s our life,” says Asgari.

“This man decides to act because nothing has changed. In the end, the war still exists, and so does the repression. But then he decides to roll the rock back up the mountain again.”

He adds: “That’s also what I’ve learnt from Italian filmmakers like Nanni Moretti. ‘The Son’s Room’ [about parents grieving the death of their son] was a very good example of that.”

In the film – sold by Salaud Morisset and produced by Milad Khosravi for Seven Springs Pictures – helping others or simply being with them takes the protagonist’s mind off suicide.

“This story is about a man who’s going to take his life, but life follows him everywhere,” says the director.

“Our lives are interconnected. Personally, whenever I want to do something, I immediately think of my mother and sisters. How will they react? I know I could destroy their lives, so I’m careful when making decisions,” he says.

“What we need, especially now, is to be together. Iran is a divided country. I wanted this family to come together, sit side by side and even dance a little. If we want any kind of change, it should happen this way.”

In Iran, but also in other places.

“During our premiere, so many people were crying. It didn’t matter where they were from. They just connected with this character, mostly because we’re talking about human values and dignity.”

“That’s what cinema is for – it can speak your language, and it can speak for everyone. In life, we sometimes hope for big things. But I’m not waiting for a bright future anymore. Just for some light.”

title: TIFF 2026: 20 International Titles to Track, From Feng-I Fiona Roan’s Shuhua Starrer to a Taxidermy Musical and a John Madden Parkinson’s Rom-Com
summary: Helen Mirren, Laura Linney, Rhys Ifans, Erin Doherty and James McAvoy star in three of the biggest U.K. titles world premiering at Toronto and making Variety’s 2026 selection of 20 International Titles to Track at this year’s Toronto.Jodie Comer sings (very creditably Variety suggests), in a fourth U.K. package, gothic rom-com “Stuffed” as romance takes […]
content:
Helen Mirren, Laura Linney, Rhys Ifans, Erin Doherty and James McAvoy star in three of the biggest U.K. titles world premiering at Toronto and making Variety’s 2026 selection of 20 International Titles to Track at this year’s Toronto.Jodie Comer sings (very creditably Variety suggests), in a fourth U.K. package, gothic rom-com “Stuffed” as romance takes unpredictable turns at Toronto.

As in 2025, multiple more Platform titles, 42% made up of movies from female directors, could have made the selection. It focuses on new titles, hence what otherwise would be startling omissions such as “Jim Queen,” or Spain’s Cannes main competition trio. The list is by no means definitive. But what it does point up is the presence this year of new and noteworthy voices, such as Scotland’s Tom Nicoll and Ireland’s David Turpin. Some of the films may feature in the Oscars race. The Platform selection of Gabriel Martins’ “On Behalf of My Son,” as Variety notes, consolidates its status as the biggest international hope this year from a Brazilian director.

The selection films will certainly deliver surprises. “Wild Wild East,” for instance, is described as “about many twists and turns, and an ending that throws a straight punch to the head.”

Popular on Variety

And yes, Variety has selected a baker’s score of films. Given the abundance of international movies at Toronto meriting attention, it would prefer to be accused of bad mathematics than bad taste.

Ancestors Leanne Sullivan

“Ancestors,” (David Turpin, Samson Films, Lunatica, Ireland, U.K., Discovery)

Beau, a young gay man in 1980s London, searches for missing friend Tiny. Featuring Éanna Hardwicke, Jack Wolfe, Jessica Reynolds, Rupert Everett and Christina Hendricks, tenderly scored and shot with many scenes of seeming dreamlike revery, a mystery which soon becomes deeper charting the phantasmagoric emotional landscape and aftermath of the AIDs crisis. “Often when there is an event like this, our instinct is not to look back at it, then sort of not to be aware of the ways in which it’s continuing to haunt us,” Turpin tells Variety. Sold by Mister Smith Entertainment. JH

Angh Jungle Book Studio

“Angh,” (Theja Rio, Winter Hymns Films, Undercover Squirrel, India, Platform)

Theja Rio expands his 2021 short into a feature centered on Anghba, a Nagaland chief presiding over an empty village in the 1960s – his people gone, his wife failing, his son unable to speak. A missionary, played by Douglas Henshall, arrives with gifts and promises that pressure everything Anghba has spent his life protecting. Rio cast the film with Nagaland locals who had never acted before, shooting on 16mm. It’s the London-based writer-director’s feature debut, produced with Nancy Nisa Beso and Bernardo Angeletti, and the only Indian film in this year’s Platform lineup – a section whose winner now heads straight into Oscar’s international feature race. NR

Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo Neon

“Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” (Miike Takashi, OLM, Nippon TV, Pressman Film, Recorded Picture Company, TF1 Films, U.S., U.K., Japan, France, Special Presentations)

Miike Takashi takes the wheel on the third entry in the “Bad Lieutenant” lineage, following Abel Ferrara’s 1992 original and Werner Herzog’s New Orleans reboot, and makes it entirely his own. Shun Oguri plays a gambling-addicted Tokyo cop dragged into a joint investigation with an FBI agent over a missing politician’s daughter (Lily James), while a former yakuza figure out for revenge works an angle neither sees coming. It’s a setup built for Miike’s tangled plotting and gonzo violence. World premiering at Toronto, screenwriter Daisuke Tengan, of Miike’s “13 Assassins,” returns to script this one. NR

Brace Your Heart Credit: Sophia Olsson

“Brace Your Heart” (Amanda Kernell, Nordisk Film Production, Forest People, Compass Films, Invictus, Nordisk Film Production Denmark, Filmpool Nord, SVT, Film i Väst, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Bulgaria, Platform)

“Sámi Blood” director Amanda Kernell talks about responsibility – and how heavy that burden can be. Her protagonist, Ejva, has been harmed but also has her family, and her Sámi community, to consider. Kernell told Variety: “What can be forgiven? And what if you live in a place where everything has to be, because it can be a matter of survival?” It’s not easy, but there’s a way out of the trauma. Speaking up, however terrifying, might be just what you need to heal. MB

Children Untold K2 Pictures

“Children Untold,” (Nishikawa Miwa, K2 Pictures, Japan, Platform — Opening Film)

Nishikawa Miwa, returning to TIFF for a fourth year, opens this year’s Platform program with a story set in Tokyo during the last days and aftermath of World War II. Orphaned at 12 and born to a pair of musicians, the film’s central girl adopts a boy’s disguise to survive the city’s underworld, while a former teacher, carrying her own guilt, keeps quiet watch over her. Adapted from Nishikawa’s own unpublished novel and starring Ami Koyae, Fumi Nikaido and Koji Yakusho, it’s a Platform opener from one of Japan’s most reliably acclaimed filmmakers, in a section whose winner now has a direct line to the international feature Oscar race. NR

The Daughters of Abraham Courtesy of TIFF

“The Daughters of Abraham,” (Hanael El Yousfi, CG Cinéma, France 2 Cinéma, France, Discovery)

At the film’s get-go, a Marseilles university lecturer quotes Aristotle’s take on happiness as the freedom to become what one is. Achieving that, however, is no slam dunk, as Arab Myriam and BFF Jewish Eva’s modern assumptions about sex and anti-patriarchy grate against their still traditional worlds. Capturing with flair and ambivalence a sense of community, its events – a Marrakech nightclub, a Marseilles Arab wedding and Jewish dinner – its dynamics and resilient impositions – El Yousfi’s stylish debut is produced by Charles Gillibert, behind many of France’s higher-profile arthouse plays (“The Chronology of Water,” “Minotaur”) and sold by Les Films du Losange. JH

Djinn Wedding Courtesy of TIFF

“Djinn Wedding” (Ferit Karahan, Ferit Karahan Films, Royal Pictures, Maya Films, Arya Yapim, Turkey, Platform)

“Can a person who denies their own darkness truly change their fate?” is the question that drove director Ferik Karahan to make his third feature film. A story about family, history and Anatolian folk tales, the film follows four siblings across three periods of time as their dark secrets and traumas begin to unravel during a family wedding. Dealing with the universal themes of loss, guilt and mourning, this is Karahan’s follow-up feature to “Brother’s Keeper,” which won the Fipresci’s Berlin Panorama Award. RP

Faith Courtesy of TIFF

”Faith,” (Paul Andrew Williams, Giant Productions, Homefront Productions, Blazing Griffin, Miria Talent, U.K. Special Presentations)

Already a talking point at Toronto after an early screening, with Erin Doherty (“Adolescence,” “The Crown”) gleaning rave reviews for her performance as a single mother charmed by a mysterious but increasingly sinister stranger (James McAvoy), then tortured by grief as horrifying tragedy occurs. Generally, the film has drawn upbeat reaction as well. “Intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitor,” says the Guardian. A drama with a supernatural build from Paul Andrew Williams (“Bull,” “Dragonfly”), an invigorating presence on the British film scene. JH

Le Faux Soir Courtesy of Goodfellas

“Le Faux Soir,” (Michaël R. Roskam, Frakas Productions, Rectangle Production, Goodfellas, Harbor Men Pictures, Belgium, France, Special Presentation)

Oscar-nominated “Bullhead” helmer Roskam hadn’t directed a feature film in his home country of Belgium since 2017’s “Race and the Jailbird.” His homecoming is a fitting one, a highly ambitious historical thriller set in 1943 and relaying the real-life case of a group of Resistance fighters who printed a fake edition of Belgium’s leading newspaper Le Soir, which had been turned into a propaganda tool during the Nazi occupation. The case is widely considered to be the world’s first media hack, with Roskam’s fast-paced thriller honing in on the past to paint a vivid picture of the present. RSR

Four Seasons in Java

“Four Seasons in Java,” (Kamila Andini, Forka Films, Indonesia, France, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Centrepiece)

Kamila Andini sets her latest against the volcanic backdrop of Mount Bromo, following Putri Marino’s Pertiwi as she returns to her village after years in prison for killing a man who tried to rape her. Old family wounds and a wary community await her, and Andini slides between registers — grounded drama one moment, something closer to myth or speculative fiction the next. Arya Saloka and Christine Hakim round out the cast. Producer Ifa Isfansyah pictured Bromo as the setting nearly a decade before shooting began. It’s Andini’s return to TIFF after winning the Platform Award in 2021 with “Yuni,” and one of this year’s most striking Southeast Asian entries. NR

Future Tense Courtesy of TIFF

“Future Tense” (Jenna Cato Bass, Causeway Films, Benchfilms and Fox Fire Film, South Africa,Australia; Centrepiece)

Five years after thrilling TIFF audiences with “Good Madam,” a Jordan Peele-esque creeper that explored the real-life horror of post-apartheid trauma, Jenna Cato Bass returns with the sci-fi feature “Future Tense.” Set in a near future on the brink of climate collapse, it unpacks weighty issues like climate change, human guilt and South African identity through the story of a mixed-race couple offered a chance to travel back in time. The film should cement Bass’ status as one of their country’s most inventive and provocative filmmakers. Specialty distributors might want to take note: Shudder swooped on “Good Madam” after its Toronto premiere. CV

Glaxo Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures

“Glaxo,” (Benjamín Naishtat, RT Features, Rei Pictures, Brazil, Argentina, Special Presentations)

“This is the story of betrayal,” says Miguelito, the narrator of “Glaxo.” In fact, he’s only half right. This is the story of seemingly endemic betrayals, braiding narratives in 1956, 1957, and 1984 – the tale of heinous police commissioner Folcada, Miguelito, besotted by his dazzling wife Miranda and his former teen friend “Flaco” Tepermann, just out of jail 25 years later. A return to the multi-genre high-style and collective psychology portrait of “Rojo” marking one of the most awaited Latin American films of the year.

Growth of the Soil Courtesy of 4 ½ Fiction

“Growth of the Soil” (Hans Petter Molland, 4 1/2 Fiction, Scanbox Entertainment, Norway, Special Presentation)

Molland, known for his collabs with Stellan Skarsgård, takes on the classic novel by Knut Hamsun and ends up with an epic love story spanning decades – the kind not seen since “Doctor Zhivago.” In his film – recently selected as Norway’s Oscar submission – two people come together in order to survive, only to realize they can’t live without each other. But their relationship, just like the wilderness that surrounds them, has to face destruction as well. That’s just the way the world works. MB

Happily Ever After Happily Ever After Toronto Film Festival

“Happily Ever After,” (Feng-I Fiona Roan, Splash Pictures, Taiwan, Special Presentations)

Feng-I Fiona Roan’s sophomore feature follows two sisters pulling in opposite directions: Kitty, the family favorite, is riding a promotion and an engagement to a wealthy man, while Claire keeps disappointing their parents chasing a life of her own. An abandoned cat that lands in their laps cracks open old wounds. Shuhua of K-pop group i-dle makes her acting debut opposite Xuan Chen, with Kuei-Mei Yang and Jack Kao rounding out the cast. Roan became the Golden Horse Awards’ first female Best New Director winner for her 2021 debut “American Girl,” and this world premiere is one of the fest’s most anticipated follow-ups from a filmmaker on the rise. NR

Idda Credit: Simona Pampallona

“Idda” (Irene Dionisio, Kino Produzioni, Rai Cinema, Andromeda Film, EDI, Wise Pictures, Italy, Platform)

A TIFF Platform buzz title, praised for its charm and sensuality, this is a portrait of friendship between two childhood friends who decide to climb Mount Etna, an active volcano on the Eastern Coast of Sicily. Carefree Sofia and the more restrained Adele couldn’t be more different, but they share an unbreakable bond that will be tested when confronted with bottled-up resentment, past secrets and the fear of change as they make their way up the treacherous mountainside. This is Irene Dionisio’s sophomore feature following her 2016 debut “Le Ultime Cose.” RP

On Behalf of My Son Courtesy of Filmes de Plástico

“On Behalf of My Son,” (Gabriel Martins, Filmes de Plástico, Netflix Brazil, Platform)

When festivals were still finding their footing following the COVID-19 pandemic, Gabriel Martins made waves at Sundance with the tender family drama “Mars One.” Four years later, the Brazilian director returns with a major production that reunites him with Rejane Faria, who plays the mother of a bus driver who apparently killed himself and dozens of passengers in a planned suicide-crash. The film comes onto the festival circuit with the weight of Netflix’s backing and gunning to become Brazil’s Oscar entry, due to be announced mid-September. Following two banner years with “I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent,” all eyes are rightly on what Brazil does next. RSR

Onwards and Sideways BBC/Jonathan Birch

“Onwards and Sideways,” (John Madden, John Gore Studios BBC, Hilltop Screen, Kaleidoscope, U.K.)

Helmed by Madden, Oscar-nominated for “Shakespeare in Love,” a romantic dramedy starring Oscar nominee Laura Linney and BAFTA winner Rhys Ifans as two people who meet having just received the same Parkinson’s diagnosis with “five good years to live,” their straight talking neurologist (Rory Kinnear) tells them. A bottle half-full, knowing yet upbeat take on the illness written by Paul Mayhew-Archer (“The Vicar of Dibley”) who lives with Parkinson’s. Set for a TIFF gala screening on Sept. 13 and U.K. theatrical release from Icon Film Distribution. CAA Media Finance co-reps North America. JH

Purgatory Courtesy of TIFF

“Purgatory,” (Lindsay Lanzillotta, Brave Jayne Films, Canada, U.S., Discovery)

Producer Lanzillotta (“The Invitation,” Spin Me Round”) takes her first spin in the director’s chair with ’80s-set coming-of-age dramedy “Purgatory,” assembling a stellar cast to create a family and community dynamic that resonates with emotion and humor. After her mother (Abby Elliott, “The Bear”) moves out to find herself, 13-year-old Beatrice is determined to fix her family, and few other teenage problems, turning to her church’s priest ( J.K. Simmons) for guidance. “Everyone has to realize that their parents are not perfect, that life is not always easy, and that the world is bigger than just themselves,” Lansillotta says. Gersh handles international sales. JP

Liam Harkins as Danny in Salvation

“Salvation,“ Tom Nicoll, (Lane Productions with Creative Scotland, U.K., Discovery)

Inspired by a self confidence guru, Danny Carter, a dishwasher, becomes a professional life coach. “I can show you how to build a new life and find true happiness,” he promises on social media. Trouble is there’s an elephant in the room: Scottish port Greenock, caught in post-industrial depression and a world dominated by domineering baby boomers such as mentee Scott’s dad who made it in easier times. So the illusions Danny sells are essentially delusions. Finely shot in often hyper character close-ups, a compassionate take on GenZ travails sparking great word of mouth and an auspicious feature debut from Scottish writer-director Tom Nicoll. JH

The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives Courtesy of TIFF

“The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” (Daniel Oriahi, EbonyLife Media, Nigeria, Centrepiece)

Based on Lola Shoneyin’s 2010 debut novel, “The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” is set within a seemingly harmonious polygamous household whose fragile balance is overturned with the arrival of the titular patriarch’s youngest wife. A dramatic comedy that crackles with trademark Nollywood wit, the film marks the return of Nigerian mogul Mo Abudu’s powerhouse production outfit EbonyLife Films to Toronto, the fifth time selected. Oriahi, who helmed the genre-bending Tribeca premiere “The Weekend” in 2024, directs a star-studded cast, back in Toronto after his action comedy “Taxi Driver: Oko Ashewo” — another EbonyLife Films production — bowed at TIFF in 2016. CV

The Smell of Apples

“The Smell of Apples” (John Trengove, Portobello Productions, Cadence, Baldr Film, Quijote Films, South Africa, Netherlands, Chile; Platform)

After establishing a foothold in Hollywood with “Manodrome,” his Jesse Eisenberg-starring portrait of toxic masculinity that competed at the 2023 Berlinale, South Africa’s Trengove returns to the native turf he mined to such powerful effect in “The Wound,” his Oscar-shortlisted gay romantic drama. Adapted from Mark Behr’s bestselling, Booker Prize-nominated novel, “The Smell of Apples” is a sensitive portrait of a sheltered 11-year-old white South African boy who gradually comes to realize the horrors of the apartheid system. Produced by Portobello Productions — whose credits include Oscar winners “Kolya” and “Ida” — Cadence, Baldr Film and Quijote Films, the film uses the intimate story of one family to tell a larger tale about the violence lurking behind an idyllic façade. CV

Stuffed Courtesy of TIFF

“Stuffed,” (Theo Rhys, Agile Films, Fresh Fish Films, BFI, Ffilm Cymru Wales, U.K., Discovery)

A taxidermy musical. Finally! But much more, starring Jodie Comer (“Killing Eve”) and opening TIFF’s Discovery program. “Odd and oddly touching,” says Variety. A macabre comedy, love story and musical – song no dance, though Comer does prance in one show-stopping turn as she belts out a song. She plays a wild haired anti-social taxidermist dreaming of stuffing a human specimen, Harry Melling, of “Harry Potter” and “Pillion” fame, is Bernie, an anonymous factory worker who volunteers for embalming. A Gothic but tender, especially when they begin JH

Sunburn Courtesy of TIFF

“Sunburn,” dir. Serville Poblete, Serve, Tinygiant, Canada, Centrepiece

After scooping a SXSW jury award for his 2026 docu short “In The Morning Sun,” Poblete turns up the heat with “Sunburn,” a hangout film set in St. James Town, the Toronto high-rise community where he grew up­. The story follows three pairs of friends on the cusp of changes they can’t yet see, trying to stay cool and fight the boredom, “kids who look like me, ” he says, “with darker skin, curly hair, raised in immigrant and working-class Toronto.” Sweeping orchestral score by Aaron Paris makes the summer day feel epic, the loose-limbed ensemble performance keeps it grounded. No surprise buyers are circling after the well received first market screening. JP

Talent for Murder Courtesy of TIFF

“Talent for Murder,” (Anton Corbijn, LD Entertainment, Brouhaha Entertainment, Lunar Pictures, Lucky Red, U.K., Italy, Gala Presentation)

“Hotly anticipated,” Variety reports, starring Helen Mirren as crime writer Patricia Highsmith, the first film for over nine years Corbijn (“Control,”“The American”) with FilmNation Entertainment handling international. The basic plot is known: callow young New York literary agent (Ehrenreich) is dispatched to Switzerland to persuade Highsmith (Mirren) to write one final Ripley thriller. His real motives are, however, rather more Ripley-esque. Co-starring Tony winner Alden Ehrenreich and “House of the Dragon” star Olivia Cooke. Set for an Oct. 23 U.S. debut by Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment. JH

Toy Gun Bandit Courtesy of TIFF

“Toy Gun Bandit,” (dir. Rémi St-Michel, Spécimen Productions, Canada, Centrepiece)

For his second feature, Rémi St-Michel explores “what happens when the insatiable need for impressing and belonging gets out of hand.” He does this through the charmingly infuriating character of 15-year-old Felix (non-professional actor Félix Munger) whose life takes an unexpected turn after a prank becomes an actual robbery. The mayhem is further intensified when Félix falls in with an aspiring gangster (David Beaudoin) and a drug addict (Sara Montpetit), the film’s shooting, editing, and sound carrying the frantic energy to the edge. From the producers of “Humanist Vampire Seeking Consenting Suicidal Person,” with h264 distributing in Canada and handling international sales. JP

Wild Wild East Courtesy Madants

“Wild, Wild East” (Jan Holoubek, Madants, Holograph, Extreme Emotions, Poland, Platform)

In his Western-y film, overseen by “The Zone of Interest” producer, Polish director Jan Holoubek takes a page from Tarantino and proves there are different ways to talk about the Second World War. Everyone’s guilty here – mostly of averting their eyes when the unthinkable happens. But it’s not just about poisonous silence, national guilt or the purpose of art when the world is ending; it’s also about many twists and turns, and an ending that throws a straight punch to the head. MB

title: ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Star Adia On Film Debut Opposite Mahershala Ali, Getting Certified as a Doula: ‘Birth Work Fills My Soul’
summary: Twenty-five-year-old newcomer Adia never really imagined becoming a movie star. Growing up, she was focused on becoming a professional dancer before a hip injury derailed that dream. That’s when the high school senior discovered acting. “I decided to take an acting class, just to try it out and see if that would be comparable or […]
content:
Twenty-five-year-old newcomer Adia never really imagined becoming a movie star. Growing up, she was focused on becoming a professional dancer before a hip injury derailed that dream. That’s when the high school senior discovered acting.

“I decided to take an acting class, just to try it out and see if that would be comparable or satiate that need to perform and to create,” Adia told Variety via Zoom from her home in Washington, D.C. “I enjoyed it, and I had fun with it, so I just kind of ran with it. I was like, ‘Ok, I’ll go out to L.A.”

Adia has two other major screen credits on her resume — she made her acting debut in the Netflix series “The Midnight Club,” created by Mike Flanagan and Leah Fong, followed by the HBO Max series “Full Circle,” which was directed by Steven Soderbergh. Not a bad start.

Popular on Variety

“Things started to fall in place as soon as I started pursuing acting, and it’s just snowballed,” she said. “It’s just very surreal.”

Even so, Adia didn’t picture a career making movies — which makes her big screen debut in the action-drama from filmmaker Bassam Tariq (“Mogul Mowgli”) all the more unexpected.

“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” which debuted on Saturday night at the Toronto International Film Festival, stars two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali as Latif, a hired assassin whose secret occupation clashes with his home life when his wife dies suddenly. The film follows Latif as he navigates single fatherhood, including a desperate search for breast milk for his infant daughter. Adia plays Latif’s strong-willed teenage daughter Fatiha, who is forced to grow up quickly as she helps her father care for her younger brother and sister.

“She was just really complex,” Adia said, explaining what drew her to the role. “That’s how young, teenage girls are. But when we see them being portrayed on screen, generally speaking, they are not [complex]. They’re pretty black and white. ‘Oh, she’s just moody, hormonal and thinking about boys, and that’s it.”

Fatiha was written differently. “This girl has crushes, yeah, but that’s the least of her,” Adia explains. “She is dealing with very deep grief. Then also having to rise to the occasion to be in a maternal role to her siblings. Here is a character with depth, with real emotion. She’s experiencing real-life things in real time and having to navigate them with a 15-year-old brain.”

“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” will be released theatrically by Amazon MGM Studios and Orion Pictures. The film debuts in NYC/LA theaters on Sept. 25, followed by a nationwide rollout in October.

Adia auditioned for the part over Zoom, then Tariq flew to D.C. to meet her during a 30-minute break she had from her classes. (Adia was studying in a film program with acclaimed Ethiopian filmmaker Haile Gerima.)

“We didn’t talk too much about the role, but he asked me, ‘How do you envision Fatiha coming to life?’” she recalls. “I did a little bit of research into the name: it’s one of the first openings in the Quran, so it means the opener, the call to action. So we talked a bit about how Fatiha is the call to her father to parenthood, to come forth and be present.” The final step in the process was a chemistry read with Ali.

“Inside, I was screaming. But I was like, ‘Get the screams out now so that you can be a regular ass bitch on this call, Adia. Like, don’t play around. You’re going to work, so please act accordingly,’” she recalls, laughing.

Adia (as Fatiha), Mahershala Ali (as Latif) and Jahleel Kamara (as Qadir) in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” from Amazon MGM Studios. Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon MGM Studios

It was kismet that she and Ali were finally meeting, since she’d auditioned to play his daughter in another project a year prior but didn’t get the part. (“So that was wild, that here I am auditioning again,” she said.) And once she was in the room with Ali, it wasn’t difficult to get in work mode. “Now I’m acting, and it doesn’t really matter who is opposite me; I’m just doing what I love, and hopefully the other person is doing what they love. And thankfully Mahershala loves doing what he does, and so it was magic.”

The role came at the time Adia was undertaking another passion — training for her doula certification.

“It’s not easy to be a full-time artist. One of the most courageous things that you can do is to commit yourself fully to your artistry,” she said. But there’s a reason behind the “starving artist” stereotype. “You’ve got to support yourself in life,” she continues. “Birth work is something that fills my soul — spiritually and emotionally — but it fills my pockets financially, as well.”

Her interest in birth work began when she was nine and witnessed her cousin give birth; the experience was life-changing, and she knew she wanted to be a part of that sacred practice as an adult.

“I was fortunate to be mentored by the midwife and the doula who were at that birth,” Adia said. But her training overlapped with her shooting schedule. “There were days when I would be on my phone in class, and I’d be on set. They’re setting up for a scene, and I have my headphones in one ear, listening to them talking about conception.”

Adia is now certified — both as a doula and a budding movie star. Her performance in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” has been hailed as a true standout among a cast that is packed with major talents, including Emmy winner Tramell Tillman, Giancarlo Esposito and John Cho.

“I do birth work as my day job, and I’ve always thought I’ll probably end up becoming a midwife,” she adds. “Life is constantly shifting and changing. These are my passions: I love film. I love birth work. I’ll see where they meet, or don’t. And what happens next? I don’t know.”

If and when those movie offers start rolling in, Adia is more prepared than ever after working with Ali. “In my first few projects, I’m new, and I’m thinking, ‘It’s just a blessing to be here. I’m just going to do my job, and I won’t say anything, and I’m not gonna make a ruckus,’” she said. “That’s not a bad thing. That works for some people.”

But Ali taught her to follow her instincts as an artist and to speak up when she wanted to try something during a take.

“Watching Mahershala model that, and then opening the space for me to do that as well, made me feel empowered to be able to show up,” she said. “It was a master class and I got paid for it, which was cool.”

title: Netflix’s ‘Scooby-Doo: Origins’ Wraps Production Ahead of 2027 Release
summary: Netflix’s “Scooby-Doo: Origins” has wrapped production, the company announced Sunday. The live-action series is set for a global release on the streamer in 2027.  Per the series’ official logline, “Scooby-Doo: Origins” is a “modern reimagining of the iconic mystery-solving group of teens and their very special dog.” “During their final summer at camp, old friends […]
content:
Netflix’s “Scooby-Doo: Origins” has wrapped production, the company announced Sunday. The live-action series is set for a global release on the streamer in 2027.

Per the series’ official logline, “Scooby-Doo: Origins” is a “modern reimagining of the iconic mystery-solving group of teens and their very special dog.”

“During their final summer at camp, old friends Shaggy and Daphne get embroiled in a haunting mystery surrounding a lonely, lost Great Dane puppy that may have been a witness to a supernatural murder,” the logline continues. “Together with the pragmatic and scientific townie, Velma, and the strange, but ever so handsome new kid, Freddy, they set out to solve the case that is pulling each of them into a creepy nightmare that threatens to expose all of their secrets.”

The show, which audiences got a first look at earlier this year, was filmed in Atlanta. (Past Netflix productions “Stranger Things” and “His & Hers” were also shot in the state.)

Popular on Variety

The previously announced cast includes McKenna Grace as Daphne Blake, Tanner Hagen as Shaggy Rogers, Abby Ryder Fortson as Velma Dinkley and Maxwell Jenkins as Fred Jones. The titular canine will be played by a real Great Dane — a first for the “Scooby-Doo” universe.

The cast also includes Paul Walter Hauser (as Scooby-Doo’s owner), Rusty Schwimmer, Peter Macon, Jona Xiao, Dani Deetté, Elysée Sanvillé, Alex Isles, Avery Kristen Pohl, Pamela Mitchell, Ross Kimball, Sara Gilbert, Wynn Everett, Sauriyan Sapkota, Bruce McGill, André Benjamin and Cathy Moriarty.

Showrunners and writers Josh Appelbaum and Scott Rosenberg (“High Fidelity,” “Everything Sucks!”) executive produce alongside Toby Haynes. Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter and Leigh London Redman executive produce via Berlanti Productions and its overall deal with Warner Bros. Television, in addition to André Nemec, Jeff Pinkner and Adrienne Erickson, who executive produce via Midnight Radio.

title: Betty Thomas, Billy Crystal & The Curious Case Of The Emmy-Thieving Imposter
summary: On Sept. 22, 1985, the Pasadena Civic Auditorium was filled with 2,700 members of the year’s television elite, gathered together for the 37th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards. Hosted by Dynasty star John Forsythe, the ceremony was broadcast on ABC to 15.8 million homes – a staggering number today – and the stage was set to […]
content:
On Sept. 22, 1985, the Pasadena Civic Auditorium was filled with 2,700 members of the year’s television elite, gathered together for the 37th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards. Hosted by Dynasty star John Forsythe, the ceremony was broadcast on ABC to 15.8 million homes – a staggering number today – and the stage was set to receive a glitterati of Emmy Award recipients: Robert Guillaume, Tyne Daly, Williams Daniels, Richard Crenna, John Larroquette, Rhea Perlman, Edward James Olmos, David Letterman and… a man called Barry Bremen.

At this moment, it’s fair to ask: Barry who?

Tall, handsome, tan and, most importantly, possessed of a palpable confidence, Bremen certainly looked the part in his chic tuxedo, trendy pink bowtie and matching cummerbund. But the truth was a lot less glitzy: he had next to zero Industry connections. And yet, he’d happily slid into his third-row aisle seat, and made small talk with his neighbor, The Man from U.N.C.L.E. star Robert Vaughn.

Watch on Deadline

In fact, in 1985, 38-year-old Bremen – married with three children and a resident of the Detroit suburb West Bloomfield in Michigan – was actually a former insurance salesman turned co-proprietor of a marketing firm. They represented Famous Amos cookies, among other sundries, and it was Bremen’s job to place them in department stores.

But Bremen had actually become famous, in a strange sort of way. Known in sporting circles as ‘The Great Imposter’, Bremen had built a reputation for his unparalleled knack for sneaking onto the field – often with the help of those closest to the action, like Kansas City Royals all-star George Brett and the legendary ABC broadcaster Dick Schaap, the latter being Bremen’s longtime friend, neighbor and insurance client.

Who is Barry Bremen?” The answer to a trivia clue appeared on ‘Jeopardy’ about the infamous sports imposter who successfully snuck onstage to accept a 1985 Emmy Award. Channel 2

Beginning in 1979, on a dare and using a warm-up uniform he swiped at an NBA game in Detroit, Bremen brashly posed as a member of the Kansas City Kings and managed to join the pre-game shootaround with Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Julius “Dr. J” Irving at the NBA All-Star Game, a feat he’d repeat two years later in 1981, outfitted as a Houston Rocket. He’d bluff his way into Major League Baseball’s 1979 All-Star Game, shagging flies in the outfield for a half-hour until he was ejected. He’d succeed again at MLB’s All-Star Game in 1986, where once exposed, he got a royal chewing-out by legendary Los Angeles Dodgers coach Tommy Lasorda.

Growing ever bolder, Bremen posed as a baseball umpire at home plate at Game Five of the 1980 World Series, and later a line judge for 1981’s Super Bowl XV. He’d even briefly danced alongside the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders in a blonde wig and short shorts. And just months before the Emmys, he’d bluffed his way into playing practice rounds with pro golfers Fred Couples, Curtis Strange and Bob Eastwood at that year’s U.S. Open.

Dick Schaap’s son Jeremy, the accomplished sportswriter, broadcaster and author, calls these stunts “harmless,” adding, “They were victimless. They were sort of charming, Walter Mitty moments.” Jeremy Schaap grew up with a family that were intertwined with Bremen’s, via his father’s friendship and boostering – so much so, that Schaap wrote and narrated ESPN’s E60 2022 documentary The Great Imposter and Me, which chronicled Bremen’s exploits.

“He had all this charm and charisma, so people wanted to embrace him,” Schaap says. “It was just a different world. The idea of eluding the security protocols, getting behind the velvet rope. This was before the [tennis champion] Monica Seles’ stabbing [in 1993], it was before 9/11. It was a different world, a world in which these kinds of stunts seemed harmless, and they didn’t make our antenna go up, in that way.”

Indeed, as a result of these hijinks, Bremen appeared alongside Johnny Carson on The Tonight Show, as well as Late Night with David Letterman, the Today Show, Larry King’s radio show, a Michelob Light commercial and my personal favorite: a guest stint on Bowling for Dollars.

Insurance salesman ‘The Great Imposter’ Barry Bremen who impersonated an NBA player at the NBA All-Stars game, with ‘The Tonight Show’ host Johnny Carson on February 9, 1979. Gene Arias/NBC/NBCU Photo Bank

Bremen was, simply put, the most accomplished charlatan in sports. But crashing the Emmys would be a whole different ball game.

In 1980, he’d expanded his repertoire by sneaking into the Academy Awards, hoping to swoop in and claim the award of a star who’d skipped the ceremony. But even when an ailing, absent Melvyn Douglas’ name was announced as Best Supporting Actor, Bremen lost his legendary nerve. “That would have been perfect—except I panicked,” he told a Washington Post reporter at the time. “I really did. I could not get out of my seat.” He’d also targeted the Emmys twice before: once, he made it inside, but balked at claiming a trophy; the second time he backed out before the ceremony.

Still, he had his sights set on gracing a major Hollywood awards ceremony’s stage.

Born in 1947, Bremen met his wife Margo when they were both teenagers studying at MSU. Speaking via phone now from her home in Scottsdale, Arizona, Margo says, “A frustrated actor, a frustrated athlete – put them together in one and you get Barry. He loved movies and he loved his athletic stuff. Being out there, being known by people, he loved being recognized as somebody. That’s who he was.”

She also knew that at 6’4″, tall, dark and handsome, Bremen could get away with a lot. “When he put on a tuxedo, he could go any place and get in anywhere,” she says. “He could make himself be a part of any situation, for the most part. He loved people. So getting in and talking with people and being around people and just mostly being himself, he was able to do things.” As Bremen readied himself for another go at crashing the Emmys, Margo recalls discussing his mission. “I remember our conversation was, ‘This is your third try. About time you get it right.'”

He momentarily encountered what might have been a major monkey-wrench when he was recognized by actor, comedian and sports enthusiast Billy Crystal, but the recent Saturday Night Live breakout Crystal did not report him to security.

Bremen would later recount to his hometown newspaper the Detroit Free Press, among other media outlets, that he put four months of planning into crashing the Emmys, but finding himself short on inside connections to obtain a ticket, he was forced to get creative. Using his real name and claiming to work for a local network affiliate, he told the local paper, “Finally I called ABC and said I was in town from Michigan and I wanted to do a story on the Emmys.”

Allowed to pay $300 for a ticket – “No one ever asked for my credentials” – he flew to Los Angeles, tuxed up and “walked through the front entrance.” He momentarily encountered what might have been a major monkey-wrench when he was recognized by actor, comedian and sports enthusiast Billy Crystal, but the recent Saturday Night Live breakout Crystal did not report him to security.

“When I got in, I realized my ticket was for the third row. It was like they were saying ‘This is for you, Barry,’” Bremen told the press after that night. He had quickly calculated that as long as he looked like he knew what he was doing, he could be onstage in but a moment. Until his moment presented itself, he made idle chit-chat with another TV icon of his youth, The Untouchables star Robert Stack. “I told him I was here to accept an Emmy and I asked him what it was like to work with some of his friends. He didn’t say much. He acted like he knew who I was, but I knew he didn’t.”

As the ceremony progressed, the biggest controversies of the night remained somewhat tame. Moonlighting star Cybill Shepherd paired orange Day-Glo Reebok high-tops with her formal black velvet gown. Then there was the increasingly anemic showing of the critically ballyhooed, 15-times-nominated TV game changer Miami Vice, which was edged out by perennial Emmy darling Cagney & Lacey. However, thanks to Bremen, the drama dial was about to be turned way up.

For him, fate seemed to intervene in the form of Mission Impossible star Peter Graves, who took the stage to present Best Supporting Actress in a Drama Series. And what would follow would change the trajectory of Bremen’s life.

“Mission Impossible is how I always see myself,” Bremen later told the Washington Post. “We always start with a Mission: Impossible concept. It always starts out, ‘Good morning, Mr. Bremen. Your mission, should you choose to accept…’ So it was incredible. Graves is my hero.”

“I’ll tell you a very private moment,” says Margo. “He and I snuck away from school and went to his parents’ house. This was back when we were in college and being together or living together was not a thing. We were breaking the rules to go home for the weekend and just have a weekend to ourselves at his house. We were lying in bed and watching the Peter Graves show, Mission Impossible, and that’s when we decided to name our first child, our first son, Noah, because there was a character Noah on the program. He just always loved the Mission Impossible thing.”

That fateful Emmy night, Graves, with his rich, baritone voice, announced the winner: Hill Street Blues actress Betty Thomas. It was her first victory after four previous nominations in the category for her role as patrol officer Lucy Bates in Steven Bochco’s highly-acclaimed, grittily realistic police drama (she’d be nominated for two subsequent seasons as well). The orchestra struck up composer Mike Post’s instrumental theme song, which had become a hit on adult contemporary radio. Bremen, who’d never seen a single episode of the cop show, nevertheless recognized that his moment had arrived.

“When I called Betty’s name she was all the way on the other side of the auditorium, and I didn’t know if she was coming. All of sudden, there’s this guy sitting below me, and I said, ‘Isn’t Betty here?’ And he said, ‘No, I’ll take it,’ and he took off with it.” Peter Graves, to the Emmy Awards press in 1985.

In interviews with the San Francisco Examiner and the Orlando Sentinel, Bremen later said, “Betty Thomas’ name was called. There was a hesitation. There were no screams for Thomas, not even a lot of clapping. I did not think she was there.”

“He couldn’t sit still,” says Margo. “He had to get up and do it. And he actually did not think she was there. He did look and she hadn’t stood up yet. And if nothing else, Barry did lots of things very fast: throw a bowling ball, swing a golf club. Fast was part of his mode.”

Bounding up to the stage at lightning speed, Bremen collected the Emmy from a puzzled Graves, who told the press backstage, “When I called Betty’s name she was all the way on the other side of the auditorium, and I didn’t know if she was coming. All of sudden, there’s this guy sitting below me, and I said, ‘Isn’t Betty here?’ And he said, ‘No, I’ll take it,’ and he took off with it.”

Bremen had stepped up to the mic with the bravado he usually reserved for sports. He’d prepared a speech, but as the magnitude of the audience, in front of him and at home, weighed on him, his nerves began to show as he spoke off the cuff. “Betty was not able to be here,” he announced, “and she asked for me to accept this award and thank everybody else who was here. And thank you and thank everybody.” The he offered a quick shout-out to an old pal: “And especially Dick Schaap.”

Imposter Barry Bremen accepting the Primetime Emmy Award on behalf of actress Betty Thomas at the 1985 ceremony. ABC

“I’m sure when my father heard his name come out of Barry’s mouth, it was not a great moment for him,” says Jeremy Schaap. “I’m sure that he was like, ‘Jesus, Barry, couldn’t you have said Otis Birdsong or George Brett? Why me?’”



Meanwhile, Betty Thomas was, in fact, very much present at the ceremony. Her ascent to the stage was delayed by both the typical surprise of winning, and then by a string of beads she was wearing breaking and spilling everywhere. As the 38-year-old actress at last stepped onto the stage, she felt a sinking feeling when she saw an unfamiliar man merrily collecting the award. “I thought I made a mistake,” she’d later tell reporters. “It was the nightmare you always hear about.”

As Bremen concluded his speech and turned away from the mic chuckling with glee, he suddenly found himself face to face with the confused but formidable Thomas – all six-feet-one-inches of her, including extra heel height. He immediately went straight-faced, pivoted away from her and began quickly offering explanations to Thomas and Graves. They moved off the stage into the wings and the show quickly shifted to a commercial. “She was a little startled,” Bremen reported. “I said to her ‘Betty, I’m sorry. I’m the imposter.’ And the guy from ABC went a little crazy.”

I keep hearing that somebody’s going to make a movie. There’s always somebody who’s like, ‘We’re going to do this!’ At one point I think Adam Sandler was interested, at one point Larry David. I hope somebody does it. Jeremy Schaap

That “guy from ABC” was Emmys producer Alexander Cohen. He seized Bremen in a fit of rage as Pasadena police officers moved in. “I ran over and jumped on his back and was ready to kill him,” Cohen later told United Press International, “but he said ‘No, no, no’ and pulled out his press clippings. I was absolutely stunned and the cops pulled him away.”

“I wanted to make sure they understood that I didn’t have a gun or something,” Bremen told the Lansing State Journal. “That I’m fun-bizarre, not crazy-bizarre.”

Still, in Thomas’ retelling in the Emmy press room later that evening, Bremen made a break for it. “It turned out that he was running backstage, out the door, and the police were chasing him, tackled him,” she said. “And it’s grand theft to take that Emmy away,” she added with a chuckle, “so he’s in jail right now.”

For his part, Graves offered bemused consolation to the actress, saying “I’m sorry, darlin’. That was a ‘mission impossible’ and I think that guy’s on his way to the cooler.” After the commercial, Thomas was allowed to return to the stage with her trophy and deliver her acceptance speech, opening with “Well, it’s definitely hard to follow an act like that, but I will.”

Meanwhile, Bremen was led out of the Civic Auditorium in handcuffs by Pasadena police, then he spent several hours in jail before he was finally released about 45 minutes after midnight on $1,500 bond provided by his attorney, who’d been on standby for just such a result. (“He always had his attorney set up to get him out of jail after,” says Margo). “They brought me in for questioning, and they got a little pushy for a while,” Bremen recounted back then, adding that behind bars “I was the only guy dressed in a tuxedo. And then there was the fact that I was conscious. You know, not drunk.”

Imposter Barry Bremen (center) is approached by Betty Thomas after he accepted her Emmy Award from Peter Graves (left). ABC

Even then, Bremen’s charm became an important part of his toolkit. “He met some guy that was in jail, and gave him the number of his mother to call and tell her where he was when he got out,” says Margo. “So yeah, even being in jail was a story for Barry.”

The tense mood lifted upon his release. “I even autographed something for some of the police officers,” Bremen said. Ultimately, he was sanguine about the arrest. “I guess I deserved it, right? I mean, you take an award from somebody on Hill Street Blues, I guess you should be thrown in jail.”

Some relief came when he discovered the grand theft charge wouldn’t stick. The Emmy statuette, originally estimated to be worth $400, was actually valued at $135, and the charge was downgraded to interfering with an event. Within a month, from Detroit, Bremen pleaded no contest and a Pasadena municipal court judge fined him $175 and sentenced him to six months’ probation.

Along with the consequences came an important takeaway: “I learned that in Hollywood awards are taken very seriously,” Bremen said.

He was genuinely penitent that he’d marred a moment of career victory for Thomas. “When I saw her come up I was very surprised and disappointed that I took something away from her.” Although he couldn’t help admitting “it was a great feeling holding that Emmy and looking out on that crowd.” And he couldn’t help but make light of the brouhaha he caused. “I guess I missed my mark. I should have accepted for Jane Curtin,” he offered, as the Kate & Allie star was a no-show at the ceremony but won the Best Actress in a Comedy Series trophy.

“Whatever you write, could you please start out with an apology to Betty Thomas?” he asked the press. In fact, he vowed to offer her a personal apology, via his attorney, who was friends with Thomas’ agent.

Thomas had been pretty good-humored about the incident at the time. “I would now like to thank him,” she deadpanned in the press room. “That was a great way to be remembered for the award.” Days later, however, the network publicist for Hill Street Blues told Newsday that Thomas wanted to put the incident behind her and curtail any further notoriety for Bremen. She reportedly had accepted his public apology but not forgiven him.

Fortunately, the night would not be Thomas’ last in the Emmy spotlight. In 1993, after a career pivot behind the camera, she became the first woman to receive a Directing Emmy for the HBO comedy Dream On, followed by additional directing nominations in 1994 and 1996. She’d later go on to helm a string of successful big-screen comedies including Private Parts, The Brady Bunch Movie and 28 Days (Deadline attempted to contact Thomas for comment but was not able to connect with her by press time).

“He was so regretful over the fact that it was her moment and he messed it up for her,” remembers Margo. “He always felt terrible and tried, I cannot tell you the number of times, to be able to apologize to her, and she would not accept his apology. And that was his one regret in his life, that he hadn’t been able to apologize to Betty Thomas.”

Betty Thomas with her Emmy at the 1985 Emmy Awards American Broadcasting Companies via Getty Images

Dick Schaap wrote an article decrying the fallout from his friend’s Emmy debacle. Although both Jeremy Schaap and Margo strongly suspect that Dick, having been name checked during Bremen’s fake acceptance speech, was pushed to pen the condemnation by his employer, ABC. “Their friendship remained very strong up until my father’s death,” says Jeremy. “So I don’t know if it was performative or real.”

The Emmy affair would signal a turning point in Bremen’s ‘career’ as a professional imposter. Says Margo, “After that, pretty much, I said ‘enough’ and that our kids were becoming teenagers and I didn’t want him to keep ending up in jail.”

Bremen died of esophageal cancer on 64th birthday in 2011, leaving behind a loving family and a colorful legacy, one that continues to captivate 15 years later. “People like people who have balls. And Barry was so positive about life,” says Margo. “What Barry’s influence did is that he showed people – first and foremost, our three children – you don’t say no to things. When opportunity presents itself, you take advantage.”

“I keep hearing that somebody’s going to make a movie,” says Jeremy Schaap. “There’s always somebody who’s like, ‘We’re going to do this!’ At one point I think Adam Sandler was interested, at one point Larry David. I hope somebody does it, because nobody would love to see themselves on the silver screen more than Barry.”

And if that happens, maybe Barry Bremen’s name will finally, legitimately, be engraved on one of those prized Hollywood trophies.

Deadline contributor Scott Huver is the author of the forthcoming true crime collection Beverly Hills Noir Volume Two: Money, Murder and Mayhem in 90210 (March 2027). His book Beverly Hills Noir: Crime, Sin, & Scandal in 90210, was published in 2024.

title: Bertil Nilsson’s TIFF Film ‘Masc’ Explores Intersectionality Of Queer, Biracial, Autistic Experience — Clip
summary: In Bertil Nillson’s feature directorial debut Masc, the writer/director teams up with co-writer and star Joshua Griffin to share a story of intersectionality and self-love. Making its world premiere last night in TIFF’s Next Wave Selects section, Masc stars Griffin as Robin, a queer, biracial man on the autism spectrum, who struggles over a year […]
content:
In Bertil Nillson‘s feature directorial debut Masc, the writer/director teams up with co-writer and star Joshua Griffin to share a story of intersectionality and self-love.

Making its world premiere last night in TIFF‘s Next Wave Selects section, Masc stars Griffin as Robin, a queer, biracial man on the autism spectrum, who struggles over a year to learn how to exist as himself.

“It’s worth saying that most of the time autistic characters are portrayed as a stereotype, not a real person,” said Nillson. “Every autistic person is different and so is Robin. He’s not intended as a representation of autism.”

The writer/director continued, “I think that’s similar to how queer characters have historically been portrayed. Thankfully we now have a much richer queer representation in films and hope our film can contribute to that, as well as adding an autistic perspective.”

Watch on Deadline

In a Deadline exclusive clip from Masc, Robin (Griffin) asks Sky (Reece King) about where to get drugs, specifically crack cocaine. A concerned friend, Sky steers Robin toward something more his speed.

Watch the clip above.

title: Vertical Saves Lily James & Pierce Brosnan Starring ‘Cliffhanger’; Spring 2027 U.S. Release Eyed – TIFF
summary: EXCLUSIVE: After the hot new distributor at TIFF last year, Row K, imploded, many films that the label scooped up at the fest were left homeless; one of the big titles they supposed shelled out eight figures for was Jaume Collet-Serra’s reboot of 1993’s Cliffhanger starring Lily James and Pierce Brosnan. In a complete surprise, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: After the hot new distributor at TIFF last year, Row K, imploded, many films that the label scooped up at the fest were left homeless; one of the big titles they supposed shelled out eight figures for was Jaume Collet-Serra’s reboot of 1993’s Cliffhanger starring Lily James and Pierce Brosnan. In a complete surprise, Vertical has risen to be the title’s savior, taking U.S. rights as the buzz around Cannes was that Neon’s new Decal label was acquiring the action adventure film.

Vertical is targeting a spring 2027 wide theatrical release for the pic.

The news comes at a time when James is starring in a buzzy festival title, The Liberation, alongside Carrie Coon and Bella Ramsey, which world premiered at Telluride and is now playing TIFF which Deadine’s Pete Hammond exclaims is an “edge-of-your-seat suspense thriller,” calling James “bewitching”. Bleecker Street is releasing the movie on Jan. 8, 2027.

Watch on Deadline

The deal for Cliffhanger was negotiated by Jarowey, SVP of Acquisitions Tony Piantedosi and Manager of Acquisitions Rachel White on behalf of Vertical and by CAA Media Finance on behalf of the filmmakers. Rocket Science has international sales.

Cliffhanger is set high in the breathtaking but treacherous Dolomites where legendary mountaineer Ray Cooper (Pierce Brosnan) runs a secluded luxury chalet with his daughters, Naomi (Lily James) and Sydney (Nell Tiger Free). When a billionaire’s son arrives for a weekend getaway, a ruthless gang launches a daring kidnapping, taking Ray hostage and leaving Sydney in the crossfire. Haunted by a devastating climbing accident, Naomi must conquer her fear of the mountains and turn the terrain against her enemies in a relentless race to save her family.

Based on the 1993 Sylvester Stallone summer hit movie which grossed over $255M WW, the latest Cliffhanger was penned by Mark Bianculli and Melanie Toast based on a story by Sacha Penn and Bianculli. Nell Tiger Free (Servant), Franz Rogowski (Passages), Shubham Saraf (Shantaram), Assaad Bouab (Franklin), Suzy Bemba (Poor Things), and Bruno Gouery (Emily in Paris) also star. Producers include Lars Sylvest of Thank You Pictures, Thorsten Schumacher of Rocket Science, Joe Neurauter and Philipp Kreuzer of Supernix, and Neal Moritz and Toby Jaffe.

“Cliffhanger is the perfect combination of an iconic title, a world-class filmmaker, an incredible cast, and edge-of-your-seat spectacle that demands to be experienced on the big screen,” Vertical Partner Peter Jarowey told Deadline. “Jaume Collet-Serra has created a relentless, visually stunning thriller that takes everything audiences love about the original and delivers it with a fresh, modern intensity. With Lily James and Pierce Brosnan leading an exceptional cast, we’re thrilled to bring this next chapter of Cliffhanger to theaters in 2027.”

Row K acquired several movies out of TIFF last year including Maude Apatow’s feature directorial debut Poetic License, Gus Van Sant’s Dead Man’s Wire, Cliffhanger and the Emilia Jones-Nick Robinson title Charlie Harper. Following the January theatrical bombing of Dead Man’s Wire, Row K realized the indie feature distribution was challenging with a number of their executives exiting. Word was that they had never even closed on several of these acquisitions (though the trades announce them, it’s often a lengthy papering process). Poetic License was scooped up by Sony Pictures Classics. Charlie Harper per Rentrak still sits at Row K with a Sept. 25 theatrical release.

title: ‘Scooby-Doo: Origins’ Season 1 Production Has Rrrr-Wrapped
summary: The cast, crew and star of Scooby-Doo: Origins can finally take a pawse, as production has wrapped on the first season of the upcoming Netflix live-action series. It’s slated to premiere globally on the streamer in 2027. For the first time in Scooby-Doo franchise history, the title character is being portrayed by a real Great […]
content:
The cast, crew and star of Scooby-Doo: Origins can finally take a pawse, as production has wrapped on the first season of the upcoming Netflix live-action series. It’s slated to premiere globally on the streamer in 2027.

For the first time in Scooby-Doo franchise history, the title character is being portrayed by a real Great Dane dog. (You can see his photo above).

Based on characters created by Hanna-Barbera, Scooby-Doo: Origins is a modern reimagining of the iconic mystery-solving group of teens and their very special dog. During their final summer at camp, old friends Shaggy (Tanner Hagen) and Daphne (Mckenna Grace) get embroiled in a haunting mystery surrounding a lonely lost Great Dane puppy that may have been a witness to a supernatural murder.

Together with the pragmatic and scientific townie, Velma (Abby Ryder Fortson), and the strange, but ever so handsome new kid, Freddy (Maxwell Jenkins), they set out to solve the case that is pulling each of them into a creepy nightmare that threatens to expose all of their secrets.

Watch on Deadline

Previously announced cast also includes Paul Walter Hauser, Rusty Schwimmer, Peter Macon, Jona Xiao, Dani Deetté, Elysée Sanvillé, Alex Isles, Avery Kristen Pohl, Pamela Mitchell, Ross Kimball, Sara Gilbert, Wynn Everett, Sauriyan Sapkota, Bruce McGill, André Benjamin and Cathy Moriarity.

Created by Joe Ruby and Ken Spears, the Scooby-Doo! franchise was launched in 1969 with the duo’s first animated series Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! for then-Hanna-Barbera (later absorbed into Warner Bros. Animation).

The series, which introduced supernatural mystery-solving teens Fred Jones, Daphne Blake, Velma Dinkley, and Shaggy Rogers and their talking Great Dane Scooby-Doo, originally aired on CBS from 1969-76, when it moved to ABC, where various versions of the show aired until 1986.

Josh Appelbaum and Scott Rosenberg serve as showrunners, writers, and executive producers. Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter, Leigh London Redman (via Berlanti Productions and its overall deal with Warner Bros. Television), André Nemec, Jeff Pinkner, and Adrienne Erickson (via Midnight Radio), and Toby Haynes (EP/Episode 101 Director) also executive produce. Warner Bros. Television is the studio.

title: Midnight Madness! A Caped Canadian Prime Minister Stars In ‘Ladies And Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney’ – Toronto Film Festival
summary: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, attended the opening of the Toronto Film Festival last year, helping introduce the documentary John Candy: I Like Me. This year, a former Canadian PM, Brian Mulroney, is appearing at TIFF, in a manner of speaking. The Conservative Party politician, who served from 1984-1993, stars in Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian […]
content:
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, attended the opening of the Toronto Film Festival last year, helping introduce the documentary John Candy: I Like Me. This year, a former Canadian PM, Brian Mulroney, is appearing at TIFF, in a manner of speaking.

The Conservative Party politician, who served from 1984-1993, stars in Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney, the rare documentary to be programmed in the festival’s Midnight Madness section. The outlandish tone suggests why it would be slotted in the midnight roster – the TIFF program describes Matthew Rankin’s film as “a satirical collage of archival footage, television nostalgia, and national mythmaking.”

One look at the key image will give a hint of what’s to come – it shows Mulroney in an outfit and pancake makeup that looks like a collision of Liberace and Count Dracula.
