Directed by Wen Muye (“Dying to Survive”) and starring Shen Teng, Jiang Qiming, Aarif Rahman, and Omar Sherif, the late-summer hit has lifted its cume to $318.4 million since opening on Aug. 11. The story tracks a Chinese chef who travels to the Middle East to run an eatery to clear family debts, only for his establishment to turn into a vital haven for civilians and orphans after regional armed conflict erupts.

Pearl River Film Group’s crime thriller “V” took second place in its fourth weekend of release, taking in $4.7 million. Directed by Han Yan (“Love Never Ends”) and featuring an ensemble led by Tony Leung Ka-fai, Zhu Yilong, Tan Jianci, and Kara Wai, the gritty production has now amassed $84.1 million since rolling out on Aug. 19.

Popular on Variety

Pearl Studio’s animated fantasy comedy “All Wishes Come True!” was in third position in its ninth frame, generating $4 million. Directed by Mu Zhengyang, the enduring family hit has reached a cumulative total of $283.4 million since its July 18 debut.

In fourth place Universal’s “The Odyssey” crossed the century mark in China, adding $3.5 million for a cumulative total of $102.9 million. Crossing the $100 million threshold pushes the film well past the China runs of “Oppenheimer,” “Tenet,” and “Inception,” leaving it second in Christopher Nolan’s local catalog only to the $122 million lifetime gross of “Interstellar.”

Rounding out the top five, Phoenix Legend Films’ time-bending fantasy romance “My Tomorrow, Your Yesterday” opened with $1.7 million over its two-day debut frame. Directed by Xiang Guoqiang and adapted from Takafumi Nanatsuki’s Japanese novel, the film stars Bi Wenjun as an architectural restorer who falls in love with a medical student played by He Landou, only to uncover that her timeline flows in reverse to his, leaving them with an expiring window together.

Mainland China’s overall weekend grosses reached $28.8 million, while the 2026 year-to-date box office stands at $4.26 billion, down 27.6% from the same period in 2025.

title: ‘Pretenders’ Review: A Superb Portrait of Chrissie Hynde and Her Legendary Band Captures Their Incandescence…and Tragedy
summary: Hynde, though she had the feelings of punk in her bones, was the most romantic songwriter of that entire scene. I don’t mean romantic as in "love songs," but as in conjuring the majestic romanticism of life. Just listen to "Kid," a song so happy and sad at the same time that it’s worthy of the Beatles.
content:
As a rock star, Chrissie Hynde has always been a bit of a paradox — gnarly but cerebral, ferocious yet guarded. And “Pretenders,” Joss Crowley’s sensational and revealing music documentary, shows you that there was a paradox — a glorious one — built into her band.

Formed in London in 1978, the Pretenders emerged from the moment when “punk” had morphed into “new wave.” But there were still musicians around who could claim to be both, and Hynde was one of them. When you listen to “Precious,” which is totally a punk song (it has the potent high-speed sizzle of something by the Ramones), the ice-cold defiance and gutter snarl of Hynde’s singing (“Made me wanna…”), the song’s total fuck-it-all vibe, are undiminished by time. Hynde, with her shag haircut and androgynous toothy scowl, had emerged from the original punk scene (she’d moved to London in her early 20s and even tried to join the Slits), and it left its mark on her. She was a blistering rocker who was going to be no one’s doll.

And yet…as fierce and defining as a song like “Precious” was, it doesn’t represent what I ultimately cherish about the Pretenders. To say what that is, I have to use a word that risks sounding innocuous: They were tuneful. They came out of the world of rage and nihilism and buzzcuts and heroin, but there was an incandescence to the songs Hynde wrote, and to how the band sounded. For years, rock critics of the post-new wave era struggled to come up with different words to communicate the concept of “jangly guitar.” But it was James Honeyman-Scott, the lead guitarist of the Pretenders, who owned jangly guitar, and in some ways invented it. He had a sound that rang. And Hynde, though she had the feeling of punk in her bones, was the most romantic songwriter of that scene. I don’t mean romantic as in “love songs,” but as in conjuring the majestic romanticism of life. Just listen to “Kid,” a song so happy and sad at the same time that it’s worthy of the Beatles.

Popular on Variety

“Pretenders,” which is built around astonishing archival footage as well as a lengthy interview with Hynde (Crowley also talks to many fascinating people in her orbit), is a movie that understands that side of the Pretenders — that they were making music so shimmering in its timelessness that it transcended the new-wave aesthetic and a lot of other things. How Chrissie Hynde wound up being that kind of songwriter is anyone’s guess. Songwriting is one of the true mysteries: a gift that drops into certain people from the heavens. But Hynde’s vocal expression was just as magical. She sounded like she was singing directly to you, and she had that unique slow vibrato, which could suffuse a single note with heartbreak.

Born in 1951 and raised in Akron, Ohio, she grew up in what’s described in the film as a “cookie-cutter postwar family.” She loved her parents but experienced their ’50s squareness as if they were aliens. At Kent State University, she was close to one of the four students killed there by the National Guard on May 4, 1970, and by the time she moved to London in the early ’70s, she was ready for anything. Which is what she got.

She was majorly into drugs. She became a pop-music critic for New Musical Express, mostly writing scathing put-downs. But she couldn’t find a band that would have her! She met Mick Jones and attempted to work with him, but he went off and formed the Clash. She tried to join the Damned, but they weren’t biting. (She finally joined a band called the Moors Murders, who were so disreputable that they all performed in masks.) Yet she was writing songs, and her gift was pure; we hear her singing a demo of “Precious” from 1976, and the Hynde mystique is there, fully loaded.

The only solution was to form her own band, which she did, joining forces with a bass player, Pete Farndon (they were in a relationship together), then inviting in James Honeyman-Scott, who turned out to be a karmic addition. Hynde just thought she needed a guitarist, but Honeyman-Scott, who was only 22, was as visionary a guitar player as The Edge. The ferocious drummer Martin Chambers, with his knifey sideburns, completed the quartet.

So here was Hynde, an American girl with a smoldering stare, and her three British male back-up musicians. That sounds like a novelty, but Hynde ruled the stage with such verve, and such effortless punk-ruffian moves, that when you looked at her, you didn’t think that this was pretty much the first time in history that a woman with a guitar slung around her neck had led a rock ‘n’ roll band. She made it look like something that had always been.

The first song their producer, Nick Lowe, wanted to put out as a single was “Stop Your Sobbing,” Hynde’s cover of a 1964 track by the Kinks. If you listen to the original, it’s got a C&W-meets-British-Invasion stodginess that makes it sound like one of those slightly boring covers that filled out the Beatles’ first few albums. But Hynde makes the song as accusatory, and grandly symphonic, as a great Phil Spector track. In her hands, it’s a brand new song, one that squares with the vantage that would define the Pretenders — a grounded yearning for love, in its very imperfection, to become a higher love. As the single was getting ready to be pressed, the band still didn’t have a name, so Hynde, inspired by the Platters song “The Great Pretender,” came up with it at the last moment.

Here’s another side of the Chrissie Hynde paradox. At 17, she became a vegetarian, and still is, mostly driven by the animal-rights aspect of it all. But as she discusses in the documentary, she also had a thing for bikers — and I don’t just mean that she liked the sexiness of riding on the back of a chopper (though she did). She was hanging out with biker-gang members who were, by her own description, homicidal, and that was part of the excitement. So when it came to her belief in punk danger, this animal-rights vegetarian wasn’t playing.

That spirit was the yin to her melodic yang. She wrote “Brass in Pocket,” a masterpiece of jangle, and didn’t even want to put it out as a single, though it went to number one and became defining. What lyrics! The song is so resonant that it’s like a movie, and it’s also one of the most romantic songs I’ve ever heard. It could be the anthem of a teenage girl (“‘Cause I’m…gonna make you see,/There’s nobody else here, no one like me”). It could be the anthem of anyone who’s looking for someone to fall for them.

The Pretenders, for a while, had a satisfying life on the road. Hynde was a disciplined performer, and the guys enjoyed the perks of rock celebrity. But they indulged too much. Watching “Pretenders,” we wait for the dark side, and when it arrives it’s simple and devastating. Pete Farndon became a heroin addict, and spiraled down to the point that they had to kick him out of the band. Okay, that happened; it’s part of the rock ‘n’ roll story. He was fired from the Pretenders on June 14, 1982. Exactly two days later, James Honeyman-Scott, who was not a junkie (he was just a rock star who liked to party too much), died in his sleep of a heart attack. He was 25 years old and had been up for four nights straight, doing cocaine. This was a genuinely shocking rock death. Just like that, the band…was no longer a band.

As “Pretenders” captures vividly in the conversation it features with Chrissie Hynde, she’s a straight-shooter who can be extremely prickly and defensive. She was, and still is (at 75, looking great in a black-leather jacket), a strutting rock star who hates to see herself on camera. She smashed through the rock ‘n’ roll glass ceiling before it was even named, yet she doesn’t like the label of feminist or groundbreaker or anything else of that ilk, because she doesn’t want to be stuck in the role-model box. She had a fierce bravado on stage, yet claims that she took no pride in her performances; she just thought she was getting away with something. Maybe that’s why she called herself a Pretender? In “Pretenders,” she’s as real as it gets.

title: ‘All That She Wants’ Review: Annie Murphy and Cooper Raiff Are Well-Matched in a Generation-Gap Romcom
summary: Millennials get their Mrs. Robinson moment with “All That She Wants,” an age-gap romcom titled after the 1992 Ace of Base hit. If you remember listening to that song on a cassingle, it’s time to ask your doctor about perimenopause. Professional dancer Emma (Annie Murphy) isn’t quite there yet, but in her early thirties, she’s […]
content:
Millennials get their Mrs. Robinson moment with “All That She Wants,” an age-gap romcom titled after the 1992 Ace of Base hit. If you remember listening to that song on a cassingle, it’s time to ask your doctor about perimenopause. Professional dancer Emma (Annie Murphy) isn’t quite there yet, but in her early thirties, she’s feeling her age. Symptoms include baby fever, exacerbated by the pregnancy announcement of her sister Macy (Zosia Mamet), and an intolerance to her pompous, long-term but non-committal boyfriend Spencer (Finn Wittrock).

In the wake of her breakup, Emma meets an intriguing guy, Luke (Cooper Raiff), at a nightclub. A grad student, he’s about a decade younger than Emma, but his old soul is enchanted by her awkward manic pixie dream girl energy. Fueled by shots and undeniable chemistry, they fall into bed in his university dorm room. Here’s the twist: In the clarity of morning, Emma spots a few family photos and realizes she used to babysit four year-old Luke, whom she once referred to as “Lil Lukey.”

Popular on Variety

“Schitt’s Creek” writer David West Read penned this script specifically for Murphy, who won an Emmy for her performance in that acclaimed comedy series, and the film is built around the expressive physical humor that made her Alexis Rose so GIF-able. But “All That She Wants” gives Murphy an opportunity to demonstrate her dramatic chops too, in a role that requires Emma to grow over time, which is marked over a couple of years in jumps from May to December (LOL).

The film is co-directed by spouses Andrew Rhymer and (in her helming debut) Scarlett Bermingham, who previously worked on the 2019 wedding rom-com “Plus One” — Rhymer as co-writer and co-director, Bermingham as a supporting player. While the tone and look of “All That She Wants” starts out quite Netflix-y, it’s the characters and performances that elevate this to future comfort-watch territory.

In his own films as director-star, Raiff has made himself the go-to younger guy for age-gap romances. His college-set debut “Shithouse” was about the connection between a freshman and his sophomore resident advisor (Dylan Gelula); he followed that up with “Cha Cha Real Smooth,” playing a bar mitzvah party-starter flirting with an older single mom played by Dakota Johnson. However, Raiff is a far more appealing romantic lead under the guidance of a different directing team, with another writer’s script. This is his warmest and most charming turn yet — his edges buffed out in a good way.

While the former babysitter hiccup is ostensibly the obstacle for Emma and Charlie’s love story, Emma gets over it pretty quickly, and that speed bump is a little too contrived and minor. The biggest hurdle is Emma’s own brain. She’s hamstrung herself with the toxic perfectionism she inherited from her mother (Christine Baranski), and the expectations that she perceives other people have for her. The title “All that She Wants” might be a little cutesy (that needle-drop is both inevitable and highly anticipated), but it’s also apt. What exactly does Emma want for herself that has nothing to do with what other people have decided she should want?

Like the maneater protagonist of the song, what Emma wants is a baby — an actual human child —whether that’s considered feminist or not. She throws herself into a career change, but her desire for motherhood doesn’t abate, and she realizes that Luke might be an ideal sperm donor. He agrees because he wants to help, and to spend time with Emma. Within the confines of this transactional relationship, will Emma let herself love Luke? Or be loved by him?

Murphy and Raiff are well-matched. Emma’s manic, quirky energy might feel slightly out of date and a little over the top, but that’s what makes Luke adore her, and because we see her through his eyes, she’s perfectly adorkable. Luke grounds Emma, but ultimately, Emma grounds herself, through purpose and family. It’s satisfying seeing the journey that this character goes on to finding her own happiness, as much within herself as with others.

Rhymer and Bermingham’s solid direction lets the performances shine against a standard-issue, spit-shiny Toronto landscape. But “All That She Wants” is more about the script. Read kicks this tale off with a meet-cute and an unconventional relationship, but finds authentic emotion and real social issues to power the characters’ journeys forward. As the anecdotal data piles up — from cultural trend pieces, to pop culture, to movies like “Babygirl” and “I Want Your Sex” — it’s no surprise that the younger man-older woman dynamic has made its way to the romantic comedy. This time, “Mrs. Robinson” finds a different, more modern kind of happy ending.

title: ‘Lanterns’ Star Poorna Jagannathan Breaks Down Zoe’s Brutal Episode 5: ‘It’s a Faustian Play She Makes’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Lanterns” Episode 5, titled “Lights Out,” now streaming on HBO Max. This week’s episode of “Lanterns” finally unmasks the Manhunter, who’s been at the heart of the mystery in Rushville throughout the season. As revealed at the end of Episode 4, the Manhunter is in fact Zoe Macon, […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Lanterns” Episode 5, titled “Lights Out,” now streaming on HBO Max.

This week’s episode of “Lanterns” finally unmasks the Manhunter, who’s been at the heart of the mystery in Rushville throughout the season.

As revealed at the end of Episode 4, the Manhunter is in fact Zoe Macon, played by Poorna Jagannathan. In an interview with Variety, Jagannathan said that she had no idea she was the Manhunter until she got the script for the fourth episode. “Everyone saw it coming except me!” she says with a laugh.

“Obviously, I’m grateful that they didn’t tell me initially, because in my audition I know I would have acted like a robot,” she says.

Popular on Variety

The episode begins by delving into how the Manhunter holds so much sway over the people of Rushville. We see Sheriff Kerry (Kelly Macdonald) years before on the run from some gangsters to whom her father owed money. They track her to the Rushville diner, where Zoe is sitting in a booth by herself. Out of nowhere, she snaps one gangster’s neck and informs the other that he will be going back to his boss and telling him that Kerry is dead.

Kerry is grateful, but obviously scared. Zoe explains that Kerry can have a safe and peaceful life in Rushville, so long as Kerry is willing to protect Zoe when the time comes.

“[Co-creator] Chris [Mundy] and Geeta Patel, the director of that episode, wanted a sense that that scene is emblematic of the contract Zoe has made with every single person in the town,” Jagannathan says. “Her survival depends on you agreeing to your survival. It’s a Faustian play she makes.”

Given that, Rushville goes into high alert, as Zoe knows that Antaan (Paul Ben-Victor) and his team will be on their way to kill her. All the citizens arm themselves and prepare for battle.

Hal (Kyle Chandler), meanwhile, has left John (Aaron Pierre) trapped in their car after forcing him into a crash at the end of the last episode. He plans to let Antaan and Will Macon’s (Garret Dillahunt) militia shoot it out while he goes after Zoe to turn her over to the Guardians.

Zoe tracks John down just as the car begins to burn. But rather than save him, she waits for it to explode. Now severely burned and barely alive, John is taken to the local hospital, where he reveals to Zoe that he knows the Guardians are the ones who created the Manhunters in the first place.

Zoe offers John a deal: She will heal his injuries so long as he lets Hal die and tells the Guardians that all is well. “She waits for John to burn, and he is hanging by a thread to life,” Jagannathan says. “What you understand is she waits for people to be at their most vulnerable point, near death — and she comes in to save them.”

On why she believes Zoe wouldn’t have let John die, Jagannathan believes the character understood that having the gratitude and protection of a Green Lantern would be “her crown jewel.”

“She quickly assessed who is her biggest threat,” she says. “She quickly assessed who could be her strongest protector, and it wasn’t Hal — it was John. She sees something in John where she knows that he is going to be the better Green Lantern.”

Antaan and his team reach Rushville, and Hal finds them at the diner. He tells Antaan that Will is the Manhunter, but Antaan is clearly suspicious. Still, they set off for Will’s ranch armed to the teeth.

Back at the hospital, John has agreed to Zoe’s terms, and she prepares to heal him using alien technology. He asks her why she chose the form of a South Asian woman, to which she replies that being an outsider allows her a “higher vantage point” from which she can infiltrate a society.

“My outsiderness over the years has definitely become my strength,” Jagannathan says. “It’s the thing that I bring to the party. So when I read that monologue, I was like, ‘OK, that’s my in.'”

“You just don’t get asked a lot of questions if you are presented as outsider,” she continues. “No one really knows what questions to ask you. You can hide in plain sight, and that’s the tactic she chose in order to come and live on this planet.”

Now fully healed, John deduces that Zoe killed Abin Sur, the Green Lantern who passed his ring to Hal, as he was going to let her go on Earth. But Zoe couldn’t risk Abin Sur one day revealing her location to the Guardians.

While Jagannathan believes that all the characters in “Lanterns” are presented with a wide range of shades of gray, Zoe is ultimately a “victim of her programming” as a Manhunter.

Antaan and his team assault Will’s ranch. He patiently waits inside for Antaan to get there, calling Zoe to thank her for giving him more time to live. Antaan arrives, and Zoe has coached Will to pretend to be the Manhunter to throw Antaan off the trail. But Antaan dispatches Will, and cuts out his heart, proving he is human.

Zoe needs to draw Hal out, so she begins firing space-based weapons onto the town in order to force him to drain his ring’s power. He manages to find her, but she escapes. With his ring nearly drained, Hal has to return to the motel to recharge it.

Once he arrives, John is waiting for him. He brutally assaults Hal as they begin a knockdown, drag out brawl that has been brewing since the season started. John gets the upper hand and nearly takes the ring, before one of Zoe’s satellite weapons blows up half the motel, forcing Hal to use what little charge is left in the ring to protect himself and John.

As the dust settles, John flees, but Zoe comes with a gun to finish off Hal in the rubble. Hal laughs, knowing that if John wanted him dead, he would have done it himself. Suddenly, we see John staring down the barrel of a sniper rifle, which is trained on Zoe. She turns around and looks at John with a softness in her eyes just before he fires.

“John is the only person she has ever encountered that she didn’t predict,” Jagannathan says. “Everyone else has always fallen into line. I think the last look is kind of game-recognized-game. It was a complete appreciation for someone whose sense of morality outdid anything and everything, and ultimately that’s the only thing that could have killed her. Someone who broke the contract, and no one ever has.”

John returns to the motel, takes the ring and lantern from Hal and walks through the rubble of Rushville. He goes to the local bar, where Lianna (Laura Linney) is waiting for him. Though he finally has what he’s always wanted, John walks away from Lianna, leaving the ring behind.

title: ’60 Minutes’ Kicks Off Much-Scrutinized 59th Season With Old Ticks, Tricks
summary: CBS News says it needs to push “60 Minutes” into the future if the show is to survive, but the first telecast of the 59th season following a shocking overhaul of its on-air and behind-the-camera staff in May and June relied on many elements from the program’s past. The new season of “60 Minutes” burnished […]
content:
CBS News says it needs to push “60 Minutes” into the future if the show is to survive, but the first telecast of the 59th season following a shocking overhaul of its on-air and behind-the-camera staff in May and June relied on many elements from the program’s past.

The new season of “60 Minutes” burnished stalwarts, and none of the new faces who have recently come aboard. Viewers on Sunday night got only a brief glimpse of Ross Douthat, and none of Sebastian Junger, Gianna Toboni, Trevor Phillips or Ariel Levy, but were rather greeted by three correspondents who already have an association with the program. Lesley Stahl has been with the newsmagazine since 1991, while Jon Wertheim joined the program in 2017. Norah O’Donnell was recently named a full-time correspondent on the show, but has contributed stories multiple times in the past.

Popular on Variety

One of the stories even featured the old-time TV-news “hidden camera,” which many people thought went out of style after ABC News got sued in 1999 — and lost — for sending reporters to take footage at Food Lion supermarkets after lying on resumes and gaining access to tape unsanitary food practices. ABC News got tripped up on charges of trespassing and fraud, and hidden-camera reporting in the modern day is typically used mostly in public spaces or overseas, where U.S. laws don’t apply.

Will viewers miss Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, or Scott Pelley? The last of that trio, all pushed out of the show following the decision to oust top producers, was on nearly every week, often crashing a story tied to events that had taken place in the days leading up to broadcast.

Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News whose work at transforming the unit for modern audiences has stirred up a lot of controversy, wants “60 Minutes” to show up in more media venues and kick up livelier discussions. Other members of CBS News have felt this way as well, wondering if the program has gotten too soft or overly reliant on stories tied to the release of new books.

There were no on-screen QR codes on Sunday’s telecast, or on-air prompts for viewers to join Stahl, Wertheim or O’Donnell for an interactive chat at CBSNews.com at some later day or time. There were no nods to listening to the stories via podcast. On Sunday morning, however, executive producer Nick Bilton sent out a note via email telling CBS News followers he would be publishing a newsletter every Monday that offered a behind-the-scenes look at the show.

Some of the window dressing has indeed changed. The opening logo is rendered more in black and white and has less red. The opening montage, which once looked as if spread out across the cover of a magazine, now looks as it takes place on a mobile tablet. One piece of the show did not change, at least in the first season broadcast. “The Last Minute,” a brief segment at program’s end that offers a few words about the program or its stories and was originally put into place by former executive producer Bill Owens., remains — perhaps because it has a regular sponsor.

The stories that were presented were segments that any longtime viewer might expect. O’Donnell nabbed an interview with one of the rescued Air Force officers whose fighter jet was shot down over Iran 34 days into the war (the segment was riveting due to its access to top military personnel, as well as the pilot, but did not offer any voice or analysis outside of the armed forces). Lesley Stahl probed the world of the so-called “pardon economy,” in which attorneys and lobbyists vow to win a presidential absolution for a convicted criminal — but don’t always deliver after they get cash (a nod should be given to The Washington Sun, the news outlet previously known as NOTUS, which interviewed one of the subjects of Stahl’s story several weeks ago). And Wertheim interviewed top personnel from the Los Angeles Rams. The show routinely tries to provide a mix of stories, one based on current events or an investigation, one focused on something overseas and one feature lighter in tone.

Bilton, who seized the reins of the show as executive producer earlier this year, may not want to shake things up overmuch in a season debut. Executives at CBS News, and parent Paramount Skydance, know only too well that “60 Minutes” generated $67 million in advertising in 2025, and saw its overall audience in the 2025-2026 season rise by 9%. Those figures will be critical for CBS News to maintain, especially as audiences continue to erode for “CBS Mornings” and remain below desired levels at “CBS Evening News.”

There are some differences, however, that the usual audience probably could not discern. Stahl’s investigation into pardons was a joint collaboration with “60 Minutes” and the CBS News investigative team, something producers at the program would likely have turned down in seasons past. Sachar Bar-On, a veteran “60 Minutes” producer, supervised the segment along with Michael Kaplan, a CBS News investigative producer and reporter. A person familiar with the show says “60 Minutes” will be “integrating more” with CBS News and its investigative unit, a move that provides more opportunity for CBS News rank-and-file doing this sort of work but also raises the specter of cost-cutting at a program with economics that already seem to work.

On Sunday night, “60 Minutes” put its most obvious foot forward: correspondents the audience recognizes, and a story mix that doesn’t deviate wildly from the norm.

Keep an eye on subsequent weeks of the program. Weiss’ overhaul of the show interrupted a critical off-season period when correspondents typically try to file and finish a segment for the fall. Bilton and crew will enjoy a cushion thanks to having the new NFL season as a lead-in every Sunday for the next several weeks. Still, they won’t have the luxury of stories that may have been in the works for weeks, which may shortchange the amount of attention they can devote to segments from new on-air personnel who are still learning the ropes.

title: Netflix To Stream Lee Chang-Dong’s Previous Works Following ‘Possible Love’ Silver Lion Win In Venice
summary: Following the Silver Lion win for Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love at this year’s Venice film festival, Netflix is set to stream more of the director’s work worldwide.  Lee’s earlier films Green Fish and Secret Sunshine are already available on Netflix, streaming from August in Italy, the UK, France, Australia, and New Zealand. Peppermint Candy and […]
content:
Following the Silver Lion win for Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love at this year’s Venice film festival, Netflix is set to stream more of the director’s work worldwide.

Lee’s earlier films Green Fish and Secret Sunshine are already available on Netflix, streaming from August in Italy, the UK, France, Australia, and New Zealand. Peppermint Candy and Oasis started streaming on Netflix in Italy and Spain on September 4.

Poetry and Burning are also planned for release in markets including Japan, the U.S., Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Availability and timing vary by country. Depending on the market, the films will be offered with subtitles in up to six languages, including Korean.

Possible Love, Lee’s first film in eight years, won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize in Venice. The film opens in South Korean theatres on September 23, followed by Australia and New Zealand on October 22, and the UK, Japan, the US, and Canada on October 23. It will premiere globally on Netflix on November 6.

Watch on Deadline

The film has been selected as Korea’s official entry for the Best International Feature category of the Academy Awards.

Since making his debut with Green Fish in 1997, Lee’s films have swept awards including Best Director at the 59th Venice International Film Festival for Oasis in 2002 and Best Screenplay at the 63rd Cannes Film Festival for Poetry in 2010. Most recently, he became the first Korean director to win the Ebert Director Award at the 51st Toronto International Film Festival.

Starring Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong, Possible Love is a story of two couples – a laid-off worker and his spouse, and a documentary filmmaker and her spouse – crossing paths to film a documentary and facing their different lives and hidden desires.

title: Steve Ballmer Apologizes To Fans, Says He Has Paid $30M NBA Fine, But Does Not Admit Guilt
summary: Steve Ballmer seems to have gotten to the acceptance stage of grief. Less than two weeks after — his word — “vehemently” denying the results of a year-long NBA investigation that found the Clippers had circumvented the salary cap and paid superstar Kawhi Leonard millions through no-show deals with sponsors, the team’s billionaire owner posted […]
content:
Steve Ballmer seems to have gotten to the acceptance stage of grief.

Less than two weeks after — his word — “vehemently” denying the results of a year-long NBA investigation that found the Clippers had circumvented the salary cap and paid superstar Kawhi Leonard millions through no-show deals with sponsors, the team’s billionaire owner posted a somewhat contrite statement acknowledging “sincere regrets…for the distraction and distress this matter has caused.” Ballmer did not, however, admit guilt. He said, “there are still disagreements concerning the findings in the report.”

He went on: “We are committing to put this chapter behind us. We have communicated to the NBA that we are complying with the penalties assessed by the league, have paid the fine, and are moving forward. While there are still disagreements concerning the findings in the report, this is not where I want to focus. Team owners should support, not distract.”

Watch on Deadline

Specifically, the Clippers will forfeit their first-round picks in the NBA Draft from 2029 through 2033. Ballmer is suspended for “all league and team activities for one year” and fined $30M. Leonard, a two-time NBA Finals MVP signed by the Clippers in 2019, was not suspended but was fined $700,000.

title: Israel’s Culture Minister Calls For Oscar-Winning Israeli Filmmakers Behind Gaza Doc ‘NAZA’ To Lose Their Citizenship
summary: The day after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor‘s bombshell Israeli documentary NAZA alleging the Israeli army targeted civilians in Gaza won the Special Jury Prize at Venice, Israel’s Culture Minister Miki Zohar announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the directing duo. According to a translation provided by X, Zohar went on to call […]
content:
The day after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor‘s bombshell Israeli documentary NAZA alleging the Israeli army targeted civilians in Gaza won the Special Jury Prize at Venice, Israel‘s Culture Minister Miki Zohar announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the directing duo.

According to a translation provided by X, Zohar went on to call the film “vile” and the Venice Film Festival honor “shocking.” He continued, “The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state.”

You can read a translation of Zohar’s full statement below.

Watch on Deadline

The win of the vile film NZA [sic] at the Venice Festival is shocking. The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state. This is exactly the reason I led the important reform in cinema so that Israeli citizens will no longer have to pay from their own pockets for the harm to IDF soldiers and the State of Israel. As Minister of Culture, I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for betraying the state.

הזכייה של הסרט הנבזי נז״א בפסטיבל ונציה מזעזעת. השנאה העצמית היוקדת של היוצרים שמוכנים לפגוע במולדתם כדי לקבל מחיאות כפיים מהאנטישמים בעולם בלתי נתפסת ומהווה בגידה במדינה.

זו בדיוק הסיבה שהובלתי את הרפורמה החשובה בקולנוע כדי שאזרחי ישראל לא ישלמו יותר מכיסם על הפגיעה בחיילי צה״ל… — Miki Zohar מיקי זוהר (@zoharm7) September 13, 2026

NAZA, a late addition to the competition lineup in Venice, received a record 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere there. On Saturday night, it won the festival’s Special Jury Prize. The film is directed by Israeli Jews Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the four directors of the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land. Abraham appears on camera, interviewing his subjects on the rooftop; they explain that “NAZA” is a Hebrew acronym used by the Israel Defense Forces to signify collateral damage (נזק אגבי, or Nezek Agavi, per an interview included in press notes), in other words, an acceptable loss of civilian life incurred while trying to kill suspected Hamas militants. The film suggests the number of “NAZA” considered acceptable in each attack was elastic. In some cases, it would be under a dozen, but in others it could be 200 or even 500 people deemed permissible collateral damage, according to Israeli military personnel interviewed in the film.

On Friday, former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett criticized NAZA and its filmmakers, saying in a statement that that he is “proud” and “deeply grateful” to the Israeli reservists and soldiers “standing between us and that next massacre.” He added, “To portray them as perpetrators of ‘genocide’ is not courageous art. It is a cowardly blood libel.”

Zohar has accused the Israeli film of betrayal before. In July, he released a video denouncing filmmakers who used government funds to criticize the country.

“For years, the formula was simple: Defame Israel and receive a check from the government,” Zohar said the video, before pledging, “Not anymore.” The minister went on to promise he would move “our money from films that Israel haters love to films that Israelis love…This is the end of the era where Israeli soldiers are blackened at the expense of Israeli citizens.”

title: ‘The Last Photograph’ Review: DC’s Zack Snyder Comes Back Down To Earth With A Violent But Surprisingly Human Action Drama – Toronto Film Festival
summary: After so many years in the DC universe, Zack Snyder comes back down to earth again with a violent but surprisingly human action thriller set in the jungles of an unidentified Latin American country. Its plotline — more of which later — could go either way, and since the director has been unfairly accused of […]
content:
After so many years in the DC universe, Zack Snyder comes back down to earth again with a violent but surprisingly human action thriller set in the jungles of an unidentified Latin American country. Its plotline — more of which later — could go either way, and since the director has been unfairly accused of dodgy politics ever since the homoerotic jingoism of 300 (2006), many may expect this to be his Sound of Freedom, the QAnon-adjacent indie hit of 2023. Thankfully, The Last Photograph is no such thing; true, it is high on testosterone, and it centers on an almost ridiculously deadpan fella-drama bromance. But a better comparison would be Peter Weir’s The Year of Living Dangerously (1982), a slightly more morally complex story of life in a volatile ideologically captured warzone.

Snyder shot the film himself and it looks just great, starting out in the basement of a grubby restaurant basement where photojournalist Joe Wallace is being seduced into having sex with a waitress. Whether it’s because his artistic eye is drawn to a beautiful butterfly or down to the ton of smack he has just injected into his arm, Joe is oblivious to her advances, much to her annoyance. The sudden sound of gunfire makes him snap to attention; running up the stairs, camera at the ready, Joe finds that the child’s birthday party that’s being thrown has been attacked by guerilla gunmen, who shoot the adult guests and kidnap the two children present. Joe is by her side when their mother is killed, and he captures the moment, almost getting himself killed in the process.

Watch on Deadline

The shockwaves from the incident reach a remote part of Scotland, where Ethan Black (Stuart Martin) is working on a sheep farm, commanding respect for his gentle rapport with the animals — right before he cuts their throats and chops up their corpses for dinner. We learn that Ethan’s brother, being the father of the birthday boy, was killed in the carnage, but that’s not, strictly speaking, the inciting incident that sends Ethan off on a revenge-o-matic killing spree. Rather, it is the fact that his sister-in-law — the woman in what will become a series of several “last” photographs, each with their own personal meaning — was the love of his life, leaving him after their one illicit fling with a Polaroid bearing the cryptic line “This is a photograph from that other world”.

Bent on tracking down the killers, Ethan flies over and heads to the photographic agency that represents Joe’s work. After paying out a bribe to find his whereabouts, Ethan finds Joe in a sleazy sex club, still bloodied and bruised after his brush with death. He has a deal to make; if Joe will come with him to identify his brother’s killers and rescue the two missing children, Ethan will pay him $10,000. Joe doesn’t take much convincing, not just because he needs the money, but because it soon becomes clear that a road trip with Ethan will feed both his adrenaline jones and cater to his prurient need for sensation, being largely deadened to the world of human relationships.

There are obvious echoes of Apocalypse Now in the story that follows, not just because there’s a literal journey upstream but because it’s all about the getting there and not the arrival: Both characters have a reckoning that awaits them. Along the way, Ethan opens up more and more about his past as a former DEA agent, telling stories that sometimes border on something out of Tropic Thunder, but as unlikely as it might sound, Martin is a surprisingly plausible as a soldier gone native, and whose once-tight bond with the local community has led him into the increasingly perilous situation he now faces. Fra Fee, as Joe, has a slightly harder task, since his role is almost entirely reactive; while Ethan bangs on mournfully about, effectively, the dangers of shagging your brother’s wife — well, who would have thought? — Joe simply gets on with his seemingly inexhaustible supply of heroin, while Ethan mocks him for hiding behind his camera.

It doesn’t sound much like fun when you lay it out like that, but there’s certainly a lot of excitement, a fair bit of tension, and at least one very unexpected laugh-out-loud moment when a driver transporting them along the way asks the pair if they like “the king”. (Clue: It’s not Elvis Presley.) But although you can take the man out of DC, the DC is very still much inside this particular man, and the niggling problem with The Last Photograph is that it sometimes forgets about its characters in a bid to hit the furiously paced action set-pieces.

That said, though, it’s good to see Snyder trying something so far out of his wheelhouse (well, at least a bit far out of it), sharpening his sometimes rusty storytelling skills without the safety net of superhero pyrotechnics.

Title: The Last Photograph

Festival: Toronto (Special Events)

Director: Zack Snyder

Screenwriter: Kurt Johnstad

Cast: Stuart Martin, Fra Fee, Costanza Andrade, Marlon Moreno, Quique Mendoza

International sales agent: CAA

Running time: 2 hrs 15 mins

title: ’60 Minutes’ Debuts New Season With A Pentagon Exclusive And Hidden Camera Expose — Amid Plenty Of Scrutiny Of The Show Itself
summary: 60 Minutes debuted its new season on Sunday with an exclusive sit down with an Air Force officer who told of his harrowing rescue in Iran. It featured a hideen camera segment on pardon brokers who collect hundreds of thousands or even millions to try to secure Trump’s clemency. And it profile the Los Angeles […]
content:
60 Minutes debuted its new season on Sunday with an exclusive sit down with an Air Force officer who told of his harrowing rescue in Iran. It featured a hideen camera segment on pardon brokers who collect hundreds of thousands or even millions to try to secure Trump’s clemency. And it profile the Los Angeles Rams and head coach Sean McVay.

Yet despite new graphics, the debut of new correspondent Ross Douthat for its one-minute ender, and an increased social media presence, the show had much the same look and feel of previous seasons. The story selection was in the realm of past seasons.

What is different, though, is the extra scrutiny the show is under, in the wake of the purge last spring of executive producer Tanya Simon and top producers, as well as correspondents Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi and Scott Pelley, each of whom has accused the executive higher ups of interference. Just this past week, the former managing editor called the show “a casualty of corporate priorities and ideological intrusion.” CBS News editor in chief Bari Weiss pushed back on the claim in June, telling The Wall Street Journal, “What’s being called ‘editorial interference’ is in reality the job description of an editor in chief.” And shortly after he became the new executive producer, Nick Bilton told staffers that the show “will never be instructed by the ownership of the company on these stories.”

Watch on Deadline

The corporate ownership has done plenty to raise suspicions, starting with the decision by the previous owners of Paramount, the parent company of CBS, to settle a lawsuit Donald Trump filed against the network for the way that 60 Minutes edited an interview with Kamala Harris. Then, new owners Skydance have waged a not-so-subtle effort to woo Trump as it sought administration sign off for its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Interference or not, the risk that 60 Minutes faces is ratings, or losing the show’s position as the No. 1 news show on television.

The first segment was Norah O’Donnell’s exclusive sit down with an Air Force colonel whose plane was shot down over Iran, who relayed the story of his survival and then rescue, calling it a “modern day miracle.” The network had extensive cooperation from the Pentagon, with interviews with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, as well as declassified footage of the operation.

The segment was narrowly focused on the rescue itself, as the officer described his free fall, major injuries and his ascent up a 7,000 foot ridgeline before being spotted two days later. The officer said at the end of the segment, “It’s a story of the teamwork, the training, of the faith, of the decisions and the leadership to do something that will live in history as an example of what America’s willing to do, in order to uphold our promise and leave no man behind.”

The sit down was one that all networks crave, and it is one that the Pentagon has been anxious to promote. There was a mention during the segment of the “costly and unpopular war that has taken the lives of 18 service members.” It remains to be seen how 60 Minutes will explore further aspects of the conflict, and if it will turn its attention to one of the more alarming stories circling in D.C.: Hegseth’s purge of top experienced generals.

The next segment put a spotlight on pardon brokers, with a hidden camera used to capture two of them, Jack Burkman and Jacob Wohl, as they tried to entice Ammon Covino, a convicted felon, and his wife, Crystal, into spending $300,000 for their alleged ability to get a pardon request in front of Donald Trump.

The camera caught Burkman telling them, “You have to put pressure on the president from all directions in a consistent way to force his hand. We literally want to put the pen in his hand and get him to sign it because he’s tired of hearing about it.”

The show pointed out that Burkman and Wohl are well known for their political stunts, so their involvement in business of pardon brokering isn’t all that shocking. In the footage that aired, they didn’t seem all that rattled by the revelation of a hidden camera. They also tried to engage in a bit of relativism, i.e. that their activity was little different from what went on in the Biden and Obama administration.

That’s why the more telling moment of Lesley Stahl’s segment were the stats: About 70% of Trump’s clemencies in his second term have not gone through the standard channels the DOJ. If the president’s pardons of the January 6th rioters are included, the figure is 92%. And while the White House claimed that Trump was behaving in an “ethically sound manner,” the segment pointedly featured a college professor who said that, despite the proliferation of brokers charging ever higher fees, “in the end, it falls on the administration.”

Also important is that the show ran through some of the notables who did get pardons, including the CEO of Binance who “boosted a Trump family crypto venture, though both sides deny any connection to the pardon,” Stahl noted.

The third segment was devoted to the Los Angeles Rams, with 60 Minutes and Bill Wertheim getting access to its preseason practice, billing the team “as maybe the — premier NFL franchise: blue chip; gold standard.”

There wasn’t mention of the drubbing that the Rams took in its opener against the 49ers, but that was perhaps foreshadowed by McVay during his interview. He said, “Success is never linear, you know? It’s– it– it’s always up and down.” He also admitted that he was “not in a good place right now,” referring to the progress of practice.

Douthat appeared for the closing segment, The Last Minute, to talk about the latest warnings about AI, but he also made a pitch for the show’s future, with the drama of the last year left unsaid. “We may have a narrow window this year, not the next 10, to make artificial intelligence safe for humanity,” he said. “That clock is ticking, and so is ours. For almost 60 years, it has meant the same thing: Journalism you can trust. Where we’re headed, we’re going to need it.”

title: Sydney Sweeney’s Naked Sports Betting Ad Ignites Backlash From Olympic Athletes: ‘Stop Sexualizing Women in Sport’
summary: Sydney Sweeney appears to be at the center of another controversy involving a commercial. The “Euphoria” actress recently stripped down for a steamy new ad for sports trading app Novig, going nude and covering parts of her with a variety of sports equipment. But not everybody is overjoyed by sports’ new naked cheerleader. Over the […]
content:
Sydney Sweeney appears to be at the center of another controversy involving a commercial.

The “Euphoria” actress recently stripped down for a steamy new ad for sports trading app Novig, going nude and covering parts of her with a variety of sports equipment. But not everybody is overjoyed by sports’ new naked cheerleader.

Over the weekend, just days after the ad dropped, several athletes took to social media to speak out against the campaign, which they accused of sexualising women’s sports.

Popular on Variety

“I don’t know wtf Sydney Sweeney was doing, but it’s 2026,” wrote British athlete Lucy Davis. “Stop sexualizing women in sport.”

Meanwhile, Ariarne Titmus, a former Australian swimming champion and four-time Olympic gold medal winner, wrote: “I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this.”

Titmus added: “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity. How do we live in a world where monetising a woman’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”

The backlash prompted many female athletes to post their own footage alongside messages about what sports actually looks like.

Among them was American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted an highlight reel, now with more than a million likes, with the caption: “Idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sports looks like.”

In a TV interview, British sprinter Amy Hunt, who became a four-time European champion earlier this summer, raised the ad after running a season’s best in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

“Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like,” she told the BBC immediately following the race.

In reference to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, Hunt added: “21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears,” before adding: “When you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty. It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time, definitely.”

Meanwhile, water polo Olympic silver medallist Tilly Kearns succinctly wrote: “I absolutely fking hate Sydney Sweeney’s new sports ad.”

In a statement on the Novig website, Sweeney said: “The campaign was about embracing a fun idea. The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humor and a playful edge.”

The star also appeared to respond to the backlash by posting to her Instagram story a series of covers from the ESPN Body Issue, which featured naked athletes.

The Novig commercial comes just over a year following American Eagle’s hugely controversial “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” campaign,” which prompted a wave of criticism for appearing to use the language of eugenics. In a now-deleted video, Sweeney said: “Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair colour, personality, and even eye colour. My jeans are blue.”

Months after the American Eagle ad, Sweeney responded by saying she was “surprised by the reaction” and that she was “against hate and divisiveness.”

title: ‘Brother’s Keeper’ Director Ferit Karahan’s ‘Djinn Wedding’ Asks: ‘Can a Person Who Refuses to Acknowledge Their Own Darkness Ever Truly Change Their Fate?’
summary: “Djinn Wedding” (“Cinlerin Düğünü”), written and directed by Ferit Karahan (“Brother’s Keeper,” “The Fall From Heaven”), will have its world premiere at Toronto as part of the TIFF Platform competition. This is Karahan’s follow-up feature to “Brother’s Keeper,” which won the Berlin Film Festival’s Fipresci Award in the Panorama section. A magic realism story about […]
content:
“Djinn Wedding” (“Cinlerin Düğünü”), written and directed by Ferit Karahan (“Brother’s Keeper,” “The Fall From Heaven”), will have its world premiere at Toronto as part of the TIFF Platform competition. This is Karahan’s follow-up feature to “Brother’s Keeper,” which won the Berlin Film Festival’s Fipresci Award in the Panorama section.

A magic realism story about family, history and Anatolian folk tales, the film follows four siblings across three periods of time as their dark secrets and traumas begin to unravel during a family wedding. It deals with the universal themes of loss, guilt and mourning.

The film stars Demit Özdemir, Kaan Yildirim, İlhan Şen, Sarp Bozkurt, Heli̇n Kandemi̇r and Evliya Aykan. It is produced by Ferit Karahan Film, Royal Pictures, Maya Films and Arya Yapim. Luxbox is handling international sales.

Popular on Variety

Ferit Karahan. Photo Credit: Brigitte Dummer

Variety spoke with director Ferit Karahan ahead of its world premiere in Toronto.

Can you tell me about the djinn and what they symbolize in Anatolian folklore?

Ferit Karahan: In Anatolian culture specifically, but also more broadly across Islamic cultures, djinn are invisible beings who share the same world as humans. Stories about them are often intertwined with the night, abandoned places, thresholds, weddings and death. I grew up in a region where these stories were still very much alive. It was part of everyday life for people to make sense of things they couldn’t explain through djinn, dreams or legends.

The reality we live with in the Middle East today can be so harsh, and at times so irrational, that even when I try to explain it to my own child, I find myself needing elements of the surreal. I don’t use them to soften reality or escape from it. On the contrary, I use them to make that reality tellable and bearable. Perhaps this is where my relationship with magical realism begins. Djinn, dreams, legends and invisible things are not alternatives to reality for me; they are another layer of it.

What were some of the themes you wanted to address in the film?

Karahan: Before I began making the film, there was a question that kept circling in my mind: “Can a person who refuses to acknowledge their own darkness ever truly change their fate?” I don’t think the most dangerous thing about human beings is that we have dark impulses. Greed, jealousy, anger or the desire for power can exist in all of us. The real danger is denying that they exist. This is what interests me in Jung’s concept of the “shadow:” we don’t destroy what we refuse to see in ourselves; we simply leave it in the dark.

What are your thoughts on present-day Turkey and its political landscape?

Karahan: I think we are living in an atmosphere of fear. People don’t know what tomorrow will bring, or even what might happen to them personally. And this fear is not unique to Turkey; it is increasingly spreading across the region, and even across the world. The war between Iran and the U.S. and the conflicts throughout the region, affect all of us. The resurgence of the far right in Europe inevitably makes me think of the 1920s and 1930s. In many parts of the world, fear is once again being used as a political instrument and people are once again being governed through fear.

The political and economic conditions in Turkey today affect towns like the one depicted in the film. The consequences of the economic crisis, migration, unemployment and diminishing access to education can sometimes be felt even more severely in smaller towns than in major cities. That is why I don’t see the town in the film as some folkloric world left behind in the past. On the contrary, to me it is very much a place of the present.



Is there a connection between this film and “Brother’s Keeper?”



Karahan: In “Brother’s Keeper,” the source of oppression was more visible: the school, authority, the system created by adults. In “Djinn Wedding,” that oppression is no longer outside the characters. It has seeped into the family, into memory, even into the ways people love one another.

“Djinn Wedding” is also a much more autobiographical film for me. “Brother’s Keeper” grew out of a real incident from my childhood, but “Djinn Wedding” comes from a much broader and more personal memory. Family, home, siblings, loss, silence, the stories that are told and the ones that are never told, all of these are much more directly connected to my own past.

There is a scene in the film where the mother is placed inside a large cauldron filled with hot water. That image actually comes from my childhood. When I was about nine years old, I saw the brother of a neighbor who had cancer being placed in a large cauldron of hot water to ease his pain. While I was writing the script, it suddenly came back to me. I suppose cinema has this strange relationship with memory: sometimes an image you have carried for years without knowing why finds its place in a story much later.

title: Oprah Winfrey to Headline Las Vegas Sphere With New Music and Arts Show ‘Aha’
summary: There is a new, immersive entertainment experience coming to the Las Vegas Sphere — and Oprah Winfrey is at the center of it. Titled “Aha,” the two-hour show is taking place four times across one weekend, from April 2-4, 2027. Winfrey will appear live on-stage and introduce performances from Grammy winner Jacob Collier, poet Ocean […]
content:
There is a new, immersive entertainment experience coming to the Las Vegas Sphere — and Oprah Winfrey is at the center of it.

Titled “Aha,” the two-hour show is taking place four times across one weekend, from April 2-4, 2027. Winfrey will appear live on-stage and introduce performances from Grammy winner Jacob Collier, poet Ocean Vuong, musician Ajeet, gospel singer Wintley Phipps and more. The ticketed event is described in a press release as a “journey of light, sound, music, storytelling, nature and shared humanity.”

“My first time at Sphere, I was blown away by this high-tech marvel of sound and images,” Winfrey said in an announcement video. “I had a big aha moment: What if this magnificent space could take us to the edge of the universe and deep within ourselves for an immersive symphony of awe, wonder and joy? Aha! Join me for the ultimate aha moment at Sphere.”

Popular on Variety

Elaborating in a press release, Winfrey continued, “‘Aha’ is a dream that came to me as I sat in awe at the opening night of U2 at the Sphere, mesmerized by the possibilities of how the space could be used as a tool for creating greater awareness and understanding of ourselves and our connection to each other. Creating this experience has felt like the culmination of what I’ve spoken about and worked towards my entire life.”

Tickets start at $145 and will go on sale here starting on Sept. 25 at 10 a.m. PT.

Max Richter is the musical director of “Aha,” which is directed by Ethan Tobman, produced by Baz Halpin and written by Tarell Alvin McCraney (“Moonlight”). The show features original works by stage designer Es Devlin and others.

The title and concept of the show will resonate with Winfrey fans: After all, it was she who popularized the term “aha moment” in the 1990s on her daytime talk show. Winfrey is the reason the phrase was added to the dictionary in 2012 by Miriam-Webster, which describes an aha moment as “a moment of sudden realization, inspiration, insight, recognition or comprehension.”

“I always love those moments when I sit down to talk to somebody and they say things that make me look at life or a situation in a completely different way,” Winfrey has explained, adding that an aha moment is like a “lightbulb, bing bing bing” moment in which “the little hairs on your arms stand up.”

title: Philomena Cunk to Quiz Michael Bay and Benedict Cumberbatch in ‘Cunk on Cinema’ as Latest Outing for Diane Morgan’s Character Gets First Look
summary: Michael Bay and Benedict Cumberbatch are set to face the ill-informed interview style of Philomena Cunk, the beloved TV idiot played by Diane Morgan, in the comedy creation’s latest outing. “Cunk on Cinema,” first announced by Variety earlier this year, will see Cunk chart the history of cinema and the world’s love affair with movies […]
content:
Michael Bay and Benedict Cumberbatch are set to face the ill-informed interview style of Philomena Cunk, the beloved TV idiot played by Diane Morgan, in the comedy creation’s latest outing.

“Cunk on Cinema,” first announced by Variety earlier this year, will see Cunk chart the history of cinema and the world’s love affair with movies in what’s been billed as her “most glamorous series to date.”

A first look from the three-part faux documentary series, from Pacesetter Productions and coming to both the BBC and Netflix, has been released, showcasing Cunk getting to grips what appears to be a Sony Venice Digital Cinema Camera (as used by Bay on “6 Underground”).

Popular on Variety

According to the description, “Cunk on Cinema” will uncover the invention of the camera, to the New Wave filmmakers of the 60s, right up to the entrance of CGI and what the future of AI holds. Cunk will attempt to “demystify it all while sitting in lumpy seats with stale popcorn, asking herself where did cinema come from? And why? What does it want? And why can’t it tell us?”

Alongside Bay and Cumberbatch, others to be quizzed by the ever-confused Cunk will include composer Daniel Pemberton (“Project Hail Mary”), screenwriter Steven E. de Souza (“Die Hard,” “Commando”), Oscar-nominated cinematographer Seamus McGarvey (“Avengers Assemble,” “Atonement”), critic Mark Kermode, and documentary-maker and author Mark Cousins (“The Story of Film: An Odyssey”).

“Cunk on Cinema,” the latest in the British mockumentary television franchise by Charlie Brooker for the BBC and Netflix, follows “Cunk on Life,” “Cunk on Earth,” “Cunk on Shakespeare” and “Cunk on Britain.”

Brooker leads a team of writers including Ben Caudell, Erika Ehler, Eli Goldstone, Jason Hazeley, Dan Maier, Morgan, Joel Morris, Michael Odewale, Kali Varghese, and Sam Ward. The director is Al Campbell. Executive producers are Brooker, Jessica Rhoades, Morgan, and Sam Ward. Navi Lamba is the BBC commissioning editor and Mark Kinsella is co-executive producer for Pacesetter Productions.

“Cunk on Cinema” will debut on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two and on Netflix outside of the U.K. and Ireland.

title: Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival Unveils New Visions Forum Lineup
summary: The 30th edition of Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival, which draws around 1,200 industry professionals, has unveiled the projects selected for its New Visions Forum. Twenty-nine projects from 15 countries will be presented during the Forum, taking place Oct. 28–30, offering their teams the opportunity to connect with potential co-production, financing, sales and distribution partners. Eight […]
content:
The 30th edition of Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival, which draws around 1,200 industry professionals, has unveiled the projects selected for its New Visions Forum.

Twenty-nine projects from 15 countries will be presented during the Forum, taking place Oct. 28–30, offering their teams the opportunity to connect with potential co-production, financing, sales and distribution partners.

Eight of this year’s selected projects are directed by first-time filmmakers, alongside new works by acclaimed and experienced directors.

These include Lindsey Sitz, a Pulitzer Prize-winning filmmaker, who comes with “Searching for SmarterChild”; Simantini Chakraborty, a close collaborator of Godfrey Reggio and director of “The Original Badass,” who presents “Impossible to Ignore”; Iranian filmmaker Ali Razi (“At Night, the Red Sky”), who pitches “Archiveless Memories, for an Imaginary Museum”; and Polish director Agnieszka Zwiefka (“Silent Trees,” “Vika!), delivering “Words We Never Say.”

Popular on Variety

The selection also features new projects by two alumni of the festival’s Emerging Producers program: Charlotte Heilstone from the U.K. and Matej Sotník from Slovakia.

The Forum will present projects from Europe, the U.S., and East and Southeast Asia, complemented this year by six upcoming projects from Montenegro, the Country in Focus of Ji.hlava’s industry program this year.

Across the selection, several recurring themes emerge: memory, archives, and what has been suppressed or silenced; individuals confronting systems and structures of power; and the intersection of personal experience with larger historical processes.

The Forum is complemented by an extensive Matchmaking Accelerator, connecting selected projects with international decision-makers and industry professionals.

The full lineup of projects can be found here.

title: Canada’s Precious Metal Productions & Black Fawn Distribution Strike Genre Slate Deal – TIFF
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Precious Metal Productions and Black Fawn Distribution, two of Canada’s buzziest indie film companies, are joining forces on a three-picture genre slate. Precious Metal Productions’ co-founding heads Canadian producer Christopher Giroux and actress-producer Ann Pirvu say the deal marks a milestone for their company which they launched earlier this year. The first project under the new agreement […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Precious Metal Productions and Black Fawn Distribution, two of Canada’s buzziest indie film companies, are joining forces on a three-picture genre slate.

Precious Metal Productions’ co-founding heads Canadian producer Christopher Giroux and actress-producer Ann Pirvu say the deal marks a milestone for their company which they launched earlier this year.

The first project under the new agreement will be a horror film directed by Giroux from an original screenplay he co-wrote with Pirvu. It is slated to begin production in early 2027.

Watch on Deadline

Giroux’s recent credits include romances Snowbound for the Holidays for Hallmark and Bee My Love, Precious Metal’s first fully fledged production, but he is no stranger to horror having taken producer credits on a string of pictures in the genre including Anything For Jackson, Bite, Pins and Needles, I’ll Take Your Dead, The Heretics and recently The Voices of Our Mother.

“We’ve always believed that Canadian filmmakers can create commercially viable films without compromising creative ambition,” said Giroux. “Partnering with Black Fawn Distribution gives us an incredible opportunity to build a slate of exciting genre films while working alongside a team that truly understands both filmmaking and audiences.”

Black Fawn Distribution, a subsidiary of horror filmmakers Chad Archibald and Cody Calahan’s Black Fawn Films, is a major distributor of genre in Canada across all platforms, with recent acquisitions including Bury The Devil, Death of A Yellowbird, It Feeds, and Violence.

In 2025, it moved into international sales kicking off with The Undertone, which then sold to A24 following a bidding war.

“It’s always been part of our mission to seek out and collaborate with creative film teams who can help bring cool new stories to life. Ann and Christopher have a proven track record of doing just that, and with a level of community and audience engagement that’s imperative in today’s marketplace,” said CF Benner, SVP Finance Operations, Black Fawn Distribution.

Giroux and actress-producer Pirvu officially launched Precious Metal Productions last January with a focus on television movies and feature films with its activities spanning original content creation as well as full-service production.

Alongside producing, Pirvu is she is best known for her roles as Nicole on the CW’s Reign and Zoe in the award-winning series Poly Is the New Monogamy.

“At the heart of what we’re building with Precious Metal Productions is a commitment to meaningful, commercially accessible stories while championing Canadian talent on both sides of the camera. Black Fawn Distribution shares our passion for fearless filmmaking, and we couldn’t think of a better distribution partner as we expand into the genre space,” she said.

Benner added: “Black Fawn Distribution teaming up with Precious Metal Productions made sense on every level, and we’re looking forward to helping this new slate of genre films connect with both Canadian and international audiences.”

title: ‘Evil Genius’ Review: Courteney Cox’s True-Crime Unpacks The Toxic Love Story At Center Of “Pizza Bomber” Case — Toronto Film Festival
summary: “You can’t make this shit up… and most of it, we didn’t,” Courteney Cox’s latest directorial outing prefaces, an appropriate warning for the chaotic nature of the unbelievable true-crime saga at the center of Evil Genius. In Evil Genius, adapted by screenwriter Courtenay Miles from the 2018 Netflix docuseries, Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong (Patricia Arquette) orchestrates the […]
content:
“You can’t make this shit up… and most of it, we didn’t,” Courteney Cox‘s latest directorial outing prefaces, an appropriate warning for the chaotic nature of the unbelievable true-crime saga at the center of Evil Genius.

In Evil Genius, adapted by screenwriter Courtenay Miles from the 2018 Netflix docuseries, Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong (Patricia Arquette) orchestrates the infamous 2003 “pizza bomber” heist that resulted in the gruesome death of Brian Wells (Tom McCarthy), who was kidnapped and forced to rob a PNC bank with a bomb stropped around his neck.

The film also dives into the inheritance scheme that sparked the heist, as well as the body in the freezer that led the police to the truth. But the heart of this story is the toxic years-long romance between Marjorie and her co-conspirator Bill Rothstein (David Harbour), an equally cunning player who was blinded by love.

Whereas many true-crime movies spend nearly the entire first act introducing its characters and creating exposition before getting to the crime at hand, Cox wastes none of the lean 94-minute runtime, immediately establishing the pair’s dysfunctional dynamic in the absurd high-stakes situation they’ve created for themselves.

Watch on Deadline

Harbour and Arquette truly get lost in their characters, with the former nearly unrecognizable in his prosthetic nose and fake beard. Hopper who? Meanwhile, Arquette is an onscreen force as the manipulative spitfire Marj. Two people with little redeeming qualities, they ultimately deserve each other.

Rounding out the ensemble as the crew of idiots to their unhinged geniuses are Michael Chernus, Garret Dillahunt, Danielle Macdonald and Owen Teague, each bringing these real co-conspirators to life with the appropriate balance of depth and dark humor.

The recreated surveillance and news footage of Wells is chilling to watch, especially given McCarthy’s grasp of the fear that ran through Wells during the police standoff in the final minutes of his life, knowing he’s a pawn in someone else’s deadly crime.

While it’s still considered a dark comedy at times, it takes the very real consequences of its subject matter seriously, unlike a previous 2011 title that may or may not have been a loose take on the tragic incident.

One such comedic element comes into play during the heist itself, as two bank employees (David Arquette and Christine Taylor) struggle to make sense of the masterminds’ overcomplicated pre-written instructions. The jokes are never at the expense of the tragedy, but at the ridiculous nature of the events that transpired around it.

Meanwhile, the movie never asks the audience to redeem these people or even empathize with them, but it questions how Marj and Bill went from two smart, lovestruck teens to where they ended up.

More than a decade after her directorial debut, Cox packs a heavy punch with Evil Genius, thanks to an incredible, committed ensemble (featuring Courteney and former sister-in-law Patricia’s daughters in cameos) and a faithful approach to the true story that still offers moments of levity during the dark tragedy captured onscreen.

Title: Evil Genius

Festival: TIFF

Section: Gala Presentations

Director: Courteney Cox

Screenwriter: Courtenay Miles

Cast: Patricia Arquette, David Harbour, Michael Chernus, Garret Dillahunt, Ryan Eggold, Gregory Alan Williams, Tom McCarthy, Owen Teague, Harlow Jane, David Rasche, Dascha Polanco, Danielle Macdonald, Thomas Michael Allen

International sales agent: Cornerstone Films

Running time: 1 hr 34 mins

title: Oprah Winfrey Heads To Las Vegas Sphere With New Immersive Experience
summary: Oprah Winfrey’s AHA, a new live immersive experience created in collaboration with a global collective of musicians, artists and storytellers will debut at Sphere in Las Vegas for one weekend, April 2-4. The project will see Winfrey appear live on stage alongside a variety of performances in what the announcement calls a “brand-new visual, musically […]
content:
Oprah Winfrey‘s AHA, a new live immersive experience created in collaboration with a global collective of musicians, artists and storytellers will debut at Sphere in Las Vegas for one weekend, April 2-4.

The project will see Winfrey appear live on stage alongside a variety of performances in what the announcement calls a “brand-new visual, musically immersive symphony of senses.”

Windfrey said “‘AHA’ is a dream that came to me as I sat in awe at the opening night of U2 at the Sphere, mesmerized by the possibilities of how the space could be used as a tool for creating greater awareness and understanding of ourselves and our connection to each other.”

The two-hour shows will feature performances by Grammy Award-winner Jacob Collier; poet and author Ocean Vuong; musician Ajeet; and gospel singer Wintley Phipps, among others. The show will utilize Sphere’s next-generation technologies, including the world’s highest-resolution LED display that wraps up, over, and around the audience creating a fully immersive visual environment. The venue also features the world’s most advanced concert-grade audio system, Sphere Immersive Sound.

Watch on Deadline

“Creating this experience has felt like the culmination of what I’ve spoken about and worked towards my entire life,” Winfrey said in the announcement.

What organizers are calling a “journey of light, sound, music and storytelling” is designed by director Ethan Tobman and produced by Emmy-winning founder of Silent House Group, Baz Halpin.

The team includes musical direction and original music from Oscar-nominated composer Max Richter; Grammy-winning musician and vocal director Jason White; Grammy-nominated composer, producer, and electronic artist Jon Hopkins; writing from Tarell Alvin McCrane, Oscar-winning screenwriter and Artistic Director of Geffen Playhouse; and original works by artist Es Devlin and the Plum Village Monks.

Presented by Live Nation, the event is executive produced by Winfrey, along with Jennifer Rudolph Walsh, producer of The Life You Want Tour, founder of Together Live, and co-founder of Godmothers bookstore; Harpo Entertainment’s EP Tara McNally Montgomery; co-founder and partner of Fulwell Entertainment, Ben Winston; social entrepreneur Andrew Maxwell Mangino; and consulting producer and Pinterest co-founder Evan Sharp.

AHA marks a new kind of spectacle for the Sphere, which debuted in 2023 with the inaugural residency of U2 and has or will soon been host to Phish, the Eagles, Kenny Chesney, Backstreet Boys, Carín León, Metallica, Anyma and more. It branched into sporting events with the UFC in September of 2024. Its ongoing presentation of The Wizard of Oz, a 75-minute 4D immersive adaptation of the classic 1939 film, in collaboration with Warner Bros., has been extremely popular.

Oprah Winfrey: Courtesy

title: Beta Cinema Posts Fresh Deals For Trudie Styler’s ‘Up Against It’ Ahead Of TIFF Debut
summary: Beta Cinema has unveiled a raft of new deals for Trudie Styler’s comedy Up Against It ahead of its world premiere as a gala presentation in Toronto later this week. The fresh deals include to Spain (Youplanet Pictures/Caramel), Greece (Spentzos Film), Turkey (Mars Production), Bulgaria (Beta Film) and Latin America (A2 Filmes). Beta Cinema reports […]
content:
Beta Cinema has unveiled a raft of new deals for Trudie Styler‘s comedy Up Against It ahead of its world premiere as a gala presentation in Toronto later this week.

The fresh deals include to Spain (Youplanet Pictures/Caramel), Greece (Spentzos Film), Turkey (Mars Production), Bulgaria (Beta Film) and Latin America (A2 Filmes).

Beta Cinema reports that the film, first announced at the post-production stage last TIFF under the title of Rose’s Baby, has now sold to more than 50 territories.

Previously announced territories include to Australia & New Zealand (Kismet), Middle East (Front Row), Italy (Rai Cinema), Scandinavia (SF-Studios), Benelux (Paradiso), Poland (Best Film) Czech Republic and Slovakia (Foxx), Former Yugoslavia (MCF), and Hungary (Cinetel).

The tender family comedy stars Oscar nominee Antonio Banderas (The Mask of Zorro) and Eva Birthistle (Bad Sisters) as a divorced couple who struggle to maintain the minimum communication required to share custody of their beloved only child Rose.

Watch on Deadline

When it’s discovered that, not only does Rose have a rare form of leukemia, but that, their best bet at keeping her healthy and alive is for Álvaro and Saffron to produce a second child who could provide a transfusion, the ex-partners are forced to bury the hatchet.

Up Against It is produced by Maven Screen Media and Tempo Productions.

Banderas and Birthistle (Bad Sisters) are joined in the cast by Úrsula Corberó (Money Heist), Arinzé Kene (The Pass, Lee), Oscar winner Forest Whitaker (The Last King of Scotland), Oscar nominee Richard E. Grant (Saltburn) and rising talent Eden Hamilton (The Railway Children Return).

The film was edited by Walter Fasano (Call Me By Your Name, I Am Love) and Nathan Nugent (Room), with Academy Award nominee Dante Spinotti (L.A. Confidential) serving as director of photography.

title: Jeremy Thomas Tributes: Figures From Across The Industry Remember Legendary UK Producer Of ‘The Last Emperor’ & ‘Crash’
summary: Tributes from across the industry have been rolling in this weekend following the death of veteran producer Jeremy Thomas. He died on September 11. He was 77 years old.
