content:
EXCLUSIVE: Patricia “Ms. Pat” Williams-Lee is expanding her relationship with Paramount under her new deal with BET Studios, spanning producing, writing, and performing across BET and Paramount platforms.

VH1 has ordered America’s Funniest People from the producers of America’s Funniest Videos, V10 Entertainment. The show is a comedy competition with Ms. Pat starring. Each episode will feature “outrageous creator-led content — savage jokes, wild stunts, pranks, bad decisions — and the kind of unforgettable social content you can’t believe someone actually posted,” the network teased. Content creators will go head-to-head for a cash prize.

Additionally, Ms. Pat Settles It, from 495 Productions, has been renewed for a fourth season. The courtroom series puts Ms. Pat on the bench to preside over real-life cases with a jury of her friends, celebrity guests and fellow comedians.

Watch on Deadline

“I’ve never had three legal jobs at the same time, so this is new for me,” joked Ms. Pat. “I love being a judge, and four seasons of any show is more than I could ask for. I also believe that real life is the only thing funnier than my favorite TV shows. America’s Funniest People is merging both of my favorite worlds together. I’m grateful to be trusted to bring both shows to life.”

“Ms. Pat has one of the most distinctive, authentic voices in comedy, and an instinct for exactly what makes people laugh,” said Laurel Weir, Head of Programming and Acquisitions for Paramount Media Networks. “She built her career on unfiltered, real-life comedy, and America’s Funniest People lets her loose on the funniest things the internet has to offer.”

America’s Funniest People is executive produced by Ms. Pat, John Stevens, Carter Skeath, and Rick De Oliveira. Saterah Moore serves as co-executive producer. Ms. Pat Settles It is executive produced by Ms. Pat, SallyAnn Salsano and Ebony McClain for 495 Productions.

title: ‘Adults’ Streaming Viewership Grows 40% In Season 2, Per FX
summary: FX’s Adults is posting rare Season 2 viewership gains amid a sophomore slump impacting most streaming series recently. Citing Disney internal streaming data, FX has revealed that Adults‘ viewership has grown more than 40% season over season across Hulu in the U.S. and Disney+ internationally over the first 12 days of release. (Both seasons were […]
content:
FX’s Adults is posting rare Season 2 viewership gains amid a sophomore slump impacting most streaming series recently.

Citing Disney internal streaming data, FX has revealed that Adults‘ viewership has grown more than 40% season over season across Hulu in the U.S. and Disney+ internationally over the first 12 days of release. (Both seasons were binge drops on streaming. Because of the series’ young skew, its linear ratings on FX/FXX are very small, with most of the viewing coming from streaming.)

International has been a major driver with a big increase off a small base. After modest turnout for Season 1, international viewership has doubled, up +100% for Season 2.

A programming move that appears to have played a key strategic role is the release of a standalone prequel episode, Marathon Day, a month ahead of the release of Season 2. It drove viewership for Season 1 of Adults, which has been up 50% since Marathon Day‘s July 31 debut.

Watch on Deadline

The U.S. Season 2 to Season 1 audience growth of 30%+ matches the increase of the show’s Rotten Tomatoes critics score, up 30% to 100% from 77% for Season 1.

Adults‘ Season 2 gains come as Hulu opted to cancel its similar comedy about 20something young New York professionals living together, Not Suitable For Work after one season. According to sources, Adults has performer better while also carrying a significantly smaller price tag.

In Adults, Samir (Malik Elassal), Billie (Lucy Freyer), Paul Baker (Jack Innanen), Issa (Amita Rao) and Anton (Owen Thiele) are five friends crashing together in Samir’s childhood home. Created by Ben Kronengold & Rebecca Shaw, the show puts a generational lens on the wins, losses and humiliations of being in your twenties.

Produced by FX Productions, Adults is executive produced by Ben Kronengold & Rebecca Shaw, Nick Kroll, Sarah Naftalis, Jonathan Krisel, Alicia Van Couvering and Rob Rosell . “Adults” is produced by FX Productions.

title: Rhea Seehorn Wins Emmy for ‘Pluribus’ After ‘Better Call Saul’s’ Legendary Shutout
summary: Hi Carol. We Are So Happy To See You Win an Emmy. We Just Want You To Be Happy. The “Pluribus” hivemind is collectively cheering the news: Rhea Seehorn has won the outstanding drama Emmy for playing novelist Carol Sturka — one of the last independent-thinking humans on Earth — on the Apple TV series. […]
content:
Hi Carol. We Are So Happy To See You Win an Emmy. We Just Want You To Be Happy.

The “Pluribus” hivemind is collectively cheering the news: Rhea Seehorn has won the outstanding drama Emmy for playing novelist Carol Sturka — one of the last independent-thinking humans on Earth — on the Apple TV series.

Seehorn beat out fellow nominees Carrie Coon (HBO Max’s “The Gilded Age”), Chase Infiniti (Hulu’s “The Testaments”), Keri Russell (Netflix’s “The Diplomat”) and Zendaya (HBO Max’s “Euphoria”).

This reps Seehorn’s first Primetime Emmy win. She was previously nominated in 2023 and 2022 for outstanding supporting actress in a drama series for “Better Call Saul,” as Kim Wexler. Also in 2022, she was nominated in the outstanding actress in a short-form comedy or drama series category for playing Kris Latimer on AMC’s “Cooper’s Bar.”

Popular on Variety

“Pluribus” has already outpaced “Better Call Saul” at the Emmys: Going into Monday’s telecast, “Pluribus” had already won four awards — including outstanding sound mixing for a comedy or drama series (one hour), original main title theme music, picture editing for a drama series and production design for a narrative contemporary program (one hour). The show has 18 nominations overall.

On the flip side, despite its wide acclaim (including for Seehorn), “Saul” never won a single Emmy during its time on the air — despite earning 53 nominations. It’s widely considered one of the most puzzling Emmy snubs of all time, given how critically acclaimed the show was over its multiple seasons. (And “Saul” holds the unfortunate record of most Emmy nominations for a series without a win.)

As for Seehorn, “Pluribus” — which reunited her with “Saul” co-creator Vince Gilligan, who created the new series — has already generated best drama actress wins at the Golden Globes and Critics’ Choice Awards, as well as individual achievement in drama at the TCA Awards. She was also nominated at this year’s SAG-AFTRA Actor Awards in the female actor in a drama category.

The 78th Emmys are taking place at the Peacock Theater at L.A. Live in downtown Los Angeles, airing on NBC and Peacock. “Law & Order SVU” star Mariska Hargitay is host, while Jesse Collins Entertainment is producing the ceremony. This year’s Emmy nominations were led by HBO Max’s “The Pitt,” with 25, followed by “Hacks” with 24 (the most ever for a comedy). After the first two Emmy ceremonies (now known as “Night 1″ and “Night 2,” Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay” was in the lead with the most wins so far this year with eight, while Apple TV headed into the final Emmy ceremony with 19 wins, the most of any outlet so far.

title: ‘Buffy’ Reunion at Emmys: Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz Mock Canceled Reunion Series, Pay Tribute to Cast Members Who Died
summary: “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz had a mini reunion at the Emmys and presented at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles Monday night. The pair started by joking about the show’s premise. “A teenage girl chosen by fate to fight vampires, demons and forces of darkness and then she […]
content:
“Buffy the Vampire Slayer” stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz had a mini reunion at the Emmys and presented at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles Monday night.

The pair started by joking about the show’s premise.

“A teenage girl chosen by fate to fight vampires, demons and forces of darkness and then she falls in love with a vampire with a soul carrying around a couple 100 years of regret,” Gellar said. “And much, much older vampire with a soul and agonizing remorse about his past. For those of you who don’t know, his character was 241 years old.”

She also pointedly said that audiences will “never know” how Buffy and Angel’s love story will end, a terse nod to the pilot to a sequel series that was announced to not have been picked up earlier this year.

Popular on Variety

Gellar also alluded to some recent big losses in the “Buffy” cast in recent years. Nicholas Brendon, who played Buffy’s friend Xander Harris, died in March at 54, and Anthony Head, who played Buffy’s Watcher Rupert Giles on all seven seasons of the show, died in June at 72. Michelle Trachtenberg, who joined “Buffy” in its fifth season as Buffy’s younger sister Dawn Summers, died in February 2025 at 39.

The duo presented the Emmy for outstanding lead actor in a limited or anthology series or movie, which ended up going to Matthew Rhys for “The Beast in Me.”

“Buffy” ran for seven seasons, beginning in 1997. Sarah Michelle Gellar starred as Buffy Summers, the titular slayer. David Boreanaz played love interest Angel in the first three seasons of the original show and made several guest appearances until the finale in 2003. He returned in his own spinoff series, “Angel,” which ran from 1999—2004.

“Buffy” also starred Alyson Hannigan, James Marsters, Charisma Carpenter, Emma Caulfield and Eliza Dushku. A revival at Hulu nearly happened with Gellar returning to mentor a new Slayer, but it was canned earlier this year.

“Buffy” was nominated for 14 Primetime Emmy Awards during its run. It won for outstanding makeup for a series and outstanding music composition for a series (dramatic underscore), both in 1998. Angel was nominated for a Primetime Emmy for outstanding makeup for a series in 2000, but it lost to “The X-Files.”

The 2026 Emmy Awards are presented by Mariska Hargitay, who took home two awards last weekend for her documentary “My Mom Jayne: A Film by Mariska Hargitay.”

title: Allison Janney Wins Emmy for Supporting Actress in Drama, Tying Record for Most Wins by a Performer
summary: “The Diplomat” star Allison Janney has won the Emmy for outstanding supporting actress in a drama series — her eighth career win as a performer, putting her in rarified air. She now ties the all-time record for the most Emmys won by a performer (eight wins overall). “This is not what I planned for this […]
content:
“The Diplomat” star Allison Janney has won the Emmy for outstanding supporting actress in a drama series — her eighth career win as a performer, putting her in rarified air. She now ties the all-time record for the most Emmys won by a performer (eight wins overall).

“This is not what I planned for this category at all,” Janney said onstage. “I’m very surprised and very, very grateful to be here. I thank all the members of the Television Academy. And of course I have to thank Debra Kahn who is our writer. So much fun. And Alex Gray, our director, who I adore, and Janice Williams, and the coolest woman on the planet, Keri Russell, who leads us all every day. And Rufus, the entire cast is divine. And I am so grateful and so lucky. And I thank you very much from the bottom of my heart.”

Janney earned her trophy on a historic night, as “Hacks” star Jean Smart joined her in tying the record. The two of them join Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, who both have eight Emmys as a performer. Janney previously won four Emmys for “The West Wing” (outstanding supporting drama actress in 2000 and 2001, then lead drama actress in 2002 and 2004), two for “Mom” (supporting comedy actress in 2014 and 2015), and one as a guest drama actress on “Masters of Sex” (2014). She has 16 Emmy nominations all together.

Popular on Variety

Janney beat out a field including Taylor Dearden (as Dr. Mel King, “The Pitt”), Fiona Dourif (as Dr. Cassie McKay, “The Pitt”), Katherine LaNasa (as Charge Nurse Dana Evans, “The Pitt”), Sepideh Moafi (as Dr. Baran Al-Hashimi, “The Pitt”), Julianne Nicholson (as Sinatra, “Paradise”) and Karolina Wydra (as Zosia, “Pluribus”).

Besides drama series and drama lead actress, “The Diplomat” was also nominated this year for drama series, drama lead actor (Rufus Sewell, as Hal Wyler), drama lead actress (Keri Russell, as Kate Wyler), drama writing, drama casting and drama guest actor (Bradley Whitford, as First Gentleman Todd Penn).

For “The Diplomat,” Janney has also received nominations at the SAG-AFTRA Actor Awards, the Golden Globes and the Critics’ Choice Awards.

The 78th Emmys are taking place at the Peacock Theater at L.A. Live in downtown Los Angeles, airing on NBC and Peacock. “Law & Order SVU” star Mariska Hargitay is host, while Jesse Collins Entertainment is producing the ceremony. This year’s Emmy nominations were led by HBO Max’s “The Pitt,” with 25, followed by “Hacks” with 24 (the most ever for a comedy). After the first two Emmy ceremonies (now known as “Night 1″ and “Night 2,” Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay” was in the lead with the most wins so far this year with eight, while Apple TV headed into the final Emmy ceremony with 19 wins, the most of any outlet so far.

title: In Emmys Monologue, Mariska Hargitay Tells Nicole Kidman to ‘Zip It, Movie Lady’ and Reveals Dick Wolf’s Real Name Is ‘Richard Penis’
summary: Mariska Hargitay opened the 78th Emmy Awards with a bang, delivering a monologue that poked fun at her long-running role on “Law & Order: SVU” and parodied a beloved piece of pop culture. “The Emmys are celebrating their 78th year, and NBC is celebrating its 100th year. And I have been on ‘Law & Order: […]
content:
Mariska Hargitay opened the 78th Emmy Awards with a bang, delivering a monologue that poked fun at her long-running role on “Law & Order: SVU” and parodied a beloved piece of pop culture.

“The Emmys are celebrating their 78th year, and NBC is celebrating its 100th year. And I have been on ‘Law & Order: SVU’ for all of them,” Hargitay joked after she was carried onto the stage by a group of backup dancers with TVs on their heads.

Hargitay is the first woman to host the Emmys in a decade and a half, a tidbit she emphasized by quipping, “Imagine that: For 15 straight years, Amy and Tina said no.”

Popular on Variety

Looking out at the starry crowd at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, Hargitay said it was “reassuring to see so many familiar faces out there. And I’m just talking about how many of you I’ve arrested on ‘SVU.'”

Speaking of the long-running NBC drama, Hargitay gave a sincere tribute to series creator Dick Wolf, who has made over 40 shows — 13 of which are currently on the air.

“Over the years, there have been a lot of jokes about his name, which is so unfair because Dick Wolf isn’t even his real name,” Hargitay said. “His real name is Richard Penis.”

Celebrating the nominees who recently wrapped their last episode, Hargitay rubbed in her steady network gig by pretending to struggle with the teleprompter as she read “series finale.”

“Fee-na-lay? Fin-a-lay? Am I saying that right?” she said. “I’m sorry guys, it’s just that I’ve never had one!”

Just when it appeared Hargitay was getting sincere — “I am truly deeply moved and so incredibly grateful to be in a room full of people who have dedicated their lives to telling stories” — the host spiraled into a familiar-sounding monologue. “At the end of the day,” Hargitay continued, “we come to TV for magic, to laugh, to cry, to care, because we need that, all of us, that indescribable feeling that we get when the lights begin to dim. Dazzling images on the silver screen, sound that I can feel.”

Suddenly Hargitay was interrupted by an audience member — Nicole Kidman! “Now, Mariska, come on,” Kidman said. “That’s mine. That’s my bit. You can’t do that.”

As Hargitay barrelled forward, delivering Kidman’s exact words from her famous AMC ad, the “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” star interrupted again: “That is my line. That is actually my line.”

“Zip it, movie lady! It’s TV’s turn tonight!” Hargitay yelled to big laughter (despite the fact that Kidman has appeared in what seems like hundreds of TV shows).

The NBC kudocast opened with a pre-recorded sketch that saw Hargitay steaming her ball gown next to Knicks star Jalen Brunson, snuggling up with best actress in a comedy winner Jean Smart and sipping boba with Jennifer Coolidge.

Following a controversial, one-and-done hosting stint from Nate Bargatze, Hargitay took the reins as the first woman to emcee the Emmys in 15 years (Jane Lynch hosted in 2011). As an NBC mainstay, the “Law & Order: SVU” star and executive producer was tapped to host the kudocast while the network celebrates 100 years. Plus, Hargitay herself has some Emmys history, with 10 nominations and three wins under her belt. (She won two awards ahead of the primetime telecast for directing and producing “My Mom Jayne,” a documentary about her mother, Jayne Mansfield.)

Ahead of her hosting stint, Hargitay teased in her Variety cover story that she wanted to do “SVU: The Musical” on the Emmys stage. She also said she couldn’t wait to hang out with the actors from “The Pitt,” adding, “I couldn’t turn it off.”

title: ‘Beast in Me’ Star Matthew Rhys Wins Emmy for Lead Actor in Limited Series
summary: Matthew Rhys has won the Emmy Award for outstanding lead actor in a limited series for “The Beast in Me” Season 2. With the win, Rhys beat out fellow nominees Riz Ahmed (“Bait”), Jason Bateman (“Black Rabbit”), Charlie Hunnam (“Monster: The Ed Gein Story”), and Oscar Isaac (“Beef”). “If you try to play me off, […]
content:
Matthew Rhys has won the Emmy Award for outstanding lead actor in a limited series for “The Beast in Me” Season 2.

With the win, Rhys beat out fellow nominees Riz Ahmed (“Bait”), Jason Bateman (“Black Rabbit”), Charlie Hunnam (“Monster: The Ed Gein Story”), and Oscar Isaac (“Beef”).

“If you try to play me off, I’ll stab you in the eyes with this,” Rhys cheekily said onstage upon receiving his statuette. “This is a real shock, not least because the caliber and company of the actors in this program. We had a holy trinity of scribes in the glorious form of Daniel Pearle, Gabe Rotter, and Howard Gordon, who really brought out the beast in all of us. We were guided so beautifully by Antonio Campos, but certainly led ferociously, fiercely, fervently by the incredible Claire Danes. Thank you for letting me join the mystery machine and bringing out the beast. You are an intimidating scene partner, but I’m very grateful for for all this.”

Rhys is a three-time nominee this year. He also shares in “The Beast in Me’s” nomination for outstanding limited series as an executive producer, while he is also up for the award for outstanding lead actor in a comedy for Apple TV’s “Widow’s Bay.” Should he also win the award for “Widow’s Bay,” he will become the first person to win two lead acting Emmys in one night.

Popular on Variety

He has received eight Emmy nominations in total throughout his career, including three nods (and one win) for the critically-acclaimed FX series “The Americans.” He was also previously nominated for his work in HBO’s “Perry Mason,” in which he played the title role. Beyond “Widow’s Bay,” he is staying in business with Apple TV with a lead role in “Presumed Innocent” Season 2.

title: Mariska Hargitay Opens The Emmys With Help From Jalen Brunson, Jean Smart & A Nicole Kidman Commercial
summary: Tonight Mariska Hargitay, who recently directed an Emmy winning documentary and also made her Broadway debut, became the first woman to host the Emmy Awards in 15 years, and at least in the show’s fairly brief opening monologue mostly steered clear of attempting to out-do the outrageous comedy talents of previous hosts Amy Poehler and […]
content:
Tonight Mariska Hargitay, who recently directed an Emmy winning documentary and also made her Broadway debut, became the first woman to host the Emmy Awards in 15 years, and at least in the show’s fairly brief opening monologue mostly steered clear of attempting to out-do the outrageous comedy talents of previous hosts Amy Poehler and Tina Fey.

Immediately following a so-so pre-taped song parody of Joan Jett’s “I Love Rock ’n’ Roll” retitled “I Love TV Screens,” in which Hargitay quipped with Jalen Brunson and Jean Smart, among others, and lip-synced to her own pre-recorded lyrics that name-dropped any number of nominees, the host took to the Emmy stage in a gorgeous, silvery-white glam gown and quickly set about keeping expectations in check.

“I am so incredibly proud to be the first woman to host the Emmys in 15 years,” she said. “For 15 straight years, Amy and Tina said no.”

Watch on Deadline

Hargitay also wasted no time getting to the Law & Order jokes. “The Emmys are celebrating their 78th year, and NBC is celebrating its 100th year,” she said, “and I have been on Law and Order: SVU for all of them.”

And another: “It is so reassuring to see so many familiar faces out there,” she said, surveying the audience, “and I’m just talking about how many of you I’ve arrested on SVU. You guys have done some unspeakable things. I’m talking to you, Martin Short.”

Hargitay then took on her boss: “I couldn’t do any of this without thanking the genius behind SVU, the legendary Dick Wolf, who has created over 40 shows, 13 of which are on the air right now, and I gotta say, you know, over the years there have been a lot of jokes about his name, which is so unfair because Dick Wolf isn’t even his real name. His real name is Richard Penis.”

With that groaner out of the way, Hargitay got serious, saying that she had been advised not to “go for sincerity” but decided to ignore that wisdom.

RELATED: The 2026 Emmys Parties & Events Photos: Netflix, BAFTA TV Tea Party & Warner Bros.

Television Group Pre-Emmys Party



“I am truly deeply moved,” she said, “and so incredibly grateful to be in a room full of people who have dedicated their lives to telling stories since the beginning of time, humans have all gathered around the light to tell stories. Back then, it was the fire in the cave, and now it’s the screen of your choice.



“But no matter how we watch, and even though we’re worlds apart, we’re all still holding a bit of that communal light, and at the end of the day, we come to TV for magic, to laugh, to cry, to care, because we need that, all of us, that indescribable feeling that we get when the lights begin to dim, dazzling images on the silver screen…”

Year

Sound familiar? If you’ve been in an AMC movie theater in the last few years you’ll recognize that speech as Nicole Kidman’s pitch for the theater chain, which Kidman, in the Emmy audience, loudly pointed out, bringing the gag to a blessedly quick end.

title: Sarah Michelle Gellar & David Boreanaz Reflect On Fate Of”May December” Romance Between Buffy And Angel In ‘Buffy The Vampire Slayer’: “I Guess We’ll Never Find Out”
summary: Buffy the Vampire Slayer stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz reunited on the Emmys stage tonight to present the award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie. While reflecting on the show celebrating 30 years since its premiere this upcoming March, Boreanaz remarked that he always thought their characters, […]
content:
Buffy the Vampire Slayer stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz reunited on the Emmys stage tonight to present the award for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie.

While reflecting on the show celebrating 30 years since its premiere this upcoming March, Boreanaz remarked that he always thought their characters, Buffy and Angel, would end up together, despite the large age gap with Angel being a 241-year-old vampire.

“I guess we won’t find out,” Gellar answered.

Earlier this year, Hulu opted not to proceed with its pilot order for a Buffy: New Sunnydale reboot that would have been directed by Chloe Zhao from a script written by Nora and Lilla Zuckerman (Poker Face).

Gellar revealed the news that the project was not going forward shortly after she attended the SXSW Film Festival for the premiere of Ready or Not 2: Here I Come.

Watch on Deadline

“David and I would like to acknowledge that it has been a tough two years for our beloved cast and crew, and we feel very lucky to have known and worked with such amazing people,” Gellar added before they opened the envelope to present the award to Matthew Rhys for his role in The Beast In Me.

RELATED: Sarah Michelle Gellar Reveals She Declined Chloé Zhao’s ‘Buffy’ Reboot “Many Times” & Why She Learned To “Never Say Never”

The show has recently lost some of its staple cast members, with Michelle Trachtenberg having passed in February 2025 and Anthony Head passing in June this year. Nicholas Brendon, who played Xander Harris, passed in March of this year.

Boreanaz, who has shows like The Angel, Bones and SEAL Team under his belt, has NBC’s reboot of The Rockford Files coming in January next year. He will succeed James Garner as James Rockford, the witty, world-weary and chronically broke private investigator Garner originated on the 1974 NBC series.

title: ‘Widow’s Bay’s Kate O’Flynn Dedicates Emmy Win To “All The Patricia’s Out There”
summary: Break out the cursed twig figurines and light up the bonfire because Widow’s Bay star Kate O’Flynn has clinched her first Emmy. Winning for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her role as Patricia, the awkward but very dutiful assistant to Matthew Rhys’ troubled mayor Tom Loftis, O’Flynn had this to say: “Thank […]
content:
Break out the cursed twig figurines and light up the bonfire because Widow’s Bay star Kate O’Flynn has clinched her first Emmy.

Winning for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her role as Patricia, the awkward but very dutiful assistant to Matthew Rhys’ troubled mayor Tom Loftis, O’Flynn had this to say: “Thank you to Katie [Dippold] and Hiro [Murai] for trusting this Lancashire lass to play a sassy broad like Patricia and Apple for saying yes.”

Widow’s Bay, the word-of-mouth Apple series horror-comedy that took TV lovers by surprise, follows mayor Loftis as he tries to revive the economy of his struggling New England island town. In the midst of renovating it into a tourist destination, the island’s long-rumored curse begins to come true, and he and the quirky, skeptical locals find themselves confronting a series of increasingly bizarre supernatural horrors.

Watch on Deadline

O’Flynn continuing her speech said, “I want to thank our mayor and all the residents of Widow’s Bay in front and behind the camera. You’re amazing, this is a role of a lifetime…[I also want to thank] the loves of my life, my darling husband and our darling daughter—another sassy broad in the making—but this is for all the Patrica’s out there. See you at sunset cocktails to celebrate.”

Widow’s Bay came into the Emmys ceremony with 19 total nominations, winning eight between Emmys Night 1 and Night 2 with O’Flynn’s win racking up a ninth win.

In August, series creator Katie Dippold told Deadline that the writer’s room for Season 2 was already under way. As for what O’Flynn would like to see happen next for character?

As for what O’Flynn would like to see happen next for her character? “I don’t know,” she told Deadline. Instead she threw her hat into the ring to also play the role of someone else too O’Flynn added: “But, I would love to play a British ancestor or Patricia or something… I like the idea of wigging up and doing a bit of a period drama. Why not?”

title: Jean Smart Ties Acting Record With Fifth Emmy Win For ‘Hacks’: “What A Ride This Has Been”
summary: Jean Smart ended her Emmy run for Hacks the way her character Deborah Vance ended her comedy career — on top. Smart tonight earned her fifth consecutive Outstanding Lead Actress In a Comedy Series win for the fifth and final season of the HBO Max show. With that, Smart has tied Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris […]
content:
Jean Smart ended her Emmy run for Hacks the way her character Deborah Vance ended her comedy career — on top. Smart tonight earned her fifth consecutive Outstanding Lead Actress In a Comedy Series win for the fifth and final season of the HBO Max show.

With that, Smart has tied Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for the most Emmys ever by a performer, eight. In addition to the five for Hacks, her haul includes two in the Guest Actress In a Comedy Series category for Frasier and one in the Supporting Actress a Comedy Series field for Samantha Who?, a rare sweep of the comedy acting trifecta.

After channeling Deborah when she got a standing ovation how only men should stay up given how uncomfortable it is for women wearing tight shapewear and high heels, Smart turned serious.

Watch on Deadline

“This one I’m dedicating to Lucia Aniello, Jen Statsky and Paul W. Downs,” she said about the Hacks creatoes/executive producers. “It all begins and ends with them.”

RELATED: Here Are The Actors Who Have Won The Most Emmys: Photo Gallery

Smart has won an acting Emmy for every eligible season of her series, the only performer to accomplish that for a show that has run for four seasons or more. The feat comes with an asterisk because Louis-Dreyfus won six Emmys in a row for her starring role in Veep. She did not complete a full sweep after losing the seventh time but had the show ended at six seasons, Louis-Dreyfus would be holding the record.

The Seinfeld alumna has the record for the most Emmys won for a single role, 6, with Smart now tied with Candice Bergen who also took five trophies for Murphy Brown.

RELATED: ‘Hacks’ Jean Smart Chases Emmy History As She Nears Julia Louis-Dreyfus & Cloris Leachman Record

Smart’s last Emmy win for Hacks comes just months after she was inducted into the Television Academy Hall of Fame.

In the final season of Hacks, Deborah (Smart), shaken up by a false death announcement, is focusing on her legacy as she teams with Ava (Hannah Einbinder) to mount one last, record-breaking standup performance.

“What a ride this has been,” Smart said at the end of her speech. You can watch it below:

title: Gavin Newsom On Kamala Harris: “I Wouldn’t Run If She Ran”
summary: The careers of Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris have paralleled each other since at least 2004, when he was sworn in as Mayor of San Francisco and she as the city’s D.A. Since then, their political fortunes have skyrocketed, with Newsom becoming a two-term governor and Harris a senator and then VP. Now, of course, […]
content:
The careers of Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris have paralleled each other since at least 2004, when he was sworn in as Mayor of San Francisco and she as the city’s D.A. Since then, their political fortunes have skyrocketed, with Newsom becoming a two-term governor and Harris a senator and then VP. Now, of course, they’re both reportedly considering runs for president in 2028. But, according the Newsom, they won’t be running against each other.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom told Jake Tapper in a new interview. “I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Tapper says he was stunned to hear that.

“Why would I?” Newsom asked. “I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do it to me…I won’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?”

Watch on Deadline

The governor then explained that, beyond friendship, such a matchup doesn’t make political sense for democrats.

“Electorally it’s a gift from God for everybody else,” the governor explained. “They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good. Why would I do this if I wasn’t trying to serve some greater good? There would be no upside whatsoever.”

Newsom also noted it would tax the same base of support.

“I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the (Venn) diagram on that is just pure crossover…I wouldn’t do that to people. I wouldn’t put them in that position.”

Newsom tells @jaketapper he won’t run in 2028 if Kamala Harris runs. pic.twitter.com/auDjNdBlyr — Alex Thompson (@AlexThomp) September 14, 2026

While Tapper may have been shocked, Newsom has said as much before. In 2023, he told Chuck Todd of the chance that they might run against each other, “Of course not. By definition, it won’t happen. I’ve said that a thousand times.”

As for not running against Trump in 2024, the governor says there were even more basic considerations arguing against his candadicy.

“I wasn’t ready,” he said. “I would have gotten crushed because I didn’t have a why. You don’t have big enough why, then you don’t belong there.”

title: Stephen Colbert Says ‘Free Speech Is Alive and Well’ After Emmy Win Despite CBS Cancellation: Late Night Is ‘Just as Vital as it Ever Has Been’
summary: “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” may have been canceled by CBS, but after taking home the award for outstanding variety series at Monday night’s Emmy Awards, Stephen Colbert is still optimistic about the state of late-night television. Speaking with CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister and Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh following the Emmy Awards, […]
content:
“The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” may have been canceled by CBS, but after taking home the award for outstanding variety series at Monday night’s Emmy Awards, Stephen Colbert is still optimistic about the state of late-night television.



Speaking with CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister and Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh following the Emmy Awards, Colbert explained that he still feels that “free speech is alive and well.”



“Because if you can’t say something because you go to jail, that is a violation of free speech,” he continued. “I think that late night is just as funny and just as vital as it ever has been, and I love watching Jimmy and Jimmy and John and John and Seth and everybody else. And I think I hope it goes on for a long time because you get to work with people like this, and that’s the greatest gift.”



“The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” won the award for its final season, which ended in May after CBS announced the series’ cancellation. The show was up for the Emmy against “The Daily Show” (Comedy Central), “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” (ABC), “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” (HBO Max) and “Saturday Night Live” (NBC).



Speaking with Wagmeister and Setoodeh, Colbert also playfully pivoted away from the topic of Donald Trump: “That’s a beautiful dress. It’s amazing. What? Oh, I’m sorry, I’m deaf in that ear,” he said when asked if he thinks his show was canceled by the president. As for his thoughts on Bari Weiss, Colbert said he’s “never heard of her. Do you know her? I hear great things.”



The host also noted that he feels “just lovely” following the win. “I’m so glad that the show got recognized, and especially last week, all the people who want the creative arts, the writers and our director, our technical director, camera, lighting, and the digital team, and then tonight, all these incredible people,” he said. “First of all, just to be together after not seeing these guys for four months, it’s incredible. And we couldn’t be more grateful to the academy and everybody who voted for the show.”



Prior to Monday night’s awards, “The Late Show” had already won four prizes during the first weekend of the Emmys: Outstanding Writing For A Variety Series, Outstanding Directing For A Variety Series, Outstanding Technical Direction and Camerawork For A Series, Outstanding Lighting Design/Lighting Direction For A Series and Outstanding Picture Editing For Variety Programming (Segment).

title: ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Review: Amanda Seyfried and Scoot McNairy Are Powerful in Tim Blake Nelson’s Twisty Dark-Side Prison Saga
summary: Tim Blake Nelson’s "The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd" is a gripping, wrenching, dark-as-midnight crime drama that taps into a phenomenon many might view as an underground secret (or maybe they just don’t know anything about it): the relationship that develops, more often than you’d think, between violent incarcerated criminals and civilians who fall in love with them.
content:
Tim Blake Nelson’s “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” is a gripping, wrenching, dark-as-midnight crime drama that taps into a phenomenon many might view as an underground secret (or maybe they just don’t know enough about it): the relationship that develops, more often than you’d think, between incarcerated violent criminals and civilians who fall in love with them. Often, it starts with an exchange of letters. But in “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” Karen (Amanda Seyfried), a teacher who’s looking for an escape from her oppressive marriage and her dead-end life, finds work leading a creative-writing class at a maximum-security prison in Oklahoma.

One of the prisoners, Wilson Shedd (Scoot McNairy), has a snaky menace about him, but he’s clearly intelligent, and he’s actually interested in reading Hemingway short stories and trying his own hand at writing. When one of the other prisoners starts to bait Karen with hostile leering comments, Wilson warns him to back down. (When he doesn’t, the situation gets taken care of in a bloodier way.) With his quiet drawl and sociopathic flatness, Wilson has a mean charm that sneaks up on you, though it takes the audience a while to realize what he’s up to regarding Karen. He’s playing her.

Popular on Variety

Early on, there’s a jarring cut: to a scene of Wilson and two other prisoners in the outside world, still in their dirty orange prison uniforms, using an axe to bust into someone’s home. They have obviously escaped. But this is quite the dramatic flash-forward, and it sets the tone and structure of the movie — that Nelson, who wrote and directed it, is going to be jumping around in chronology, in what feels almost like a “Pulp Fiction” time loop, to undercut any tidy narrative stability. The fractured time scheme works powerfully; it keeps the audience on edge and triggers connections we wouldn’t otherwise make.

That said, to plug into the drama of “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” you need to accept that Amanda Seyfried’s Karen, who seems smart and canny and aware of things, could start receiving confessional letters from a prisoner like Wilson and be seduced by them — drawn into his spell of damaged “vulnerability.” Surveying Seyfried’s no-nonsense crispness, you might say, “Nope, that wouldn’t happen.” But the film lays the emotional groundwork for it (she convinces herself that he can save her), and part of what’s scary and fascinating is that what happens does chafe against our common sense, and the common sense we want our heroine to have. This, the film seems to be saying, is not a rational relationship. It’s a bond of counterintuitive danger, and that’s its allure.

Tim Blake Nelson is a great actor who’s been directing independent dramas for 30 years. I’ve been a fan ever since I saw his first one, “Eye of God” (also a bleak crime film with a tricky time scheme), back at the Sundance Film Festival in 1997. I thought he became major with “The Grey Zone” (2001), a Holocaust drama unlike any other. It put you right there in the camps, along with the Sonderkommando (the Jewish prisoners who led victims into the gas chambers and then disposed of the bodies); it had a queasiness you couldn’t shake off. “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd” is only Nelson’s sixth feature, and it’s his strongest since “The Grey Zone.” It holds you with the stark realism of its craft (this is a film about criminals but not a “thriller”), and with what it’s about: how human violence carves out its own realm of existence, and then feeds on itself.

The staging has an ominous matter-of-fact authority, whether it’s Karen fighting with her lout of a husband (Grant Harvey) or Wilson using the hardware-store tools Karen sneaks into him to start chiseling away at his escape. I’ve never seen Scoot McNairy give a performance this rich — it’s as if he’s playing someone like Gary Gilmore, his personality wary and contained, magnetically so, until he draws on the violence that’s been simmering in him for a lifetime. (Even when he does, it’s contained.) There’s a nice Black family, the Lawsons (William Jackson Harper and Devyn A. Tyler), who are taking a trip with their kids (Xuri Selah and Eric Blount) in their SUV, and what happens to them on a picnic is so horrifying that I nearly had to turn away. Yet Nelson directs a scene like this with unfussy bravura, so that there’s a need to look, to confront what evil is.

There’s one more level of violence in “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd.” Let’s call it state-sanctioned violence. What should we do with people like Wilson Shedd? Should they become the lightning rod of our vengeance? Or if not, are we refusing to close the circle? There is nothing supernatural about “The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd,” but as the film’s title suggests, Wilson undergoes more than one death. There’s the one that society hands him. And there’s the one he inflicted on himself, the one we might call not soul murder but soul suicide. Maybe society should have left it there, but you could also say that it’s our responsibility to put a man like this one out of his misery.

title: Mariska Hargitay Leads a Brisk Yet Celebratory Emmys in a Return to Form: TV Review
summary: Last year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host in Nate Bargatze and the result was an unmitigated disaster. This year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host and were rewarded with an effusive, yet efficient tribute to television at its best. Watching “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star — and “My Mom Jayne” […]
content:
Last year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host in Nate Bargatze and the result was an unmitigated disaster. This year, the Emmys bet on an unorthodox host and were rewarded with an effusive, yet efficient tribute to television at its best.

Watching “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star — and “My Mom Jayne” director, and Broadway leading lady and New York Knicks superfan — Mariska Hargitay emcee the Emmy awards’ 78th ceremony, I thought often of stand-up comedian Nikki Glaser. After Jo Koy’s abysmal, contemptuous turn leading the Golden Globes, Glaser rescued the broadcast, raised her own profile and ultimately became a repeat host by embracing enthusiasm. And while Bargatze’s Emmys performance last year wasn’t quite as infamous as Koy’s, a countdown clock preemptively chiding honorees for enjoying their moment a little too much showed a similar lack of regard for the evening’s ostensible purpose. Hargitay went in the other direction, throwing herself into multiple musical numbers and generally showing herself to be a fan of television as well as one of its most visible ambassadors. The approach paid off.

It helped that Hargitay, while game, wasn’t exactly earnest: a seemingly sincere monologue about the power of storytelling turned out to be a feint, transitioning into a ripoff of the AMC Nicole Kidman ad called out by the Australian actor herself. (The bit was also a self-aware wink on the part of Kidman, who Hargitay brushed off as “movie lady” but spends most of her time on the small screen these days.) But the novice host clearly took the job seriously, going through more outfit changes than her good friend Taylor Swift on an average night of the Eras Tour. Hargitay even got Swift herself to show up for a pre-taped segment, even if the cameo didn’t entirely justify an overlong parody of the pop star’s conspiratorial fanbase.

Popular on Variety

The Emmys had room to spare because the show had bumped several awards to the earlier ceremony once known as the Creative Arts Emmys, including supporting actor and actress in a limited series. (Winners Linda Cardellini and David Harbour of “DTF St. Louis” still got to appear in the main show as presenters.) The move was controversial — when the Oscars tried something similar a few years ago, demoting most of the technical awards to a pre-show, the time savings weren’t enough to justify the slight and the strategy was swiftly reversed.

But on Sunday at the Emmys, the results spoke for themselves with a brisk show that miraculously came in a few minutes under time. One Hargitay-led song, a riff on Supertramp’s “Goodbye Stranger” repurposed into an ode to series finales with an assist from Andrew Rannells, wasn’t necessary. But a dedicated tribute to Dolly Parton, led by fellow country luminary Reba McEntire, was certainly nice to have — as were extended honors for Catherine O’Hara and Rob Reiner. Even letting John Mulaney riff for several minutes before presenting lead actor in a drama felt like a good use of airtime. After all, the award itself was almost an afterthought: everyone in the room knew it was about to go to Noah Wyle of “The Pitt” once again, and deservedly so.

The modern Emmys love a sweep, which can give the proceedings a monotonous feel. It’s nonetheless hard to begrudge the love for horror comedy “Widow’s Bay,” a tide so strong it seemingly transcended categories and propelled star Matthew Rhys to a double acting win for his turn in Netflix’s “The Beast in Me” as well as the Apple TV breakout. An original story and therefore an underdog, “Widow’s Bay” also yielded the best speech of the night in creator Katie Dippold’s commitment to shamelessly show off her new trophy. And the plaudits were more evenly distributed in drama, which delivered surprise wins for Allison Janney of “The Diplomat,” Tom Pelphrey of “Task” and, to my personal delight, director Saul Metzstein of “Slow Horses.”

An unexpected result is not always the best one; much as I love Sally Field, I’m baffled by her performance in “Remarkably Bright Creatures” edged out Sarah Pidgeon’s bewitching embodiment of Carolyn Bessette in “Love Story.” It’s still good to know the Emmys can veer a bit off book in its production choices and deliver a solid, enjoyable show. After all, the pool of late night luminaries from which networks have reliably drawn their awards talent is shrinking, despite Stephen Colbert’s pleas to preserve the institution as a talent pipeline after the cancellation of “The Late Show.” Figures like Hargitay — familiar mainstays, but with untapped reserves of talent — are now the next best option in the search for steady hands. Hargitay herself, we’ve seen, was more than ready to step up to the plate.

title: Apple TV Wins 28 Emmys Thanks to ‘Widow’s Bay’ Sweep, HBO Max Takes Second Place With Help From ‘The Pitt’ and ‘DTF St. Louis’
summary: “Widow’s Bay” was the most-awarded show at the Emmys this year, winning 14 trophies total. The Apple TV comedy already had eight wins under its belt at the start of Monday night’s ceremony, having picked up awards including guest comedy actress (Betty Gilpin), comedy casting and music supervision at last week’s Creative Arts Emmys. At […]
content:
“Widow’s Bay” was the most-awarded show at the Emmys this year, winning 14 trophies total.

The Apple TV comedy already had eight wins under its belt at the start of Monday night’s ceremony, having picked up awards including guest comedy actress (Betty Gilpin), comedy casting and music supervision at last week’s Creative Arts Emmys. At the Primetime Emmys, it won every category it was nominated for, adding six to its haul: outstanding comedy series, lead comedy actor (Matthew Rhys), supporting comedy actor (Stephen Root), supporting comedy actress (Kate O’Flynn), comedy writing and comedy directing. This was a record-breaking sweep: “Widow’s Bay” has now won more Emmys in a single year than any comedy series in history.

As a result, Apple TV was the most successful studio at the Emmys this year. The tech giant-turned-streamer took home 28 trophies total, including six “Pluribus” wins, three for “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” three for “Palm Royale,” one for “Slow Horses” and one for “Mr. Scorsese.”

Popular on Variety

This is the first time at the top of the tally for Apple, a major achievement indicating continued growth after it had the No. 1 show last year — “The Studio” with a then-record-breaking 13 wins — but still trailed behind HBO Max and Netflix overall. In fact, 2026 marks only the second time in 20 years that a platform besides HBO Max or Netflix has led the Emmys. (FX triumphed over them in 2024.)

HBO Max came in second place this year with 21 Emmys. At the top of the heap with seven awards each were “DTF St. Louis” and “The Pitt,” which were named outstanding limited series and outstanding drama series, respectively. They tied with two other shows to become the titles with the second-most wins after “Widow’s Bay”: “The Traitors” on Peacock and “The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny” on NBC.

With its six awards for Apple, “Pluribus” tied with “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” as the third winningest show at the Emmys. Fourth, fifth and sixth place went, respectively, to “Spider-Noir” with five wins, “The Muppet Show” with four and “Beef” with three — with each of the three shows earning all of its gold at the Creative Arts Emmys rather than the primetime ceremony.

After HBO Max, as the No. 3 platform, was Netflix with 16 wins spread quite evenly across “Beef,” “Love on the Spectrum,” “Bridgerton,” “The Beast in Me” and more.

See a full breakdown below of the Emmys by program and by platform below.

title: Emmys 2026 Snubs and Surprises: Colbert’s Final Season Wins, Oscar Isaac Can’t Stop Matthew Rhys, Taylor Swift Crashes the Party and More
summary: The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are here, and much like a passing glance at a cloudless night sky, the stars are out! But this is no time for puns! Television’s biggest night was hosted by “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” icon Mariska Hargitay, and there were plenty of big wins and upsets. See some […]
content:
The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are here, and much like a passing glance at a cloudless night sky, the stars are out!

But this is no time for puns! Television’s biggest night was hosted by “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” icon Mariska Hargitay, and there were plenty of big wins and upsets.

See some of the night’s biggest snubs and surprises below.

Surprise: “DTF St. Louis” takes limited or anthology series.

Despite being a more subtle character study compared to buzzy heavy hitters like the second season of “Beef” and the Matthew Rhys-led “The Beast in Me,” it ended up with seven statues, including top honors.

Popular on Variety

Snub: Actors who aren’t white.

My colleague Clayton Davis wrote about it at length, but every lead and supporting acting award went to a white performer this year. Why is this still happening in 2026?

Surprise: Taylor Swift was in two places at once.

Swift did indeed support her BFF Hargitay’s hosting gig, pre-taping a comedy sketch so she could also attend her husband Travis Kelce’s first game of the season with the Kansas City Chiefs.

Snub: Oscar Isaac can’t block a record evening.

Isaac’s performance in “Beef” was predicted to win by the pundits, but Rhys pulled off a record win, taking both lead actor in a limited or anthology series or movie and lead actor in a comedy series.

Surprise: “Slow Horses” takes drama directing honor.

With starry and showy noms like Noah Wyle and Vince Gilligan, “Slow Horses” director Saul Metzstein sneaked in with a win for the episode “Scars.”

Snub: The supporting actresses of “The Pitt” cancel each other out.

While Allison Janney is brilliant, it’s likely that “Pitt” vote splitting opened the lane for her work on “The Diplomat” to be recognized.

Surprise: Gilligan nabs writing honor for “Pluribus.”

The writing category is always full of surprises, and the dramatic side of the category was no different, with Gilligan’s out-there “Pluribus” besting more down-to-earth storytelling.

Surprise: Stephen Colbert’s final season of “The Late Show” takes home variety series kudos.

A bit of background: In 2015, outstanding variety series was broken into two categories: outstanding variety sketch series and outstanding talk series. This year, the split was reversed; the categories were merged. Given all of the controversy about his show ending, Colbert certainly had a shot at winning the combined category, as he won talk series last year. But it had to squeeze by the juggernaut of John Oliver’s “Last Week Tonight,” which consistently won the variety sketch series statue.

Surprise: John Mulaney delivers a tight stand-up segment an hour into the show.

It’s no surprise that Mulaney was funny, but his introduction to lead actor in a dramatic series squeezed so many laughs and inside-baseball showbiz jokes that it gave the night a great jolt. Also bonus for nominee Mark Ruffalo chuckling along in the crowd. That man deserves a hearty laugh!

Surprise: Kate O’Flynn takes home hardware for the year’s wackiest character.

Despite what the pundits may have predicted, it seems so wonderful that a character as deliciously weird as Patricia Moyer can be victorious at a major award show. O’Flynn is just too undeniable on “Widow’s Bay.”

Surprise: The show was three minutes short!

Brevity is the soul of wit, and this year’s ceremony kept things tight! “Leave ’em wanting more” is a mantra that other award shows could stand to learn …

Surprise: Palpable sexual tension between Hargitay and Jean Smart in the opening segment!

There was a moment that, while the duo was lounging in bed together watching TV, Smart gave an unmistakable look to her bedmate. Should have kept that camera rolling!

Snub: Fashion lovers looking for some entertainment.

Very few celebs brought their A-game to the red carpet and ceremony. Let’s spice things up a bit next year!

Surprise: Why would the Emmys air opposite Monday Night Football?

Believe it or not, there are many TV addicts who also love sports. It’s the first week of the NFL returning, the year’s first Monday Night Football and it’s a Kansas City Chiefs game. Award show ratings are struggling … why go up against a gridiron giant?

title: Apple Takes Victory Lap After Emmy Bonanza: “You Can’t Predict These Things”
summary: Eddy Cue joined Apple in 1989, the year that shows such as Cheers and L.A. Law were dominating the Emmys. Fast forward 37 years and it is Apple that dominated the ceremony with a record-breaking night for Widow’s Bay and an assist from the likes of Pluribus and Slow Horses. The tech giant landed 28 […]
content:
Eddy Cue joined Apple in 1989, the year that shows such as Cheers and L.A. Law were dominating the Emmys.

Fast forward 37 years and it is Apple that dominated the ceremony with a record-breaking night for Widow’s Bay and an assist from the likes of Pluribus and Slow Horses.

The tech giant landed 28 television Emmys (29 if you’re counting commercials), beating the likes of HBO and Netflix, and Katie Dippold’s Matthew Rhys-led horror comedy broke the comedy record with 14 wins.

“It’s an amazing night,” Cue told Deadline after the show. “We started this seven years ago. We said we really want to try to make the best shows on television, get the greatest storytellers to give them the opportunity to do their best work, and this is certainly just the best example of that.”

Watch on Deadline

Cue said that when Apple TV (then known as Apple TV+) launched in November 2019, he didn’t consider such a night possible.

However, unlike some others may have been tempted to do, Cue didn’t laud the fact that it beat Netflix and HBO in terms of total wins (with far fewer submissions) over his rivals.

“I don’t think it’s the right way to think about it,” he said. “They’re incredible companies that do amazing work, and what we thought is that we could do something really special and something that unique to Apple, which was let’s not try to make the most, let’s try to make the best, and that was our number one goal. We figured if we did that, viewers would recognize it. Obviously, the Academy recognized it, and it’s great to see those the people that we work with are the best in the world, and we give them a platform.”

Eddy Cue, John Ternus, Zack Van Amburg and Jamie Erlicht (Photo by Chad Salvador/Getty Images)

Cue, who is SVP, Services and Health at Apple, said that such an awards haul doesn’t change the way that it does business in Hollywood or impact its overall programming strategy.

“We’re trying to create the best shows we can, that tell the best stories that you can to get human emotion, and we do that. If we can do that, then everything else, will come,” he said. “I’ve been at Apple for 38 years, and we’re trying to make the best product. If I knew how to make 200 great TV shows, we would.”

The night clearly belonged to Widow’s Bay’s. The show won 14 awards including Outstanding Comedy Series (making it two years in a row after The Studio’s success last year), and wins for Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn, Stephen Root, Hiro Murai and Dippold.

But the timing of the show’s launch, so close to the Emmy deadline that its final three episodes were not eligible, suggests that the streamer had no idea it had such an awards darling on its hands.

“It’s comedy, it’s horror. That’s the beauty of life. You can’t predict these things,” he added. “My favorite line is we probably say 1000 noes for every yes, and then we get behind the thing that we’re doing and work with the creators to let them make the best work. Widow’s Bay is a great example. That’s such an amazing story.”

The television rights to the Emmys are currently being shopped and there’s some suggestions that the broadcast wheel – which sees ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC air it once every four years – will not continue in its current form.

After a night like this (and last year), would Apple consider getting into the Emmy business?

“I haven’t thought about that, so I have no idea,” said Cue.

Apple will certainly be thinking about this year’s Emmys for some time to come.

title: ‘The Pitt’ Celebrates Wins With Season 3 Update; Noah Wyle On Enjoying Latest Success Years After ‘ER’ – Emmys Backstage
summary: For a second year in a row, The Pitt has been honored with the Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series. The hit HBO Max medical drama scored five additional wins this year: Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for Noah Wyle, Outstanding Casting in a Drama Series, Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series […]
content:
For a second year in a row, The Pitt has been honored with the Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series. The hit HBO Max medical drama scored five additional wins this year: Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for Noah Wyle, Outstanding Casting in a Drama Series, Outstanding Guest Actor in a Drama Series for Ernest Harden Jr., Outstanding Original Music and Lyrics, and Outstanding Prosthetic Makeup.

The cast, executive producers and writers continued the celebration backstage tonight to discuss their accomplishments. Deadline asked Wyle, creator R. Scott Gemmill and producer John Wells for some Season 3 teasers; the new season is currently shooting in Los Angeles.

“I can tell you that we’re going to be back to work tomorrow morning, hitting it hard with a very dramatic storyline. We are midway through our season on episode 8 of 15, and the episodes are turning out great. I watched episodes 4 and 5 today. Episode 5 Shawn [Hatosy] directed and it’s wonderful. I think you’re going to be in for a really great season,” said Wyle.

RELATED: ‘The Pitt’s Noah Wyle Touts Local Roots After Repeat Emmy Win: “I’m A Hollywood Kid, Raised On Television”

Gemmill added, ” Yeah, we took everyone on an amazing journey this season. Everyone brought their A-game like they always do.”

Going into a third season, Gemmill admits he is feeling a bit of pressure following the huge success of the show’s first two seasons.

“It’s so great to have the recognition. So we feel obligated to really try our best and not settle and keep pushing and pushing, and making Noah cry even more,” Gemmill joked. He added, “Whatever I can do to make it work. I joke, but we have a real responsibility to show the lives of these real-life emergency medicine heroes and try to do them justice.”

Wyley noted how much more he is able to appreciate the success that comes from working on such a critically acclaimed series. The first time around on ER, the actor was in his early 20s.

“That was such a wonderful sort of heady time, and I was on my back foot through most of it. It was only after that experience had come and gone that I really wished I had made more of it, enjoyed it more, and taken more deep breaths. I promised myself that if it ever happened again, if lightning was ever going to strike again, that I would really take time and smell the roses,” Wyle said.

title: ‘Pluribus’ Creator Vince Gilligan Reveals That Season 2 Is Already Mapped Out – Emmys Backstage
summary: Rhea Seehorn was the first to tell the press backstage at the Primetime Emmys on Monday that Pluribus creator Vince Gilligan has completed the first two scripts of Season 2. “I don’t have anything,” the Best Actress for Drama Series winner said, meaning she hasn’t seen the scripts. Gilligan, who won tonight for Drama Series […]
content:
Rhea Seehorn was the first to tell the press backstage at the Primetime Emmys on Monday that Pluribus creator Vince Gilligan has completed the first two scripts of Season 2.

“I don’t have anything,” the Best Actress for Drama Series winner said, meaning she hasn’t seen the scripts.

Gilligan, who won tonight for Drama Series Writing, explained, “It took us a while, we figured it out, but Season 2 is not technically all written. We’ve broken it out, which is the hard part. In other words, the plot of all episodes (is figured out). The first and second are written.”

“The rest of them are in various stages of being written, but we know what the whole season is, and we will share it soon with Rhea. Sometimes the actors like Karolina and Samba, sometimes they don’t necessarily want to know. They kind of want to be surprised, which I kind of like that.”

Season 1 ends with Carol demanding the alien hive mind deliver an atom bomb in a crate, which they make good on. Carol tells Manousos, who like her is one of the few humans untouched by the alien virus, “You win. We save the world,” using the bomb as her insurance policy if the collective tries to force a conversion of them.

Gilligan and Seehorn both discussed how they adore fans’ theories on what the show is about, read Covid, AI, grief and isolation.

Gilligan said that when it comes to AI and the pandemic being inspirations, “The idea (for this show) predated both those things.”

Said the creator taking home his fifth Emmy tonight, “Someone said that it’s sort of a contemplation of loss. I think all these things are true. They all have validity. I really like hearing other people tell me what my show is about.”

title: Sally Field Reflects On Filming ‘Remarkably Bright Creatures’ In Canada: “Let’s Keep Our Neighbors Close” — Emmys Backstage
summary: Sally Field would like the United States to play nice with its neighbors to the north. After winning an Emmy award on Monday night for Netflix’s Remarkably Bright Creatures, the actress used some of her time backstage with press to advocate for a friendly relationship with Canada, where the film adaptation was shot. “I do […]
content:
Sally Field would like the United States to play nice with its neighbors to the north.

After winning an Emmy award on Monday night for Netflix‘s Remarkably Bright Creatures, the actress used some of her time backstage with press to advocate for a friendly relationship with Canada, where the film adaptation was shot.

“I do know this that this film was about things that matter to me greatly about friendship, family, and home, and that it was on Canada, our neighbors, magnificent Canada, that I felt so welcomed,” she said. “Fight for it. Stand up for it. Don’t give it away. Resist.”

The small round of applause she received when she mentioned Vancouver, where one of her sons lives, invigorated her further: “Yes, let’s hear it for Vancouver. It’s a filming city, and honestly, guys, let’s keep our friendships. Let’s keep our neighbors close.”

Watch on Deadline

Field didn’t go into detail on her sentiment, but it’s not difficult to draw conclusions about what she might have been alluding to given the strained relations between the U.S. and Canada due in large part to President Trump’s tariff war with the country.

The U.S. has also long lost production to Canada, particularly Vancouver, as well as other territories abroad, which has sparked a years-long effort to bring back domestic film production. Trump recently backed a federal film tax incentive for the first time, opening the door for a potential bipartisan bill before the end of the year.

In addition to accepting an Emmy for her role in Remarkably Bright Creatures, Field also took the stage Monday night to participate in a tribute to her friend Dolly Parton. While speaking with press, she expanded on honoring her Steel Magnolias co-star.

“She was a friend. I admired her. I loved working with her. I never stopped loving her. There were moments where we tried to reach each other, but this is a weird world I live in. This acting world, where you where you do films and you’re so bonded with this group of people,” she said. “It’s like being in battle together. You save each other’s lives, and you got each other’s backs, and you spend 24/7 with each other. We would go shopping together, all of us and go to Walmart together. Can you imagine all of us coming into Walmart?”

Field admitted she hadn’t reunited with Parton in recent years, as “Dolly and I lived so far apart,” but she added: “The times we did reach out, I think she felt that way about me. So I loved her.”

content:

Emmy history was made tonight by Matthew Rhys, who became the first actor to win across all three lead categories (Comedy, Drama & Limited Series/Movie) and is the first man to win two lead acting awards in the same year.

And Jean Smart won her eighth career Emmy, tying Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for the most Emmys ever by a performer.
