title: Top Marketers on How Creators, TikTok, Spotify and Pinterest Help Fuel Fandom
summary: The era of AI and social media platforms has blown open the marketing playbook for bringing audiences to entertainment and experiences. That was the sentiment shared by six top marketers who spoke Thursday at Variety‘s Entertainment and Technology Summit in Los Angeles. The subject of the creator economy and its impact on selling everything from […]
content:
The era of AI and social media platforms has blown open the marketing playbook for bringing audiences to entertainment and experiences. That was the sentiment shared by six top marketers who spoke Thursday at Variety‘s Entertainment and Technology Summit in Los Angeles.

The subject of the creator economy and its impact on selling everything from soap to soap operas was a dominant theme of the day. And it was center stage in the panel with executives from Archrival, TikTok, Spotify, Pinterest, AMC Global Media and Lionsgate, which was moderated by Dea Lawrence, Variety‘s publisher and co-president.

Entertainment marketers once closely guarded their marketing materials and spooned out their campaigns with tactical precision on timing and platforms. Social media and social video in particular require studios and creatives to allow their fans to offer their takes on their favorite properties. It’s particularly prevalent on TikTok, of course.

Popular on Variety

“That participatory culture of co-creation is so unique to us, and that’s why [TikTok] participants are very engaged in creating,” said Dawn Yang, global head of entertainment for TikTok. “We have over 12 million TV and film posts that are posted by our users every day now, and that just gives you the perspective how much content there is around just stories that they love and want to share with everyone.”

Briana McElroy, global head of digital marketing for Lionsgate, reinforced Yang’s point by sharing her own experience.

“We actually hire fans to make our TikTok content for Lionsgate brand. If you consume it, you’ll know it — it’s called edits on TikTok,” McElroy said. “That’s wildly popular, and it’s really a lot of kids — 17 year olds, 18 year olds, 15 year olds — it’s their way of expressing their love for a person or a movie or a musician. They create these incredible visual pieces. The temptation is to try to replicate that on our end. But we thought, why do that? If we’re talking about authenticity, the best way to do it is to let the fans themselves do it. So on TikTok, that piece of advertising is incredible.”

Ben Harms, chief growth officer at youth culture marketing agency Archrival, offered a strong point of view on what it takes to win today and in the future.

“The brands that are going to win over the next 10 years are the ones that understand how to truly add value into consumers’ lives,” Harms said. He pointed to Spotify as a prime example. “While we have so much data and we’ve optimized and engineered everything, there is this sense that we’ve sort of lost the magic of the world in a lot of ways. And what we find that’s working for brands today is when they’re building ecosystems of experiences and human connection that go far beyond attention and just getting noise out there to really building meaningful connections with consumers.”

Sara Pollack, global head of consumer marketing for Pinterest, also reinforced that today’s fans often want to craft elaborate tributes and nods to favorite personalities and titles. On the Pinterest platform, fans hunt for inspiration for expressing their love.

“It’s like they’re coming to Pinterest to figure out how to turn that fandom into real world moments and experiences that they share with others that feel rich and fulfilling,” Pollack said. She cited a recent brand partnership that Pinterest struck with Warner Bros. to promote the theatrical release of “Practical Magic 2.”

“We saw that there’s a ton of Gen Z sourcing happening for really like specific things like herbal apothecaries, crystal meanings, tarot readings. This is all really adjacent to the film,” Pollack said. “So for Gen-Zers who maybe didn’t see the first [film], but clearly would be an immediate fan of the second, given what they’re already looking for — that was an opportunity for us to come together and actually build a real world pop-up experience where people could come and get tarot card readings. They could custom make candles. They could figure out how to create their own brew of tea. And that means that from every moment forward, it’s an actual connection to to the film and to Pinterest that goes beyond just an impression or a share or a like.”

Jenny Haggard, global head of thought leadership at Spotify, added her perspective that marketers too often use “Gen Z” as a broad brush. Spotify has made a point of understanding this cohort with an annual report that studies the consumption habits of the demo defined as ages 14-29 — which is a pretty broad range of life stages, Haggard observed.

“The first mistake we see marketers make is they treat Gen Z as one group,” she said. “I don’t know about you, but I was a very different person from when I was a teeny bopper dancing to NSYNC in my bedroom than when I was 29 and young professional working and living in New York. What we’ve learned is that life stage is a better predictor of behavior than birth year, and so I think we as marketers need to stop doing that.”

Haggard also made a strong stand that the conventional wisdom that teens and young adults don’t have the patience to watch long-form content.

“As an industry, it’s now common practice to make ads that are six seconds long,” she said. “I went into our dashboards and found that a third of older Gen Zs on Spotify are streaming 100% of two-hour-long podcast episodes. So what that tells me is that Gen Z isn’t allergic to long-form content; they’re allergic to shitty content. We all know this. James Cameron would be out of a job if people didn’t like long form content. To me, it’s about creating better content. That is our responsibility as marketers.”

Kim Granito, chief marketing officer for AMC Global Media, echoed Haggard comments that the new world order puts pressure on marketers to be as creative as fans.

“It’s our job as marketers to make sure that we are creating on ramps for them to find and experience [entertainment] exactly where they want to,” Granito said. “There are fans of ‘The Walking Dead’ has been around for 15 years. There are people that show up for every single spinoff series, but don’t necessarily post about it or do things, and there are other fans that dress up as Negan every year at Comic Con and bring their families and friends along. The passion and love that they have for that IP is the same. It’s expressed differently. So I think it’s our job as marketers to create as broad a pathway and is layered, choose-your-own-adventure journey for them to make it their own.”

(Pictured: Variety‘s Dea Lawrence, TikTok’s Dawn Yang, Lionsgate’s Briana McElroy, Spotify’s Jenny Haggard, AMC Global Media’s Kim Granito, Archrival’s Ben Harms and Pinterest’s Sara Pollack)

title: With Lucas Museum About to Open, Mellody Hobson Steps Down From LA28 Olympics Board
summary: Just days before the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens to the public, co-founder Mellody Hobson has stepped down from the board of directors of Los Angeles Olympics organizing committee LA28, Variety has confirmed. Hobson indicated that the demands of overseeing the Lucas Museum, which opens Tuesday after a Friday gala, were too great to […]
content:
Just days before the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens to the public, co-founder Mellody Hobson has stepped down from the board of directors of Los Angeles Olympics organizing committee LA28, Variety has confirmed.

Hobson indicated that the demands of overseeing the Lucas Museum, which opens Tuesday after a Friday gala, were too great to continue serving on the board, according to an email reviewed by LAist. Business executive Hobson is co-founder of the museum with her husband George Lucas.

The 35-person board is led by Casey Wasserman, who was forced to give up his stake of his management company after the Epstein files revealed his messages with Ghislaine Maxwell.

Popular on Variety

An activist group called the Fair Games Coalition has sought to meet with Hobson over their concerns about the Olympics and Paralympics, including housing and workers’ needs. The coalition is also concerned about the games’ effect on the South Los Angeles area that is home to the Lucas Museum.

“The Fair Games Coalition is deeply disappointed that Mellody Hobson responded to requests to meet with faith leaders, workers and community members calling for living wages, affordable housing, immigrant protections, and Games that benefit all Angelenos by announcing she was resigning from the LA28 Board,” the group said in a statement.

“Mellody Hobson could have used her influence on the LA28 Board to stand with our communities, support living wages, and defend immigrant workers. Instead, she chose the easy way out. That is deeply disappointing,” Rev. Gary Williams, Senior Pastor of St. Mark United Methodist Church, a member of the Fair Games Coalition, said in the group’s statement.

title: Paranormal Comedy ‘Don’t F — k With Ghosts’ Premieres On Demand, Launches Original YouTube Channel (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: “Don’t F***k With Ghosts,” a paranormal hybrid comedy from 5’7 Films, is now available to rent or buy in the U.S. on Amazon, Apple TV and Fandango at Home. The debut comes alongside the launch of Potluck Originals, an original YouTube channel from 5’7 Films in partnership with The Moment Lab. In the film, real-life […]
content:
“Don’t F***k With Ghosts,” a paranormal hybrid comedy from 5’7 Films, is now available to rent or buy in the U.S. on Amazon, Apple TV and Fandango at Home. The debut comes alongside the launch of Potluck Originals, an original YouTube channel from 5’7 Films in partnership with The Moment Lab.

In the film, real-life brothers-in-law Stu Stone and Adam Rodness play exaggerated versions of themselves who are convinced they’ve discovered the next paranormal sensation. The duo assembles a team consisting of a former Playboy star-turned-ghost-hunter, a professional wrestler and local psychics to bring home proof that ghosts are real.

“Are ghosts real? That’s exactly why we made this movie,” said Stone, who also co-wrote and directed the film. “And we’re still not telling. You’ll have to watch it yourself.”

Popular on Variety

The film also stars Tony Nappo and Josh Cruddas, with guest appearances from professional wrestler Colt Cabana, paranormal podcaster Bridget Marquardt and Michael Rapaport. Rodness serves as producer and co-wrote the film with Stone.

Following its Canadian debut, “Don’t F***k with Ghosts” is distributed in the U.S. by Filmhub and is a co-production between Stone and Rodness’ 5’7 Films and Winnipeg-based Fairpoint Films, in association with Toronto-based Farmhouse Productions. Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat executive produces alongside Kyle Bornais, Ira Levy, Ryan Kimel, Kent Sobey and Kevin Healey.

Potluck Originals, the YouTube channel from 5’7 Films in partnership with The Moment Lab, will feature a mix of unscripted and hybrid content. The channel debuts with 8-episode documentary series “The Great American Ghost Hunt,” where Bridget Marquardt takes celebrities on ghost hunts, including Howie Mandel, Jason Mewes, Symba, Marla Sokoloff, Alisan Porter, members of K-pop group FiveAlive and Cherie DeVille.

Stone’s credits include serving as an actor on projects like “Donnie Darko” and “Magic School Bus”; more recently, he directed genre comedies out of Toronto. Rodness’ credits include Netflix’s “Hemlock Grove” and “Shazam!,” as well as working as a music video producer with Drake, Eminem and Usher.

Together, Stone and Rodness have been behind feature films including 2020’s “Faking a Murderer.”

title: Orville Peck on His New Album ‘Mule,’ Battling Addiction and Making Out With a Pro Football Player
summary: Orville Peck has a ritual he does before every concert. He hugs and tells each member of his band, “I love you.” And that’s what the country music star did at Madison Square Garden on June 20, 2023, at the opening of his “Bronco” tour. But this night was different from all the others. Just […]
content:
Orville Peck has a ritual he does before every concert. He hugs and tells each member of his band, “I love you.”

And that’s what the country music star did at Madison Square Garden on June 20, 2023, at the opening of his “Bronco” tour.

But this night was different from all the others. Just hours before the show, his team found him overdosing in his hotel room.

“It was sort of a disturbing show because me and my band were completely aware before we even stepped on stage that I was canceling the tour and I was going to rehab the next morning,” Peck tells me. “I did a shot on stage of Patron. It was contractual because they sponsored the tour. I remember taking the shot and just looking at my band and everyone just looking at me and thinking, ‘How the hell have we ended up like this?’ It was a very dark night. It was very difficult.”

Popular on Variety

It’s now a little over three years later, and a sober Peck is spending Wednesday afternoon at the Hollywood Bowl rehearsing for his headlining debut at the legendary amphitheater on Friday.

“I’ve gotten really good at compartmentalizing events like this, so I tried not thinking about it until the last few days because I’d overwhelm myself,” says Peck. “I put way too much pressure on myself, and then I actually end up not enjoying shows like if I overthink it. I’ve just started allowing myself to get excited, and I’m kind of freaking out now.”

Friday also marks the release of his new album, “Mule,” a collection of 12 tracks (plus a prologue) that chronicles his drinking and using, his time in treatment (he actually has a song called “Rehab Blues”) and his now-sober life.

“I think a big struggle for me, why my addiction ramped up so badly, was truthfully just trying to navigate these compartmentalized worlds I’d created in terms of navigating public life and being someone who suddenly there were thousands of people who had opinions about everything I did and going home and living as a normal person with problems and issues and trauma,” Peck explains.

Orville Peck at Baby’s All Right on May 19, 2025 in New York City. Rolling Stone via Getty Images

“Mule” is his fourth studio album following “Stampede” (2024), “Bronco” (2022) and “Pony” (2019). Peck, who is never seen in public without a Western styled mask partially covering his face, is a trailblazer in the country music world for being an out gay artist since the start of his career. He’s become a queer icon who has collaborated with Kylie Minogue, Shania Twain and Noah Cyrus. He made his Broadway debut playing the MC in “Cabaret.” Who else but Peck could get Willie Nelson to duet on “Cowboys Are Frequently Fond of Each Other,” a song about same-sex love and lust in the boots and Levi’s crowd?

“’Mule’ spoke to me because a mule is part horse, part donkey and they’re sort of bred specifically for working and they’re known for being stubborn,” Peck says. “They also have a connotation with drug trafficking … I think that’s funny.”

Peck’s longtime partner and his family have all supported his truth-telling on “Mule.” “A lot of this album is, of course, about me, but I also intended it to be a thank-you to many people and an apology to some people and an explanation to other people,” he says.

In “Ring the Bell,” Peck sings, “I love the Lakers, the Mets and the Longhorns, made out with a guy on the Raiders.” That slice of kiss-and-tell is sure to get inquiring minds digging to identify who the pro athlete is.

“I’m going to preface this by saying that I did receive permission to sing that lyric from the subject in question and he was very thrilled,” Peck says. “I told him, ‘Look, I’m gonna keep it sort of ambiguous and mysterious, but I would like to include this in this song.’ He was very, very honored.”

He continues, “I would never have done it if it were somebody who was hiding or fearful of it coming out. This person would have probably allowed me to say their name if I wanted, but I didn’t think it was necessary. People can use their own common sense and discovery to try to figure out who it may be, but that’s all I’ll say.”

For the record, Carl Nassib became the first active NFL player to publicly come out as gay while playing for the Las Vegas Raiders in June 2021. Peck declines to confirm or deny Nassib was his makeout partner.

Peck first performed the entire album earlier this month during both shows of a two-night run at San Francisco’s Castro Theatre.

“Even in rehearsals, I could barely make it through some of the songs,” Peck says when I ask if he has trouble not crying while singing some of his new material. “These are very deep wounds. What better therapy is there than getting up and being able to express these songs? Then there are people listening and relating, and they’re sharing their pain. It’s a spiritual experience.”

Watch the video for Peck’s latest single “Already Gone” below.

title: FCC Approves 49.5% Foreign Ownership of Paramount-Warner Bros.
summary: The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday approved Paramount’s petition to allow 49.5% of its equity to be held by foreign entities once the Warner Bros. Discovery deal is complete. Paramount owns 28 TV stations, and thus must get the FCC’s approval for foreign ownership over 25%. Its acquisition of WBD is backed by three Gulf […]
content:
The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday approved Paramount’s petition to allow 49.5% of its equity to be held by foreign entities once the Warner Bros. Discovery deal is complete.

Paramount owns 28 TV stations, and thus must get the FCC‘s approval for foreign ownership over 25%. Its acquisition of WBD is backed by three Gulf state sovereign wealth funds.

In approving the petition, the FCC dispensed with concerns over national security and improper influence, noting that the foreign funds — from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi — will not own voting stock.

“We are persuaded by Paramount’s argument that the Foreign Investors therefore will not be able to wield any influence, let alone control, over decisions involving the Licensees,” the commission’s decision states.

Popular on Variety

A Paramount spokesperson said Thursday that the company appreciates the FCC’s review of the matter, and noted that the Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners will own 100% of the voting stock in the combined company.

“At a time when the media industry faces unprecedented competitive pressure from dominant big tech companies, a combined Paramount-WBD will have the scale and resources necessary to compete, invest, innovate, and deliver premium content to audiences worldwide,” the spokesperson said.

The merger is on hold pending the outcome of an antitrust suit filed in July by California and 11 other states. A trial is scheduled to begin next March.

Free Press, a media advocacy organization that has repeatedly raised alarms about the Trump administration, opposed Paramount’s request, arguing that foreign investors may well end up with a majority of the company’s equity.

“Control over for-profit, commercial domestic news media by any government is an extraordinary situation that would surely strike most Americans as unseemly, precisely because of the utility of the news media as a propaganda tool for those governments,” the organization wrote in its opposition.

A handful of Democratic senators also expressed concerns about the issue.

“The FCC has never approved a significant ownership stake of an American broadcaster by a

sovereign wealth fund — that is, an investment entity controlled by a foreign government,” wrote Sen. Maria Cantwell and others in May. “The plain text of the Communications Act prohibits ownership by ‘a foreign government or representative’ without regard to voting rights. And the FCC’s prior approval of foreign ownership of equity in broadcasters has been limited to entities based in allied NATO, Five Eyes, or friendly neighboring countries.”

Anna Gomez, the Democratic FCC commissioner, echoed those concerns in a comment on X on Thursday.

“The FCC just let some of the most repressive governments in the world indirectly control nearly all of a combined Paramount-Warner Bros,” she wrote. “An investment this large in one of America’s biggest media companies doesn’t just buy equity, it secures influence over what gets said and made.”

Though the foreign funds will own 49.5% of the equity when and if the merger goes through, Paramount sought permission for them to own up to 100%, given the potential need for future investment. The commission approved the request, provided that Paramount must obtain further approval if the entities are to own voting shares.

title: Curry Barker, Alex Gibney, Siân Heder, Rachel Morrison & Bassam Tariq On Taking Chances & Conquering Obstacles – Deadline & DGA’s Art Of Directing At TIFF
summary: Bold decisions during filming, biggest challenges and first Directors Guild of America cards were among some of the topics we that came up during Deadline and the DGA’s Art of Directing panel at the Toronto Film Festival that featured a conversation with Curry Barker, Siân Heder, Alex Gibney, Rachel Morrison and Bassam Tariq. Check out […]
content:
Bold decisions during filming, biggest challenges and first Directors Guild of America cards were among some of the topics we that came up during Deadline and the DGA‘s Art of Directing panel at the Toronto Film Festival that featured a conversation with Curry Barker, Siân Heder, Alex Gibney, Rachel Morrison and Bassam Tariq.

Check out the panel conversation here and scroll down for more photos from the event.

Barker was at TIFF for the one-year anniversary of Obsession, which world premiered a year ago, was picked up by Focus Features, and grossed more than $500,000 at the global box office. He revealed to us that one of the most stressful moments on his latest Focus Features/Blumhouse Atomic Monster production Anything But Ghosts, which co-stars Aaron Paul, was that “we had a 130-page script and we had 26 days to shoot it. I’m also starring in it and directing and I’m the lead character. I have more lines than anyone in the movie.”

“Zach Kregger just told me, ‘You have to cut 30 pages’ and I probably should have listened to him. So, did my manager; he told me that, too,” shared Barker during the conversation at the Bisha Hotel. “But I didn’t cut a single page because I wanted to shoot all of it. And the hardest day on Obsession was the easiest day on Anything But Ghosts.“

As is apparent in the social media barbs he’s taking from SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Gibney’s biggest problem while shooting his new documentary Musk was that “Nobody wanted to talk to me, either because they were terrified and the central subject didn’t want to talk to me. In fact, as I asked [Musk] for an interview, he responded with a tweet. And the tweet was ‘Gibney is a douche.’ To which I responded ‘Douché.'”

How did he get around some of these problems?

“We collected everything that he had ever said, either on audio or video, and we production designed an avatar for the main interview where we had two angles: one looking direct to camera, one off to the side. Then as we edited the film and got it down to length, we then animated the character that we had created and it became the avatar.”

RELATED: ‘Musk’ Review: World’s Richest Man, And His Digital Avatar, Thrashed In Damning Alex Gibney Doc – Venice Film Festival

Still, even if Gibney had landed Musk for an interview, the director observed, “He keeps repeating the same lines over and over and over again. So I’m not sure I would have gotten a revolutionary interview or something that would have been truth-seeking. But it certainly would have been interesting and I would have enjoyed it.”

Tariq was in Toronto with his Mahershala Ali-starring Orion action movie Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, about an American Muslim hitman who goes to war with a mentor godfather-type in his mosque in addition to a vicious far-right David Koresh type played by John Cho. The filmmaker shared that a production schedule of 30 days with five action set pieces was the ultimate uphill. That, in addition to adhering to filmmaking advice from his late editor-mentor Jonathan Oppenheim, which was, “In the first five minutes of the film, you tell the audience how to watch the movie.”

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother debuts in cinemas on September 25.

RELATED: ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Review: Mahershala Ali Is The Glue That Binds A Dour Texas-Set Action Drama – Toronto Film Festival

Morrison on her Prime Video romantic drama Love of Your Life starring Margaret Qualley, Aaron Pierre, Gabriel Basso and Patrick Schwarzenegger, said that “My line producer would say that the greatest challenge was shooting in three countries, four cities, different states, which doesn’t happen anymore at the studio level. There’s a real tendency to pick a tax incentive state, shoot some plates and everything against green screen. I really wanted to shoot things on the ground.” The pic which streams on Oct. 14 was shot in London, Portugal, New Orleans and Boston.

RELATED: ‘Love Of Your Life’ Review: Margaret Qualley On A Quest To Find Herself In Wandering Romantic Drama Of Grief And Renewal – Toronto Film Festival

For CODA Oscar winner Heder and her new Apple movie Being Heumann, about disability-rights activist Judy Heumann who led 100 disabled people to storm a federal building in 1977, it was “trying to create an accessible set, which was a crazy journey because it hadn’t been done before.”

The movie stars 12 disabled leads and 60 disabled background actors.

“We had to build our trailers from scratch. We had to build a hair and makeup trailer from scratch. We created like Ramp Villages, and from beginning to end, it was just there was no map for how to build an accessibility team and take care of people’s bodies while you’re making a movie.”

“It’s cool that now there’s these trailers,” said Heder about making strides for the community.

“There was one accessible trailer in all of North America; because [a production] never expects more than one wheelchair user to ever be working at the same time.”

Being Heumann has a one-week play in cinemas on November 6 before hitting Apple TV on November 13.

title: Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch’s Total Pay Declines To $31M In Fiscal 2026 From $33M In Prior Year
summary: Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch’s total compensation in fiscal 2026 fell to $31 million, from $33 million in the prior year. The pay figures for Murdoch and other execs were disclosed in an SEC filing on Thursday. Murdoch, who was reaffirmed last September as the heir to Rupert Murdoch’s media empire in a settlement reached […]
content:
Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch‘s total compensation in fiscal 2026 fell to $31 million, from $33 million in the prior year.

The pay figures for Murdoch and other execs were disclosed in an SEC filing on Thursday.

Murdoch, who was reaffirmed last September as the heir to Rupert Murdoch’s media empire in a settlement reached in a Nevada court case involving the mogul and his four eldest children, made a base salary of $3 million. The remainder of his compensation came from a bonus, stock and option awards, non-equity incentive plan compensation and other sources.

President and COO John Nallen was the next-highest paid exec last fiscal year, taking home $18.1 million, up from $15.3 million in fiscal 2025.

Watch on Deadline

Fox has been a well-oiled machine in recent quarters, with high-demand programming like sports and news helping offset declines in linear viewing. Shares in the company have slid 11% in 2026 to date, largely due to broader uncertainty about the media business.

After initially staying on the sidelines during the streaming wars, the company under Murdoch’s direction last August launched subscription streamer Fox One, a complement to fast-growing free outlet Tubi. The company has also made forays into podcasting and the creator space, and last June placed a big bet on the strategy of owning the pipes for streaming with a proposed $22 billion takeover of Roku. The merger is slated to close in the first half of 2027.

Along with the executive compensation figures and other disclosures, the SEC filing revealed November 4 as the date of the company’s annual shareholder meeting. The meeting will be held virtually at 10 am. ET.

title: Hollywood Sign Gets A ‘Fast & Furious’ Makeover
summary: Universal Studios Hollywood last night turned a onetime billboard into — what else? — a giant, illuminated billboard. The theme park used projection mapping to shower the ionic Hollywood Sign in colorful video imagery from the Fast & Furious films as well as its ambitious new roller coaster themed to the franchise, which opened yesterday. […]
content:
Universal Studios Hollywood last night turned a onetime billboard into — what else? — a giant, illuminated billboard.

The theme park used projection mapping to shower the ionic Hollywood Sign in colorful video imagery from the Fast & Furious films as well as its ambitious new roller coaster themed to the franchise, which opened yesterday.

Universal partnered with the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce to create the promotion for it’s like-named Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift ride, which officially opened earlier in the day.

Originally erected to read “Hollywoodland” as an advertisement to lure real estate investors in 1923, the now-named Hollywood Sign has become a major symbol of Los Angeles that has transcended its commercial roots.

The sign has been seen in everything from Seinfeld to Beavis and Butt-Head Do America to The Day After Tomorrow. It’s been featured in promotional photos for Paramount’s 1992 film Cool World, The Muppet Movie and band photos photos for Fleetwood Mac and Blondie.

See video below of last night’s event.

title: ‘Up Against It’ Review: Antonio Banderas & Eva Birthisle In Trudie Styler’s Witty Comedy About Divorced Couple Forced To Conceive Baby To Save Their Daughter – Toronto Film Festival
summary: With a concept that is like a twisted version of The Parent Trap, director Trudie Styler’s sly comedy with drama shows what happens when the messy unforeseen circumstances of life and death interrupt a nasty divorce. Up Against It, an apt title, had its world premiere today at the Toronto Film Festival. Antonio Banderas stars […]
content:
With a concept that is like a twisted version of The Parent Trap, director Trudie Styler‘s sly comedy with drama shows what happens when the messy unforeseen circumstances of life and death interrupt a nasty divorce. Up Against It, an apt title, had its world premiere today at the Toronto Film Festival.

Antonio Banderas stars as Alvaro, father to Rose (Eden Hamilton), a daughter he loves as much as he truly hates her mother, his about to be ex-wife Saffron (Eva Birthisle), who returns the hate and maybe magnifies it. With their divorce about to become final, the complication of complications arises when Rose’s childhood cancer appears to return in the form of leukemia. This poor girl, dealing with her failing body, now has to contend with the broken marriage of her parents on top of the new diagnosis.

Bitterly opposing each other but brought together with the realities of an urgent life-and-death situation presented by their trusted doctor (Forest Whitaker), the battling co-parents are thrust into a rather mind-boggling and radical decision: the only hope for Rose is for mom and dad to conceive another genetically matching child, to create an IVF savior sibling for her. This surprise on the eve of making their much desired breakup official brings out all the old resentments, personal wounds and recriminations, as well as a new and awkward (to say the least) need for intimacy they will have to find to unlock the love they once had as they come together to save their only child.

Watch on Deadline

In pure movie fashion we have to wonder, a la Parent Trap, if the kid can somehow bring these warring parents back together in maybe more ways than one. The complications also arise with the current partners of both Alvaro and Saffron: Arinzé Kene, playing a genuinely nice guy and a real antidote for Saffron after her turbulent marriage to Alvaro, is not quite understanding of how this could happen and how it will affect their relationship, and same problem exists for Alvaro’s new love played by Úrsula Corberó. Suddenly it is very crowded in that bed as what they all thought was ancient history and about to officially end for good is now hitting a huge roadblock.

As both parents need support from their new partners, the real issue is Rose, who faces the only medical solution that has a shot at saving her as well as an extended family that threatens to fall apart — again. The film parallels the trauma of a broken body with that of a broken home. Yes, she desperately needs to heal, but the toxic relationship of the grown-ups surrounding her might be just as awful.

The screenplay by Chloe King and Camille Griffin is an original twist on those family divorce comedies like the aforementioned Parent Trap and 1984’s Irreconcilable Differences, among others. The new wrinkle of a life-threatening illness forcing the battling parties to make a truce and warm up to each other against all odds is a clever one that is realistically played out here because both Banderas and Birthisle manage to keep the priorities front of mind for Alvaro and Saffron. There isn’t a lot of exposition or explanation as to how these two people got to the point of wanting to kill each other (figuratively, not literally), but the body language and attitudes expertly expressed by both stars tell us all we need to know. Their relationship is now a combustible and lethal one, so it takes something like childhood cancer in a young daughter conceived out of their onetime love for each other to bring them together.

Hamilton is irresistible as Rose, and Banderas and Birthistle are excellent here, as are Corberó and Kene as the confused new partners in their lives. Whitaker nicely plays the no-nonsense doctor whose priorities dictate the complex solution at hand. Richard E. Grant turns up as a friend, but the role is so brief you wonder why he would take it.

The handsome-looking film shows off London locations at their best, and Styler, with the help of a screenplay that doesn’t resort to clichés, has pulled off a smart and sophisticated story of dysfunctional adults who, in the worst of times, must learn the true definition of love and family and what really matters.

Producers are Styler, Celine Rattray and Piers Tempest.

Title: Up Against It

Festival: Toronto (Gala Presentations)

Director: Trudie Styler

Screenwriters: Chloe King and Camille Griffin

Cast: Antonio Banderas, Eva Birthisle, Eden Hamilton, Richard E. Grant, Forest Whitaker, Úrsula Corberó, Arinzé Kene

Sales agents: CAA (domestic); Beta Cinema (International)

Running time: 2 hr 2 mins

title: ‘The Traitors: New Blood’ EPs Break Down NBC Premiere, Sweetening the Pot for the Faithful and Why the Civilian Cast ‘Played Hard Straight Away’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for the two-hour series premiere of NBC’s “The Traitors: New Blood,” now streaming on Peacock. “The Traitors” castle isn’t just for the rich and famous anymore. Peacock’s Emmy-winning franchise has arrived on NBC, with “The Traitors: New Blood,” a new season composed entirely of civilian players in the game […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for the two-hour series premiere of NBC’s “The Traitors: New Blood,” now streaming on Peacock. “The Traitors” castle isn’t just for the rich and famous anymore. Peacock’s Emmy-winning franchise has arrived on NBC, with “The Traitors: New Blood,” a new season composed entirely of civilian players in the game of murder, mayhem and more money than ever before. In the show’s two-hour series premiere, host Alan Cumming welcomed 22 appropriately bloodthirsty competitors to his Scottish castle and immediately threw them into the deep end of the loch. Because of the show’s international popularity, the players walked into the castle knowing exactly where to go and what to investigate. Feeling right at home with the game is exactly what the creative team wanted. “To have a sense of familiarity meant they felt comfortable in their surroundings and they played hard straight away,” executive producer Sam Rees-Jones tells Variety of the premiere. At the first roundtable, with a sly tap on the shoulder, Cumming chose Tomica Adams (a pilot from Boston, MA) and Joe Vanella (a funeral director from Wantagh, New York) as his first Traitors of the season. But during their midnight confab in the turret, he informed them a third Traitor was incoming, and that they had to pick the person. In addition to their first murder (RIP faux college basketball coach and real lawyer Kim Daily), the Traitors chose two “accomplices” to audition to become their fellow chaos agent. Courtesy of Euan Cherry/NBC

Katie Fites (a marketing manager from Jacksonville, Florida, and the youngest player at 23) and Xavier Scruggs (former MLB player turned analyst) got to work scheming and stirring the pot against each other to claw their way to the turret. But the ultimate test came in the second hour when they were directed to deceive the Faithfuls in plain sight by stealing a cleverly titled book on crime and punishment and delivering it to the Traitors. The premiere leaves audiences hanging on whether they manage to smuggle the book out without the Faithful seeing it..

What is for sure is that the blood of the Faithfuls has already been spilled. In addition to Daily’s murder, a tense first roundtable saw Mississippi realtor Kriste Lewis go for the jugular on San Diego construction manager Madeline Kostopulos over a throwaway comment she believed proved she was one of the cloaked killers. Caught in the crossfire was Kostopulos’ ally and resident eye candy, New York business executive Victor Vollbrechthausen, who took heat for immediately snagging a shield of protection in the first challenge. The pair nearly split the vote evenly.

Popular on Variety

Below, “The Traitors: New Blood” executive producers Rosie Franks, Mike Cotton and Rees-Jones go deep on slimming down their hit for broadcast, why they incentivized identifying Traitors for the first time and how including an all-civilian cast makes the game so much more personal.

Being on broadcast means these episodes run for about 41-42 minutes, along with the commercial breaks. That’s very different from the Peacock episodes, which often exceed an hour. How does the time constraint change the storytelling and the rhythm of the show? Mike Cotton: I would say that was one of our biggest challenges. In truth, the game is the game. We call it a game, but there’s always a cycle. It’s a day in the castle. There’s always breakfast, someone gets murdered, there’s the mission, there’s a roundtable, and the Traitors meet in the turret. We haven’t changed that, in terms of how they played the game. But we had to look at different places where we could create cliffhangers, and so we put quite a lot of thought and work into that before we started shooting to make sure that the audiences still got what “The Traitors” was. We always say we’re like a murder mystery, but we treated it a bit like a drama. Where’s a good place for a cliffhanger? We actually put quite a lot of planning in our pre-production to work out those different points that could cliffhanger the episodes. One thing we didn’t want to do is cut it like it’s a drama. We didn’t want to make the episodes faster or fit everything into a short amount of time. We still wanted to breathe and be able to explore the characters, and I feel like we’ve achieved it. Courtesy of Euan Cherry/NBC

You’re at a disadvantage this season where you don’t have the backstory of celebrities to help you prep. In the premiere, we see one of the competitors holding a card that asks their preference to play as a Traitor or Faithful. Is that something you’ve always done, or is that new reconnaissance this season? Sam Rees-Jones: No, that was something new for the civilians. What we loved about this version was Alan inviting these players. He sent out these invitations, so it should feel like these players are actually being invited to this crazy experience in the Highlands of Scotland. And within that invitation was whether they wanted to be a Traitor or a Faithful. Rosie Franks: Alan always asks them in the “gold chats” by the fire in the premiere what role they want to play in the game. But this just felt like a really nice throughline from the opening of the raven flying across America, dropping the invitations, and this is like their RSVP. Rees-Jones: We pick Traitors only if they want to become a Traitor, because it’s a hard job. There’s a lot to do, so they should want to become a Traitor. But what we always say to everyone is that once you enter the game, you could be made a Traitor at any point. As you can see at the end of Episode 1, we picked our original two Traitors, and then we left it in their hands who they were going to pick as the third one and that was Katie and Xavier.

Cotton: You’re right, though. It’s more difficult working out who those initial Traitors should be when they’re a cast of regular people who we don’t have a history with on a reality show or on television. That then comes down to casting, and really digging into who these people are and the characters that they are. We don’t decide who the Traitors are until everyone’s arrived at the castle. So they’ve been on the train, and we’ve seen them interact. They’ve all sat down with Alan and had quite in-depth chats with him about whether they want to be a Traitor or not.

That uncertainty extends to the cast’s hunt for Traitors as well. The celebrities often have pre-existing relationships and feuds that can guide accusations. But in this premiere, the cast is largely at a loss on who to target at the first roundtable. Franks: What’s so exciting is that they all come in with a completely clean slate. It’s a game about identity, and they can basically be whoever they want. But we’re watching them get to know each other, and we’re getting to know them at the same time. So it’s a level playing field for the viewers and the players, which is really exciting to watch. You feel very much like you’re part of the process.

One of the biggest differences between the celebrity and civilian editions is the impact of the money. Watching celebrities play challenges for money doesn’t quite have the same thrill because, depending on their personal wealth and situation, $250,000 may be life changing or it may be a drop in the bucket. But for the “New Blood” cast, it is different. Mark Zgoda makes a comment after the first challenge, where they add $50,000 to the prize pot: “That’s a full person’s salary already added to the pot.” This money will simply mean more for these players. How does that change the game play? Rees-Jones: We love that moment, and I’m glad you mentioned it. That perfectly summarized all of their approaches to the game, to the challenges, to the missions, and yeah, the money means so much to them. As far as the game is concerned, what it means is that they all have to work together really hard to build that prize pot. But ultimately, that also means that betrayal cuts even deeper. Because the whole game is built around the Faithfuls and the Traitors coming together to put up that prize pot, which in one mission can be as much as the person’s yearly salary, then when treachery happens, it hurts even more. But to see the missions play out and to see them throw themselves into it, whatever their age or physical ability, was amazing. You see what it meant to them at the end of Episode 1 when they win a huge amount of money.

Alan also reveals in the premiere that, for the first time, each Traitor banished from the castle will earn a $15,000 bonus for the prize pot. Is that in addition to the possible $250,000 they can raise? Rees-Jones: It’s in addition to the $250,000. We’ve talked about it for a while. Obviously, the most important thing is to get a Traitor out. But we felt there was something really interesting in that added incentive.

That could make the difference between speaking up or staying quiet at the roundtable if you know there is more money on the line. Franks: Exactly!

In the premiere, as soon as they arrive in the castle, you let them roam free. But after several seasons of this show, this cast has been watching at home and they clearly know the place. A few even knew which book to pull to open the secret room in the library. Does that much familiarity with the castle pose any issues? Cotton: I love that they knew the castle! The castle is a real place. It’s not like it’s a “Big Brother” house that’s reconstructed every year. So I think we all love the fact they felt at home immediately in there, and that they knew the game and they knew the rhythm of it. Every year is a different murder mystery, so we put a lot of plans in place to keep the players on their toes. But we never change the core game of Traitors versus Faithfuls. It will never change the overall rhythm of the game, but we always, every season, put in new twists and turns just to keep them guessing even if they think they know it and the castle. Rees-Jones: I think it actually really helped this cast. To have a sense of familiarity meant they felt comfortable in their surroundings and they played hard straight away.

James and Oliver Phelps are here! Fred and George Weasley from the “Harry Potter” movies are seen being mischievous in the premiere. What can you tease about their role this season? Rees-Jones: That is their role! They’re mischievous, mysterious castle creepers.

What a job title to have. Rees-Jones: Yeah, it was just a fun tongue-in-cheek extension of the murder mystery world. You have Alan’s castle, and you would imagine in that world there would be people that are keepers of the castle. So there’s some fun to be had with little scenes that can be peppered throughout the season. Cotton: One of the things I’m most excited about with the NBC version is that we have a chance to expand this world to a broader audience. In the U.K., the show has become a massive shared viewing experience, like a family hit. People gather with their children to watch the show. Although it’s about betrayal and murder, there’s also elements of “Harry Potter” and magical fantasy within the show as well. So I feel like who [James and Oliver] are, and that world they’re from, sort of ties in neatly with the world of “The Traitors” too.

In the first challenge, there is a decoy crate filled with salmon. Was this an acknowledgement that there is apparently not enough salmon in Scotland for your previous casts, who protested the lack of smoked salmon at breakfast before? Franks: It’s always about the salmon!

It’s hard not to make that connection given how much your last celebrities talked about it!

Franks: Yes, we do like putting in little Easter eggs like that for the fans.

In previous seasons, the music in the show has been appropriately moody but generic. “New Blood” has covers of real songs, including Justin Timberlake’s “Cry Me a River” at a particularly sinister moment. Was this something new available to you on broadcast?

Franks: That was one of the things we were so excited about in terms of making the show feel familiar but also fresh, that we were going to be able to use some commercial music in this version. I don’t know how you felt watching it, but I feel like there’s tonally a shift in the way that it feels and I think the commercial music definitely helps with that.

You don’t often speak about why you chose the Traitors, but you did let them choose two accomplices to audition for the third Traitor slot. We don’t yet see who wins, but what did you think about their two choices, Katie and Xavier? Cotton: I love that the Traitors chose Katie and Xavier, because they chose almost completely opposite people.

The height difference alone! You can barely get them both in the same camera frame. Cotton: Right! They are so different that it was surprising and really thrilling for us when it happened.

title: Universal Still Plans Overseas Release for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Documentary Despite Mogul’s Legal Threats
summary: Contrary to a recent report, Universal is moving forward as planned with the international release of Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” sources familiar with the project told Variety. Though a release date has not yet been set for the overseas rollout, that’s not unusual for a film like “Musk,” a nearly 4-hour long documentary […]
content:
Contrary to a recent report, Universal is moving forward as planned with the international release of Alex Gibney‘s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” sources familiar with the project told Variety.

Though a release date has not yet been set for the overseas rollout, that’s not unusual for a film like “Musk,” a nearly 4-hour long documentary that’s being released theatrically in North American on Oct. 9 by the indie distrib Bleecker Street.

Despite recent legal threats from Musk over the documentary’s content, Universal has always been enthusiastic about releasing the film internationally, the sources added. “Musk” is set to stream on HBO in the first quarter of 2027.

Popular on Variety

After the documentary premiered at the Venice Film Festival, the tech mogul began posting comments on X, calling the doc “a hit piece,” though it was not clear whether he had seen the film.

Musk asserted that Gibney had “just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind).” Among the interviews featured in Gibney’s film is one with Ashley St. Clair, a MAGA influencer who had a child with Musk. The documentary portrays a text exchange between the two about the 2024 presidential election.

Musk’s attorney Alex Spiro threatened to file a defamation lawsuit before the film’s release in October, pointing to Musk’s texts with St. Clair.

Variety critic Owen Gleiberman wrote in his review of “Musk” in Venice, “Once you start piecing together Musk’s scandals and cut corners and slipshod management, you see that he’s a creator of mirages who promises more than he delivers … Musk, as the documentary makes clear, is a genuine if flawed technocratic visionary, a messianic opportunist, and something of a crackpot,”



Universal and Gibney had no comment.

title: Nick Kroll Delivers Heartfelt Appeal for Productions to Shoot in L.A.: ‘It Will Bring Life Back’ to the City
summary: Nick Kroll said upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent,” which he co-created and stars in, is a “love letter” to Los Angeles — and he expressed hope that a “thriving” entertainment production community will bring “vitality” to the city. The comedian, writer, producer, director and actor was a featured keynote speaker at the Variety […]
content:
Nick Kroll said upcoming Netflix comedy series “A Hundred Percent,” which he co-created and stars in, is a “love letter” to Los Angeles — and he expressed hope that a “thriving” entertainment production community will bring “vitality” to the city.

The comedian, writer, producer, director and actor was a featured keynote speaker at the Variety Entertainment & Technology Summit presented by EY, held Thursday in L.A.

Kroll explained why he “needed” to film “A Hundred Percent,” which is expected to debut on Netflix in 2027, in L.A. “It feels like it’s about people who live in Los Angeles. I’ve lived here for almost 20 years,” he said.

Popular on Variety

He co-created “A Hundred Percent” with his friend Gabe Liedman (creator of “Q-Force” and showrunner of the first season of “PEN15”), and stars in the show alongside Sam Richardson, Jason Mantzoukas and Vanessa Bayer, with Diane Lane joining the cast in a recurring role.

“We genuinely felt like it was a love letter to the city that we live in. And we really, honestly, have the best crew, had the best people, who were in such a happy mood making a show in Los Angeles,” said Kroll, who was interviewed on stage by Angelique Jackson, senior entertainment writer at Variety. “It was an awesome experience, and I’m so grateful to the city for helping make that happen. I hope it continues to grow because I think all of the doldrums that we’ve all been feeling for so many years will hopefully begin to work itself out.”

Kroll continued: “The more that we have a thriving, ongoing shooting community here in Los Angeles, it will bring life back. Not only money, but just like it will bring a vitalization, a vitality to the city that I think I have missed from when I moved here, and like the dream of coming to Hollywood and making things and being around people who are making things.”

When the audience responded with a round of applause, Kroll then quipped: “That said, I’m personally moving to Austin to start a podcast network.”

“A Hundred Percent,” Kroll said, is a “show about the world of thought leaders, self-help gurus, wellness influencers, and much of where they sort of live are on panels like this, in sad ballrooms” — he gestured to the Four Seasons room where he was speaking at the conference — “where you only get pitchers of water, tiny mints, and if you really search, a San Pellegrino, but that’s not what matters.”

Kroll said his goal with any project is “just trying to first and foremost work with the most talented people I can find.” In the case of “A Hundred Percent,” he said Liedman, the cast and the writers “are the funniest people… It’s just an incredibly talented group.”

“Just surround yourself with quality people, because assholes — they’re just the worst, you know. So that’s what I would say,” Kroll said. He added, “That’s a pretty profound statement, if Variety wants to lead with that.”

In addition to his work on “A Hundred Percent,” Kroll is an executive producer of the FX sitcom “Adults,” which follows five 20-something friends living together in Queens, New York (in one of the group’s childhood homes). He has also served as EP and voice actor for several Netflix animated series, including “Mating Season,” “Human Resources” and the Emmy-nominated “Big Mouth.”

Kroll and “Adults” creators Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw started developing the show several years ago, “and then we cast the next generation of incredibly funny comedic performers, and they fucking killed it.”

“Adults” comes under Kroll’s long-running first-look deal with FX, a relationship with the network that began more than 15 years ago. He said he loves making fun of FX’s “fearless” tagline but said it’s true that “they are genuinely incredibly innovative in how they launch stuff and how they’re willing to take shots. And in the case of ‘Adults,’ Season 1 found an audience, but it wasn’t as big an audience as everyone wants. And so we shot this prequel episode to give a new way into the show.”

Through that episode, Kroll explained, “audiences found it, really responded to it, and then were able to understand the show and the characters in a way that they entered into the rest of the season and stuck around.” In Season 2, bucking typical TV trends, the show’s ratings grew by 40% domestically and 100% internationally. “It’s a testament to FX and John Landgraf at the head of it to trust us to build something to keep with something that they know is quality and that’s what it comes down to.”

About creating engaging TV shows, Kroll said, “I really think it’s such incredible competition for people’s attention that you really have to figure out a way to grab them, but also hold them gently, so that they don’t run away. And that’s the hard thing to figure out. That’s the game we’re all in right now.”

At the beginning of his talk, Kroll riffed on the previous panel about AI in the entertainment industry — in which there was a sentiment expressed that humans will always find a way to keep the tech in check — Kroll commented, “Don’t underestimate the ability of machines to find a way to destroy us as well,” adding, “I say that generally without much alarm.”

title: Battling Misconceptions and Figuring Out Use Cases: Entertainment Leaders Navigate AI’s Place in the Industry
summary: In a world where AI is capturing every conversation, a series of experts is trying to figure out what it actually means for the world of entertainment. “I think the word ‘AI’ is doing too much right now,” says Mira Line, Google’s vice president of technology and society. ”One of the things that we’re doing, […]
content:
In a world where AI is capturing every conversation, a series of experts is trying to figure out what it actually means for the world of entertainment.

“I think the word ‘AI’ is doing too much right now,” says Mira Line, Google’s vice president of technology and society. ”One of the things that we’re doing, especially with the industry, is figuring out, well, what does AI mean in the industry? How do you break it down?”

Lane made her comments alongside several entertainment and tech personalities during the “Entertainment and Media in the Age of AI” panel, one of several AI-focused conversations happening at Variety’s Entertainment and Tech Summit presented by EY. Moderated by Variety business editor Todd Spangler, the conversation saw executives from Netflix (Girish Balakrishnan, the streamer’s senior director, creative innovation), Lionsgate (Kathleen Grace, its chief AI officer), Hasbro (Bertie Thomson, head of its AI-focused studio Sixth Wall), Teads (Annaka Vasquez, senior vice president of sales) and Adobe (Meagan Keane, Pro Video’s head of business strategy) come together to walk through AI’s place in entertainment and the use cases for versions of the technology — once people figure out how to talk about it.

Popular on Variety

That comes down to building relationships with creators about how it can be used, including where it fits within the production landscape. Balakrishnan highlighted Netflix’s public framework for how the company uses AI within its production pipeline (on a generative level, for roughly 300 programs), a model he said “builds trust with the creative community” and gives those members ”a pathway to navigate to drive use cases that are meaningful to the creative process.”

The industry is already landing on other frameworks surrounding AI’s place in the industry, such as the Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute-led “Human Generative Workflows” paper published last month. Lane helped develop the paper, which she said breaks down the use cses in ways that can help AI-backed productions reach a still-elusive goal: being copyrightable.

“We did a whole exercise around tooling and looking at everything from de-noising techniques to fully synthetic characters,” she said. “Let’s start thinking about the vocabulary and breaking it down so it’s not just AI as one big monolithic.”

Adobe has tried to help distinguish that in its own tools, Keane said, delineating between “assistive,” “corrective“ and “generative” functions. That allows users who’ve found those use cases to prosper, she said. “People don’t even really realize that they’re AI anymore because so much of the conversation has shifted to generative,” she said.

Some of that trust built between companies and those working in the AI space has offered up another elusive item in the field: intellectual property, including renowned brands and high-profile characters.

“[Companies] are very careful about how we use those creative assets to maintain the integrity of the brand,” Vasquez said about Teads’ work with ad sales. “We have AI models to build the creative, but for those world’s largest brands, there’s a lot of scrutiny around that. So what I’m looking forward to, and the brands that we partner [with] look forward to, is what are the guardrails in place?”

Hasbro, through its Sixth Wall work, has worked to implement proprietary guardrails for the ElevenLabs-backed AI replicas of characters it licenses, such as those of Cobra Commander and Optimus Prime. While companies can license those characters for interactive experiences — one hypothetical Thomson offered was a Waymo with the voice of Prime — those can’t be manipulated in the way many unauthorized clips of Hasbro characters have been.

“If you think about the existence of lots of unauthorized characters out there… they’re not necessarily safe for our brand,” Thomson said. “Whereas working on the authorized AI version of the character means that, for these actors, it has a protective value for them too, and also for us as IP owners.”

Still, each company is still working through public misconceptions surrounding AI, whether the idea models are preparing for humanity’s imminent destruction or the notion that full-fledged blockbusters can be create with a quick prompting of ChatGPT.

“They don’t understand that, when you’re making really premium movies, TV shows, really engaging stories the way that Lionsgate and others on the stage do, the technology you have to use there is more complex than just prompting. It’s a whole process,” Lane said. “There’s a lot of consideration that goes into everything we make, and in my role, I’m here [saying] here are the tools you could use to make your thing better, bigger, more, and get to the end of the production faster. You choose what’s best for the story, and then, great, you chose the thing that’s best for your story, and it’s better. It’s not necessarily what people think of in pop culture. It’s not like ChatGPT. We just can’t throw something onto that.”

In the end, each leader said they wanted the technology to help creatives tell better — and more — stories, not feel like they have to adopt the technology for the sake of staying ahead.

“Filmmakers aren’t asking, ‘Do I want to use AI or not?’ They’re looking to solve meaningful creative problems that they’re faced with on their shows,” Balakrishnan said, citing several Netflix programs that made use of generative AI. “I think those are the opportunities that creators are looking for, and that’s where AI comes specific as an option to be able to solve real creators.”

It can also, in Grace’s view, help studios find and distribute new stories from creators who’ve utilized AI tools to help bring their visions to life. She cited the worlds of “John Wick” and “The Hunger Games” as examples of work the company has done to sell well-liked IP, and that it wants to have “all kinds of filmmakers we work with.”

“Just look at the range of our slate from this year: ‘Housemaid,’ ‘Michael,’ ‘Sunrise [on the Reaping]’,” she said. “Those are all very different filmmakers and different stories. To me, it’s just more creative people, and in some ways, easier to find them because the tools are democratized. Is it going to be an exciting challenge to bring in more talented people who have access to tools? Yes, but I’m interested to see what happens.”

title: ‘Resident Evil’ Video Game References: All the Zombies, Weapons and Easter Eggs in Zach Cregger’s Reboot
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters. “Resident Evil” is one of the longest-running horror video game series, and for a time it was the highest-grossing film series based on a game (until Universal’s “Super Mario” movies dethroned them). The games started out as scary, third-person shooters that […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters.

“Resident Evil” is one of the longest-running horror video game series, and for a time it was the highest-grossing film series based on a game (until Universal’s “Super Mario” movies dethroned them). The games started out as scary, third-person shooters that packed in scares even while the graphics were low on pixels.

The original Capcom game released in 1996 and introduced gamers to heroes Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine who must escape a spooky mansion filled with zombies. They later uncover the Umbrella Corporation, a pharmaceutical company that let loose a zombie virus while experimenting with bio-weapons. The 1998 sequel ramped things up and brought in Chris’ sister Claire Redfield and Leon S. Kennedy, who had to escape the zombie-infested Raccoon City. Later sequels, remakes and reboots spread the zombie virus into hillbilly homes, vampire villages and further around the world as the Umbrella Corporation’s disease took hold.

The games have been massive hits for gamers and horror fans alike, and they were adapted into six live-action movies helmed by Paul W.S. Anderson and starring Milla Jovovich. After a failed reboot with 2021’s “Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City,” the film franchise is getting revamped again by “Barbarian” and “Weapons” director Zach Cregger, who’s made a fully original story separate from the games. The movie takes place in Raccoon City and features the Umbrealla Corporation, but star Austin Abrams’ character Bryan is simply a medical courier who’s in way over his head during a not-so-routine delivery.

Check out all of the video game references from Cregger’s movie below.

title: Barbra Streisand Decries Trump’s “Unchecked Ego” Amid His Assertion That The Kennedy Center May Be Torn Down
summary: “You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego,” wrote Kennedy Center honoree Barbra Streisand. She was referring to President Donald Trump’s attempts to close down or, in his words, issue a warning that the center would be […]
content:
“You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego,” wrote Kennedy Center honoree Barbra Streisand. She was referring to President Donald Trump‘s attempts to close down or, in his words, issue a warning that the center would be “ripped down” unless a renovation plan is carried out and his administration gets recognition for it.

Trump has long complained that the center is old and needs to be renovated. Congress included more than $250 million in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year for just that. But since Trump’s takeover of the center weeks into his second term, the institution has seen a drop in ticket sales and, after the president’s name was added to the complex in December, another wave of artist cancellations.

What followed was a saga in which Trump’s name was added on the front of the building and then, when order by a judge, it was removed. But a tarp was then placed over the entire edifice as if to hide it.

Watch on Deadline

Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this week that the renovation will not take place unless courts lift a judge’s order that has prohibited his name from being enshrined on the facade of the complex. Then came the president’s threat on Wednesday that the center may be ripped down unless a renovation plan is carried out and his administration gets recognition for it.

A federal judge today said that the Kennedy Center must give the court 30 days notice before proceeding on any demolition of the complex.

Sharing a photo of herself and the late president, streisand noted that the center was renamed in the wake of Kennedy’s death as a memorial, and for good reason.

“The Kennedy family and other American leaders wanted a meaningful way to preserve his legacy. Re-naming the Cultural Center in JFK’s honor was a fitting choice, because he was a true champion of the arts.”

In fact, being honored by the center meant something greater that other awards.

“In 2008, I was deeply honored to be included in the 31st annual class of Kennedy Center Honorees. For me, and for so many artists, that honor represented something larger than a career recognition. It represented a belief in the importance of art to the life of a democracy.”

She continued, “That is why what is happening to the Kennedy Center is so galling and painful to witness.”

Another reaction came from Kennedy’s niece, Maria Shriver, who wrote on Tuesday, “That a sitting president would not let any renovations to a public building go on unless he gets to first put his name in the said building… What a sad state of affairs. What a tragedy. Actually, how small minded, how narcissistic. Actually great men, devoted to public service and the public good do not act like this.”

title: UTA Partner Josh Katz Exits Agency After 30-Year Run
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Josh Katz, a longtime UTA Partner and Motion Picture Talent Agent, has left the company after a 30-year run. Sources close to the agency indicated that Katz left of his own accord. The veteran rep himself declined to comment when contacted by Deadline. No next destination was given. It’s expected that Katz will remain […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Josh Katz, a longtime UTA Partner and Motion Picture Talent Agent, has left the company after a 30-year run.

Sources close to the agency indicated that Katz left of his own accord. The veteran rep himself declined to comment when contacted by Deadline. No next destination was given.

It’s expected that Katz will remain in the industry — possibly as a manager — though whether or not he’ll bring clients with him to his next venture is not yet clear. During his time at UTA, he worked with talents such as Rhea Seehorn — the Better Call Saul star fresh off her first Emmy win for Pluribus — along with Rob Delaney, Josh Duhamel, SNL alums Bill Hader and Bobby Moynihan, Nicholas Braun, Nick Offerman, Jessica Biel, Emerald Fennell, Michael Showalter, and many more.

Katz has been a partner at UTA since 2013. A homegrown talent who grew up loving movies, he joined the agency through the mailroom in 1996 — set on a path toward becoming an agent when he read an essay from its co-founder Jeremy Zimmer, who served as CEO for nearly 13 years, ending in June 2025.

Watch on Deadline

A native New Yorker, Katz came to UTA after graduating from SUNY Albany.

content:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains details on Big Brother Season 28, Episode 35, which aired on Thursday, September 17.

Big Brother Season 28 is down to its final weeks, and the latest episode featured a double eviction, the last Block Buster challenge, and two more housemates joining jury.

In Week 10 of the competition, Yash Patel was crowned as the Head of Household (HOH) and would not only have immunity for the week, but also put three people up for eviction.

At the nominations ceremony, Yash put up Barrett Pfeiffer, Drew Campbell, and Melody Morris for eviction.

The nominated houseguests still had the opportunity to save themselves from the block by winning the Power of Veto (POV) competition. In an endurance competition, Yash and Drew were the final two, and after striking a deal, Drew won the Veto.

Watch on Deadline

title: ‘Vintage Violence’ Review: Eugene Kotlyarenko’s Blood-Splattered Rom-Com Is A Fun Crime-Fueled Trip Through Japan’s Denim Trade — Toronto Film Festival
summary: Six years after his unhinged social media age horror Spree, writer/director Eugene Kotlyarenko takes a more optimistic approach with his action-packed rom-com out of Japan. In Vintage Violence, Carter (Cole Sprouse) is an urban explorer who finds a haul of rare denim in a mineshaft. When Izumi (Kiko Mizuhara) invites him to offload the merchandise […]
content:
Six years after his unhinged social media age horror Spree, writer/director Eugene Kotlyarenko takes a more optimistic approach with his action-packed rom-com out of Japan.

In Vintage Violence, Carter (Cole Sprouse) is an urban explorer who finds a haul of rare denim in a mineshaft. When Izumi (Kiko Mizuhara) invites him to offload the merchandise in Tokyo, the pair ends up in the crosshairs of the yakuza in a twisty, high-octane trip through the country’s thriving denim market.

Much how he used the found footage of a livestream in Spree to contribute to the social media atmosphere, Kotlyarenko similarly introduces this world with Carter’s urbex stream in Colorado, which Izumi watches on the other side of the world in Toyko. It’s an interesting use of modern tech to drive the narrative, painting a quick but thorough portrait of these two strangers before they even meet.

Kotlyarenko also cleverly uses the connectivity of an abandoned AirPod to provide an adrenaline-fueling soundtrack for an intense chase scene, which makes utilizes the skipping music to build the chaotic tension.

Watch on Deadline

Being as Vintage Violence explores the potential of human connection via the internet, sharing locations becomes the ultimate sign of trust and intimacy in this perpetually online rom-com.

Sprouse and Mizuhara manage to establish a believable chemistry as they flirtatiously get to know each other in the virtual opening montage, bringing a playful infatuated quality to their dynamic before they’re even in the same room.

While act one gets us invested in their budding romance, all hell breaks loose in act two with an entertaining ensemble of bad guys on their trail.

Nijirô Murakami slips effortlessly into the role of Izumi’s shady boyfriend Hiro, who masterminds a shady plot involving Carter’s denim after he racks up debt with the yakuza. Hio Miyazawa channels his inner eccentric Bond villain as Edoga, a dangerous denim-obsessed yakuza boss. But it’s Pierre Taki as the disgraced gangster Ko who gives a devilishly fun performance, seeking vengeance years after his finger was taken as punishment.

Using Tokyo as the film’s setting provides gritty, vibrant playground for Kotlyarenko to explore a twisty yakuza plot and shed light on Japan’s growing sex tourism industry, which has come to attracts unsavory visitors from the US. Meanwhile, the film uses the symbolism of denim to represent the old glory of America as a beacon of the West.

Don’t let the title fool you. If Spree was Kotlyarenko’s cynical comedic take on horror in the social media age, Vintage Violence is an optimistic rom-com with an exciting action twist, that’s still not afraid of a little gross-out factor—not just in the form of the quintessential Japanese blood spray, but also a graphically detailed makeout scene that will have audiences losing it.

Vintage Violence is an addictive fusion of genre set through Kotlyarenko’s hyper-stylized cinematic aesthetic, which is grounded seamlessly by charming performances from Sprouse and Mizuhara.

Title: Vintage Violence

Festival: TIFF

Section: Midnight Madness

Director-screenwriter: Eugene Kotlyarenko

Cast: Cole Sprouse, Kiko Mizuhara, Nijiro Murakami, Pierre Taki, Hio Miyazawa

US sales agent: WME

Running time: 1 hr 45 mins

title: ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators Wanted Green Lantern For Their DC Crossover Episode But Had To Settle For The Flash
summary: SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from Thursday night’s episode of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails to Save the Universe. As the title of this week’s episode (“Spoiler: We Couldn’t Get Green Lantern”) suggests, the creators of Stuart Fails to Save the Universe really did want the Green Lantern to be at the center of the […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from Thursday night’s episode of HBO Max‘s Stuart Fails to Save the Universe.

As the title of this week’s episode (“Spoiler: We Couldn’t Get Green Lantern”) suggests, the creators of Stuart Fails to Save the Universe really did want the Green Lantern to be at the center of the show’s DC comic crossover.

Unfortunately, the man without fear was already booked.

“They told us we couldn’t have him because of [HBO’s live-action series] Lanterns, which I understood,” Zak Penn, one of the series’ creators, revealed to Deadline. “Chuck [Lorre] was a little grumbly about it, but Bill and I pointed out to him that Flash was actually perfect. If we needed something that’s going from dimension to dimension, Flash worked even better than Green Lantern.”

Like Penn says, the episode ultimately sees Stuart (Kevin Sussman) and his friends stuck inside a comic book, where Mr. Freeze is terrorizing Gotham City. To get out of that dimension, they go off in search of Golden Age Flash for help.

Watch on Deadline

“It was half opportunity and half what they encouraged us, but Golden Age Flash appealed to us a lot, just because he’s kind of silly. No offense to Golden Age Flash,” Penn said.

If it seems kind of backward that the gang would trek all the way to Central City to enlist The Flash to help them take on a villain in Batman’s territory, that’s the point. The writers reveled in the opportunity to poke fun at the more far-fetched notions accepted in comic lore.

“Bill [Prady] and I were laughing a lot [about] the whole notion of Gotham City isn’t where New York City is, which makes no sense,” Penn said. “All those things were just kind of built up humor and things that we felt about comic books. So, the next obvious decision was, in terms of a villain, let’s put the villain who seems right and that people know more, and then have our characters comment on the fact that he’s the wrong villain for this piece.”

Penn is surely considered the superhero expert of the group as a Marvel vet who also famously wrote a script for a Suicide Squad film that went unused. However, he says his fellow creators Prady and Lorre, as well as several of the other writers, had their own affinity for DC comics to draw upon for the episode.

He and the writers thought a commentary on how a layperson would navigate a comic locale like Gotham City “seemed like the perfect sense of humor for our show.”

“If you were in the DC universe, it would be pretty boring a lot of the time because you’d just be sitting around waiting for planes,” he laughs, adding that the irony is there’s also a bit about that exact notion in an early episode of Lanterns.

That other DC show didn’t steal all Stuart‘s thunder, though, and in fact there is plenty that the comedy series can get away with that its drama counterparts cannot in that the writers can lean into the quirks of these convoluted superhero universes rather than shy away.

“One of the things about this show that’s really fun is that you know when you work on an actual comic book movie, you really have to be rigorous about the consistency of the reality, because people will pick you apart if you’re not, and on this show we kind of took the attitude of ‘we’re going to purposely break things and then have the characters notice that the multiverse doesn’t work as well as it should,'” Penn explained.

Similarly, Penn says the episode could adopt a visual style more consistent with comic books without asking the audience to do more work suspending their disbelief.

“[Director] Robbie McNeill deserves a lot of credit, because he really added a bunch of stuff, like the way the frames panel at certain points, which is something that I don’t always think is effective. Back in the early days of comic book movies, when people did that, I think it really took you out of it,” Penn told Deadline. “But this show’s sense of humor needs that, so it was really helpful.”
