title: Naomi Watts Says She’d Like To Work With Paul Thomas Anderson & Praises The Advancements Older Women Have Made In Hollywood — San Sebastián
summary: “I started, by Hollywood standards, quite late,” Naomi Watts began this morning when quizzed on whether the treatment of older women in Hollywood has improved during a press conference at the San Sebastián Film Festival. The British-Aussie actor is at the Spanish festival to receive an honorary Donostia Award for career achievement. “I launched with […]
content:
“I started, by Hollywood standards, quite late,” Naomi Watts began this morning when quizzed on whether the treatment of older women in Hollywood has improved during a press conference at the San Sebastián Film Festival. The British-Aussie actor is at the Spanish festival to receive an honorary Donostia Award for career achievement.

“I launched with Mulholland Drive, and I was 30 or 31,” Watts continued. “And I was told that I better get my skates on because it all finishes at the age of 40, but here we are today. I’m in my late 50s now.”

Watts continued to praise the improvements in the Hollywood industry that have prolonged women’s careers.

“Look at the Emmys just last week, there were a number of women in strong categories over 50, so that’s heartening to see,” she said. “I do think things have changed. Women are consumers of film and TV. Their stories should be reflected. Everybody needs to see their story reflected in storytelling, so that narrative had to be shifted, and I’m grateful to be a small part of that shift.”

Watch on Deadline

Here in San Sebastian, Watts is also joined by her Housewife cast and director, Ben Shirinian. The film will screen this evening at the festival following Watts’ Donostia Award presentation.

Set in 1964, The Housewife follows Hermine (Watts) and her hardworking husband Russel (Luke Evans), who enjoy a seemingly normal life in New York City — until the fateful day Hermine meets The New York Times journalist Joseph Lelyveld (Tye Sheridan). Following a tip from a Holocaust survivor, Joseph is investigating the possibility that Russel might be a Nazi in hiding. As his inquiry deepens — and his exchanges with Hermine become increasingly intimate — Joseph discovers a series of revelations far stranger and more complicated than he could have imagined.

Watts described the role as a challenging “mind twister.”

“The storyline was compelling. It is based on true events, and so it really drew me in,” she said.

Elsewhere during the press conference, Watts was asked whether she had any professional goals or directors that she’d still like to work with. She responded: “Paul Thomas Anderson is someone I’ve wanted to work with for a long time.”

Anderson debuts his next feature, a concert filmed at Carnegie Hall with Geese frontman Cameron Winter, next month at the New York Film Festival. A24 will release that film in cinemas.

San Sebastián runs until September 26.

title: White House Blocks MS NOW Journalists From Entry and Confiscates Their Badges After Donald Trump Bans Network, Along With CNN and Politico
summary: President Donald Trump doesn’t like the coverage of him by MS NOW, CNN and Politico — and as of Saturday, the White House started enforcing the president’s ban on those news organizations from accessing the facility. MS NOW said some of its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning. The […]
content:
President Donald Trump doesn’t like the coverage of him by MS NOW, CNN and Politico — and as of Saturday, the White House started enforcing the president’s ban on those news organizations from accessing the facility.

MS NOW said some of its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning. The network, formerly known as MSNBC, said it will “take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

In a report on the network, MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Garnder described what happened when she arrived to try to get in to the White House.

Popular on Variety

“I showed my badge, and then when I was inside where we have magnetometers, I attempted to scan my badge, which we have to do to get into the White House grounds. It did not work,” Gardner said. “There was a red beeping light, and so the officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled. I asked why I could not get inside; he said it was above him.”

An MS NOW photographer also was denied entry and had their badge taken, according to Gardner. However, she said, an MS NOW producer was able to get through and into the White House.

Trump Friday said on social media that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico “effective immediately” from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.”

Staffers from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were able to remain on the White House grounds on Friday.

The three news outlets have all said or suggested they will fight Trump’s ban, and the situation could lead to legal action as they seek to overturn the president’s block on their White House access. CNN said Friday the action represented “an illegal assault” on its constitutionally protected First Amendment rights to conducting reporting “without hindrance or interference from the government.” A Politico rep said, “We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.”

Trump told reporters in an Oval Office briefing Friday afternoon that there was no single story that triggered him to ban the news outlets, but was rather a cumulative effect of their “purposely negative” coverage. He also suggested that the New York Times and the Washington Post would be next in line to be barred from the White House.

Here’s the full statement MS NOW released Saturday: “Earlier this morning, MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars. MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy. We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters, and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the President, the administration, and the issues that impact the American people.”

title: Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players
summary: No Spanish industry initiative is likely to drive more conversation at this year’s San Sebastián Festival than the latest moves by the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT). Over the past 12 months, state-backed venture capital fund SETT, the investment driver of the Spain Audiovisual Hub, has plowed €215.6 million ($252.3 million) into Spain’s film, […]
content:
No Spanish industry initiative is likely to drive more conversation at this year’s San Sebastián Festival than the latest moves by the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT).

Over the past 12 months, state-backed venture capital fund SETT, the investment driver of the Spain Audiovisual Hub, has plowed €215.6 million ($252.3 million) into Spain’s film, TV, video game and new technology sectors, sparking matching private-sector investment of a further €230 million ($269.1 million), says María González Veracruz, Spain’s secretary of state for digitalization and artificial intelligence.

That’s around four times the average budget of Spain’s core subsidy fund at the country‘s ICAA Film Board.

Popular on Variety

In other ways, SETT, which is part of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation, also harbors a revolution. Since the 1940s, Spanish governments have offered subsidy grants and loans for individual films, and from around 2015, tax breaks on shoots in Spain.

In contrast, SETT invests up to 10 years in companies with a portfolio of productions, requiring co-investment from private-sector partners, and looking to give them an edge in the international market. It also backs private-sector investment vehicles.

“We are moving from an era of encouraging an ecosystem to consolidating a truly international audiovisual industry,” says González Veracruz.

Eleven of 15 SETT investments have been made public to date, with beneficiaries including animation sector leaders (Anima Kitchent, Amuse Animation, Planeta Junior), new Spain-based production companies (Good Films Studios Spain, Ítaca Films Madrid, Moonlighting Studios Spain), post-production facilities (Lazona Audiovisual Hub, the Refinery) and a full chain-of-value production-distribution player (Impulse Studio).

Also underscoring the range of SETT’s portfolio, risk capital fund partners include Aurora Media Inversiones, led by the Secuoya Content Group, Culture CAP7, which targets small- to medium-sized enterprises, and elevated genre specialist Moby Dick Film Capital.

Serving as a “public catalyst for growth, employment, innovation and talent, which are all core elements of the audiovisual sector,” SETT brings to the table the weight and power of the Spanish government and European Union backing, says SETT director general Javier Ponce.

With the Spain Audiovisual Hub a key element of Spain’s post-COVID Recovery Plan, SETT’s funding is financed through the European Union’s Next Generation funds, Ponce notes.

Its model has been built on three pillars, adds SETT audiovisual director María Coronado: “First, it adopts an industrywide approach, rather than a project-based one, addressing the entire audiovisual business ecosystem. Second, its investment facilities are directed at the equity capital of companies or regulated investment vehicles. Third, it promotes public-private partnership instruments in the medium to long term.”

Companies must represent a “worthwhile business opportunity,” she adds.

As global markets have contracted to some 75% of peak TV, according to Ampere Analysis, however, where are these opportunities? The key to SETT is its specific operations. SETT has taken a 46% stake for €19.8 million ($22.6 million), for instance, in Good Films Studios Spain, set up at Spain’s Ciudad de la Luz, one of Spain’s biggest studio complexes. It aims to make competitive English-language movies, budgeted at €15 million-€25 million ($17.5 million-$29.3 million) “with stars of international theatrical market value,” says GFSS head Miriam Segal, producer of “Good,” with Viggo Mortensen and “The Infiltrator,” starring Bryan Cranston.

Attracting such stars, however, is ever more difficult, she adds. “So it makes making independent films at this level very, very hard. So to have a government body like SETT and hopefully new producer-driven tax incentives, it’s like I died and went to heaven,” says Segal. “In a world that’s receding, to have a country with the vision to support filmmakers, independence, training and creation of an industry is very exciting.”

Established in Madrid by Roberto Butragueño and Andrés Sánchez Pajares and co-owned by SETT, Impulse Studio offers everything, from upstream development to financing, production, post-production, international sales and distribution.

“When we talk with potential partners on projects or potential investors, we have the stamp of security of government backing,” says Sánchez Pajares. With SETT’s support, we can bring “hard equity” to the table, retaining part of the IP, “and offer all services at any phase of a project,” says Sánchez, Impulse Studio CEO. “I think that will allow us to sit at tables where we were not able to talk to date.”

Further growth opportunities turn on scaling up animation projects aimed at the preschool audience. In another move, investing €9.2 million ($10.7 million) and partnering with Planeta Junior and Amuse Animation, SETT co-bought select distribution rights to hit preschool toon series “Milo,” sold to 186 territories, across multiple formats.

“‘Milo’ represents a strategic opportunity in the field of technology development, particularly in software, video games and mobile applications,” says Coronado.

“Spain has already established itself as one of Europe’s most attractive production hubs, thanks to its combination of creative talent, production incentives, and infrastructure,” says Maria Rua Aguete at London-based consultancy Omdia. “The next logical step is for Spain to transition from being a production destination to building globally competitive Spanish companies that own and export intellectual property.”

EU Next Generation funds ran out on Aug. 30. SETT doesn’t aim to stop here, however. “The audiovisual sector will remain one of SETT’s strategic areas of activity and will continue under new fund, España Crece. We have begun discussions with [Spanish state bank] ICO to define the procedures and framework for collaboration between the two institutions, ensuring the continuation of co-investment in strategic technologies and sectors,” says Ponce.

A Drill Down on Further SETT Investments

“The goal of the Hub’s second phase is clear: that Spain continues to be not only a great place to film, but also a great place to create, produce, finance, and export content, technology, and intellectual property to the world,” says González Veracruz.

She adds: “It’s a portfolio that reflects an industrial, technological, domestic and international view of Spanish audiovisual production.”

A breakdown of announced SETT investments:

*South Africa’s Known Associates Group and SETT have invested a joint €25 million ($29 million) to launch Moonlighting Studios Spain, a Madrid-based production company, and post-pro The Refinery, with facilities in the Basque Country and the Canary Islands.

*Alongside DNEG, “The Odyssey’s” sole VFX partner, SETT has taken €24.9 million ($29.1 million) equity in the Canary Islands’ Anima Kitchen, behind pre-school animation series hits “Cleo & Cuquín.” Anima Kitchent is renowned for leveraging YouTube, where it has over 67 million subscribers, in order to launch and consolidate IPs.

“The real edge is the combination: strong IP and production values paired with data analysis that tracks audience trends in real time. Producing quickly and at high quality is precisely what makes that IPs travel into new markets,” comments Pablo Hernández, executive president of the Canary Islands ZEC tax benefit zone.

*SETT has put up €20 million ($23.4 million) of a total €45 million ($52.65 million), the rest coming from Mexico’s Ítaca Films and investor Omega Capital, to found Ítaca Films Madrid, an international content studio. “For Ítaca Films, SETT represents much more than financing. It’s an instrument which institutionalises the industry, strengthens producers and shows that creativity, when it counts on structure and solid bases, can grow and develop better,” says Ítaca’s Santiago García.

*Focused on the creation, ownership and global distribution of kids & family IPs, Amuse Labs, a new Canary Islands animation company, has received a €6.4 million ($7.3 million) investment from SETT in return for a 48% equity position. Amuse Studios will become Amuse Labs’ second-largest shareholder.

*SETT has taken a 46% equity participation for €1.1 million ($1.3 million) in Lazona Audiovisual Hub, along with Lazona (36%) and El Alamedia Estidios (13%), billed as a Madrid creation and post-production factory aiming to meet the large demand for post-production services in the Spanish capital.

title: Naomi Watts Believes Standards Have Changed for Older Women in the Industry: ‘Look at the Emmys Last Week… That’s Heartening to See’
summary: British actor Naomi Watts, at the San Sebastián Film Festival to receive this year’s prestigious Donostia Award, spoke about opportunities in the industry for women over 50. Talking a week after Sarah Paulson told Variety about the lack of film offers following her spellbinding portrait of Marcia Clark in “The People v. O.J. Simpson: American […]
content:
British actor Naomi Watts, at the San Sebastián Film Festival to receive this year’s prestigious Donostia Award, spoke about opportunities in the industry for women over 50. Talking a week after Sarah Paulson told Variety about the lack of film offers following her spellbinding portrait of Marcia Clark in “The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story,” Watts said, “things have changed.”

Watts recalled entering the industry late “by Hollywood standards,” starring in David Lynch’s lauded “Mulholland Drive” at 31 years old. “I was told at the beginning that I better get my skates on because it all finishes at the age of 40. And here we are today. I’m in my late 50s. Look at the Emmys last week [and] the number of women in strong categories over 50. That’s heartening to see.”

Popular on Variety

Nominees over the age of 50 included Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”), Jean Smart (“Hacks”), and Allison Janney (“The Diplomat”).

“I do think things have changed,” she added. “Women are consumers of film and TV, and their stories should be reflected. That narrative had to be shifted. And I am grateful to be a small part of that shift.”

The actor is also at the Basque festival with Ben Shirinian’s feature debut “The Housewife.” The film, the Donostia Award Screening, stars Watts, Tye Sheridan, Luke Evans, Michael Imperioli and Lena Olin. Set in 1964 and based on a true story, the film tells the tale of a young journalist who tracks down a potential Nazi officer living secretly in New York and befriends the suspect’s charming wife.

Prodded about the parallels between a film about World War II and the Holocaust and the ongoing wars today, specifically the ongoing war in Palestine, Watts said: “It’s a very, very scary time what is going on in the world globally.” “We must be vigilant, we must pay attention, and not let that happen again. Hopefully this film sparks a dialogue. We don’t give answers; we hopefully send you away with questions of how did this happen and, who do you relate with in this story, and how we can avoid this happening ever again.”

“We have to tell these stories; storytelling is important, particularly now,” she reiterated, noting how she vows to continue supporting minorities and representation on screen. “I’m proud to be a part of the LGBTQ community. Minorities are being attacked right now, and it’s frightful and unacceptable. My heart is with these communities, particularly my family. I’ll do whatever I can to stick up for minorities.”

As for playing an immigrant in the U.S. as an immigrant to the country herself, Watts said she “moved to America with hopes and dreams,” all of which she has already “surpassed.” “Hermine, the woman I play in this story, was there post-World War II, when things were much more sunny and bright. Her story was about trying to find a new place and erase the past, which she was able to do for a period of time.”

“In terms of me, I have American children, I do love America, and what’s going on today is complicated and certainly nerve-wracking, but I have faith that things will work out in time,” she added about the U.S.’s current political climate.

Watts noted how the role was “very complicated,” and she had a “huge amount of fear” when taking on the adaptation of the harrowing true story. “It was like nothing I ever played before: this duality of this woman who had done horrific things, heinous crimes, and yet blending into society as a normal person – very much a good citizen, a good wife, baking cookies, showing up to church. That duality and living with that secret was interesting to me as an actor.”

“I am always looking to do new things even though I might have a repetitive theme in my work – grief and identity— things that are meaningful to me,” she continued. “This character is like nothing I’ve ever played. I’m at an age now when some might joke I’m in my villain era, but this is an extreme one and not a joke. I felt compelled to play this story.”

When asked about the similarities between her role in “Mulholland Drive” and “The Housewife,” especially how both characters broach these notions of duality, Watts said both roles are “deeply psychological and confronting,” but while she didn’t particularly enjoy playing Hermine, she has nothing but wonderful memories of her time on set with the late Lynch, who died early last year.

“‘Mulholland Drive’ was nothing but fun,” she said. “It was coming at a time in my life when I didn’t have any breaks after years of struggle, so every day on set was just a wonder. Getting to learn how Lynch works and directs was truly wonderful. I’ll never forget those days.”

The actor called working with Lynch “an incredible break.” “I had been working to get a film role for a good 10 years before that lucky break came. I was very much a journeyman actor, working wherever I could, but I had a lot of rejection. really was quite shut down, not bringing good energy into rooms I was asked to audition in. It took someone like David Lynch to see through the veneers I had created. We had a beautiful conversation, and he gave me the role of a lifetime.”

“I’m forever indebted to David Lynch; he is in my heart forever,” she went on. “This is a film that has remained in people’s consciousness for decades, and I think it really launched me because every great filmmaker saw this film.”

The San Sebastián Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26.

title: Anthony Page Dies: Tony-Winning, Emmy-Nominated Director Of Stage & Screen Was 90
summary: Anthony Page, the prolific British stage, film and TV director who won a Tony Award for his 1997 Broadway production of A Doll’s House and was twice Emmy-nominated for acclaimed TV movies in the 1970s, died September 11 at a London residential care home. He was 90. Page’s death has been confirmed by press representative […]
content:
Anthony Page, the prolific British stage, film and TV director who won a Tony Award for his 1997 Broadway production of A Doll’s House and was twice Emmy-nominated for acclaimed TV movies in the 1970s, died September 11 at a London residential care home. He was 90.

Page’s death has been confirmed by press representative Jo Allan to British news outlets.

The director of the 1977 Oscar-nominated film I Never Promised You A Rose Garden starring Kathleen Quinlan as a young woman struggling with schizophrenia, Page was Emmy nominated for his direction of two high-profile TV-movies in the mid-1970s: Pueblo (1973), which chronicled the capture of an American spy ship in North Korea, and 1975’s The Missiles Of October, a drama starring Martin Sheen and William Devane about the 1962 Cuban missile crisis. Both projects won multiple Emmy Awards.

On Broadway, Page is best remembered for directing a string of acclaimed and starry productions during the 1990s and 2000s, beginning with his Tony-nominated A Doll’s House starring Janet McTeer (herself a Tony nominee for the role). In 2003 he directed a revival of Tennessee Williams’ Cat on a Hot Tin Roof starring Ashley Judd, Jason Patric, Ned Beatty and Margo Martindale, and two years later directed a revival of Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf that starred Kathleen Turner as Martha opposite Bill Irwin’s George.

Watch on Deadline

Page made his final Broadway appearance in 2009 with a revival of Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, starring Irwin, John Goodman, John Glover and Nathan Lane.

Born Anthony Frederick Montague Page on September 21, 1935, in Bangalore, British India, Page attended Oxford before relocating to New York to study with famed acting teacher Sanford Meisner. By the mid-1960s he had begun a long association with London’s Royal Court Theatre where he directed and, from 1969 to 1972, served as co-artistic director.

Page made his Broadway debut with 1965’s Inadmissible Evidence, a John Osborne play starring, among others, Nicol Williamson. He returned to Broadway in 1983 with a revival of Shaw’s Heartbreak House starring Philip Bosco, Rosemary Harris, Rex Harrison and Amy Irving. Page would not return to Broadway until his string of star-driven revivals began with A Doll’s House in ’97.

For the screen, Page directed, among others, 1979’s The Lady Vanishes starring Cybill Shepherd, Elliott Gould and Angela Lansbury. Television credits include 1981’s The Patricia Neal Story and Bill starring Mickey Rooney as a mentally disabled man; the 1983 sequel Bill: On His Own; 1988’s Scandal In A Small Town starring Raquel Welch; and, in 1994, seven episodes of the British mini-series Middlemarch.

His final credit was the 2008 British TV film My Zinc Bed, written by playwright David Hare and starring Uma Thurman, Jonathan Pryce and Paddy Considine.

Page is survived by his husband and partner of 40 years Kenneth Butler.

title: John Wilson on ‘The History of Concrete’ and What’s Wrong With the Documentary Space: ‘People Are Retelling Stories That Have Already Happened’
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “The History of Concrete,” now in theaters. John Wilson’s new documentary “The History of Concrete” is, of course, about the history of concrete. But it’s also about selling a documentary titled “The History of Concrete,” which, it turns out, is almost as hard as concrete. It sees […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “The History of Concrete,” now in theaters.

John Wilson’s new documentary “The History of Concrete” is, of course, about the history of concrete. But it’s also about selling a documentary titled “The History of Concrete,” which, it turns out, is almost as hard as concrete.

It sees the filmmaker, best known for his HBO series “How To,” traveling across the world — to concrete conventions in Las Vegas and New Orleans, to ancient buildings in Italy and to graves in undisclosed locations. But he also documents the Zoom meetings in between, where he pitches the idea to Hollywood executives and tells them the film’s title. Underneath their deep sighs, you can almost hear them mutter: Who wants to watch a movie called “The History of Concrete”?

“I genuinely did want to make the definitive movie about concrete,” Wilson says of the doc, now in theaters via Magnolia Pictures. “I ended up incorporating the meta aspects about a year or so into the process, because I felt like that was becoming a more interesting story. And I wanted to make something that another filmmaker could learn something from, about how things are produced, because that was always a mystery to me growing up.”

Popular on Variety

Of course, it’s not all slabs of rock. Wilson finds humanity in the cracks of “The History of Concrete,” letting his camera guide him toward a professional “gum buster,” a grieving local musician and dozens of other fascinating characters. It is perhaps the filmmaker’s most substantial — and heart-forward — work to date.

“The History of Concrete” by John Wilson John Wilson

In the film, as you’re struggling to sell said film, I kept thinking: It’s John Wilson, obviously he’s not going to make a boring movie about concrete!

It doesn’t matter. In terms of the money, we were asking for what a Netflix documentary would cost. Our budget ask was also scaled to what “How To” would cost, so I didn’t think we were being that outrageous. The struggle is actually a lot more real than what’s on screen in the film. I just didn’t want to weigh it down with more struggle.

People laugh when they hear the title, but you laugh knowing that the movie is done. It’s a lot different when someone is asking you directly for money to make this thing that doesn’t exist yet. Would you give your own money to make “The History of Concrete”? Even if it’s me, I don’t know. It’s a strange proposition.

The documentary space has mutated slightly, and I think people value the wrong things a lot of the time. That’s what I wanted to comment on, in a way.

What are the things people value?

People are focused on retelling stories that have already happened — whether it’s a triple homicide or a musician who has gone through all the motions of their career. Certain people with money have a hard time with imagination and this idea of art-making for the sake of it. You need to go through several layers of approval. I didn’t realize how hard it was going to be.

Structurally, the film is similar to “How To.” Was working in the feature-length format freeing or more challenging?

It was freeing in that I was able to have more durational subjects — like the 3,100-mile race that takes place over the course of a few months. I don’t know if I would have been able to cover that as substantially in an episode of the show. Same with one of the main characters I spent a lot of time with near the end of the film. I spent a year and a half with him, and I wouldn’t have been able to do that without the elasticity of a feature film. But emotionally, it is a little different than the show, and while superficially it shares a lot of the same qualities, I set out to make something that was much broader in scope and almost felt like a prequel to the show, because it’s kind of the foundation on which the rest of the work was built.

The subject of the film is literally our foundation. I found it notable that you chose to explore concrete, a hard topic, in a physical sense, but you can’t help but be led to the softness — the humanity.

Yeah, and Jack, the musician I spent a lot of time with, has the softest heart of all. In the world of hard surfaces, he’s got a really soft interior.

How do you view your responsibility to these subjects, specifically him? Do you approach it as a journalist? Do you have an ongoing relationship with him outside of the film?

I met him at a liquor store right next to my house, so he’s the kind of person I’d see all the time. So in that case, I treated it as if he’s someone I’m going to see frequently. But also, my friend Francis Carr, who was one of my producers, would mostly correspond with Jack whenever he was going to have a show or something like that. There was a bit of distance — it wasn’t just him and me. I think there’s some value to a certain level of journalistic distance when making something like this, just because I’m dealing with so many people at the same time.

Has he seen the film?

I think he saw part of it in the Rockaways. But he was rehearsing, because he was playing the after party next door during the screening, so he couldn’t fully watch it. He’s going to be at one of the premieres at IFC over the weekend.

I expect that one of the most talked-about moments of the film will be the Kim Kardashian scene. You’re at a GQ dinner and filming Dwyane Wade as he gives a toast to Kim, and she’s looking right into your camera. It’s all very unsettling. How uncomfortable was that to film?

The discomfort started when I entered the room, and the filming only eased that discomfort. I had just never seen an uninterrupted shot of Kim Kardashian before, and I knew this was going to be the only chance for me to get it. I wasn’t pursuing it, but I thought it was a very rare environment, and there’s something very awkward and strange about these celebrity events. I wanted to capture that somehow by not including any score and just letting the moment play out, so you have a POV of what it’s like to be sitting across from someone like that at dinner.

Did you have any interaction with her at all?

No.

So how does that work? Were you nervous about putting her in the film? Do you expect to hear from her?

It’s a miracle that this film exists and is being released as is — that’s what I’ll say. It was an event that was being documented by someone else too, an internal magazine film-and-photo team. I have no idea where that kind of stuff ends up, but I know it won’t be treated anywhere near how I would treat it. So I think that’s how the footage is able to be in the movie, because it was an event that was captured by someone else as well. But I don’t know where that material will ever end up.

The shot of Tim Robinson got the biggest laugh of the entire film at the screening I was at. Were you expecting that to be such a punchline?

No. Originally we did not have Tim at the end of that shot, because we just wanted you to sit with the strangeness of that eye-contact moment I was having with Kim. We ended up putting the Tim thing in just because it performed really well when we showed it to people, and I realized comedically you needed something to pop that tension bubble. I love reveals that someone else has been there the whole time. I showed the film internationally in a couple of places, and that shot was crickets. There are some places in the world that don’t know Tim in the same way people do here — same with Hallmark and Chef Boyardee. They don’t know what that stuff is.

Is there one shot in the movie you’re proudest of?

The shot I really liked a lot was when I’m filming the sidewalk and you see my shadow, but then I’m zooming into the sidewalk, and the light changes really dramatically around me, and my shadow just disappears into the sidewalk. It happened randomly, and it felt very poetic in a way that I didn’t really plan. But on top of that, I think my favorite shot is when the tattoo preservation guy asks his dad where Chef Boyardee is buried. The timing of that was just incredible, and how casual he was.

It turned out to be your kicker!

I remember trying to figure out what the last shot of the movie should be when I was talking to [producers] Josh [Safdie] and Ronnie [Bronstein] and Eli [Bush]. I was thinking about going to Chef Boyardee’s grave, but we had to have the movie ready in four days, and I didn’t know how I was going to get it. They said, “You have to get that shot,” so I went and shot it by myself on Christmas Eve, which was the day before we locked the movie. So now I know where Chef Boyardee’s grave is.

Wow, that’s fascinating that the final shot was so last-minute.

It was because we got into Sundance as I was still filming the movie. But it also kind of ties in with the Christmas theme of it all, even though you would never know I filmed that on Christmas Eve.

title: Box Office: Zach Cregger’s ‘Resident Evil’ Scares Up $26 Million on Opening Day
summary: With fall right around the corner, movie theater-goers are ready to be spooked — and Sony’s zombie horror “Resident Evil” has arrived at the perfect time. “Resident Evil” earned $26.3 million domestically across 3,684 screens on opening day, making it far and away the No. 1 new release on Friday. By Sunday, Sony’s new take […]
content:
With fall right around the corner, movie theater-goers are ready to be spooked — and Sony’s zombie horror “Resident Evil” has arrived at the perfect time.

“Resident Evil” earned $26.3 million domestically across 3,684 screens on opening day, making it far and away the No. 1 new release on Friday. By Sunday, Sony’s new take on the horror franchise is expected to make around $55 million, making it the largest debut in “Resident Evil” franchise history. (2010’s “Resident Evil: Afterlife,” previously the highest-grossing installment, made $26 million at the box office over its opening weekend.)

Based on Capcom’s popular horror video games, the film was directed by Zach Cregger — who last frightened audiences with 2025’s “Weapons” and 2022’s “Barbarian.” (“Weapons” opened to $43 million and ended its box office run with $270 million globally.) Austin Abrams takes the lead in the gory reboot co-written by Cregger and Shay Hatten as a medical courier who must contend with a zombie outbreak while making a delivery to Raccoon City General Hospital.

Popular on Variety

Some die-hard fans were unsure about Cregger’s mission to create a new, original story for the reboot (and thus omit established characters from the “Resident Evil” video game universe), though it seems such concerns were for naught as early reviews and word-of-mouth for the film have been strong. While Variety’s Owen Gleiberman referred to the prior “Resident Evil” films as “hyperviolent, hyperkinetic video-game zombie sludge,” he called Cregger’s take on the IP a “sweetly executed piece of escapist trivia” that has “a quirky relatability.”

The Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock-led “Practical Magic 2” took second place on Friday, bringing in an additional $3.1 million in its second week. Over the weekend, the witchy sequel is expected to earn another $10.4 million, bringing the film’s cumulative total to $48.2 million.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” both remained in the Friday top 5. Sony’s comic book sequel landed at No. 2, bringing in another $1.53 million, while Universal’s “The Odyssey” took in an additional $ 1.36 million for a fourth-place finish. Those additions bring “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” to a staggering $944.15 million domestic gross, and “The Odyssey” to $609.8 million.

Vertical’s “The Weight,” another newcomer, pulled in around $1.17 million across 1,504 theaters on Friday, placing it fifth. Per rival estimates, the historical thriller is expected to make $2.3 million through its opening weekend. Director Padraic McKinley’s debut feature stars Ethan Hawke as a battle-scarred veteran hired to smuggle a fortune in gold across 100 miles of impenetrable wilderness. Russell Crowe also stars.

From GKids, “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” opened to $540,000 across 2,173 theaters on Friday, per competitor numbers. The Steve Cox and Matthew Walker-directed animated flick is expected to bring in roughly $1.4 million through the weekend. Per the logline, the film follows Shaun the Sheep (voiced by Justin Fletcher) on Halloween Eve as “excitement turns to dismay when the clumsy Farmer ruins the pumpkin patch. Shaun tries fixing it with science experiments, but things go wrong when a wild beast appears in the woods.”

title: ‘Resident Evil’ Star Austin Abrams on His ‘Tragic’ Transformation, ‘Not Trying to Look Cool’ While Screaming and the One Scene He Wasn’t Allowed to Shoot
summary: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters. There’s not a moment in “Resident Evil” where star Austin Abrams isn’t making you laugh, scream or feel bad for the zombie-infested nightmare his character Bryan finds himself in. For almost the entire 95-minute runtime, he’s either running, shooting or getting […]
content:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters.

There’s not a moment in “Resident Evil” where star Austin Abrams isn’t making you laugh, scream or feel bad for the zombie-infested nightmare his character Bryan finds himself in. For almost the entire 95-minute runtime, he’s either running, shooting or getting covered in gore from various undead monsters, like a rat-filled behemoth, a roly-poly ball of bodies or an acid-puking fiend. After teaming with director Zach Cregger on last year’s horror hit “Weapons,” Abrams takes center stage in “Resident Evil” and proves he’s more than capable of leading a feature on his own.

Based on the popular horror video game series, “Resident Evil” tells a fully original story with some nods to the original source material that fans will love. Abrams plays a bumbling medical courier who finds out his girlfriend is pregnant, but agrees to one last delivery before heading home. He must make his way to a hospital in Raccoon City (which is ground zero for the zombie outbreak in the games) to drop off a mysterious package, but the snowy drive is far from easy. Almost immediately, he hits a strange woman with his car, then buckles her in and starts driving her to the hospital without realizing she’s slowly turning into a zombie. They get pulled over by a cop and things quickly go awry. Bryan is able to escape to a nearby farmhouse, but the woman doesn’t stop pursuing him for the entire movie.

Popular on Variety

Bryan finds a shotgun at the farm to defend himself, but he realizes the undead creatures will stop at nothing to kill him. After blasting apart the woman and an infected farmer, their bodies fuse together with stringy tendrils from inside each of them. Bryan books it out of there and gets picked up by some scientists from the Umbrella Corporation (an evil institution from the games) who explain that the package he’s delivering contains an antidote to the zombie virus.

Along the way, Bryan gets bit by a zombie but hides the wound, which slowly infects him. As his condition worsens, he makes it to the Raccoon City hospital, but he doesn’t get the chance to use the antidote. He transforms into a gigantic, tentacled monstrosity in the Umbrella Corporation lab and rips apart the scientists trying to save the world. With their bodies fused to his own, the monstrous Bryan roars atop the hospital as a military helicopter takes aim at him.

With Variety, Abrams discusses how he transformed into the monster, the cold and messy shooting conditions he endured and the one scene the “Resident Evil” team couldn’t allow him to film.

©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection

How did you find the right sound for Bryan’s scream? You really go all out, and it’s played for laughs but also works for a horror movie. Is it similar to your real scream?

There wasn’t a method behind that. It’s just letting all inhibitions down and not trying to look or sound cool and just letting it come out. I can’t tell you that it was weeks of labored work trying to figure it out. I don’t know the last time a scream naturally came out, so I’m not really sure. Whatever it is is what felt right, especially in the moment for the character. It was something where you didn’t know what was gonna what come out. You don’t want to know. It’s better to just like feel it and let whatever happens happen.

If Bryan isn’t screaming then he’s usually muttering “fuck!” under his breath. Are you muttering or talking to yourself like that in real life?

I don’t know if I can say I’m muttering “fuck, fuck” all the time. It was relatively easy thinking about the situation that you’re in at the time. In my daily life, god, that would mean something was really wrong if you did that all the time in your regular life. Those are signs that things are not going well. Please, if that’s happening, something needs to change.

I was not expecting you to turn into a monster at the end of the movie. What was your first reaction to reading that surprising moment in the script?

That’s what I love about Zach’s work. He’s willing to take those risks and kill off the person that you’re following the whole time — and not just that, have them ruin everything that they were just fighting for. It definitely was surprising, and also tragic. Everything that this character went through, the change that he has, how he feels with his girlfriend and all this sacrifice is essentially for nothing. It tells the story of why this virus got out and continued to go out and that there was this possibility of it being fixed. I think it’s a cool origin story.

How much of your monster form was practical vs. CGI and other special effects?

A lot of it was capturing it. It would be hard to build a suit like that. It was kind of a mixture. It’s definitely me, and there’s definitely some stuff they put on my face. I don’t know how they would add all the other different people on me and stuff like that. I don’t know what they fully keep as you or not. But we definitely went through the actions of it.

What kind of direction was Cregger giving you during the monster fight at the end? What was going through your head?

What’s going through your head is I look like a fucking idiot right now. It’s so funny because the thing with all that stuff is you can feel dumb, but the less you commit to it, the dumber you look. So actually, the more you commit to it, the more people are just like, “Whoa, that looks cool.” But you know, “More monster.” He would say that a lot. “More roar. Scarier. Monster more. Keep monstering. Don’t stop monstering. Come on, imagine you’re a big, scary monster.” I don’t know, I’m fucking making shit up right now. It was fun. I can’t remember specific notes. A lot of it was just playing around in in this open space and imagining stuff.

The movie ends with Bryan facing off against a military helicopter. Do you have an idea of what happens to him after? Is that something you’d want to see explored in another movie?

I don’t know. I’m not sure. I really don’t know. Whatever you want, you want it to be best for the story, and I love Zach. But beyond that, I just don’t know. I don’t want to put in some sort of theories about things.

The other big part of the movie is Bryan’s relationship with his pregnant girlfriend Michelle, who we never see in person. Who voiced her, and did you ever meet in person or was it just a voice on the phone?

I think that’s Zach’s wife Sara [Paxton]. We had someone else at the time. She wasn’t where we were shooting at the time, so it’d be too hard to try to patch a call and then it drops out and gets unreliable. We had someone else reading it, but I think he knew he wanted to put Sara in as a fun kind of Easter egg.

Did you create any more backstory for his and Michele’s relationship than what we see in the movie?

Yeah, to some degree. There was a coming up with that just for myself, but I don’t know how deeply Zach and I went into it at the time. But it’s something that you need to know to make a full person that feels like there’s dimensions behind what you’re seeing.

How cold was it shooting in Prague?

Everyday is kind of up and down, but there were days where it was definitely quite cold. I don’t mind that stuff though. There were day where it was this kind of rain that would then freeze to your jacket. So then you’d be covered in this outer layer of ice. But I enjoy that stuff. There were some days where we thankfully got real snow, which was pretty awesome, like fully blanketed. The farmhouse stuff is mostly actual snow that was happening. The temperature was also all in Celsius, which I cannot remember. There were a couple days that everyone was particularly having a tough time. But, whatever, man, it’s just temperature.

How do you push through the cold when you’re shooting and not let it affect you?

You just feel it. You let it be a part of the thing. But like I said, it’s not really a big deal. It’s just cold. You know who was concerned was the woman in the dress playing the pedestrian. If there’s anyone to be concerned it was her because she had to do scenes where she was having to lay down in the snow. She was really a killer and not complaining and getting it done. If there’s anyone to pat on the back, it’s her because everyone else got to be fully clothed and not in a summer dress.

The other thing that stood out to me was all the running you do. Did you train at all to be able to run like that in the snow?

I don’t know if this is the way to do it, but you want the person to not be a runner. I want to see the person struggling with it. So no, there wasn’t a particular kind of running prep because I feel like it’s just more interesting to watch someone that’s out of breath and you’re like, “I don’t know if they can do this.”

What was the messiest and bloodiest scene you had to shoot?

Definitely once we got down to the maternity ward stuff. At that point, you’re completely soaked in this blood and this floor that’s completely blood. People were getting taken out constantly or almost going down. At that point in that movie, there’s not a part of me that’s not completely covered in blood and goo.

How did you shoot the jump down to the ground from the farmhouse?

That is one of the only ones that we had a stunt team come in and do. Other than that, it felt it was important to do everything. That was one where, well, I don’t know what to say they just wouldn’t let me do it. But our great stunt guy that did it, he didn’t have any wires on him or anything. He just took the fall. I remember him afterwards saying he really hit his tailbone pretty hard.

title: ‘Vintage Violence’ Review: Cole Sprouse Heads Up a Hyper-Online Gonzo Freakout in Japan
summary: Eugene Kotlyarenko has built a career on drawing upon his widely-viewed cinephilic base of knowledge to consider more contemporary forms of hyper-online, of-the-moment provocation, and “Vintage Violence” is no exception. As with Kotlyarenko’s arguably best-known film, 2020’s “Spree,” live-streaming is key: “Vintage Violence” introduces obnoxious social media celebrity Carter (Cole Sprouse) mid-stream before quickly spinning […]
content:
Eugene Kotlyarenko has built a career on drawing upon his widely-viewed cinephilic base of knowledge to consider more contemporary forms of hyper-online, of-the-moment provocation, and “Vintage Violence” is no exception. As with Kotlyarenko’s arguably best-known film, 2020’s “Spree,” live-streaming is key: “Vintage Violence” introduces obnoxious social media celebrity Carter (Cole Sprouse) mid-stream before quickly spinning out into a gangsters-vs-everybody-and-each-other free-for-all. Zipping around Tokyo, Kotlyarenko underlines the of-the-moment-ness of his scenario at every turn, but the film is a surprisingly slow ride despite the overload.

Per his press kit bio, Kotlyarenko specializes in films “exploring love and cultural madness in the age of social media,” of which “Vintage Violence” is definitely one. Carter’s jam-packed introduction finds him in vertical vision while chat-box commenters provide both random insults and background information about the character at a speed almost impossible to process; more relevant details are being dispensed than can possibly be fully absorbed.

Popular on Variety

The impressive density of this overload, which embraces the possibilities of relatively new technology to find novel ways to deliver and compress context, diminishes as Carter is drawn to Japan by Izumi Adachi (Kiko Mizuhara). She lures him with promises of fabulously large sums to be made by selling the vintage denim he found mid-stream — i.e., a duffel-bag-sized Macguffin that can set the protagonists in perpetual motion. (The denim was also apparently integral to the making of the production: per the end credits, “This film was made with the generous support of Levi’s and Levi’s Japan.”)

There is no meaningful trace of the past beyond fetishizable commodities in Kotlyarenko’s film, only the relentless present; shooting with his characteristically tilt-and-zoom-heavy fluidity, cinematographer Sean Price Williams amplifies that twitchy energy.

Appropriated from a John Cale album, the title accurately describes scenes of bloodletting committed by bizarre, scenery-chewing yakuza members, and the energy hovers somewhere around a bloodier-than-baseline Takashi Miike movie from the mid-2000s. But, per his conceptual preference, Kotlyarenko’s riff on familiar territory is texturally very now, and the setpieces are often based around tech that didn’t exist 20 years ago. The best of these is a chase where Carter’s phone is stolen and he chases down the thief, gauging his proximity by how much his bluetooth earbuds start crackling; the closer he gets, the more unbroken the sound.

Kotlyarenko is cinematically omnivorous: Beyond the copious Japanese filmmakers he references, “Vintage Violence” riffs on everything from “North by Northwest” to “Wanderlust.” As the plot progresses, increasingly outré elements are introduced: a hotel that seems to have been founded by the same TV programming team that made content in Olivier Assayas’s “demonlover,” or a gangster whose severed finger has been replaced by a spray bottle of poisonous mist. This kind of non-stop maximalism in the service of cult-movie scenes that scream “clip me and put me online!” can quickly grow old, and while “Vintage Violence” is admirably committed to living up to the mayhem of its forebears, like many of them the cumulative effect is more enervating than energizing.

The film internalizes potential objections about a foreign director making a film that claims insight into Japanese characters’ interiority, with Carter being ritualistically insulted as a gaijin, or outsider. Sprouse is a serviceable lead, adapting to new forms of mayhem while slowly reaching a form of moral rehabilitation, for which he’s rewarded with a romantic arc. For all its determination to be firmly of the Now and provide midnight-movie crassness, “Vintage Violence’s” constituent parts can be surprisingly stock.

title: ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Sees Mary Embark on Married Life in First Images
summary: BritBox have given fans of their hit Jane Austen-inspired series “The Other Bennet Sister” an early Christmas present with a first look at a new three-part special set to drop this holiday season. Ella Bruccoleri returns as the awkward Mary Bennet opposite Dónal Finn as Tom Hayward, who proposed in the Season 1 finale – […]
content:
BritBox have given fans of their hit Jane Austen-inspired series “The Other Bennet Sister” an early Christmas present with a first look at a new three-part special set to drop this holiday season.

Ella Bruccoleri returns as the awkward Mary Bennet opposite Dónal Finn as Tom Hayward, who proposed in the Season 1 finale – with Mary accepting.

“But with marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs. Hayward?” reads the logline for the Christmas special.

Returning alongside Bruccoleri and Finn are Ruth Jones as Mrs. Bennet, Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley, Laurie Davidson as Mr. Ryder, Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins.

Popular on Variety

Joining the cast for the first time is Nerys Amber-Stocks as Mary’s housemaid Lucy.

“The Other Bennet Sister” is based on Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name. Season 1 was adapted by Sarah Quintrell, who has also written the three-part special based on new storylines by Hadlow.

Earlier this year, producer Jane Tranter told Variety that while “The Other Bennet Sister” was conceived as a limited series, “the characters just live on.” She said any further seasons “really depends on Janice and her thinking.”

“At the moment we’re concentrating on looking at the novels of Jane Austen, because that’s what we always set out to do,” Tranter added. “But having set up ‘The Other Bennet Sister,’ you can’t help but think ‘What would happen if – ?’ so we’ll see. We’ll see what Janice says, and Sarah, obviously.”

The first season garnered plenty of fans, with Variety‘s reviewer Aramide Tinubu describing the show as “immensely charming and thoughtful.”

“The Other Bennet Sister” is produced by Bad Wolf for the BBC and BritBox North America. Asim Abbasi returns to direct.

title: BritBox Reveals First Look At ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special
summary: BritBox is giving a first look at the three-part Christmas special The Other Bennet Sister starring Ella Bruccoleri and Dónal Finn. Check out the photo above. The Other Bennet Sister continues the story of Mary Bennet following the events of the first 10 episodes. Produced by Bad Wolf for the BBC and BritBox North America, […]
content:
BritBox is giving a first look at the three-part Christmas special The Other Bennet Sister starring Ella Bruccoleri and Dónal Finn.

Check out the photo above.

The Other Bennet Sister continues the story of Mary Bennet following the events of the first 10 episodes. Produced by Bad Wolf for the BBC and BritBox North America, production recently wrapped in Wales.

Bruccoleri (Down Cemetery Road, Wicker) returns as Mary, with Finn (Young Sherlock, SAS Rogue Heroes) as her husband Tom Hayward. The 10th episode of the series saw Mary agreeing to wed Tom setting up the question, as BritBox puts it, “with marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs. Hayward?”

Also returning are Ruth Jones (Gavin & Stacey, Stella) as Mrs. Bennet, Tanya Reynolds (Ted Lasso, Sex Education) as Caroline Bingley, Laurie Davidson (A Cruel Love: The Ruth Ellis Story, The Girlfriend) as Mr. Ryder, Varada Sethu (Doctor Who, Andor) as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert (My Oxford Year, Chloe) as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close (Sunflower Child) as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson (The Coroner, COBRA) as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright (The A Word, APOSTASY) as Kitty Buncock, and Anna Fenton-Garvey (The Nevers) as Charlotte Collins. Nerys Amber Stocks (Out There, Mammoth) also joins the cast as Mary’s housemaid Lucy.

Watch on Deadline

Screenwriter Sarah Quintrell (The Power, Ellen), who wrote nine of the 10 episodes of the series, has written all three additional episodes based on storylines by author Janice Hadlow. Asim Abbasi (Cake) has returned to direct.

Based on Janice Hadlow’s novel, The Other Bennet Sister followed Mary Bennet, the oft-overlooked middle sister in Pride & Prejudice as she navigated the societal pressures of Regency England, where marriage is both aspiration and necessity.

In its first 90 days on BritBox in North America, The Other Bennet Sister delivered a record-breaking performance, driving five times more new subscribers than any previous launch and achieving the highest streaming rate of any title launch on the service. According to BritBox, nearly half (47%) of its active subscribers have watched the series in that timeframe, which also helped drive the strongest quarter of subscriber growth in BritBox history and the service’s highest-ever week of signups.

title: ‘Resident Evil’s Austin Abrams Recalls “Harrowing” Stunt Shoot For Zach Cregger’s Video Game Adaptation: “You Don’t Wanna F*ck Up”
summary: As Zach Cregger puts audiences in the player’s POV with Resident Evil, Austin Abrams had to begin with Level One. The actor admitted he wasn’t familiar with the Resident Evil video games or movies before taking the lead in Cregger’s adaptation, now playing in theaters, explaining the horror gaming genre “really goddamn rocks your nervous […]
content:
As Zach Cregger puts audiences in the player’s POV with Resident Evil, Austin Abrams had to begin with Level One.

The actor admitted he wasn’t familiar with the Resident Evil video games or movies before taking the lead in Cregger’s adaptation, now playing in theaters, explaining the horror gaming genre “really goddamn rocks your nervous system.”

“Not that I was like an anti-fan,” explained Abrams. “The movies, I haven’t seen, and the games were something that just felt too frightening to engage with. I mean that genuinely. I remember playing Dead Space, a very different game, but kind of a similar vibe, and literally just panic playing the beginning of it and being like, ‘I can’t do this.'”

After Cregger recounted filming a stunt that “would’ve killed” Abrams if it had gone wrong, the actor admitted the experience was also “harrowing” for him, running down a snow-covered road as zombies jumped off roofs and splattered on the pavement around him.

Watch on Deadline

Following his work with Cregger on last year’s horror hit Weapons, Abrams was “very grateful” to reunite with the horror auteur and work together to build the role of Brian, an original character that did not appear in the games.

Austin Abrams and director Zach Cregger on the set of ‘Resident Evil’ (2026) Dusan Martincek/Sony Pictures Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection

“One, you don’t wanna fuck up the shot,” Abrams said. “Also, you don’t wanna make a wrong move or something goes wrong. So, it’s kind of scary each time.”

“It was definitely doing the best you can to create a person that feels tangible, and they have a gravity to them, and also you understand them,” he said. “So, there was definitely a process there of discovering that, and also just who do you want to see in this situation. Because it was just kind of an avatar that, when I think of that word, I think of like a blank slate almost. That’s not necessarily interesting to see, and so it was, who do you want to see go through this? That was kind of a guiding light a little bit too.”

Read on about Austin Abrams’ starring role in Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil, now in theaters.

DEADLINE: I love seeing you and Zach work on this together after Weapons. What was it like reuniting for Resident Evil?

AUSTIN ABRAMS: It was awesome, man. In a lot of ways, it was really interesting cause it kind of felt like we just picked up where we left off, even though it was a different project, and different character. But dude, I love Zach, I love working with him, I love what he makes. It was great, and [I’m] just very grateful that he would trust me enough to handle this project.

DEADLINE: Were you a fan of the Resident Evil games, or even the movies before?

ABRAMS: No, none of it. Not that I was like an anti-fan. … the movies, I haven’t seen, and the games were something that just felt too frightening to engage with. I mean that genuinely. I remember playing Dead Space, a very different game, but kind of a similar vibe, and literally just panic playing the beginning of it and being like, “I can’t do this.” Cause it really goddamn rocks your nervous system until you get used to it. But no, it was always something that was just like, when you’re a kid and you’re looking at an R-rated movie or something, you’re like, “God, that’s so scary,” and it feels like this big looming thing. That was essentially what this was for me. So, it wasn’t until coming into this project that I started to get familiar with them.

Austin Abrams in ‘Resident Evil’ (2026) Sony Pictures Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection

DEADLINE: Tell me about working with Zach to build your character Brian, because I know he said that Brian is kind of an avatar for him and how he would make these decisions. But also tell me about infusing the character with some of your sense of humor and comedic timing.

ABRAMS: Well, you can’t play an avatar, in terms of being a character. That’s just kind of a general idea, so it was definitely doing the best you can to create a person that feels tangible, and they have a gravity to them, and also you understand them. So, there was definitely a process there of discovering that, and also just who do you want to see in this situation. Because it was just kind of an avatar that, when I think of that word, I think of like a blank slate almost. That’s not necessarily interesting to see, and so it was, who do you want to see go through this. That was kind of a guiding light a little bit too.

DEADLINE: Tell me about his relationship with his girlfriend and how this news from her kind of impacts his whole fight for survival.

ABRAMS: He learns that someone he really is in love with, that also is someone that wants to go to the next level of their relationship. And I feel like Brian has been, up until this point, he seems a little bit incapable and scared of that. He essentially has this moment where this possibility of a huge life change where he would really need to step up in a real way, that I think he’s been avoiding up until when you see him. He’s kind of faced with that and terrified of that, and then he starts to go through this actual horror movie. We have all of our little issues in life or things that feel really big, but then when something real happens, when you almost die, when someone you love dies, when it’s actually like, all of this could end—well, all this will end, not could end, it will end, and it could end at any second. It puts everything into perspective. So, I think he gets kind of put into perspective and starts to realize, “What do I actually want?”

DEADLINE: What it was being immersed in Zach’s take on Raccoon City. Did you have a favorite creature that you had to fight?

ABRAMS: Practical sets are always great, so something like the sewer was a really cool practical set. I mean, that that guy in the trailer, the big man in the sewer was really kind of crazy to look at, ’cause he really looked like a real, just humongous dude. I mean, I don’t even know how tall that guy would have been, and then there’s another creature that’s a little funnier, kind of towards the end. It’s kind of hilarious and really kind of surprised me.

Austin Abrams in ‘Resident Evil’ (2026) Dusan Martincek/Sony Pictures Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection

DEADLINE: I’m also curious about shooting a lot of these stunts. I know Zach said the one with the falling zombies, if you would have made one wrong step, it could have been disastrous. What was it like for you filming that one?

ABRAMS: I would say, it’s harrowing, man. I mean, if you imagine yourself; I’m gonna run this way, and they’re gonna call action, and I need to do it at a certain pace, so that everything goes well and goes right, and also you need to not slip, and the ground is all wet, with this kind of combination of some real snow, but then the fake snow or whatever, you’re just in sneakers that don’t have any grip, and there’s these things falling. One, you don’t wanna fuck up the shot. Also, you don’t wanna make a wrong move or something goes wrong. So, it’s kind of scary each time.

DEADLINE: It looks awesome though. After doing Whalefall also, do you prefer working in snow or working in a water tank?

ABRAMS: I mean, working in water is pretty fun. A lot of Whalefall was working in like a small amount of water. It wasn’t like a lot. A lot of it wasn’t working directly in water, it was kind of like a little kiddie pool. But when you’re fully in water with the suit on and everything, that’s nice. But also I love the aesthetic of a horror movie with snow, like The Shining. It’s just really something that’s beautiful, that really gives a feeling to me, kind of like, you shouldn’t be outside. You see it, you see the character, and you know where you wanna be. You wanna be inside next to a fire with a cat, watching a movie or reading a book or something. It just adds a whole other element, this person should not be out here doing this right now, that I think is just really enjoyable to watch.

Austin Abrams in ‘Resident Evil’ (2026) Dusan Martincek/Sony Pictures Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection

DEADLINE: What do you think about your “scream king” status? It seems like you’ve really solidified that with Tragedy Girls, Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark and Weapons.

ABRAMS: I don’t really have any feelings about that, one way or the other. I guess that’s just kind of an idea and a concept, so nothing really strong comes to mind. You’re just doing the work that feels interesting at the time, especially working with Zach and doing two back-to-back, basically. But no, I don’t have too many thoughts around that. Things will all ebb and flow. It’s not a goal in mind, at least.

title: As Fall Approaches, Camden International Film Festival Spends Time With ‘The Illusion Of An Everlasting Summer’
summary: The 2026 Camden International Film Festival in mid-coast Maine has reached its midway point. The prestigious all-documentary festival continues Saturday with the world premieres of Sierra Pettengill’s Argonauts at the End of History and Nicole Costa’s No Money No Honey. Friday saw the world premieres of two other nonfiction features: Dependence, directed by Grace Harper […]
content:
The 2026 Camden International Film Festival in mid-coast Maine has reached its midway point.

The prestigious all-documentary festival continues Saturday with the world premieres of Sierra Pettengill’s Argonauts at the End of History and Nicole Costa’s No Money No Honey. Friday saw the world premieres of two other nonfiction features: Dependence, directed by Grace Harper Brighouse, and Windows of Time, directed by Hubert Taylor and Cyrus Moussavi.

The 22nd edition of the festival is once again attracting many of documentary’s most acclaimed filmmakers, including Oscar winner Alex Gibney, with his new film Musk; Oscar winner Laura Poitras with her short film They’re Here, co-directed by Rachel Lauren Mueller; two-time Academy Award winner Barbara Kopple with Union Town, and Oscar-shortlisted director Luke Lorentzen with Boatbuilders, about the meticulous crafting of a gorgeous 56-foot wooden sailboat at the Brooklin Boat Yard in Maine (the magnificent vessel was spotted Friday in Camden harbor).

Watch on Deadline

The Gibney, Poitras, Kopple, and Lorentzen films all headed to Camden from their world premieres at the Venice Film Festival just a few days ago. Screening on Thursday night was a film that bowed in August at the Locarno Film Festival: The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer (La ilusión de un verano sin fin) by the Argentinian photographer Alessandra Sanguinetti, making her directorial debut.

Cousins Guillermina “Guile” Aranciaga (left) and Belinda “Beli” Stutz in ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’ MUBI

The documentary invites viewers into the world of two captivating girls, cousins Guillermina “Guile” Aranciaga and Belinda “Beli” Stutz, growing up in a farming area of the Argentinian Pampas. Beginning in 1999, Sanguinetti followed the girls’ lives as they tended to the animals on the farm, frolicked in nearby waters, and engaged in flights of fancy and imagination – often playing dress up, sometimes with Beli in the role of a dashing young man, mascara applied to her upper lip to pass for a mustache.

Director Alessandra Sanguinetti in conversation with Zaina Bseiso, senior programmer of the Camden International Film Festival. Matthew Carey

At a Q&A following the screening moderated by CIFF Senior Programmer Zaina Bseiso, Sanguinetti explained that her original intention was to make a series of photographs about farm animals, “Seeing life through their eyes. And that’s where I met the girls’ grandmother that appeared in the film, and through the grandmother is how I met them.” Later, Sanguinetti shifted her focus to taking still images of Guile and Beli.

‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’ MUBI

“When I was photographing them, I felt like it wasn’t enough. I couldn’t hear them… I thought, ‘Photography’s just too flat. I have to film this,’” Sanguinetti explained. “I would put the video camera on the tripod and photograph them at the same time. And then I realized they were acting for the video camera. So, then I started playing with them saying, ‘Oh, why don’t we pretend this? Why don’t we pretend that?’ And it was just play between the three of us.”

The filmmaker continued, “I could tell they started feeling sort of like the stars of their own life with the video. When I was photographing them, I felt more like a little dictator. I was more precious with the light and the framing and all of that. And with the video it just felt free. With video, I feel like I’m living with the people… With photography… I feel like I’m watching from the outside. The video just made me feel that I was part of it all.”

Cousins Belinda “Beli” Stutz (left) and Guillermina “Guile” Aranciaga in ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’ MUBI

Remarkably, The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer follows Guile and Beli over a quarter of a century as they move from girlhood into young adulthood and adulthood. As is common with many documentary projects, the narrative took shape in the edit bay.

“I wasn’t sure what it was until I started editing. I had a certainty that it was them, it was the animals as witnesses, time, time, time, the grandmother,” Sanguinetti said. “But then with the editing, you just start seeing the threads, the patterns in the lives that you can’t see in the moment. Like Guillermina, that’s the most literal one. She’s been talking about being a spinster, being alone, since she’s nine. And a lot of things, like self-prophesizing things I discovered through the editing.”

Audiences in Locarno and now in Camden have seen the final version of the documentary. But the protagonists haven’t.

“Guillermina has seen versions of the film. She hasn’t seen it finished. And Belinda, I kept offering to show her as I was making different versions of it and she was like, ‘No, I don’t want to see it. I want to see it when it’s out,’” the director shared. “They know the material I have. They know I have infinite material of them. Belinda knows that she’s breastfeeding [her child]. So that’s not going to be a shock. What might be a shock for her is the arc because I created that. It’s faithful, but it’s missing 80-percent of their lives. This is just the story of them through my eyes, this little bit of their life.”

The Illusion of an Endless Summer next plays at the San Sebastián Film Festival in Spain and will screen in October at Film Fest Gent in Belgium, the Chicago International Film Festival, and Mill Valley in Northern California.

The Camden International Film Festival continues through Sunday in the towns of Camden and Rockland. Prizes will be presented in two juried categories — the Harrell Award and the Cinematic Vision Award. The Fowlie Award, named for festival founder Ben Fowlie, will go to the audience choice for favorite feature-length documentary, and comes with a $10,000 prize.

title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico Journalists Denied White House Entry Following Donald Trump’s Announced Ban
summary: UPDATED: President Donald Trump is following through on pledge to ban journalists he doesn’t like from the White House: This morning, CNN and MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, as well as Politico announced that their journalists had been denied access to the White House grounds. Both networks announced this morning that their journalists were denied access […]
content:
UPDATED: President Donald Trump is following through on pledge to ban journalists he doesn’t like from the White House: This morning, CNN and MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, as well as Politico announced that their journalists had been denied access to the White House grounds.

Both networks announced this morning that their journalists were denied access and their White House press badges confiscated. Later, Politico reported that the same thing happened to one of its correspondents, Cheyenne Haslett.

At 10 a.m. ET, CNN announced it, like MS NOW earlier, had been denied access. The network’s White House correspondent Betsy Klein said she and a photographer attempted to enter the grounds as usual but were not allowed in.

CNN has released the following statement: “Early today, CNN journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.”

Watch on Deadline

Earlier, in a statement posted on social media today, MS NOW wrote, “Earlier this morning, MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars. MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy. We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters, and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the President, the administration, and the issues that impact the American people.”

Politico editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger wrote in an email to the newsroom, “We stand by her and all reporters covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights.”

Yesterday Trump announced that he intended to ban MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House due to what he claims are “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

This morning, MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner appeared on screen to detail what happened when she arrived at the White House, as did CNN’s Klein later.

Watch the reports from Gardner and Klein below.

“I showed my badge,” she said, “and then when I was inside where we have magnetometers, I attempted to scan my badge, which we have to do to get into the White House grounds. It did not work. There was a red beeping light, and so the officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled. I asked why I could not get inside. He said it was above him.”

Gardner said an MS NOW photographer also was denied entry and had a badge confiscated, although an MS NOW producer was able to gain White House entry.

Gardner added that MS NOW journalists were permitted on the White House grounds yesterday, and that today’s actions were the first stemming from Trump’s threats.

CNN’s Klein reported her nearly identical experience, with her badge setting off an alarm and being confiscated. She said White House security referred her to the White House press team.

“I asked him if he could provide an explanation as to why it had been deactivated,” Klein said on-air to CNN’s Kasie Hunt. “He said he had no further information. I asked him once more if he had any more details he could share with me, and he said that I should be referred to the White House Press Office.”

She added that CNN reporters would continue reporting on White House business. “We can do our job anywhere,” she said.

In Trump’s first term in 2018, the White House revoked the credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then working for CNN. The network sued, and a federal judge ruled in their favor. The judge, Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, concluded that Acosta was not granted due process when his hard pass was revoked.

This term, the White House restricted the Associated Press from the press pool, the smaller group of correspondents who are given access to the Oval Office and other areas with limited space. The White House cited the AP’s refusal to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, per Trump’s executive order. The AP sued, and a federal judge ruled that the restriction violated the First Amendment.

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden, another Trump appointee, wrote, “The Court simply holds that under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists — be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere — it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints. The Constitution requires no less.”



The decision is on appeal.

Trump has been clear that his denial of access is over news coverage. He told reporters on Friday, “There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposefully negative stories. If they want to write them, that’s fine, but I do not have to let them into my, into the people’s house.”

Here is @betsy_klein's account of how she found out the government had deactivated her White House press pass. pic.twitter.com/j4AwhsJRUd — Brian Stelter (@brianstelter) September 19, 2026

BREAKING: MS NOW denied access to the White House. Statement from MS NOW. https://t.co/TWT3ejfW7w via @YouTube — MS NOW (@MSNOWNews) September 19, 2026

title: Singer Aaron Rowe Defends Ed Sheeran After Dropping Out of Tour: ‘It Was Human F—ing Error’
