summary: Aaron Rowe, who was one of the opening acts on Ed Sheeran’s tour before pulling out after Macklemore’s dismissal over his support for Palestine, has now issued an impassioned defense of the singer. “I think you are all focusing on the wrong person here. All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that. […]
content:
Aaron Rowe, who was one of the opening acts on Ed Sheeran’s tour before pulling out after Macklemore’s dismissal over his support for Palestine, has now issued an impassioned defense of the singer.

“I think you are all focusing on the wrong person here. All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that. When you really should be focusing on the likes of Robert Kraft. You really should be focusing on the Zionist lobbies that are trying to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide, the genocide that is happening in Palestine right now by Israel,” said Rowe in a video posted to his Instagram account Friday.

He continued: “Look, I know Ed’s statement could have been a lot better, and I do think that Macklemore shouldn’t have been pulled off the tour. I fully believe it was panic station over there, and they rushed the decision because they didn’t know what to fucking do because they were getting it from all angles. That’s a mistake… I haven’t had a chance to fucking talk to Ed too much, but I fully believe he knows that was a mistake.”

Popular on Variety

Rowe went on to point out that most of the artists in Sheeran’s opening lineup support Palestine. “Look who’s on the fucking lineup, yeah? Beoga, the most pro-Palestine group out there…. fully pro-Palestine, fucking Macklemore. Need I say more? Me, everyone knows my fucking stance on Palestine. Like, if Ed Sheeran was a fucking Zionist, why would he have all these fucking people on the fucking tour? It was human fucking error.”

The Irish singer-songwriter’s video comes as Sheeran continues to receive backlash for Macklemore’s removal from the tour. In addition to Rowe, Finneas, another opener, also dropped out of the tour. When Rowe dropped out, he acknowledged that Sheeran had “changed my life,” a point he honed in on again in this video.

“I know Ed Sheeran has done so much for so many fucking people, including artists like me, who he’s literally changed their entire lives. All he has inside of him is kindness. That is who Ed Sheeran is. And yes, like every other human being, he makes fucking mistakes.”

Rowe concluded: “You should be using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere. Someone who tried to shut down free speech. Someone who tried to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide. That’s what you should be using your energy on, not fucking Ed Sheeran, for fuck’s sake.”

For the main event, Burmese fighter Joshua Van (17-2-0) defends his flyweight title belt against Brazilian Alexandre Pantoja (30-6-0) in a marquee match. It’s scheduled for […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

After Islam Makhachev defended his welterweight title against Ian Machado Garry during UFC 330 in August, the Ultimate Fighting Championship travels from Philadelphia to Los Angeles for UFC 331. For the main event, Burmese fighter Joshua Van (17-2-0) defends his flyweight title belt against Brazilian Alexandre Pantoja (30-6-0) in a marquee match. It’s scheduled for five rounds.

On Saturday, Sept. 19, UFC 331: Van vs. Pantoja takes place at Crypto.com Arena in L.A., California. The event starts at 5 p.m. ET/2 p.m. PT, while the main card is set to begin at 9 p.m. ET/6 p.m. PT.

In late 2025, Joshua Van defeated Alexandre Pantoja in 26 seconds to win the UFC Flyweight Championship belt during UFC 323. Van has reigned as champion for nearly a year, while Pantoja worked to get back into the octagon to reclaim the title. title: Orville Peck Dedicates Performance to ‘All the Gay Cowboys’: ‘We Exist, We Walk Among You’
summary: Orville Peck made his headlining debut at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night. But it wasn’t the first time the country singer performed at the legendary amphitheater. He performed at the outdoor venue during Willie Nelson’s 90th birthday celebration in 2023. About a year later, Peck, who is openly gay, and Nelson duetted on a […]
content:
Orville Peck made his headlining debut at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night. But it wasn’t the first time the country singer performed at the legendary amphitheater.

He performed at the outdoor venue during Willie Nelson’s 90th birthday celebration in 2023.

About a year later, Peck, who is openly gay, and Nelson duetted on a cover of “Cowboys Are Frequently Secretly Fond of Each Other,” Latin country musician Ned Sublette’s 1981 song about same-sex love and lust among the boots and saddles set. The Nelson collaboration is featured on Peck’s 2024 duets album “Stampede.”

“It’s a song that’s very pertinent to my interests,” Peck said, inspiring cheers and applause from the audience. “It’s about gay cowboys. I don’t know if you notice, but I’m a gay cowboy.”

Popular on Variety

He continued, “We exist. We walk among you. There’s probably some here. I think I see a bunch.”

Raising an arm into the air, Peck said, “Let’s dedicate this one to the incredible, incredible Mr. Willie Nelson. I’m sure he’s enjoying an edible somewhere.”

Before launching into the song, Peck said, “This is for all the gay cowboys.”

The song includes Nelson crooning, “And I believe to my soul that inside every man there’s the feminine/And inside every lady there’s a deep manly voice loud and clear/And a cowboy may brag about things that he’s done with his women/But the ones who brag loudest are the ones that are most likely queer.”

The two sing together, “Cowboys are frequently secretly fond of each other/What do you think all them saddles and boots was about?/And there’s many a cowboy who don’t understand the way that he feels for his brother/And inside every cowboy there’s a lady that’d love to slip out.”

A music video for the track was filmed on Nelson’s Luke Ranch in Spicewood, Texas.

The concert also included a surprise appearance by Noah Cyrus, who joined Peck on stage to duet on “Atchafalaya.” A music video for Peck and Cyrus’ “How Far Will We Take It?” featured a pre-“Heated Rivalry” François Arnaud in a love-triangle storyline.

During his encore, Peck covered Dolly Parton’s “I Will Always Love You.” Opening acts included Lucius and Deloyd Elze.

Friday also marked the release of Peck’s fourth studio album, “Mule.” The album chronicles his battle with addiction before getting sober in 2023.

“These are very deep wounds,” Peck told me during an interview on Wednesday. “What better therapy is there than getting up and being able to express these songs? Then there are people listening and relating, and they’re sharing their pain. It’s a spiritual experience.”

In the song, “Ring the Bell,” Peck sings of kissing an unidentified pro football “Raiders player.”

“I did receive permission to sing that lyric from the subject in question, and he was very thrilled,” Peck said. “I told him, ‘Look, I’m gonna keep it sort of ambiguous and mysterious, but I would like to include this in this song.’ He was very, very honored.”

He added, “I would never have done it if it were somebody who was hiding or fearful of it coming out. This person would have probably allowed me to say their name if I wanted, but I didn’t think it was necessary. People can use their own common sense and discovery to try to figure out who it may be, but that’s all I’ll say.”

title: Spain’s National Film Prize Honoree Carmen Machi: ‘Acting Has Been the Driving Force of My Happiness and Also a Balm for My Darkest Moments’
summary: Actor Carmen Machi, best known for her role as Aida in the wildly popular Spanish series “7 Lives” and spin-off “Aida” as well as her pivotal roles in Almodóvar classics “Talk to Her” and “Broken Embraces,” received the 2026 National Film Prize at the San Sebastian Festival, a prestigious honor that has been granted to […]
content:
Actor Carmen Machi, best known for her role as Aida in the wildly popular Spanish series “7 Lives” and spin-off “Aida” as well as her pivotal roles in Almodóvar classics “Talk to Her” and “Broken Embraces,” received the 2026 National Film Prize at the San Sebastian Festival, a prestigious honor that has been granted to a bevy of Spanish greats, including Oscar winners and nominees Penélope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Antonio Banderas, director Fernando Trueba (“Belle Epoque”) and El Deseo producer Esther Garcia, among many others since the Spanish Ministry of Culture launched it in 1980.

The award, presented by the Institute of Cinematography and Audiovisual Arts (ICAA), an agency under the Ministry of Culture, comes with a €30,000 ($34,437) prize.

Popular on Variety

In remarks before Machi came up to accept her award, Diego San José, the co-screenwriter of Spanish blockbuster “Spanish Affair” (“8 apellidos vascos”) in which Machi also starred, quipped: “I would say that Carmen is already part of our national heritage, like an aqueduct or like the Burgos Cathedral, but much better preserved than those two examples

“Besides, Carmen has something that neither an aqueduct nor a cathedral has, and that is that when we look at you, we see ourselves. Today, Carmen, as you go up to collect this award, you carry inside you all those women you have portrayed from the beginning: Your mother, your aunts and your neighbors accompany you.”

Machi also starred in “Celeste,” created by San José, which won her best actress as well as best series at Series Mania’s International Panorama last year. Superb in Carlota Pereda’s Sundance hit “Piggy,” Machi has demonstrated her chops for drama and melodrama, incarnating the oldest version of a heinously messianic mother in “La Mesías,” from Javier Ambrossi and Javirr Calvo, now behind “La Bola Negra.”

Spanish Minister of Culture Ernest Urtasun said that he had rarely received so many messages of delight when the ministry announced in June that the award would go to “a truly great actress of innate talent and extraordinary versatility,” whom he compared with such figures as Anna Magnani, the late Marisa Paredes and Julieta Serrano.

Said Machi: “I’ve always been fascinated by cinema,” relating how her bedroom was filled with clippings and stills of Marlon Brando and how she would hide behind the sofa at the black-and-white movies her parents were watching, and how, struck by a scene, she would run alone to her room and try to recreate scenes in front of the mirror, trying to feel what the protagonist felt, often ending up in tears.

“It was something that fascinated me. It gave me a strange sense of freedom. I was just a little girl. Then I would leave the room and go back to waiting. I never imagined that that game, which was a refuge to overcome my insecurity and my shyness, would become my craft and my way of life,” she confessed.

“This profession has given me a wonderful life. It is and has been the driving force of my happiness and also a balm for my darkest moments.”

John Hopewell contrinuted to this article.

title: Miley’s ‘Bass Persuades’ Is Pretty and Passable, but Surprisingly Light on Bass… or Persuasion: Album Review
summary: The title track and first single from Miley Cyrus’ “Bass Persuades” was a classic act of misdirection, we now learn. Released two and a half weeks prior to the album, the song promised a tenth album full of bangers (with an S or Z, take your pick), mildly scolding the young people for not being […]
content:
The title track and first single from Miley Cyrus‘ “Bass Persuades” was a classic act of misdirection, we now learn. Released two and a half weeks prior to the album, the song promised a tenth album full of bangers (with an S or Z, take your pick), mildly scolding the young people for not being interested enough in the dance floor — whatsa matter with kids today? — and aiming to redirect them there with a combination of throbbing rhythms and spoken-word instructions loosely borrowed from the catalogs of Madonna and Lady Gaga. For better or worse, it seemed as if Cyrus was going to drop some of her stylistic eccentricities, along with her last name, and deliver a pure club record.

But that was our supposition, not hers, even if borrowing the single’s title for the whole project did seem to make a promise the full record isn’t prepared to deliver on. The new album, which came out Friday sans press previews, opens with “Bass Persuades” being followed by a second number in a faintly similar vein, “Different Religion,” but then it rarely returns to that territory until the 38-minute collection wraps up with its 10th track, a revved-up and unnecessary remix of the title track. What comes in between includes a surprising number of love ballads and a few odd outliers. It’s eclectic, but not “Endless Summer Vacation”-level eclectic. One thing no one will ever remember about it is the album having a surfeit of bass.

Popular on Variety

So how about persuasion? It’s a little light on that, too — pleasant, passable and occasionally compelling, but slight, with hooks that never quite reach the peaks you hope for out of a great pop song, and a bit of an “is that all there is?” feeling at the end of its relatively short length. It will be no one’s favorite Miley album, nor anyone’s least favorite. The overall feel is of something enjoyable on its own terms but a little undercooked in almost every regard, as if the star had been in a rush to deliver product to her new label, even as its primarily lovestruck lyrics — some of which are quite good — surely do reflect where the singer is at in her off-screen life. But for those who admired her previous album, the barely year-old “Something Beautiful,” for finding a cool and interesting retro aesthetic and pretty much sticking with it, “Bass Persuades” seems kind of centerless, more like an in-between project meant to mark time between bolder musical statements than any kind of arrival.

The core message of the album seems to be that things are going pretty well — make that extremely well — with fiancée Maxx Morando, who is a writer-producer collaborator on all but two of the tracks. Hearing Miley in a besotted state turns up mixed results. The third track, “Let’s Get Married,” is an abrupt left turn from the two bang-ier numbers that precede it into synthy easy listening/AC flavors, and what it delivers is not worth the whiplash; while it will probably be heard at some weddings to come, there may be a lot of attendees who would be itchy to please skip ahead to the vows.

Fortunately, that syrupy aside is a low point from which the album fairly quickly recovers. “Orbit,” next up, is just as romantic but one of the collection’s better tracks, as a power ballad — or even just ballad, without so much emphasis on the power — that applies some clever turns of phrase and thought to what could be a tired metaphor. Her significant other is the center of her solar system: “Place a marble on the floor / When you walk in the room, it’ll roll to you” is an image that makes for a lovely mash note.

The romantic reveries sometimes give way to things sillier and saucier. “Neon Signs” isn’t a particularly memorable tune unto itself, but the increasingly ridiculous spoken interactions between Cyrus and duet partner Andrew Wyatt may put a smile on your face before all is cooed and done. And/or make you cringe, since, as Wyatt murmurs at the end between the pair’s sexy bedroom oohs and aahs, “Some people think I’m creepy, but others think I’m just right.” An album this immersed in relatively straightforward love songs could use this moment of awkward verbal snogging.

The album’s best song, “Aftermath,” arrives halfway through, and as the one track that really accelerates into something more impassioned, it would have made an ideal climax for the record, if not for one problem: it’s the only sad song on the album, and thus would be a strange way to wrap up an otherwise cheerful collection. Still, it’s good to know that Miley can take a philosophical moment to ponder The End of All Things — including, inherently, her relationship — as a sort of intermission in an album that’s otherwise characterized by romantic buoyancy.

There is one other dark track on the album, sure to be its most talked-about number — “Innocent Ways,” which has Cyrus singing at length about a sibling, which many listeners will presume to be Noah. “I want better for my sister / She calls me only when it’s late night and she’s high / Her mind is spinning / Eight nights in a row / She’s been in a crisis / She looks just like me when she cries.” There needs to be some form of crisis to offer some dramatic tension in an album that doesn’t have much, so if she has to borrow the angst from a family member, fair enough. Amusingly, Miley seems to resent her sister for wearing a Blondie T-shirt without actually listening to Blondie music. More intriguingly, she sings, “Fall out from the fame / Claim my mother’s maiden name,” suggesting that this is a family that thinks a lot about last names and how to claim or ditch them. Besides just being legitimately lyrically fascinating, “Innocent Ways” is also the album’s most heated banger — and working out deep-rooted sibling issues over the din of the club is a concept we can get behind.

“Snow” ends the album on a sweeter, if relatively inconsequential-feeling, note, and ought to be the record’s closer, but then Miley evidently thought nine is not enough and makes it an even 10 with the remix of the title track no one asked for. Ending with the most obvious form of filler is not the best look, although, as a non-fan of the original track, I could personally appreciate the amphetamine version of the number a little more.

Maybe the album seems so short because Miley has booked Hollywood Bowl shows themed around it, and those will be awfully short performances if she sticks primarily to these nine numbers, which presumably she won’t. It doesn’t feel like “Bass Persuades” is going to be an Event Album for Cyrus fans; her followers are notorious for finding her records polarizing, to the extent that an album like “Something Beautiful” earns comments calling it either one of her best or one of her weakest — and yet it wouldn’t be surprising if the fan base is unanimous in finding this new one belongs somewhere in the mid-section of any ranking. “Not bad” is probably not the reaction being sought when someone starts afresh in a business part of their career. But say this for her: she’s someone who never makes the same album twice. So if this one is neither overwhelming nor underwhelming but just kind of whelming, it won’t diminish the appetite for what mode she’ll be in come Miley Mach 11.

title: Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present”
summary: Enjoying the show? Then please put away your cellphone. That was the message delivered by Cate Blachett from the London stage of National Theatre’s Lyttelton Theatre after the curtain call of Electra/Persona, the new play written and directed by Benedict Andrews that combines the Sophocles tragedy Electra with Ingmar Bergman’s Persona. Still in her stage […]
content:
Enjoying the show? Then please put away your cellphone.

That was the message delivered by Cate Blachett from the London stage of National Theatre’s Lyttelton Theatre after the curtain call of Electra/Persona, the new play written and directed by Benedict Andrews that combines the Sophocles tragedy Electra with Ingmar Bergman’s Persona.

Still in her stage costume of a black t-shirt and baggy black trousers, Blanchett, who stars opposite Nina Hoss in the play, spoke in a heartfelt and calm manner directly to the audience in an address that has been widely shared on social media. (Watch it below.)

Said Blanchett, “There are few places on this planet where we can simply be together and be present. I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way – but for anyone who is filming the show, please don’t, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us. So thank you very much.”

Watch on Deadline

The speech was greeted enthusiastically by the National Theatre audience.

The play, which runs through October 10, has Blanchett and Hoss sharing the roles of Electra/Elisabeth and Clytemnestra/Alma, with a coin toss determining who plays what role on any given night.

Here’s how the National Theatre describes the production as “a thrilling production [that] fuses ancient myth and modern psychology in a powerful exploration of identity, and the fragile line between who we are and who we play.”

The synopsis continues, “Electra. A daughter consumed by grief and rage, clinging to the idea of justice as her world comes apart. Persona. During a performance of Electra, an actress suddenly falls silent. What follows is a rupture: two women drawn into an intense, unsettling encounter where speech breaks down and the boundaries between self and role give way.”

In addition to Blanchett and Hoss, the cast features Ella Lily Hyland.

title: Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic”
summary: The Motion Picture Editors Guild is praising California’s bill offering tax incentives for productions that shoot outside the state but bring their post work to California. The bill, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom yesterday, expands the state’s film and television tax credit program and creates a new tax credit to support workers in all areas […]
content:
The Motion Picture Editors Guild is praising California’s bill offering tax incentives for productions that shoot outside the state but bring their post work to California.

The bill, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom yesterday, expands the state’s film and television tax credit program and creates a new tax credit to support workers in all areas of post-production, including picture editorial, sound, music, visual effects, and finishing.

“This is a historic day for Editors Guild members and for California’s film and TV workers more broadly,” said Editors Guild National Executive Director Scott George in a statement today. “AB 186 ensures that the California Film and TV Tax Credit Program continues to drive the recovery of our industry in its historic home, while AB 2319 will complement the program by making sure that even projects shooting outside of our state can come back to California to employ Editors Guild members in post-production.

George also praised Assemblymember Nick Schultz and “all the legislators who recognize the value of entertainment industry workers to our state’s economy, to the California IATSE Council for its powerful advocacy, and, of course, to our partners in the California Post Alliance.”

Watch on Deadline

Newsom signed the bill AB2319 into law Friday, also signing AB186, which exempts certain productions from caps on tax credits.

The post-production bill was overwhelmingly passed the Assembly and Senate at the end of the legislative session, receiving broad, bipartisan support. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass advocated for the measure, as did other local leaders in Southern California. Initial funding of $10 million will be allocated to get the program started

The Editors Guild and the California Post Alliance co-sponsored the bill, which they say is “a necessary step to level the playing field for editors, assistant editors, mixers and other post-production workers who have seen their work lured away to other states and countries with powerful tax incentives.”

“We owe this victory not only to lawmakers and, of course, to Gov. Newsom, but also to the activism of our members and partners,” said F. Hudson Miller, President of the Editors Guild. “Post-production professionals work behind the scenes in dark rooms, unseen, to craft entertainment that dazzles. But for months our union has asked members to get out there and make some noise in order to save our industry. They absolutely delivered.”

The post-production bill complements California’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program 4.0, passed last year, which provides $750 million to incentivize in-state filming and address runaway production to other areas.

Newsom said in a statement, “California is the nation’s entertainment capital. It is the home of storytellers, dreamers, artists, entrepreneurs, and creators who define culture for the rest of the world. This legislation protects the extraordinary people who make this industry possible and makes it unmistakably clear: California is still the future of film and television. We have the talent. We have the infrastructure. We have the creative community. And we have an ecosystem that simply cannot be replicated anywhere else.”

title: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Creator Reacts to Netflix Cancellation: ‘I Hope Serenity Will Always Have a Place in Your Heart’
summary: Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson is looking back on the romantic drama’s 5 Season run. “Living in Serenity for five seasons has been a privilege and a blessing,” Anderson shared in the caption of an Instagram post Saturday. “The people I’ve met and […]
content:
Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson is looking back on the romantic drama’s 5 Season run.

“Living in Serenity for five seasons has been a privilege and a blessing,” Anderson shared in the caption of an Instagram post Saturday. “The people I’ve met and worked with — our incredible writers, cast, crew, executives, and producers — have touched my heart and changed my life.”

She continued: “And our fans have been amazing in their passion for our characters. Thank you all. Though our journey has sadly come to an end, I hope Serenity will always have a place in your heart. Keep pouring it out!”

Popular on Variety

The Netflix show first premiered on the platform in May 2020, and starred JoAnna Garcia Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley. Originally adapted from the book series by New York Times best-selling author Sherryl Woods, the streamer announced that the show continuously ranked among Netflix’s Global Top 10 in over 60 countries after announcing its return for a fifth season in 2025.

The “comfort drama,” as described by Netflix, followed the lifelong friendship between Maddie (Swisher), Dana Sue (Elliott), and Helen (Headley) “as they juggle relationships, family and careers in the charming small town of Serenity, S.C.”

Though “Sweet Magnolias” may be coming to an end, Netflix announced that Swisher and Anderson would be teaming for a new drama series titled “Ladies of the House.”

Variety previously reported that Anderson will serve as showrunner, with Swisher potentially starring and executive producing with Kate Gordon under their Rolling Clover banner, alongside executive producers at Black Label Media.

The logline reads, “When the charismatic owner of a winery dies unexpectedly, his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives. Good friends and good wine will aid in the journey to hang on to the winery, but what matters most is that they find a way to hang on to each other.”

title: Henry Winkler Says His Name Was Cut From ‘Scream’ Poster Because ‘You Were the Fonz’ and It Would ‘Knock the Balance of Horror Off’
summary: Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days. The “Happy Days” star played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original “Scream” film, which went on to become one of the most successful horror franchises. But despite his character’s entrance receiving applause during screen tests for the […]
content:
Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days.

The “Happy Days” star played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original “Scream” film, which went on to become one of the most successful horror franchises. But despite his character’s entrance receiving applause during screen tests for the 1996 movie, Winkler revealed the studio refused to put his name on the poster.

“The studio comes to me and says, ‘We can’t put your name on the film. We cannot put you anywhere near the poster,’” Winkler said in an interview for “In Depth With Graham Besinger.” When he asked why, the studio said, “Well, you were the Fonz, and you will knock the balance of horror off if we let them know you’re in it.”

Popular on Variety

Although it left him feeling “insulted,” the actor didn’t overtly protest the studio’s decision.

“I said, ‘OK. What can I do?’ I went home upset,” the actor said. “I was bewildered a little bit.”

He later learned the same people who had informed him his name wouldn’t be used on the poster were also the ones who asked him if he would do press for the film’s release. Winkler ultimately agreed, noting he obliged for himself, director Wes Craven and the movie as a whole.

Now, looking back 30 years later, Winkler said the experience taught him to navigate the unknown.

“That’s the lesson. You just show up,” he said, also pointing out that “you have no idea what’s going to happen, but that’s out of your control.”

“Scream” also starred Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, David Arquette, Drew Barrymore and Matthew Lillard. The franchise’s latest film, “Scream 7,” became the highest-grossing installment with $176.9 million.

title: Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Were Clowned for Buying the Staten Island Ferry. They Just Proved Everyone Wrong.
summary: “There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.” As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Ferry Comedy Show, a reel from The Free Press popped up. Professor Arthur Brooks was making the case that “Gen Z is perhaps the most risk-averse generation in history.” Now, […]
content:
“There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.”

As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Ferry Comedy Show, a reel from The Free Press popped up. Professor Arthur Brooks was making the case that “Gen Z is perhaps the most risk-averse generation in history.”

Now, I’m no psychologist. I’m a social media editor. And I theorize that some of that fear Brooks describes comes from our overexposure to a digital world that, seemingly, has all the answers. And when someone makes a decision outside the purview of algorithmic logic — like buying an abandoned ferry for $280,000 at a city auction — they are at the mercy of, well, being completely clowned.

Popular on Variety

That’s exactly what the news cycle did to Pete Davidson and Colin Jost after they joined a group of investors to buy the decommissioned John F. Kennedy in 2022. Built in 1965, the JFK was the oldest ferry in the Staten Island fleet when it was retired last August due to mechanical failures. Davidson and Jost intended to transform the vessel into a floating entertainment venue.



“Davidson, who’s no longer with SNL, might need to call his agent to book those gigs — turning the 57-year-old ship into a nightspot is likely to cost millions,” The New York Daily News reported. The headline read: “Retired NY Ferry Bought by Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Is Full of Asbestos, Roaches, Say Ex-Crew Members.”

The social media hate laid on thick, too: “Have you heard of the hottest club in the city?” one person tweeted (per the LA Times). “It’s called ‘Tetanus’ and it’s located in the rusted belly of a decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. You’ll dance the night away while also always being just moments away from drowning.”

Years had passed without hearing about the ferry until I got an unexpected email in my inbox: “EMBARGOED: Invite to NYC’s Most Unexpected Comedy Club From Pete Davidson and Colin Jost.”

As it turned out, the “SNL” comedians partnered with Snapple to give New Yorkers an “unexpectedly refreshing break from the daily grind,” transforming their vessel into the Snapple Staten Island Ferry for a free, one-night-only floating comedy show.

Could the comedians have listed tickets for $200 a pop and still packed the ferry? Undoubtedly. Instead, they dropped a limited batch of free tickets at 3 p.m. each day (Sept. 3-8). The resulting buzz and scramble among young New Yorkers to secure tickets (not totally unlike the IMAX 70mm frenzy surrounding “The Odyssey”) was much more valuable than the low six figures a sold-out show might have grossed at the door.



Those lucky enough to make it aboard became a test audience for two brand comebacks, each fiercely looking to win over a younger generation before betting on a much bigger, more calculated swing.

The first is Snapple, which started phasing out its signature glass bottles in 2017, replacing them with plastic (the transition was complete by 2021). The company justified the brand’s “massive makeover” as a decision made “with the evolution of sustainability in mind.” The operational savings from slashing the cost of manufacturing a bottle to roughly a third of what it once was probably looked pretty savory to the big-wig execs at Keurig Dr Pepper. Consumers weren’t as quenched.

Sean K Fitzpatrick

Snapple eventually budged in the fall of 2025, launching a limited glass-bottle revival at select bodegas and retailers across New York, citing a “demand for nostalgia from an OVERWHELMING number of consumers.” The brand has yet to commit to a wider or permanent return, but it was clearly testing the waters with this major brand activation.

Hosting Snapple’s revival party was Davidson and Jost’s own comeback project to replenish the New York comedy scene, taking the form of a floating, popsicle-orange vessel. They once played the purchase off as a joke on “SNL,” with Jost quipping, “We thought the whole thing through” (sarcasm implied). But four years later, this one-night-only comedy show offered them a real opportunity to float their idea.

The main room was packed. Because the ferry, naturally, didn’t have one big corridor, an overflow room projected a live feed of the main stage (shaped like a blocky ‘T’).

“You’re media, right?” an event coordinator asked me. “Yes!” I had zoned out. “Then we better put you up here.” She whisked me straight to the front and pointed at two young women, who immediately jolted to their feet and shuffled toward the far end of the bench running parallel to the stage.



“I, uh, I’m sorry I took your seats,” I told the two women as I sidestepped past them. They glanced at each other and giggled. “It’s okay,” one of them said. “Trust me.”

It took me a couple of minutes to figure out what she meant. Then I pulled out my phone to take a picture of the stage: a black barstool, a (glass!) Peach Tea Snapple and a mic stand. I wasn’t just in the front row. I was in the hot seat. The very hot seat, directly under the mic stand. Stage lights beamed down on me, and the ferry cabin itself was extremely muggy. (I guess in Davidson and Jost’s master plan, A/C hit the cutting room floor.)

The room skewed younger millennials and older Gen Z. Most toward the front looked like (or probably were) influencers who’ll look good on camera. Usually, I’ll recognize at least a few media friends in a crowd like this. Not here. I tried making friendly banter with the dude sitting next to me. He was cordial, but his energy read: Nope.

At nine o’clock sharp, the lights went dark. Davidson and Jost emerged from beneath the neon Snapple Island Ferry sign to rapturous applause. This would be the first and last time we’d see the two co-hosts all night.

I’ve encountered Davidson and Jost in the wild before, but this tight vantage point popped any illusion of celebrity. Picture sitting in the front row of a movie theater.

“This is something we’ve wanted to do for like five years, so thank you guys for coming out,” Davidson opened. “And thank you to our sponsor, Snapple.” After holding a beat for the applause, Davidson exclaimed, “The glass is back, baby!”

Jost added: “I also feel like we should acknowledge our former sponsor: my accountant’s suicide note.” He smirked. “Snapple asked me to say this.”

They then turned to the first of three lingering storylines from the news cycle they clearly wanted to address. First, the aforementioned clowning.



“The amount of shit that people have talked,” Davidson said. “Well, suck it!”

“Everyone feeling hot and nauseous? That’s a good feeling,” Jost asked the crowd before moving on to news topic numero dos. “Obviously we’ll get going soon. We’re gonna stop at the Strait of Hormuz.” But when Jost looked over at Davidson to tee up the next punchline, it became clear the geopolitical reference sailed right over his head.

“I like how you thought I would know what that is,” Davidson quipped back. He glanced down at the shot clock. 8:17 remaining. The sweat was palpable.

“I love that this is our body language,” Davidson said, leaning into their candid awkwardness as he and Jost stood marooned on opposite ends of the oversized T-shaped stage. “It’s truly like we’re waiting for someone to start a fight.”

Laughing along with the crowd, Jost admitted, “We don’t know exactly what to do.” The audience roared. That unvarnished honesty, the willingness to take themselves down a notch, clearly resonated with the audience of young people accustomed to spending hours each day swiping through content engineered to mask imperfection.

“We have an incredible show. There are so many great comedians here,” Jost said. “Macklemore is here tonight.” The crowd erupted. Jost stalled on a few uhs, his eyes scanning the room as he debated whether it was worth taking the joke any further.

Davidson took advantage of the moment. “You wanted to make a stance tonight, right?” he poked. “Colin was talking mad shit backstage, dude. He was like, ‘Macklemore doesn’t have shit on what I’m about to say.’”

Red in the face, Jost quickly rowed back to safer waters. “So, in other news…” From there, the remainder of their opener centered on Davidson’s recent concussion. But the lineup of fierce rising comics (with considerably less to lose) didn’t shy away from the insecurities and taboos their Gen Z audience might be too anxious to confront.

Matt Richards, who served as emcee for the night (effectively filling the role many of us presumed Davidson and Jost would play), set the tone for the night by chugging an entire Snapple in one go and then telling a story of how he tried to suck his own penis as a teenager. “Happy to say it didn’t work out,” Richards said. “If it did, I wouldn’t be here.” In an alternate timeline, he’d “live under a bridge and suck my own dick all day.”

As the crowd observed Richards, he gauged their reactions, taking the temperature of how far he could push them. The other comics were about to dive into some risqué material — he was just warming them up.

Richards wiped a bulk of sweat from his forehead. The humidity was becoming hard to ignore. Playfully, he advised Davidson and Jost to sort out the A/C situation before the next show. That’s what I was thinking.

When Chris Rock sat down with Variety’s Selome Hailu for his first in-depth interview since “The Slap,” he recalled “dying a death” during a stand-up set in Oakland in ’96. He was workshopping his controversial “Black People Versus N—s” bit, which would eventually appear in his landmark HBO special “Bring the Pain” that helped catapult Rock into rock-star comic status.

“People wanted to fight because I didn’t have it right yet,” Rock explained in his cover story interview. “You gotta go over the line to find the line. That’s what people don’t understand. When a comedian gets in trouble for saying something at the club, it’s like, ‘Dude, that’s what the club’s for.’”

Overcoming the fear of vulnerability, on both sides of the stage, is what makes the club special. A physical vessel where smartphones, despite the event’s plea for ample social coverage, were repeatedly told to stay tucked away.

At one point, a Staten Island photographer named Sean lowered his camera to snap a portrait on his phone of “Impractical Jokers” star Sal Vulcano mid-set. Vulcano immediately stopped. “No cellphones, sir,” he said. “It’s right up in my face.” Sean held up his DSLR, cutting Vulcano’s budding rant short.

“This guy’s just like- oh, you work here?” Vulcano said, his tone instantly changing. “Okay, you’re not fired. You’re great. I love you.”

Even an Impractical Joker, after hundreds of public challenges and punishments designed to push the limits of embarrassment, could still tense up when a cellphone camera caught him experimenting with a new bit. “That was the ending,” he told the crowd after telling a story about buying health insurance for his newborn. “I thought that would get a bigger laugh.”

The crowd loved it. He was hyper-fixated on grading his performance.

Perhaps that’s why crowd work is so effective. Is there any other setting better designed to experience a flash of public humiliation?



“I like this guy,” Richards said, pointing at me. “You look like a Disney villain.”

“Gaston!” He belted out a Disney song.

Caitlin Peluffo stormed the stage with material in the — let’s call it — advanced workshopping stages. After boldly announcing to the crowd that she was “dropping eggs,” she turned to ask if I knew what ovulating was.

I responded with a sarcastic “Ehh!” and bobbed my head. “Go figure,” she said. “I wouldn’t expect anything less from a man wearing khakis.”

After another minute or two of hyper-sexual jokes, she circled back to me.

“Do you like pussy?”

The camera whipped in my direction.

I froze. Then hit her with the same ambiguous emote.

Why did I just do that? I literally-

“You’re really wishy-washy on the answer, sir.”

“You gotta leave a little mystery.”

“Leave a little mystery?”

Gulp.

“Those pants aren’t leaving any mystery, I’ll tell you that,” she fired back. “You’re not circumcised, I can tell.” The crowd woo-ed. “That’s okay. I like me a full-body boy,” she continued. “I’m not an easy cum. You better crack your knuckles.”

I cracked my knuckles on both hands. She smiled. Peluffo got what she needed from me. Mercifully, she moved on to her next victim.

“Are you a tough cum or an easy cum?” she asked an attractive, reserved young woman. “Which one are you?” I had never seen a face more red in my entire life. “ANSWER THE FUCKING QUESTION!”

“I’m easy!” she finally blurted out.

“Fuck!” Peluffo shot back. “You’re probably cumming right now.”

On the way out, ferry workers dressed in sailor uniforms were handing departing guests free Snapple. I grabbed a glass peach tea and popped a squat on the pier. It really does taste better.

As I sat there taking in the night, the sound of clinking glass got louder and louder. Sure enough, I spotted a small procession bolting away from the boat with entire cases of Snapple.

I walked over and asked a few of the workers why they were giving them away. A woman with a dyed-blonde bob leaned toward me, lowering her voice.

“Please, take one now and leave before anyone sees you,” she said. “We need to get rid of all of these before the end of the night.”

title: ‘The Smell of Apples’ Review: A Sun-Soaked but Chilling Child’s-Eye View of Apartheid-Era Privilege and Denial
summary: Every surface period detail is present and correct to an eerie degree in “The Smell of Apples”: the gawkily short seasonal school uniforms, the ickily patterned kitchen tiles, the garden chairs like steel satellite dishes, the orange-and-brown daisy print that anyone of a certain age will recognize from sundry towels, mattresses and beach umbrellas. Production […]
content:
Every surface period detail is present and correct to an eerie degree in “The Smell of Apples“: the gawkily short seasonal school uniforms, the ickily patterned kitchen tiles, the garden chairs like steel satellite dishes, the orange-and-brown daisy print that anyone of a certain age will recognize from sundry towels, mattresses and beach umbrellas. Production designer Birrie Le Roux has crafted a pristine one-way time capsule to mid-1970s white South Africa; DP Lennert Hillege shoots it to softly lit, summer-burnt perfection. But there’s not a whisper of nostalgia to “The Smell of Apples,” director John Trengove‘s slowly, then suddenly, piercing evocation of affluent Afrikaner family life in that era, and the litany of egregious abuses and inequalities propping it up. It’s told through the eyes of a naïve 11-year-old boy, but there’s no halo to his innocence — just a growing awareness of how much he doesn’t know, none of it good.

Drawn from a well-regarded 1993 novel by Mark Behr that has become a popular set text in South African schools and universities, “The Smell of Apples” joins other recent literary adaptations like Oliver Hermanus’ “Moffie” and Embeth Davidtz’s “Don’t Let’s Go to the Dogs Tonight” in articulating the experiences of white people living inside an Apartheid bubble just on the verge of bursting. It’s a discomfiting and not especially fashionable point of focus; as in those films, we get only deliberately glancing, peripheral views of the black majority, their anguish never openly voiced. But these glaring blind spots, however hard to watch, are the point. “The Smell of Apples” intelligently demonstrates the effortful compartmentalization and denial that kept a system of white supremacy in place.

Popular on Variety

It’s a successful homecoming for Trengove, the Johannesburger who made a searing feature debut with the Sundance prizewinner “The Wound,” about ritual initiation and repressed sexuality in the traditional Xhosa community, before heading to the U.S. for his Jesse Eisenberg-starring follow-up “Manodrome,” a commendably ambitious but stifled manosphere study. “The Smell of Apples” resumes those films’ preoccupation with toxic masculine influence across generations, as well as their queer framing — though in a surprising departure from the novel, the latter is restricted to subtextual intimations.

Indeed, Trengove and co-writer Christopher Ciancimino’s impressively minimalist adaptation strips away much of Behr’s structural foreshadowing and underlining, including the novel’s flash-forwards to the child protagonist’s adult military service in the South African Border War. As it is, there’s an ample sense on screen of the plunging darkness toward which the country is headed, before any kind of dawn can establish itself, while it’s impossible not to feel the military’s past, present and future stranglehold on young Marnus Erasmus (Dawian van der Westhuizen, a real talent) at every turn. The only son of Johan (Hilton Pelser), the country’s youngest Army general, Marnus has a world of macho Afrikaner ideology to live up to, but already the boy, timid and fair and small for his age, suspects he might be a disappointment.

Johan generally treats Marnus with bluff good humor, though you can see the anxious scrutiny with which he sizes his son up — and when that worry gets the better of him, it emerges violently. Marnus’ best friend Frikkie (Wian Carstens) is a strapping, bullish lad, and when he’s over, which is often, Johan tends to treat him like another, stronger son — Marnus may feel a little frozen out by their bond, but he’s too shy and stoic to say so. “A father looks at his sons and sees his own shortcomings,” says enigmatic houseguest Mr. Smith (Alejandro Goic) to Marnus, and that’s no great comfort. Nor is Mr. Smith himself: a Chilean Army general, fresh from his role in the Pinochet coup, with whom Johan is covertly consulting about matters beyond Marnus’ understanding.

His homemaker mother Leonor (a superb Maude Sandham) and his 17-year-old sister Ilse (Karoline Watson) complete the immaculate family portrait, but there’s unrest there too. Ilse, a high-flyer at her conservative Afrikaans high school, is gradually catching wise to her father’s entitlement and cruelty, and to the injustices of the Apartheid government; Leonor puts on a brave face as she projects exactly the image her husband needs her to, but is unnerved by the barbed critiques of her liberal sister Karla (Inge Beckmann), who, by Johan’s decree, is not welcome in the family’s rambling, lushly landscaped Cape Town home.

The person who keeps that home shipshape, of course, is not Leonor but Doreen (Celeste Matthews Wannenburgh), the family’s black live-in maid — a longtime fixture whom Marnus takes too much for granted to fully realize his emotional attachment to her. (Her routine pet name for him is kleinbaas, which translates as “little boss,” and it’s said with weary affection but no irony.) The family, of course, would say Doreen is a valued part of the household, though her place in it is made quite clear when her orphaned teenage grandson Neville (Courtlin Baron) arrives to stay in her servants’ quarters, and is made most unwelcome by the master of the house. An exquisitely composed shot of Doreen, slumped in the kitchen half-light as she eavesdrops on the family’s dining-room discussion of Neville’s fate, encapsulates a world of upstairs-downstairs, black-white hierarchies.

Over a tight five-day timeline — as Marnus and Ilse finish school ahead of the December holidays, and the family prepares for their summer vacation — these various tensions impact one another in tacit but perhaps terminal ways. Some are mere faultlines, others crack into unavoidable conflicts, though they collectively unmask the ugly face of authority in South Africa in ways even the young, fanciful Marnus can’t blithely look past. The sins of the father are ultimately presented in a literal, stomach-churning slideshow that haphazardly alternates benign family snaps with gleeful photographic evidence of Johan’s war crimes.

It’s a queasy climactic setpiece — one that tests, in particular, the brittle wifely composure so precisely enacted by Sandham — though matters here don’t come quite as tidily to a head as they do in Behr’s novel, which culminated in a shocking act of transgression that you sense may be afoot in the film, though it’s never confirmed. “The Smell of Apples” isn’t less powerful for this elision: It works toward a state of forced family stability, everyone that bit more frightened and mistrusting of each other, but held stiffly in place by their own privilege and power. You can feel Trengove’s film, so beautifully crafted and impeccably paced, sometimes bristling against its own fine construction — anticipating the destruction of this walled-off, deeply ugly idyll.

title: Melissa Barrera Says It’s “So Beautiful” To See Support For Macklemore Speaking Up On Palestine: “I Didn’t Get That When It Happened To Me”
summary: Nearly three years after she was fired from the Scream franchise for speaking up in support of Palestinians, Melissa Barrera sees the tides changing. The actress recently expressed how “emotional” it made her to see Fennias and Ed Sheeran’s other openers dropping out of his Loop Tour in support of Macklemore, who was dropped from […]
content:
Nearly three years after she was fired from the Scream franchise for speaking up in support of Palestinians, Melissa Barrera sees the tides changing.

The actress recently expressed how “emotional” it made her to see Fennias and Ed Sheeran‘s other openers dropping out of his Loop Tour in support of Macklemore, who was dropped from the tour over his “Free Palestine” remarks.

“It was so beautiful to see Finneas and the band and all the opening acts pulling out in support of Macklemore. It made me emotional,” Barrera told the Associated Press. “You know, I didn’t get that when it happened to me. I didn’t have any of that happen. It was too soon. People were too scared. But it’s good to see that almost three years later, at least things have changed.”

Watch on Deadline

Spyglass fired Barrera in November 2023 over her social media posts on the Israel-Hamas conflict and the “atrocities being committed against Palestinians,” explaining the company has “zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech.”

Following her ousting, Jenna Ortega also exited the franchise, later noting that the sequel “was all kind of falling apart” without Barrera to play its new “final girl” Sam Carpenter. Director Christopher Landon dropped out of the project as well, citing “highly aggressive and really scary” death threats targeting his children.

Neve Campbell was then brought back to reprise her role as OG “final girl” Sidney Campbell for Scream 7 in March 2024, with original Scream (1996) writer Williamson on board to direct. She previously sat out Scream VI (2023) over the low pay offer.

As the seventh installment of the slasher franchise premiered at Paramount Studios in February, “Free Palestine” protesters lined up outside the entrance to the lot. Back when the first trailer for Scream 7 was released last October, fans quickly began slamming the movie on social media, calling for a boycott.

title: Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38
summary: Rose Friedman, an NPR editor and reporter who shaped the public radio network’s arts & culture coverage and co-created its popular reading guide Books We Love, died of cancer Thursday, September 17, at her home in New York City. She was 38. Her death was announced on-air by NPR’s Elizabeth Blair, who called Friedman one […]
content:
Rose Friedman, an NPR editor and reporter who shaped the public radio network’s arts & culture coverage and co-created its popular reading guide Books We Love, died of cancer Thursday, September 17, at her home in New York City. She was 38.

Her death was announced on-air by NPR’s Elizabeth Blair, who called Friedman one of the outlet’s finest journalists.

In an obituary and tribute posted on NPR’s website, Blair said, “Rose Friedman was an editor to the end. She said she wanted the second line of her obituary to acknowledge her role as a shop steward for SAG-AFTRA, the union that represents NPR’s editorial workers. She wanted the line to say that her ‘proudest achievement’ was helping convince NPR to increase its paid parental leave.”

Friedman joined NPR as an editorial assistant in her early 20s in 2010. She later served as an editor and reporter, becoming deeply sourced in the publishing industry, editing book reviews and features and writing appreciations of book world personalities such as author Herman Wouk and editor Sonny Mehta.

Watch on Deadline

She co-created what was initially called the Book Concierge, later renamed Books We Love. Reading over hundreds of titles nominated by NPR staff and critics, Friedman narrowed the list to the popular reader’s guide.

“She was voracious,” novelist Meg Wolitzer, who worked with Friedman on a number of NPR reviews and features, said to NPR. “What a gifted, delightful, brilliant, deeply kind person. And I would say a true enthusiast. I got so much working with Rose.”

Raised in Newton, Mass., Friedman is survived by her partner Andrew Anastasi, two children, parents and two sisters.

title: Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out AGs For Betrayal In Deal Talks With Paramount: “A Win Only For David Ellison”
summary: Whatever the true state of settlement talks this weekend between Paramount, a coalition of state Attorneys General and the Writers Guild of America to end the antitrust action over the $111 billion Warner Bros Discovery merger are, the people against the deal from the beginning are not going quietly. “As Trump tries to ban CNN […]
content:
Whatever the true state of settlement talks this weekend between Paramount, a coalition of state Attorneys General and the Writers Guild of America to end the antitrust action over the $111 billion Warner Bros Discovery merger are, the people against the deal from the beginning are not going quietly.

“As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said Saturday morning as the current WBD-owned cabler newser and MS Now journalists were denied access to the Executive Mansion. “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.”

Compared to Sen. Warren, the A-list supported Block the Merger is truly pissed off and feeling betrayed.

Watch on Deadline

“The rumored ‘deal’ to usher the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger forward is an insult to everyone who has stood up against this harmful transaction and to the hundreds of thousands of workers, journalists, and consumers who will be hurt if it goes forward,” the DC-based group told Deadline today of reported behind closed doors negotiations underway right now. “Let’s be very clear: an agreement based on unenforceable concessions is a win only for David Ellison. It is an L for everyone else.”

As leaks of talks between the AGs, led by California’s politically ambitious Rob Bonta, and the Ellison-run Paramount flooded the media late Friday, the possible L (loss) that BTM are spotlighting could include guardrails of CNN editorial independence, some selloffs, and job assurances. The hope down on Melrose is such a deal would render moot the March 2, 2027, trial start date currently on the calendar in federal court – and all the financial and political blast radius that comes with it for the Trump-friendly Ellisons.

To that, with massive job, production and tax revenue losses on the table, Paramount’s Plan B for the last eight weeks has been to pressure Bonta from all sides to make a deal ASAP. Two days of court-ordered settlement talks have already been set for mid-October, but that’s procedural in the judicial system and widely expected to go nowhere fast.

Also, mid-October doesn’t quite line up with Ellison’s balance sheet.

Looking at an October 1 date in which a $7 million a day ticking fee to WBD shareholders begins as well as a September 24 hearing on a Hail Mary desire for a $1.88 billion bond from the states and the very not flush WGA, Ellison’s crew has been leaking more than ever threats to exit California for a red state.

Even as the likes of outgoing CA Governor Gavin Newsom acknowledged privately at the recent 78th Primetime Emmys that the Ellisons were being too heavy handed, the multi-pronged pressure campaign seems to have paid off. Whereas Bonta once accused Paramount of “blackmail” with its threats and theatrical promises, the reelection-seeking AG now has his lieutenants in the room with Ellison’s execs.

The latest word on the wire is the parties could have an agreement before the official start of Yom Kippur this weekend.

Word is also out there that New York AG Letitia James isn’t as “in step,” according to a source, with Bonta as she previously was when it came to burying the hatchet with Para. There is also the wildcard of the WGA, who joined the AGs’ July 13 suit after filing an anti-merger action of their own.

“This is such bullsh*t,” an industry insider told Deadline this morning of the ParaBros talks. “Bonta should have called their bluff, instead he caved,” she added, noting such tactics are typical of Democratic politicians in the MAGA era.

Block the Merger, with its support from such names as Bryan Cranston, Hannah Einbinder, Bradley Whitford, W. Kamau Bell, Kristen Vangsness, Jane Fonda and Rati Gupta, wasn’t quite as blunt today in its statement, but the vibe was very much the same.



“Thousands of industry leaders took a risk when they spoke out publicly about the harm the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger would cause,” said the outfit, which also counts Noah Wyle, Denis Villeneuve, Atsuko Okatsuka, Damon Lindelof and Sophia Coppola among its backers. Claiming that more than 75,000 people have joined them to tell the state AGs to stand strong, including national leaders like Warren, the group said, “We know a bad deal when we see one. AG Bonta and his fellow state AGs should reject this deal, stand strong, and fully block the merger with no concessions.”

That mention of Warren may have greater significance this weekend than initially apparent. Like everyone else, Paramount is keenly aware of what the polls are projecting going into November’s midterms. If the midterms actually occur and if the new Congress is actually seated (two big ifs in America right now), then a projected Democratic majority in the House and the Senate have promised to probe and even break-up mega-media mergers.

Even with Oracle founder Larry Ellison the primary backer of his son’s ParaBros dreams, the even older Ellison’s net worth, which has been declining of late, may not be able to handle the strain of months and months of such probes. So perhaps it is the first week of November, not October 1, that is the calendar date the younger Ellison is hoping to beat the clock on this weekend.

Paramount has been in “no comment” mode for weeks since the Melrose lot got burned on allegations of leaks detailing past preliminary talks with Bonta’s gang.

AG Bonta’s office did not respond Saturday to Deadline’s request for comment on Warren and Block the Merger’s opposition to the talks.

title: Ruby Rose Remembers ‘Best Friend’ Hayden Panettiere: ‘All That She Ever Wanted Was to Have Her Story Told’
summary: Ruby Rose got emotional when asked about her friend, Hayden Panettiere, who died Aug. 16 at 36. Rose told Entertainment Tonight that Panettiere was her “best friend” and that they “spoke every day for five years.” “I didn’t even think we were going to be friends,” Rose said, tearing up. “I didn’t know if I […]
content:
Ruby Rose got emotional when asked about her friend, Hayden Panettiere, who died Aug. 16 at 36.

Rose told Entertainment Tonight that Panettiere was her “best friend” and that they “spoke every day for five years.”

“I didn’t even think we were going to be friends,” Rose said, tearing up. “I didn’t know if I wanted to have any celebrity friends, because I didn’t have a great experience with the industry.”

She shared how the two of them first met, saying, “I saw her, she saw me, and I just remember thinking, ‘Oh, no.’ And then she ran up anyway and was like, ‘Hey, I’m Hayden. Can we go talk somewhere? We’ve got a lot in common.’ I just laughed.”

Popular on Variety

The two quickly became close after realizing they “had everything in common,” Rose said. Throughout their five-year friendship, they texted each other every day to check in.

“Hayden, all that she ever wanted was to have her story told her way, on her terms,” Rose said.

Panettiere, who was known for her roles on “Heroes,” “Nashville,” “Scream 4” and “Scream VI,” openly spoke about her struggles with drug and alcohol addiction in her 2026 memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning.” Days after her death, the Drug Enforcement Administration joined the investigation, working with South Carolina’s Greenville Police Department to determine her cause of death.

Hollywood stars shared tributes online after news of her death became public, including Jack Coleman, who played her father on “Heroes.”

“I’m heartbroken. I couldn’t begin to put my thoughts into words until now, and they will be inadequate,” Coleman wrote. “I’ve loved Hayden since day one of the pilot of ‘Heroes,’ 20 years ago, when she introduced herself by shouting ‘daddy’ and throwing her arms around me. From that day on, she called me daddio. She was Haydini, because she was a magician.”

title: Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’
summary: Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside Ed Sheeran’s concert at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night as the singer returned to the stage for the first time since Macklemore was dropped from his Loop Tour following his onstage remarks in support of Palestine. For attendee Jodi Rhoden, an organizer at Writers Against the War in Gaza, […]
content:
Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside Ed Sheeran’s concert at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night as the singer returned to the stage for the first time since Macklemore was dropped from his Loop Tour following his onstage remarks in support of Palestine.

For attendee Jodi Rhoden, an organizer at Writers Against the War in Gaza, the protest represents something “much bigger than us.” “It’s much bigger than Ed Sheeran. It’s much bigger than Macklemore. It’s a movement for Palestinian lives, and it’s not going to stop until Palestine is free.”

Rhoden also noted that while there are many people who have “lost their livelihoods for speaking the truth about this genocide,” she feels the “tide is turning”: “You can see that with the way that Ed Sheeran fans are reacting, and the way that people are rallying behind that for more. It seems like we’ve really hit a tipping point, and public opinion has changed.”

Popular on Variety

Grace, an 18-year-old college student, said it was important for her to attend the protest “because we have to continue talking about Palestine.” Going into the evening, she is hoping that Sheeran “acknowledges what he did was wrong and says he wants to free Palestine.”

The demonstration, which drew a crowd of around 100 participants, was planned for 4:30 p.m. outside the South Philadelphia stadium, ahead of Sheeran’s 8 p.m. performance. Organizers said speakers from Writers Against the War on Gaza, the Boycott Cooknsolo Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann were expected to participate. The Philly Palestine Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann had also circulated calls for supporters to demonstrate outside the venue.

The protest comes amid mounting fallout from Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s U.S. stadium tour. The rapper had opened Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and Sept. 5 concerts at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he performed his 2024 pro-Palestinian protest song “Hind’s Hall,” displayed footage from Gaza and called for a “Free Palestine” from the stage.

Days later, tour promoter Messina Touring Group announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The promoter said several stadiums had indicated they would not permit concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup and that keeping him on the bill could jeopardize the remainder of the tour.

Macklemore subsequently said New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft played a central role in the decision. Kraft’s company owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform Sept. 25 and 26, and Macklemore alleged that Kraft rallied other stadium owners behind an ultimatum that the rapper be removed.

Kraft acknowledged that he opposed Macklemore performing at Gillette Stadium, saying in a statement that his participation in the two concerts there “would cross that line.” Kraft argued that Macklemore’s presentation of the Israel-Hamas war ignored the actions of Hamas and contributed to divisiveness and hate. Macklemore has defended his advocacy for Palestinians and rejected accusations that it amounts to antisemitism.

Sheeran, meanwhile, has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by the tour promoter and venues rather than by him. The singer said he had spoken with venue owners, promoters and activists in an effort to reach a resolution but was unable to do so.

The decision prompted a wider exodus from the Loop Tour. Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga — the Irish group that had been performing as part of Sheeran’s live band — all withdrew following Macklemore’s removal. Saturday’s Philadelphia show was consequently pushed from its originally advertised 5:30 p.m. start to 8 p.m., with Sheeran listed as the only act on the bill.

The controversy has also prompted a local debate over the decision to exclude Macklemore from the publicly owned stadium. The Philadelphia chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations sent an open letter to the Philadelphia Eagles, the City of Philadelphia, Lincoln Financial Group and others criticizing the move and raising questions about free expression and advocacy for Palestinian rights. The organization also filed a public-records request seeking information about who told Messina Touring Group that Macklemore could no longer perform at the venue.

Ahead of Saturday’s demonstration, Philadelphia police said they were coordinating with the venue and event organizers and would adjust staffing according to public-safety needs. A police spokesperson separately said officers had been in communication with Sheeran’s team over security arrangements for the concert.

title: ‘Ride Or Die’ Canceled By Prime Video After One Season, Being Shopped By Paramount TV Studios
summary: EXCLUSIVE: This is a shocker — one of the streaming hits of the summer will be no more, at least on its original platform. Prime Video has opted not to renew Ride Or Die starring Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer for a second season. The lead studio behind the buddy spy comedy, Paramount Television Studios, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: This is a shocker — one of the streaming hits of the summer will be no more, at least on its original platform. Prime Video has opted not to renew Ride Or Die starring Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer for a second season. The lead studio behind the buddy spy comedy, Paramount Television Studios, is shopping the series to other buyers, I hear.

The lack of quick renewal should’ve been a sign. Still, the cancellation has taken everyone involved in Ride of Die by surprise. That is because the action comedy has been well received and, according to available data, it has performed well.

Part of the current wave of “white wine thrillers” — series featuring adult female leads — Ride or Die launched on July 15 with a fraction of the marketing money Amazon put behind its YA summer lineup that got a big Obsession Is In Session promo campaign, including Elle, Off Campus, Every Year After and Sterling Point, all of which have been renewed.

Watch on Deadline

Ride Or Die snuck up under the radar to immediately hit the No. 1 slot in the daily U.S. rankings, eclipsing even big-budget film Masters of the Universe. The action comedy made Luminate’s weekly US rankings with just two days of release logging 927K views, twice as many as Elle drew for its first two days in the U.S. (477K) and almost four times Off Campus‘ 245K views back in May. Ride Or Die zoomed to No.1 in U.S. minutes watched in its first full week on Luminate, also doubling Elle‘s and almost tripling Off Campus‘ haul over the comparable periods, a trend that continued in Week 3.

The strong domestic performance carried onto the Nielsen Weekly Top 10 where Ride Or Die debuted at No.8 on the overall streaming chart and at No. 3 among originals with 869M minutes viewed. It climbed to No. 4 overall and No. 2 on the streaming originals charts in its second week with 922M minutes. Over its first 14 days of release, Ride Or Die is said to be Prime Video’s most watched new scripted series in the U.S. from 7/30/25 to 7/29/26.

Globally, Ride Or Die was the No.1 most watched Prime Video original series for the its first three weeks. Elle held the No.1 slot for two weeks, Off Campus for five. Completion rate-wise, Ride Or Die is believed to be in the range of several renewed Prime Video series, including Mr. & Mrs. Smith, Scarpetta and Elle.



A crowd pleaser that has also scored with reviewers, Ride Or Die has logged 96% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics and 85% with audiences.

Ride or Die was one of two series centering on 50-something female friendships that launched in July to similarly strong U.S. viewership and reviews. The other, Peacock’s The Five Star Weekend, has been renewed for a second season.

Created by Tessa Coates, Ride or Die follows best friends Debbie Claybourne (Spencer) and Judith Burton (Waddingham) who thought they knew everything about each other, except Judith turns out to be an international assassin. When a mysterious figure emerges from Judith’s past and a hit goes horribly wrong, both of their worlds are turned upside down as they’re forced to go on the run together.



Season 1, which ended on several cliffhangers that set up major storylines for a second installment, also stars Ed Skrein, Calam Lynch, Savannah Steyn, Jamie Parker, Jacky Ido, with Sylvia Hoeks and Bill Nighy.

Ride or Die Season 1 was produced by Paramount Television Studios (the series originated at Skydance Television), Amazon MGM Studios as well as Andy and Barbara Muschietti’s Double Dream and Spencer’s Orit Entertainment. Coates, showrunner Matt Miller, and director Peyton Reed executive produce alongside Spencer for Orit Entertainment; Waddingham; Andy Muschietti, Barbara Muschietti, and Irene Yeung for Double Dream; Brian Clisham; and Stephanie Kluft.

title: Aaron Rowe Defends Ed Sheeran After Dropping Out Of Tour: “Human F*cking Error”
summary: Although Ed Sheeran has no more openers on his Loop Tour, at least one artist is coming to his defense after dropping Macklemore over his pro-Palestine remarks. On Friday, after departing the tour, Aaron Rowe defended Sheeran for his “human f*cking error” in caving to Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft’s demand that he remove Macklemore […]
content:
Although Ed Sheeran has no more openers on his Loop Tour, at least one artist is coming to his defense after dropping Macklemore over his pro-Palestine remarks.

On Friday, after departing the tour, Aaron Rowe defended Sheeran for his “human f*cking error” in caving to Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft‘s demand that he remove Macklemore from the tour, arguing that instead, people should be “using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere.”

“I’m gonna be honest, I think you are all focusing on the wrong person here. All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that, but you really should be focusing on the likes of Robert Kraft,” he began in the video on Instagram. “You really should be focusing on the zionist lobbies that are trying to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide, the genocide that is happening in Palestine right now, by Israel.

Watch on Deadline

“Look, I know Ed’s statement could have been a lot better, and I do think that Macklemore shouldn’t have been pulled off the tour. I fully believe it was panicked stations over there, and they rushed to a decision because they didn’t know what to do, because they were getting it from all angles.”

Rowe continued, “That’s a mistake from a person. And I haven’t had a chance to fucking talk to Ed too much, but I fully believes he knows that was a mistake.”

Pointing out that all of Sheeran’s openers were pro-Palestine, Rowe said, “If Ed Sheeran was a fucking zionist, why would he have all these fucking people on the fucking tour? It was human fucking error. You all know my stance on Palestine. I’ll tell you right now, first hand, I know Ed Sheeran has done so much for so many fucking people, including artists like me, who he’s literally changed their entire lives. All he has inside of him is kindness. That is who Ed Sheeran is, and yes, like every other human being, he makes fucking mistakes.”

After calling out the Irish government’s role in the Israel-Hamas conflict, Rowe turned his attention back to Kraft, urging others to do the same.

“In the music industry, within the media, there are people with so much money and fucking power, that they’re able to basically shut down any opinion they don’t agree with. You should be using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere, someone who tried to shut down free speech, someone who tried to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide. That’s what you should be using your energy on, not fucking Ed Sheeran, for fuck’s sake,” added Rowe.

On Monday, Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his tour amid an outcry around his “Free Palestine” onstage remarks. Sheeran subsequently released a statement saying it was the “promoter’s decision” after Kraft assembled several of the tour venues to give him an ultimatum.

Following the statement, Rowe and fellow openers Finneas and Lukas Graham dropped out of the tour, along with Sheeran’s backing band Beoga.

title: Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta ‘Don’t You Dare’ Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: ‘Do Not Cave’
summary: Mark Ruffalo is encouraging California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramount Skydance and keep David Ellison from acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery. “Don’t you dare, [Rob Bonta], do not cave,” Ruffalo wrote on X. “5,670 filmmakers put their necks on the line for […]
content:
Mark Ruffalo is encouraging California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramount Skydance and keep David Ellison from acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery.

“Don’t you dare, [Rob Bonta], do not cave,” Ruffalo wrote on X. “5,670 filmmakers put their necks on the line for you to fight this merger. Another 75,000+ and counting have signed to tell you not to concede in just 3 weeks. You work for the people — the very people who will be hurt if you let this lousy deal filled with empty promises go forward. Please sign to send a message to the AGs and Paramount. Reject the deal. The people don’t want it!”

Ruffalo is one of Hollywood’s most outspoken stars about opposing the merger. He recently found himself in a back-and-forth with Paramount, in which a studio rep called him “antisemitic” for calling out the Ellisons’ connection with Israel.

Popular on Variety

Paramount Skydance’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. was approved by the Department of Justice in June. However, the deal was put on hold thanks to the antitrust lawsuit from Bonta and his team of state AGs. The Wall Street Journal, citing anonymous sources, reported Friday that Paramount Skydance and Bonta are in “advanced talks” to reach a settlement.

Ruffalo isn’t the only one asking Bonta to hold his ground. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote on Facebook Saturday morning that President Donald Trump banning CNN from the White House is a warning of things to come if Paramount Skydance swallows Warner Bros. (Trump also banned MSNOW and Politico).

“As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Warren wrote. “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.”

title: ‘Ride or Die’ Canceled by Prime Video After One Season
summary: “Ride or Die” has been canceled by Prime Video after one season, Variety can confirm. The streamer’s Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer-led buddy dramedy premiered in July of this year. It was first reported that Spencer and Waddingham were teaming up for the series in December 2023. Per the show’s official logline, “‘Ride or Die’ […]
content:
“Ride or Die” has been canceled by Prime Video after one season, Variety can confirm.

The streamer’s Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer-led buddy dramedy premiered in July of this year. It was first reported that Spencer and Waddingham were teaming up for the series in December 2023.
