The project marks a reunion between Dharma Productions and Leo Media Collective following “Bad Newz” (2024) and “Kesari: Chapter 2” (2025). It also continues Dharma’s run of films drawn from real events and figures, including “Kesari,” “Raazi” and “Shershaah.”

title: Latido Takes Isaki Lacuesta’s ‘Flamenco Sketches,’ San Sebastian’s Zabaltegi-Tabakalera Closer (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain – Madrid-based Latido Films has picked up international sales rights to Isaki Lacuesta’s “Flamenco Sketches” (“Jaleos”), the latest film from Isaki Lacuesta, one of Spain’s most singular filmmakers, which plays this week at the San Sebastian Film Festival. Lacuesta has twice won San Sebastian’s top prize, the Golden Shell, with “The Double […]
content:
SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain – Madrid-based Latido Films has picked up international sales rights to Isaki Lacuesta’s “Flamenco Sketches” (“Jaleos”), the latest film from Isaki Lacuesta, one of Spain’s most singular filmmakers, which plays this week at the San Sebastian Film Festival.

Lacuesta has twice won San Sebastian’s top prize, the Golden Shell, with “The Double Steps” and “Between Two Waters.”

“Flamenco Sketches” will close San Sebastian’s Zabaltegi-Tabakalera section. Using a vast array of archive footage, the film takes a freewheeling journey through the history of flamenco.

Popular on Variety

“Isaki Lacuesta is without any doubt one of Spain’s most creative and innovative directors,” said Latido president Antonio Saura. “With ‘Flamenco Sketches’ he takes us on an unrivalled road of discovery of art, perception and joy.”

Rather than offering a conventional history, the director builds the film as something closer to flamenco itself: stories begin, mutate, collide and disappear; images, music and ideas summon themselves intuitively.

The film jumps from flamenco’s first appearances in the mid-19th century to the arrival of trains, clocks and standardized time; from Thomas Edison’s early moving images of Spanish dancer Carmencita to the relationship between flamenco and the artistic avant-garde; from Vicente Escudero and Man Ray to Francis Picabia, Joan Miró and Marcel Duchamp.

The project has been years in the making. Speaking to Variety in 2024, Lacuesta described it as “a kind of ‘One Thousand and One Nights,’ a story that explains tales, tales of flamenco.”

“What do Edison, Hitler, Leni Riefenstahl, Tarantino and Camarón de la Isla all have in common?” he said. “They all have stories that have to do with flamenco. Flamenco has always been modern and attached to modern history.”

Lacuesta and his co-writers Pedro G. Romero and Luis Parés also probe what happens when an spontaneous, living form is recorded and ‘preserved.’ The film continually circles the paradox of the art form surviving through mutation and contradiction, even as attempts are made to establish what constitutes “real” flamenco.

Its cast of voices includes figures from flamenco, and the arts more broadly including rapper C. Tangana, director of the memorable “La guitarra flamenca de Yerai Cortés,” dancer Rocío Molina, artist Pedro G. Romero and french philosopher and art historian Georges Didi-Huberman.

“Flamenco Sketches” is produced by Tono Folguera for Lastor Media and Guillermo Cascante for Goroka Contents, with Lacuesta’s La Termita Films as co-producer. BTeam Pictures handles Spanish distribution, with Latido selling worldwide outside Spain.

The title echoes Miles Davis’ “Flamenco Sketches,” but Lacuesta’s own sketchbook, like the jazz great, revels in contradiction.

title: Secuoya Studios Taps Carla Gómez to Lead Latin American Development as Regional Expansion Accelerates (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Spain’s Secuoya Studios has tapped Carla Gómez as head of development and executive producer for Latin America, strengthening its creative and production operations in the region. Bringing more than two decades of experience in the television and streaming sector, Gómez will oversee the development of original projects from initial concept through production. She also brings […]
content:
Spain’s Secuoya Studios has tapped Carla Gómez as head of development and executive producer for Latin America, strengthening its creative and production operations in the region.

Bringing more than two decades of experience in the television and streaming sector, Gómez will oversee the development of original projects from initial concept through production. She also brings a catalogue of intellectual property and projects developed through her boutique development company, Cielito Studio.

Her appointment follows Secuoya’s announcement in April that it was granting its Latin American operation greater autonomy over development, production and greenlight decisions, targeting Mexico, Colombia and the U.S. Hispanic market.

Popular on Variety

The regional business is headed by Daniel Hernández Bocanegra, managing director of Secuoya Studios in Latin America, with Pierluigi Gazzolo serving as a strategic adviser through Farniente Media.

“Carla Gómez’s arrival marks an important step in the continued strengthening of both our team and our strategy in Latin America,” Hernández Bocanegra said. “We share the same commitment to working closely with local talent and stories to develop distinctive content capable of connecting with international audiences.”

Gómez has worked with content teams at ViX, HBO and Viacom, produced for NBCUniversal and, most recently, served as a development consultant for Netflix in Colombia.

Her executive credits include ViX productions “Isla Brava,” “El Gallo de Oro,” “La Mujer del Diablo” and “María Félix: La Doña,” alongside HBO Latin America’s “Sierra Madre” and Nickelodeon’s “Grachi” and its U.S. adaptation, “Every Witch Way.”

“I strongly believe in the ‘local for local’ vision: content created within the region, for our audiences and their cultures,” Gómez said.

‘La celda de los milagros’ Courtesy of Secuoya Studios

Secuoya’s regional production drive has already yielded Netflix hit “La Celda de los Milagros,” which topped the streamer’s global non-English-language film rankings for the week of Feb. 16-22. The film recorded 21 million worldwide views in the first half of 2026, according to Netflix.

The studio’s Latin American slate also includes the upcoming “Belleza,” produced with BH5 for Miércoles Entertainment, and “La Corona,” a collaboration with Black Sheep Productions, Startling, Infinity Hill and Runaway Films.

title: Presley Gerber Dies: Model, Son Of Cindy Crawford & Rande  Gerber Was 27
summary: Presley Walker Gerber, a model and the only son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, has died. A representative for the family confirmed the news to Deadline. He was 27. A statement from the family read as follows: “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time.” An L.A. County Medical […]
content:
Presley Walker Gerber, a model and the only son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, has died. A representative for the family confirmed the news to Deadline. He was 27.

A statement from the family read as follows: “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time.”

An L.A. County Medical Examiner’s report says Gerber died at a rehab facility. An investigation into the cause is ongoing.

Gerber was signed to IMG models and appeared in a 2018 Pepsi ad with his mother. His modeling career began with a 2015 Bruce Weber shoot. He soon was doing runway work at the various fashion weeks around the globe.

He recalled the whirlwind in a 2023 interview with the podcast Studio 22.

Watch on Deadline

“My whole life changed within a month and it was just a very profound experience because I had to grow up quickly,” said Gerber.

In 2019, he was arrested for a DUI in Beverly Hills and sentenced to three years’ probation. Then 19, Gerber was also ordered to complete a DUI program.

His younger sister, Kaia Gerber, currently plays Susan Reynolds in Ryan Murphy’s The Shards.

title: Paramount Settlement Talks Prospects Dim For Now As Gang Of Four AGs Resist Quick Ellison Deal
summary: EXCLUSIVE: As Hollywood celebrates Yom Kippur tonight, a framework for a settlement of the antitrust suit hampering Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery has hit some political potholes, even as some hoped for a quick deal. Four of the 12 Attorneys General that took the David Ellison-run company to federal court are breaking […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: As Hollywood celebrates Yom Kippur tonight, a framework for a settlement of the antitrust suit hampering Paramount‘s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery has hit some political potholes, even as some hoped for a quick deal.

Four of the 12 Attorneys General that took the David Ellison-run company to federal court are breaking with the California AG Rob Bonta-led faction that wants to put the high stakes dispute to rest, at least for the time being. Along with the Golden State, the blue state coalition that sued Paramount and WBD back on July 13 is made up of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

A March 2, 2027 trial date has been set in the matter, much to Paramount’s chagrin.

Watch on Deadline

Now, as the pressure turns into a court of public opinion vice for blue state reps, it is Minnesota AG Keith Ellison who has taken the reins in resisting an agreement with David Ellison (no relation, but the irony is undeniable). A longtime Democratic powerbroker, the North Star State’s Ellison is joined in the Gang of Four by NY’s powerful AG Letitia James, Connecticut’s William Tong and, indications are, Washington state’s Nick Brown.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison

The quartet is concerned that settlement parameters are “too lenient to Paramount,” we hear. The states want Bonta to slow down and not overreact to threats of Paramount leaving California or other external pressures.

Specifically, as more and more fellow Democrats, Hollywood A-listers and activists urge rejecting a settlement with the MAGA adjacent Para, the Gang of Four are pessimistic of the power of a proposed CNN Editorial Board. “It has no teeth,” an individual close to discussions tells Deadline. “(David) Ellison wants a deal, Bonta is feeling pressure to make a deal. Both want an off-ramp. The worry among the four states that have yet to sign off on a settlement is that some “window decorating” around CNN plus some cable sell-offs could be enough for Bonta to walk away from the larger legal battle with Paramount after months of hanging tough.

Over a weekend of remote talks, as the October 1 deadline for a $7 million a day ticking fee to WBD shareholders gets closer, a variety of items have been discussed. To that, with court-ordered settlement talks already on the books for mid-October, the notion of significant financial penalties if ParaBros fails to keep its theatrical release promises has been floated. There’s also a question of making the two studios completely separate for at least two years as a temporary solution.

As it stands tonight, things are in a state of suspended animation until next week, with one M&A vet telling us the Yom Kippur respite could either “make or break” the talks going forward.

United with the AGs from almost the get-go, the WGA has been on the sidelines of current talks, we’re told. Yet, with outrage and now protests from the star-studded Block the Merger group (Oakland today, NYC Monday and outside Paramount in L.A. on September 22), the guild has been getting an earful from members, sources say. Additionally, the leadership of the WGA and other Tinseltown guilds have been in contact with NY’s James to “gauge the temperature” around any settlement.

In what one source called a “civil atmosphere,” the parties have also been very much aware of the busy calendar this week after the holiday. On September 24, a hearing is set before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on Para’s Hail Mary desire for a $1.88 billion bond from the AGs and the WGA to cover the “extraordinary losses” the company says it will suffer waiting for the trial to start next spring. The very next day, with the politics of Trump and the midterms never far from anyone’s mind, the AGs and the WGA have to reply to a motion by red states Iowa and Montana to take the whole matter to the Supreme Court.

Neither Keith Ellison or Letitia James’ offices responded Sunday to Deadline’s request for comment on any settlement or gearing down. Paramount brass and Rob Bonta’s office also had nothing to say tonight about the state of the talks. However, the usually quick with a statement CA AG did post a Yom Kippur message on his Threads account.

Read between the lines if you think there is something between the lines:

At the opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Arts on September 19, the Paramount legal tussle was the talk of the shindig. One well-placed guest said to be in close touch with the parties told several attendees that while a deal wasn’t 100% done, the deep freeze between Bonta and Paramount’s Ellison was “unstuck.”

Battling a tough campaign for reelection, L.A. Mayor Karen Bass was said to have stated to fellow Lucas attendees that a deal was “close.” Earlier Saturday, before the Narrative Art gathering began, the once merger-opposing Bass seemed to put her preferences out in the open.

There’s no place like home. Keep Hollywood in Hollywood. pic.twitter.com/53S0iKn8Aj — Karen Bass (@KarenBassLA) September 19, 2026

David Ellison wasn’t at George Lucas‘ soiree, nor was still WBD boss David Zaslav. The Paramount CEO was also nowhere to be seen ringside or elsewhere Saturday night at the Paramount+ streamed UFC 331 from DTLA’s Crypto.com Arena.

Whether the Force is strong with proponents or opponents of a settlement, one idea certainly being considered for everyone to save face is as a hold-separate arrangement. The corporate mechanism could allow the antitrust suit to proceed, but take the ticking fee financial strain off the deep-pocketed Ellisons and their recently DOJ-approved Gulf State backers.

Even if the companies are held separate in a compromise deal, it would be good news for Paramount’s expense ledger but possibly bad news for its stock and that of WBD. The market has shown over the past two months that it doesn’t like limbo, and neither does the industry, which has grown restless about the damage already being done by the merger delay. (Sworn foes of the merger would argue that a period of stasis is better than what they see as heavier carnage were the merger to proceed.)

A hold-separate agreement has been struck before, including in the case of Time Warner and AT&T’s $85 billion merger in 2018. It also factored into Nexstar’s acquisition of TV station rival Tegna, which was opposed by state AGs and DirecTV — though in that instance it was after the merger had already closed in a still-pending lawsuit.

The past several weeks have seen a constant stream of leaks that Paramount will leave California if it doesn’t close the ParaBros deal or get a settlement soon. Even as the ambitious Bonta has cancelled previous settlement talks and called Team Ellison’s tactics “blackmail,” a growing chorus that includes outgoing Governor Gavin Newsom, likely next Governor Xavier Becerra, incumbent Bass and IATSE have urged this all be settled “in the boardroom, not the courtroom.” Add to that reports to the L.A. Board of Supervisors is predicting big job losses if ParaBros become a reality. On the other hand, there have also been Paramount-commissioned reports to the powerful Supervisors promising even bigger job losses if the Melrose lot leaves, but an employment and production bonanza if the deal goes through.

With all that, worth noting that AG Keith Ellison’s radio silence today is very different from how adamant Ellison was earlier this summer when he took Paramount to town as the AGs suit hit the docket:

In contrast to AG Ellison’s current silence, ever since reports surfaced of a potential settlement emerged on September 18, Congressional Democrats, many of whom could hold key committee chair roles if their poll-leading party takes control after the midterms, have been very vocal about Bonta and gang’s need to “hold the line” against a rushed deal. “With Trump and his billionaire allies crushing independent media, we need state AGs to stand strong against more corporate media monopolies,” Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy tweeted Sunday. “The AGs should keep fighting to block Paramount’s illegal merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.” Murphy was joined by dozens and dozens of his colleagues, including New Jersey’s senior Senator Cory Booker.

The long time foe of the merger weaved in the latest attack on the press by Ellison pal Trump in a tweet today:

Trump just locked CNN out of the White House. Now his billionaire allies want to own it. State attorneys general: Don't settle. Hold the line. Block this merger. — Sen. Cory Booker (@SenBooker) September 20, 2026

Just sayin’

Dade Hayes contributed to this report

title: Jake & Logan Paul Address Troops At The Pentagon
summary: The day before National POW/MIA Recognition Day, Jake and Logan Paul addressed troops gathered at the Pentagon. From the podium, Logan Paul told those gathered that touring the building was “a cool experience.” He added, “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight […]
content:
The day before National POW/MIA Recognition Day, Jake and Logan Paul addressed troops gathered at the Pentagon.

From the podium, Logan Paul told those gathered that touring the building was “a cool experience.”

He added, “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight for their country.”

The visit was documented in a video and images posted today to the Department of Defense page on X. With swelling music, it showed smiling service members listening intently to the brothers. It also showed the duo meeting with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

Last Thursday, we welcomed Logan and Jake Paul to the Pentagon to meet with our warriors. pic.twitter.com/NiRJVWb2Rc — Department of War 🇺🇸 (@DeptofWar) September 20, 2026

That same day, it appears Jake Paul met with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Watch on Deadline

In a post with photos from the visit, Bessent wrote, “Jake’s path from content creator to entrepreneur and professional boxer is a distinctly American story.”

Great to welcome @jakepaul to the Treasury Department today.



Jake’s path from content creator to entrepreneur and professional boxer is a distinctly American story. 🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/7Pn0EGbOy0 — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) September 18, 2026

The brothers, who are YouTube stars with experience in boxing and wrestling earlier this month landed a fight competition series at Hulu and ESPN.

The untitled series, which previously had the working title Fight Island, is a major statement from Disney and is intended to appeal to young, male audiences.

The series comes from Brent Montgomery’s Wheelhouse, which is behind series such as Netflix’s Million Dollar Secret and A&E’s Duck Dynasty reboot, and Jake Paul’s Most Valuable Promotions.

Peter White contributed to this post.

title: Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review
summary: For decades, law-enforcement procedurals have been staples on television, and when they are done well, these series build loyal fanbases that stick with them for years. NBC’s newest drama, “Line of Fire” is from “Quantico” creator Joshua Safran and loosely based on executive producer Jenna Bush Hager’s experiences with the United States Secret Service. The […]
content:
For decades, law-enforcement procedurals have been staples on television, and when they are done well, these series build loyal fanbases that stick with them for years. NBC’s newest drama, “Line of Fire” is from “Quantico” creator Joshua Safran and loosely based on executive producer Jenna Bush Hager’s experiences with the United States Secret Service. The show has all the makings of becoming a classic in the canon of beloved police procedurals. “Line of Fire” follows the Hollingsworth family: Secret Service Agent Mike Hollingsworth (Peter Krause); his estranged wife, U.S. Marshal Jane Hollingsworth (Hope Davis); and their three adult children, FBI Agent Clare Hollingsworth (Kat Cunning), Secret Service Agent Mike “Micah” Hollingsworth Jr. (Tommy O’Brien) and DOJ analyst Russ Hollingsworth (Taylor Bloom). Mike, Jane and their children try to keep things professional, but continually cross personal boundaries because of their agencies’ proximity. Boasting intense family dynamics and several truly intriguing cases, “Line of Fire” has a depth, intensity and a hint of soapiness that works perfectly within the genre.

The 10-episode first season (two episodes were available for review) opens in Crozet, Virginia. A U.S. Marshal, under the guise of being a delivery driver, attempts to track down a missing fugitive. Unfortunately, before the morning breaks, both the Marshal and the outlaw lay dead in the woods. The next day, Jane arrives at the crime scene, determined to figure out what happened. Needing a bit more reach than the Marshals can offer, Jane calls in her daughter, Clare, for her expertise and for the FBI’s resources. Though Clare is eager to help, Jane’s team is not exactly pleased that the FBI is encroaching on her territory. For her part, Clare isn’t thrilled when her mother badgers her about bringing her mysterious new boyfriend to dinner to finally meet the family.

Popular on Variety

Back in Washington, D.C., Mike is set to finish out his final week at the Secret Service Headquarters before retiring. Yet, he’s increasingly concerned Micah is skirting his professional duties for a personal relationship with Sydney (Savannah Lee Smith), the president’s college-age daughter. Elsewhere, Russell is ready to get his feet wet at the DOJ, but his family’s constant requests complicate his role. Chaos and dysfunction are par for the course for the Hollingsworths. But when a seemingly standard case unearths long-buried secrets that threaten the family’s safety, each person must decide whether their jobs are worth more than the people they love.

From bank robberies to cartel killings and even contending with the First Family’s drama in the White House, all of the cases the Hollingsworths handle are interesting. Still, the Hollingsworth family dynamic anchors “Line of Fire.” Though they’ve been long separated, Jane and Mike have a solid friendship; one that can only be formed after knowing and loving someone intimately for half your life. Not only do the former couple share children, but Mike and Jane also share secrets — shocking ones they keep close to their chests. The siblings, each with unique relationships with their parents and each other, are also well mapped out.

Though only two episodes were available to screen, the family feels well lived-in: a boisterous clan with varied personalities becomes the ecosystem that shapes the series. In the pilot, Mike and the siblings arrive at Jane’s house for a chaotic and hilarious family dinner to meet the beau Clare has avoided introducing them to. Immediately, the audience gets a full sense of who these people are and how this family functions. Yet, that doesn’t make any of the cases sprinkled within the show any less worthwhile. In fact, it makes the conspiracy sitting at the center of “Line of Fire” even more gripping.

“Line of Fire” has all of the essential elements that make procedural dramas so fun. With a stellar cast and some detailed mysteries which will likely stretch across the season (and into the next, assuming there is one), changing the Hollingsworth family dynamic as we know it, it’s clear NBC has a gem on its hands.

“Line of Fire” debuts Sept. 21 on NBC, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Mondays.

title: ‘Hot Ones’ Producer First We Feast Sets New Series ‘Hot Ones: Game Night’ Hosted by Joe Santagato (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: First We Feast is preparing to launch a new show in the “Hot Ones” franchise dubbed “Hot One: Game Night,” Variety has learned exclusively. The new series will be hosted by The Basement Yard’s Joe Santiago and will premiere Sept. 30 at 7 a.m. ET on the First We Feast YouTube channel. The guest in […]
content:
First We Feast is preparing to launch a new show in the “Hot Ones” franchise dubbed “Hot One: Game Night,” Variety has learned exclusively.

The new series will be hosted by The Basement Yard’s Joe Santiago and will premiere Sept. 30 at 7 a.m. ET on the First We Feast YouTube channel. The guest in the first episode will be Doctor Mike, with upcoming guests including Neil deGrasse Tyson, Frank Alvarez and more.

The official description of the series states “the new show brings the heat of ‘Hot Ones’ to a custom-themed board game. Celebrity guests will roll the dice, move across the board, and take on challenges and questions inspired by their personalities and backstories, winning prizes in the process…As the stakes get higher, Joe and his guests work together to conquer the game. Falling behind comes with a painful consequence: taking on the infamous Wings of Death.”

Popular on Variety

This marks the latest original series from First We Feast, which includes the smash hit show “Hot Ones,” “Hot Ones Versus,” “Hot Ones Wing Pong,” “Pro Moves,” “Heat Eaters” and more.

“I’ve always been a huge fan of “Hot Ones,” so joining the universe and working with the First We Feast team has been incredible,” said Santagato. “I grew up having game nights with friends and family, so using that as an interview format is so cool to me. You never really know someone until you’ve played a board game with them so you really get to see a new side of these guests when they’re competing and trying to win. I also really appreciate the fact that they trust me as an executive producer because it gives me the opportunity to be involved creatively and help shape the game and each episode. I was so excited when I signed on that I forgot I’d actually have to eat insanely spicy wings every episode. You never really get used to the spice but it’s totally worth it!”

Originally launched in 2012 at Complex Media, First We Feast has grown into a major cultural hub thanks to the popularity of “Hot Ones.” The brand now boasts more than 27 million followers across platforms.

“’Game Night’ marks an exciting new chapter for First We Feast,” said Chris Schonberger, CEO of First We Feast. “For the first time we’ll be welcoming a new host into the Hot Ones cinematic universe. In Joe and his COO Greg Dybec we’ve found our ideal partners—true creative collaborators who share our vision for producing the most innovative celebrity interview formats on the internet.”

title: Chile’s ‘Erratics,’ Blending Denis Lavant, Speculative Fiction and Ghost Cinema, Bows at San Sebastián New Directors Competition
summary: Blending speculative fiction, ghost cinema and Patagonian hauntology, Chilean Thomas Woodroffe’s debut feature “Erratics” (“Bloques erráticos”) holds its world premiere at the San Sebastian Festival’s New Directors sidebar. It tracks the ghost of French filmmaker Lucien Castelnau who wakes up in the stunning landscapes of Patagonia where he has spent a century trapped inside a […]
content:
Blending speculative fiction, ghost cinema and Patagonian hauntology, Chilean Thomas Woodroffe’s debut feature “Erratics” (“Bloques erráticos”) holds its world premiere at the San Sebastian Festival’s New Directors sidebar.

It tracks the ghost of French filmmaker Lucien Castelnau who wakes up in the stunning landscapes of Patagonia where he has spent a century trapped inside a glacier. “As he wanders through a technological society built upon the remnants of forgotten histories, he encounters traces of indigenous memory, displaced communities and visions of a world that no longer resembles the one he left behind,” the synopsis goes, exploring “what becomes of images, memories and artworks that fail to find their audience…. can a film truly exist if it is never seen?”

“Like an erratic boulder carried by ice and abandoned in a place where it does not belong, Lucien becomes a wanderer between times, searching for meaning, recognition, and a place for his unfinished legacy,” it says.

Popular on Variety

Castelnau is played by French actor Denis Lavant (“Beau Travail”) whose evocative voiceover adds to the haunting imagery of the film.

The origins of “Erratics” lie in an unexpected act of serendipity, says Woodroffe. “Six years ago, a friend told me about an academic research on ancient photographs of Patagonia. When I asked her to send it to me, she got confused and sent me the wrong paper. The research was about a recent discovery of the ethnographic documentary ‘La Terre de Feu’ (1925), at La Cinémathèque de Toulouse. This serendipity was the starting point of ‘Erratics.’”

Reflecting on the film’s spirit, Woodroffe says: “I believe in the possibility of cinema to be a ghost, to invoke voices from remote times and bring them back to life in the present.”

As a director, screenwriter, cinematographer and colorist, Woodroffe has sought to bridge filmmaking and film preservation. He first broke out with his short “Astral Fever,” which had its world première at 1976 Biennale, and won a special mention in the Nest competition at San Sebastián. He served as cinematographer on Diego Céspedes’ “The Summer of the Electric Lion,” a Grand Prize winner at Cannes’ Cinéfondation. He has been pursuing a Master’s degree in Film Preservation at Elías Querejeta Zine Eskola in San Sebastián.

Paris-based MPM Premium handles the international sales of “Erratics,” bolstering the company’s commitment to some of the most original voices in modern-day Latin American cinema. Recent titles it has represented include “Rains Over Babel” (Sundance 2025), “The Red Hangar” (Berlinale Perspectives 2026) and “The Riverbank“ (“A Margem do Rio,” Locarno Competition 2026).

Says Natalia Isotta, head of festivals & Ibero-American sales at MPM Premium: “As a sales company, our work is to help films find their audience. Rarely do we encounter a film that turns that very journey into the heart of its own story.”

“Erratics” is produced by Fiebre SpA (Chile), La Belle Affaire Productions (France) and Un Puma (Argentina). Aside from Lavant, the cast includes Francesca Bozzano, Dominique Legoupil, Reinaldo Caro, Daniel Muñoz, and distinguished film directors Dominga Sotomayor (“La Perra”) and Felipe Gálvez (“The Settlers”).

title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Reprises His Oscar-Winning Role in David Fincher’s Tarantino Sequel
summary: Netflix has released a trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” in which Brad Pitt reprises his Oscar-winning role as the stuntman first introduced in Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” The film is set to premiere in Imax theaters on Nov. 25, before hitting the streamer Dec. 23. Directed by David […]
content:
Netflix has released a trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” in which Brad Pitt reprises his Oscar-winning role as the stuntman first introduced in Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” The film is set to premiere in Imax theaters on Nov. 25, before hitting the streamer Dec. 23.

Directed by David Fincher, the film sees the return of Cliff Booth” — “only this time it’s 1977 and it’s a very different Hollywood,” as Netflix put it in the trailer announcement. The film takes place eight years after the events of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” when Booth has traded stunts for being a “studio fixer.”

While Leonardo DiCaprio is not returning as Hollywood star Rick Dalton, Timothy Olyphant will reprise his original role of James Stacy. Scott Caan, Elizabeth Debicki, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Carla Gugino, Holt McCallany and JB Tadena will play new characters in the sequel.

Popular on Variety

The trailer opens with Booth causing chaos at the Beverly Cinema, which has been owned by Tarantino since 2007. Mud-wrestling, murder and car chases ensue. At one point, Debicki’s character asks Booth about his work as Dalton’s stunt double. “You worked with Rick Dalton for a number of years. What brought an end to your engagement?” she asks. “Oh, Rick got too fat for me to double him anymore,” he replies.

In an August 2025 interview on “The Church of Tarantino” podcast, Tarantino got candid about why he wouldn’t return to direct the film. “I love this script, but I’m still walking down the same ground I’ve already walked,” he said. “It just kind of unenthused me. This last movie, I’ve got to not know what I’m doing again. I’ve got to be in uncharted territory.” (The director has notably said that his 10th feature film will be his last; “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” was his ninth.)

But that doesn’t mean he isn’t excited to see how Fincher directs it. “I think me and David Fincher are the two best directors,” he continued. “So the idea that David Fincher actually wants to adapt my work, to me, shows a level of seriousness towards my work that I think needs to be taken into account.”

Tarantino serves as a producer alongside Pitt, David Heyman, Ceán Chaffin and Stacey Sher. Erik Messerschmidt serves as the film’s director of photography. The film was shot on-location in Los Angeles.

Watch the trailer below.

title: MS NOW, CNN, Politico Allege Trump, White House Staffers Violated First Amendment in New Suit
summary: MS NOW, CNN and Politico are suing President Donald Trump and other administration officials over a decision by Trump to ban the three news organizations from newsgathering at the White House, the latest fracture in the relationship between the president and the national media. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a […]
content:
MS NOW, CNN and Politico are suing President Donald Trump and other administration officials over a decision by Trump to ban the three news organizations from newsgathering at the White House, the latest fracture in the relationship between the president and the national media.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the three news organizations said in a statement. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

The three news companies are filing suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. “There could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment,” they alleged Monday in a court filing.

Popular on Variety

MS NOW, CNN and Politico sought an order that would keep officials from taking any more action to ban its staffers from reporting at the White House and calling for an immediate restoration of the credentials required to access the grounds.

The Constitution “protects the liberty and property interests that news organizations and White House reporters have in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford them to cover the White House for the benefit of the public,” the companies alleged in a legal filing. “No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim — with no notice, no process, and no warning — as the President did here.”

The news organizations have precedent on their side. In 2018, the first Trump administration banned Jim Acosta, then a top White House correspondent for CNN, from White House newsgathering following an incident in which the reporter tried to hold on to a microphone as a government staffer tried to pull it away from him. A federal judge ordered Acosta’s credentials to be restored on a temporary basis as CNN pursued legal remedies. The White House subsequently dropped the matter, and CNN ended its legal efforts.

The suit adds to a growing pile of legal entanglements between the federal government and the national media. Disney’s ABC in August filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission, raising the pitch of that company’s efforts to countermand unusual pressure from the Trump administration to force the company’s stations to submit licenses for early renewal proceedings.

The U.S. Constitution, the companies alleged, “does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on that official’s dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is patently unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.”

In addition to Trump, the suit names as defendants Steven Cheung, White House communications director; Secret Service director Sean Curran; and Susan Wiles, White House chief of staff.

A copy of the lawsuit is available at this link.

In a post Monday morning on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

title: ‘Stuff The British Stole’ Producer WildBear Entertainment Reshuffles Top Team To “Get Ahead” Of Industry Transformation
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Australian factual producer WildBear Entertainment has unveiled a new look for its management team amid “the biggest transformation we’ve seen in decades” for the entertainment industry. A eight-strong team will lead activities the company, which is known for the likes of Stuff the British Stole, Rise of the Dictators and Every Little Thing. WildBear […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Australian factual producer WildBear Entertainment has unveiled a new look for its management team amid “the biggest transformation we’ve seen in decades” for the entertainment industry.

A eight-strong team will lead activities the company, which is known for the likes of Stuff the British Stole, Rise of the Dictators and Every Little Thing.

WildBear co-founder Michael Tear will remain CEO, and under him will be join co-founder Serge Ou, who becomes Head of Creative Services, leading on production, post-production, design and visual effects. Alan Erson takes on a newly created role as Managing Director of Premium Television, and will oversee the WildBear factual slate and creative strategy.

Exec producer Craig Meade is upped to Head of International TV and Harriet Pike segues from COO to Chief Strategy and Growth Officer, which WildBear is calling a “pivotal new role.” Pike will oversee international activities and expand her to include digital and post services, catalog and rights and commercial opportunities.

Watch on Deadline

Both Meade and Pike will work with distributor Wild Thring Media on new commissioning opportunities, co-productions and global potential of WildBear’s content.

Rounding out the new-look top team are Caroline Nicols, who is Chief Financial Officer, Matt Nightingale, who becomes Head of Production and Miranda Kelly, who is Head of Production Finance.

WildBear is one of Australia’s oldest factual-focused producers, having started life more than four decades ago. The company now has around 100 staff across Australia and New Zealand, and it currently produces around 150 hours a year.

“Our industry is undergoing the biggest transformation we’ve seen in decades and while WildBear has always quietly weathered every change, the time felt right to really get ahead of things, analyse all the forces at work and decide how we best want to meet the challenges ahead to steer our own future,” said Tear.



“The new leadership structure brings together some of the strongest creative and commercial talent in Australia and sends a clear message to the market about our abilities and intentions. It gives us the focus to continue producing bold, world-class factual content at scale – telling ambitious true stories for a range of audiences – while expanding internationally, building new partnerships and creating greater long-term cross-platform value from our intellectual property, rights and creative services.”

title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Trailer: Brad Pitt Revisits The Character That Won Him An Oscar In David Fincher’s Latest
summary: We have the first trailer for David Fincher’s latest, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Directed by Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino, the film will premiere in IMAX on November 25 for a two-week engagement, followed by its release on the streamer on December 23. Pitt, who earned an Oscar for his role […]
content:
We have the first trailer for David Fincher’s latest, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Directed by Fincher from a screenplay by Quentin Tarantino, the film will premiere in IMAX on November 25 for a two-week engagement, followed by its release on the streamer on December 23.

Pitt, who earned an Oscar for his role as Cliff Booth, returns to play the character, but this time it’s 1977, and Hollywood looks very different. The film is a follow-up to Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. The film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Peter Weller.

Once Upon a Time in Hollywood premiered in 2019 and was written and directed by Quentin Tarantino. The film featured a cast that included Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Austin Butler, Dakota Fanning, Timothy Olyphant, Mike Moh, Margaret Qualley, Al Pacino, Emile Hirsch, Bruce Dern, Luke Perry, and many others.

Watch on Deadline

Pitt’s Cliff Booth plays a stunt double and DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton’s best friend, driver, and personal assistant. Cliff is a World War II special ops veteran who lives in a trailer with his pit bull. The character struggles to find work following an altercation with Bruce Lee and rumors that he killed his wife.

Tarantino’s film went on to win two Academy Awards: one for Pitt in Best Supporting Actor and another for Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for Best Production Design.

Buzz for Cliff Booth has been building since it was announced in 2024 that Pitt and Fincher were teaming on the project that Tarantino originally wanted to direct. Once Tarantino gave his blessing for Fincher to come aboard, Netflix was the obvious stop given the director’s exclusive deal there.

Watch the trailer above.

title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban
summary: UPDATED: CNN, Politico and MS NOW are suing Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex. In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry […]
content:
UPDATED: CNN, Politico and MS NOW are suing Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex.

In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”

The new organizations said in a joint statement, “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.



“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool on Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. As a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York, signaling that other networks declined to serve as replacements because of the president’s targeting of CNN.

Watch on Deadline

The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions.

“President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.”

The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling.

The outlets are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster.

In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that

it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.”

The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants.

Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

In 2018, in the case of Acosta, a federal judge ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.”

The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban.

“Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked.

Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations.

In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings.

Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. Karl moved on to another topic.

title: Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Cancels  2026 Edition
summary: Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Foundation has cancelled the 2026 edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival, saying in a statement that the sixth edition had been postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027. The announcement follows weeks of speculation over whether the 2026 edition, scheduled to unfold from December 3-12 in the Red […]
content:
Saudi Arabia‘s Red Sea Film Foundation has cancelled the 2026 edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival, saying in a statement that the sixth edition had been postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027.

The announcement follows weeks of speculation over whether the 2026 edition, scheduled to unfold from December 3-12 in the Red Sea port city of Jeddah, would take place amid tensions across the entire Gulf region due to the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war.

Aside from retaliatory strikes on neighboring territories, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, Iran has also sought to take control of the Strait of Hormuz connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, a key shipping route for their oil and other goods.

Beyond direct threats from Iran, Saudi Arabia is also dealing with a flareup in its conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi group in recent weeks.

Watch on Deadline

The foundation did not mention the geopolitical tensions saying rather that the decision “followed a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale.”

Since the event’s launch in 2021, in the wake of Saudi Arabia’s lifting of its 35-year cinema ban at the end of 2017, it has grown into the Gulf region’s main film festival with a steady flow of high-profile Hollywood guests, burgeoning industry events, and wide Middle East and international participation.

Aside from geopolitical tensions beyond its control, the festival has also been subject to internal debate about its future direction in recent months.

In June, the foundation’s longtime Managing Director Shivani Pandya Malhotra, who helped spearhead the launch of the festival having joined the body in 2019, stepped down with a number of her close team members leaving as well.

In the backdrop, there are also wider questions around Saudi Arabia’s larger commitment to the film industry, with the country’s entertainment focus shifting to the video game sector and sports such as boxing and soccer.

The foundation made it clear in its statement that the festival will be back for sixth edition in 2027 with “a renewed vision and a programme that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world.”

It also emphasized that it will continue its year-round mission of supporting filmmakers and strengthening the film industries through the Red Sea Fund, Red Sea Labs and its wider programmes and initiatives.

As part of this continued commitment, the foundation said it will introduce year-round programming at Culture Square in Jeddah from November 2026, establishing it as an ongoing destination for film screenings, cultural events and specialised film-industry programmes.

“The Red Sea Film Foundation extends its sincere appreciation to filmmakers, partners, guests and audiences for their continued trust and support. We look forward to welcoming the global film community back to Historic Jeddah in 2027 for a sixth edition that celebrates cinema, creativity and cultural dialogue,” concluded its statement.

In the meantime, Gulf neighbor the United Arab Emirates announced last week that it is reviving the Dubai International Film Festival following a 10-year hiatus, with a scheduled December 8, 2027 opening date, which could see it clash with the Red Sea.

In the backdrop, Qatar’s Doha Film Festival is pushing on with plans for its second edition running this November 19-27, 2026.

title: BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast
summary: BAFTA winner Adeel Akhtar (Sherwood) and Academy Award nominee Ciarán Hinds (Belfast) have joined the cast of A24’s BBC drama series Ministry of Time. Also announced this morning are Hong Chau (The Whale), Tamara Lawrance (Get Millie Black), Emily Fairn (The Responder), Josh Finan (Say Nothing), Aisling Loftus (Sherwood), Tawfeek Barhom (Cairo Conspiracy) and Nahuel […]
content:
BAFTA winner Adeel Akhtar (Sherwood) and Academy Award nominee Ciarán Hinds (Belfast) have joined the cast of A24‘s BBC drama series Ministry of Time.

Also announced this morning are Hong Chau (The Whale), Tamara Lawrance (Get Millie Black), Emily Fairn (The Responder), Josh Finan (Say Nothing), Aisling Loftus (Sherwood), Tawfeek Barhom (Cairo Conspiracy) and Nahuel Pérez Biscayart (120 Beats Per Minute) and Hélène Patarot (Paris, Je T’aime).

They join Aoife Hinds and Billy Howle in the series, which is based on Kaliane Bradley’s debut novel of the same name. Alice Birch (Normal People) is adapting the show, with Aneil Karia (Top Boy) is lead director on the six-part series, which is produced by Beef and Dreaming Whilst Black maker A24 for BBC iPlayer and BBC One.

The show follows the professional friendship between Sophy (Hinds) and Graham (Howle), which “develops into an intense forbidden romance that reveals the transporting power of love across centuries, just as the sinister nature of the Ministry’s true intentions increasingly puts them in danger.”

Watch on Deadline

Akhtar will play Quentin Ackerly, Sophy’s ‘handler’ at The Ministry, and while Aoife Hinds’ her real-life dad Ciarán will be Sophy’s father, Peter, with her mother, Patarot playing her on-screen mom Channary.

Hong will play Adela, the Vice-Secretary of Expatriation; Lawrance is Simellia, a ‘bridge’ alongside Sophy; Fairn will one of Commander Gore’s fellow ‘expats’, Margaret Kemble; Finan plays Captain Arthur Reginald-Smyth and Aisling Loftus is Anne Spencer. Barhom and Pérez Biscayart also star as the elusive Brigadier and Salese.

Filming on the six-part show is currently taking place in and around London, UK. A24 is executive producing alongside Birch, Bradley, Karia and Jo McClellan for the BBC. Frances du Pille is the producer and A24 has international distribution rights.

title: Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement: What the Guilds, AGs and Activists Are Saying
summary: After almost a year in the trenches pulling together his historic combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, David Ellison has finally emerged victorious. On Monday, the Silicon Valley heir confirmed he’d reached a settlement with a group of state attorneys general, who sued to block the merger over antitrust concerns. The proposed merger […]
content:
After almost a year in the trenches pulling together his historic combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, David Ellison has finally emerged victorious. On Monday, the Silicon Valley heir confirmed he’d reached a settlement with a group of state attorneys general, who sued to block the merger over antitrust concerns.

The proposed merger was met with heated opposition by activist groups, top talent like Mark Ruffalo and whispers by Ellison’s legacy media competitors. But groups like the Hollywood labor guilds are celebrating the settlement news, as the staring contest between Ellison and the AGs caused paralysis in development and spending seemingly across the board at both companies.

Here are the cheers, jeers and looming fears of the players involved in “ParaBros”:



WGA

The outspoken union acknowledged that their own active litigation against the ParaBros. merger could no longer continue once the state AG’s settled, largely over the cost of duking it out in court.

Popular on Variety

“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large. Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial. Consequently, we have also settled our lawsuit with an agreement from Paramount to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys’ fees in the litigation. Though we were not successful in blocking the merger, our advocacy brought more attention to the harms that this merger—and others like it—will cause. We will continue to fight the harms of industry consolidation.

As the number of outlets to sell our work to and the corresponding diversity of programming shrinks, we need industry-wide structural separation between streamers and studios in order to promote competition in programming, like the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules once required in broadcast television. We will continue to fight for these goals.”

DGA

The Directors Guild of America highlighted protections that the AG’s negotiated (read a comprehensive list of those here).

“We congratulate the parties on reaching an agreement that addresses a number of critical concerns related to the Paramount/WBD merger. The AG agreement contains important binding and enforceable commitments that protect theatrical film and television markets and domestic film jobs. Equally important, it brings clarity and stability to the industry during a period of decreased production. We especially thank California Attorney General Rob Bonta, and New York Attorney General Letitia James, for their leadership. We intend to continue our discussions with Paramount regarding domestic television production, with a focus on ensuring a competitive and robust marketplace that protects jobs.”

SAG-AFTRA

The actors union underscored the power of collective bargaining.

“The settlement of the Attorneys General antitrust lawsuit, announced today, addresses some of our deep concerns about production levels and investment in U.S. production… We will continue to approach our relationship with Paramount with professionalism and the intention to work well together. We hope that the process of engaging with the attorneys general has impressed upon them the fact that in addition to collective bargaining, our members rely on the law to help protect our interests. These are the lowest standards that our employers must meet. All of the companies have the opportunity to exceed their legal obligations and make additional efforts to ensure that our workplaces are healthy and that employers honor our dignity.”

Mark Ruffalo

“Task” star Ruffalo is the face of celebrity dissent over the merger, engaging in an ugly back-and-forth with Paramount after promoting what the studio called “antisemitic tropes.”

“Gavin Newsom hands huge win to Trump and his billionaire cronies,” Ruffalo wrote simply on X, referring to California Governor Newsom.



California Attorney General Rob Bonta

If Ruffalo is the face of celebrity dissent, then Bonta was the final boss. Ellison’s most vocal opponent said this about his own settlement deal on Monday:

”Today, we have secured a settlement that resolves our antitrust concerns of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger — concerns that the merger will lower output and increase prices — by guaranteeing massive investment in domestic film production and providing enforceable guardrails to help keep cable prices competitive. Let me be clear: This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger. But we believe this settlement, which resolves our antitrust concerns in every market alleged in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and puts workers’ needs, concerns, and futures first, is the best course of action. When we get down to brass tacks, what we heard over and over from people who would be most directly and immediately impacted by the merger is that what matters most is consistent film output, domestic production, and protecting the livelihoods of workers above and below the line. As such, our settlement provides court-enforceable commitments for more films, an infusion of an additional $1.5 billion into home-grown film production, and protections for workers who are impacted by the merger. There’s no Hollywood without the people who work on and off screen to make the magic happen, and today’s settlement protects workers, jobs, and Hollywood.”

More to come …

title: WGA Settles Antitrust Lawsuit With Paramount Over Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
summary: The Writers Guild of America East and Writers Guild of America West, jointly the WGA, have settled their lawsuit to block the proposed merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery per a statement released by the organization Monday. The settlement comes following the news that Paramount has reached a deal with 12 state attorneys […]
content:
The Writers Guild of America East and Writers Guild of America West, jointly the WGA, have settled their lawsuit to block the proposed merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery per a statement released by the organization Monday.

The settlement comes following the news that Paramount has reached a deal with 12 state attorneys general, removing a major obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large. Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial,” reads the statement.

Popular on Variety

The WGA also noted that while they “were not successful in blocking the merger,” the organization’s “advocacy brought more attention to the harms that this merger—and others like it—will cause. We will continue to fight the harms of industry consolidation.”

The WGA filed the lawsuit to block the proposed $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance back in July. At the time, the organization alleged it would violate federal antitrust law and would cause specific harm to writers.

“With fewer competitors, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity would have both the incentive and the ability to lower costs by suppressing writers’ wages and reducing output. Writers will be paid less and have fewer employment opportunities,” the WGA complaint stated.

The WGA’s lawsuit was filed following a prior antitrust lawsuit by 12 Democratic state attorneys that same month, which similarly alleged that the merger would give Paramount-WBD anticompetitive power in theatrical and basic cable TV markets.

Read the WGA’s full statement here:

“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large. Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial. Consequently, we have also settled our lawsuit with an agreement from Paramount to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys’ fees in the litigation.

Though we were not successful in blocking the merger, our advocacy brought more attention to the harms that this merger—and others like it—will cause. We will continue to fight the harms of industry consolidation.

As the number of outlets to sell our work to and the corresponding diversity of programming shrinks, we need industry-wide structural separation between streamers and studios in order to promote competition in programming, like the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules once required in broadcast television. We will continue to fight for these goals.”

title: David Ellison Says Paramount Hopes to Close Warner Bros. Deal in ‘Approximately Two Weeks’ in Staff Memo
summary: David Ellison’s endgame is in sight. Following a dramatic weekend of negotiations with a collection of state attorneys general and the WGA, the mogul’s path to combining Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery is now clear. In a Monday address to staff, Ellison said his team’s goal is to “close in approximately two weeks. That […]
content:
David Ellison‘s endgame is in sight. Following a dramatic weekend of negotiations with a collection of state attorneys general and the WGA, the mogul’s path to combining Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery is now clear.

In a Monday address to staff, Ellison said his team’s goal is to “close in approximately two weeks. That said, closing is really just the starting line. Bringing two companies this size together takes time, and we’ll share information as it becomes available.”

The mood is celebratory on the Paramount lot, insiders said, despite the fact that most of Hollywood is observing Yom Kippur (the most reverent of the Jewish High Holy Days). One source joked that several of Ellison’s top lieutenants will be making “guilt donations” to select charities for working through the day.

Popular on Variety

While brief, the memo focused on the combined power that “ParaBros” will now wield to provide jobs and increase content volume (a stark narrative shift from the previously opposed group of AGs, who said the merger would be anticompetitive).

“This is an exciting moment for our company and our industry. If you’re like me, you’re in this business because you love the art of visual storytelling – the chance to entertain, unite and inspire the world through extraordinary stories,” added Ellison. “Together, Paramount and WBD can do more of that, for audiences everywhere. And we can’t wait to get started.”

Read Ellison’s full memo to staff:

Team,



Just a few moments ago, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, on behalf of himself and 11 other State AGs, announced a settlement that clears the path forward on the lawsuit blocking our merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. We have also reached a settlement with the Writers Guild of America.



With both groups’ concerns now addressed, we have complete clearance for this merger and can move toward closing. There’s still work ahead to get this deal across the finish line, but we’re excited to bring these two iconic companies together, as it means more opportunity for our creatives, production crews and employees across the business, and more great entertainment for audiences everywhere.



We’re grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, and to the WGA, for engaging in good faith to reach this resolution. The agreement includes a number of commitments, including 30+ films annually and expanded U.S. film production – meant to help revitalize our industry and support the people behind it, here at home. Since we launched this bid, our goal has been to build a stronger Hollywood: more stories told, greater choice for consumers, stronger competition. Combining these companies gives us the opportunity to do just that.



This is an exciting moment for our company and our industry. If you’re like me, you’re in this business because you love the art of visual storytelling – the chance to entertain, unite and inspire the world through extraordinary stories. Together, Paramount and WBD can do more of that, for audiences everywhere. And we can’t wait to get started.



I know you have questions about what happens next – your role, your team and how we will work day to day. We don’t have all the answers yet, and I won’t pretend otherwise. We are tentatively planning to close in approximately two weeks. That said, closing is really just the starting line. Bringing two companies this size together takes time, and we’ll share information as it becomes available. In the meantime, if you have questions or concerns, please visit the Integration Hub, reach out to your manager or HR representative, or email internalcomms@paramount.com.



Thank you for your patience, commitment and hard work throughout this process. I know it’s created real uncertainty, and for some of you, real anxiety – that’s not lost on me. Our people are what make this company one of the best in the world, and I’m truly grateful for your dedication and support. I’m confident we’re going to build something special together in the years ahead.



Let’s go!



David

title: Neil Jordan on Restoring ‘Interview With the Vampire’ for 4K and Why the Film Didn’t Have Jump Scares
summary: Thirty-plus years after its original release, Neil Jordan’s Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise starring gothic vampire movie “Interview with the Vampire” is available in 4K and on 4K UHD Blu-ray. The bonus features include never-before-seen deleted scenes, as well as two special features: “Eternal Night and Deadly Light,” where Jordan and film editor Mick Audsley […]
content:
Thirty-plus years after its original release, Neil Jordan’s Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise starring gothic vampire movie “Interview with the Vampire” is available in 4K and on 4K UHD Blu-ray.

The bonus features include never-before-seen deleted scenes, as well as two special features: “Eternal Night and Deadly Light,” where Jordan and film editor Mick Audsley discuss the approach to cinematography and the gothic romanticism achieved by director of photography Philippe Rousselot. Another feature, “Interview with the Vampire: Creating the World,” with Jordan and production designer Dante Ferretti showcases the detailed sets, augmented locations and costumes of the film.

Marking the film’s release in 4K, Jordan spoke with Variety about the release, the deleted scenes and whether he’d ever consider shooting for Imax.

It’s been 32 years since the film’s release. What does it mean to finally have the film in 4K?

We can restore the movie to the way we originally shot it. The last time I saw the film was on the 25th anniversary. I asked Warner Bros. for a 35mm print. But either the cinema or the projector lights were so low, or the print had been so degraded or something, it was so dark I couldn’t see the film. So to be able to restore it, and to scan it frame by frame, is just a wonderful opportunity. I’m glad it exists so you can basically bring a movie to life again and remind yourself why you shot it in the first place.

We have to talk about the deleted scenes, like the moment with Louis in the church and inside the confessional as the priest is telling him about the capacity to forgive…

Why is that not in the finished movie? I don’t know. I swear to God, I was looking at it with Mick Audsley, the editor and I was saying, “Why did we not include that? It’s dramatic. it’s bloody, it’s tortured — it’s everything the movie is. Maybe it was for reasons of length. Or maybe the character Louis — his sense of suffering and his declarations of suffering — were all becoming a bit too much.

This film has had a lasting impact, and then there was the TV show. Why do you think “Interview With the Vampire” has such lasting appeal?

Anne Rice changed the perception of this thing that doesn’t exist. She took the story of Bram Stoker’s “Dracula,” that image of Dracula and of the vampire. She placed it in the 18th and 19th centuries. She set it in this glamorous French Louisiana background and made the question of eternity the focus. What would it be like if you were given the gift of eternal life? What would it be like to live forever? How bored would you get with your partner — be it Tom Cruise, Brad Pitt or Kirsten Dunst? Most people can’t survive a marriage. How would you survive eternity with somebody else? She retouched the archetype of a vampire. It affected everything. It definitely affected the “Twilight” novels. In some ways, it made them far too cutesy and Heathcliffian in a way. But Anne’s stuff is still dangerous, and it deserves to be continually explored.

How did you keep that danger in the film?

I saw it as a film about a doomed family. That’s what I thought was the center of it. That’s why I thought the part of Claudia is so important. In the book, she’s about six, or a bit younger. When she was 11 or 12, she still was a child. If you go to 14 or 15, you’re talking about a different kind of period of development. To me, it was a story about two men who are obsessed with each other. One tries to leave, and the other says, “OK.” He creates the child from the two of them. They’re stuck with each other, and she’s stuck with them and she doesn’t know why she became this thing.

That, to me, was a fascinating story and that was a story that would sustain an entire movie.

The problem with it was I found, is that because we’re telling a story from the heart, from the perspective of the monster — from Louis’s perspective, and also from Lestat’s perspective in a way — the studio kept saying to me, “Oh, is it scary?” I had to say to them, “Look, you’re not going to get jump scares out of this because these people — you can’t kill them. You can harm them, you can burn them or expose them to daylight. But you can’t even chop off their heads effectively. How do you scare the scariest creature that has ever existed? You can’t. So it becomes something different. It becomes about dread. It becomes about what Anne wrote about: the punishment of time. But that’s perhaps not the best subject for a horror movie in general. That’s what I had to grapple with, to make it kind of terrifying. The terror had to come from within, or the terror had to come from the ideas of these characters themselves.

So much of that dread comes from the visual language of the film — the way it’s directed, the cinematography, the lighting. What was one of the most challenging sequences for you to shoot?

The big stuff is not that difficult. We were lucky enough to be at a period before CGI had taken over the world and taken over cinema. Everything that we saw in the film had to be photographed. We built that New Orleans set, and we burned it. We had cameras across the Mississippi. It probably was one of the last times when you could actually do that.

CGI was just in its infancy, and we had a great special effects supervisor, Rob Legato, who had just set up Digital Domain with James Cameron, but that whole movement of cinema into something that is not essentially unreal hadn’t begun yet — or at least I wasn’t aware of it.

The most difficult scene to shoot is where Tom has that prostitute in his room, and she gradually realizes that she’s with two vampires. He puts her in a coffin, and Lestat is trying to force Louis to admit who he is. That was a difficult set of scenes to shoot. I think we went on for about eight days. That was the essence of the movie: Lestat getting Louis to embrace the monster within him.

That just reminds me of one of the other deleted scenes, the ones the one at the beginning, where Lestat is sitting down and then he gets up and he’s got the bullet hole through his hand. Why did that get left on the cutting room floor?

Maybe there was something slightly theatrical about it that you know that didn’t deserve to stay within the film. I don’t remember why these scenes were not in the final cut. I just know that the first time I showed the movie, saying to David Geffen and to Warner about this, “Look, this film is too long and David insisted on previewing what we had shot in front of an audience. The audience watched it, said, “Oh, the film is too long.” I had already worked out how to compress certain things. But it’s I’m glad those scenes are available to people and fans of the movie to see.

I want to go back to format for a second. Audiences love seeing movies in Imax, even Imax 70mm. If you were making this movie today, would you consider shooting it in Imax 70mm?

I spoke with Christopher Nolan last night. I was asking him about that. I’m not sure I would be able to wheel those bloody cameras around. I do like to be able to hold a camera on my shoulder, I love 35mm. I love the way you hear the film whirring through the gate. I’m not sure I’d be able to handle Imax. If I ever get to make another big studio movie, I’ll definitely look into it. I will.

What would you say to somebody that has never seen your “Interview with the Vampire?

I’d say it’s a companion piece to an earlier movie I made, “The Company of Wolves.”

This interview has been edited and condensed.

Watch the deleted scene below.

title: What’s in the Paramount Settlement With States: Commitment to Not Sell Studio Lots, Additional $300M Yearly Investment in U.S. Film Production, CNN Oversight and More
summary: The details of Paramount’s deal with 12 states settling their antitrust case — paving the way for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the biggest merger in Hollywood history — have been revealed. Among the top-line items: Paramount is agreeing to keep its operations in California and has committed to not sell the Paramount Studios […]
content:
The details of Paramount’s deal with 12 states settling their antitrust case — paving the way for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the biggest merger in Hollywood history — have been revealed.

Among the top-line items: Paramount is agreeing to keep its operations in California and has committed to not sell the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in the state for at least five years. That comes after Paramount Skydance chief David Ellison had threatened to pull up stakes from the Golden State if he couldn’t close the WBD deal by Oct. 1.

Under the terms of the proposed settlement, Paramount will invest at least an additional $300 million on film production in the U.S. annually — for a total of $1.5 billion over five years — and is obligated to release at least 30 movies for theatrical distribution per year (something Ellison has repeatedly promised he would do).

Popular on Variety

The company also has agreed to have a third-party entity — a “news editorial independence board” — oversee news operations of CNN and CBS News, a measure intended to maintain their editorial independence under Paramount’s ownership.

The terms of the settlement would conclude at the end of the fifth calendar year that follows the closing, so if the Paramount-WBD merger closes before the end of this year as expected, the commitment period would run through Dec. 31, 2031.

David Ellison said in a statement: “We are grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, as well as the WGA, for engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution that serves all parties, and to Governor Newsom for his support throughout this process.
