Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and — most importantly — the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling. We’re confident this agreement does exactly that, memorializing a series of commitments that include 30+ films annually and expanded U.S. film production to help revitalize our industry here at home.”

The merged Paramount-Warner Bros. will face penalties if it doesn’t meet those requirements, including potential divestiture of assets. The text of the proposed settlement with the states, which requires approval by the judge overseeing the case, is available at this link.

Also Monday, the Writers Guild of America announced a settlement with Paramount resolving the WGA’s antitrust suit over the Warner Bros. merger. Under that agreement, WGA obtained a concession from Paramount “to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years.”

Here are the key points from the Paramount settlement with the state AGs, which came after a marathon weekend of negotiations between the two sides:

Movie commitments: Paramount-Warner Bros. is required to release minimum numbers of annual film releases in both the wide release and “tentpole” categories, among others; spend at least $300 million more annually on film production in the United States than was spent in 2025; and agree to commitments regarding pricing to theaters. In years one and two, at least 20 of 30 movies must be “wide release films”; that goes up to 21 of 32 movies for years 3-5. At least four of the films must be “independent films,” and at least 50% of the movies must be produced or jointly produced with another company. The merged company is required to operate a fund for purchasing indie films and make an annual contribution of $5 million per year, for a total of $25 million over five years. If the company doesn’t meet those obligations, after a six-month grace period it would be forced to divest its entire ownership interest in Miramax Studios.

Basic cable commitments: The merged company is required to conduct separate negotiations for the distribution of basic cable channels owned by Paramount and Warner Bros. for five years. The settlement puts restrictions on changes to affiliate fee negotiations and agreements with distributors, as well as a restriction on the use of confidential information of either Paramount or Warner Bros. in the negotiations of affiliate fees for the other. If the company does not uphold those commitments, it will be required to divest the following channels: BET, BET Gospel, BET Her, BET Hip-Hop, BET Jams, and BET Soul; VH1; Comedy Central; Smithsonian; Destination America; and Science,

Maintaining both WB and Paramount lots: The company must maintain the production lots of both Paramount (5555 Melrose Ave. in Los Angeles) and Warner Bros. (4000 Warner Blvd. in Burbank, California) through at least the end of 2031.

Employment commitments: The company must honor collective bargaining agreements and commit $47.5 million to a “workforce fund” over five years for training and career development for employees who are laid off as a result of the merger.

News oversight board: The new Paramount-WB must form a “News Editorial Independence Board” to establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels.” The proposed settlement requires both an internal “compliance monitor” and an independent “monitoring trustee” to ensure the merged company’s compliance with the terms. In addition, a “State Committee” of five states will also oversee enforcement and monitor compliance.

Payment of states’ legal fees: The company will reimburse the 12 states for “reasonable attorneys’ fees and reasonable economic expert fees” they have incurred in an amount of not more than $40 million.

title: Paramount-Warner Bros Penalty If Merger Fails To Release 30 Pics A Year: Divest Miramax
summary: One of the settled terms negotiated by the Gang of Four AGs in Paramount’s union of Warner Bros is that if the combined merger doesn’t yield the annual film commitment of 30-plus films, they may have to divest Par sister label Miramax. Such a divestiture would be required if Paramount fails to make up for […]
content:
One of the settled terms negotiated by the Gang of Four AGs in Paramount’s union of Warner Bros is that if the combined merger doesn’t yield the annual film commitment of 30-plus films, they may have to divest Par sister label Miramax.



Such a divestiture would be required if Paramount fails to make up for the shortfall of movies within six months.

California AG Rob Bonta, specified during this AM’s presser about the settlement, “Two penalties, they fail to meet the requirements of those films, one is a structural one, a divestiture, if you will of a corporate asset of Miramax. That is one of the penalties.”

Today’s settlement also reads, “If, upon the expiration of the Theatrical Cure Period, the Combined entity has failed to cure the shortfall, the Combined entity shall divest its entire direct and indirect ownership interest in Miramax studios (“Miramax Divestiture Assets”), on commercially reasonable terms, to a bona fide acquirer approved by the State Committee (such approval not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed) within twelve (12) months of the expiration of the Theatrical Cure Period (the “Miramax Divestiture”).

Watch on Deadline

It also notes, “The Combined Entity may not reacquire any part of or interest in the Miramax Divestiture Assets during the Commitment Period.”

It’s an intriguing penalty to put upon a merged company when you’re trying to get them to pump up their volume, especially as Bonta noted today that the combined merger’s theatrical output needs to include four films annually that are considered indie versus 20% which are classified as blockbusters.

Miramax, mind you, is not a huge piece of the Paramount empire, not near the size of say, CBS.

Interesting to note, that Paramount’s highest grossing movie of the year is a Miramax co-production, Scary Movie with $231.9M worldwide (and $108.2M domestic). Miramax also has the No. 1 TV series on Netflix worldwide, The Gentleman. At this time, there are no other Miramax movies dated on the Paramount theatrical release schedule in Rentrak.

Note that not every movie that Miramax makes, goes directly to Paramount. The movie label, which raises funds through foreign sales and other types of independent financing, conducts business with various studios around town, (i.e. the Jason Statham franchise The Beekeeper, and upcoming Supermax, Serendipity and 4 Kids Walk into a Bank are with Amazon MGM Studios; 2023 Oscar winner The Holdovers was released by Focus Features after that studio won distribution rights for $30M. Also the last Bridget Jones sequel went through Universal).

Paramount closed a 49% stake in Miramax in 2020, with 51% controlled by Qatar based owner beIN Media Group. At the time of closing, ViacomCBS shelled out $150 million of the $375 million pricetag and committed to invest $225 million – comprised of $45 million annually over the next five years – to be used for new film and television productions and working capital. The deal was originally orchestrated in 2019 by then Paramount motion picture studio chief Jim Gianopulos.

“This agreement is the opposite of Disney-Fox,” Bonta also said this morning. “All the things we saw with the Disney-Fox merger: a massive decrease in film production, in film output; less films being made. This doesn’t just guard against that, and protect against the downside. It locks in a massive upside. Thirty films per year for two years, 32 films a year for the next three with requirements for what kind of films those are.”

The other penalty if Paramount-Warner Bros misses 30 films a year per Bonta: “For each film that they fail to make, should they fail to make any, $30M is paid to be split three different ways, but 90% of it goes to workers.”

title: WGA Gets No Writer Layoffs At CBS News, $17.5M For Health Fund As Guild Confirms Settlement Of Lawsuit Against Paramount-WBD Merger
summary: The WGA has confirmed that its own lawsuit over the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger also has been settled, following the same move by the state attorneys general announced Monday morning by California AG Rob Bonta. In a statement, the guild acknowledged that it could not go it alone. “We continue to believe the merger will […]
content:
The WGA has confirmed that its own lawsuit over the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger also has been settled, following the same move by the state attorneys general announced Monday morning by California AG Rob Bonta. In a statement, the guild acknowledged that it could not go it alone.

“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large,” WGA said. “Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial.”

WGA revealed what concessions they got out of Paramount as part of the settlement.

Watch on Deadline

“Consequently, we have also settled our lawsuit with an agreement from Paramount to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys’ fees in the litigation,” the guild said.

The five-year term matches that of the provisions the AGs got from Paramount.

While begrudgingly settling, the WGA vowed to keep up the fight, focusing on a reinstatement of fin-syn rules for the streaming era.

“As the number of outlets to sell our work to and the corresponding diversity of programming shrinks, we need industry-wide structural separation between streamers and studios in order to promote competition in programming, like the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules once required in broadcast television. We will continue to fight for these goals.”

You can read the full statement below.

During his press conference, Bonta was asked to address the WGA litigation.

“That’s a separate lawsuit with a separate resolution, they sued on their own, of course, adjacent to us,” he said. “We’re grateful that they sued alongside us and stood up for their principles and their convictions, and they had their own pathway to a resolution. But it’s resolved as well.”

Bonta said he believed the WGA settlement, like their own, was reached over the weekend bust stressed that “they made their own decisions about their own case, independent.”

“We were never in the same room. They had their own discussions; there was some opportunities for information sharing between the Writers Guild and the states, but they brought their own case,” he said during Monday’s press conference in Los Angeles. “They decided whether or not they wanted to resolve their case and on what terms. And they decided in the end that they would resolve their case.”

While both lawsuits were brought on antitrust grounds, the WGA focused heavily in its own suit about the impact that the merger would have on workers. Just last week, a report commissioned by the Los Angeles County supervisors warned that the proposed Paramount-Warner Bros. merger would erase another 4,500 jobs in the area. That’s after years of production decline that has led to plummeting work opportunities already domestically.

Bonta and the state AGs addressed some of these concerns as well in their own settlement, ensuring a financial penalty if the combined company fails to meet its theatrical release commitments that would largely be split among the major entertainment unions and the California Film and Television Fund.

“This agreement is the opposite of Disney-Fox,” Bonta told reporters, invoking a deal that contributed to a massive wave of consolidation and reduced competition among the major film and TV studios. “The things that we saw in the Disney-Fox merger: a massive decrease in film production, in film output, less films being made. This doesn’t just guard against that and protect against the downside. It locks in a massive upside: 30 films per year for two years, 32 films per year for the next three, with requirements, of course, about what kind of films those are.”

In addition to $30 million fee, the new Paramount-Warner Bros. would be legally required to divest from Miramax if the film production requirements aren’t met.

“This settlement centers workers, thinks about workers [and] their future,” he said, adding later: “I think with this agreement and the commitments of Paramount to have its headquarters here and be here, there is a very bright future for production, job creation, for workers, for the economy here in California, here in LA, and also across the country.”

It’s worth noting that, while Paramount and Warner Bros. did contractually commit to keeping their famed studio lots in Hollywood, there is only a verbal commitment from the companies and from Paramount-Skydance CEO David Ellison for the studio headquarters to remain in the Golden State, too.

Here is WGA’s statement.

title: Roel Reiné To Direct ‘Lunar Colony’; Billed As Sci-Fi Thriller Meets Space Age ‘Romeo & Juliet’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Roel Reiné (Halo) has signed to direct sci-fi thriller Lunar Colony, which takes its cue from an imagined future reality in which mankind had colonized the moon. The production brings together Centerboro Productions, Sintered Steel Productions and Convoke Media, which began talking to buyers about the project at TIFF last week. Set in 2060, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Roel Reiné (Halo) has signed to direct sci-fi thriller Lunar Colony, which takes its cue from an imagined future reality in which mankind had colonized the moon.

The production brings together Centerboro Productions, Sintered Steel Productions and Convoke Media, which began talking to buyers about the project at TIFF last week.

Set in 2060, the feature takes place nearly three decades after humanity established Terra 2.0, a permanent civilization on the Moon. As Earth becomes increasingly dependent on the colony’s resources, tensions between the two worlds threaten to ignite a new struggle for power and control.

When Tiara and Josh, two young people raised on opposite sides of the Earth–Moon divide, fall in love, their relationship challenges political loyalties, family expectations and the forces determined to keep their worlds apart.

Watch on Deadline

Inspired by NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to return humankind to the moon and establish a permanent base there, the feature is written by Cerise Fukuji.

It is produced by Patricia A. Beninati (Hubble: 20 Years of Discovery) through Centerboro Productions; Todd Slater of Convoke Media (Bella, The Optimist); Fukuji (Ted Bundy: Dialogue with the Devil) through Sintered Steel Productions; Marilyn G. Haft (Grace Is Gone); Ram Paul Silbey (Stranger in the Woods); Nina Demarchi; and Line Producer Stephen Marinaccio (Jack Ryan, Ghosts of Beirut).

“Roel brings an extraordinary ability to combine cinematic scale with authentic, character-driven storytelling. His work creates immersive worlds while keeping audiences emotionally invested, and we could not imagine a more exciting filmmaker to bring Lunar Colony to life,” said Beninati

“The film imagines where today’s Artemis missions and renewed global race to the Moon could lead just a few decades from now, but at its heart is something timeless—a classic romance in the vein of Romeo and Juliet.”

Reiné, who previously explored the futuristic spaces worlds as one of the directors on the 2022-24 TV series Halo, said he had been drawn to the project for its human element.

“Underneath the scale of the science fiction, it is a deeply human story about freedom, love and the world we choose to leave behind. I want the Moon to feel completely real, beautiful, brutal and industrial; a civilization built for survival but not necessarily for freedom, while Earth, damaged and exploited, still holds something humanity has lost,” he said.

“At the center are Tiara and Josh, two people from opposite worlds whose connection challenges everything they have been taught. Visually, I want this film to feel epic and immersive, but always tactile, grounded and emotional. That contrast is what makes the world of Lunar Colony so exciting to me.”

Production is targeted for 2027, with principal casting currently underway.

Reiné is represented by David Saunders and Jack Leighton at IAG; Beninati, by Marilyn G. Haft Law, and Fukuji by Buchwald. Nina Demarchi and Ram Paul Silbey are represented by Centerboro Productions.

title: Taylor Frankie Paul Says She Doesn’t “Desire To Move Forward” With ‘The Secret Lives Of Mormon Wives’
summary: The drama in the world of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives continues. Taylor Frankie Paul, the embattled star of the Hulu reality series, revealed on social media that she doesn’t “desire to move forward” with the show as relations within the ensemble have seemingly frayed. This comes only a week after it emerged that […]
content:
The drama in the world of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives continues.

Taylor Frankie Paul, the embattled star of the Hulu reality series, revealed on social media that she doesn’t “desire to move forward” with the show as relations within the ensemble have seemingly frayed.

This comes only a week after it emerged that Paul, whose season of The Bachelorette was suspended after a domestic fracas involving her ex-partner, was set to return for Season 6 of the Jeff Jenkins-produced series.

Last week, cast member Mikayla Matthews said that she “will not be continuing the show at this moment” with a series of social media posts that seemed to imply it was because of Paul’s return.

Watch on Deadline

“The ONLY reason I’m leaving the show is because I was told a certain person was coming back,” Matthews wrote on Instagram Stories. “I told them before agreeing to do [Season] 6 that I wasn’t going to film if that certain someone came back because it’s UNETHICAL and kids are involved.”

Cast members Mayci Neeley and Layla Taylor seemed to support Matthews. “I am finishing this current season that we are filming and then not sure for after that,” Neeley posted to TikTok.

On Instagram, Paul wrote, “My gratitude goes to all the networks that supported me throughout this and gave me the chance to return. However, I don’t desire to move forward like this. I originally was willing to be removed to let them all continue on with less stress and I’m back to that point. Some of the girls know what I’ve been through and then to turn and collectively pile on with their “statements” knowing there has been ongoing abuse through the system the last 8 months on top of what I’ve endured. Almost the entire cast plus some, going at me….laughing about my kids is disgusting.”

Paul noted that production and crew were the ones who checked in on her during a tumultuous year and accused others of “bullying for months now”.

The reality star also claimed that her cast members, which also include Jen Affleck, Jessi Draper and Miranda Hope, wanted her to “lead the way of pay”. “My voice was the only one that can make it happen and then they would work from what I demanded. I’m grateful I never followed through with their requests of demands and I’m grateful I kept same pay out of fairness and integrity,” she added.

“However, it’s a pleasure to remove myself so they can continue, because I’ve almost convinced myself I’m deserving of all this pain and to a certain degree absolutely this is consequences of my actions. My question has been how much suffering and scrutiny is going to be enough…I’m just relieved to be out,” she concluded.

Season 5 of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives premiered on September 10 but only featured five episodes as a a result of the production hiatus caused by Paul’s legal issues.

Last month, the streamer renewed the show for a further 20 episodes, which was set to be broken into Seasons 6 and 7. Cameras had started rolling, but it’s not clear what Disney, Jeff Jenkins Productions and the other cast members will do now.

title: Read The Proposed Consent Decree To Settle The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
summary: As entertainment figures and politicos weigh in on the settlement of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, the parties submitted details of a consent decree for a judge’s approval. Among other things, the five-year decree requires a minimum number of annual film releases and another to spend $300 million more on domestic U.S. film production than […]
content:
As entertainment figures and politicos weigh in on the settlement of the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger, the parties submitted details of a consent decree for a judge’s approval.

Among other things, the five-year decree requires a minimum number of annual film releases and another to spend $300 million more on domestic U.S. film production than was spent in 2025. It also sets levels of U.S. film production if Congress establishes a federal film tax credit. If there is a breach, one remedy is to divest the company interest in Miramax.

Restrictions also were placed on affiliate fee negotiations for cable channels, and requirements for negotiating separately. If there is a breach, Paramount may be on the hook to divest channels including BET, VH-1, Comedy Central, Smithsonian, Destination America and Science.

The consent decree also sets up a news editorial independence board to oversee CBS News and CNN, including establishing a set of standards and principles.

Watch on Deadline

Read the proposed consent decree.

The decree also requires Paramount to continue the operation of its lot and that of Warner Bros.

title: Tom Cruise Says AI Is ‘Coming and It’s Going to Happen,’ but ‘People Want to See Real Things’: ‘Keep Creating’
summary: Despite the threat of AI to the film industry, Tom Cruise is confident that people will always “want to see real things” on screen. At an intimate BAFTA “Life in Pictures” conversation in London on Monday night, Cruise looked back on his four-decade career including acclaimed roles in “Top Gun,” “Jerry Maguire,” “Magnolia” and the […]
content:
Despite the threat of AI to the film industry, Tom Cruise is confident that people will always “want to see real things” on screen.

At an intimate BAFTA “Life in Pictures” conversation in London on Monday night, Cruise looked back on his four-decade career including acclaimed roles in “Top Gun,” “Jerry Maguire,” “Magnolia” and the “Mission: Impossible” franchise as well as to the future with his upcoming movie “Digger.”

On the topic of how the “Mission: Impossible” films have been at the forefront of new technology — with 2025’s “The Final Reckoning” even taking on AI as its villain — moderator Edith Bowman asked Cruise for his take on how it will impact the industry.

Popular on Variety

“Here’s the thing: There is nothing like human,” Cruise began, explaining that one of the reasons he is so bullish on keeping the theatrical experience alive is because it brings people together.

“I have nothing against streaming or anything like that,” he continued, saying that seeing a film in theaters is simply “a different art form.”

He pointed to this summer’s box office — which broke all-time industry records by grossing $4.76 billion from May 1 to Labor Day — as an example of the enduring desire for human stories and craftsmanship.

“People want that experience. They’re going to movie theaters,” Cruise said, adding: “I always believe in humanity.”

Cruise concluded that in the face of AI, creatives must “keep creating.”

“You know, it is coming and it’s going to happen,” Cruise said of AI. “But people want to see real things.”

The movie star also teased “Digger,” directed by “The Revenant” helmer Alejandro G. Iñárritu, in which he plays a wealthy oil tycoon. Cruise looks nearly unrecognizable in the role, sporting a fat suit and prosthetics he said initially took six hours to apply.

“I’ve never read a movie like this,” Cruise said. “It’s the most original film and one of the most moving films I’ve ever seen.”

“Digger” hits theaters on Oct. 2 via Warner Bros.

title: Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’
summary: Christina Applegate has shared a first look at her life outside the hospital following a months-long stay amid her ongoing battle with multiple sclerosis. In the video, shared on Applegate’s Instagram account, the “Married… with Children” star is seen showing off her blonde hair while wearing a black zip-up hoodie. “Fresh hair color, new weird […]
content:
Christina Applegate has shared a first look at her life outside the hospital following a months-long stay amid her ongoing battle with multiple sclerosis.

In the video, shared on Applegate’s Instagram account, the “Married… with Children” star is seen showing off her blonde hair while wearing a black zip-up hoodie. “Fresh hair color, new weird spot on my cheek haha thank you @davestanwell for brightening up my cloudy day,” Applegate wrote.

The Emmy winner also shouted out those who have been supporting her: “Love you and love to you all out there,” she wrote.

Popular on Variety

News first broke that Applegate had been hospitalized back in March, though the next month, she took to Instagram to share that she’d been “getting stronger and better every day.”

“Thank you for the outpouring of love and well wishes,” she wrote in her caption on Monday. “Health issues are a constant for me, but I’m a strong chick and I’m getting stronger and better every day. I’m taking a moment to focus on my health, but I’ll be back with more to say soon enough.”

Applegate first announced her MS diagnosis in Aug. 2021, and made her first public appearance when she attended her Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony the following year.

When she took the stage during the ceremony, the “Dead to Me” actor began to cry when talking about her daughter.

“The most important person in this world is my daughter,” Applegate said. “You are so much more than even you know. You are so beautiful and kind and smart and interesting. I’m blessed every day that I get to wake up and take you to school…thank you for standing by me through all of this.”

Speaking to the audience, Applegate added, “Every single one of you. I love you [all] so much.”

title: ‘Daredevil: Born Again’ Ending With Season 3
summary: Daredevil is hanging up his mask after three seasons on Disney+. Marvel’s “Daredevil: Born Again,” starring Charlie Cox as the blind lawyer-turned-vigilante, is ending with the upcoming Season 3, Variety has confirmed. The third and final season wrapped production a couple of months ago and is expected to premiere on Disney+ in 2027. Co-creator and […]
content:
Daredevil is hanging up his mask after three seasons on Disney+.

Marvel’s “Daredevil: Born Again,” starring Charlie Cox as the blind lawyer-turned-vigilante, is ending with the upcoming Season 3, Variety has confirmed. The third and final season wrapped production a couple of months ago and is expected to premiere on Disney+ in 2027. Co-creator and showrunner Dario Scardapane has also exited the series, which is in the midst of post-production.

Cox originally debuted as the blind hero on Netflix’s “Daredevil,” which ran for three seasons from 2015-2018 and kicked off the mini, street-level Marvel universe on the streamer. It spawned “Jessica Jones”, “Luke Cage” and “Iron Fist” spinoffs and culminated with the team-up series “The Defenders.” Disney+ revived the show as “Daredevil: Born Again” in 2025 and brought back several of the main cast members, including Vincent D’Onofrio as Wilson Fisk, aka the Kingpin of New York City, Deborah Ann Woll as Karen Page, Elden Henson as Foggy Nelson and Wilson Bethel as Bullseye.

Popular on Variety

“Born Again” Season 2 started reuniting Netflix’s “Defenders” cast by bringing back Krysten Ritter as the super-strong private detective Jessica Jones in a supporting role, plus Mike Colter had a cameo in the finale as her lover Luke Cage. Paparazzi photos also leaked during Season 3 production, showing Finn Jones back as Danny Rand, aka the martial arts expert Iron Fist, alongside Ritter and Colter. They’re expected to team up once again to take down Kingpin, who’s been stripped of his title as New York City mayor. Meanwhile, Daredevil has found himself in jail, and his identity was made public in the wake of the Season 2 finale.

Hollywood Reporter first reported the news of the series ending.

title: Rob Bonta, Facing Skeptics, Defends ‘Very Strong’ Paramount Deal
summary: Rob Bonta defended the antitrust settlement that allows Paramount to merge with Warner Bros. on Monday, saying in a 45-minute press conference that the deal includes independent monitoring and will result in more jobs in Hollywood. But the deal does not include the three words — robust structural remedies — that California’s attorney general had […]
content:
Rob Bonta defended the antitrust settlement that allows Paramount to merge with Warner Bros. on Monday, saying in a 45-minute press conference that the deal includes independent monitoring and will result in more jobs in Hollywood.

But the deal does not include the three words — robust structural remedies — that California’s attorney general had said was the goal since filing suit in July. And while he went to some lengths to argue that the deal represents a “strong” outcome, he also acknowledged it was not his preferred result.

“I don’t think these two companies should merge,” he said. “But that’s not something that we are focused on with our resolution here.”

Popular on Variety

Bonta had come under increasing pressure in the last few weeks, as Gov. Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra, the cinema trade group, and labor leaders all expressed hope for a settlement. Paramount also did its best to increase the leverage on Bonta, threatening to relocate to Tennessee and seeking a court order to force the 12-state coalition to pay $1.88 billion for delaying the deal.

In the press conference, Bonta sought to downplay that pressure. “That’s not what I’m thinking about, that’s not my focus,” he said. making the case that the A.G.’s victories in court put pressure on Paramount to offer significant concessions.

“We got the antitrust resolution that we wanted,” he said. “Very strong remedies and commitments to address the concerns that we raised.”

As to whether he thought the states could have prevailed at trial next spring, he said that courtrooms “always have risk.” He also acknowledged concerns that prolonging the case would create “uncertainty” in Hollywood, an issue that had been raised by Paramount and some labor unions.

“This deal gives certainty about the future of production right here in L.A.,” he said, noting that Paramount had committed to increasing domestic production and to not selling its L.A. lots for at least five years. “That also generates important certainty for this industry that I think is craving it.”

He also argued that the outcome is dramatically different from the Hollywood’s last major merger, the Disney-Fox deal, which went unchallenged by antitrust authorities and led to reduced production.

“This agreement is the opposite of Disney-Fox,” he said. “The things that we saw in the Disney-Fox merger — a massive decrease in film production… this doesn’t just guard against that and protect against the downside; it locks in a massive upside.”

Bonta was alone at the podium, without his trial team or representatives from the other 11 states involved in the suit. He was also not joined by the Writers Guild of America, which filed its own antitrust suit and also resolved it over the weekend.

In a statement, the WGA said that the settlement terms “fall far short of adequately protecting writers,” but that it could not bear the cost of continuing its suit without support from the states.

William Tong, the attorney general of Connecticut, also expressed dismay that the deal does not include divesture of CBS and CNN, which he said was needed to save “ethical and independent journalism.”

“We fought aggressively for that remedy,” he said. “I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more.”

Bonta noted that all 12 states signed on to the settlement. He also said the WGA was not involved in the states’ negotiations.

“They brought their own case,” he said. “They decided whether or not they wanted to resolve their case and under what terms.”

Bonta said there was no key moment or provision that unlocked the deal, and struggled to offer a timeline of how the agreement came together.

“These days have blurred because we’ve been in some deep and robust conversations,” he said.

title: Taylor Swift Set For Inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors
summary: Taylor Swift will have to find space for yet another award. MTV said Monday that the Queen of Pop Present will be the first recipient of its MTV VMA Artist Director Honors, set to be presented Sunday during the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. The inaugural prize celebrates a sustained and influential body of work […]
content:
Taylor Swift will have to find space for yet another award. MTV said Monday that the Queen of Pop Present will be the first recipient of its MTV VMA Artist Director Honors, set to be presented Sunday during the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards.

The inaugural prize celebrates a sustained and influential body of work from artists who have pushed creative boundaries and developed a clear directorial voice.

Swift has won Best Director at the VMAs four times and was nominated three other times. Among the untold number of accolades during her career, she is the only person to win the Album of the Year Grammy four times, most recently for Midnights in 2024, ande has 14 Grammy Awards overall on 58 nominations. She has racked up 11 consecutive No. 1 album since Fearless in 2008, along with topping the chart with four re-recorded LPs in 2021 and 2023, and has 15 No. 1 singles.

Her mammoth 2023-24 Eras Tour grossed more than 2.07 billion from nearly 150 shows around the world and spawned Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour, which became the top-grossing concert movie of all time with $180.8 worldwide.

RELATED: Grammy Album Of The Year Winner Through The Years – Photo Gallery

MTV noted that Swift has brought an increasingly expansive approach to storytelling, creating interconnected narratives, cinematic worlds and recurring details that invite audiences deeper into each project. The inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors recognizes that body of work, the cable channel said, while also underscoring the growing role artists play in shaping how their music is brought to life on screen.

CBS and MTV will simulcast the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards live at 7:30 p.m. ET/4:30 p.m. PT from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on September 27. The show also will stream live on Paramount+.

title: John Oliver Calls Out “Soon-To-Be Business Daddy” David Ellison & Throws Stephen Colbert Under The Bus

The comedian is known to take jabs at his “business daddies,” and amid the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, Oliver took a swipe at Ellison. While discussing UnitedHealthcare and its denial of insurance claims, Oliver gave an example […]
content:
John Oliver took a dig at “soon-to-be business daddy” David Ellison on the latest episode of Last Week Tonight.

The comedian is known to take jabs at his “business daddies,” and amid the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, Oliver took a swipe at Ellison.

While discussing UnitedHealthcare and its denial of insurance claims, Oliver gave an example of a patient who had to pay $95,000 out of pocket for cancer treatment after a claim was denied.

“Having access to wealthy parents just cannot be the system to get badly needed healthcare even if it is apparently the system that lets you be in charge of HBO,” Oliver said. “Yeah, my soon-to-be business daddy has a literal business daddy. And to be very clear, I deeply respect that and I would never make fun of you for it, unlike that pesky Stephen Colbert.”

Colbert ended his run as host of The Late Show earlier this year amid Skydance’s acquisition of Paramount and after Colbert called the CBS parent company, which settled a lawsuit with Donald Trump, a “big fat bribe.” The merger between Skydance and Paramount Global would close a month after the show was confirmed to be ending.

Watch on Deadline

“The Late Show With Stephen Colbert will end its historic run in May 2026 at the end of the broadcast season,” CBS said in a statement. “We consider Stephen Colbert irreplaceable and will retire The Late Show franchise at that time. We are proud that Stephen called CBS home. He and the broadcast will be remembered in the pantheon of greats that graced late-night television.”

title: Paramount To Keep Headquarters In Los Angeles Post-Merger: “We Aren’t Going Anywhere”
summary: Paramount is not leaving California — at least not anytime soon. The settlement of the anti-trust lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general calls for the company, which is set to acquire WBD shortly, to keep both the Paramount lot on Melrose and the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank for the next five years. “We […]
content:
Paramount is not leaving California — at least not anytime soon. The settlement of the anti-trust lawsuit filed by 12 state attorneys general calls for the company, which is set to acquire WBD shortly, to keep both the Paramount lot on Melrose and the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank for the next five years.

“We wanted those lots to be protected, they are part of the the broader solution, and I believe that the future of this merged company is in Los Angeles for many years to come for the foreseeable future,” California AG Rob Bonta said during his press conference about the settlement Monday morning.

Bonta was asked about the status of the Paramount headquarters, currently located in Los Angeles.

Watch on Deadline

“I believe that will be the case, that they will have their headquarters in California for the foreseeable future,” he said, adding, “It’s not part of the deal, I believe there will be public statements.”

There had been no public statements on the matter. Paramount Chairman and CEO David Ellison did not address it in his official statement or his company memo on the settlement Monday, the latter of which noted the combined company’s commitment to producing 30+ movies a year and expand U.S. film production.

Hours later, Ellison stepped in to clear the confusion.

“Let me be clear: the newly merged company will be headquartered in Los Angeles,” he said. “We aren’t going anywhere. Our history is here and this is where our future is being built.”

This brings to an end weeks of tension that culminated in an alleged ultimatum that Paramount would move its headquarters to Tennessee, Texas or Georgia if the anti-trust lawsuit filed by the state AGs was not settled by October 1 when a costly ticking fee to WBD was set to kick in.

Per the settlement’s consent decree, the bulked up post-merger Paramount “shall not sell or close the Paramount or Warner Bros. Lots and shall use commercially reasonable efforts to operate the Lots in a manner consistent with past practices, including leasing use to third parties and producing films and television shows.”

title: Tom Cruise Earns Applause With Six-Minute Monologue On Why Art Beats AI In Filmmaking: “There Is Nothing Like Human”
summary: Tom Cruise earned spontaneous applause at a BAFTA event in London after spending more than six minutes eulogizing about the power of art over AI. Speaking at a BAFTA: Life in Pictures event, during which Cruise reflected on his screen career, host Edith Bowman posed what she described as the “AI question” about how the […]
content:
Tom Cruise earned spontaneous applause at a BAFTA event in London after spending more than six minutes eulogizing about the power of art over AI.

Speaking at a BAFTA: Life in Pictures event, during which Cruise reflected on his screen career, host Edith Bowman posed what she described as the “AI question” about how the technology will disrupt the medium Cruise loves.

The Top Gun and Mission: Impossible actor embarked on a monologue about human craft in filmmaking and the potency of the theatrical experience. His answer re-trod plenty of familiar Cruise messages, but his passion prompted an outbreak of applause from an otherwise low-key audience.

“There is nothing like human,” Cruise responded, before traversing through an answer that touched on camera lens technology and cinemas vs. streaming. Although he did not speak about the downsides of AI directly, he said a blockbuster summer at movie theaters — including engagement from young audiences — shows that “people want human experience.”

Watch on Deadline

“What you put attention on, you give life,” Cruise told the audience of BAFTA members, adding that he does not want to lose the craftspeople who dedicate their careers to creating movies. “People wanna see real things,” he added.

Cruise has previously spoken about artificial intelligence during the 2023 SAG-AFTRA negotiations, during which the actor pushed for protections concerning the technology. He has repeatedly emphasized the importance of people in filmmaking.

During the BAFTA event, which was staged to mark his upcoming movie Digger, Cruise spoke about how he got Alejandro González Iñárritu to read him the script over two nights before he committed. The Jerry Maguire actor described the film as “one of the most original and moving” movies he has ever worked on.

The pic is gearing up for its October 2 theatrical release. It stars Cruise as an oil baron named Digger Rockwell who is charged with saving the day to avert an environmental catastrophe that he caused in the first place.

The end is near for Daredevil: Born Again. The series starring Charlie Cox as the titular character, will end with the upcoming third season, Deadline has confirmed.

Season 1 of Daredevil: Born Again followed Fisk who goes from being a gangster to a NYC autocrat mayor. Season 2 saw the return of Krysten Ritter’s Jessica Jones character. Also in the Season 1 ender, Jon Bernthal’s Frank Castle/Punisher returned and, in the very end, broke out of Fisk’s Red Hook prestige jail.

RELATED: 2026 TV Series Renewals Photo Gallery

Watch on Deadline

Daredevil: Born Again came out strong ratings-wise in its first season, racking up the best series premiere on Disney+ for 2025, with 7.5 million viewers worldwide in its first five days. US viewership dropped about 50% in Season 2, per Luminate data.
