His film credits, which collectively have grossed more than $1.75 billion worldwide, include his role as the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Australian actor and filmmaker Angus Sampson has signed with Buchwald and Sweeney Entertainment for representation.

Sampson is best known for his multi-year run as Cisco in Netflix’s hit legal drama The Lincoln Lawyer from David E. Kelley. His film credits, which collectively have grossed more than $1.75 billion worldwide, include his role as the Organic Mechanic in Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga, opposite Anya Taylor-Joy and Chris Hemsworth, and in Mad Max: Fury Road, alongside Charlize Theron and Tom Hardy. He also starred as Tucker throughout the Insidious franchise.

Sampson also was praised for his memorable performance as Bear Gerhardt in Season 2 of FX’s Fargo. His additional film and TV credits include Warner Bros.’ They Will Kill You, opposite Patricia Arquette; CBS’ NCIS: Sydney; HBO Max’s Our Flag Means Death; AMC’s The Walking Dead; and Searchlight’s Next Goal Wins.

Watch on Deadline

Sampson also starred in the dark comedy film The Mule, which he also wrote, directed, and produced.

Sampson continues to be represented by Creative Representation in Australia and Felker, McGinnis & Ryan.

Buchwald is a full-service talent agency based in Los Angeles and New York, representing top-tier talent across the entertainment industry, with departments spanning film, television, theater, literary, branding and creators, animation, voiceover, sports, podcasting, publishing, commercial, and broadcast.

Sweeney Entertainment is a full service artist management and production company with clients working across film and television overseen by managers David Sweeney and Peter Edwards. On the producing side, Sweeney is an Executive Producer on the upcoming Netflix series Calabasas and has numerous projects in active development.

title: ‘Wonder Woman’ Director Patty Jenkins Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Is ‘Such Chaos’: ‘The Studio System Is in Bad Shape’
summary: Patty Jenkins, Halle Berry, Regina King, Misty Copeland and others gathered at downtown Manhattan’s Locanda Verde on Tuesday morning for Tribeca and Chanel’s Through Her Lens luncheon. The timing was notable for an event centered on emerging filmmakers, coming just 24 hours after news that the Paramount-Warner Bros. deal is essentially complete — a consolidation […]
content:
Patty Jenkins, Halle Berry, Regina King, Misty Copeland and others gathered at downtown Manhattan’s Locanda Verde on Tuesday morning for Tribeca and Chanel’s Through Her Lens luncheon. The timing was notable for an event centered on emerging filmmakers, coming just 24 hours after news that the Paramount-Warner Bros. deal is essentially complete — a consolidation that many in Hollywood fear could have profoundly negative effects on the industry.

“I didn’t even look at it, frankly. I’ve been tuning all of that out,” “Wonder Woman” director Patty Jenkins, who has a longstanding relationship with Warner Bros., tells Variety of the news. “It’s such chaos. I think the studio system is in such bad shape that I’m kind of tuning it out.”

Popular on Variety

Still, Jenkins remains optimistic about the industry’s future. Asked whether she would make a film with Warner Bros. under Ellison’s leadership, she says, “You never know.”

“I never say no to anything because so many people have different projects,” she continues. “Something may come along, and they’ve been making some great films, and who knows.”

Despite the turmoil within the studio system, Jenkins believes emerging filmmakers face fewer barriers than they did when she was starting out. She points to films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession” as encouraging proof that talented directors can make films on shoestring budgets — and find box office success.

“People are able to make their own films and it’s a game-changer,” she says. “I see it coming and I’m so excited about it — the democratization of being able to get your films to your audiences.”

Tribeca boss Jane Rosenthal, who co-founded Tribeca and Chanel’s Through Her Lens program 11 years ago, takes a somewhat different view, arguing that young filmmakers actually face more obstacles than when she started out. “The business is really kind of a mess,” she says, noting that streaming has contributed to an uptick in the number of films being made. Still, she adds, “Who knows what this merger is gonna do.”

One potential silver lining of the merger, according to Rosenthal, is that it could create an opening for new models of independent film distribution. “You see what AMC is doing, let’s see what that really means,” she says, referring to the indie distribution venture announced by the country’s largest theater chain last month.

That hopeful, solution-oriented attitude carried throughout the event, which kicked off this year’s Through Her Lens program. The initiative brings together five filmmaking teams for workshops, one-on-one mentorship and industry conversations before culminating in a live pitch to a jury. One team will receive full financing to produce its short film with support from Tribeca Studios, while the remaining four will receive development grants.

Berry, King and Meg Ryan were announced as this year’s jury members alongside cinematographer Autumn Durald Arkapaw (“Sinners”) and “Sterling Point” actress Ella Rubin.

Emmy Rossum, who attended Tuesday morning to support the initiative, says she “just wants the best people to tell stories” — and, she adds, “to be seen by lots of people in theaters and on streaming.”

title: ‘Crew Girl’ Renewed for Season 2 at Netflix
summary: Netflix’s latest YA drama series “Crew Girl” is racing right into Season 2, the streamer announced on Wednesday. “Crew Girl” came out on Sept. 10 and rowed to the top in the Netflix English TV Top 10, where it has remained since its release, climbing to number two this week. It reached the top 10 […]
content:
Netflix’s latest YA drama series “Crew Girl” is racing right into Season 2, the streamer announced on Wednesday.

“Crew Girl” came out on Sept. 10 and rowed to the top in the Netflix English TV Top 10, where it has remained since its release, climbing to number two this week. It reached the top 10 in more than 90 countries and now has more than 16 million views.

“I am beyond excited for Crew Girl season two!” star Miku Martineau said. “There’s so much left to explore with the characters, the romances and the rowing team, it’s going to be a ride for sure! All I know is that it will definitely be a packed, juicy, drama-filled second season so I’m ready to get back in a boat and on camera! #teamteagan.”

The eight-episode inaugural season follows 16-year-old Teagan Tao (Martineau) as she adapts to her new life after her father’s financial fraud forced her family to move across the country and back to her mother’s close-knit hometown. Tao must navigate the choppy waters of her elite prep school Easton Academy and its all-boys crew team. Unwilling to give up her own rowing dreams, she finds a spot for herself as coxswain, leading the team to victory and falling in love with some of her teammates along the way. To celebrate the team’s success, former-stroke seat Josh (Samuel Braun) opened up to his family about his ongoing health issues, while his replacement Cam (Kyle Clark) romantically rejoiced with Tao.

Popular on Variety

Along with the unanswered questions about her complicated love life and family circumstances, the season ends with Tao’s nemesis, Britney (Sage Linder), pledging to help create a girls crew team.

Fans will have to sit tight for the second season to see if Tao is team Josh, team Cam or team girls crew.

The Netflix original series is executive produced by Vivian Lin, Jeff Norton, Lindsay Macadam, Hillary Zwick Turner, Tony Chung, Lori Massini and Matthew Hornburg, Mark J.W. Bishop, Jennifer McCarron for Blue Ant Studios.

title: Mahershala Ali Says ‘I Agree’ That Marvel Not Making ‘Blade’ Is the ‘Biggest Failure’ of Kevin Feige’s Career: ‘I Don’t Know Why It Didn’t Happen’
summary: Mahershala Ali is dumbfounded like the rest of us when it comes to Marvel’s inability to get his “Blade” movie reboot off the ground. Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige told the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast over the summer that he was “feeling like a gigantic loser and failure” for bungling Ali’s “Blade,” and now the […]
content:
Mahershala Ali is dumbfounded like the rest of us when it comes to Marvel’s inability to get his “Blade” movie reboot off the ground. Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige told the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast over the summer that he was “feeling like a gigantic loser and failure” for bungling Ali’s “Blade,” and now the actor told GQ that he agrees with that assessment.

“That’s a Kevin Feige question,” Ali said when asked why Marvel never got to the point of putting “Blade” into production. “They had, as you said, a two-time Oscar-winning actor under contract and you got billions of dollars. That’s a question for them. I don’t mean anything personal to you, but I don’t know why it didn’t. To this day, I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know that it was—Kevin, he said it was the biggest failure of his career and I agree.”

Marvel originally announced “Blade” in July 2019. Bassam Tariq (who now directs Ali in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”) was the first director to join the movie, but he exited in September 2022 roughly two months before it was set to begin shooting. Variety reported in November 2023 that “Blade” had gone through at least five writers, from “Watchmen” scribe Stacy Osei-Kuffour to Michael Starrbury. Yann Demange stepped in as the movie’s director after Tariq’s exit, but Demange ended up dropping out in June 2024.

Popular on Variety

Amid the film’s development struggles, Ali’s interest in playing Blade has never wavered. He told Variety on the “Jurassic World Rebirth” red carpet last summer: “I’m ready. Let them know I’m ready.” In an interview with GQ earlier this year, Ali called out Marvel point blank by saying: “You had me under contract, they have billions of dollars, if they wanted to do the movie, we would’ve done the movie. So we’re not doing the movie.”

Speaking to press in July 2025, Feige explained how the prolonged delays on “Blade” were a symptom of Marvel’s “over-expansion” into Disney+ streaming content where “for the very first time ever, quantity trumped quality.” When Marvel began to reevaluate its development process, the “Blade” movie was one of the projects that stalled.

“Blade” was the latest example of Ali’s career never being sure-footed despite being a two-time Oscar-winning actor for “Moonlight” and “Green Book.” The actor told GQ in his latest interview that he thought his career would break through after the Oscar wins, yet he still found himself fighting to be cast in HBO’s “True Detective” Season 3 as opposed to getting any offers.

“I don’t feel any bitterness or disappointment around that. I want to be careful of it coming off that way because it’s honestly not how I feel,” Ali explained. “If anything, there’s sort of a relief in the epiphany of like, ‘Oh, ain’t nobody coming to save you. You got to build your boat. They’re not coming. There’s no helicopter coming. Get to cutting wood.'”

Ali also said in the interiew, “I don’t know why I constantly feel like I have to remind people of stuff or prove myself to people, but that’s just how this business works. And it exhausts me. And so then you start thinking about: How long do I have to do this this way, or do it at all?”

Watch Ali’s full interview with GQ in the video below.

title: 5 Things the Fall Festivals Told Us About the Oscar Race, From Julianne Moore and John Malkovich to ‘La Bola Negra’ and ‘I Play Rocky’
summary: The fall festival triple crown ended the way it always does, with a Toronto audience getting the last word. On Sunday, those words were in Spanish. “La Bola Negra,” the sprawling Netflix epic from Los Javis, took TIFF’s People’s Choice Award, capping three weeks in which Venice handed its Golden Lion to May el-Toukhy’s “Woman […]
content:
The fall festival triple crown ended the way it always does, with a Toronto audience getting the last word. On Sunday, those words were in Spanish.

“La Bola Negra,” the sprawling Netflix epic from Los Javis, took TIFF’s People’s Choice Award, capping three weeks in which Venice handed its Golden Lion to May el-Toukhy’s “Woman Unknown” and Telluride did what Telluride does, launching contenders without ranking a single one. Three festivals, three very different kinds of potential voters. Put their verdicts side by side, and the shape of the 99th Academy Awards starts to come into focus.

Here are five things the festivals told us.

Popular on Variety

“Wild Horse Nine” Searchlight Pictures

Venice and Telluride agreed on one thing, and that’s John Malkovich.

Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine” premiered in competition on the Lido to a 13-minute standing ovation. The next day, Searchlight brought it to Telluride as the surprise patron screening, timed to John Malkovich’s Silver Medallion tribute. And nine days later, Venice closed the loop and handed him the Volpi Cup for best actor.

Malkovich plays a dying CIA agent sent to Easter Island in the tense days before Chile’s 1973 coup, and the performance is equal parts menace and, of all things, tenderness. He’s been nominated twice, for “Places in the Heart” and “In the Line of Fire and hasn’t been back since the Clinton administration. Between the prize, the tribute and the ovation, the Academy has been handed a narrative with a bow on it. Searchlight opens the film Nov. 6.

“La Bola Negra” Carla Oset/Netflix

“La Bola Negra” is the international feature front-runner, and it’s playing well beyond the category.

The directing team known as Los Javis has everyone’s attention now.

Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi won best director at Cannes in May, carried the film to Telluride and then took Toronto’s top prize. Shot on 35mm and inspired by Federico García Lorca’s unfinished work of the same name, Spain’s Oscar selection moves among 1932, 1937 and 2017, following three generations of gay men across nearly a century of Spanish history.

A subtitled Netflix film that festivalgoers won’t stop talking about is exactly where you want to be heading into the international feature race. But People’s Choice changes the size of the conversation. Over the last decade, nine of 10 winners landed a best picture nomination, with only 2024’s “The Life of Chuck” missing. Two of them, “Green Book” and “Nomadland,” won the whole thing.

That gives Netflix, which has never won best picture, every reason to campaign across the board. And consider this — stars Guitarricadelafuente and Penélope Cruz weren’t even in Telluride to work the room, and the movie still had people talking.

I Play Rocky” Courtesy of TIFF

Toronto’s audience is signaling a wide-open and competitive best picture field.

We know the internet wants to call the race already for Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” and it’s definitely at the top of the heap for films that have screened and performed, but there’s six more months to go.

First, some housekeeping. Social media spent the weekend asking how “La Bola Negra” could win People’s Choice but not the International People’s Choice Award. TIFF officials tell Variety there’s no separate ballot, and the international prize isn’t limited to non-English-language films but to non-North American ones. “La Bola Negra” received the most votes overall, so the international honor went to the next highest non-North American film. That’s how a British drama, spoken in English and starring an Irish actor, ended up with it.

Behind “La Bola Negra” came Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” and Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann,” two crowd-pleasers with clean, sturdy narratives built to gain a legion of lovers during a long season. Heder knows how far that love can travel, after riding “CODA” from Sundance all the way to best picture.

Over the last decade, two of every three films finishing in Toronto’s top three went on to a best picture nomination. In 2019, all three (“Jojo Rabbit,” “Marriage Story” and “Parasite”) made the lineup and “Parasite” won. In 2020, only “Nomadland” did and it won, too.

That statistic can be a bit uncomfortable for two presumed heavyweights, “Wild Horse Nine” and “The Debut,” neither of which cracked the top three. But missing the podium isn’t fatal. In 2017, “The Shape of Water” was one of the most talked-about titles in Toronto, finished outside the top three and won best picture anyway. The same for 2016’s “Moonlight” from Barry Jenkins, who toppled the TIFF audience winner, “La La Land” at the Oscars. But on the other hand, the winner of the Cannes best director prize has never won the Oscar for directing. The last Cannes winner to convert to an Oscar nominee was Paweł Pawlikowski for “Cold War” (2018) and before that was Bennett Miller for “Foxcatcher” (2014).

Halle Bailey and Julianne Moore in “The Debut” A24

The best actress race has a front-runner, and she already owns an Oscar.

Julianne Moore walked into Telluride as a name on the lineup. She walked out as the actress to beat.

In “The Debut,” Jesse Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, Moore plays Mona Friedman, a meek New Jersey homemaker who stumbles into a community theater musical and discovers she can’t stop. The role lets her be funny, fragile and completely unguarded, often in the same breath and she sells Eisenberg’s original songs like a woman who has waited her whole life for someone to ask.

The Telluride crowd applauded in the middle of the movie during a rehearsal scene opposite Paul Giamatti and again before the credits rolled. Festival audiences rarely do that even once.

The complication is “Still Alice.” Moore won best actress for it 11 years ago, and voters know exactly what she can do. That’s the double edge of chasing a second Oscar: the respect is already banked, and urgency is harder to manufacture. A24, which opens the film Dec. 11, will need to sell this as a Moore the Academy hasn’t seen before, not a victory lap.

Then there’s Venice. Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for “Woman Unknown,” the Danish postwar drama that also took the Golden Lion, a double the jury can only award unanimously. By her own account, it’s her first lead role and her first film festival. Arcel isn’t a name the Academy knows. Still, a performance attached to a Golden Lion demands a look, especially now that the prize makes “Woman Unknown” eligible for international feature under the Academy’s new rules.

Andrew Scott stars as Ian Charleson and Olivia Colman as Margaret Johnson in “Elsinore.” Anthony Dickenson

The field is broad, and we shouldn’t expect “locks” any time soon.

There’s a lot of themes circling movies of the fall. Many are about the craft of acting, and the actors branch loves watching those. The actors branch is the Academy’s largest; it alone decides the four acting categories and it votes on best picture like everyone else. Hand actors a movie about their own work and history, and they lean in. That helps movies like “Elsinore” and “The Debut” down the line.

If you look at history, “All About Eve,” a movie about a Broadway star and the understudy coming for her crown, earned a then-record 14 nominations and won best picture. “Shakespeare in Love” beat “Saving Private Ryan.” “The Artist” won with a silent film star who can’t survive the talkies. “Birdman” won with a faded actor staking everything on a Broadway opening. “Black Swan,” “La La Land” and “Judy” handed Natalie Portman, Emma Stone and Renée Zellweger each their own individual Oscar statuettes. And only six months ago, Jessie Buckley won best actress for “Hamnet,” a film that builds to a crowd at the Globe Theatre watching Shakespeare’s “Hamlet.”

Obviously, the branch’s affection has limits as it tends to favor movies about the craft, not the business. Case in point: Damien Chazelle’s “Babylon” cast Margot Robbie and Brad Pitt as silent-era stars and came away with zero acting nominations.

In a time of mergers and AI, real people doing the real artistic work might just do the trick.

Moral of the story is that it’s still early, and anything can change between now and nomination voting in January.

title: White House’s Trump TV 24-Hour Livestream, Launched After He Banned CNN and MS NOW, Slammed by Critics as ‘Literally State-Run TV’
summary: President Donald Trump has banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House coverage, and the three outlets are suing him, alleging it abridges their First Amendment rights. In response to Trump’s ban of the news outlets, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and Fox News — which along with CNN provide the White House […]
content:
President Donald Trump has banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House coverage, and the three outlets are suing him, alleging it abridges their First Amendment rights. In response to Trump’s ban of the news outlets, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and Fox News — which along with CNN provide the White House TV pool coverage — announced Monday they were suspending pool coverage of the president at events because of his ban on the news outlets.

On Monday at 7 p.m. ET, the White House — possibly in response to the TV pool blackout — launched Trump TV, a 24-hour livestream populated with reruns of Trump speeches combined with live coverage of other events featuring administration officials. The first video streamed on the Trump TV station was Trump’s July 3, 2026, speech at Mount Rushmore, in which he dubbed his political rivals “godless” and “evil” communists.

Popular on Variety

“Watch the Trump Administration’s biggest moments all in one place,” the White House says in the description on YouTube for “TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station.” “Top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time. Stay informed and stay up to date!”

What’s the purpose of Trump TV? “The press, in some cases, reported inaccurately or not at all on the Administration’s many record breaking accomplishments on behalf of all Americans,” according to White House head of digital strategy Kaelan Dorr, writing in a post on X. “Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration’s greatest hits, unfiltered.”

The launch of Trump TV was quickly derided by critics as “state-run” television, akin to government-controlled outlets in other countries. Among those blasting the move was California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a frequent Trump critic.

“First, Trump banned independent news from the White House. Now, he’s launching what is quite literally state-run TV to try drowning out the fact that he and his corrupt administration are failing the American people,” Newsom wrote on X. “This is truly autocratic behavior from a failed President.”

Ed Krassenstein, a prominent progressive social-media personality, commented on the White House’s post about Trump TV: “State-run TV like Russia. Fascism is awesome!”

Prior to the Trump TV launch, Weijia Jiang, CBS News’ senior White House correspondent (and former White House Correspondents’ Association president), opined on “Fox News Sunday” that the U.S. “cannot have” state-run TV in discussing Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

“America cannot have state TV,” Jiang said. “That’s what makes America America… because you need independent actors to be able to be the observers. And if the government is only showing you what it wants, then you have to question: What are we missing?”

title: ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Off To Slower Start Than ‘Ed Gein’ As ‘Crew Girl’ Surges On Netflix Weekly TV Rankings
summary: Netflix viewers responded lukewarm to the latest addition in Ryan Murphy’s cinematic universe of infamous killers last week. Meanwhile, the streamer seems to have found the right audience for its latest YA offering. Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story debuted atop the English TV list for the week of September 14 to 20, raking in 12.1 […]
content:
Netflix viewers responded lukewarm to the latest addition in Ryan Murphy‘s cinematic universe of infamous killers last week. Meanwhile, the streamer seems to have found the right audience for its latest YA offering.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story debuted atop the English TV list for the week of September 14 to 20, raking in 12.1 million views through its first four days of availability, which appears on par with last season’s premiere weekend for The Ed Gein Story. But, the third season hit Netflix on a Friday, giving it one less day than The Lizzie Borden Story to amass that viewership.

It’s truly on par with Season 2’s The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story opening week performance, because that title was released on a Thursday and had four days to hit 12.3 million views.

Watch on Deadline

With that in mind, it’s difficult to gauge the overall appetite for this series as it continues, though the latest suggests that it is at least waning, which is in line with the streamer’s well-documented problem retaining its audience on many of its biggest continuing series.

It appears the No. 2 title on the English TV list has found its audience after a modest opening earlier this month. Crew Girl sprinted to 11.3 million views in its second week on the platform, more than doubling its viewership from its opening weekend. The streamer also renewed the a frothy, coming-of-age teen drama about a 16-year-old girl who becomes the coxswain of an elite private school’s all-male rowing team.

The Gentlemen once again claimed two spots on the TV rankings. Season 2 retained its third place spot with 6 million views, while Season 1 came in at No. 5 with 3.4 million views.

It’s a sleepier week in film, with Tyler Perry’s Why Did I Get Married Again? leading the pack on the English film list with 9.7 million views. The Whisper Man came in at No. 2 with 6.2 million.

title: Kara Swisher Says She’s Leaving CNN Now That Settlement Clears Way For Paramount-WBD Merger
summary: Kara Swisher said that she will depart CNN now that a legal settlement has cleared the way for Paramount to acquire the network’s parent, Warner Bros. Discovery. On her Pivot podcast with Scott Galloway, posted on Tuesday, Swisher said that she has “asked my agent to get me out of my contract. It ends December […]
content:
Kara Swisher said that she will depart CNN now that a legal settlement has cleared the way for Paramount to acquire the network’s parent, Warner Bros. Discovery.

On her Pivot podcast with Scott Galloway, posted on Tuesday, Swisher said that she has “asked my agent to get me out of my contract. It ends December 31, so it’s only a few months, right? I just can’t. … I was trying to figure out ways I could work with them in some like licensing way, but then I thought, ‘F— these guys! I don’t want to work for them. I just don’t.”

On Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a settlement of a state AG lawsuit to block the merger, which includes the creation of an independent editorial board to oversee journalistic standards. But Swisher called such a board “dingbat nonsense,” citing the toothless nature of a board set up to oversee The Wall Street Journal when it was purchased by Rupert Murdoch in 2007.

Swisher has been a contributor to the network since 2023 and headlined an original series, Kara Swisher Wants to Live Forever, earlier this year. She said that the network had been trying to keep her.

Watch on Deadline

“I have a lot of regard for the executives there now,” Swisher said. “I have other things that make more money, that matter more and have a bigger audience … I just don’t want to work” at the network with the David Ellison-led takeover.

Swisher has been a critic of David Ellison and his father, Larry Ellison, and their purchase of WBD.

She added, “I think they are terrible media owners. I would rather work for Rupert Murdoch.”

She said, “I can’t leave yet, but I will leave as soon as I can.”

A CNN spokesperson declined to comment.

At CNN, the pending merger has generated plenty of anxiety as to the pending changes under the new owners. At a Politico summit last month, Paramount’s Chief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim talked about plans for CNN and said that Ellison “wants to bring it back to news,” a remark that suggested that the network wasn’t doing so now and was in for a major shift in the way it covers stories.

title: Mary Beth Barone Writes & Stars Opposite Joe Alwyn In Rom-Com ‘Still We Met’; Lena Dunham Among EPs
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Mary Beth Barone, the comedic multi-hyphenate who just set up the A24 rom-com series Hard Feelings at Hulu, has written and will star opposite Hamnet‘s Joe Alwyn in Still We Met, an original romantic comedy loosely inspired by her own experiences. Marking the narrative feature directorial debut of Zackary Drucker, the filmmaker behind the […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Mary Beth Barone, the comedic multi-hyphenate who just set up the A24 rom-com series Hard Feelings at Hulu, has written and will star opposite Hamnet‘s Joe Alwyn in Still We Met, an original romantic comedy loosely inspired by her own experiences.

Marking the narrative feature directorial debut of Zackary Drucker, the filmmaker behind the Emmy-nominated short-form docuseries This Is Me, the film follows a young woman at a crossroads who meets a charming British stranger and spends one unforgettable night wandering New York, revealing more than either intended.

Production is set to begin this fall in New York, with Jack Heller and Caitlin de Lisser-Ellen producing for Assemble Media (The Man I Love, Skeletons), alongside Alex Bach and Daniel Powell of Irony Point (I Think You Should Leave with Tim Robinson). Lena Dunham and Michael Cohen are exec producing under their Good Thing Going banner — which was behind Dunham’s recent Netflix series Too Much — with Madison Wolk co-producing for Assemble Media alongside Blake Mars for Good Thing Going.

Watch on Deadline

Still We Met marks the feature screenwriting and acting debut of Barone, a popular stand-up comic who writes and stars opposite Benito Skinner in the Amazon/A24 comedy Overcompensating. She recently wrapped production on the show’s second season and took to Netflix to unveil her hour-long special Galaxy Brain, which debuted in the streamer’s Top 10. We were first to report on her new TV vehicle Hard Feelings, which is being fast-tracked at Hulu after landing with the streamer in a competitive situation.

Barone told Deadline, “I am beyond excited to contribute to my favorite movie genre with the incredible producers at Assemble, Irony Point, and Good Thing Going. To have decorated documentary filmmaker Zackary Drucker directing is a true honor and Joe Alwyn in the role of Isaac just could not be more perfect. It’s a very personal project. I’m so lucky to have the opportunity to share it with the world.”

Barone’s co-star Alwyn has most recently been seen starring in Chloé Zhao’s Academy Award-winning film Hamnet, Brady Corbet’s Golden Globe winner The Brutalist, and Hamlet opposite Riz Ahmed. Upcoming, he will be seen in Sam Esmail’s Panic Carefully, alongside Julia Roberts, Eddie Redmayne and Elizabeth Olsen and Apple TV’s The Husbands.

Other past credits for Drucker include the Sundance-premiering HBO doc Enigma, Peabody Award-winning film The Stroll and The Lady and the Dale, as well as Hulu’s Queenmaker: The Making of an It Girl.

Drucker is repped by CAA and Elsa Ramo; Barone by Entertainment 360, UTA, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; and Alwyn by CAA, Management 360, Independent Talent Group, and Peikoff Mahan.

title: Sony Scoops Up TIFF Michelle Yeoh Thunder Road Action Thriller ‘The Surgeon’
summary: In another sign of life for films looking for acquisitions out of film festivals, the Thunder Road and Tango thriller The Surgeon starring Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh is seeing its North American and some foreign rights won by Sony Pictures after multiple bids. Sony also took rights in Latin America, Italy, China, and Hong Kong. […]
content:
In another sign of life for films looking for acquisitions out of film festivals, the Thunder Road and Tango thriller The Surgeon starring Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh is seeing its North American and some foreign rights won by Sony Pictures after multiple bids.

Sony also took rights in Latin America, Italy, China, and Hong Kong.

After IFC decided to unload its buzzy River out of TIFF Midnight Madness, which Sony was outbid on by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster, the other buzzy title at the Great White North festival was The Surgeon.

In the fast-paced, pulse pounding, Thin Lizzy infused soundtrack action pic, Yeoh plays an expert surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient, only to turn 35 years of surgical expertise against her captors and outwit them in a fight for survival. The pic was directed by Roshan Sethi, M.D. and also stars Martin Freeman, Laurie Davidson, Yuri Kolokolnikov, and Joseph Mydell. In addition to directing such movies as the 2025 romantic comedy A Nice Indian Boy and being the co-creator of Fox medical series The Resident), Sethi is a practicing radiation oncologist at a Boston hospital.

Watch on Deadline

Following A Nice Indian Boy, Sethi drew from his background as a physician to deliver a pulse-pounding ride that pays homage to genre films, from kidnapping thriller to surgical drama to home invasion in The Surgeon. Eleven reviews out of TIFF have The Surgeon at 100% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes.



Pic is produced by John Wick franchise producers Basil Iwanyk, Erica Lee, and Diarmaid McGrath of Thunder Road, Tango’s Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Tango’s Neil Shah, Steve Klinsky, Adam Kolbrenner of Lit Entertainment Group, John Schoenfelder, and Russell Ackerman. Theresa Page, Kim Szarzynski, Yeoh, 193’s Patrick Wachsberger and Ashley Stern, Mahal Sourgose, Eric Harbert, Jay Schuminsky, Patrick White, David Martin, Macdara Kelleher, Eoin Egan, Cáit Collins, and Andrew Schwartzberg serve as executive producers.



Yeoh also appeared in other official selection at this year’s TIFF, Bai Xue’s It’s My Time. Yeoh won Best Actress at the 2023 Oscars for Everything Everywhere All at Once.



The deal was negotiated by WME on behalf of the filmmakers. 193, a Legendary company, handled international sales rights. The deal was negotiated on behalf of the studio by Joe Matukewicz, President, Sony Pictures Worldwide Acquisitions; Virginia Longmuir, EVP Business Affairs, and Elan Kovo, VP Business Development & FP&A. Sethi is represented by CAA and Lit Entertainment Group.

title: ‘Crew Girl’ Renewed For Season 2 At Netflix
summary: There will be more Crew Girl in our future. Netflix has renewed the popular YA drama for a second season. Written by Vivian Lin, Crew Girl is described as a frothy, coming-of-age teen drama about a 16-year-old female rower Teagan (Miku Martineau) who becomes the coxswain of a dysfunctional all-boys rowing team at an elite […]
content:
There will be more Crew Girl in our future. Netflix has renewed the popular YA drama for a second season.

Written by Vivian Lin, Crew Girl is described as a frothy, coming-of-age teen drama about a 16-year-old female rower Teagan (Miku Martineau) who becomes the coxswain of a dysfunctional all-boys rowing team at an elite East Coast Prep School. Warring rivals, messy romantic entanglements, and betrayed friendships spill drama both in and out of the boat. Not to mention her complicated relationship with her mom, Ella (Jessica Paré). The team’s a mess, her life’s a mess. Can she fix both and win?

In the first season of the show, Teagan asserts herself as a true leader despite trying out for a spot on the all-girls’ rowing team at Gravenhurst Academy as part of an offer from her teammate Baloo Garner’s (Jude Wilson) twibling Britney (Sage Linder). She entertains switching schools from Easton Prep very briefly, but her teammate affectionately known as Crab Catcher (Jarrett Carlington) convinces her to stay.

Watch on Deadline

“I am beyond excited for Crew Girl season two! There’s so much left to explore with the characters, the romances, and the rowing team, it’s going to be a ride for sure!” Martineau said. “All I know is that it will definitely be a packed, juicy, drama filled second season so I’m ready to get back in a boat and on camera! #teamteagan”

L-R: Miku Martineau as Teagan, Sage Linder as Britney, Alaska Leigh as Amber and Olga Petsa as Juliet Morny in ‘Crew Girl’ Season 1

A love triangle ensued between Teagan, Josh and Cam in Season 1, with a sweet kiss shared between Teagan and Cam in the finale after she had a casual fling with Josh. But after she kisses Cam, Britney resurfaces and so does her offer of an all girls rowing team, this time at Easton Prep itself. For context, Britney was dating Josh at the beginning of Season 1, but they broke up at the Fall Formal before he and Teagan got together.

“I find their relationship very complicated. Yes, Josh sort of started [it] but it’s not really about Josh. It’s about these two [girls] who are incredibly competent at the top of their game because they suss each other out the first time that they meet each other,” Lin said of the tension between Teagan and Britney. “And it’s like, ‘I don’t want to lose to you’ is always in both of their minds. So, what does that look like? And now on the water?”

In addition to Martineau and Paré, cast includes Sam Braun (The Marshmallow Experiment, Time Cut, Bad Genius) as Josh Regis; Kyle Clark (Hello, Goodbye and Everything in Between, The Baby-Sitter’s Club, Riverdale) as Cam Dillinger and Thomas Cadrot (Scream, So Help Me Todd, Family Law) as Coach Hayden.

The series is produced by Blue Ant Studios. Lin serves as writer, executive producer and showrunner. Jeff Norton (Geek Girl, Finding Her Edge), Lindsay Macadam, Hillary Zwick Turner, Tony Chung, and Lori Massini also serve as executive producers.

title: Tom Cruise Welcomes Prince William and Kate Middleton at ‘Digger’ World Premiere in London: ‘We Love Them and Really Appreciate What They Do for the Arts’
summary: Tom Cruise world premiered his new film “Digger” on Tuesday night to an enthusiastic audience in London that included some royal guests. Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales got a front row seat to Cruise’s latest transformative role, this time as wealthy oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s satirical black comedy. “Digger’s” […]
content:
Tom Cruise world premiered his new film “Digger” on Tuesday night to an enthusiastic audience in London that included some royal guests.

Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales got a front row seat to Cruise’s latest transformative role, this time as wealthy oil tycoon Digger Rockwell in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s satirical black comedy. “Digger’s” world premiere also doubled as a Royal Film Performance, an event held by The Film and TV Charity that is attended by members of the U.K. royal family with its proceeds donated to charity.

In a speech before the start of the film, Cruise thanked William and Kate for being there. “We want to thank the royal highnesses for supporting this event, and just to tell them that we love them and we really appreciate what they do for the arts, for this country and for the world,” he began.

Popular on Variety

Cruise also thanked the Film and TV Charity and then turned his attention to producer Mary Parent — whom he called “absolutely brilliant” — and, of course, his director.

“Alejandro,” Cruise began. “You are one of one, and I have so admired your films from the very first one. And to have the opportunity to work with you has been one of the great dreams of mine and a pleasure.”

He continued, “You’ll see — this character, what he’s created, I’ve never seen anything like it. I don’t know, his mind is just extraordinary.”

“Digger” follows Cruise’s titular character — the “most powerful man in the world,” according to the film’s synopsis — as he “races to prove he is humanity’s savior before the disaster he unleashed destroys everything.” Alongside Cruise, the film stars Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons.

Cruise has been making the promotional rounds for the film over the past few weeks, appearing on the cover of GQ, “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” and Travis and Jason Kelce’s “New Heights” podcast (notably after watching the Kansas City Chiefs’ first game of the season next to Taylor Swift).

He also gave an intimate talk at London’s BAFTA headquarters on Monday night, delivering an impassioned monologue on why he believes human skill and craftsmanship will always prevail over AI.

“You know, it is coming and it’s going to happen,” Cruise said of AI. “But people want to see real things.”

He added, “People want that experience. They’re going to movie theaters. I always believe in humanity.”

“Digger” opens in theaters on Oct. 2 from Warner Bros. Pictures.

title: Ari Emanuel on Outrunning ‘Entourage,’ the Art of the Phone Call and the Stolen Commission that Still Hurts
summary: The Thomas Guide is a map that painstakingly details how to navigate Los Angeles by car. It’s a spiral-bound relic that almost none of your junior executives remember. Your assistant thinks it’s a ranking of pale British heartthrobs. Your intern will stare at you, unblinkingly and for minutes, if you even ask. But Ari Emanuel […]
content:
The Thomas Guide is a map that painstakingly details how to navigate Los Angeles by car. It’s a spiral-bound relic that almost none of your junior executives remember. Your assistant thinks it’s a ranking of pale British heartthrobs. Your intern will stare at you, unblinkingly and for minutes, if you even ask.

But Ari Emanuel has used it as a kind of blueprint to build an empire. The familiar byways of Century City, the lofty heights of the Bird Streets, the humble beginnings south of Olympic Boulevard — he’s traveled all of them. The guide is also one of the ways the super agent anchors “Roll the Calls,” a memoir of the TKO chief executive and WME Group executive chairman’s rage-fueled rise to the top of show business that hits shelves this week.

As the book rolls out, coupled with upcoming live events including in Los Angeles, Variety scored 18 (anger-free!) minutes with Emanuel to discuss his tome and outlook on the business today. Here he dissects the art of the phone call, the stolen commission that still keeps him up at night and the unholy rise of the text message.

Popular on Variety

Why was this the right time to jump in and tell your life story?

Well, it’s been a hell of a ride. I know [this memoir] was shocking to people, because most of my life I’ve just been a voice for clients. This book is really for two [groups] of people. First, the parents that come to me with anxiety having to raise kids with ADHD and dyslexia — and how to find a way to deal with that. Looking back at it, my mom and dad let me go through it and struggle while still making sure I had all the tools. It was incredible because it taught me to be a free thinker. That’s helped me in business and helped me with the people in my life. The other [group] — I wrote this book as my own version of the Thomas Guide, to surviving [the industry]. To succeed, you have to realize how hard it is. You have to be relentless, consistent, have emotional endurance. And it doesn’t come quickly. I didn’t have a “Plan B.” It was only “Plan A.” I wanted to show that sacrifice through stories and hopefully give other people a road map to get there.

Have you realized that in recent years many agents don’t “roll calls” anymore?

I’ll tell my assistants — not my current two, because they’ve gotten it — but I ask them to call [someone] and I’ll follow up and ask if they talked to them. The assistants will say, “Well, I texted.” But that’s not what I asked for. I asked you to call. I understand that texts and DMs are how we have the conversation now, but I like the personal [nature] of a phone call. I’ll also have my assistant call back after 15-20 minutes. They’ll say, “We just left word.” Call again!

Do you text?

I’m a one-word texter. Maybe two words.

I bet.

You can also just leave a voice note now.

You know people can keep those files, right? What do you think the talent agencies look like in 10 years?

The overall content business — from live sports to live events, movies, TV, podcasts, social, concerts, books, lectures — it’s all going to expand. I also think we’ll see more production … and costs will come down because of AI. The creators will keep making small movies that make a lot of money [like “Obsession”]. You’re going to start seeing a lot of new development around that. Steve Jobs [once spoke about] a study about humans. That they were the slowest-moving mammals until the invention of the bicycle, then became the fastest. So, whatever [Hollywood looks like in the future], we’ll still need legs to pedal those bikes.

It seems like the agencies are under increased pressure to consolidate, like the rest of Hollywood. Is that a good thing?

I have no idea. There will probably need to be more consolidation. But remember — Charlie Bludhorn took over Paramount all those years ago and wrote off the movie business. Then, out of nowhere, they made “The Godfather” and “Chinatown.” Barry Diller announces five years ago that the movie business is dead, then he tries to buy Paramount. When I started in the business, they said packaging was over. They said half hours were dead. They said dramas were over. This is a business that has gone on for over 100 years and it’s not going anywhere. I haven’t thought through what that means for talent agencies, but they’re going to be around. People are talented. They’re going to have to be represented.

There are many revelations in “Roll the Calls,” but something I can’t get over: You write that, in the mid-‘90s, you put the “architecture” together for CJ Entertainment to buy a minority investment in the startup DreamWorks. You said Jeff Berg, the head of ICM Partners at the time, took that entire commission for himself.

I give him credit. He owned the company. Jeff Berg took the money. [So I said], “Yeah, great. See you later. I’ll make my own.”

How much would you have cleared for that transaction?

I don’t know how much he made. But he paid for a house, probably. I didn’t own a house at that point, I had a duplex.

About 10-15 years ago, I think a lot of people in your life would’ve said you’ll never outrun Ari Gold — Jeremy Piven’s caricature of you from “Entourage.” But I’m not sure. I think you may have.

You know, my wife has helped. My new marriage, and the work I’ve done on myself has helped. Looking back, it was a great ride but I don’t want to be that guy anymore.

So you’re not going to help reboot “Entourage’ any time soon?

No, definitely not.

Talk to me about the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger and where we stand today.

I’m sitting here watching CNBC on mute. I’ve stated this publicly in op-eds, but we’ve had six bad years between COVID and the strikes. Based on all the indications from people in distribution, in film, in the cable [sector] – it seems that this isn’t about anything other than CNN and politics. Let’s move on from that and make a deal.

title: ‘Digger’ First Reactions Split Over Tom Cruise’s ‘Baffling,’ ‘Unpleasant’ and ‘Brave’ New Movie: ‘The Divide on This Is Going to Be Wide’
summary: Tom Cruise’s star vehicle “Digger” has finally been unveiled to members of the film press, who have been left divided by the satirical black comedy. The latest directorial effort from “Birdman” and “The Revenant” Oscar winner Alejandro González Iñárritu is being called everything from “baffling” to “unpleasant” to “fascinating stuff.” Most film journalists seem to […]
content:
Tom Cruise‘s star vehicle “Digger” has finally been unveiled to members of the film press, who have been left divided by the satirical black comedy. The latest directorial effort from “Birdman” and “The Revenant” Oscar winner Alejandro González Iñárritu is being called everything from “baffling” to “unpleasant” to “fascinating stuff.” Most film journalists seem to agree on one thing: “Digger” is like nothing you’re expecting.

“This is Tom Cruise’s most dynamic and interesting role in years,” writes Next Best Picture founder Matt Neglia. “It provides him plenty of space to preach to the back row but not enough to dig deeper and deliver a performance that could’ve had far more power and nuance had Alejandro González Iñárritu’s ambitious narrative not been so imbalanced in favor of its zany but empty theatrics.”



Variety’s awards pundit Clayton Davis adds: “I respect the swing and what Alejandro González Iñárritu is going for. Tom Cruise and John Goodman are delivering stellar work, and the production design and cinematography are impressive. In the end, not all the dots connect, and I wish the film leaned harder into the absurdity and satire it kept reaching for. Shocker! The divide on this one is going to be wide.”

Awards Radar’s Joey Magidson called the movie a “mess,” claiming that “not a whole lot works here” and “this wasn’t enjoyable,” while critic Edward Douglas added: “I cannot say that ‘Digger’ is very good, although I could tell what Iñarritu and Cruise were going for… I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore.” A similar opinion was shared by journalist Mike Ryan, who called the movie “unpleasant.”

Popular on Variety

IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill was more positive, writing the movie “not only showcases Tom Cruise’s best performance since ‘Magnolia,’ it’s one of the most visually inventive, conceptually audacious, and unpredictable studio movies ever made. Takes so many bold aesthetic swings it makes ‘Bardo’ look like an episode of ‘The Golden Girls.'”

Anne Thompson of IndieWire was also high on the movie, calling it “a brave and gorgeous art film that will not score with mainstream audiences but will play best for the Academy, especially crafts and actors.”

“Digger” stars Cruise as Digger Rockwell, a wealthy tycoon who must save the world when one of his oil rigs malfunctions and causes an environmental catastrophe across the planet. The film’s supporting cast includes Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons.

For Cruise, “Digger” notably marks his return to adult-oriented drama after more than a decade playing action movie heroes. In the last 10 years, Cruise’s only non-action movie is the 2017 crime comedy “American Made.” One would have to go back 20 years to add more non-action movies to Cruise’s roster, such as the musical “Rock of Ages,” the political drama “Lions for Lambs,” the comedy “Tropic Thunder” and the historical thriller “Valkyrie.” Cruise’s return to more dramatic fare has raised the eyebrows of Oscar pundits since “Digger” was announced a few years ago, but the wildly divisive reactions to “Digger” may upend his expected awards campaign.

Prior to the film’s release, much of the buzz surrounding “Digger” has related to Cruise’s wild transformation into the title role. The actor appears under heavy makeup and prosthetics that originally took six hours to apply. Cruise worked with the movie’s makeup department to get the transformation time down to an hour.

“I had a guy there with a stopwatch and I’m like, ‘OK, you see that time, six hours? By the time we’re done, we’re going to get it under an hour,’” Cruise said on the “New Heights” podcast. “They were like, ‘No, I’m not doing that, it will never happen.’ I’m like, ‘OK, first of all, if you say no, you can’t do it, you will never get there. So can we agree that we’ll maybe make it a little less?’ So with each piece that was going on, it was timed and then we’d drill and practice.”

“Digger” opens in theaters Oct. 1 from Warner Bros. Check out first reactions in the posts below.

title: Spike Lee, Bowen Yang, Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco and Chance the Rapper Front J.Crew’s 40th Anniversary Barn Jacket Campaign
summary: J.Crew is celebrating 40 years of its signature Barn Jacket with a sprawling new campaign featuring everyone from Spike Lee and Bowen Yang to Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco, Chance the Rapper and Scottie Pippen. Unveiled Tuesday, the campaign brings together 160 people photographed across New York City, Los Angeles, Austin, Boston and Chicago, marking what […]
content:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

J.Crew is celebrating 40 years of its signature Barn Jacket with a sprawling new campaign featuring everyone from Spike Lee and Bowen Yang to Amandla Stenberg, Dave Franco, Chance the Rapper and Scottie Pippen.

Unveiled Tuesday, the campaign brings together 160 people photographed across New York City, Los Angeles, Austin, Boston and Chicago, marking what J.Crew calls its most ambitious portrait project to date. The lineup spans actors, musicians, athletes, designers, artists and local personalities, with Jenny Slate, Hari Nef, Vince Staples, Ryan Beatty, Owen Thiele, Aly Raisman and Chloe East also among the familiar faces modeling the brand staple.

Photographer Robert Nethery shot the cast in a stripped-down portrait style, with each subject putting their own spin on the Barn Jacket. Accompanying films bring members of the group together to discuss personal style, their respective cities and the jacket’s staying power.

“The scale of this campaign is extraordinary, but its power comes from the individuality within it,” J.Crew chief marketing officer Julia Collier said in a statement. “We brought together 160 people across five cities to show how one iconic piece can take on an entirely different life through every person who wears it.”

First introduced by J.Crew in 1986, the Barn Jacket has become one of the retailer’s most recognizable pieces, borrowing from traditional workwear with its boxy silhouette, utility-minded construction and easy layering appeal.

For its anniversary, J.Crew is also introducing a new 2026 version of the jacket with updated proportions. The wider anniversary collection comprises 29 styles across women’s, men’s and kids offerings, ranging from the familiar cotton canvas construction to new fabrics, finishes and embellished takes.

“The Barn Jacket has always had an ease and utility that make it incredibly versatile,” said Olympia Gayot, J.Crew’s creative director of women’s and kids. “The shape is timeless, but it takes on a completely different personality depending on who is wearing it and how they style it.” Gayot added that the piece can skew “polished, rugged, feminine, oversized, familiar or unexpected,” pointing to that adaptability as a reason it has remained a mainstay in J.Crew’s assortment for four decades.

The Barn Jacket campaign builds on J.Crew’s recent effort to reintroduce archival staples to a new generation. The brand launched its “Next Rollneck Generation” last fall and more recently an updated version of its rollneck sweater fronted by Emma Chamberlain.

title: All the Top Shows, Movies and Networks in the Merged Paramount-Warner Bros: ‘Yellowstone,’ ‘Harry Potter,’ ‘Mission: Impossible’ and DC Under One Roof

What differentiates this deal — which is now in the clear to move forward — from others is the sheer amount of brands and intellectual property in play. […]
content:
In line with mega-mergers that have come before, the impending marriage of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery will lead to a media company packed with assets. What differentiates this deal — which is now in the clear to move forward — from others is the sheer amount of brands and intellectual property in play.

David Ellison’s newly merged entity will house a mountain of content, given that Paramount (which was acquired last year by Skydance Media) and Warner Bros. (which was bought by Discovery) have already doubled up their respective lineups of TV shows, movies, streamers and networks. Ellison told employees Monday he expects the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close in about two weeks following the settlement of the 12-state antitrust lawsuit that sought to block the deal.

Popular on Variety

The programming list alone is a monster to contend with, spanning Harry Potter (which is about to be revived with a new HBO series) and “Game of Thrones” at Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount’s “Yellowstone” universe and Nickelodeon empire. title: Mahershala Ali On ‘Blade’ Being A Big Failure For Kevin Feige: “100%. He Should Feel That Way”
summary: Mahershala Ali says he still doesn’t know why the long-aborning reboot of Marvel’s Blade franchise never happened. “That’s a Kevin Feige question,” the actor told GQ in a recent interview of why the film fell apart. “I don’t know why it did to this day. I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know […]
content:
Mahershala Ali says he still doesn’t know why the long-aborning reboot of Marvel‘s Blade franchise never happened.

“That’s a Kevin Feige question,” the actor told GQ in a recent interview of why the film fell apart. “I don’t know why it did to this day. I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know that it was Kevin, he said it was the biggest failure of his career and I agree. 100%. He should feel that way.”

For the record, Marvel boss Feige told the Happy Sad Confused podcast of the film in July: “I am feeling like a gigantic loser and failure that we didn’t get off the ground with Mahershala.”

Marvel first confirmed the Blade reboot starring Ali at Comic-Con in 2019. But the project was hit with multiple delays, including directors Bassam Tariq and Yann Demange’s exits from the film and the 2023 WGA strike.

Watch on Deadline

Feige hinted at another issue in a 2025 sit-down with the press at Marvel’s Burbank HQ.

“You can start and have a good script and make it a great script through production, but we didn’t feel confident we could do that on Blade,” he said. “We didn’t want to do that to Mahershala and didn’t want to do that to us.”

While Ali doesn’t sound bitter about the failed project, he does register some frustration about the five-plus years he put into it.

“I’m saying no to things in that time because they own my schedule basically,” the two time Oscar winner told GQ. “I spent a year training. Yeah. I trained so hard ’til I blew my knee out.”



He continued, “I literally moved, uprooted my family. Moved to Atlanta. We’re there waiting to go and they just keep pushing it back pushing it back pushing it and we don’t…it doesn’t happen.”

Ali has since moved on, making a different film with Tariq called Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which just screened at Toronto. The actor gets to showcase the swordfighting skills he learned for Blade and, more importantly, put his prodigious acting abilities to good use. Deadline called his performance “the glue that binds” the film.

Of his experience with Blade, Ali told GQ, “In the end, the failure became a blessing in disguise. It helped me stop waiting for the golden ticket and start building my own path.”

title: Trump DOJ Official Minimizes State AGs’ Paramount-WBD Settlement, Says It Yielded No New Antitrust-Related Commitments
summary: A top Justice Department official is minimizing the concessions state attorneys general received in the settlement of their antitrust lawsuit to block the Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery merger. Stanley Woodward, associate attorney general, said in a statement Tuesday, “After a thorough review of the Paramount/WarnerBros deal, DOJ concluded that market dynamics create the necessary incentives to […]
content:
A top Justice Department official is minimizing the concessions state attorneys general received in the settlement of their antitrust lawsuit to block the Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery merger.

Stanley Woodward, associate attorney general, said in a statement Tuesday, “After a thorough review of the Paramount/WarnerBros deal, DOJ concluded that market dynamics create the necessary incentives to protect competition.

“The only antitrust related provisions in the States’ settlement require that Paramount honor its already-stated commitments to maintain and grow its movie and TV businesses.”

The DOJ signed off on the $111 billion merger in June, with no concessions from Paramount of requirements of divestitures. Merger opponents criticized the DOJ’s review as insufficient amid Paramount’s wooing of the Trump administration, and the next month a dozen state attorneys general sued to halt the transaction.

Watch on Deadline

But a settlement was announced Monday that includes a set of behavioral conditions to last for five years, including a commitment by Paramount to release 30 films for the first and second years, and 32 films for the third, fourth and fifth years. The consent decree also includes a theatrical release window of at least 45 days. Paramount CEO David Ellison had previously stated he would commit to such windows and to the 30-movies-per-year releases.

Woodward said in his statement, “Consumers benefit when transactions close quickly after federal enforcers have concluded a substantive review. Under President Trump’s leadership, DOJ will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.”

At a press conference Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the 12 states in the litigation, repeatedly said the settlement would be an “enforceable commitment,” including that it would “significantly increase domestic production in the United States, and necessarily production right here in L.A., in Hollywood.” Among other things, he said, Paramount also would spend $300 million more each year in domestic film production, while agreeing to conduct Paramount and Warner Bros cable channel negotiations independently. The settlement also includes an independent monitor to oversee compliance, Bonta’s team noted.

Bonta had previously indicated that only a structural remedy — like a commitment to divest assets — would suffice when it came to a settlement. The consent decree does contain requirements to sell off Miramax and selected cable channels if there are breaches of the settlement terms.

Just last week, before the settlement was reached, the DOJ sided with Paramount in its motion to require that the state AGs put up a $1.88 billion bond as the litigation dragged on. The trial had been scheduled for March, but Paramount faced having to pay a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to Warner Bros. Discovery for each day that the merger didn’t close after September 30.

title: Anne Wilson Song ‘My Jesus’ Inspires New Film With Aliza Kate Barlow To Lead; Gavin Casalegno, Beau Bridges Among Cast
summary: EXCLUSIVE: A new film inspired by Anne Wilson’s hit song “My Jesus” is gearing up to begin production next month, with Aliza Kate Barlow making her feature debut starring as the Christian country singer. My Jesus, which hails from Lionsgate and Kingdom Story Company (I Can Only Imagine, Jesus Revolution), also stars Gavin Casalegno (The […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: A new film inspired by Anne Wilson‘s hit song “My Jesus” is gearing up to begin production next month, with Aliza Kate Barlow making her feature debut starring as the Christian country singer. My Jesus, which hails from Lionsgate and Kingdom Story Company (I Can Only Imagine, Jesus Revolution), also stars Gavin Casalegno (The Summer I Turned Pretty), Monica Potter (Parenthood), Charles Esten (Outer Banks) and Beau Bridges (Matlock).

Kay Oyegun wrote the screenplay based on Wilson’s book My Jesus: From Heartache to Hope, and will make her feature directorial debut.

Clockwise from top left: Aliza Kate Barlow, Gavin Casalegno, Monica Potter, Kay Oyegun, Beau Bridges and Charles Esten Anita Lashey, Getty, Getty, Jami-lyn Fehr Hall, Getty, Courtesy

Casalegno will play Anne’s brother Jacob; Potter will play Anne and Jacob’s mother, Lynn; Esten will play Kent, their father; and Bridges will play their grandfather, Bob.

Watch on Deadline

The music-driven, coming-of-age film follows the inspiring story of Anne, a teenager who is driven by a life-altering moment to post a video of herself singing online, triggering an avalanche of responses and catching the attention of executives across the Christian and country music industries. But finding her voice means Anne must also navigate the impact her gift has on everyone around her, including the changes it brings to her family and friends and the weight of her own expectations. Along the way, she must redefine how she views herself, her place in the world, her relationship with God, and ultimately her purpose.

“Anne’s story is the ultimate wish-fulfillment story — a regular girl finds a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to share her gift with the world — but what sets her story apart is that her true gift is a testament to the power of faith, family, friendship, love and devotion,” said Erin Westerman, President of Lionsgate Motion Picture Group. “Her journey isn’t just evocative and emotional — it shows how trusting that faith changed her life in every way. Kay has a wonderful take on this touching story, and we’re passionate about bringing it to life.”

The song “My Jesus” topped Billboard’s Hot Christian Songs chart and spent seven weeks at No. 1 on the Christian Airplay chart, making Wilson the first female solo artist to lead the latter with a debut single since the chart launched in 2003. Her album of the same name went on to receive a Grammy nomination for Best Contemporary Christian Music Album.

“We couldn’t be more honored to bring Anne’s story to the big screen with Kay and this talented cast. My Jesus is a story for a generation that loves the communal experience of going to the movies and is increasingly bold and unapologetic about their faith. Working alongside our incredible partners at Lionsgate to deliver an experience for that audience that feels fresh, entertaining, and deeply authentic is beyond exciting for all of us at Kingdom Story Company,” said Brandon Gregory, President and COO of the studio.

Joshua Walsh, Brandon Gregory, Andrew Erwin and Daryl LeFever will produce for Kingdom Story Company, with Jim Miller, Matthew West and Robert Deaton serving as executive producers. Meredith Wieck and Maria Ascanio are overseeing for Lionsgate. Gaby Ludlow at Kingdom Story and Phil Strina at Lionsgate negotiated the deals.

Barlow is a singer-songwriter and actress who grew up in Birmingham, AL. She has performed live across the country, and her original music has garnered over 2 million streams across Apple Music and Spotify. She is represented by Artium Talent, Authentic Talent and Literary Management, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

Casalegno most recently starred for three seasons on Prime Video’s The Summer I Turned Pretty, and will reprise his role in the theatrical feature based on the series. Additional credits include The Devil’s Mouth, the horror film produced by Lionsgate for Amazon Prime Video. He is represented by UTA, Luber Rocklin and Skrzyniarz & Mallean.

Potter starred in the films Con Air, Along Came a Spider and Patch Adams, as well as the long-running NBC series Parenthood. She is represented by Gersh and Pop Art Management.

Esten currently stars as Cain Ross on Homestead: The Series for Angel Studios and is known for his performances as Deacon Claybourne on ABC’s Nashville and as Ward Cameron in Netflix’s Outer Banks. Next, he will appear in the films Flint and Drummer Boy. He is represented by Artists & Representatives.

Bridges is an Emmy winner who currently recurs as Howard “Senior” Markston on CBS’ legal drama Matlock, starring opposite Kathy Bates. His film and TV credits include The Fabulous Baker Boys, Norma Rae, The Descendants, Without Warning: The James Brady Story, The Second Civil War, Masters of Sex and Homeland. Bridges is represented by CAA.

Oyegun is a writer and director who previously executive produced and helmed several episodes of the NBC series This Is Us. She most recently served as writer and executive producer of Apple TV’s miniseries Imperfect Women. She is represented by Underground and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

title: Top Creator Attorneys On “Turning Creative Authority Into Economic Authority” & Forging A New Entertainment Business Model At Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit
summary: It’s no secret that Hollywood is rapidly changing, and one of several driving forces is the arrival of the creator economy. Some of the industry’s top minds gathered at PMC’s Los Angeles headquarters last week for Deadline’s inaugural LA Law Summit to discuss how technology that allows anyone the ability to establish a completely unmitigated […]
content:
It’s no secret that Hollywood is rapidly changing, and one of several driving forces is the arrival of the creator economy.

Some of the industry’s top minds gathered at PMC’s Los Angeles headquarters last week for Deadline’s inaugural LA Law Summit to discuss how technology that allows anyone the ability to establish a completely unmitigated relationship with one’s audience has forced an entire rethink on how the entertainment industry does business.

“The creator economy is evolving very quickly. It’s something that has come such a long way over the last decade, and now it feels like it’s very much at the heart of entertainment” said Matt Dysart, Partner, Entertainment at Greenberg Glusker LLP. “I think about the creator economy as a space where creators [and] entertainers take advantage of lower barriers to entry to effectively establish an unmediated relationship with their audience. Effectively, the only mediator you have to work with is the algorithm.”

Dysart was joined by Ethan Cohan, Partner at Del Shaw Moonves; Jack Whigham, President and co-founder of Range Media Partners; and director-producer Anthony Hemingway.

RELATED: Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit: Nina Shaw & Patricia Glaser Honored On Day Of Big Ideas, Big Insights; Watch The Video Presentations

They all agreed that breaking down those barriers between creatives and their audience has resulted in more economic opportunity for creators.

Hemingway is the producing director for Hulu’s All’s Fair, and his work also includes directing episodes of television across CSI: NY, Treme, True Blood and Shameless, among others. He put it quite succinctly: “It’s really ultimately about turning creative authority into economic authority.”

There are countless examples of creators who have achieved success without a traditional studio or network backing them, from Joe Rogan to Charli D’Amelio. Digital-first creators are not the only ones benefiting from the business model, either.

“It’s become a term that some people look at as very narrow, but it really doesn’t make a difference whether you’re somebody with a thousand followers on your Instagram channel or you’re an Academy Award-winning actor who wants to establish secondary businesses or even primary businesses,” Cohan said. “You’ve got this opportunity to cut everybody else out and just go straight to the consumer.”

That’s not to say there is no longer value in the old way of doing things. There’s balance to be found by mining both the wisdom of the traditional studio system and the creator economy, this group argued.

“Any time there’s that disruption in distribution, there’s so much opportunity, there’s a lot of unknowns, but I think that’s what we try to capitalize on,” said Wigham. “At the end of the day, you are still connecting storytellers with distribution. As someone who was, historically, in the lanes of traditional film and TV, I was at least smart enough to know what I don’t know.”

Watch the full video above and check back Wednesday for more from Deadline’s inaugural L.A. Law Summit. Also check out video of our awards presentations to law legends Patricia Glaser and Nina Shaw here.

Deadline’s inaugural L.A. Law Summit was sponsored by Blank Rome LLP, Davis Wright Tremaine LLP, Greenberg Glusker LLP, Del Shaw Moonves Tanaka Finkelstein Lezcano Bobb & Dang LLP, Glaser Weil Fink Howard Jordan & Shapiro LLP, and Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP.

title: CAA Signs Fashion Commentator, Red Carpet Host Nicky Campbell
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Nicky Campbell has signed with CAA for representation. A red-carpet host, correspondent, fashion commentator, stylist, and creator known for his viral takes on celebrity fashion and red-carpet style, Campbell is the co-creator and host of Gloves Off, a digital fashion talk series in which he sits down with celebrity guests to revisit their red-carpet […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Nicky Campbell has signed with CAA for representation.

A red-carpet host, correspondent, fashion commentator, stylist, and creator known for his viral takes on celebrity fashion and red-carpet style, Campbell is the co-creator and host of Gloves Off, a digital fashion talk series in which he sits down with celebrity guests to revisit their red-carpet histories. To date, the show has featured Charli xcx, Sarah Paulson, Olivia Munn and Mark Ronson, among other notables.

In recent years, Campbell’s work in television has included serving as a correspondent for Netflix at the 2025 SAG Awards, appearing in Season 22 of Project Runway, and speaking on a panel for Live from E! for the Grammys and Oscars in 2026. Most recently, he co-hosted NBC’s TikTok pre-show livestream from the red carpet at the 78th Emmy Awards, alongside Trisha Paytas.

Named to the TIME100 Creators list in 2025, Campbell has partnered with brands including Tiffany & Co., HBO, Neiman Marcus, Boss, Coach, Bottega Veneta, Audemars Piguet, and YSL Beauty, and is the stylist for Grace Gummer and Mark Ronson. He graduated from Parsons School of Design and began his career at Thom Browne and Vogue. Later, he became the first Digital Editor at the Council of Fashion Designers of America before leading social and digital strategy for the launch of Balmain Beauty with Estée Lauder.

title: David Worth, Director of ‘Kickboxer’ and DP of ‘Any Which Way You Can,’ Dies at 86
summary: David Worth, director of films including “Kickboxer” and DP on numerous films including Clint Eastwood’s “Any Which Way You Can,” died Sept. 4 in Sunland, Calif. He was 86. Worth started out as director of photography on low-budget movies before Clint Eastwood hired him as cinematographer on “Bronco Billy” and “Any Which Way You Can,” […]
content:
David Worth, director of films including “Kickboxer” and DP on numerous films including Clint Eastwood’s “Any Which Way You Can,” died Sept. 4 in Sunland, Calif. He was 86.

Worth started out as director of photography on low-budget movies before Clint Eastwood hired him as cinematographer on “Bronco Billy” and “Any Which Way You Can,” both released in 1980.

After serving as director of photography on Jean-Claude Van Damme’s “Bloodsport,” he moved into directing, with 1989’s “Kickboxer” starring Van Damme. Worth went on to direct several episodes of the “Air America” TV series and features including “Shark Attack 2” and “Shark Attack 3.”

Among the other films he shot were “China Cry: A True Story,” “Lady Dragon,” “American Tigers,” “Raptor Island,” “Man With the Screaming Brain” and “Alien Apocalypse.”

Popular on Variety

“His work was also his joy, and his family frequently joined him on location around the world during his long career,” his daughter Christina said, “He was irreverent, funny, and in jovial spirits to the very end.”

Worth was also an author, teacher, and received his master’s degree in 2016. His books include “Milestones in Cinema: 50 Visionary Films & Filmmakers,” “Orson Welles Crash Course in Cinematography and “Zen & the Art of Independent Filmmaking (a cautionary tale).”

He is survived by his daughter, Chrystina Myers, a son, David Wertheimer, a brother and two grandsons.



Van Damme remembered Worth on Instagram, writing: “I am deeply saddened by the passing of my friend David Worth. From ‘Bloodsport’ to ‘Kickboxer,’ David’s talent and vision helped create two martial arts classics that changed my life.”

title: Clavicular Posts Video After Being Charged With Rape and Drugging: ‘Theres Better Ways to Make Money Then Suing Someone’
summary: “Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular has shared his first video on social media since news circulated Monday that the online personality had been charged with rape and drugging in Massachusetts. In the video posted to both TikTok and Instagram, Clavicular includes a compilation of screenshots of text messages with a contact named “Leksy,” a video of himself […]
content:
“Looksmaxxing” influencer Clavicular has shared his first video on social media since news circulated Monday that the online personality had been charged with rape and drugging in Massachusetts.

In the video posted to both TikTok and Instagram, Clavicular includes a compilation of screenshots of text messages with a contact named “Leksy,” a video of himself with the text, “Theres better ways to make money then suing someone because they don’t want you,” and a photograph of a handwritten letter with text reading “Interesting…” Underneath the post, he wrote that “Greed is a sin” in the Instagram caption, and the following under the TikTok: “Yeah still texting me to this day… totally not just trying to be greedy and get a check.”

On Monday, when outlets first reported the charges, Clavicular posted to X, writing, “Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money. Greed is evil.”

Popular on Variety

The charges against Clavicular were first filed on Sept. 8 and show that the influencer (whose real name is Braden Peters) faces one count of rape, one count of drugging someone for sexual intercourse and one count of procuring liquor for someone under 21 years of age. The alleged offenses occurred on May 23, 2025, and an arraignment is set for Oct. 14. Clavicular is not currently in custody. Clavicular’s representative, Mitchell Jackson, told NBC News that he “has not been physically served.”

While the victim was not named in accordance with Massachusetts law, reports have found that the timeline may match a civil lawsuit brought against Clavicular by 18-year-old influencer Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, who had accused him of battery, fraud and sexual misconduct in a series of events that took place in 2025. In July, Clavicular denied the allegations and filed a motion to dismiss several counts of the lawsuit.

In recent years, Clavicular has gained online attention and internet fame, notably on TikTok, thanks to provocative videos that show the 20-year-old “looksmaxxing”: injecting substances into his face, bone smashing and other practices.

title: ‘The Housewife’ Review: Naomi Watts Anchors a Watchable but Underpowered True Story of Hidden Nazism in Suburban Queens
summary: Long before the relevant authorities do, you’ll figure out the secret that immigrant homemaker Hermine Ryan (née Braunsteiner) holds close to her chest in “The Housewife” — a giveaway that may be the fault of some heavy-handed direction and scripting, but speaks to the detail and integrity of Naomi Watts’ lead performance, which often seems […]
content:
Long before the relevant authorities do, you’ll figure out the secret that immigrant homemaker Hermine Ryan (née Braunsteiner) holds close to her chest in “The Housewife” — a giveaway that may be the fault of some heavy-handed direction and scripting, but speaks to the detail and integrity of Naomi Watts‘ lead performance, which often seems a step ahead of the film around her.
