content:
EXCLUSIVE: The Challenger, Prime Video‘s ’80s-set NASA limited series, has expanded its cast with the addition of six as recurring: William Fichtner (Lucky), Kevin Carroll (Widow’s Bay), Eric Lange (Lucky), Adelaide Clemens (R.J. Decker), Louisa Jacobson (The Gilded Age) and Hunter Burke (Sweet Magnolias).

Fichtner plays Nobel physicist Richard Feynman, with Carroll as his fellow physicist, Professor Arthur Walker. Lange portrays General Donald Kutyna (of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident), with Clemens as NASA astronaut Rhea Seddon, Jacobson as Tam O’Shaughnessy — partner of Kristen Stewart’s astronaut and physicist Sally Ride — and Burke as astronaut Steve Hawley.

Inspired by Meredith E. Bagby’s 2023 book The New Guys, The Challenger chronicles the events leading up to the Challenger disaster, the investigation that followed, and Ride’s groundbreaking journey as the first American woman in space.

Watch on Deadline

The Challenger disaster was of course the 1986 breakup of NASA’s eponymous space shuttle shortly after launch, which left all seven crew members dead.

Marking Stewart’s television starring debut, The Challenger is created by Maggie Cohn (The Staircase, American Crime Story), who serves as writer, executive producer, and showrunner. James Hawes (One Life, Slow Horses) directs and also executive produces, along with Kyra Sedgwick and Valerie Stadler for Big Swing Productions; Cohn, Hawes, and Bagby; Stewart, Dylan Meyer, and Maggie McLean for Nevermind Pictures; and Darryl Frank and Justin Falvey for Amblin Television.

Other previously announced cast includes Will Arnett as George Abbey, Danny Huston as William Rogers, Sofia Black D’Elia as Judy Resnik, Paul Sparks as Larry Mulloy, Boris McGiver as William ‘Bill’ Lucas and Shea Whigham as Roger Boisjoly.

Fichtner is repped by Paradigm, Thruline Entertainment, Principal Entertainment, and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern; Carroll by Innovative Artists and Susanna Griffith Talent and Josiah Akinyele at ColorCreative; Lange by Innovative and Trademark Talent; Clemens by Gersh, Untitled Entertainment, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; Jacobson by CAA, Untitled, and Schreck Rose Dapello; and Burke by Alexander White Agency and Haven Entertainment.

title: Carlos Sanson Jr, Rosario Dawson, George Lopez & Gina Rodriguez To Lead Cast Of ‘House Of Guerrero’
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Following news of Gina Rodriguez’s directorial feature debut House of Guerrero, the lead cast has been set. Carlos Sanson Jr (Bump, Paper Dolls) is taking the lead of the boxing drama, joined by Rosario Dawson (Ashoka, 25th Hour), George Lopez (Lopez vs. Lopez, Blue Beetle) and Rodriguez. The project comes from Wayfarer Studios, 1Community, […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Following news of Gina Rodriguez’s directorial feature debut House of Guerrero, the lead cast has been set. Carlos Sanson Jr (Bump, Paper Dolls) is taking the lead of the boxing drama, joined by Rosario Dawson (Ashoka, 25th Hour), George Lopez (Lopez vs. Lopez, Blue Beetle) and Rodriguez. The project comes from Wayfarer Studios, 1Community, and I Can and I Will Productions.

House of Guerrero has commenced production in Los Angeles and California’s Imperial Valley, “capturing the distinct landscapes and communities of Los Angeles and El Centro while drawing on the deep history of Latino boxing and the region’s enduring professional fighting culture. Set against the backdrop of communities where boxing has long served as a pathway to identity, discipline, opportunity, and pride, the film brings an authentic sense of place and culture to the story of the Guerrero family,” notes a release for the film.

The original story by Rodriguez and Bernardo Cubría follows Alex Guerrero (Sanson), whose promising boxing career is cut short before he gets one last shot at stepping back into the ring with his embattled ex-fighter father Alejandro (Lopez) in his corner. Struggling with the grief and loss of his mother Elsa (Dawson), Alex turns to his older sister Paloma (Rodriguez), a gifted boxer herself, to become his new trainer and help him rediscover the fighter he once was.

Watch on Deadline

“The level of talent Gina has assembled for House of Guerrero is truly exceptional,” said Andrew Calof, Producer and President of Production and Development for Wayfarer Studios. “We’re only a few days into shooting, and you can already feel the laughter, the love, and the raw emotion coming through in these performances. This is a film that will have audiences on their feet cheering. With Gina at the helm, we’re in the hands of a true filmmaker with a remarkable vision and instinct for storytelling. More exciting casting news is coming soon!”

“Latinos have always been a powerful force in boxing, as passionate fans and as champions who have shaped the sport,” said Budnick of 1Community. “It was vital to us to tell a story that felt both authentic and deeply respectful of the enormous impact Latinos have had on boxing. That authenticity starts with the cast, and it’s a tremendous honor to welcome Gina, Carlos, George, and Rosario to the Guerrero family.”

House of Guerrero is produced by Budnick and Ameet Shukla from 1Community, Rodriguez’s I Can And I Will Productions with Molly Breeskin, and Justin Baldoni and Calof from Wayfarer. Steve Sarowitz and Jamey Heath are executive producing for Wayfarer, with Sherrese Clarke and Niija Kuykendall from HarbourView Media Group, alongside Clare LoCicero and Alice S. Kim.

Wayfarer Studios, 1Community, HarbourView Media Group and Clare LoCicero are co-financing the feature with tax credit financing provided by Three Point Capital. UTA Independent Film Group is representing the film for worldwide sales. Casting is by Mary Vernieu and Lindsay Graham Ahanonu. Cast deals were negotiated by Eric W. Thompson.

Sanson is represented by M88 and United Management; Dawson is represented by CAA and Untitled; Lopez is represented by UTA and 3 Arts Management; and Rodriguez is represented by WME.

content:
The United Kingdom led all territories in nominations at this year’s International Emmys, landing 14 nods total — including Disney+’s “A Thousand Blows” in drama and Netflix’s “Man vs. Baby” in comedy. Brazil followed, with nine nominations, then Spain with five.

Meanwhile, not making the cut was Bell Media/Crave’s “Heated Rivalry,” although a Bell Media rep confirmed that it had been submitted. “Heated Rivalry” was a phenom earlier this year both internationally and in the U.S., where it ran on HBO Max — but because it was a Canadian commission with no U.S. production partners, it wasn’t eligible for the Television Academy’s Primetime Emmy consideration. Hence, it was eligible for an International Emmy, but it wasn’t among the nominees announced on Wednesday.

Besides “A Thousand Blows,” other drama series that did make the cut included France’s “Carême,” Argentina’s “Menem” and India’s “Real Kashmir Football Club.” On the comedy side, besides “Man vs Baby,” nominees include Argentina’s “División Palermo — Season 2 [Community Squad],” Spain’s “Old Dog, New Tricks” and India’s “Vir Das: Fool Volume.”

Popular on Variety

All told, the International Academy of Television Arts & Sciences revealed 64 nominees across 16 categories and spanning 22 countries.

“The International Emmy Awards are as competitive as ever, with an outstanding range of entries from around the world vying for a coveted nomination,” International Academy presidentCEO Bruce L. Paisner said in a statement. “We look forward to bringing the global television community together to celebrate these exceptional programs and performances.”

Winners will be announced at the 54th International Emmy Awards Gala in New York on Monday, Nov. 23.

Nominees this year also came from Argentina, Belgium, Canada, Chile, China, France, Germany, India, Japan, Mexico, the Netherlands, Norway, the Philippines, Portugal, Qatar, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea and Türkiye.

title: Pete Byrne, Naked Eyes Vocalist Who Sang ‘Always Something There to Remind Me,’ Dies at 74
summary: Pete Byrne, vocalist for the British new wave band Naked Eyes, died in Los Angeles on Sept. 14 after a brief illness. He was 74. Byrne founded Naked Eyes in 1982 with his college friend Rob Fisher. Their debut album “Burning Bridges” reached No. 32 on the Billboard 200, and the duo achieved four top […]
content:
Pete Byrne, vocalist for the British new wave band Naked Eyes, died in Los Angeles on Sept. 14 after a brief illness. He was 74.

Byrne founded Naked Eyes in 1982 with his college friend Rob Fisher. Their debut album “Burning Bridges” reached No. 32 on the Billboard 200, and the duo achieved four top 40 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 across their two studio albums in 1983 and 1984: the Burt Bacharach cover “Always Something There to Remind Me,” “Promises, Promises,” “When the Lights Go Out” and “(What) In the Name of Love.”

Naked Eyes, which never toured, broke up after their second album.

Popular on Variety

In addition to his work with Naked Eyes, Byrne provided backing vocals on Stevie Wonder’s 1985 hit “Part-Time Lover,” as well as songwriting for film, television and for the Olsen twins.

Byrne continued writing, recording and touring throughout the U.S. and internationally after Fisher’s death in 1999. He released “The Real Illusion” as a solo album in 2001 before reforming Naked Eyes in 2005. The reimagined group released “Fumbling with the Covers” in 2007, “Disguise the Limit” in 2021 and a remaster of the original “Naked Eyes” self-titled album in 2025.

Born in Islington, North London, Byrne was part of a duo with Jeff Starrs from 1976 to 1977 and the band Studio from 1977 to 1979 with Clive Wright, Stash Huchrack and Richard Fenton. From 1979 to 1982, Byrne was in the band Neon which included Fisher, as well as future Tears for Fears members Neil Taylor, Manny Elias, Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal.

Peter is survived by his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve; his three children, Merlin, Dylan and Chloe; and his ex-wife, Elena.

title: Los Angeles Lakers Release Official Photo Book Chronicling Seven Decades of Purple-and-Gold History
summary: The Los Angeles Lakers are putting nearly eight decades of basketball history on the coffee table. The franchise has teamed with luxury art-book publisher Taschen for “Lakers: An Official History of the Purple & Gold,” a 528-page authorized history spanning the team’s beginnings in Minneapolis through the Showtime era, its turn-of-the-millennium three-peat and its most […]
content:
The Los Angeles Lakers are putting nearly eight decades of basketball history on the coffee table.

The franchise has teamed with luxury art-book publisher Taschen for “Lakers: An Official History of the Purple & Gold,” a 528-page authorized history spanning the team’s beginnings in Minneapolis through the Showtime era, its turn-of-the-millennium three-peat and its most recent championship runs.

NEW RELEASE Lakers: An Official History of the Purple & Gold Buy Now $100

Edited by Vikki Tobak, the book takes a particularly Los Angeles approach to the traditional sports retrospective, examining not only the team’s championship history but its broader ties to Hollywood, celebrity, fashion and fan culture. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar contributes the foreword, Lakers governor Jeanie Buss writes the introduction and former head coach Phil Jackson provides the afterword.

Bold-faced contributors include Magic Johnson, Shaquille O’Neal, Pau Gasol, LeBron James and Luka Dončić are among the players featured alongside Pat Riley, Paula Abdul, Flea, Jack Nicholson, Lou Adler, Dyan Cannon and others.

Across 10 chapters, the book traces the franchise from Minneapolis through Showtime, the Shaq-and-Kobe three-peat, the back-to-back titles of 2009 and 2010 and the 2020 championship. Each title run receives its own gold-themed section highlighting the roster, head coach and key playoff moments.

And because it’s a Taschen tome, there’s plenty here for design obsessives, too. Special layouts include a four-page gatefold displaying the Lakers’ 17 championship rings, another tracking the evolution of the team’s uniforms and a four-page spread dedicated to retired numbers. Historic promotional material, play diagrams and postgame analysis notes are also included.

“The Lakers are a global phenomenon,” Buss said in announcing the release, describing the book as “a love letter to everyone who has been part of that story.”

“Lakers: An Official History of the Purple & Gold” is available now on the Taschen website, with a wider retail release set for Oct. 1.

title: ‘Les Misérables’ Review: A Starry, Lavishly Empty, French-Language Version of Victor Hugo’s Epic
summary: Nobody sings in the latest adaptation of Victor Hugo’s 1462-page cinder-block classic, but the absence of rousing musical numbers does not mean that Fred Cavayé’s “Les Misérables” is going for gritty realism. The 179-minute film, enjoying a reported $37m budget and a host of Big French Stars trapped in starchily archetypal Big French Roles, spackles […]
content:
Nobody sings in the latest adaptation of Victor Hugo’s 1462-page cinder-block classic, but the absence of rousing musical numbers does not mean that Fred Cavayé’s “Les Misérables” is going for gritty realism. The 179-minute film, enjoying a reported $37m budget and a host of Big French Stars trapped in starchily archetypal Big French Roles, spackles its resources across the screen in a manner that has come to stand in for “epic” (wide vistas of battlefields; gliding aerial angles on meticulous, digitally rendered 19th-century cityscapes; taverns and courtrooms teeming with costumed extras) but that actually just provides a lot of weightless distraction for how curiously unmoving it all is. Three gusty hours of lots to look at and nothing to see.

You do not have to be any stripe of “Les Misérables” fan — in fact, you don’t have to have read, seen, attended or listened to a single one of well over a century’s worth of books, movies, TV shows, theater adaptations, radio plays, musical productions and comics — to find Cavayé’s film familiar. The story of Jean Valjean’s decades-spanning beef with Inspector Javert is like chlorine in the water supply: you’ve ingested it whether or not you realize. What is of note, however, is how little this version distinguishes itself from its predecessors, as though Cavayé, who makes efficient work of streamlining the book’s sprawl into just three hours, was aiming to create a kind of median, ur-“Misérables” against which all future “Misérables”-es could be measured. But in going for definitive, it ends up derivative, with cramped ambitions making a big production feel paradoxically small. Small enough to be better suited to a smaller screen — why this is not a streaming-service miniseries is anyone’s guess, especially given Netflix is a production partner.

Popular on Variety

The casting is less perplexing. The role of Valjean, previously taken in Francophone versions by Jean Gabin, Jean-Paul Belmondo and Gerard Depardieu among other luminaries, is practically an earned honor at this point, a medal that can pinned to the chest of any French actor maturing into his “national treasure” phase. Vincent Lindon certainly fits that bill; it’s less clear if he fits with newbie actor Ryan Fartout who plays hot, young Valjean, whose rippling musculature is, as the film begins, being heartlessly exploited in construction labor. (Presumably because it will be 200 years until Calvin Klein launches their Eternity fragrance and needs him to model for it.)

Valjean’s famous bread-theft-to-feed-his-starving-family here becomes a footchase/fight setpiece before he is caught and consigned to an ever-lengthening prison sentence. Eventually released, the resentful ex-con experiences a Damascene conversion due to the Christian compassion of Monseigneur Myriel (Frédéric Pierrot). Years later, Valjean, now played by Lindon, has reinvented himself as M. Madeleine, the deeply decent proprietor of a glass factory and the popular mayor of Montreuil.

Javert (Tahar Rahim) has been on a different trajectory. He becomes crueler as he rises through the law enforcement ranks, spurred by self-hatred (he smashes a lot of mirrors) and frequent apparitions of his mother, who forced him into thievery as a boy and then abandoned him when he got caught pilfering a pocket watch — just one of several such timepieces that pop up throughout “Les Misérables” as a symbol of wealth, but also a reminder of all the time that is passing while you are watching “Les Misérables.” Which is not, to be fair, to suggest that the film is laggardly. Edited at a brisk clip by Mickael Dumontier, urged along by Christophe Julien’s adventure-and-action-pummelled score, it skims quickly along the surface of the narrative, unburdened by subtext or psychological complexity or socio-political texture. Instead, we get a lot of plot.

Javert is posted to Montreuil and becomes obsessed by the suspicion that there’s more to M. Madeleine than meets the eye. Elsewhere the venal Thénardiers (Benjamin Lavernhe and Camille Cottin) are introduced scavenging gold teeth from the bodies of fallen soldiers on the battlefield of Waterloo. In the greatest misfortune of a very unlucky life, Fantine (Noémie Merlant) stops at the tavern the Thénardiers run on her way to Montreuil with her angelic daughter Cosette. Mme Thénardier, knowing a mark when she sees one — she has scarcely a single line of dialogue that is not about how better to fleece some poor sap — persuades the young mother to leave the girl with them so she can bilk regular sums out of Fantine for her upkeep. But Fantine gets fired from M. Madeleine’s factory, and turns to selling her hair, then her teeth and finally her body, which M. Madeleine only discovers when Fantine is already on her deathbed. Filled with remorse, he vows to watch over Cosette, raising her as a surrogate father. Cosette (Megan Northam) then falls for Marius (Vassili Schneider) who despite his privileged background is a leftist resistance agitator who has also befriended the Thénardiers’ daughter Éponine (ensemble MVP Marie Colomb).

What, exactly, are we doing here, people? Why, in the year 2026, do we need another “Les Misérables,” in particular one so uninterested in reflecting its own time? Even the barricades of the Paris Commune in the finale are little more than bloodied background color. Though perhaps, given the recent controversy surrounding the production’s parent company, Canal+, reportedly blacklisting filmmakers who criticized the growing influence of their right-wing billionaire majority shareholder, a more trenchantly political take on labor resistance and the plight of the working poor would have been an irony too much for this stolidly irony-free project. Whatever the case, in a rather transparent attempt at justifying yet another retread, the final words of the narration run something like, “As long as misery exists, stories like this must always be told.” Which means if we’re ever going to staunch the flow of endless, interchangeable “Les Misérables” adaptations, all we have to do is eradicate human misery. So maybe let’s get to work on that.

title: Hayley Williams Speaks Out on Death of Ex-Husband Chad Gilbert: ‘Have Not Known If It’s Appropriate’ to Comment, but ‘I Will Forever Be Grateful’
summary: Hayley Williams has spoken out about the death of her former husband, New Found Glory guitarist Chad Gilbert, who died Sunday. In a social media tribute post, the Paramore singer admitted she put a pause on commenting for a few days because she “had not known what to say or if it’s appropriate,” given their […]
content:
Hayley Williams has spoken out about the death of her former husband, New Found Glory guitarist Chad Gilbert, who died Sunday. In a social media tribute post, the Paramore singer admitted she put a pause on commenting for a few days because she “had not known what to say or if it’s appropriate,” given their estrangement. But Williams said she was ultimately compelled to put her voice forward to honor Gilbert’s impact on the music scene they shared.

The marriage between Gilbert and Williams was a short one — they wed in 2016 and divorced the following year — and it did not appear to end altogether amicably. But the couple were together a much long time than the marital record would indicate, with their relationship having begun in 2008,.

Williams’ tribute on her Instagram Stories reads:

“Have not known what to say or if it’s appropriate. But I feel sure now that I want to bc life is made of the paths we cross and the reasons we cross them are infinite.

“Chad is indeed a legend in the scene and my time connected to him taught me a lot. He introduced me to people that continue to shape my life in beautiful ways, and to music and culture that has made life a lot richer.

“There isn’t much that hasn’t already been said about what he contributed to the musical world a lot of us grew up in. His influence and attitude guided the genre forward. His passion for fostering the community was inspiring and sticks with me.

“I will forever be grateful that from him I gained a deeper understanding and a reverence for the community and the culture of hardcore.

“Sending love and my sympathies to his family, NFG fam, and all his friends.”

In a joint announcement when they split in 2017, Gilbert and Williams collectively said, ““Marriage is not for the faint of heart. There is a challenge to trying to understand your own heart in the context of a relationship… and there is goodness in considering another heart, even in spite of your own. Love is an absolute risk. And it’s up to each of us to stay hopeful even when the outcome isn’t what we’d originally hoped for.”

title: ‘The Great Experiment’ Trailer: Directors Stephen Maing And Eric Daniel Metzgar Document America At Crucial Moment Of Division
summary: EXCLUSIVE: President Lincoln, quoting the Bible, famously said of America on the brink of civil war, “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” In our present moment of intense political division, those words seem particularly relevant. The new documentary The Great Experiment, directed by Stephen Maing and Eric Daniel Metzgar, explores this era of political […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: President Lincoln, quoting the Bible, famously said of America on the brink of civil war, “A house divided against itself cannot stand.” In our present moment of intense political division, those words seem particularly relevant.

The new documentary The Great Experiment, directed by Stephen Maing and Eric Daniel Metzgar, explores this era of political antagonism, covering the period from 2017-2021 that culminated with the attack on the U.S. Capitol and President Biden’s inauguration. The film’s title comes from our first president, George Washington, who described America’s democratic form of government as “our last great experiment.”

We have your exclusive first look at the film in the trailer above.

Watch on Deadline

A border wall in ‘The Great Experiment’ Courtesy of Stephen Maing

The Great Experiment opens in New York City at IFC Center on October 16 for a week-long engagement, followed by a Los Angeles opening at Laemmle Glendale beginning October 23. From there, the film will “embark on a nationwide social cinema tour designed to bring the film back to the regions and communities featured throughout the documentary,” according to a release, “extending its exploration of how people navigate division and fostering meaningful local dialogue.” Among the planned theatrical tour stops are Milwaukee, Boston, San Diego, San Francisco, Berkeley, New Orleans, Austin, Baltimore and Memphis, with additional cities and community screenings expanding continually.

‘The Great Experiment’ Courtesy of Stephen Maing

“The Great Experiment is an epic poem in documentary form – a mirror held to an American nation at war with its own reflection, asking not who is right, but whether the experiment itself can survive,” notes a synopsis. “Filmed in striking black and white across the US from 2017 to 2021, the film engages the recent past with the critical distance of archival footage, considering the results of what George Washington called ‘our last great experiment’ in democracy. Its approach is spatial and observational, less interested in the ideological binary of left and right than in the vast, complicated country that lies between. Much as Robert Frank traveled the U.S. in the mid-1950s, bearing witness to the seen and unseen in his landmark photobook The Americans, the film weaves these lives together not to resolve their contradictions, but to hold them in the same frame long enough for something surprising to come into focus.”

The documentary held its world premiere at True/False in Columbia, MO in March and has gone on to screen at CPH:DOX in Copehagen, DC/DOX in the nation’s capital, Full Frame in Durham, NC, and RiverRun International Film Festival based in Winston-Salem, NC, among others. It is set to screen at the upcoming Woodstock Film Festival in New York and Montclair Film Festival in New Jersey.

Guns at a religious ceremony in ‘The Great Experiment’ Courtesy of Stephen Maing

The Great Experiment is produced by Farihah Zaman, Stephen Maing and Eric Daniel Metzgar. Executive producers include Anne Marie Stein, Richard MacMillan, Agnes Mentre, Lyda Kuth, and Kirsten Johnson. Co-executive producers are Rachel Traub and Jihan Robinson.

In a directors’ statement, Maing and Metzgar note they filmed in dozens of regions throughout the United States: “…Eschewing traditional interviews and narration for immersive observation, this documentary explores the vast connections between personal needs, deeply held values and the impreciseness of political affiliation. At a time when many Americans were defined by their allegiance or disavowal of Trump, we set out to film in a way that decentered that binary and, in lieu of a more expansive frame, that could account for people’s feelings of profound disconnection with sensitivity to more social and structural factors in our identities. Our hope was to build a captivating cinema of encounters and juxtapositions that might suggest how someone like a gay Trump supporter may not just be indignant in his allegiance but also on living on the margins of the margins – without a confident sense of belonging to nation, movement or affiliation.

“During our process, we thought about the immediacy and visual ambition of observational films like Fred Wiseman’s High School and Ron Fricke’s epic cinematic poem Baraka, but also the more challenging associative style of narrative exploration as seen in projects like Hale County This Morning, This Evening [directed by RaMell Ross] and Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message —particularly the way any single cut point invites viewers to engage the deeper connections between moments and the historical placement of imagery across time.”

The directors continue, “Shot in black and white, the film engages the recent past with the critical distance of archival footage — inviting the kind of clear-eyed reckoning that only distance, real or imagined, makes possible.”

Watch the trailer for The Great Experiment above.

title: Mason Thames To Star In Coming-Of-Age Comedy ‘Narcs’ For Sony Pictures
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Mason Thames, the 19-year-old actor out of the How to Train Your Dragon and Black Phone franchises, has inked a deal to star in Narcs, a new coming-of-age comedy from Sony Pictures. Plot details for Narcs are being kept under wraps. John Phillips, whose writing credits include the R-rated comedies No Hard Feelings, Good […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Mason Thames, the 19-year-old actor out of the How to Train Your Dragon and Black Phone franchises, has inked a deal to star in Narcs, a new coming-of-age comedy from Sony Pictures.

Plot details for Narcs are being kept under wraps. John Phillips, whose writing credits include the R-rated comedies No Hard Feelings, Good Boys and Dirty Grandpa, is set to make his directorial debut here.

Script is by Jordan & Justin Shipley (creators of TBS comedy Wrecked) with a rewrite by Phillips & frequent collaborator Gene Stupnitsky, who’s producing through his Big Name Entertainment banner. Robert Lamonaca is exec producing via Big Name, alongside Phillips.

Thames cemented his status as a young star capable of commanding major studio vehicles with roles in a pair of Universal projects — the 2021 horror flick The Black Phone and 2025’s live-action How to Train Your Dragon. He’s subsequently gone on to reprise in sequels to both; The Black Phone 2 released in 2025, whereas the live-action How to Train Your Dragon 2 is due for release on June 11, 2027.

Watch on Deadline

While previously appearing in Netflix’s Incoming, from Dave and John Chernin, Thames has gotten further opportunities to demonstrate his comedic chops recently via Idiots, Macon Blair’s R-rated road trip flick acquired by Independent Film Company after premiering at Sundance, as well as the Green Day project Nimrods. Upcoming, the actor will also be seen starring in the John Wick spin-off Caine helmed by Donnie Yen. He is repped by WME, Brillstein Entertainment Partners and Goodman, Genow.

Phillips is repped by UTA, Underground and Schreck Rose. Justin & Jordan Shipley, who are currently developing the animated sci-fi series Mikey & the Last Mike with Hulu/20th and Amblin, are repped by WME, Haven Entertainment and Hansen, Jacobson. Stupnitsky, who most recently directed Sony Pictures’s No Hard Feelings, starring Jennifer Lawrence, is repped by WME and Mosaic.

title: Judge Says He’ll Rule “As Soon As I Can” On Trump’s Ban On CNN, Politico And MS NOW; Expresses Concern Over Due Process
summary: A federal judge said that he will rule “as soon as I can” on whether access should be restored to CNN, Politico and MS NOW after Donald Trump’s banned them from the White House because of their coverage of him. In a 45-minute hearing on Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly noted thta he is […]
content:
A federal judge said that he will rule “as soon as I can” on whether access should be restored to CNN, Politico and MS NOW after Donald Trump‘s banned them from the White House because of their coverage of him.

In a 45-minute hearing on Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly noted thta he is bound by D.C. circuit precedent over White House access, including a 1977 decision in Sherrill vs. Knight and a 2020 decision in Karem Vs. Trump, the latter having to do with the revocation of report Brian Karem’s credentials.

Kelly told the attorneys at the outset that. based on precedent, “wasn’t followed here.”

The judge also noted that he previously presided over a CNN lawsuit against the administration after they revoked the hard pass of its then-chief White House correspondent, Jim Acosta. Kelly ruled that his pass had to be restored because he was not given notice.

Watch on Deadline

More to come.

title: HBO’s Casey Bloys & Par’s George Cheeks Go To ‘War’ Together: Execs’ Joint Premiere Appearance Creates Intrigue With WBD Merger Closing
summary: Casey Bloys’ social calendar has been getting a lot of attention over the past several months — especially the timing of some of his engagements. The Chairman and CEO of HBO and Max Content is a fixture at all of the streamer’s events, so him attending the red-carpet premiere of the new limited series War […]
content:
Casey Bloys‘ social calendar has been getting a lot of attention over the past several months — especially the timing of some of his engagements.

The Chairman and CEO of HBO and Max Content is a fixture at all of the streamer’s events, so him attending the red-carpet premiere of the new limited series War in New York on Tuesday night was not a surprise. His plus-one, George Cheeks, was.

Cheeks is Chairman of TV Media for Paramount, a company in the final stages of acquiring HBO parent Warner Bros Discovery.

Bloys and Cheeks’ joint appearance was arranged weeks ago, sources said, with Bloys inviting his friend to a premiere of a buzzy new show. They kept the affair relatively private by not posing for photos together. (The image above is a collage.)

Still, the sight of top Paramount and WBD TV executives together stirred a lot of buzz at the event, coming just a day after a settlement in 12 state attorneys general’s antitrust lawsuit was announced, paving the way for the Paramount-WBD merger to close in the next two weeks after months of uncertainty.

Watch on Deadline

Bloys similarly got tongues wagging in March when he was spotted lunching with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos just a couple of weeks after Netflix had walked away from its proposed merger of WBD following the late $111 billion bid by Paramount.

The HBO boss’ social engagements are being closely scrutinized because what he will do next is one of the most intriguing questions surrounding the Paramount-WBD merger.

Paramount CEO David Ellison and Sarandos have both spoken highly of Bloys, who is coming off another strong Emmy season at HBO where he is under contract through 2027.

Bloys is expected to be a key part of Ellison’s plans for the combined Paramount-WBD. It is the way streaming leadership is structured with the planned merger of Paramount+ and HBO Max that would determine whether Bloys and Paramount Chair of Direct to Consumer Cindy Holland both stay or one of them leaves as it’s likely neither would report to the other.

Current speculation is that Bloys would stay on, with Netflix chatter remaining in the background. Cheeks, the only Paramount co-CEO to continue after the company’s 2025 acquisition by Skydance, is part of Ellison’s senior management team and is expected to carry on, with his role possibly adjusted post-WBD merger.

So, Cheeks’ visit to the War premiere may have been a precursor, similarly to then-Discovery CEO David Zaslav’s attendance of the Season 3 premiere of HBO’s Succession alongside Bloys while the Discovery-WarnerMedia merger was still being finalized.

The situation is a little different as Bloys and Cheeks are considered peers with their areas not expected to overlap if both stay on at Paramount, making their premiere date two potential co-workers hanging together.

HBO/Sky’s drama War stars Dominic West and Sienna Miller as tech entrepreneur Morgan Henderson and film star Carla Duval in the grips of an acrimonious divorce.

Dade Hayes contributed to this report.

title: Jessie Blackhall Joins Untitled
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Jessie Blackhall has joined Untitled as a manager based in the New York office. Blackhall comes over from Aperture Talent, a subsidiary of Wilhelmina International, where she spent the past decade building and leading the talent agency across its New York and Los Angeles offices, spearheading the development of Wilhelmina’s digital and creator division. […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Jessie Blackhall has joined Untitled as a manager based in the New York office.

Blackhall comes over from Aperture Talent, a subsidiary of Wilhelmina International, where she spent the past decade building and leading the talent agency across its New York and Los Angeles offices, spearheading the development of Wilhelmina’s digital and creator division.

Blackhall brings with her clients including Barbie Ferreira and Shay Sullivan, among others. She’s the third in a string of recent talent, creator, and crossover management hires at Untitled, following Alyssa Manning and Dani Jacobson, as the company continues to expand its capabilities in the space.

Blackhall, who began her career at CESD, told us: “I’m incredibly excited to be joining Untitled Entertainment at such an exciting moment for the company. I’ve long admired Untitled as one of the leading forces in talent management, with an incredible reputation and a forward-thinking approach. Watching the company’s growth and expansion over the past few years has been exciting, and I’m thrilled to be part of that momentum.”

Watch on Deadline

The Untitled Partners commented, “Jessie has spent the past decade building something from the ground up, and that experience gives her a perspective that is both rare and incredibly valuable. She understands what it takes to identify opportunity, earn trust, and create an environment where talent can grow. We’re excited for the perspective she’ll bring to Untitled as we continue to grow our creator and crossover business and expand our presence in New York.”

The last couple of years have been a time of major expansion and evolution for both Untitled and Initial Group, the TPG-backed global entertainment company, which snapped up the company as a foundational acquisition in 2024. Grandview came to operate under the Untitled banner that same year, and Initial has since further expanded with the acquisition of Silver Tribe Media — now Initial Digital — plus a strategic investment in music management company Good World Management, and the acquisition of Brookside Artist Management, whose Emily Gerson Saines joined Untitled as a partner. The company announced the promotion of six to partner in August.

title: Barry Diller Drops Bid to Acquire MGM Resorts: ‘We Didn’t Feel the Mix Was Coming Together’
summary: People Inc., the media company controlled by Barry Diller, is scrapping its proposed bid to acquire MGM Resorts International. People Inc. (which changed its name from IAC this spring) owns about 27% of MGM Resorts. In June, the company submitted formal offer for the hotel and resorts operator to acquire all outstanding shares of MGM […]
content:
People Inc., the media company controlled by Barry Diller, is scrapping its proposed bid to acquire MGM Resorts International.

People Inc. (which changed its name from IAC this spring) owns about 27% of MGM Resorts. In June, the company submitted formal offer for the hotel and resorts operator to acquire all outstanding shares of MGM that People Inc. does not already own for $48.30 per share in cash.

But on Wednesday, People Inc. said it was withdrawing the offer.

Popular on Variety

Diller, who serves as People Inc.’s chairman and senior executive, said in a statement, “There are lots of ingredients that go into a proposal of this kind on its way to completion. We didn’t feel the mix was coming together in the way we had hoped and have decided not to pursue taking the company private at this time.”

Diller added, “What is undimmed is our belief in the future of MGM Resorts. We continue to hold 66.8 million shares representing approximately 27% of MGM Resorts and have total confidence in both the management and the Company’s prospects.”

The media mogul added, “People Incorporated is doing just fine with its principal publishing business achieving its 11th quarter of growth with plenty of cash to both invest in its business and purchase its stock.”

People Inc. remains “open to and interested in the possibility of a strategic transaction with MGM Resorts and look forward to considering a range of alternatives,” Diller said.

Back in June, Diller had said MGM Resorts “represented a rare kind of business: one with real-world assets that AI cannot easily replicate or disintermediate and exceptional digital growth opportunities.”

The company’s Dotdash Meredith publishing unit in July 2025 had changed its name to People Inc., and Diller subsequently decided to apply that name to the whole enterprise.

Diller originally formed Silver King Broadcasting in 1996 as a media holding company and change its name to IAC (InterActiveCorp) in 2004. IAC over the years has owned and operated more than 200 companies and overseen over 100 minority investments. It has spun off 11 businesses including Match Group, Expedia, LendingTree, HSN (now part of QVC Group, which recently filed for bankruptcy), Ticketmaster (now part of Live Nation Entertainment) and Angi.

In late 2021, IAC acquired Meredith in a $2.7 billion deal, three years after Meredith bought Time Inc. (and following Meredith’s sale of titles including Time, now owned by Salesforce’s Marc Benioff; Fortune; and Sports Illustrated). Today, People Inc.’s 40-plus brands include People, Food + Wine, Southern Living, Travel & Leisure, Allrecipes, Better Homes & Gardens, InStyle, Verywell, Investopedia and EW.

title: Original ‘Willy Wonka’ Oompa-Loompa Rusty Goffe ‘Shed a Tear’ at Gene Wilder’s Voice Recreated by AI: ‘It Was Lovely Hearing It Again’
summary: “Have a scrumdiddlyumptious day!” is how Rusty Goffe, who played an Oompa-Loompa in the 1971 adaptation of “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” opposite Gene Wilder, signs off our Zoom call after we speak earlier this month. With such Wonka-isms rolling off his tongue with ease, it’s no surprise that when Netflix, which acquired the […]
content:
“Have a scrumdiddlyumptious day!” is how Rusty Goffe, who played an Oompa-Loompa in the 1971 adaptation of “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” opposite Gene Wilder, signs off our Zoom call after we speak earlier this month.

With such Wonka-isms rolling off his tongue with ease, it’s no surprise that when Netflix, which acquired the rights to Roald Dahl’s literary estate five years ago, planned to make a Wonka-inspired game show Goffe was clearly top of their list to bring back.

In “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” which launched on Sept. 23, he stars alongside his son Ben Goffe — also an actor who has appeared in “Artemis Fowl,” among other titles — as well as a host of new Oompa-Loompas. (Unlike in the original film, these Oompa-Loompas “come in all shapes and sizes now,” as the contestants are told during the show.). Also back is Wilder, albeit only his voice, which has been, somewhat controversially, recreated in AI with the blessing of his wife, Wilder himself having died in 2016.

Popular on Variety

Over the course of nine episodes, viewers will see 12 contestants take part in a series of increasingly wacky challenges in the hopes of winning a “lifetime’s supply of money” (approximately $3 million, calculated as an annual six-figure salary over 30 years), all played out on Wonka-themed set pieces, including the famous elevator and, of course, the edible candy room, complete with chocolate waterfall.

Ahead of “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket” launching, Goffe, now 77, spoke with Variety about how he came to work on the competition show, what it was like to step back into the world of Wonka — and his feelings at hearing Wilder’s voice recreated by AI.

How did this come about? Did Netflix reach out to you?

Well, I just had a phone call from my agent in New York saying they want you in Netflix, talking about “Wonka.” [I said] “Being in ‘Wonka?’ That was a long time ago.” And they said “Yeah, they still want you.” So that’s how I got into it, and I really loved the new one.

Once you knew it was a game show, were you wondering what that format might be?

I was wondering how is this going to happen. But after a couple of days, I got used to it. The contestants were in their own bubble, so when they came on, you just nodded to them, because they were trying to get answers from your face, how they’re doing. So we’re not giving anything away. I was really pleased — thrilled — this time to have my son with me, Ben. [He’s] 33 years of age, an Oompa-Loompa!

What was it like for him to step into that iconic role?

Well, he’s grown up with “Wonka” through me, and he loved the first one, and when [Netflix] said about Ben being in it, he jumped at the chance. “Yeah, yeah, I’m going to be an Oompa-Loompa,” you know, because he’s an actor. He’s done Shakespeare, many, many movies.

Did you give any give him any tips?

No. None whatsoever. I was an Oompa-Loompa. You’re the new one. Learn — on the job!

What was it like for you stepping back into the world of “Wonka”?

It was bizarre, going into the studio, into the chocolate room, in fact. And it was all modern. They still had a river. They still had a waterfall. It was absolutely fantastic, it was. And the river — last time, it was just dirty water, it smelled because we were pouring real cream and real sugar into it, and with the hot lights, it was melting. It was melting, and poor Michael Böllner, who played Augustus Gloop [in th 1971 film], he had to fall in it when he was a kid. And they ask him now, “What was it like, Michael? What was the river like?” [In a German accent] “It vas stinky vater!” in his best German. But it was lovely. But unfortunately, he wasn’t there, it was just myself and my young son, who wasn’t there in the original.

Did you keep anything from the set of the original film?

Mmmmmm, yes. I might have a golden ticket, a real one or two. My children’s inheritance.

Would you have wanted to be a contestant on “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” if you weren’t part of the cast?

No. It was great being the Oompa-Loompa just watching them, because I knew what they were going to win, lose, what’s going to happen if they lost [a challenge]. Which is not good on some occasions.

Did you ever think that the original film would have such a lasting impact that you’d still be revisiting that world so many years later?

I am still absolutely amazed how big it still is. I get to go and do conventions, mainly in the States, and people say, “Yeah, we loved it. We came out the theater, when we saw the new ones. We came out the theater, but we were still singing ‘Oompa-Loompa doompa dee do’ — your movie.” They loved it. But I was surprised how big it still was and still is! And I thank the people for keeping it alive. If it wasn’t for the fans, it’d be gone.

This time round there seems to be more diversity among the Oompa-Loompas…

[These] Oompa-Loompas, they weren’t just short. We had one bodybuilder, big guy, a tall guy, three ladies, a small man, and Ben. It was wonderful to have this diverse [cast of] people.

Netflix has also brought Gene Wilder’s voice back for the show with AI, which has prompted some discussion. Was it weird hearing his voice again after so many years?

Well, “weird” is not the word. It was lovely hearing his voice again, because I loved that man. He was a gentle, fantastic character, very funny, very, very kind, and to hear him in the show, I was so pleased that Netflix had done it. He is Mr. Wonka. He is Willy Wonka. Gene Wilder is Willy Wonka.

Was it uncanny hearing him again, or is it just like he’s standing there?

It’s just him standing there. I did shed a tear when I first heard it, because I loved the man so much. But then I thought he wouldn’t want me to do that. He’d want me to be an Oompa-Loompa, get out there, do the job. Yeah, that that was Gene. He was a lovely, lovely man.

Did you have a favorite moment of filming this new show?

Yes, the breaks! It was one of the best moments of my life to do “Wonka” again. I started my career on “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” and now I am pleased to announce to Variety that I’ve ended my career on “Willy Wonka’s The Golden Ticket.”

This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: The Best Pop Culture Halloween Costumes for 2026: From Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Shrubs to Taylor Swift’s Knicks Shirt
summary: Expect to see plenty of hockey jerseys, hospital scrubs and suspiciously elaborate shrubbery on the streets this Halloween. Some revelers will be channeling Ilya and Shane from “Heated Rivalry,” others will be pulling overnight shifts as the doctors of “The Pitt” — and the most committed friend groups may skip dressing as Bad Bunny altogether […]
content:
Expect to see plenty of hockey jerseys, hospital scrubs and suspiciously elaborate shrubbery on the streets this Halloween. Some revelers will be channeling Ilya and Shane from “Heated Rivalry,” others will be pulling overnight shifts as the doctors of “The Pitt” — and the most committed friend groups may skip dressing as Bad Bunny altogether and show up as the bushes from his Super Bowl halftime show.

As usual, the year’s biggest movies and TV shows provide a gold mine of costume inspiration. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” offers a particularly cinematic couples costume in Zendaya’s Athena and Matt Damon’s Odysseus, while “KPop Demon Hunters” practically begs for a three-person HUNTR/X get-up. Elsewhere, “Off Campus,” “Backrooms,” “Euphoria” and “Widow’s Bay” offer options ranging from exceedingly easy to the kind of niche reference that will earn approving nods from fellow obsessives.

Musicians, meanwhile, have supplied some of the year’s most immediately recognizable looks. Harry Styles’ tiny red shorts from the “Dance No More” video are destined for Halloween parties, while Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” album cover offers another ready-made pop-star transformation. And for anyone whose costume philosophy is simply “more rhinestones,” there’s always Dolly Parton.

Shop the best pop-culture Halloween costumes for 2026 below:

Nikki in ‘Obsession’

©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection

Channel Inde Navarrette’s Nikki with the horror hit’s instantly recognizable red-and-black zebra halter, black bottoms and plenty of gold jewelry. Bonus points for a Willow prop — and a little fake blood if you want to take things in a more sinister direction.

Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Bushes

Christopher Polk/Billboard

For one of the year’s most absurdly specific group costumes, skip dressing as Bad Bunny himself and go as the greenery surrounding him during his Super Bowl performance. All you really need is head-to-toe green, some faux foliage and friends willing to commit to the bit.

Super Bowl Grass Costume PRE-ORDER Now

Athena and Odysseus in ‘The Odyssey’

Melinda Sue Gordon

Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” gives couples an elevated alternative to the standard toga costume: think weathered linen, leather and patinated bronze rather than pristine Grecian robes. Matt Damon’s battle-worn Odysseus and Zendaya’s draped, earth-toned Athena make an especially good pairing.

‘Celebrity Row’ at MSG

Getty Images

Sometimes the best celebrity costume is also the easiest: recreate Taylor Swift and her crew’s matching Stevie Nicks concert shirts for a group look that requires little more than merch, jeans and Swift-level enthusiasm. It’s niche enough to reward anyone who spent the year chronically online.

Hannah and Garret in ‘Off Campus’

Liane Hentscher/Prime Video

Prime Video’s buzzy hockey romance makes Hannah and Garrett an easy couples costume: she can channel Hannah’s signature campus looks while he throws on a Briar U hockey jersey. For a more overtly Halloween-ready option, recreate the show’s bunny-and-magician pairing.

Operatives in ‘Backrooms’

Courtesy Everett Collection

Hazmat suits have rarely felt more zeitgeisty. Suit up in protective gear, respirators and utility equipment to become one of the operatives venturing into the fluorescent-lit nightmare of “Backrooms” — particularly effective if your entire friend group commits.

Magick in ‘Euphoria’

Eddy Chen

If your Halloween philosophy is “more is more,” Magick offers plenty to work with: dramatic makeup, maximalist styling and the kind of hyper-specific fashion choices that have always made “Euphoria” a costume gold mine. Consider it an excuse to pull out every rhinestone in your makeup drawer.

Neck Brace Buy Now $9.99

Ilya and Shane in ‘Heated Rivalry’

sabrina lantos

The internet’s favorite hockey couple is practically made for a two-person costume. Go straightforward with rival hockey jerseys, or recreate one of Ilya and Shane’s more memorable off-ice looks for something that devoted “Heated Rivalry” fans will clock immediately.

Rozanov Jersey Buy Now $39.99

‘The Pitt’ Doctors

Warrick Page/MAX

Few costumes require less explaining — or shopping — than the doctors of “The Pitt.” Grab some medical scrubs, an ID badge and a stethoscope, then spend the evening looking appropriately exhausted for the full Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center effect.

Scrubs Costume Buy Now $29.99

Dolly Parton

Big blonde hair, bigger lashes, rhinestones and enough fringe to be visible from across the room: Dolly Parton remains one of pop culture’s most foolproof Halloween transformations. The trick is not to exercise restraint.

Olivia Rodrigo Album Cover

Geffen

Rodrigo’s third album offers a very 2026 costume for anyone looking beyond her already Halloween-friendly “Sour” and “Guts” eras. Recreate the cover’s styling and makeup, then carry around a mock vinyl sleeve in case anyone needs the reference spelled out.

Harry Styles in ‘Dance No More’ Music Video

YouTube

Possibly the easiest excuse you’ll ever get to wear tiny red shorts on Halloween. Styles spends much of the “Dance No More” video dancing in custom Marc Jacobs short-shorts and sneakers, making the look both instantly recognizable and surprisingly simple to copy.

Huntr/x in ‘Kpop Demon Hunters’

NETFLIX

Rumi, Mira and Zoey are tailor-made for a three-person costume: colorful stagewear, pop-star hair and makeup and, naturally, demon-hunting accessories. Netflix has even released officially licensed HUNTR/X costumes, though the trio’s highly distinctive looks are ripe for DIY interpretations too.

Patricia in ‘Widow’s Bay’

Apple TV

Patricia’s distinctive “Widow’s Bay” look offers a more unexpected choice for anyone who wants their costume to inspire a few “wait, I know this” reactions. Nail the hair, wardrobe and character-specific accessories and let the year’s horror obsessives do the rest.

title: Roseanne Barr Rages Against Ex Co-Star Michael Fishman for Saying ‘Roseanne’ Reboot Was ‘Rightfully Canceled’: ‘You F—ing Little Worm’ and ‘Brainwashed Bigot’
summary: Roseanne Barr and her original “Roseanne” co-star Michael Fishman are still feuding over the cancellation of the show’s 2018 reboot. Fishman made headlines in August for saying “the show was rightfully canceled” after Barr posted a tweet that appeared to link Barack Obama’s advisor Valerie Jarrett, who is Black, to “Planet of the Apes.” Barr […]
content:
Roseanne Barr and her original “Roseanne” co-star Michael Fishman are still feuding over the cancellation of the show’s 2018 reboot. Fishman made headlines in August for saying “the show was rightfully canceled” after Barr posted a tweet that appeared to link Barack Obama’s advisor Valerie Jarrett, who is Black, to “Planet of the Apes.” Barr was accused of being racist but has long maintained that was not her intention.

During a new interview on the “Can’t Be Censored” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly), Barr was asked to weigh in on Fishman’s comments supporting ABC’s decision to pull the 2018 “Roseanne” reboot. She did so by unleashing a tirade against her former co-star.

Popular on Variety

“He fucking doesn’t even fucking know what I said, even though I’ve explained it 10,000 times for nine years on the Internet,” Barr said. “He hasn’t even taken the time to listen to what I say because he’s a bigot. And he’s a brainwashed bigot.”

Barr claimed that Fishman once asked her to clarify her controversial tweet that got the reboot canceled, to which she told him: “Let me explain this, Michael, go and fuck yourself and stay fucked ‘till the day you die. Don’t put my name in your fucking mouth; shut the fuck up. You are an ignoramus and a bigot, and you have no idea what I said because it contradicts the Democratic Party platform that you’ve had shoved down your throat and up your ass. So just fuck you. You have no geopolitical context whatsoever to discuss what I said.”

“Roseanne” was canceled after Barr tweeted: “muslim brotherhood & planet of the apes had a baby=vj.” The tweet was widely perceived as a racist insult toward Valerie Jarrett, although Barr claims otherwise. She stressed in her new interview that she was evoking the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and that “Planet of the Apes” is a nickname she used to describe the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“You think I said Black people look like monkeys,” Barr continued in her lashing out at Fishman. “Go fuck yourself, you little fucking worm. And I’m glad they fired you because I was the only reason you were ever on that show. They wanted to get rid of you in the reboot and I made them take you back.”

Barr is referring to Fishman’s abrupt exit from “The Conners,” the ABC sitcom that continued the “Roseanne” franchise sans Barr following the reboot’s cancellation. “The Conners” ran for seven seasons, with Fishman reprising D.J. Conner for four seasons before revealing in 2022 that “I was told I would not be returning for season 5.” It’s never been confirmed why ABC dropped him.

Fishman has always opposed Barr’s tweet. He “vehemently” condemned the post after the “Roseanne” reboot was canceled and called his co-stars’ comments “reprehensible and intolerable.” She fired back at the time by posting: “You throw me under the bus.”

In a video posted to his Instagram in August, Fishman spoke out against claims that it was “woke crap” that got the “Roseanne” reboot canceled.

“I get these kinds of ignorant and inaccurate comments daily,” Fishman said. “After eight years, turning the other cheek is really not helping. So, I guess the world failed to learn the lesson, so I’m going to point out — we are perpetuating a lie, and people are using a political smokescreen to justify the indefensible… Those justifications, they’re leading to real consequences, real crimes, situations like Trey Reed and Tasha Fortune, because dehumanizing people is never a joke.”

Fishman acknowledged that comedians can make people laugh at the “darkest” of topics, but “sadly, in this case, there was no joke. And the show was rightfully canceled.”

title: Jeff Garlin Says ‘Undiagnosed Bipolar’ Made Him ‘Mean’ on ‘The Goldbergs’ Set; Wendi McLendon-Covey Responds: ‘I Remember Things Differently’
summary: Jeff Garlin revealed in a recent interview on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly) that he had undiagnosed bipolar disorder during the making of ABC’s “The Goldbergs,” which he notably exited from after an HR investigation into multiple claims of inappropriate conduct against him. The 1980s-set family sitcom, which ran for 10 seasons […]
content:
Jeff Garlin revealed in a recent interview on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly) that he had undiagnosed bipolar disorder during the making of ABC’s “The Goldbergs,” which he notably exited from after an HR investigation into multiple claims of inappropriate conduct against him. The 1980s-set family sitcom, which ran for 10 seasons and 229 episodes from 2013 to 2023, starred Garlin opposite Wendi McLendon-Covey. Garlin exited in 2021.

“At the time, I was undiagnosed bipolar,” Garlin said on the podcast, noting he got his diagnosis after exiting the series. “I was miserable on the show, and I was miserable with my performance. And [Wendi] was always trying to tell me, ‘Hey, you’re really great on the show.’ I didn’t believe her. I just got to the point where I had to quit, and she was very resentful.”

Popular on Variety

Garlin added, “Being bipolar, I was either one of three things: dark, dark, dark, dark, didn’t talk and look at anyone; happy to the point of mania, never turning off my thing; or mean — really, really mean.”

McLendon-Covey reacted to Garlin’s comments on Instagram by disputing his comments: “Huh. Let’s just say I remember things very differently, as does the crew, the other actors, the writers, and our executives.”

When Garlin exited “The Goldbergs” in 2021, two sources close to the production confirmed to Variety that it was a mutual decision between the actor and the network. Shortly before, Garlin addressed allegations against him in an interview with Vanity Fair, acknowledging that an HR investigation into his on-set behavior had been ongoing for the past three years and dismissing a rumor that he had been fired from the series.

“We have a difference of opinion, Sony and myself. Okay. My opinion is, I have my process about how I’m funny, in terms of the scene and what I have to do. They feel that it makes for a quote ‘unsafe’ workspace,” Garlin said at the time. “Now, mind you, my silliness making an unsafe workspace — I don’t understand how that is… I am always a kind and thoughtful person. I make mistakes, sure. But my comedy is about easing people’s pain. Why would I ever want to cause pain in anybody for a laugh? That’s bullying. That’s just uncalled for.”

The allegations against Garlin ranged from unwanted hugging and touching people on set to telling jokes that made others uncomfortable. McLendon-Covey later said during an interview with Andy Cohen for SiriusXM that Garlin’s exit was “a long time coming.”

“That it finally happened, it was like, ‘Ok, finally someone is listening to us.’ But that was kind of hard though because we had lost George Segal in real life,” she added. “To have to go through another loss on a sitcom…you can’t keep asking your audience to mourn people. That’s not why they tune in… I’m exhausted by that topic and the PTSD of it all. I just feel like the less people know about that, the better. No one benefits from knowing anything.”

“The Goldbergs” was in the middle of filming its ninth season when Garlin was fired. As Variety exclusively reported at the time, producers decided to keep Garlin’s character on the show for the rest of the season by using off-camera dialogue and unused takes pulled from earlier episodes, as well as previously shot images of Garlin. The actor’s stand-in was also used in group scenes, but he was shot from the back. The final result was visually awkward and earned so many complaints on social media that McLendon-Covey even weighed in at the time.

“This season threw us for a loop because it’s hard to incorporate someone who doesn’t want to be there and wants to leave mid-scene, and we weren’t about to rewrite the second half of the season,” the comedian wrote on Twitter at the time. “We’re doing our best.”

When “The Goldbergs” kicked off its 10th and final season last fall, the show killed off Garlin’s character.

title: Did O.J. Simpson Have An Accomplice? Peacock Doc Offers “Real Evidence” Suggesting He Did
summary: Peacock is launching a two-part documentary that claims to offer “real evidence” that suggests members of O.J. Simpson’s inner circle may know more than they’ve let on about the brutal murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman. The NBCUniversal streamer has ordered OJ’s Accomplice from Ample Entertainment. The two-part doc will premiere in December […]
content:
Peacock is launching a two-part documentary that claims to offer “real evidence” that suggests members of O.J. Simpson’s inner circle may know more than they’ve let on about the brutal murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman.

The NBCUniversal streamer has ordered OJ’s Accomplice from Ample Entertainment.

The two-part doc will premiere in December and will “challenge long-held assumptions about the case that captivated a nation”.

Nicole Brown Simpson – O.J’s ex-wife – and Ron Goldman were murdered on June 12, 1994. Former NFL star Simpson was charged with the murders and became a fugitive after failing to turn himself in to the LA Police Department and instead took off in a White Ford Bronco on a ride that was watched live by millions.

However, O.J. Simpson was acquitted of both murders in 1995 after an eight-month trial, although Goldman’s father filed a civil suit against the Naked Gun star and a jury found him responsible for the deaths.

Watch on Deadline

Peacock is exploring the fact that law enforcement “never seriously considered the idea” that Simpson may not have acted alone.

The documentary “challenges the dominant narrative around the O.J. Simpson murder saga and offers real evidence suggesting that what we thought we knew about the most obsessed-over crime story of all time could be all wrong.”

It will feature interviews with Kato Kaelin and Nicole Brown’s sister, alongside never-before-heard first-person accounts from eyewitnesses and presents new information “raising questions as to whether members of OJ’s inner circle may have been there that night.”

Created by Ample boss Ari Mark, who exec produces alongside Sumit David, Sphere Abacus is handling international distribution of the two-parter.

Ample Entertainment is behind series such as Netflix’s This Is The Zodiac Speaking and Peacock’s Diddy: The Making of a Bad Boy.

title: ‘Dynamic Duo’ & Untitled ‘Gremlins’ Head To Fall 2028 Amid Warner Bros Release Date Changes
summary: Warner Bros has made some release date changes, unrelated to its pending marriage with Paramount. The DC Robins-origin puppet meets animation feature, Dynamic Duo, is moving from June 30, 2028 to Sept. 22, 2028. The reason being is because Warner Bros distribution believes this will be a good back-to-school animated feature slot for not just […]
content:
Warner Bros has made some release date changes, unrelated to its pending marriage with Paramount.

The DC Robins-origin puppet meets animation feature, Dynamic Duo, is moving from June 30, 2028 to Sept. 22, 2028. The reason being is because Warner Bros distribution believes this will be a good back-to-school animated feature slot for not just K-12, but also teens and college kids. The movie has the potential to his the Spider-Verse crowd.

Coincidentally, this shifts Dynamic Duo away from Paramount’s big feature take of video game Call of Duty on June 30. There are no Paramount movies on Sept. 22, 2028.

Also shifting forward, is Chris Columbus-directed untitled Gremlins, which is moving from Nov. 19, 2027 to Oct. 6, 2028 (Warners has had good luck in that first weekend of October with Joker). Gremlins wasn’t up against any Paramount movies on its 2027 date, nor is it on its new weekend.

Watch on Deadline

Dynamic Duo marks the first joint project between DC Studios and the Bill Damaschke-led WBPA.

The 6th & Idaho movie scripted by Matthew Aldrich is being made by a new animation studio out of New Orleans named Swaybox and that studio’s husband-and-wife creators Arthur Mintz and Theresa Andersson. Mintz will direct this movie, which follows the early days of Dick Grayson and Jason Todd aka the Robins.

InSneider recently announced the VoiceOver cast for Dynamic Duo: Mason Thames as Dick Grayson, Logan Kim as Jason Todd, Lee Pace as Red Hood One, and Steve Buscemi as Red Hood 2.

The third Gremlins has a script from Carl Ellsworth, Zach Lipovsky and Adam B. Stein. Kristie Macosko Krieger and Holly Bario are producing for Amblin Entertainment alongside 26th Street Pictures’ Columbus, Michael Barnathan and Mark Radcliffe. Steven Spielberg is executive producing. Joe Dante directed the first two Gremlins movies.

title: Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek Blames Bob Iger For Ouster In New Memoir
summary: Bob Chapek, fired as Disney CEO in 2022 after less than three years, lays the blame for his ouster squarely on Bob Iger in an upcoming memoir, according to the New York Times, which obtained a copy. Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth comes out Sept. 29 from […]
content:
Bob Chapek, fired as Disney CEO in 2022 after less than three years, lays the blame for his ouster squarely on Bob Iger in an upcoming memoir, according to the New York Times, which obtained a copy.

Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth comes out Sept. 29 from Gallery Books, a division of Simon & Schuster.

“My abrupt dismissal hurt my reputation, leaving those close to me, outsiders and some within the kingdom trying to figure out what I did wrong,” Chapek writes. “The answer, again, is nothing.” Instead, he claims that Iger, who had handpicked him for the job, relentlessly and intentionally sabotaged him.

Chapek’s belief on that front is no secret but he lays out his thoughts and defends his tenure publicly at length for the first time in the book. He calls himself a disrupter and writes, “I didn’t get a chance to finish what I started.”

Watch on Deadline

Iger resigned abruptly as Disney CEO in February of 2020 after an epic run but remained as executive chairman for two years, retaining control over creative endeavors at the company and reporting directly to the board of directors. Chapek reported to both the board, and to Iger. The two clashed. Chapek suggests that Iger believed he could reclaim the job whenever he wanted, the NYT says.

Describing Iger’s exit from Disney, Chapek wrote, “I have been told by several high-ranking people both in government and private business that in their opinions, the real reason he left the company so abruptly was his anticipation of the arrival of Covid.”

Disney declined to comment.

The company has denied the pandemic had anything to do with Iger’s exit. Iger has said he wanted to wind down after a successful run. He felt at the time that Chapek was the right person for the job.

“I had been CEO for about 15 years. I started the company in 1974 at ABC. I had been around a long time. There were plenty of things in the world that I was interested in that I either wanted to do or wanted to learn more about. I had not really had a day off in I don’t even remember,” Iger told a NYT DealBook conference in 2023 about his departure. He said he was “disappointed in what I was seeing, both during the transition period when I was still there and while I was out. But I really worked hard at distancing myself from it because one, I couldn’t do anything about. It in a way, it wasn’t my business at all, really. It was his business to run.”

Soon after he started as CEO, Chapek was being pilloried on several fronts including management decisions that vexed key executives, and a public fight with star Scarlett Johansson that alienated talent. The company’s response to legislation (dubbed the ‘Don’t Say Gay’ bill) in Florida angered both Disney employees and Gov. Ron DeSantis. His ouster came shortly after Disney reported a greater than expected $1.5 billion streaming loss for its latest quarter.

Chapek’s apparent rubber stamp by the Disney board, followed by his rocky tenure, was used as ammunition by activist investor Nelson Peltz in a bruising proxy fight with the Mouse House.

Iger returned as chief executive after Chapek was fired and remained in the job through March of this year. Josh D’Amaro, head of Disney’s giant theme parks and experiences business, was named CEO after a considerably more robust executive search process.

Chapek, a 30-year Disney veteran, had also been running parks and experiences when he was anointed chief. He had worked with D’Amaro and says he was instrumental in the current CEO’s ascent. “I consistently suggested the idea of promoting him,” Chapek wrote. “He had been a relative unknown in the corporate hierarchy before I singled him out.”

title: Brad Caleb Kane Found It “Hard” Ignoring ‘Crystal Lake’ Fan Theories, Teases “Certain Explanations” Given In Prequel: “It’s Grounded In Reality”
summary: As the first Crystal Lake trailer debuted last week, longtime fans of Jason Voorhees ran wild with online speculation about how the Peacock show approaches his story. Series creator Brad Caleb Kane recently assured Deadline that although the Friday the 13th prequel does “give certain explanations” about the masked killer, the series is much more […]
content:
As the first Crystal Lake trailer debuted last week, longtime fans of Jason Voorhees ran wild with online speculation about how the Peacock show approaches his story.

Series creator Brad Caleb Kane recently assured Deadline that although the Friday the 13th prequel does “give certain explanations” about the masked killer, the series is much more “grounded in reality” than fans are giving him credit.

“Listen, it’s hard for me to look at the theories that are bandied about, like, ‘There’s a strange yellow door. Are they making Jason a government super soldier? Is that the route they’re going down?'” he said. “And I just want to tell people that my wife said, ‘Don’t engage yet. Just let them have their theories and do their thing.’ But I don’t want people watching, thinking that we’re doing some sort of Stranger Things, Eleven, government super soldier. It’s not that, it’s its own thing.”

Kane continued, “It’s grounded in more reality. It’s grounded in things that were going on in the 60s and 70s that sort of intersect with the theme of mistrusting our institutions. I don’t want to say too much more because I don’t want to get into spoiler territory, but I didn’t want people to think that we’re doing Stranger Things. This exists in the world of Friday the 13th, it’s grounded.”

Watch on Deadline

Following last week’s trailer, which teased a yellow door in what looks like a top-secret facility, Kane took to social media to poke fun at the speculation. “Everybody chill!” read a meme of Arnold Schwarzenegger’s Mr. Freeze that he shared on Instagram.

As the first 'Crystal Lake' trailer debuted last week, longtime fans of Jason Voorhees ran wild with online speculation about how the Peacock show approaches his story.



Series creator Brad Caleb Kane recently assured Deadline that although the 'Friday the 13th' prequel does… pic.twitter.com/dDTFdyPPLl — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 23, 2026

Streaming Oct. 15 on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. As two strangers begin digging into her mysterious past, Pam goes to murderous lengths to keep her secrets buried.

title: Peter Byrne Dies: Naked Eyes Singer Who Scored ’80s Hits ‘Always Something There to Remind Me’ & ‘Promises, Promises’ Was 74
summary: Peter Byrne, the singer and songwriter for the band Naked Eyes who scored 1980s hits with “Always Something There to Remind Me” and “Promises, Promises,” died peacefully in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, September 14, after a brief illness. He was 74. His death was announced on the band’s official website. One of the most […]
content:
Peter Byrne, the singer and songwriter for the band Naked Eyes who scored 1980s hits with “Always Something There to Remind Me” and “Promises, Promises,” died peacefully in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, September 14, after a brief illness. He was 74.

His death was announced on the band’s official website.

One of the most popular, if fleeting, British New Wave bands of MTV’s golden era, Naked Eyes was founded in 1982 by Byrne and keyboardist Rob Fisher, who had been college friends in their native Bath, England, and had performed together in a band called Neon from 1979 to 1982. (That band also included Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal, who would go on to form Tears for Fears.)

Within two years Naked Eyes had scored four Top 40 hits on Billboard’s Hot 100. The highest charting was “Always Something There to Remind Me” which peaked at #8 during the summer of 1983. A cover of the 1963 song written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for Dionne Warwick, the Byrne-Fisher demo of “Always Something There to Remind Me” was strong enough to convince EMI Records to sign the duo that would become Naked Eyes.

The band had three subsequent top 40 hits, the most successful of which was “Promises, Promises,” written by Byrne and Fisher and not to be confused with the Bacharach-David song of the same title that was a hit for Warwick. Both songs were included on the band’s debut 1983 album Burning Bridges, as was a third, less successful single “When the Lights Go Out.”

DEADLINE RELATED VIDEO:

The band’s second album, 1984’s Fuel For The Fire, featured a modest hit “(What) In the Name of Love,” but failed to match the success of the debut album, prompting Naked Eyes to disband (the group never toured). Fisher died in 1999 at the age of 42 following cancer surgery.

Born June 9, 1952, in Bath, Byrne continued writing, recording and touring following Fisher’s death, releasing the solo album The Real Illusion in 2001 under Pete Byrne, followed by two albums under the Naked Eyes name: Fumbling with the Covers in 2007 and Disguise the Limit in 2021. A remaster of the original Naked Eyes self-titled album was release in 2025.

In 2008 Byrne’s Naked Eyes took part in the U.S. “Regeneration” tour with Belinda Carlisle, ABC and the Human League, and in 2024 joined a similarly ’80s themed tour of the U.S. and Canada with Wang Chung, Men Without Hats and The Motels.

Outside of Naked Eyes, Byrne’s work included providing backing vocals on Stevie Wonder’s 1985 hit “Part-Time Lover,” as well as songwriting for film and television. He wrote the song “I Am The Cute One” in 1993 for the Olsen Twins.

Byrne is survived by his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve; children Merlin, Dylan, and Chloe; and ex-wife Elena. A private service will be held for the family.
