The series is produced by 20th Television, a part of Disney Television Studios.

The original “Scrubs” premiered in 2001 and ran for nine seasons on NBC and then ABC.

title: Serbia’s Screen Industries in Crisis Amid Claims That Blacklists, ‘State-Sponsored Censorship’ Are Designed to ‘Starve Independent Production’
summary: The Serbian film and television industries are in a state of crisis, with independent production in the Balkan powerhouse crippled by what leading industry groups describe as “a coordinated campaign of state-sponsored censorship.” Nearly two years after a devastating train station disaster that killed 16 people and sparked mass demonstrations against the government of President […]
content:
The Serbian film and television industries are in a state of crisis, with independent production in the Balkan powerhouse crippled by what leading industry groups describe as “a coordinated campaign of state-sponsored censorship.”

Nearly two years after a devastating train station disaster that killed 16 people and sparked mass demonstrations against the government of President Aleksandar Vučić, independent producers say they’re being shut out by state-aligned media and starved of financing by the national funding body, Film Center Serbia, which has not announced a public call in nearly two years.

“There are virtually no independent sources of financing left in Serbia,” said one leading film and TV producer, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of potential repercussions.

Popular on Variety

“Whether you are looking for public funding for a film, financing from the national broadcaster, or investment from the other major media companies, all of the major sources of financing are now state-owned or state-controlled,” they added. “If you are considered politically undesirable, there is really nowhere else to go.”

Earlier this year, a coalition of leading film guilds and professional associations issued a desperate plea to the international film community, alleging in an open letter that “political interference, informal blacklists of filmmakers and public attacks on artists have become systemic” in the once booming Balkan biz.

“The Serbian film industry is currently facing a coordinated campaign of state-sponsored censorship,” read the letter, which was signed by eight industry bodies. “While Film Center Serbia continues to project a ‘business as usual’ image internationally, the reality is a total freeze on funding calls designed to starve independent production.”

The tragedy at the Novi Sad railway station, where a concrete canopy collapsed in November 2024, killing 16 bystanders, sparked nationwide protests — among the largest in Europe in recent memory — and became a symbol of entrenched corruption in the Vučić administration. Prime Minister Miloš Vučević stepped down in the aftermath, though the president has rejected ongoing calls for his resignation.

Director Jelena Maksimović, whose Venice-bound debut feature “Until the Day Ends” is set against the student protests that galvanized the nation, told Variety that “the attempt to silence us is part of a broader attack on workers, on collective organizing and on the possibility of imagining a society based on solidarity, equality and freedom.”

Producer Jelena Angelovski echoed her remarks, adding that “those who do not see eye to eye with the regime [are] thoroughly obstructed in their efforts to make films, regardless of whether or not these films are openly political.”

“For close to two years now all institutional funding for film production has been entirely suspended, except for those who are propagating the right-wing nationalist government’s corrupted ways,” she said.

The systematic silencing of opposition voices is part of what Angelovski describes as a broader strategy by the Vučić regime of “actively and by all possible means — from administrative to those involving physical violence and imprisonment — repressing all forms of opposition to its authoritarian and criminal methods of governance and its highly reactionary politics.”

Critics accuse the country’s largest media groups, including the state-owned Telekom Srbija and the United Media conglomerate, of blacklisting creatives opposed to the right-wing government, what the veteran producer characterizes as “actors and filmmakers who are considered acceptable and those who are not.”

“Your public statements, your social media activity and whether you take part in protests can determine whether you get a role or a job,” they said.

United Media did not respond to a request for comment. Aleksandra Martinović, chief multimedia and content officer at Telekom Srbija, rejected allegations of bias at the company and its production arm, TS Media, insisting the group is “completely open” to work with any and all talent, regardless of their political beliefs.

“Our results and our projects show what we are doing and the way we work,” she said. “We are completely open-minded.”

Meanwhile, as the political deadlock shows no signs of resolution, Serbian industry professionals worry about the consequences that their silencing will have on society at large.

“This kind of censorship is leaving people without work and without a space for their voices to be heard,” said the veteran producer. “And when you systematically remove critical voices from film, television and the media, what you are left with is an increasingly dark and controlled public space.”

title: Tom Hiddleston Recalls Trekking to Everest for ‘Tenzing’ and Kevin Feige Telling Him ‘Thor’ Wasn’t ‘Going to Be the Only Film’ He Would Play Loki In
summary: British actor Tom Hiddleston has a privileged view and understanding of the Marvel Cinematic Universe phenomenon, having starred as Loki in “Thor,” only the second film of a now ever-expanding franchise. Speaking at the Zurich Film Festival, where he is presenting the opening film “Tenzing” and receiving a Golden Eye Award, the actor recalled those […]
content:
British actor Tom Hiddleston has a privileged view and understanding of the Marvel Cinematic Universe phenomenon, having starred as Loki in “Thor,” only the second film of a now ever-expanding franchise. Speaking at the Zurich Film Festival, where he is presenting the opening film “Tenzing” and receiving a Golden Eye Award, the actor recalled those early Marvel days as “larger than life.”

Hiddleston said transitioning from working with British auteur Joanna Hogg on “Unrelated” and “Archipelago” was not so much of a shock, as both Hogg’s work and his role as Loki were about dealing with family issues, in a way. “The difference [with Marvel] was in the scale of the resources, the size of the crews, the size of the sets. It was so larger than life.” The actor would go on to play the famed character in seven movies and two seasons of “Loki.”

His memories of those early days are largely about “a very vivid, happy, immediate, fast friendship with Chris Hemsworth that had both of us feeling like we were the two luckiest guys in the world.” The actor said they were both very aware of being given “this extraordinary opportunity to play these magnificent characters and bring them to life for the first time.”

Popular on Variety

“We were immediately bonded,” he added. “It was a shared excitement about being invited to make a film like this. Marvel Studios had made one film at that time, which was ‘Iron Man,’ which we both loved, and we were being directed by Kenneth Branagh, Anthony Hopkins was playing our father, Rene Russo was playing our mother, and we had extraordinary resources. We had an amazing, brilliant creative stunt department where we would train for sequences of dizzying choreography. We both loved movement and these opportunities.”

Of the project’s scale, Hiddleston said, “It was a different dimension.” “The scenes themselves were very deep. They were full of turbulence, turmoil, soul and emotion […] The material was really deep, so the combination of those things was a thrill.”

The Brit thanked late screenwriter Don Payne for developing Loki’s “complex” backstory, and recalled an early conversation with Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige, who told him “Thor” wasn’t “the only film you’re going to be in.”

“He said: ‘Well, we’ve made an ‘Iron Man’ film, we’re going to make a ‘Thor’ film, we’re going to make a ‘Captain America’ film, and then we’re going to make an ‘Avengers’ film, which is Thor, Captain America, Iron Man, Black Widow, the Hulk and Hawkeye forming a team. In the first edition of the first ‘Avengers’ comic, from 1967, the villain is Loki, and we want you to be the villain.”

“I never expected to be playing the character for this long,” he added. “But he’s a brilliant character of such depth and dimension […] “I knew where we had started in ‘Thor,’ and I wanted to get back to his capacity for love and his belonging to his family. I wanted to somehow find a way of completing that arc. It’s a long journey.”

Hiddleston kept his lips sealed about the highly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday,” saying only that “it is coming.” And it is indeed, with the premiere date set for Dec. 18.

Apple Original Films

The “Crimson Peak” actor also spoke at length about Jennifer Peedom’s “Tenzing,” which chronicles the tale of the first-ever ascent of Mount Everest. The Brit plays climber Edmund Hillary, with Genden Phuntsok playing the titular Sherpa Tenzing Norgay. Willem Dafoe, Caitríona Balfe and Tenzin Jigmey are also in the cast of the Apple TV film.

“I’ve been compelled by Everest for as long as I can remember,” he said, noting how he learned how to ski in the Swiss and French Alps, but has always been drawn by the highest of mountains. “What moved me so much about, um, about Jen’s screenplay and the premise and the promise of her film, which she sent to me three years ago with a beautiful letter, was that it was to put Tenzing Norgay at the center of his own story, to reframe that narrative from a different perspective and bring him into the foreground.”

Hiddleston praised Peedom’s 2015 documentary “Sherpa,” which portrayed in depth the Sherpa culture near Everest and the exploitation of local climbers by wealthy Westerners chasing the dream of summiting the mighty mountain. After reading the script, watching the documentary, and meeting Peedom, Hiddleston signed up for the project, which led him to climb to Everest’s base camp alongside the director, Phuntsok, and a high-altitude medical specialist. That experience connected him with the physicality of the role, but also its spirituality.

“I love that this film really reveals the deeply spiritual relationship that Tenzing had with the mountain, not a mountain to be conquered, but a goddess to be revered, a mother into whose lap he might climb,” he added.

“I think Hillary was really open to that depth of feeling,” he went on. “They did this extraordinary thing. Amazing. They achieved the impossible, like stepping on the moon. After that, their lives were changed forever; summiting Everest became possible, and thousands and thousands of people have done it since.”

The Zurich Film Festival runs Sept. 24 – Oct. 4.

content:
Benjamin Netanyahu‘s arrival to New York City was meet with chants of “Free Palestine” outside the United Nations on Thursday.

Hannah Einbinder and Susan Sarandon were among around 100 protesters being detained on video while blocking Bibi’s entrance to the U.N. building, where he spoke with global leaders at the U.N. General Assembly. Deadline has reached out to the NYPD.

Also present at the demonstration were Cynthia Nixon, Elliot Page, Chelsea Manning, Sarah Sherman, Mary Beth Barone and Caleb Hearon, protesting Netanyahu and Israel’s ongoing strikes on Gaza since the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel.

Videos of the demonstration show protesters chanting, “Free, free Palestine! Stop the genocide!”

Watch on Deadline

“Netanyahu, you can’t hide! We charge you with genocide!” others chanted.

As dozens of delegates walked out of Netanyahu’s speech, he declared to applause from others, “If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much.”

title: How ‘All American’ Survived Long Enough To End Its 8-Season Run As The Lone YA Series Left At The CW: An Oral History
summary: All American entered the television scene nearly eight years ago as yet another trailblazing coming-of-age story on a network with a history and a 2018 fall slate full of them. It’ll end its eight-season run on Monday as the lone symbol of a bygone era at The CW. Inspired by the life of former NFL […]
content:
All American entered the television scene nearly eight years ago as yet another trailblazing coming-of-age story on a network with a history and a 2018 fall slate full of them. It’ll end its eight-season run on Monday as the lone symbol of a bygone era at The CW.

Inspired by the life of former NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger, the series debuted in October 2018 and began what would increasingly become an uphill battle to stay on the air.

Yet, as the television landscape (and the world) changed rapidly around it, All American always found a way. It stood its ground on issues from racial injustice to mental health awareness to substance abuse to exploitation in youth sports time and time again. When money was tight, the series faced slashed budgets and shrinking episodic orders that continually tested the cast and crew’s determination to keep it alive.

Not only did it stay alive, it ran for eight seasons and more than 100 episodes — a milestone that has long been celebrated on television and is becoming increasingly rare. It survived several major disruptions, including the COVID-19 pandemic, a historically long writers and actors strike, and an exodus of series regulars after Season 6. It’ll hang up its hat on Monday as the last of its kind on The CW, which has largely abandoned young adult television after the network made a name for itself over decades of evolution with the genre. And, despite the network’s storied history in the YA space, All American will stand as one of the few that put a primarily Black cast on broadcast television.

Watch on Deadline

Through more than a dozen conversations with the cast and writers, Deadline has weaved together an oral history of the series from those nerve-wracking early days on Season 1 to the bittersweet end of production in December 2025.

The CW

On October 2, 2018, about a week before the premiere of The CW’s new high school football series All American, news broke that creator and showrunner April Blair would be replaced by co-executive producer Nkechi Okoro Carroll. Though she had been consulting on the series since the earlier days of the writers room, Okoro Carroll had not been involved with shaping the pilot or the original idea for the series, but she would now be responsible for preserving the ethos of this incredibly nascent show through the end of its first season and, with any hope, beyond.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: I’d been on an overall deal at 20th [Century Fox Television], and I’d just come over and signed an overall with Warner Bros. and was working on a pilot pitch to take out for them. They asked if I would read a script that was called, I think, Spencer at the time, and consider staffing temporarily on that show while I was working on my pitch to take out and just help out there. I’ve loved YA shows my whole life. I still do. I always will. I remember getting that sort of tingly feeling when I read the script and just being like, ‘Oh, this reminds me of how I used to feel watching the original Beverly Hills 90210 and all the other sort of YA shows I loved from way, way back in the day.’

So I agreed to take a meeting, but then Greg [Berlanti] asked me to sit down and watch the pilot, and you don’t say no to Greg Berlanti. And at the time I was like, ‘Oh, it’ll be cool to watch the pilot,’ but I wasn’t really thinking anything of it. After a while, I forgot I was watching it for consideration for coming on to the show, and I was just watching it as a fan. By the time the pilot ended, I was in tears, and I was just so emotionally invested in these characters, and it was special. I remember walking out of the conference room I was screening in and seeing Greg, and he just had this big smile on his face, because he knew that it was special. He knew the minute I saw it, I was going to be like, ‘Oh my gosh.’ From there, the rest was history. [The writers room was] full of a bunch of us who’d come up on these YA shows, who had a genuine love and respect for the genre, and really could see the potential in these characters and where we could take these stories. It’s crazy to think that was eight years ago.

The pilot episode of All American introduces viewers to 16-year-old Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), a star quarterback at South Crenshaw High School who gets recruited by the head coach of Beverly High, Billy Baker (Taye Diggs), to instead play ball in one of the wealthiest locales in Los Angeles. It was Ezra’s first big television gig, as it was for many of the young actors who made up the original teenage cast.

Thinking back, Season 1 was full of contradicting emotions. Fear, excitement, a nervous sense of optimism about the show they were making.

DANIEL EZRA: All I remember about the pilot was being terrified someone was going to change their mind and send me home.

MONET MAZUR: There was something about the script that just grabbed you from the moment you read it, and I just thought, ‘Wow, this is not a story I would usually see myself in, or a part I necessarily had been cast playing before,’ but in those 60 pages, I knew immediately that I wanted to do it. You don’t have that feeling a lot.

TAYE DIGGS: A lot of the issues that the show was dealing with when it came to African Americans and fathers and sons, all that I was literally going through in real life relationships. I love the relationships and how the character — I don’t want to say [Billy] was flawed, but he’s very human.

The CW

KARIMAH WESTBROOK: It was one of my biggest dreams to become a series regular on a hit drama series. I had been living in Los Angeles for about 18 years, and it was a busy season of auditioning for new potential shows. I hadn’t booked anything yet, and when I read the script for All American, I absolutely loved it. The story felt real and relatable…What resonated with me about the script was the storyline of a talented kid with a dream being raised by a single mom, doing the best she could for her children, in a community that wasn’t always safe.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Honestly, my goal for the first season was: Do not get us canceled. Season 1 shows are so tough, and especially with me coming over and stepping in as showrunner. Everyone worked their tail off on that first season and put their whole heart and soul into it, and we could all feel how special it was. I had put some unrealistic sort of weight on my shoulders of ‘do not fail them, do not fail them, do not fail them.’

MONET MAZUR: The expectation was so high, and we were all just so excited to be there without even knowing where the show would go, or how successful it would become. It did feel like that from the very beginning, that there was just something magical about it, and we had no idea how topical and timely everything would become.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: I was very, very grateful for my partner in crime, Jamie Turner. We came up in this business together. I knew, as sort of the football aficionado that he is, and how much he loved the genre as much as I did, that I needed to bring his special sauce to the mix toward the back half of Season 1.

JAMIE TURNER: At that point in my career, I had primarily worked on cop procedurals, so a lion’s share of the work that’s done in a procedural writers’ room is built around case beats, plot twists and propulsion. But in the family drama space, you get to slow down a little and focus on character, conflict and emotional journeys. It’s also a great environment for you to tap into your personal well and share stories about yourself that could add layers and depth to the characters you’re writing for.

NKECHI OKORO CARROL: So once we were able to get that done, it just suddenly felt like everything was cooking on all cylinders. Everyone always brought an extra something to the table that made it so special.

BRE-Z: I remember all of us just being all ears, eyes wide open just to dive into these characters and bring them to life as best as we could. The beginning days were just a lot of fun, a lot of laughing, a lot of talking, a lot of learning, and going back and forth about these characters and what we’d do if we were them, and also reminiscing on our own high school experiences.

CHELSEA TAVARES: I was Bre-Z’s first on-screen kiss. I remember she was really nervous, so I took her to the side so she could peck my lips without the cameras, and after that we just started cracking jokes on each other. It’s weird, but she was like a big sister to me. Our chemistry was very natural and effortless from day one.

The CW

MICHAEL EVANS BEHLING: Me, Daniel [Ezra] and Greta [Onieogou] were all brand new to California itself, so that was really scary and lovely. But we all had each other. It was amazing to lean on those individuals and have fun going to work.

DANIEL EZRA: Mike and I essentially hid in his apartment for two years.

MICHAEL EVANS BEHLING: We’ve talked about this before — we didn’t leave my apartment for all of Season 1. We were so petrified of Los Angeles to the point where we’d have a full week of work, and then on Saturday morning he’d come over around 11 in the morning, and we’d watch cartoons all day long. We would do that for Saturday and Sunday, and just order food, and it was fantastic. We got to bond and chat. I can remember bonding with Greta really well, just because she didn’t have a car, and so she would [go back and forth] getting rides from me and Daniel, because we all lived in North Hollywood at the time, which was really awesome.

GRETA ONIEOGOU: We all got close very quickly, I think. For most of us, it was our first really, really big job, and so we were sort of catapulted into this. When the show got super popular, especially over COVID, we were sort of catapulted together, so it made us all really close having this really unique experience all together. Long hours on set, spending a lot of time laughing, and it was a lot of fun.

CHELSEA TAVARES: Mike threw really fun parties! I think by the second season, when we would all go out together. That’s when the fans started noticing everybody, especially girls would scream when they saw Daniel, Mike, and Cody [Christian].

While the show had a fairly small broadcast audience in that first season, it completely took off on Netflix. By the time that the show returned for Season 2, it was already benefitting from a boost in popularity. Then, just as it seemed All American was hitting a stride, COVID almost killed the show, but in a weird way, ended up being its biggest blessing.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: We started shooting Season 2, and Season 1 had done okay on the network, and then when it re-aired on Netflix, it picked up an even bigger audience. That was when we were really starting to feel the rumblings of, ‘Oh, people are talking about us.’ We were no longer sort of ‘The Little Show That Could.’ We found out about our Season 3 pickup fairly early, while we were shooting Season 2, so that felt great to know, like, ‘Oh, we’re not on the bubble anymore. We don’t have to wait to see what happens.’ Then COVID hit while we had just started writing scripts for Season 3. Production was down, and all of a sudden everyone was stuck at home, and word of mouth started spreading about this show, All American.

JAMIE TURNER: From the first day I landed in the writers’ room to our last day filming Season 1, I always felt like there was something special about this show from the writers’ room to our cast to our incredible crew. We were instant family, which is rare. I even told my reps between Season 1 and 2 to hold off on any potential staffing meetings for other shows until we learn if we’ll be picked up for Season 2. I was clearly betting on the show, but I was also betting on the culture, cause I had a feeling this show would blow up the moment it landed on Netflix. Next thing you know, the rapper Wale, Coach Deion Sanders and a host of celebrities started shouting us out on social media and the show hit another gear in terms of popularity and man did it soar.

The CW

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: I was constantly on the phone with the studio and the network, all of us trying to figure out if there is a safe way to bring the show back during COVID, and how we would shoot football and everything. I almost didn’t even realize what was happening in the zeitgeist until I sort of looked up and it was everywhere.

DANIEL EZRA: I don’t think there was much belief in us, in NK or the show for a long time. Everything was a fight. It always feels good proving people wrong.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Quite frankly, it was that continued passion and love from our audience that kept us on the air. It was always the thing I could go back to as I was pitching the new season to the studio and network as part of our pickup process, what this show meant to the fans and the communities, and what would feel absent from television if it wasn’t on the air. The response from our audience gave me the material I needed during those pitches to be like, ‘Hey, grandparents down to their grandkids are arguing about watching the show together. We pulled off a generational show that is really appealing across the board to all ages,’ and it really allowed us to go the distance.

The show resonated for many of the same reasons coming-of-age stories have always endured: it took seriously the lives and struggles of people of all ages, even kids, who felt like they had the weight of the world on their shoulders. It lent empathy to hard conversations about race and class and identity, refusing to minimize the reality of being a teenager as the country entered yet another era of reckoning about its sociopolitical structures.

Whatever the world was talking about, the show would be talking about, too. Even if the world didn’t seem ready for the conversation yet, All American was going to have it.

TAYE DIGGS: I was proud of the bravery to handle and talk about certain issues — racism, and being a young Black man, with how young Black men have to deal with police, being a part of an interracial relationship, all of this was real issues that we weren’t afraid to deal with. I was very, very proud that we chose to face these issues head on.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Even as early on as when we did the cop stop in Episode 103, which was one of the first scripts I wrote for the series, I remember we were having long debates in the writers’ room about [how] the only way it made sense for us to bring it to the screen was if we were going to have an honest conversation about what it looks like when these boys come home from that. If we were going to have an honest conversation about the first time I had to have a conversation with my son about being stopped by the cops and how to carry yourself and knowing you were giving up a piece of their childhood the minute you had to have that conversation.

KAREEM J. GRIMES: We don’t see a lot of roles of African American men fighting and getting custody of their child. Billy Baker giving [Preach] a second chance at life to right his wrongs and become a teacher…that’s real life. Everybody’s an ex-something, and everybody deserves a second chance, sometimes [a] third chance. This show displayed that from Season 1 all the way to 8, and I’m just grateful to be a part of a show like this.

KARIMAH WESTBROOK: The most fulfilling part for me in telling the adult stories was the message of taking accountability and the power of forgiveness. I love how the adults were able to overcome the things that happened in the past and come together, eventually building a stronger connection. I also love how we fought for the best for our kids.

The CW

MICHAEL EVANS BEHLING: [One of] the hardest scenes was Olivia’s overdose scene. It hit home for me and my family, and so to tap into that was probably the hardest [scene] I’ve ever [shot] in all of my career.

JAMIE TURNER: One [scene] that has stayed with me the whole series happened during Episode 205 when Layla threw a birthday party for Liv and Jordan that spiraled out of control. Towards the end of the episode, there’s a moment between Layla and her dad, JT, where he tells her for the first time that her mother suffered from depression. The way Layla processed that information and lived in the heartbreak was so beautifully nuanced by Greta Onieogou and perfectly captured by the director of that episode, David McWhirter.

GRETA ONIEOGOU: I think that the mental health episodes, especially when it was particularly bad, were always tough. A lot of times you have to go to some pretty challenging places, but I think what we’re able to portray in those episodes make a lot of people feel seen and heard in a way they might not have [seen] beforehand on television. I think it’s worth it.

There was a brief moment, around the start of the third season, when All American seemed to finally have the wind in its sales. Not only was the flagship series doing well, the franchise was growing. It became popular enough to spawn a three-season spinoff series set at an HBCU in Atlanta, All American: Homecoming. Eventually, after a short period of smooth sailing, the show faced the harsh reality that is bound to confront any long-running series eventually: cast exits.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: I mean, that was just always a reality as a show gets longer and longer. I always thought it was a miracle every season that we were able to hold on to someone like Taye. It was leading into Season 5 where Taye and I started talking about it, just because I knew he had another project coming out that I was a huge fan of, and so was happy to facilitate him sort of [shooting] both, because selfishly, as a fan, I wanted to watch him in the other series as well. But it also got me thinking, I was like, ‘Oh, I feel like we’re on borrowed time.’

Diggs was the first of the major cast members to depart. His exit came in Season 5, Episode 11, when Billy dies saving his team during a bus crash.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL When Taye and I had that conversation, I was like, ‘Look, I fully support you. I respect you, and if you feel like you want to do other things right now, I completely understand that. This is how it would have to be done, though, in order to maintain the core of who the character of Billy is, and also in a way that his leaving the show wouldn’t be a blip, and it would be something that kind of leaves an impact in all of our characters that is something that all of us deal with in real life.’

The CW

TAYE DIGGS: I thought it was so cool at first. I remember her saying they were going to give me a really great send off, something really intense, and I was very, very flattered and honored. But then, a few months later I was like, ‘Oh wait, there’s no way I can come back even if I change my mind.’ So that part stung.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: There were three of us in the writers’ room who lost our fathers at a young age. I was 24. Another one of my writers was in her early 20s. So it was that thing of — we knew, I knew Billy would never voluntarily leave the family, not after he fought so hard to get them back. So when I had that conversation with Taye, it took him a moment to be like, ‘Oh wow, it would really be goodbye.’ I was like, ‘Well, yes, of course, but we flash back to stuff.’ I’m constantly talking to my father, who’s no longer here. So I knew we were going to do episodes where the kids would have conversations with their dad, and we’d be able to bring Taye back. But I thought it was important that if he was leaving, that’s truly the only way he would leave his family behind. I knew, because of the caliber of actor we had on the show and how amazing this cast has been, that it gave us a chance to go through another real-life moment that so many people experience of losing a parent truly before you’re ready, and how that forever changes you.

DANIEL EZRA: Everything got a little less bright after Taye left. I missed having scenes with him, but it forced everyone to step up to play the arc of our characters individually and collective grief.

JAMIE TURNER: Losing Billy was not only a difficult decision, but it also re-set the series cause he was the only character from the pilot who had history with every single character on the show, which is unique in itself. Thanks to NK, who encouraged us to slow down and grieve Billy with pace, love and intention, we were able to tell four beautiful stories on the heels of his death that centered around Laura, Liv, Jordan and Spencer. That gave us a chance to really see how people grieve differently and what’s the expectation for them moving forward. Jordan’s journey resonated with me the most, mainly because he lived in Billy’s shadow for most of his life, but now he was being pushed to stand on his own and learn what being his own kind of Baker man looks like. Per usual, Mike Behling was incredible.

MICHAEL EVANS BEHLING: Taye was always a big advisor, and I was fortunate to have him take me under his wing in the early days. And one of the things I can remember him telling me was just to believe in myself, and I was there for a reason. I can recall feeling like I was a fish out of water on the set, working with a lot of people who were much, much more seasoned than me. He could kind of see that and feel that in me, and he was a big motivator for me to just trust my gut and go with whatever I was thinking, because I was there for a reason. I carry that with me to every set I go through now.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: We got to do it in such an individual way with each character, not just with Olivia and Jordan and Spencer, obviously, but what happens as a wife when you lose your life partner — Monet killed that storyline — and even for Grace, whose relationship with Billy was complicated, but he was always a second father to her children.

The CW

MONET MAZUR: That season in particular was really hard, because it was a slow burn how she went through the process and grieved. Every episode was like a slightly different stage of grief, and so to stay in that for months at a time was exhausting. I cried a lot, a lot, a lot, a lot every day. I was crying.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: It just gave us an opening to really dig deep into these characters, to set them up for adulthood and what their adulthood would now look like. They rose to the occasion.

Season 6 faced its own hurdles as the start of production and the eventual premiere was significantly delayed by the 2023 writers and actors strike. By the time that the writers reconvened, the future of the series was once again in question.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Season 6 was the first time where I felt like, if this show does not return, we cannot end it in a way that feels open-ended or unfinished, because as a fan of TV shows myself, and as a fan of these characters, it just felt like they deserved some version of a wrap-up and a launch into a new chapter that could be the opening for a new season, should we be so blessed, which is why we were sort of like, ‘Okay, we are building towards Layla and Jordan’s wedding and building towards Spencer getting into the NFL and Olivia and Spencer getting engaged.’

DANIEL EZRA: I knew Season 6 he was going to finally get the girl, reach the NFL and win the Super Bowl. His story felt complete. He got everything he wanted when we met him.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: To a certain degree, I always knew where these characters were going to end. It was just a question of if they were going to end there sooner or later. With Daniel making the decision that he felt like he’d completed the heart of Spencer’s arc in Season 6, really it then became a question of: What does that do to everyone else in his life, and where they are in their journey?

It became clear very quickly that this would be difficult to accomplish within the 13-episode order that Season 6 had previously received.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: I would feel so cheated as a fan of Spencer and Olivia’s if I didn’t get to see them finally get married. I went to Greg Berlanti and had a conversation with him and Sarah Schechter about needing more episodes for this season, and why I wanted to complete Spencer and Olivia’s sort of journey, and also why I wanted those two extra episodes to also hint at the introduction of a new cast that could really be the launching point for Season 7. They were completely on board, and then it was a question of does the CW have room for an additional two episodes? Thanks to [CW President] Brad Schwartz, who really did fight that battle with getting us those two additional episodes for Season 6, so we could have Spencer and Olivia’s wedding, and that felt like a completion of their journey.

The CW

By all accounts the series could have ended here. But, why did it have to? These characters’ stories had ended, but that didn’t mean there weren’t stories left to tell at South Crenshaw and Beverly.

Toward the backend of Season 6, the writers had tested out some new, younger characters’ storylines to see if audiences would respond to the introduction of a new generation of high school students.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Amina had been part of the show on and off as one of the younger characters, Preach’s daughter, and was a very sort of big part of Preach’s story arc over the seasons. So as we were looking at that new generation, she felt like an organic piece of it. That’s why we have the episode in Season 6 where our OG cast were working at that Shakespeare after-school program at Crenshaw, and we got to meet teenage Amina, and we got to meet Khalil, and we just got to get a sense of what that transition would look like if our guys kind of had to sort of become the responsible ones in the room.

ALEXIS CHIKAEZE: I actually started on the show as a co-star. I was at USC at the time. I hadn’t worked in a while, actually, like in like a year or so. Then the day I did my audition was possibly, like, the worst day I had at school. So I remember just walking to class, and I was supposed to be flying back home to Texas, and my agents reached out saying they sent my tape to producers and they loved it, and I just remember absolutely crying.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Alexis, who plays Amina, there was something in her audition that was so captivating, that was such a beautiful mix of the feisty girl we met as a young girl on the street who stepped to Preach with all the strength and power and fearlessness to be like, ‘Who are you? What do you have to do with my mom? I think you might be my father’ — and keep that essence, but also bring in a lot of the insecurities that hit in your teen years for a girl, and especially as boys enter the mix. She’s growing up without her mom, and what all of that meant. Alexis just brought such a beautiful quality to it that, in that episode we sort of realized, ‘Oh, we actually think there could be something special here.’ In the original iteration of the show, it really felt like these two girls, Olivia and Layla, were fighting over Spencer. I wanted a girl to have the power of — there were these guys who were rivals but also united in that they thought there was something to love about Amina.

ALEXIS CHIKAEZE: I remember getting in there, and they just — everyone — Daniel, Mike, Greta, Sam, Chelsea — everyone seemed so big, but big not in a sense that they were these big personalities. They were just real, and the light that shined on each of them was just so bright, and they were so kind, and they were so welcoming, and they were so calm. That was such a breath of fresh air. I was only set for one episode.

ANTONIO J. BELL: I was tapped in early on. [I auditioned], I want to say somewhere between six and eight times. I heard no so many times, I thought that ‘you’re not supposed to fit for this particular project.’ Snowfall and All American, I was reading for a lot. So, when Khalil came around, I was grateful.

The CW

KAREEM J. GRIMES: By that time, it was just a family. When we got this new reboot of characters [we wanted] to just make sure to let them know, ‘Hey, you’re coming into a family, and we want to welcome you with open arms.’

ANTONIO J. BELL: I was pleasantly surprised, because oftentimes you come into shows later in the game, or you’re not a series regular, so everyone has their bonds established. Sometimes people are jaded, and maybe over their gig, but it was great to see that that wasn’t the case here. Everybody was still having fun. Everyone was still happy to be there. So Alexis and I, and at the time, they really welcomed us with open arms, even from Day 1. So that was really dope to be a part of the family from day one, even though we didn’t know that we would even come back.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: We tested out the idea of Amina growing up, the idea of what her classmates now looked like and what that world could look like, and but then again, I was in the state of mind of, ‘but if it’s the final season, then so be it.’ Then I went to Starbucks, and this rarely happens, because I’m behind the scenes, but the barista recognized my name, and she was like, ‘Oh, are you the NK that’s affiliated with All American?’ And I said, ‘Yes.’ And then she burst into tears and started talking about how the show had changed her life and how she had dropped out of college, but because of the show it made her realize her dreams are worth pursuing. So she returned to college and actually graduated and got her degree and everything, and so, like, I’m crying, she’s crying. As I was leaving, she thanked me, and she said, ‘I just hope a show like this is around for my brother as he grows up, so that he has that too.’ It was when she said that, it really hit me, and I literally got in my car, I drove back to the lot, I ran into the writer’s room, and I was like, ‘We cannot end the show.’ Then it became really intentional, putting together a little sizzle reel that alluded to what the Season 7 storyline could be.

JAMIE TURNER: It was important for us to find a way to preserve the legacy of the show for the first six seasons by organically tying it to the next generation, hence Cassius’ (Osy Ikhile) Kilmonger-inspired journey and its connection to the Bakers.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Introducing this whole idea that Billy might have a half brother that no one knew about, which meant a whole side of the Baker family was out there somewhere in the world, and given that Jordan had lost his dad, and his sister is getting married and moving clear across America, like he would be so obsessed with finding whatever family he could find and hold on to. Everyone saw the vision, and we ended up getting greenlit for our Season 7.

JAMIE TURNER: But it was also important for Cassius, KJ (Nathaniel McIntyre), Khalil, Amina and Tori (Lauryn Hardy) to feel different from the original cast while still using some of the universal themes that worked so well in the past for our OG cast. For instance, KJ and Khalil are an amalgam of Spencer, and Amina definitely has some of Olivia’s radical DNA and in some ways Tori and Layla have dealt with the same level of heartbreak and foolishness when it comes to relationships.

The CW

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: Writing that Season 7 premiere script was truly one of the, honestly, toughest processes for me personally as a writer. I think that might be the script that I’ve written the most revisions of before I ever gave it to anyone to read. Just for me personally, I was so hard on myself as I was doing that, because I was like, is this good enough to launch a new chapter of the show? Does this just feel like another episode? I wanted it to feel both like a season premiere and a series premiere at the same time, and eventually it got there, or eventually my fingers just got tired.

LAURYN HARDY: I know I’ve said this before, but I am a fan of this show, so I have auditioned for this show before. To finally get cast on the show was genuinely the greatest moment of my life. I don’t know why I really resonated with Tori in general. I loved the idea of playing this powerful character who is not afraid to speak her mind, you know? She’s powerful, but she also has a vulnerability.

ANTONIO J. BELL: Growing up, I was a variation of Khalil. I [didn’t do] really well in school, and it wasn’t because I wasn’t smart. It was just because I didn’t fit that program. I didn’t understand why I was doing it. I didn’t really have the tribe that he had in my corner to really push me to want to excel in academics, so some of the same challenges he had, I had early on. I had a bit of a temper growing up and had to do a lot of work with myself to understand my shadow and get a little better at relating to people, so a lot of the elements of [Khalil being] misunderstood I really, really, really related to.

NATHANIEL MCINTYRE: One of my early memories was the table read, coming from New York, feeling super excited that I booked this role on such a dope show. Everybody was so excited to introduce us and include us in this story as it’s been taking a shift with Spencer’s character leaving the show. It was a whole new generation, so everybody was really excited for us to come in and fill in those shoes a bit, and I was just ready.

OSY IKHILE: I wanted to bring a different coach vibe. I didn’t want to try and emulate Billy or any other coach that did that before. I really wanted to lean more into the best-friend vibe that was written on the page and really honor that between Cassius and KJ. It was the first time that I could really draw from my own experiences with my father, which wasn’t always the best, and use that for the character in a healing way, but also in an honest portrayal of Cassius as well.

Season 7 premiered in early 2025 with the refreshed young cast at the center of stories that felt new and familiar at the same time. Where Olivia had given a voice to the voiceless on her podcast, Amina would soon be throwing herself in front of her fellow students to protect them from an ICE raid. KJ would come to grapple with the Baker family legacy right alongside Jordan. Tori was settling into her own convictions just as Layla once had, and Khalil was torn between his dreams and his reality, much like Spencer used to be.

The CW

Now, they were being guided by those who came before them, both on and off screen. The series was renewed for its final season last summer, setting the stage for 13 episodes to finally, truly bid farewell to a show that had withstood so much.

NKECHI OKORO CARROLL: I cried almost every day of the final season. I knew what the final episode would be, always. Whatever season we’re in, when the series ends, even if it meant I had a flash forward in time or something, it would allow for this ending. So, there was some peace in knowing that, even with OG actors having left the show, the heart of that did not change. Now, the tougher issue was building to [that], now that we knew this was going to be our final season. What is the most organic path to this final moment to launch into the next chapter of their lives and what feels the most satisfying for these characters?

Even before the writer’s room came back, Jamie and I would sit and talk for hours about what felt like the right journey, and that’s ultimately how I landed on the timeline of this season spanning only one week in the character’s lives, because I didn’t want this season to be about this being a new chapter of growth for them. I wanted this season to be about: Has everything they’ve been through over the last seven to eight years prepared them for what is arguably one of the toughest weeks of all of their lives, as these crossroads start to intersect? Has it prepared them to meet the moment? And hopefully the answer is yes. That’s truly the question.

The CW

The final season welcomed back many of the original characters, and somewhere along the way, the assurance that the story was culminating in exactly the way Okoro Carroll intended becomes clear in something that Layla says to Khalil about the strength of chosen family after reminiscing on her own messy youth: “I learned love in this house,” she tells him. “I learned what it means to be family, and it’s not a fairytale. It isn’t perfect. It’s a journey with one constant: the people who are there for you no matter what.”

The series finale on Monday will include much of the original cast on screen together again, including Ezra and Logan. Ezra also returned to direct the episode.

DANIEL EZRA: [It was] like coming home. The show gave me more than I could have asked for. That was encapsulated in returning for the series finale as a director and an actor. Stepping away at Season 6 was the right move for me as an actor, but ending it how we started was the only way I wanted to close it as a human.

title: Michael Lewen To Direct High-Concept Comedy ‘White Knight’ For Screen Gems
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Shortly on the heels of releasing his new comedy Tiny Fugitives, Michael Lewen has inked a deal to direct White Knight, a high-concept comedy that landed at Sony’s Screen Gems earlier this year, as we first reported. White Knight‘s plot is being kept under wraps, though the film is described as outrageous, R-rated fare. […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Shortly on the heels of releasing his new comedy Tiny Fugitives, Michael Lewen has inked a deal to direct White Knight, a high-concept comedy that landed at Sony’s Screen Gems earlier this year, as we first reported.

White Knight‘s plot is being kept under wraps, though the film is described as outrageous, R-rated fare. It’s based on a spec by Christopher William Young, which Unknown Quantity’s Chris Bremner brought into the studio, where he has a deal. This followed Unknown Quantity Creative Executive Brandon Xie’s discovery of the script on the Black List website. Young is a Florida State grad who celebrated his first sale here as a writer while still working as a bartender at a popular L.A. hotspot.

Bremner and Jeff Arkuss will produce via Unknown Quantity.

Watch on Deadline

Lewen comes to White Knight after writing and directing Tiny Fugitives, a comedy that released nationwide in theaters via Inaugural Entertainment on September 18. Johnny Knoxville stars in the flick from Point Grey Pictures and Tango Entertainment. Prior to his work on that film, Lewen made his feature directorial debut with Hello, Goodbye and Everything in Between, a rom-com produced by Ace Entertainment in association with Lionsgate that was acquired by Netflix and premiered in 2022.

Lewen began his career at Apatow Productions, where he oversaw a wide range of acclaimed film and television projects, including Trainwreck, The Big Sick, The King of Staten Island and three seasons of Netflix’s Love. In television, he most recently exec produced the pilot of HBO Max’s Vegas High alongside Michael Showalter. He also directed “Sarah From College,” an episode of Love written by Apatow and featuring Vanessa Bayer alongside stars Gillian Jacobson and Paul Rust.

Lewen is repped by WME and Christopher D. Abramson, P.C.

content:
EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures and Will Gluck’s Olive Bridge Entertainment have tapped Amélie Hoeferle and Graham Campbell to star in Fake Skating adaptation. Based on Lynn Painter’s New York Times best-selling book, Deadline recently broke the news that Josh Boone would direct. Morgan Lehmann and Victoria Bata penned the first draft of the script with Boone and his writing partner Knate Lee handling revisions.

Here is Painter’s social media post announcing the news:

Set for a summer release next year, Fake Skating is an emotional high school hockey romance about childhood sweethearts whose icy reunion in their hockey-loving hometown unexpectedly thaws when they fake a romantic relationship.

Watch on Deadline

Deadline first reported the studio coming on to the project this past March and moved fast to get Boone on board once they heard he was high on the project. Once the greenlight was given, Boone spent the remainder of the summer testing actors for its two leads with Boone and execs ultimately landing on the two rising stars.

Painter is the #1 New York Times and internationally best-selling author of Better Than the Movies, The Do-Over, Betting on You, Maid For Each Other, First and Forever, Nothing Like the Movies, and Fake Skating. Winner of the 2025 Goodreads Choice Award for Young Adult Fiction, Fake Skating has nearly 500,000 copies in print and has appeared on the New York Times YA Hardcover Bestseller list 48 times since its release in September 2025, holding the #1 spot for 15 of those weeks. The novel has also been translated into 16 languages.

Netflix is working on a film adaptation of Painter’s Better Than The Movies, directed by Julia Hart and starring David Iacono and Beatrice Kitsos.

RELATED: Everything We Know About Netflix’s ‘Better Than The Movies’ Feature Adaptation So Far

Gluck and Jacqueline Monetta are producing and Madison Jones is executive producing on behalf of Olive Bridge Entertainment. Painter will also serve as an executive producer.

Hoeferle stars in the hit young adult series Sterling Point on Prime. Her other credits include Eddington and The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. She is repped by Gersh, Affirmative Entertainment, The Lede Company, and Jackoway Austen.

Campbell gained attention in the Tony Award-winning play Appropriate opposite Sarah Paulson. Recently, he can be seen in FX’s The Shards and the critically acclaimed film Late Fame which premiered at the Venice Film Festival and just released in theaters by Magnolia. He is repped by CAA, Anonymous Content, The Lede Company and Jackoway Austen.

Olive Bridge Entertainment is repped by UTA and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern. Painter is repped by UTA and BookEnds Literary Agency.

title: ‘Séance’: Vivian Kerr Victorian Gothic Thriller Conjures Fall Theatrical Release – Watch Clips
summary: EXCLUSIVE: The Vivian Kerr directed and starring Victorian Gothic thriller Séance will begin a limited U.S. theatrical release on Oct. 2, followed by a North American VOD release Friday Nov. 13. Also written and produced by Kerr, Séance will open with a one-week run at the Laemmle Royal in Los Angeles, before widening to dates […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: The Vivian Kerr directed and starring Victorian Gothic thriller Séance will begin a limited U.S. theatrical release on Oct. 2, followed by a North American VOD release Friday Nov. 13.

Also written and produced by Kerr, Séance will open with a one-week run at the Laemmle Royal in Los Angeles, before widening to dates in San Francisco, Phoenix, Houston, Palm Springs, and Sedona, with more cities to be announced. Rue Dangeau will release Séance on North American VOD platforms.

Also starring Scottie Thompson (NCIS), Jilon VanOver (Hatfields & McCoys) and Connor Paolo (Gossip Girl), Séance is an intense four-hander set over the course of one night, as two couples confront the deficits in their marriages, the temptation of adultery, and the disturbing possibility their house is haunted by a recently deceased loved one. The feature is inspired by the August Strindberg play Creditors.

The movie was shot in Los Angeles with cinematography by Johanna Coelho (HBO Max’s The Pitt), costume design by Nina Fuller, and production design by Bri Jones.

Pic was also produced by Makenna Tuttle, Savannah Lindblad, Marion Kerr, and Rachel Stander, with Sanatan Kadakia and Suresh Cedrick Pereira serving as EPs.

The film currently holds 100% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes off 22 reviews.

Séance marks Kerr’s second feature as a writer-director following Scrap which starred Anthony Rapp and Lana Parrilla. That pic world premiered at the Deauville American Film Festival and went on to play 44 festivals worldwide before its December 2025 release.

Through her production and distribution company Rue Dangeau, Kerr is also coming off the 2026 Sundance world premiere of independent pilot, Soft Boil, which she produced and stars in. Directed by Alec Goldberg and starring Camille Wormser, the pilot went on to screen at Slamdance, SeriesFest, Just for Laughs, and Cinequest, winning audience awards at both SeriesFest and Just for Laughs.
